Red-team checks: for valid parameters this is the standard mass, checked against the explicit value 3/32 at r = 2, p₀ = 1/2, p = (1/4, 1/4), k = (1, 1).

With `hr : 0 ≤ r` and `hp₀ : 0 ≤ p₀`, `0 ≤ negativeMultinomialWeightReal r p₀ p k`: Γ is positive at positive arguments, factorials are positive, p₀^r ≥ 0 (`Real.rpow_nonneg`) and p_i ≥ 0 by type; normalisation of the weights is not needed, as the docstring says. Lean subtlety: at p₀ = 0 the real power gives 0^r = 0 for r > 0, which is nonnegative, so allowing p₀ = 0 here is harmless. Red-team checks: both hypotheses are needed (at r = 1, p₀ = -1 the zero vector gets -1; at r = -1/2 one category with count 1 gets Γ(1/2)/Γ(-1/2) < 0 times a positive factor).

With `hr : r ≠ 0`, `negativeMultinomialWeightReal r p₀ p k = Real.Gamma (r + ∑ i, (k i : ℝ)) / (Real.Gamma r * ∏ i, ((k i).factorial : ℝ)) * p₀ ^ r * ∏ i, (p i : ℝ) ^ k i`, i.e. the mass is Γ(r + Σ k_i)/(Γ(r) Π k_i!) · p₀^r Π p_i^(k_i), the defining branch; r ≠ 0 is needed because r = 0 uses the point-mass convention.

`negativeMultinomialWeightReal 0 p₀ p k = if k = 0 then 1 else 0`: at shape zero the mass is 1 at the zero count vector and 0 elsewhere, the definition's shape-zero convention (needed because Mathlib's `Real.Gamma 0` is 0).
`negativeMultinomialWeight r p₀ p k = ENNReal.ofReal (negativeMultinomialWeightReal r p₀ p k)`: the extended mass is the positive part of the real mass; true by definition.

With 0 ≤ r and 0 ≤ p₀, `(negativeMultinomialWeight r p₀ p k).toReal = negativeMultinomialWeightReal r p₀ p k`: converting the extended mass back to a real number returns the real mass. Lean subtlety: `ENNReal.toReal (ENNReal.ofReal x) = x` only for x ≥ 0; the hypotheses supply that nonnegativity through `negativeMultinomialWeightReal_nonneg`.

For a self-orthogonal binary code of positive length, the discriminant of Construction B is 4 times that of Construction A. Lean ↔ maths: `IntegralLattice.discriminant L` is by definition the absolute value (`Int.natAbs`) of `L.determinant`, the determinant of the Gram matrix of the integral form in a ℤ-basis of the carrier (independent of the basis by `determinant_eq_gramDet`), i.e. the usual |det Gram|; the right side is the discriminant of `ConstructionA.integralLattice 2 C.toAddSubgroup _`, the Construction A lattice with the same form x·y/2; `hC : C.IsSelfOrthogonal` makes both lattices integral and `[Nonempty ι]` says the length is positive. A full sublattice of index k carrying the same form has its discriminant multiplied by k² (`IntegralLattice.discriminant_eq_mul_relIndex_sq`), and here the index is 2 by `relIndex_lattice` (self-orthogonal codes are even). Lean subtlety: the discriminant is ℕ-valued (an absolute value) and is computed in a basis picked by `Module.Free.chooseBasis` (classical choice), which is harmless because the Gram determinant does not depend on the basis up to sign; `[Nonempty ι]` is needed because the empty case has index 1, not 2. Red-team checks: the coordinate hypothesis is needed, since with no coordinates both discriminants are 1; specialised to the zero code of length 3 (32 = 4·2³, as for D_3 with doubled form) and to the Golay code (4 = 4·1).

`Module.finrank ℤ (integralLattice C hC) = Fintype.card ι`: the ℤ-rank of the carrier is n, the length of the code, since a full lattice in ℚ^ι has rank dim_ℚ ℚ^ι = |ι| (`IntegralLattice.finrank_carrier`). Lean subtlety: `Module.finrank` is 0 for modules of infinite rank, but the carrier is finitely generated and free, so this is the genuine rank. Red-team checks: gives rank 24 for the Golay code; its left side is in simp normal form.

For z ∈ ℤ^ι, `(fun i ↦ (z i : ℚ)) ∈ lattice C ↔ (fun i ↦ (z i : ZMod 2)) ∈ C ∧ 4 ∣ ∑ i, z i`: the integer vector z (cast into ℚ^ι) lies in Construction B exactly when its coordinatewise reduction mod 2 (the cast ℤ → `ZMod 2`) is a codeword and 4 divides the sum of its coordinates, which is the definition of Leech and Sloane, Sphere packings and error-correcting codes, Canad. J. Math. 23 (1971), Section 3.1, read for integer coordinates. Red-team checks: used to decide membership of (1,-1) for the code {00,11} and of 1 and 2 for the full code of length one; its left side is in simp normal form.

Construction B of a self-orthogonal binary linear code C, as an integral lattice in ℚ^ι with the bilinear form x·y/2. Lean ↔ maths: a Tau Ceti `IntegralLattice (ι → ℚ)` is a structure consisting of a ℤ-submodule `carrier` of ℚ^ι that is a full lattice (`IsLattice ℚ`: finitely generated and ℚ-spanning), a symmetric ℚ-bilinear `form` on ℚ^ι, and `le_dual : carrier ≤ form.dualSubmodule carrier`, i.e. the form takes integer values on pairs of carrier vectors; the body takes `ConstructionA.integralLattice 2 C.toAddSubgroup _` (carrier Construction A, form `ConstructionA.form 2 = (2 : ℚ)⁻¹ • dotProductBilin`, i.e. x·y/2 by `ConstructionA.form_apply`) and restricts it with `restrictFull` to the full sublattice `lattice C`, keeping the form (`integralLattice_carrier`, `integralLattice_form`). The hypothesis `hC : C.IsSelfOrthogonal` unfolds to C ≤ `euclideanDual C` (any two codewords have F₂ dot product 0) and is converted by `toZModSubmodule_toAddSubgroup_le_euclideanDual_iff` into the integrality hypothesis of Construction A, since for integer vectors x·y ≡ (x mod 2)·(y mod 2) modulo 2. The carrier is Construction B of Leech and Sloane, Sphere packings and error-correcting codes, Canad. J. Math. 23 (1971), Section 3.1, and the form x·y/2 is the same as scaling the coordinates by 1/√2; self-orthogonal codes are even, matching the source's assumption, and among even codes self-orthogonality is exactly what integrality needs. Red-team checks (verified in Lean): for the zero code it is the checkerboard lattice D_n with doubled form (carrier and form checked, discriminant 4·2³ = 32 at n = 3); for the self-orthogonal code {00,11} it is odd, so evenness genuinely needs double evenness; for the Golay code it has rank 24, discriminant 4 and is even, and the Leech file glues in one odd shift to obtain the Leech lattice.

`(integralLattice C hC).carrier = lattice C`: the vectors of the bundled Construction B lattice are exactly the Construction B set, by construction (`restrictFull_carrier`). Its left side is in simp normal form.

`(integralLattice C hC).form = ConstructionA.form 2`: the bilinear form of the bundled Construction B lattice is the Construction A form `(2 : ℚ)⁻¹ • dotProductBilin`, i.e. x·y/2, since `restrictFull` keeps the form of the Construction A lattice.

For a doubly even code every Construction B vector has even norm x·x/2, i.e. Construction B is an even lattice. Lean ↔ maths: `IntegralLattice.IsEven L` is by definition ∀ x : L, Even (L.integralNorm x), where `integralNorm x` is the integer value of the form on (x, x), here x·x/2; `hC : BinaryCode.IsDoublyEven C` unfolds to 4 ∣ `hammingNorm c` (the weight) for every codeword c, and the lattice is built from `hC.isSelfOrthogonal` (doubly even codes are self-orthogonal, so it is integral). Construction A is already even, since x·x ≡ wt(c) modulo 4 for x reducing to the codeword c (`ConstructionA.isEven_integralLattice_two_of_isDoublyEven`), and Construction B is a full sublattice carrying the same form, so it inherits evenness (`isEven_restrictFull`). `(lattice C).IsLattice ℚ`: Construction B is a full lattice in ℚ^ι, where Mathlib's `Submodule.IsLattice ℚ M` means M is finitely generated over ℤ (`fg`) and its ℚ-span is all of ℚ^ι (`span_eq_top`). It sits inside the finitely generated Construction A lattice and contains 4 times every Construction A vector, and those multiples already span. Red-team checks: it needs only finitely many coordinates, which the definition already assumes (`[Fintype ι]`).

`(integralLattice C hC).IsNondegenerate`: the class says the ambient form on ℚ^ι has trivial kernel; here the form x·y/2 is a nonzero multiple of the dot product, which is nondegenerate on ℚ^ι, and `restrictFull` keeps the form, so the instance is inherited from Construction A.

`(integralLattice C hC).IsPosDef`, which unfolds (`IsPosDef` is `L.form.toQuadraticMap.PosDef`) to x·x/2 > 0 for every nonzero x ∈ ℚ^ι: Construction B is positive definite because its form is `ConstructionA.form 2` (`ConstructionA.form_posDef`).

Defines the Construction B set of a binary linear code C of length n = |ι| as a ℤ-submodule of ℚ^ι: the integer vectors that reduce modulo 2 to a codeword of C and whose coordinate sum is divisible by 4. This is exactly Construction B of Leech and Sloane, Sphere packings and error-correcting codes, Canad. J. Math. 23 (1971), Section 3.1, which states it for codes whose words all have even weight; for an arbitrary code the set equals that of its even-weight subcode, so nothing is lost by allowing every code. Red-team checks: for the zero code it is exactly twice the checkerboard lattice D_n (verified in Lean); for the full code of length one it is 4ℤ inside ℤ; for the Golay code it is the half-lattice from which the Leech file builds the Leech lattice.

`x ∈ lattice C ↔ x ∈ ConstructionA.lattice 2 C.toAddSubgroup ∧ ∃ k : ℤ, ∑ i, x i = 4 * k`: a rational vector lies in Construction B exactly when it lies in Construction A (it is an integer vector reducing to a codeword) and its coordinate sum is 4k for some integer k; this holds by definition.

For an even binary code of positive length, Construction B has index exactly 2 in Construction A. Red-team checks: specialised at d = −7, p = 2, r = 0, giving two distinct factors (2 ∤ −7, proved); the inert case d = 5, p = 2 has no root and is covered by the companion maximality criterion (proved).

For a squarefree non-square d and a prime p dividing d (`[Fact p.Prime]`, `hp : (p : ℤ) ∣ d`) in the ring of integers `𝓞 K` of `K = QuadraticAlgebra ℚ (d : ℚ) 0`, which is ℚ(√d), `Ideal.span {(p : 𝓞 K), integralSqrt …} ^ 2 = Ideal.span {(p : 𝓞 K)}`: since `integralSqrt (omega_sq_eq_algebraMap_int (d := d))` is by definition ω regarded as an element of `𝓞 K` (`integralSqrt hx := ⟨x, _⟩`, squaring to d by `integralSqrt_sq`), i.e. √d, this is (p, √d)² = p𝓞_K in the ring of integers of ℚ(√d), whatever d is modulo 4 (no mod-4 hypothesis appears), which is Marcus, Number Fields, Thm. 25(1). Correct because (p, √d)² is generated by p², p√d and d = pm with p ∤ m (squarefreeness), every generator is divisible by p, and p and m coprime puts p itself in the ideal. Red-team checks: specialised at d = 2, p = 2; the proof uses squarefreeness only to get p² ∤ d (recorded as a generality note, not a correctness issue).

Claim: the prime-decomposition law for ℚ(√d) when d ≢ 1 (mod 4): for a squarefree non-square integer d ≡ 2 or 3 (mod 4) and any prime p (2 included) such that X² − d has a root r modulo p, one has p𝓞_K = (p, √d − r)(p, √d + r). The proof is Dedekind's criterion in the order ℤ[√d] = `QuadraticAlgebra ℤ d 0` (the product equals (p) unless p divides both 2r and (r² − d)/p, which squarefreeness of d rules out), transported to 𝓞_K along `ringOfIntegersEquiv hsf hd4`, whose inverse sends ω to √d. Lean subtlety: `d % 4` is the Euclidean remainder `Int.emod`, which lies in {0, 1, 2, 3} also for negative d ((−3) % 4 = 1), so `hd4` is exactly d ≢ 1 (mod 4), and squarefreeness leaves d ≡ 2, 3 (mod 4); p : ℕ and r : ℤ enter through casts into ℤ and 𝓞 K. Red-team checks: specialised at d = −1, p = 5, r = 2, giving (5) = (5, i − 2)(5, i + 2) with distinct factors, and at d = −1, p = 2, giving (2) = (2, i − 1)²; no contradiction among the hypotheses; the condition d ≢ 1 (mod 4) is needed at p = 2.

For squarefree non-square d with `hd4 : d % 4 ≠ 1`, a prime p and `hr : (p : ℤ) ∣ r ^ 2 - d` (r² ≡ d mod p), in the ring of integers `𝓞 K` of `K = QuadraticAlgebra ℚ (d : ℚ) 0`, which is ℚ(√d), `Ideal.span {(p : 𝓞 K), integralSqrt … - r} ^ 2 = Ideal.span {(p : 𝓞 K)} ↔ (p : ℤ) ∣ NumberField.discr K`: p𝓞_K is the square of the prime (p, √d − r) exactly when p divides the discriminant of K, which is 4d (`discr_eq_four_mul_of_mod_four_ne_one`), as in Marcus, Thm. 25. For squarefree non-square d with `hd : d % 4 = 3` in the ring of integers `𝓞 K` of `K = QuadraticAlgebra ℚ (d : ℚ) 0`, which is ℚ(√d), `Ideal.span {(2 : 𝓞 K), integralSqrt … - 1} ^ 2 = Ideal.span {2}`: since `integralSqrt (omega_sq_eq_algebraMap_int (d := d))` is by definition ω regarded as an element of `𝓞 K` (`integralSqrt hx := ⟨x, _⟩`, squaring to d by `integralSqrt_sq`), i.e. √d, this is (2) = (2, √d − 1)² in the ring of integers ℤ[√d] of ℚ(√d); Marcus, Number Fields, Thm. 25 writes 2 = (2, 1 + √d)², the same ideal since (2, 1 + √d) = (2, √d − 1). Claim: for an integer p × n matrix A with linearly independent rows and k = n − p, the full lattice of integer solutions of A x = 0 has a ℤ-basis whose sup norms have product at most k!/2^(k−1) · sqrt(det(A Aᵀ))/D, with D the gcd of the p × p minors. Lean ↔ mathematics: `A : Matrix (Fin p) ι ℤ` is a p × n integer matrix (n = `Fintype.card ι`); `hA : LinearIndependent ℚ (A.map ((↑) : ℤ → ℚ)).row` says its rows, read in ℚ^n, are linearly independent (Mathlib's `Matrix.row A` is A as the family of its rows); `√((A * Aᵀ).det : ℝ)` is the square root of the Gram determinant det(A Aᵀ); `A.minorGcd` is by definition `Finset.univ.gcd fun e : Fin p ↪ ι ↦ (A.submatrix id e).det`, the normalized gcd D of the p × p minors; `LinearMap.ker A.mulVecLin` is the kernel of x ↦ A x on ℤ^ι, i.e. the lattice of all integer solutions; `b : Basis (Fin (Fintype.card ι - p)) ℤ (LinearMap.ker A.mulVecLin)` is a ℤ-basis of it with n − p elements, so it generates the whole integer kernel; `‖x‖` for `x : ι → ℤ` is Mathlib's sup norm on a finite product, max_i |x i| (the norm on ℤ is the absolute value), and the bound `(Fintype.card ι - p).factorial / 2 ^ (Fintype.card ι - p - 1) * √((A * Aᵀ).det : ℝ) / (A.minorGcd : ℝ)` is k!/2^(k−1) · sqrt(det(A Aᵀ))/D. It is the basis version of Bombieri and Vaaler's Theorem 2: the integer kernel has covolume sqrt(det(A Aᵀ))/D, and a basis built from the successive minima loses at most the factor k!/2^(k−1) against the product of the minima, which Minkowski's second theorem with Vaaler's cube-slice volume bound bounds by the covolume. Unlike Theorem 2 the vectors generate the whole integer kernel: for A = (0 0 1) the independent solutions (1,1,0) and (1,−1,0) meet Theorem 2's bound 1 but span a sublattice of index 2, whereas this statement gives a basis of the whole plane with bound 1. Lean subtlety: the factor is real division (k! is cast to ℝ), not ℕ floor division; `Fintype.card ι - p - 1` is truncated, so at k = 0 the factor is 0!/2^0 = 1 and both sides are 1; `Fintype.card ι - p` is truncated ℕ subtraction, but `hA` forces p ≤ n, so it is the honest n − p; `Real.sqrt` of a negative number would be 0 and `x / 0 = 0`, but under `hA` det(A Aᵀ) > 0 and D ≥ 1 (`minorGcd_ne_zero_iff`), so neither junk value enters. Red-team checks at 956e316250: the rank hypothesis is load-bearing; the factor is real division (statement printed with coercion types); the file's own example evaluates A = (0 0 1) with bound 1; only the standard axioms; no Mathlib duplicate found.

Claim: for an integer p × n matrix A with linearly independent rows there are n − p linearly independent integer solutions x_1, …, x_{n−p} of A x = 0, each with coprime coordinates, with ∏_l max_i |x_{l,i}| ≤ sqrt(det(A Aᵀ))/D, where D is the gcd of the p × p minors of A. Lean ↔ mathematics: `A : Matrix (Fin p) ι ℤ` is a p × n integer matrix (n = `Fintype.card ι`); `hA : LinearIndependent ℚ (A.map ((↑) : ℤ → ℚ)).row` says its rows, read in ℚ^n, are linearly independent (Mathlib's `Matrix.row A` is A as the family of its rows); `√((A * Aᵀ).det : ℝ)` is the square root of the Gram determinant det(A Aᵀ); `A.minorGcd` is by definition `Finset.univ.gcd fun e : Fin p ↪ ι ↦ (A.submatrix id e).det`, the normalized gcd D of the p × p minors; `x : Fin (Fintype.card ι - p) → ι → ℤ` is a family of n − p integer vectors, `A *ᵥ x l = 0` is A x_l = 0 (`Matrix.mulVec`), `LinearIndependent ℤ` for integer vectors is the same as linear independence over ℚ (clear denominators), `Finset.univ.gcd (x l) = 1` says the normalized (nonnegative) gcd of the coordinates of x l is 1, i.e. x l is primitive, and `‖x‖` for `x : ι → ℤ` is Mathlib's sup norm on a finite product, max_i |x i| (the norm on ℤ is the absolute value), so the conclusion `∏ l, ‖x l‖ ≤ √((A * Aᵀ).det : ℝ) / (A.minorGcd : ℝ)` is Bombieri–Vaaler's inequality. This is Bombieri and Vaaler, On Siegel's Lemma, Invent. Math. 73 (1983), Theorem 2 (p. 12), checked against the paper: same hypotheses (M linearly independent equations with integer coefficients), same sup norm, same bound; the formal version also allows p = n (empty family, bound |det A|/|det A| = 1) and adds coprimality, which costs nothing since dividing a solution by the gcd of its coordinates only lowers its norm. It follows from the subspace version applied to the kernel of A, using that the lattice of integer solutions has covolume sqrt(det(A Aᵀ))/D (Cauchy–Binet and the duality between the row space and the kernel). Lean subtlety: `Fintype.card ι - p` is truncated ℕ subtraction, but `hA` forces p ≤ n, so it is the honest n − p; `Real.sqrt` of a negative number would be 0 and `x / 0 = 0`, but under `hA` det(A Aᵀ) > 0 and D ≥ 1 (`minorGcd_ne_zero_iff`), so neither junk value enters; the casts ℤ → ℝ on det and D are the obvious ones. Red-team checks at 956e316250: the rank hypothesis is needed (for A = (0 0) the bound collapses to 0 and the conclusion is false, compiled); specialised to A = (1 1) (bound sqrt 2) and A = (2 2) (D = 2, det = 8, bound sqrt 8/2), both compiled; norm confirmed to be the sup norm; only the standard axioms.

Claim: the lattice of integer points of a k-dimensional subspace V of ℚ^n has a ℤ-basis whose sup norms have product at most k!/2^(k−1) · H(V). Lean ↔ mathematics: `V : Submodule ℚ (ι → ℚ)` is a subspace of ℚ^ι; `V.intPoints` is the ℤ-module V ∩ ℤ^ι (by definition the preimage of V under ℤ^ι → ℚ^ι, `mem_intPoints`); `b : Basis (Fin (finrank ℚ V)) ℤ V.intPoints` is a ℤ-basis of it indexed by k = dim V elements, so the vectors generate all integer points of V, not just a sublattice of finite index; `(b l : ι → ℤ)` is the l-th basis vector as an integer tuple and `‖x‖` for `x : ι → ℤ` is Mathlib's sup norm on a finite product, max_i |x i| (the norm on ℤ is the absolute value); the bound `(finrank ℚ V).factorial / 2 ^ (finrank ℚ V - 1) * V.subspaceHeight` is k!/2^(k−1) · H(V), where `V.subspaceHeight` is the absolute Euclidean height H(V) (over ℚ the relative Arakelov height to the power 1/[ℚ : ℚ] = 1, the Euclidean length of the primitive integral Plücker vector of V by `subspaceHeight_eq_height2_plucker`), and `covolume_intLattice` proves it equals the covolume of the lattice V ∩ ℤ^ι in the real span of V, which is Bombieri and Vaaler's H(V). It combines two classical facts: from vectors attaining the successive minima one builds a lattice basis whose i-th vector has norm at most max(1, i/2) times the i-th minimum, and the product of these factors over i = 1..k is k!/2^(k−1); and Minkowski's second theorem with Vaaler's lower bound 2^k for the volume of a central slice of the cube shows the product of the minima is at most the covolume. Lean subtlety: the factor elaborates in ℝ, `((k)! : ℝ) / 2 ^ (k - 1)`, an honest real quotient and not ℕ floor division (confirmed by printing the statement with coercion types); the exponent `k - 1` is truncated ℕ subtraction, so at k = 0 it is 0 and the factor is 0!/2^0 = 1, the intended value, both sides being 1 there (empty product, H(0) = 1); `[LinearOrder ι]` only orders the Plücker coordinates in the definition of `subspaceHeight`; since `covolume_intLattice` identifies the height with an order-free covolume, the statement does not depend on the chosen order. Red-team checks at 956e316250: confirmed the factor is real division, not integer floor division (statement printed with coercion types); specialised to V = Q^2, where the bound is 2!/2 · 1 = 1; k = 0 case checked; no hypotheses to drop; no Mathlib duplicate found.

Claim: every subspace V of ℚ^n of dimension k contains k linearly independent integer points, each with coprime coordinates, whose sup norms have product at most the absolute height H(V). Lean ↔ mathematics: `V : Submodule ℚ (ι → ℚ)` is a subspace of ℚ^ι for a finite index type ι; `z : Fin (finrank ℚ V) → ι → ℤ` is a family of k = dim V integer vectors; `LinearIndependent ℤ` for integer vectors is the same as linear independence over ℚ (clear denominators); `z l ∈ V.intPoints` says the rational image of z l lies in V (`mem_intPoints`; `intPoints` is by definition the preimage of V under ℤ^ι → ℚ^ι), i.e. z l ∈ V ∩ ℤ^ι; `Finset.univ.gcd (z l) = 1` says the normalized (nonnegative) gcd of the coordinates of z l is 1, i.e. z l is primitive; `‖x‖` for `x : ι → ℤ` is Mathlib's sup norm on a finite product, max_i |x i| (the norm on ℤ is the absolute value), so `∏ l, ‖z l‖` is the product of the sup norms; `V.subspaceHeight` is the absolute Euclidean height H(V) (over ℚ the relative Arakelov height to the power 1/[ℚ : ℚ] = 1, the Euclidean length of the primitive integral Plücker vector of V by `subspaceHeight_eq_height2_plucker`), and `covolume_intLattice` proves it equals the covolume of the lattice V ∩ ℤ^ι in the real span of V, which is Bombieri and Vaaler's H(V). This is the subspace form of Bombieri and Vaaler's sharp Siegel lemma: for V the kernel of an integer matrix A of full row rank it is exactly their Theorem 2 (On Siegel's Lemma, Invent. Math. 73 (1983), p. 12), because that kernel lattice has covolume sqrt(det(A A^T))/D. The proof takes lattice vectors attaining the successive minima with respect to the slice of the cube [-1,1]^n by the real span of V, whose gauge is the sup norm; Minkowski's second theorem, combined with Vaaler's bound that every k-dimensional central slice of the cube has volume at least 2^k, bounds the product of the minima by the covolume, and vectors attaining the minima are primitive. Lean subtlety: `[LinearOrder ι]` only orders the Plücker coordinates in the definition of `subspaceHeight`; since `covolume_intLattice` identifies the height with an order-free covolume, the statement does not depend on the chosen order; for V = 0 the family is indexed by `Fin 0`, so the independence and gcd clauses are vacuous and the product is the empty product 1 ≤ H(0) = 1. Red-team checks at 956e316250: no hypotheses beyond V; the norm is confirmed to be the sup norm (the vector (1,-2) has norm 2); specialised to V = Q^2, where H = 1 and it yields two independent primitive vectors with product of norms at most 1; only the standard axioms; no Mathlib duplicate (leansearch, leanfinder, loogle, grep of the pinned Mathlib).

For `e : G ≃ₜ* H`, Mathlib's type of group isomorphisms that are also homeomorphisms (isomorphisms of topological groups), `Amenable G ↔ Amenable H`: amenability is invariant under isomorphism of topological groups; each direction is `Amenable.of_surjective` applied to e, respectively to `e.symm`, viewed as surjective continuous homomorphisms.

Claim: a topological group G is amenable when there is a left-invariant mean on the space UCB(G) of bounded left uniformly continuous real functions on G. Lean ↔ mathematics: `Amenable G` is a Prop-valued class with the single field `∃ m : Mean G, m.IsLeftInvariant` (`amenable_iff`); the topological group is given by `[Group G] [TopologicalSpace G] [IsTopologicalGroup G]` with no further hypotheses; `UCB G` is the subalgebra `ucb G` of `G →ᵇ ℝ` (real bounded continuous functions on `G`) cut out by `∀ ε > 0, ∀ᶠ u in 𝓝 1, ∀ x, |f (u * x) - f x| < ε` (`mem_ucb_iff`), i.e. sup_x |f(ux) − f(x)| → 0 as u → e, which is BdHV's UCB(G): the bounded f for which x ↦ f(x·) is continuous into ℓ∞(G); `Mean G` extends `UCB G →ₚ[ℝ] ℝ` (a real-linear map that is monotone for the pointwise order `UCB.le_def`, equivalently nonnegative on nonnegative functions) with the field `map_one' : m 1 = 1`, which is BdHV's mean (positive and normalised, Definition G.1.2); `m.IsLeftInvariant` is m(f(g⁻¹·)) = m(f) for all g and f. Lean subtlety: (i) BdHV call UCB(G) the left uniformly continuous functions, while in Mathlib's terms the condition is uniform continuity for the right uniformity (`mem_ucb_iff_uniformContinuous`); the formula, not the label, is what matters, and it agrees with BdHV; (ii) the means are real-valued on real functions, whereas BdHV use complex-valued means on complex functions; the library proves the two versions of amenability equivalent (`amenable_iff_exists_complexMean`); (iii) BdHV translate by x ↦ f(gx), Lean by x ↦ f(g⁻¹x), which gives the same condition since every g is quantified; (iv) `UCB G` sits inside `G →ᵇ ℝ`, so continuity is built in, but it follows from the uniform condition anyway (`continuous_of_forall_eventually_dist_mul_lt`); continuity of the mean is not assumed but is automatic (`Mean.lipschitzWith`), as in BdHV Remark G.1.3. Source: Bekka–de la Harpe–Valette, Kazhdan's Property (T), Definition G.1.4 with Definition G.1.2, checked page by page against the 2007 draft; as there, no Hausdorff, local compactness or countability assumption is imposed. Red-team checks: a finite group and the discrete integers are amenable (compiled); the free group on two generators with the discrete topology is not amenable, by its paradoxical decomposition (compiled, standard axioms only), so the definition is neither vacuous nor always true; the pinned Mathlib (2cabef97) has Følner filters and says it has no definition of amenability.

Claim: if a group is amenable for a group topology, it is amenable for every coarser group topology. Lean ↔ mathematics: `t₁ t₂ : TopologicalSpace G` are two topologies on the same group, both group topologies by `[@IsTopologicalGroup G t₁ _] [@IsTopologicalGroup G t₂ _]`; `h : t₁ ≤ t₂` says t₁ is finer than t₂; `ha : @Amenable G _ t₁ _` is amenability for t₁ and the conclusion `@Amenable G _ t₂ _` is amenability for t₂; the proof applies `Amenable.of_surjective` to the identity map, which is a continuous surjective homomorphism from (G, t₁) to (G, t₂). Lean subtlety: Mathlib orders topologies so that `t₁ ≤ t₂` means t₁ is FINER (has more open sets), the reverse of the inclusion one might expect; with that reading the direction is the right one (finer to coarser), and in particular amenability of G as a discrete group gives amenability for every group topology (used by `Amenable.of_discrete`). Red-team checks: the identity is continuous from the finer to the coarser topology (`continuous_id_of_le`), which is what the statement needs.

Claim: a continuous homomorphic image of an amenable topological group is amenable. Lean ↔ mathematics: the hypotheses `[Amenable G]`, `φ : G →ₜ* H` (Mathlib's `ContinuousMonoidHom`, a continuous group homomorphism) and `hφ : Function.Surjective φ` say G is amenable and φ is a continuous homomorphism onto H; the conclusion `Amenable H` says, by `amenable_iff`, that `UCB H` carries a left-invariant mean; the proof pushes the invariant mean of G forward by f ↦ m(f ∘ φ) (`Mean.map`, `Mean.map_apply`) and uses that every h ∈ H is some φ(g) (`Mean.IsLeftInvariant.map`). Lean subtlety: none (both groups carry arbitrary group topologies, with no Hausdorff or local compactness assumption, as in the definition). Source: it contains Bekka–de la Harpe–Valette, Proposition G.2.2(i) (2007 draft), that G/N is amenable when G is, and needs no closedness of N. Red-team checks: specialised to the quotient map `QuotientGroup.mk' N` onto `G ⧸ N` for an arbitrary normal subgroup N (compiled); surjectivity cannot just be dropped, since the trivial group is amenable and maps into the free group on two generators, which is not; a dense image would suffice (recorded separately).

Claim: a mean m on the bounded left uniformly continuous functions is left invariant when m(L_g f) = m(f) for all g ∈ G and all f. Lean ↔ mathematics: the body is `∀ (g : G) (f : UCB G), m (UCB.leftTranslation g f) = m f`; `UCB G` is the subalgebra `ucb G` of `G →ᵇ ℝ` (real bounded continuous functions on G) cut out by `∀ ε > 0, ∀ᶠ u in 𝓝 1, ∀ x, |f (u * x) - f x| < ε` (`mem_ucb_iff`), i.e. sup_x |f(ux) − f(x)| → 0 as u → e; `Mean G` extends `UCB G →ₚ[ℝ] ℝ` (a positive real-linear functional) with `map_one' : m 1 = 1`, which is a mean; `UCB.leftTranslation g` is the translation operator, with `(UCB.leftTranslation g f) x = f (g⁻¹ * x)` by the simp lemma `UCB.leftTranslation_apply`, so the body says exactly m(f(g⁻¹·)) = m(f) for all g, f. Lean subtlety: BdHV write the translate as x ↦ f(gx) rather than x ↦ f(g⁻¹x); since the condition is required for every g and g ↦ g⁻¹ is a bijection, the two conditions are the same. Source: Bekka–de la Harpe–Valette, Kazhdan's Property (T), Definition G.1.2(iii) with the left action of Definition G.1.4 (checked in the 2007 draft). Red-team checks: the Dirac mean at the identity of the discrete integers is not left invariant (compiled), so the condition has content; the library proves the uniform average on a finite group left invariant.

From `hm : m.IsLeftInvariant`, `m (UCB.leftTranslation g f) = m f` for all `g : G`, `f : UCB G`: a left-invariant mean has the same value at f and at its translate x ↦ f(g⁻¹x) (`UCB.leftTranslation_apply`); it is the definition applied to g and f, tagged as a simp rule.

From `hm : m.IsLeftInvariant` and `hφ : Function.Surjective φ` for `φ : G →ₜ* H`, `(m.map φ).IsLeftInvariant`: the push-forward mean f ↦ m(f ∘ φ) on `UCB H` (`Mean.map_apply`) is invariant under translation by every h ∈ H, since every h is some φ(g) and invariance under φ(g) is `map_apply_leftTranslation`; correctly stated (the red team records separately that a dense image would suffice).

From `hm : m.IsLeftInvariant`, `m.map φ (UCB.leftTranslation (φ g) f) = m.map φ f` for `φ : G →ₜ* H`, `g : G`, `f : UCB H`: the push-forward mean f ↦ m(f ∘ φ) (`Mean.map_apply`) is invariant under translation by every element φ(g) of the image of φ, because (L_{φ(g)} f) ∘ φ = L_g (f ∘ φ) (`UCB.compRightAlgHom_leftTranslation`); no surjectivity or density of φ is assumed or needed.

Claim: the left-invariant means form a convex set. Lean ↔ mathematics: `toContinuousLinearMap` sends a mean to the same functional regarded as an element of the continuous dual `UCB G →L[ℝ] ℝ` (`coe_toContinuousLinearMap`; a mean is automatically 1-Lipschitz, `Mean.lipschitzWith`); `toContinuousLinearMap '' {m | m.IsLeftInvariant}` is the image of the set of left-invariant means in that dual, and `Convex ℝ S` is ordinary convexity, so the statement says that a convex combination a·m + b·n (a, b ≥ 0, a + b = 1) of two left-invariant means is again (the functional of) a left-invariant mean. Lean subtlety: `Mean G` is not itself a vector space, so convexity is stated for the image in the dual space; `toContinuousLinearMap` is injective (`Mean.toContinuousLinearMap_injective`), so nothing is lost. Source: Bekka–de la Harpe–Valette, Remark G.1.6 (2007 draft), uses that the means form a convex subset of UCB(G)*. Red-team checks: no hypotheses beyond the topological group structure; the proof is the convexity of all means (`convex_range_toContinuousLinearMap`) plus linearity of the invariance condition.

`m.IsLeftInvariant ↔ ∀ g f, m (UCB.leftTranslation g f) = m f`: a mean on `UCB G` is left invariant iff it takes the same value at f and at every translate x ↦ f(g⁻¹x) (`UCB.leftTranslation_apply`); this is the definition unfolded (`Iff.rfl`), stated so other modules can use it without unfolding.

Claim: a continuous homomorphism φ : G → H pushes a mean m on G forward to the mean f ↦ m(f ∘ φ) on H. Lean ↔ mathematics: `G →ₜ* H` is Mathlib's type of continuous monoid homomorphisms; `UCB.compRightAlgHom φ : UCB H →ₐ[ℝ] UCB G` is the pullback f ↦ f ∘ φ (`UCB.compRightAlgHom_apply`), which lands in `UCB G` because φ sends neighbourhoods of 1 to neighbourhoods of 1 (`compContinuous_mem_ucb`); `Mean G` extends `UCB G →ₚ[ℝ] ℝ` (a positive real-linear functional) with `map_one' : m 1 = 1`, and the body `mk₀ (m ∘ₗ compRightAlgHom φ) …` builds the mean from that linear functional, with positivity from monotonicity of the pullback (`UCB.monotone_compRightAlgHom`) and the value 1 at 1 because the pullback of the constant 1 is the constant 1, so `(m.map φ) f = m (f ∘ φ)` (`Mean.map_apply`). Lean subtlety: none. Source: this is the map used in Bekka–de la Harpe–Valette, Proposition G.2.2(i) (2007 draft), where UCB(G/N) is regarded as a subspace of UCB(G). Red-team checks: evaluation formula, identity law and composition law hold.

`m.map φ f = m (UCB.compRightAlgHom φ f)` for `φ : G →ₜ* H` and `f : UCB H`: the pushed-forward mean evaluates f as m(f ∘ φ), since `UCB.compRightAlgHom φ f` is f ∘ φ (`UCB.compRightAlgHom_apply`); true by construction (`mk₀_apply`).

`m.map (ContinuousMonoidHom.id G) = m`: pushing a mean forward along the identity continuous homomorphism of G returns it, since f ∘ id = f; equality of means is pointwise equality on `UCB G` (`Mean.ext`).

`(m.map φ).map ψ = m.map (ψ.comp φ)` for `φ : G →ₜ* H`, `ψ : H →ₜ* K`: pushing forward along φ and then ψ is pushing forward along the composite ψ ∘ φ (`ψ.comp φ`), since (f ∘ ψ) ∘ φ = f ∘ (ψ ∘ φ) (`UCB.compRightAlgHom_comp`).

`Amenable G ↔ ∃ m : Mean G, m.IsLeftInvariant`: G is amenable iff there is a left-invariant mean (a positive normalised real-linear functional, `Mean G`) on `UCB G`, the bounded left uniformly continuous functions; it unpacks the one-field class `Amenable`.

Correctly stated: between two graphs with the extension property, of any cardinalities, n-tuples a and b are α-back-and-forth equivalent at every ordinal level α exactly when they have the same atomic type, so the back-and-forth hierarchy collapses at level 0. Lean to mathematics: `BFEquiv α n a b` is Tau Ceti's ordinal back-and-forth relation, defined by recursion on α: at 0 it is `SameAtomicType`, at α + 1 it keeps level α and requires every one-point extension on either side to be matched at level α (`BFEquiv.add_one`), and at a limit it requires every smaller level (`BFEquiv.limit`), the standard relation a ≡_α b; `SameAtomicType` under `G.structure` and `H.structure` is agreement of equalities and adjacencies (`SimpleGraph.sameAtomicType_iff`). The direction → is `BFEquiv.sameAtomicType`; ← uses extension in both directions, hence both hG and hH. Lean subtlety: α ranges over `Ordinal.{o}` in a universe independent of V and W; harmless, the statement holds in every universe. Checks at 5f78b5307b: compiled that hG cannot be dropped: for the edgeless graph on ULift ℕ against the Rado graph the empty tuples have the same atomic type, but equivalence at every level would give a potential isomorphism (potentialIso_iff_bfEquiv_all) carrying the extension property to the edgeless graph, which lacks it.

Correctly stated: if H has the extension property, every partial isomorphism between n-tuples a of G and b of H extends to any further vertex x of G, the one-point extension step in Cameron's proof that two countable graphs with property (*) are isomorphic. Lean to mathematics: the graphs are read as first-order structures through Mathlib's `G.structure` and `H.structure`, which interpret the one binary symbol `adj` as `G.Adj` and `H.Adj`; under these, `SameAtomicType (L := Language.graph) a b` is by `SimpleGraph.sameAtomicType_iff` exactly the pair of conditions a i = a j ↔ b i = b j and G.Adj (a i) (a j) ↔ H.Adj (b i) (b j) for all i, j, i.e. a i ↦ b i is a well-defined isomorphism of the induced finite subgraphs; `snoc a x` is the tuple a with x appended, so the conclusion gives a vertex y of H for which (a, x) ↦ (b, y) is still such an isomorphism. Only H carries a hypothesis; G is arbitrary. Lean subtlety: tuples `Fin n → V` may repeat entries; harmless, since the equality clause forces repeated entries to correspond, and when x is already some a i the lemma returns b i. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: hH is used in the proof, axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound only.

Correctly stated: every graph with the extension property, of any cardinality, has internal Scott rank 1 in Tau Ceti's convention. Lean to mathematics: `internalScottRank V` is by definition the supremum over all finite tuples a of `orbitRank a + 1`, where `orbitRank a` is the least ordinal α such that every tuple of the same structure that is α-back-and-forth equivalent to a (`BFEquiv`) is equivalent to it at every level; in a graph with the extension property the same atomic type already gives equivalence at every level, so every orbit rank is 0 (`IsExtensionPair.orbitRank_eq_zero`, from isExtensionPair G G) and the supremum is 0 + 1 = 1. Lean subtlety: the number depends on the convention: this definition adds one to each orbit rank, so every structure, the empty one included, has rank at least 1 (`one_le_internalScottRank`); under a convention that counts the least stabilisation level itself (Tau Ceti's `selfStabilizationOrdinal`, which is 0 here) the same fact reads 0. The statement is exactly about the Tau Ceti definition its name and docstring cite. Checks at 5f78b5307b: specialised at the Rado graph; hG used; axioms standard.

Correctly stated: every finite partial isomorphism from an arbitrary graph G to a graph H with the extension property extends to contain any further vertex of G, the forth step of the back-and-forth argument (Cameron, The random graph, proof of Fact 2). Lean to mathematics: `Language.graph.IsExtensionPair V W` is Mathlib's `FirstOrder.Language.IsExtensionPair`: for every `FGEquiv` f (an isomorphism between finitely generated substructures of V and W) and every m : V there is g ≥ f with m in the domain of g; the language of graphs is relational with the single binary symbol `adj`, interpreted by `G.structure` and `H.structure` as adjacency, so finitely generated substructures are finite vertex sets with their induced adjacency and an `FGEquiv` is an isomorphism of finite induced subgraphs. Lean subtlety: `SimpleGraph.structure` is a definition, not an instance, so the statement installs the two structures with `letI`; harmless, the statement is about exactly these structures. Audit at 5f78b5307b: derived from exists_sameAtomicType_snoc through Tau Ceti's isExtensionPair_iff_forall_exists_snoc; hH used; no hypothesis on G.

Correctly stated: any two countable graphs with the extension property are isomorphic, Cameron's Fact 2; the docstring's gloss 'the theory of the random graph is ℵ₀-categorical' refers to this, the graphs with the extension property being the models of that theory. Lean to mathematics: `G ≃g H` is Mathlib's `SimpleGraph.Iso`, a `RelIso G.Adj H.Adj`, i.e. a bijection e : V ≃ W with G.Adj a b ↔ H.Adj (e a) (e b), so `Nonempty (G ≃g H)` says G ≅ H; `[Countable V]` and `[Countable W]` say the vertex sets are countable; `G.HasExtensionProperty` unfolds (`hasExtensionProperty_def`) to: for all disjoint finite vertex sets s, t there is z ∉ t adjacent to every vertex of s and to no vertex of t, and z ∉ s follows from looplessness, so this is property (*) with z distinct from u_1, …, u_m, v_1, …, v_n (equivalence with the explicit z ∉ s, z ∉ t form compiled). Lean subtlety: `Countable` includes finite and empty types, while the theorem is about countably infinite graphs; harmless, because the extension property with s = ∅ and t the whole vertex set forces infinitely many vertices (compiled for every `[Finite V]`, and for the empty and one-vertex graphs), so no case holds vacuously. The isomorphism is obtained non-constructively (`Nonempty`, through potential isomorphism and Tau Ceti's countable_potentialIso_iff_iso). Source: P. J. Cameron, The random graph (arXiv:1301.7544, the 1997 chapter), §1.1, property (*) and Fact 2, 'Any two countable graphs satisfying (*) are isomorphic.' Checks at 5f78b5307b: specialised to the Rado graph; compiled that hG cannot be dropped (the edgeless graph on ℕ is not isomorphic to the Rado graph); both hypotheses used; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: if G has the extension property and H is potentially isomorphic to G, then H has the extension property, for graphs of any cardinality. Lean to mathematics: the hypothesis `PotentialIso (L := Language.graph) V W` (a nonempty family of finite partial isomorphisms from G to H closed under forth and back extension, read through `G.structure` and `H.structure`) is Karp's potential isomorphism, and the conclusion `H.HasExtensionProperty` unfolds to: for disjoint finite s, t ⊆ W some z ∉ t is adjacent to all of s and none of t; the proof enumerates s ∪ t, pulls it back along the family to G, solves the adjacency pattern there and pushes the solution forward. Lean subtlety: the structures are installed with `letI` in the hypothesis; harmless. Checks at 5f78b5307b: both hypotheses used; used in compiled probes to show that the edgeless graph on ULift ℕ is not potentially isomorphic to the Rado graph.

Correctly stated: any two graphs with the extension property, of any cardinalities, are potentially isomorphic (back-and-forth equivalent in Karp's sense). Lean to mathematics: `PotentialIso V W` is Tau Ceti's definition: a nonempty set S of finitely generated partial isomorphisms (`L.FGEquiv`) such that each f ∈ S has an extension g ∈ S containing any given vertex of V in its domain and one containing any given vertex of W in its range; for the language of graphs, read through `G.structure` and `H.structure`, these are isomorphisms between finite induced subgraphs. The witness is the system of tuple pairs with the same atomic type, a back-and-forth system because each graph forms an extension pair with the other (isExtensionPair, used both ways). Lean subtlety: the structures are installed with `letI`, and the vertex types may live in different universes; harmless. Checks at 5f78b5307b: compiled that the conclusion fails without hG (the edgeless graph on ULift ℕ and the Rado graph are not potentially isomorphic, since of_potentialIso would carry the extension property to the edgeless graph).

Correctly stated: for a countable graph G with the extension property, a graph H of any cardinality satisfies the Scott sentence of G exactly when H has the extension property. Lean to mathematics: `scottSentence V` is Tau Ceti's canonical Scott sentence of the countable structure (V, G.structure), an L_{ω₁ω} sentence (`Sentenceω`) built at the least internal stabilisation level, and `SentenceInf.Realize φ W` is its satisfaction in (W, H.structure); its models are exactly the structures potentially isomorphic to V (`potentialIso_of_realize_scottSentence`, and conversely `PotentialIso.infEquivAt` with `realize_scottSentence_self`), and by potentialIso and of_potentialIso those graphs are exactly the ones with the extension property. Lean subtlety: `[Countable V]` is required because the Scott sentence is only defined for countable structures (its conjunction runs over an enumeration of the tuples of V); W is unrestricted, and H is an explicit argument. Checks at 5f78b5307b: compiled that the edgeless graph on ℕ does not satisfy the Rado graph's Scott sentence; hG used.

Correctly stated: a countable graph is isomorphic to the Rado graph exactly when it has the extension property; with the Rado graph's own extension property this is the theorem that, up to isomorphism, the Rado graph is the unique countable graph with property (*). Lean to mathematics: `G ≃g radoGraph` is Mathlib's `SimpleGraph.Iso`, a bijection V ≃ ℕ preserving and reflecting adjacency, so `Nonempty (G ≃g radoGraph)` says G ≅ R. `radoGraph` is `SimpleGraph.fromRel fun i j => j.testBit i`, and `radoGraph_adj` unfolds it to i ≠ j ∧ (j.testBit i ∨ i.testBit j): i and j are adjacent when the i-th binary digit of j or the j-th binary digit of i is 1, which is Rado's description as Cameron gives it ('x and y are adjacent if the xth digit in the base 2 expansion of y is a 1 or vice versa'); for i < j the second disjunct is false because i < 2^j, so i < j are adjacent exactly when bit i of j is set (compiled), and the graph is symmetric and loopless by construction. `G.HasExtensionProperty` unfolds (`hasExtensionProperty_def`) to: for all disjoint finite vertex sets s, t there is a vertex z ∉ t adjacent to every vertex of s and to no vertex of t; z ∉ s follows from looplessness, so this is Cameron's (*) with z distinct from the given vertices (equivalence with the explicit z ∉ s, z ∉ t form compiled), and `[Countable V]` is countability of the vertex type. Lean subtlety: `Countable` includes finite and empty types, whereas the Rado graph is countably infinite; harmless, because s = ∅ and t = all vertices shows that no graph on a finite type has the extension property (compiled for every `[Finite V]`, and for the empty graph on `Empty` and the one-vertex graph), and a finite type admits no bijection with ℕ, so for finite V both sides are false rather than vacuously true. The witness of the extension property must lie outside t, which is what makes this work: without that clause the condition would be weaker. `Nonempty` asserts existence of an isomorphism non-constructively. `[Countable V]` is needed only for ←; the → direction holds for any V (compiled), and the universe of V is arbitrary. Source: P. J. Cameron, The random graph (arXiv:1301.7544, the 1997 chapter), §1.1, property (*) and Fact 2, and §1.2 for Rado's construction. Checks at 5f78b5307b: compiled that the theorem yields the extension property of the Rado graph (from the identity isomorphism) and an isomorphism between any two countable graphs with the extension property, across universes; the edgeless and complete graphs on ℕ are not isomorphic to it; adjacency values 0~1, 1~2, 0~3, 1~3, 2~4, 0~5, 2~5 and non-adjacency of 0,2, of 2,3 and of 3,4 by computation; the hypotheses are consistent (the Rado graph itself); axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: for φ : G →* H and a commutative ring k, the chain-level square commutes — pushing G-coinvariant chains k ⊗_{k[G]} C_•(EG; k) to the H-coinvariant chains of EH along `singularChainsCoinvariantsMap` of `φ.universalGSpaceMap` (relabel join vertices by φ), then identifying with C_•(BH; k) by `singularChainsRepCoinvariantsTensorIso`, equals identifying with C_•(BG; k) first and then applying `(singularChains k).map` of the induced map `φ.classifyingSpaceMap : BG → BH`; `≫` is composition in diagrammatic order, so this is the naturality square of the chain identification. It is the general quotient-covering naturality instantiated at the orbit maps of the Milnor joins (see the reuse finding RT-20261029-3e29e8). Checks (earlier audit at 956e3162, statement unchanged at 5f78b530): not a definitional tautology, no hypotheses beyond the group and ring structures.

Correctly stated: the identification H_n(BG; k) ≅ H_n(G; k) is natural in the group — for every homomorphism φ : G →* H (no hypothesis on φ), the square H_n(BG; k) → H_n(BH; k) → H_n(H; k) equals H_n(BG; k) → H_n(G; k) → H_n(H; k). Lean ↔ maths: `HomologicalComplex.homologyMap ((singularChains k).map (TopCat.ofHom φ.classifyingSpaceMap)) n` is the map on singular homology induced by Bφ, where `φ.classifyingSpaceMap` is by definition the map of orbit spaces induced by `φ.universalGSpaceMap` (relabel join vertices by φ, `classifyingSpaceMap_proj`), and it is strictly functorial (`classifyingSpaceMap_id`, `_comp`); `groupHomology.map φ (𝟙 (Rep.trivial k G k)) n` is Mathlib's change-of-group map H_n(G, A) → H_n(H, B) for the pair (φ, A → Res_φ B), here with the identity of k, since restricting the trivial H-module k along φ is by definition the trivial G-module k — so it is the standard map H_n(G; k) → H_n(H; k) induced by φ; `.hom` of `classifyingSpaceSingularHomologyIsoGroupHomology` is the comparison H_n(BG; k) → H_n(G; k), and `≫` is diagrammatic composition, so the equation is exactly the commuting square. Lean subtlety: typing `𝟙 (Rep.trivial k G k)` as a morphism `Rep.trivial k G k ⟶ Rep.res φ (Rep.trivial k H k)` relies on that definitional equality, which is the intended identity on coefficients; G, H, k share one universe u (as for the isomorphism itself). Checks at 5f78b530: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; applied with no further hypothesis to the non-injective surjection ℤ → ℤ/2 (k = ℤ, n = 1); combined with Mathlib's `groupHomology.map_id` it forces B(id)_* = 𝟙, consistent with `classifyingSpaceMap_id`; roadmap ClassifyingSpaces item 17 asks for this naturality; no Mathlib or other Tau Ceti statement of it (grep of `groupHomology.map` uses).

Correctly stated: the same naturality square for the inverse comparisons H_n(G; k) → H_n(BG; k): `groupHomology.map φ (𝟙 _) n ≫ iso_H.inv = iso_G.inv ≫ (Bφ)_*`, obtained from the `hom` version by cancelling the isomorphisms (`Iso.comp_inv_eq`, `Iso.inv_hom_id_assoc`). Checks at 5f78b530: standard axioms; the two sides are not reducibly defeq (`with_reducible rfl` fails), so it is not a tautology.

Correctly stated: for every group G, commutative ring k and n : ℕ it gives an isomorphism of k-modules H_n(BG; k) ≅ H_n(G; k), group homology with trivial coefficients. Lean ↔ maths: the source `((singularChains k).obj (TopCat.of (classifyingSpace G))).homology n` is the n-th homology of `singularChains k`, an abbrev for Mathlib's `singularChainComplexFunctor (ModuleCat k)` at the coefficient module k, i.e. the singular chain complex C_•(X; k), evaluated at `classifyingSpace G`, which is by definition the orbit space `MulAction.orbitRel.Quotient G (universalGSpace G)` (quotient topology) of `universalGSpace G`, the realization of the countable join G * G * ⋯ with the weak topology on which G acts freely by relabelling vertices — Milnor's EG → BG; the target `groupHomology (Rep.trivial k G k) n` is Mathlib's group homology of the trivial k[G]-module k. The isomorphism is not an arbitrary one: its body is `IsQuotientCoveringMap.singularHomologyIsoGroupHomology` applied to the orbit map `classifyingSpaceProj G`, the comparison that reads C_•(EG; k) as a free k[G]-resolution of k (EG is contractible) whose coinvariants are C_•(BG; k). Lean subtlety: G has no topology (a discrete group, as intended), and G, k and the spaces all live in one universe u, as Mathlib's `groupHomology` and `singularChains` require; any group or ring can be lifted to a common universe, so nothing is lost. Checks: the earlier red-team audit at 956e3162 compiled specialisations to the trivial group (homology vanishes above degree 0), H_1(BG; ℤ) ≅ Gᵃᵇ, H_1(Bℤ; ℤ) ≅ ℤ and H_0 = coinvariants, with standard axioms; at 5f78b530 the declaration and its dependencies are unchanged, and a probe used it with the new naturality theorem at φ = id to recover that B(id) induces the identity on homology.

Correctly stated: two R-bilinear maps β, β' : Γ^d_R(M) × Γ^d_R(M) → P are equal as soon as their scalar extensions agree on the pairs (γ_d(Σᵢ Xᵢ ⊗ mᵢ), γ_d(Σⱼ Yⱼ ⊗ nⱼ)) for all finite families m, n, with the Xᵢ and Yⱼ two disjoint sets of polynomial variables. Lean ↔ maths: `LinearMap.BilinMap R V P` is V →ₗ V →ₗ P; `LinearMap.BilinMap.baseChange A β` is Mathlib's extension of scalars A ⊗ V × A ⊗ V → A ⊗ P (a ⊗ x, a' ⊗ y ↦ aa' ⊗ β x y, `baseChange_tmul`) at A = `MvPolynomial (Fin p ⊕ Fin q) R`; `X (Sum.inl i)` and `X (Sum.inr j)` are the two disjoint groups of variables; `(gamma R M d).toFun _` is the universal law γ_d after this scalar extension. Why true: by `gamma_toFun_sum_tmul` the extended value is Σ_{a,b} X^a Y^b ⊗ β(∏ mᵢ^[aᵢ], ∏ nⱼ^[bⱼ]), so the coefficient of X^a Y^b recovers β on each pair of generators of Γ^d, which span (`homogeneousSubmodule_ext_prod_dp` twice); this is the bilinear analogue of `homogeneousLawMap_injective`. Lean subtlety: as there, the hypothesis needs scalar-extended values (ground values would not determine β in small characteristic); the variables are indexed by `Fin p ⊕ Fin q`, so every finite family is covered. Checks at 5f78b530: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; re-elaborated with R, M, P in three different universes; consumed on main by `homogeneousLawEquiv_symm_homogeneousMul` in RobyAlgebra.lean (multiplicativity of the representing map); no Mathlib or other Tau Ceti ext lemma of this form (git grep for `BilinMap.baseChange` across TauCeti and pinned Mathlib).

Correct: the underlying law of `homogeneousLawMap R M N d f` is `f.toPolynomialLaw.comp (gamma R M d)`, i.e. f ∘ γ_d — the unfolding equation of the definition (`rfl`). Earlier audit at 956e3162: in simp normal form.

Correctly stated: Roby's theorem (Roby 1963, Théorème IV.1, read in the Numdam copy) — for modules M, N over a commutative semiring R and every degree d, composing with the universal law γ_d is an R-linear isomorphism between linear maps Γ^d_R(M) → N and polynomial laws M → N homogeneous of degree d. Lean ↔ maths: `HasWeakFDerivOn μ Ω u U` (Tau Ceti, Sobolev/WeakDeriv/Basic) says that for every direction v, u and x ↦ U x v are locally integrable on Ω and ∫ ∂ᵥψ · u dμ = -∫ ψ · U(·)v dμ for every scalar test function ψ ∈ 𝓓(Ω, ℝ) — the weak-derivative identity relative to μ; `U : E → E →L[ℝ] ℝ` is the weak differential and `‖U x‖ₑ` its operator norm, which on an inner product space is the Euclidean length |∇u(x)| of the weak gradient; `∫⁻ x in Ω, ‖U x‖ₑ ∂μ` is the [0, ∞]-valued Lebesgue integral of |∇u| over Ω. Proof as in the textbook: integration by parts turns ∫ u div φ into -∫ U(φ), and |U(φ)| ≤ |U| because |φ| ≤ 1. Lean subtlety: the right side is a lintegral, never a junk value: it is ∞ when |U| is not integrable on Ω, and then the bound is trivially and correctly true; the weak derivative is taken with respect to the same μ, so no Haar hypothesis is needed for this inequality (earlier audit). Correctly stated (uniqueness): for selfadjoint a, a finite measure μ on ℝ equals μ_a iff ∫ f dμ = φ(f(a)) for every continuous f : ℝ → ℝ. Proof: μ and μ_a both live on the compact set K ∪ spectrum(a), where polynomials are uniformly dense in continuous functions (Weierstrass), so equal moments force equal measures (Tau Ceti's `Measure.ext_of_forall_integral_pow_eq_of_support`). Correctly stated: it defines the law (distribution) μ_a of an element a of a unital C⋆-algebra with respect to a positive linear functional φ: for selfadjoint a, the finite Borel measure on ℝ, concentrated on the spectrum, with ∫ f dμ_a = φ(f(a)) for f continuous on the spectrum. Correctly stated: for selfadjoint a and p ∈ ℝ[X], `((∫ x, p.eval x ∂(law φ a) : ℝ) : ℂ) = φ (aeval a p)`, where `aeval a p` is ordinary polynomial evaluation p(a) in the ℝ-algebra A: the defining identity at f = p plus `cfc_polynomial` (the functional calculus agrees with polynomial evaluation) — exactly the identity τ(P(X)) = ∫ P dμ_X of T. Tao, 254A Notes 5 'Free probability', Theorem 9 for real polynomials. Selfadjointness is needed (the earlier red-team audit (2026-10-29, same text)).

Correctly stated: the defining identity of the law — for selfadjoint a and f continuous on the spectrum of a, ∫ f dμ_a = φ(f(a)). Lean ↔ maths: `ha : IsSelfAdjoint a`; `hf : ContinuousOn f (spectrum ℝ a)` (autoParam) asks continuity on the spectrum only; `cfc f a` is Mathlib's continuous functional calculus f(a); `∫ x, f x ∂(law φ a)` is the Bochner integral, cast by `((… : ℝ) : ℂ)` to compare it with φ(f(a)) ∈ ℂ. Proof: unfold the law as the pushforward of the Riesz measure on the spectrum (an integral along a measurable embedding) and apply the Riesz representation identity for g ↦ Re φ(g(a)), whose real part is all of φ(g(a)) because g(a) is selfadjoint and φ is positive. Lean subtlety: (i) `cfc f a` is 0 by definition when f is not continuous on the spectrum or a is not selfadjoint — both excluded by `hf` and `ha`; (ii) the Bochner integral would be 0 for a non-integrable f, but f is μ_a-integrable (`integrable_law`), so the left side is a genuine integral; (iii) without `ha` the identity still holds as 0 = 0, recorded as minor generality finding RT-20261029-3e2fa3, not a correctness issue. Source: T. Tao, 254A Notes 5 'Free probability', Theorem 9 (τ(P(X)) = ∫ P dμ_X, the polynomial case). Checks: the earlier red-team audit (2026-10-29, same text) specialised it at A = ℂ (law δ_r) and at A = ℂ² with the averaging state; Delta red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the file, moved unchanged from Law.lean by #24988, recompiled in isolation on Mathlib 1b1ccf4b.

Correctly stated: for selfadjoint a and every n : ℕ, `((∫ x, x ^ n ∂(law φ a) : ℝ) : ℂ) = φ (a ^ n)`: the moments of μ_a are the moments φ(aⁿ) of a (n = 0 gives the mass φ(1)), since `cfc (· ^ n) a = a ^ n` (`cfc_pow_id`). Checked (the earlier red-team audit (2026-10-29, same text)): A = ℂ² with the averaging state and a = (1, −1) gives (1 + (−1)ⁿ)/2.

Correctly stated: for selfadjoint a, `(((law φ a).real Set.univ : ℝ) : ℂ) = φ 1`, the total mass of μ_a is φ(1) — the defining identity at f = 1, with `cfc 1 a = 1`. Lean subtlety: `Measure.real` is `ENNReal.toReal` of the measure, which would turn ∞ into 0, but μ_a is a finite measure (instance), so this is its true mass. Checked (the earlier red-team audit (2026-10-29, same text)): φ = 2·id on ℂ, a = 1 gives mass 2; selfadjointness is needed since non-selfadjoint elements have zero law.

Correctly stated: `(law φ a).restrict (spectrum ℝ a) = law φ a`, the same concentration statement as an identity of measures (restricting μ_a to the spectrum changes nothing), for every a; it follows from `law_compl_spectrum` by `Measure.restrict_eq_self_of_ae_mem`.

Correctly stated: for every convex body K and index i < dim E, Tau Ceti's foundational successive minimum `MeasureTheory.successiveMin L K i` — by definition sInf{r : ℝ≥0 | i < Set.finrank ℝ (r • K ∩ L)}, the least r such that the lattice vectors in r•K span a subspace of dimension > i — equals λ_i, after the coercion ℝ≥0 → ℝ. A set spans dimension ≥ i+1 exactly when it contains i+1 independent vectors, so both infima run over the same factors. Lean subtlety: both sides use the junk value 0 in the same degenerate cases, so the equality holds with no hypothesis on L or K (checked in the earlier audit); `NNReal.coe_sInf` transports the infimum, and an index i : Fin (finrank ℝ E) forces 0 < dim E < ∞.

Correctly stated: for a discrete spanning L and 0 ∈ interior K there is an ℝ-basis b of E (`Basis (Fin (finrank ℝ E)) ℝ E`) with b_i ∈ L, gauge(b_i) = λ_i, b_i ∈ λ_i•K, and every lattice vector of gauge < λ_i in `b.flag i.castSucc`, Mathlib's flag = span of b_0, …, b_{i−1}. b need not be a ℤ-basis of L and K need not be symmetric, as the docstring says.

Correctly stated: some ℤ-basis b of L (`Basis (Fin (finrank ℝ E)) ℤ L`) has every lattice vector of gauge < λ_i in the real flag `(b.ofZLatticeBasis ℝ L).flag i.castSucc`, the ℝ-span of b_0, …, b_{i−1} — a lattice basis adapted to the minima, obtained from the real basis by a flag-preserving change (Evertse, Lemma 2.1, read). No bound on the gauges of the b_i is claimed, as the docstring says.

Correctly stated: for a discrete spanning lattice L and a symmetric convex body K with 0 in its interior, some ℤ-basis b of L has b_i ∈ (max(1, (i+1)/2)·λ_i)•K for every i — zero-based, i.e. b_j ∈ max(1, j/2)λ_j K in 1-based numbering: the classical bound of Cassels, as quoted in arXiv:1801.00979 (|g(1)| = λ_1, |g(j)| ≤ ½ j λ_j for j ≥ 2) and Aliev–Smyth arXiv:0704.1747 (|b_j| ≤ max{1, j/2} λ_j), both read. Lean ↔ maths: `[DiscreteTopology L]` with `[IsZLattice ℝ L]` (L spans E over ℝ) make the ℤ-submodule L a full-rank lattice; `K : ConvexBody E` is Mathlib's convex body (nonempty, compact, convex) and `hK : 0 ∈ interior (K : Set E)` puts the origin in its interior; `hsymm : ∀ x ∈ K, -x ∈ K` is central symmetry; `b : Basis (Fin (finrank ℝ E)) ℤ L` is a ℤ-basis of L, and `(b i : E) ∈ (max 1 (((i : ℕ) : ℝ) + 1) / 2) * successiveMin L K i) • (K : Set E)` is membership in the stated dilate. Lean subtlety: `((i : ℕ) : ℝ) + 1) / 2` is real division of the cast index (checked with `pp.numericTypes`), not ℕ division; Lean subtlety: `successiveMin` is an `sInf` of a set of reals and `sInf ∅ = 0` in Lean; the hypotheses here (discrete spanning L, 0 ∈ interior K) make that set nonempty and the infimum attained (`successiveMin_isLeast`), so λ_i is the genuine minimum, not the junk value. Checks: the earlier probes re-compiled at 5f78b530: the statement applied to the standard lattice ℤ² ⊂ ℝ² with the (symmetric) closed unit ball, all hypotheses met; standard axioms.

Correctly stated: for a discrete spanning L and a symmetric convex body K with 0 in its interior, some ℤ-basis b of L has ∏ gauge(b_i) ≤ (n!/2^{n−1})·∏ λ_i, n = dim E — the product of the factors max(1, (i+1)/2) over i < n is n!/2^{n−1}. Lean subtlety: the factor elaborates as `(↑(finrank ℝ E).factorial : ℝ) / (2 : ℝ) ^ (finrank ℝ E - 1)` (checked with `pp.numericTypes`), so the division is real, while the exponent `finrank ℝ E - 1` is truncated ℕ subtraction: for n ≥ 1 it is n−1, and for n = 0 it is 0, giving 0!/2⁰ = 1 with both products empty, the intended reading. Checks: product identity checked for small n (earlier audit); gauges are nonnegative so the factorwise bounds multiply.

Correctly stated: the minima are attained simultaneously — for a discrete spanning lattice L and a convex body K with 0 in its interior there are ℝ-independent a_0, …, a_{n−1} ∈ L with gauge(a_i) = λ_i for every i (Evertse, Lemma 2.8, read: linearly independent v_i ∈ L with v_i ∈ λ_i C; Evertse assumes C symmetric, which is not used). Lean ↔ maths: `[DiscreteTopology L]` with `[IsZLattice ℝ L]` (L spans E over ℝ) make the ℤ-submodule L a full-rank lattice; `K : ConvexBody E` is Mathlib's convex body (nonempty, compact, convex) and `hK : 0 ∈ interior (K : Set E)` puts the origin in its interior; `gauge (K : Set E) x` is Mathlib's Minkowski functional inf{r > 0 | x ∈ r • K}, which for 0 ∈ interior K satisfies gauge x ≤ t ↔ x ∈ t • K for t > 0, so gauge(a_i) = λ_i says a_i ∈ λ_i•K on the boundary; `a : Fin (finrank ℝ E) → E` with `LinearIndependent ℝ a` is n independent vectors, which need not form a ℤ-basis of L, as the docstring says. Lean subtlety: `successiveMin` is an `sInf` of a set of reals and `sInf ∅ = 0` in Lean; the hypotheses here (discrete spanning L, 0 ∈ interior K) make that set nonempty and the infimum attained (`successiveMin_isLeast`), so λ_i is the genuine minimum, not the junk value. Checks: the earlier probes re-compiled at 5f78b530; hypotheses jointly satisfiable (ℤ² and the unit cube); standard axioms.

Correct: for a discrete spanning lattice (`[DiscreteTopology L]` with `[IsZLattice ℝ L]` (L spans E over ℝ) make the ℤ-submodule L a full-rank lattice), 0 ∈ interior K and a proper subspace V (`hV : V ≠ ⊤`), some w ∈ L \ V has least gauge among the lattice vectors outside V — L ⊄ V since it spans, and only finitely many competitors have smaller gauge; V proper is needed.

Correct: for discrete L (`[DiscreteTopology L]`) in finite-dimensional E and 0 ∈ interior K, `{x | x ∈ L ∧ gauge K x ≤ r}` is finite: it lies in the bounded dilate (max r 0 + 1)•K, which meets a discrete subgroup in finitely many points. Lean subtlety: without 0 ∈ interior K the gauge can take the junk value 0 off every dilate, so the hypothesis is needed (earlier audit); symmetry is not.

Correctly stated: if a_0, …, a_{n−1} are ℝ-independent lattice vectors with gauge(a_i) ≤ λ_i, every lattice vector v with gauge(v) < λ_j lies in span_ℝ{a_0, …, a_{j−1}} — the lattice input to Minkowski's second theorem. Lean ↔ maths: `gauge (K : Set E) x` is Mathlib's Minkowski functional inf{r > 0 | x ∈ r • K}, which for 0 ∈ interior K satisfies gauge x ≤ t ↔ x ∈ t • K for t > 0; the conclusion `v ∈ span ℝ (a '' Set.Iio j)` is membership in the span of the a_i with i < j. Lean subtlety: 0 ∈ interior K is needed to read gauge v ≤ t as v ∈ t•K; no discreteness is assumed or needed (earlier audit).

Correctly stated: for a discrete spanning L and 0 ∈ interior K, `Monotone (successiveMin L K)` on the indices `Fin (finrank ℝ E)`, i.e. λ_0 ≤ λ_1 ≤ … ≤ λ_{n−1} (Evertse, Lemma 2.8). Lean subtlety: without the hypotheses the junk value breaks monotonicity — for ℤ² and the segment [−1,1]×{0}, λ_0 = 1 > λ_1 = 0 (probe re-compiled at 5f78b530).

Correctly defined: the successive minima of a lattice L ⊂ E with respect to a convex body K — λ_i is the least t ≥ 0 such that t•K contains i+1 vectors of L linearly independent over ℝ (Evertse, Diophantine approximation lecture notes, Ch. 2, §2.3, read), zero-based. Lean ↔ maths: the body is `sInf {t : ℝ | 0 ≤ t ∧ ∃ v : Fin (i + 1) → E, LinearIndependent ℝ v ∧ ∀ j, v j ∈ L ∧ v j ∈ t • (K : Set E)}` — the infimum of the admissible dilation factors, with `t • (K : Set E)` the pointwise dilate and `LinearIndependent ℝ v` independence over the reals (not over ℤ); indices are `i : Fin (finrank ℝ E)`, zero-based, so λ_0 is the first minimum and λ_{n−1} the last (n = dim E). Lean subtlety: when no dilate contains i+1 independent lattice vectors (L of rank ≤ i, or K a segment through 0 with i ≥ 1) the set is empty and Lean's `sInf ∅ = 0` gives λ_i = 0 where the mathematics has no value — as the docstring now says (#22844); every main result assumes a discrete spanning L and 0 ∈ interior K, which makes the set nonempty and the infimum a minimum (`successiveMin_isLeast`). In infinite dimension `finrank ℝ E = 0`, so there are no indices at all. Checks: the earlier probes re-compiled at 5f78b530: λ_0 = λ_1 = 1 for ℤ² and the unit cube, λ_0 = 1 < λ_1 = 10 for the box [−1,1]×[−1/10,1/10], and the junk case λ_0 = 1 > λ_1 = 0 for the segment [−1,1]×{0}; standard definition, no Mathlib copy.

Correctly defined: λ_i extended to all i : ℕ by `if hi : i < finrank ℝ E then successiveMin L K ⟨i, hi⟩ else 0` — the minimum below the dimension and 0 from it on, a bookkeeping device. Lean subtlety: the value 0 beyond the dimension is a stated convention (and agrees with the foundational minima there, `successiveMinNat_eq`); below the dimension it inherits `successiveMin`'s junk-value caveat, as the docstring now says.

Correct: for finite-dimensional E (section variable), the extension equals the foundational minimum at every i : ℕ — below the dimension by `coe_successiveMin`, and from it on both are 0 (no subspace has dimension > dim E); finite dimension is needed (earlier audit).
Correct: for i ≥ dim E the extension is 0, the stated convention (`dite_eq_right`).
Correct: for i < dim E the extension is λ_i (`dite_eq_left`).
Correct: at a `Fin` index the extension (applied to `(i : ℕ)`) is λ_i; a simp rule, by definition.

Correctly stated: if K ≤ K' (`hKK'`, inclusion of convex bodies) and 0 ∈ interior K, then λ_i(L, K') ≤ λ_i(L, K): the vectors attaining λ_i(L, K) in λ_i•K lie in λ_i•K'. The interior hypothesis sits on the smaller body, where it makes the defining set nonempty; nothing is assumed of K'.
Correctly stated: if L ≤ M (`hLM`) with L discrete and spanning and 0 ∈ interior K, then λ_i(M, K) ≤ λ_i(L, K): the vectors attaining λ_i(L, K) also lie in M; M needs no hypothesis.

Correct: for e : F ≃L[ℝ] E, the minima of the pulled-back lattice `ZLattice.comap ℝ L e` (Mathlib's pullback, as for covolumes) with respect to e⁻¹(K) equal those of L with respect to K, at indices with the same value; it is `successiveMin_map` for e⁻¹.
Correct: the unfolding equation λ_i = sInf{t ≥ 0 | t•K contains i+1 ℝ-independent vectors of L}, by `rfl` (needed because module-system definitions do not unfold downstream).

Correctly stated: `IsLeast S (successiveMin L K i)` for S exactly the set in the definition — λ_i belongs to S and is a lower bound, i.e. the infimum is attained (Evertse's minima); this is what rules out the `sInf ∅ = 0` junk under the hypotheses discrete spanning L and 0 ∈ interior K.

Correctly stated: λ_i is the least t ≥ 0 with i+1 ≤ dim span_ℝ{x ∈ L | gauge K x ≤ t} (`IsLeast`), the gauge form in Evertse's proof of Lemma 2.8 (read). Lean subtlety: at t = 0 only the zero vector has gauge 0 (0 ∈ interior K), so t = 0 never qualifies and the gauge/dilate translation for t > 0 suffices; symmetry is not assumed.

Correct: if t ≥ 0 and t•K contains i+1 independent lattice vectors (`hv`, `hvL`, `hvK`), then λ_i ≤ t, since t lies in the defining set (bounded below by 0, `csInf_le`); t ≥ 0 is part of that set and needed.

Correctly stated: for a discrete spanning L, 0 ∈ interior K and t ≥ 0, λ_i ≤ t ↔ t•K contains i+1 ℝ-independent vectors of L (`∃ v : Fin (i + 1) → E, LinearIndependent ℝ v ∧ ∀ j, v j ∈ L ∧ v j ∈ t • K`); so the infimum is a minimum, as in Evertse's definition. Correctly stated: for t ≥ 0, λ_i ≤ t ↔ i+1 ≤ finrank ℝ (span ℝ (L ∩ t•K)) — the lattice vectors in t•K span a subspace of dimension ≥ i+1 (Evertse §2.3, read); `Module.finrank` of a subspace of the finite-dimensional E is its honest dimension, so no finrank junk.

Correct: 0 ≤ λ_i with no hypotheses — an infimum of nonnegative reals is nonnegative, and the junk value `sInf ∅ = 0` is too (`Real.sInf_nonneg`).

Correctly stated: for a discrete spanning L and 0 ∈ interior K, 0 < λ_i for every i — λ_i is the gauge of a nonzero lattice vector, and nonzero vectors have positive gauge since K is bounded (Evertse, Lemma 2.8, 0 < λ_1). Lean subtlety: in the excluded degenerate cases the junk value 0 appears, so the hypotheses are needed.

Source: Evertse §2.3 (read).

Correctly stated: for dim E > 0 (`hE`, so the index 0 exists) and t ≥ 0, λ_0 ≤ t ↔ t•K contains a nonzero lattice vector — a single vector is independent iff nonzero; λ_0 is Minkowski's first minimum.

Correct: for real t and complex z, ‖exp(π i t z)‖ = exp(−π t Im z) — `‖cexp w‖ = Real.exp w.re` and Re(π i t z) = −π t Im z; with t = ‖γ+v‖² it is the size of each theta term. Its proof is now the one-line `simp [Complex.norm_exp]` (red-team chore #22907, proof only).

Correct: for t ≥ 0 (`ht`) and y ≤ Im z (`hz`), ‖exp(π i t z)‖ ≤ exp(−π y t), since −π t Im z ≤ −π t y; both hypotheses are needed (for t < 0 the inequality reverses, earlier audit), and y may be any real.

Correctly stated: θ_{γ+L} is holomorphic on the upper half-plane as a function of z ∈ ℂ: `DifferentiableOn ℂ (thetaCoset L γ ∘ ofComplex) {z : ℂ | 0 < z.im}`, i.e. complex differentiable on Im z > 0. Correctly stated: for y > 0 (`hy`), `HasSumUniformlyOn` says the partial sums of v ↦ exp(π i ‖γ+v‖² τ) converge to θ_{γ+L} uniformly on {τ : ℍ | y ≤ Im τ} — the Weierstrass M-test with the summable Gaussian majorant exp(−π y ‖γ+v‖²); y > 0 is needed (no uniform decay as Im τ → 0).

Correctly stated: for M ≤ L inside a discrete L in finite dimension and τ ∈ ℍ, `HasSum (fun y : L ⧸ M.submoduleOf L => thetaCoset M (Quotient.out y) τ) (thetaSeries L τ)` — Θ_L(τ) is the (convergent) sum over the classes y of L/M of the coset theta series θ_{x_y+M}(τ), x_y a chosen representative: the splitting into cosets of roadmap target 3B. It holds because an absolutely convergent series may be summed fibrewise (`HasSum.tsum_fiberwise`).

Correctly stated: for a discrete subgroup L of a finite-dimensional real normed space, any γ ∈ E and τ ∈ ℍ, the family v ↦ exp(π i ‖γ+v‖² τ) is (absolutely) summable over L. Checks: the earlier probes re-compiled at 5f78b530: its γ = 0 case recovers the convergence of the Jacobi theta series at L = ℤ ⊂ ℝ, where all hypotheses hold.

Correctly defined: the theta series of the translate γ + L, θ_{γ+L}(τ) = Σ_{v ∈ L} exp(π i ‖γ+v‖² τ), for arbitrary γ ∈ E (the dual-lattice condition is added only where needed), as roadmap target 3A defines it. Correct: for w ∈ L, θ_{(γ+w)+L} = θ_{γ+L} — v ↦ w + v is a bijection of L (`Equiv.addLeft`), and `tsum` is invariant under reindexing by an equivalence. Correct: the defining formula θ_{γ+L}(τ) = Σ'_{v ∈ L} exp(π i ‖γ+v‖² τ), by `rfl`; docstring added by #22907.
Correct: if γ − δ ∈ L then θ_{γ+L} = θ_{δ+L}: θ depends only on γ mod L (write γ = δ + (γ − δ)); unconditional for the same reindexing reason; the hypothesis is needed (L = 0).

Correct: θ_{−γ+L} = θ_{γ+L}, reindexing by v ↦ −v (`Equiv.neg L`) and ‖−(γ+v)‖ = ‖γ+v‖ — the symmetry asked for in roadmap target 3B; unconditional, as reindexing preserves `tsum` even without summability.
Correct: for γ ∈ L, γ + L = L and θ_{γ+L} = Θ_L (from the two previous lemmas); the hypothesis is needed (L = 0).
Correct: `thetaCoset L 0 = thetaSeries L`, since ‖0 + v‖ = ‖v‖ termwise; equality of functions ℍ → ℂ.

Correctly defined: the theta series of a lattice, Θ_L(τ) = Σ_{v ∈ L} exp(π i ‖v‖² τ) for τ in the upper half-plane, with the π (not 2π) normalisation fixed by the roadmap (ThetaSeries target 3A), so that Θ_ℤ is the Jacobi theta function Σ_n exp(π i n² τ). Checks (ab0153c6, statement unchanged): instantiated at the round sphere Sⁿ (Ric = (n−1)g, not flat) and at flat Euclidean space with the Levi-Civita connection; standard axioms.

(7.9) R_ij;^j = ½ S;i, read). Correct definition of displacement interpolation. `IsDisplacementInterpolation p μ`, for a curve of laws `μ : I → ProbabilityMeasure X` indexed by `I = [0, 1]`, holds iff there is a probability measure `η` on the path space `C(I, X)` (a dynamical transference plan, Villani Def. 7.19) such that: (i) `∀ᵐ c ∂η, c ∈ geodesicPaths X`, where `geodesicPaths X` is by definition the set of continuous paths with `dist (c s) (c t) = |s - t| * dist (c 0) (c 1)`, i.e. constant-speed minimizing geodesics, the minimizers of the action ∫|γ̇|^p (Villani Example 7.9); (ii) `η.timeMarginal t = μ t` for every t, where `timeMarginal` is by definition `η.map (fun γ ↦ γ t)`, the push-forward (e_t)_#η; (iii) `eLpNorm (fun z ↦ edist z.1 z.2) p η.endpointLaw = wassersteinEDist p (μ 0) (μ 1)`, where `endpointLaw` is `η.map (fun γ ↦ (γ 0, γ 1))`, whose marginals are μ 0 and μ 1 by (ii), so (iii) says (e_0, e_1)_#η attains the infimum over couplings that defines W_p, i.e. is an optimal coupling. This is Villani's Def. 7.20 (dynamical optimal coupling) with μ_t = (e_t)_#Π, which Villani calls a displacement interpolation in Thm 7.21. Lean subtlety: the definition itself carries no `[BorelSpace X]`, and in pinned Mathlib `Measure.map` along a map that is not a.e.-measurable is a Dirac mass, so in a non-Borel measurable space the marginals could be junk; every theorem that uses the definition (here and in Geodesic/DisplacementInterpolation.lean) assumes `[BorelSpace X]`, under which evaluation is continuous hence measurable (`ContinuousMap.measurable_eval`) and `timeMarginal` is the genuine push-forward. Optimality is stated with `eLpNorm`, so it covers p = ∞ (essential supremum) and, as the docstring says, the case W_p = ∞, where any plan of infinite cost qualifies. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: witness t ↦ δ_t on ℝ (plan = Dirac mass at the segment from 0 to 1) compiled; non-witness t ↦ δ_{t²} refuted in Lean (constant speed fails at t = 1/2); the path t ↦ t² is outside `geodesicPaths ℝ`.

Correct: for 1 < p < ∞ and a complete separable metric space X (no geodesic hypothesis), every geodesic segment γ of P_p(X) from μ to ν is a displacement interpolation: there is a probability measure η on C(I, X) concentrated on constant-speed geodesics with η_t = γ t for every t ∈ [0, 1] and optimal endpoint law. Lean ↔ maths: `h : IsGeodesicSegment γ μ ν` for `γ : ℝ → WassersteinSpace p X` says γ 0 = μ, γ 1 = ν and W_p(γ s, γ t) = |s - t| W_p(μ, ν) on [0, 1] (`dist` on `WassersteinSpace` is the real W_p); `hp1 : 1 < p` and `hp : p ≠ ∞` are 1 < p < ∞; in the conclusion `IsProbabilityMeasure η` makes η a dynamical transference plan (Villani Def. 7.19), `∀ᵐ c ∂η, c ∈ geodesicPaths X` is concentration on paths with dist (c s) (c t) = |s - t| dist (c 0) (c 1), `η.timeMarginal t = γ t` is (e_t)_#η = μ_t, and `eLpNorm (fun z ↦ edist z.1 z.2) p η.endpointLaw = wassersteinEDist p μ ν` says (e_0, e_1)_#η, whose marginals are γ 0 = μ and γ 1 = ν, attains W_p, i.e. is optimal (a compiled corollary turns this into `IsOptimalCoupling (edist ^ p.toReal) η.endpointLaw μ ν`). This is Villani Cor. 7.22, (ii) ⇒ (i) ('a geodesic in the space of laws is the law of a geodesic'), proved there for locally compact length spaces, with Remark 7.27 noting representation theorems without local compactness; the Lean proof goes through the superposition principle for absolutely continuous curves. Lean subtlety: `p.toReal` is the exponent (finite by `hp`); `dist` is `ENNReal.toReal` of W_p, harmless as laws of finite p-th moment are at finite distance; the time marginals are genuine push-forwards because evaluation is continuous; only the values of γ on [0, 1] matter. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: applied to a non-constant geodesic from δ_0 to δ_1 in P_2(ℝ) (distance 1) it yields a plan with marginals δ_0 and δ_1 (compiled); `hp1` and `hp` load-bearing; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Correct: for μ, ν ∈ P_2(E), E separable Banach, there is a coupling π with x - y square integrable under π, W_2(μ, ν)² = ∫ ‖x - y‖² dπ (so π is optimal), and the laws of (1 - t)x + ty under π forming a geodesic segment of P_2(E) from μ to ν. Checks: compiled.

Correct: for E separable Banach and an optimal coupling γ of μ, ν ∈ P_2(E) for the cost |x - y|², some geodesic segment c of P_2(E) runs from μ to ν and, for every t ∈ [0, 1], the coupling (x, (1 - t)x + ty)_#γ is optimal between μ and c t. Correct: on a separable Banach space E and for 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞, if π is a coupling of μ, ν ∈ P_p(E) with `eLpNorm (fun z ↦ edist z.1 z.2) p π = wassersteinEDist p μ ν` (optimal), then some geodesic segment γ of P_p(E) from μ to ν has γ t = law of (1 - t)x + t y under π for every t ∈ [0, 1]: the linear interpolation of an optimal plan is a Wasserstein geodesic. Lean ↔ maths: `hπ : IsCoupling π μ ν` says π has marginals μ and ν; `π.map fun z ↦ (1 - t) • z.1 + t • z.2` is the law of (1 - t)x + ty under π (a continuous map, so a genuine push-forward); `IsGeodesicSegment` is for the real W_p metric. This is Villani Cor. 7.22, (i) ⇒ (ii), with the affine segments as the random geodesics.
