Correct: if a probability plan η is concentrated on constant-speed geodesics, its laws at times 0 and 1 are μ, ν ∈ P_p(X), and its endpoint law is optimal (`hopt`), then there is a geodesic segment γ of P_p(X) from μ to ν with γ t = η_t for every t ∈ [0, 1] (Villani Cor. 7.22, (i) ⇒ (ii)). Lean ↔ maths: `IsGeodesicSegment γ μ ν` in `WassersteinSpace p X` means γ 0 = μ, γ 1 = ν and dist (γ s) (γ t) = |s - t| dist μ ν for s, t ∈ [0, 1], with `dist` the real W_p (`WassersteinSpace.dist_def`); since γ t is an element of `WassersteinSpace`, the conclusion also says every η_t has finite p-th moment. Lean subtlety: `dist` is `(wassersteinEDist …).toReal` and `ENNReal.toReal ∞ = 0`, harmless because laws of finite p-th moment are at finite W_p; values of γ outside [0, 1] are unconstrained. Checks: compiled; the hypotheses are jointly satisfiable (Dirac/segment witness).

Correct: for a Polish geodesic space X and every 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞, the Wasserstein space P_p(X) is a geodesic space. Lean ↔ maths: `WassersteinSpace p X` is by definition the type of probability measures μ with `HasFiniteMoment p μ` (∃ x, `MemLp (edist x ·) p μ`), i.e. P_p(X), and for p = ∞ the laws at essentially bounded distance from a point; its metric is `dist μ ν = (wassersteinEDist p μ ν).toReal` (`WassersteinSpace.dist_def`, checked by `rfl`), where `wassersteinEDist p μ ν` is the infimum over couplings π of `eLpNorm (fun z ↦ edist z.1 z.2) p π`, i.e. of (∫ d^p dπ)^{1/p}, or of the π-essential supremum of d at p = ∞; `IsGeodesicSpace Y` says any two points x, y are joined by some `γ : ℝ → Y` with γ 0 = x, γ 1 = y and dist (γ s) (γ t) = |s - t| dist x y on [0, 1], a constant-speed geodesic; `[Fact (1 ≤ p)]` with `p : ℝ≥0∞` is 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞; `[MetricSpace X] [CompleteSpace X] [SecondCountableTopology X] [BorelSpace X] [IsGeodesicSpace X]` is a Polish geodesic space with its Borel σ-algebra. The proof lifts an optimal coupling to a plan on geodesic paths and takes its time marginals (displacement interpolation). Source: Villani Cor. 7.22 gives this existence for p > 1 on complete separable locally compact length spaces (which are geodesic, so they satisfy the Lean hypotheses); the Lean statement also covers p = 1, p = ∞ and geodesic spaces that are not locally compact. Lean subtlety: `ENNReal.toReal ∞ = 0` could make `dist` lie, but any two laws in P_p(X) are at finite W_p (`WassersteinSpace.wassersteinEDist_ne_top`), so `dist` is the true W_p; geodesics are selected measurably only almost everywhere (Jankov–von Neumann), inside an existential, so no `Classical.choose` value enters the statement; evaluations on C(I, X) are continuous, so the time marginals are genuine push-forwards and not Mathlib's Dirac junk for non-measurable maps; a geodesic is only constrained on [0, 1]. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the instance is found for p = 1, 2, ∞ and for X = ℝ, ℝ × ℝ; the segment it provides satisfies W_p(γ s, γ t).toReal = |s - t| · W_p(μ, ν).toReal (compiled); for δ_0, δ_1 in P_2(ℝ) the distance is 1, so the geodesics are not trivially constant; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Correct: for 1 < p < ∞ and X complete separable metric, a curve `γ : ℝ → WassersteinSpace p X` is a geodesic segment from γ 0 to γ 1 iff t ↦ γ t on [0, 1] is a displacement interpolation: Villani Cor. 7.22's equivalence (i) ⇔ (ii), without local compactness. (1) Claim: the depth of a regular local ring R over itself equals its Krull dimension. (2) Lean ↔ mathematics: `IsLocalRing.depth (ModuleCat.of R R)` is Mathlib's depth of R with respect to 𝔪. It is defined by the vanishing of Ext^i(R/𝔪, R), and `IsLocalRing.depth_eq_sSup_length_isRegular` shows it is the largest length of an R-regular sequence in 𝔪. It is cast from ℕ∞ to `WithBot ℕ∞`. `ringKrullDim R` is Mathlib's Krull dimension, the supremum of lengths of chains of primes. `[IsRegularLocalRing R]` is Mathlib's regular local ring: Noetherian, local, with 𝔪 generated by dim R elements (Stacks 00KU). So the equation is depth R = dim R. The proof combines depth ≤ dimension of the support (Tau Ceti `IsLocalRing.depth_le_supportDim`) with the regular sequence of length dim R from `isRegular_of_ofList_eq_maximalIdeal`. (3) Lean subtlety: the cast ℕ∞ → WithBot ℕ∞ only makes the two sides comparable. Both are finite natural numbers here (R ≠ 0 and R is Noetherian local), so the equality is not a ⊤ or ⊥ coincidence. (4) Source and checks: Stacks Lemma 10.106.3 (00NQ). Compiled at 5f78b5307b: specialised to fields (depth 0), ℤ_p (depth 1) and ℤ_p⟦X⟧ (depth 2, with Tau Ceti's `ringKrullDim_of_isDiscreteValuationRing`). Axioms standard. No Mathlib duplicate (exact?, leansearch, git grep).

(1) Claim: every regular local ring R is Cohen–Macaulay as a module over itself, i.e. depth R = dim R. (2) Lean ↔ mathematics: the only hypothesis is Mathlib's class `IsRegularLocalRing R`, which extends `IsLocalRing R` and `IsNoetherianRing R` and adds `(maximalIdeal R).spanFinrank = ringKrullDim R`: 𝔪 is generated by dim R elements. `spanFinrank` is the least number of generators, and dim R never exceeds it, so this is Stacks Definition 10.60.10 (00KU) of a regular local ring. The conclusion `Module.IsCohenMacaulay R R` is Tau Ceti's definition (CohenMacaulay/Basic): `Subsingleton M ∨ (depth (ModuleCat.of R M) : WithBot ℕ∞) = supportDim R M`, i.e. M = 0 or depth M = dim Supp M. That is Stacks Definition 10.103.1 (00N3), 'dim(Supp M) = depth(M)'. `depth` here is Mathlib's `IsLocalRing.depth`: the least i with Ext^i(R/𝔪, M) ≠ 0. For a finite nonzero module over a Noetherian local ring, Mathlib's `IsLocalRing.depth_eq_sSup_length_isRegular` shows it equals the largest length of an M-regular sequence in 𝔪, which is the textbook depth. `supportDim R R = ringKrullDim R` (`Module.supportDim_self_eq_ringKrullDim`). So with M = R the statement reads depth R = dim R, the meaning of 'R is Cohen–Macaulay'. R is an arbitrary type in any universe, with no other hypothesis. (3) Lean subtlety: the definition has an extra disjunct `Subsingleton R` (the zero module counts as Cohen–Macaulay by convention), but a local ring is nontrivial, so that branch cannot apply. The proof indeed goes through `Module.isCohenMacaulay_iff_depth_eq`, the depth = dimension disjunct. Depth is ℕ∞-valued and is cast to `WithBot ℕ∞` to be compared with `ringKrullDim`. Both sides are finite here: R ≠ 0, so the depth is not ⊤, and a Noetherian local ring has finite dimension, which is neither ⊤ nor ⊥. So the equality is not a ⊤ = ⊤ junk coincidence. `ModuleCat.of R R` lives in R's own universe, where the `Small` instance the depth needs is automatic. (4) Source and checks: Stacks Lemma 10.106.3 (00NQ), 'In particular R is Cohen–Macaulay'. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b, compiled in Lean: the theorem applies to every field, to ℤ_p and to ℤ_p⟦X⟧ (via Tau Ceti's power-series instance), so the class has witnesses and nothing is vacuous. Through `depth_eq_ringKrullDim` their depths come out as 0, 1 and 2. The unfolded form `Subsingleton R ∨ depth = supportDim` is accepted by `exact` of the theorem. Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. No Mathlib declaration states it (exact?, leansearch, leanfinder, loogle, git grep at Mathlib 1b1ccf4b).

(1) Claim: in a regular local ring (R, 𝔪), a minimal system of generators of 𝔪 (a regular system of parameters) is an R-regular sequence, in any order. (2) Lean ↔ mathematics: `Ideal.ofList rs = maximalIdeal R` says the entries of the list rs generate 𝔪. `rs.length ≤ (maximalIdeal R).spanFinrank`, where `Submodule.spanFinrank` is the least size of a generating set, says the list is a minimal generating system. A generating list is never shorter than that (`Submodule.spanFinrank_span_list_le_length`), so its length is exactly spanFinrank 𝔪, which is dim R by the defining equation of `IsRegularLocalRing`. `RingTheory.Sequence.IsRegular R rs` is Mathlib's regular sequence: each entry is a nonzerodivisor on R modulo the earlier entries, and R/(rs) ≠ 0. This is the standard definition. A `List` is an ordered sequence, and every ordering of a minimal generating set satisfies the hypotheses, so the theorem is Stacks' 'x_1, …, x_d is a regular sequence'. (3) Lean subtlety: `spanFinrank` is defined as `(spanRank p).toNat`, which would be 0 for an ideal that is not finitely generated. That is harmless here: the class includes `IsNoetherianRing R`, so 𝔪 is finitely generated and spanFinrank 𝔪 is its true minimal number of generators. Lists with repeated entries or zeros fail one of the two hypotheses, as they should. (4) Source and checks: Stacks Lemma 10.106.3 (00NQ), first assertion. Compiled at 5f78b5307b: [p] is ℤ_p-regular and [p, X] is ℤ_p⟦X⟧-regular by this theorem. Both hypotheses are needed: [p, p] generates 𝔪 of ℤ_p but is not ℤ_p-regular (the length bound excludes it), and [0] meets the length bound but is not regular (the generation hypothesis excludes it), both compiled. Axioms standard. No Mathlib analogue (exact?, leansearch, leanfinder, loogle, git grep).

For L finite-dimensional with nondegenerate Killing form over a field of characteristic zero and any exponent monoid A, every 2-cocycle c with trivial coefficients on K[A] ⊗ L agrees with some coboundary df on all pairs (1 ⊗ x, a), so c − df vanishes on constant loops. For L finite-dimensional with nondegenerate Killing form over a field of characteristic zero (L semisimple), every 2-cocycle with trivial coefficients on L[t,t⁻¹] is the residue cocycle of some invariant symmetric form plus a coboundary: H² is covered by residue classes. Lean ↔ mathematics: `loopAlgebra K ℤ L` is Mathlib's abbreviation for `AddMonoidAlgebra K ℤ ⊗[K] L`, i.e. K[t,t⁻¹] ⊗ L with the base-changed bracket (finitely supported Laurent polynomials; the mode t^m ⊗ x is `AddMonoidAlgebra.single m 1 ⊗ₜ x`); `TrivialLieModule K _ K` is K with zero action, so the cochains have trivial coefficients; `twoCochain` is Mathlib's submodule of bilinear maps with c(u,u) = 0, `twoCocycle` is the kernel of Mathlib's Chevalley–Eilenberg `d₂₃` (for trivial coefficients the identity c([x,y],z) − c([x,z],y) + c([y,z],x) = 0), and `d₁₂ f (u,v) = ⁅u, f v⁆ − ⁅v, f u⁆ − f ⁅u, v⁆`, which is −f([u,v]) here, so `LinearMap.range (d₁₂ …)` is the space B² of coboundaries; `twoCochainOfBilinear K ℤ L Ψ _` is Mathlib's residue cochain (u,v) ↦ Σ_a a·Ψ(u_{−a}, v_a), whose value on (t^m⊗x, t^n⊗y) is n·Ψ(x,y) when m+n = 0 and 0 otherwise (`residuePairing_single_tmul`), i.e. Res(f dg)·Ψ(x,y); the conclusion `∃ Ψ (_ : Ψ.lieInvariant L) (hΨs : Ψ.IsSymm) f, ↑c = twoCochainOfBilinear K ℤ L Ψ hΨs + d₁₂ K _ _ f` is c = c_Ψ + df with Ψ invariant (Mathlib's Ψ(⁅x,y⁆,z) = −Ψ(y,⁅x,z⁆)) and symmetric and f a linear functional on the loop algebra. Lean subtlety: `c` is a bundled cocycle and `↑c` its underlying cochain; Ψ is not claimed unique (that is the injectivity in `smul_twoCochainOfBilinear_mem_range_d₁₂_iff`); `TrivialLieModule K _ K` is a type synonym of K; no junk values. Proof: normalise c on constant loops (`exists_apply_one_tmul_eq_d₁₂_apply`, Whitehead's first lemma mode by mode), then `exists_eq_twoCocycleOfBilinear_iff` with perfectness from IsKilling. Checked against Mathlib's definitions in Mathlib/Algebra/Lie/Loop.lean, Cochain.lean, InvariantForm.lean and Killing.lean, and the TauCetiRoadmap AffineLieAlgebras A1 text (mode recurrence reduces polynomial values to the residue class; nonzero class detection and one-dimensionality for simple 𝔤). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: hypotheses all used (Whitehead, perfectness); axioms standard.

`residuePairing R A L Φ (1 ⊗ₜ x) a = 0`: the residue pairing vanishes when its first argument is the constant loop t⁰ ⊗ x (`1 = single 0 1`), since only the a = 0 term survives and it carries the factor 0 · Φ.

The residue pairing on modes: `residuePairing R A L Φ (single m 1 ⊗ₜ x) (single n 1 ⊗ₜ y) = if m + n = 0 then n • Φ x y else 0`, i.e. Res(t^m d t^n)·Φ(x,y) = n·Φ(x,y)·δ_{m+n,0}, read off Mathlib's definition Σ_a a·Φ(f_{−a}, g_a) (Loop.lean); `n • ·` is the A-action on R (for A = ℤ, multiplication by the integer n).
`residuePairing R A L (t • Φ) = t • residuePairing R A L Φ`: the residue pairing is linear in the form, immediate from the defining sum Σ_a a·Φ(f_{−a}, g_a); a simp lemma in normal form.

For perfect L (`derivedSeries R L 1 = ⊤`), each mode t^{a+b} ⊗ x lies in the R-span of the brackets [t^a ⊗ y, t^b ⊗ z] = t^{a+b} ⊗ [y,z]: the base-changed perfectness `ExtendScalars.mul_tmul_mem_span_lie` with t^a·t^b = t^{a+b} (`single_mul_single`).

The argument: on (x_m, y_{−m}) the cochain is −m·Ψ(x,y) while every coboundary is −f([x,y]_0), independent of m. Lean subtlety: `μ⁻¹` uses `0⁻¹ = 0`, and the hypothesis `hμ : μ ≠ 0` is genuinely needed: at μ = 0 the right side would read `evalAt 0 = constantCoeff = 1 = 0`, false, whereas on an infinite I the point 0 lies in the spectrum of every row-compact u (compiled: the identity is not row compact and row-compact maps form an ideal), so the statement without `hμ` is false (compiled counterexample u = 0 on `C₀(ℕ, K)`); nothing is claimed about 0, as the docstring says; `charCoeff` and `evalAt` are `tsum`s that would be 0 on a non-summable family, but for row-compact u the principal minors of each size are summable (`Matrix.summable_principalMinor` with r = `u.rowNorm`, compiled) and H_u is entire (`IsRowCompact.isEntire_charPowerSeries`), so `evalAt` is a genuinely convergent sum at every point (`IsEntire.hasSum_evalAt`, compiled) and its zeros are true zeros; `[DecidableEq I]` only serves to form the minors. IHÉS 12 (1962), §7 Prop. 11 (p. 80, read in the Numdam scan): for a ∈ K, 1 − au is invertible in L(E, E) iff H(a) ≠ 0; since μ − u = μ(1 − μ⁻¹u) this is the Lean statement (the result is in §7, after the determinant of §5 and resolvent of §6). Correctly stated: for q ≠ 0, evaluating Laurent polynomials at K is injective, so K and K⁻¹ satisfy no Laurent-polynomial relation and ℂ[T, T⁻¹] ≅ U⁰ = ℂ[K, K⁻¹]. Correctly stated: for q ≠ 0 the lowering generator F of U_q(sl₂) is transcendental over ℂ, i.e. no nonzero complex polynomial vanishes at F, so ℂ[X] ≅ U⁻ = ℂ[F]. Correctly stated: for every nonzero complex q, multiplication p ⊗ r ⊗ s ↦ p(F)·r(K)·s(E) is a ℂ-linear isomorphism ℂ[X] ⊗ ℂ[T, T⁻¹] ⊗ ℂ[X] ≅ U_q(sl₂), i.e. U⁻ ⊗ U⁰ ⊗ U⁺ ≅ U. Lean ↔ mathematics: `UqSl2 q` is by definition `RingQuot (UqSl2.Rel q)` of the free complex algebra on E, F, K, K⁻¹ with relations KK⁻¹ = K⁻¹K = 1, KE = q²EK, KF = q⁻²FK and EF − FE = (q − q⁻¹)⁻¹ • (K − K⁻¹), which is exactly the presentation of U_q(sl₂) over ℂ in Baseilhac, Quantum coadjoint action and the 6j-symbols of U_q sl_2 (arXiv:1101.3440), Def. 2.1 and Thm 2.4(1) (KEK⁻¹ = q²E, KFK⁻¹ = q⁻²F, [E,F] = (K − K⁻¹)/(q − q⁻¹)). `ℂ[X]` is `Polynomial ℂ` and `ℂ[T;T⁻¹]` is `LaurentPolynomial ℂ`; `⊗[ℂ]` is the tensor product over ℂ (right-bracketed) and `≃ₗ[ℂ]` a ℂ-linear isomorphism — rightly not an algebra isomorphism, since the factors of a tensor-product algebra commute while F, K, E do not. The equivalence is `LinearEquiv.ofBijective` of that map, bijective because it sends the tensor basis X^a ⊗ T^b ⊗ X^c to the PBW vector `pbwBasis q (a, b, c)` = F^a K^b E^c; this makes the statement equivalent to the PBW theorem (Thm 2.4(1) of the source: the F^t K^s E^r, t, r ∈ ℕ, s ∈ ℤ, are a basis), and `triangularEquiv_symm_pbwBasis` checks the inverse on that basis. The base field is ℂ only, as the Quantum Groups roadmap Q8 specifies. Lean subtlety: the presentation divides by q − q⁻¹ through Lean's total inverse, so at q = ±1 the relation silently becomes EF = FE ((q − q⁻¹)⁻¹ = 0⁻¹ = 0) and q² = 1 makes K commute with E and F; the red team compiled that every two elements of `UqSl2 1` and of `UqSl2 (-1)` commute, i.e. there `UqSl2 q` is the commutative ℂ[E, F, K^{±1}], not a quantum group (the source requires q ∉ {−1, 0, 1}). Also `kUnit q ^ b` with b : ℤ is a power in the unit group (UqSl2 q)ˣ, so negative b gives powers of K⁻¹, not a junk inverse. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: compiled witnesses `triangularEquiv q (X ⊗ₜ (T 1 ⊗ₜ X)) = f q * k q * e q` (by simp), `(triangularEquiv q).symm (e q * f q) = X ⊗ₜ (1 ⊗ₜ X) + (q − q⁻¹)⁻¹ • (1 ⊗ₜ (T 1 ⊗ₜ 1) − 1 ⊗ₜ (T (-1) ⊗ₜ 1))` (the commutator's U⁰ term), and `e q * f q ≠ f q * e q` when q² ≠ 1 (so the target is genuinely noncommutative generically); `triangularEquiv 1` elaborates; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; the file elaborates in about 1.7 s.

Correctly stated: for a reductive group G over any field k with solvable k̄-points, the characters of G_k̄ separate points scheme-theoretically: the common kernel of all characters of G_k̄ is the trivial subgroup. Lean ↔ mathematics: `G` (bound by `let`) is `FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat.baseChange (K := AlgebraicClosure k) H`, i.e. O(G_k̄) = k̄ ⊗_k O(G), and the hypotheses are those of `torus_of_geometricallySolvable`. `_root_.CommHopfAlgCat.characterKernelIdeal G.obj` is by definition (`characterKernelIdeal_def`) `kernelHopfIdeal` of the canonical bialgebra map `MonoidAlgebra.liftGroupLikeBialgHom : k̄[X] → O(G_k̄)` from the group algebra of the group-like elements X, which are the characters G_k̄ → G_m; `kernelHopfIdeal f` is the image of the augmentation ideal of k̄[X] (`kernelHopfIdeal_def`), the ideal generated by the χ − 1, cutting out the intersection of the kernels of all characters (`characterKernelIdeal_toIdeal_le_ker_iff`: a point lies in it iff every character takes the value 1 there). `HopfIdeal.augmentation k̄ G` is the kernel of the counit, the ideal of the identity subgroup. So the equation says ⋂_χ ker χ = {e} as closed subgroup schemes, not only on k̄-points. Lean subtlety: (i) contravariance: a larger Hopf ideal is a smaller subgroup and the augmentation ideal is the largest Hopf ideal (`HopfIdeal.le_augmentation`), so equality with it means the trivial subgroup, not the whole group (that would be the zero ideal); (ii) the `let` in the statement is only an abbreviation: rewriting and simp with the lemma work (checked). The proof: G is a torus, so G_k̄ is split and O(G_k̄) is spanned by its group-like elements (diagonalizable, Milne 12.7–12.8); hence evaluation from k̄[X] is surjective and the image of its augmentation ideal is the augmentation ideal. Source: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Groups (2017), Definition 12.7, Theorem 12.8, Theorem 20.1(c). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms standard; both hypotheses load-bearing; the statement is true and holds for every torus by the same proof (compiled; recorded as a generality finding), and it would fail without solvability (for GL₂, whose characters are the powers of det, the common kernel is SL₂).

Correctly stated: a reductive group over any field k whose k̄-points form a solvable group is linearly reductive (every finite-dimensional representation is semisimple), in every characteristic. Lean ↔ mathematics: the hypotheses `reductiveCommHopfAlgProperty k H` and `geometricallySolvablePointsCommHopfAlgProperty k H.obj` are those of `torus_of_geometricallySolvable` (G smooth, geometrically connected, R_u(G_k̄) = e; G(k̄) solvable as an abstract group under the convolution product). The conclusion `linearlyReductiveCommHopfAlgProperty k H.obj` is by definition `Coalgebra.IsLinearlyReductive k H`: every comodule V over O(G) with `Module.Finite k V`, i.e. every finite-dimensional representation of G, is `Comodule.IsCompletelyReducible`, i.e. semisimple, which is Milne's Definition 12.52. The proof is G is a torus (`torus_of_geometricallySolvable`) and tori, being of multiplicative type, are linearly reductive (`torusCommHopfAlgProperty.linearlyReductive`; Milne 12.54). Lean subtlety: `IsLinearlyReductive` tests only comodules whose carrier lies in k's universe; harmless, since every finite-dimensional representation is isomorphic to one on kⁿ. This is not the characteristic-p falsehood 'reductive implies linearly reductive': the solvability hypothesis is essential (GL₂ in characteristic 2 is reductive but not linearly reductive, `GeneralLinear.not_linearlyReductiveCommHopfAlgProperty_coordinateHopfAlgebra`, compiled alongside). Source: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Groups (2017), Definition 12.52, Proposition 12.54, Theorem 20.1(c). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms standard; the one-line derivation compiles in a downstream module; hypotheses consistent (every torus satisfies both, compiled).

Correctly stated: a reductive group G over any field k (any characteristic, perfect or not) whose group of k̄-points is solvable is a torus. Lean ↔ mathematics: `H : FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat k` is the coordinate ring O(G) of an affine algebraic group of finite type over k, and `FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat.baseChange (K := AlgebraicClosure k) H` is k̄ ⊗_k O(G) = O(G_k̄), with k̄ Mathlib's `AlgebraicClosure k`. `reductiveCommHopfAlgProperty k H` unfolds (`reductiveCommHopfAlgProperty_iff`) to `Algebra.Smooth k H` (G smooth), `geometricallyConnectedCommHopfAlgProperty k H.obj` (Spec(O(G) ⊗_k K) connected for every field extension K/k), and: every Hopf ideal I of O(G_k̄) that is normal (`I.IsNormal`: the conjugation coaction maps I into O(G) ⊗ I, i.e. V(I) is a normal closed subgroup), whose quotient is geometrically connected and satisfies `smoothUnipotentCommHopfAlgProperty` (smooth, every geometric point acting unipotently on every finite-dimensional comodule) equals `HopfIdeal.augmentation` (the kernel of the counit, the ideal of {e}); since R_u(G_k̄) is the largest connected normal smooth unipotent subgroup, this is exactly Milne's condition R_u(G_k̄) = e. `geometricallySolvablePointsCommHopfAlgProperty k H.obj` is by definition `Group.IsSolvable (WithConv (H →ₐ[k] AlgebraicClosure k))`: the k-algebra maps O(G) → k̄ are G(k̄), `WithConv` gives them the convolution product (the group law of G), and `IsSolvable` is Mathlib's abstract solvability; for smooth connected G this is solvability of the algebraic group (Milne 16.34 (c)⇔(d) over k̄, 6.31 for base change). The conclusion `torusCommHopfAlgProperty k H` unfolds (`torusCommHopfAlgProperty_iff`) to: for some n there is an isomorphism of Hopf k̄-algebras from `DiagonalizableGroup.coordinateRing k̄ (SplitTorus.characterGroup (ULift (Fin n)))`, the group algebra k̄[Multiplicative (Fin n →₀ ℤ)] = k̄[t₁^±1,…,t_n^±1] with group-like t_i, i.e. O(G_m^n), to O(G_k̄); that is G_k̄ ≅ G_m^n, Milne's Definition 12.14 of a torus, with no claim that G splits over k. Lean subtlety: (i) solvability is asserted only for the abstract group of k̄-points, which cannot see nilpotent structure; harmless because reductivity includes smoothness; (ii) `FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat.{u, u} k` puts O(G) in k's universe, harmless since every finite-type k-algebra is a quotient of a polynomial ring in that universe; (iii) the unipotence test on subgroups of G_k̄ uses points with values in `AlgebraicClosure (AlgebraicClosure k)`, an algebraic closure of k̄, hence isomorphic to k̄; (iv) `ULift (Fin n)` is universe bookkeeping for ℤⁿ, and n = 0 is the trivial group; no division, cardinality or junk value occurs. Over imperfect fields the statement is right as written because reductivity is tested on G_k̄, which excludes pseudo-reductive non-reductive groups (Milne 6.48). Source: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Groups (2017), 6.46 (reductive means R_u(G_{k^a}) = e), Definition 12.14 (torus), Theorem 20.1(b),(c) (over any field, a connected group variety is solvable iff of semisimple rank 0, and reductive of semisimple rank 0 iff a torus). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; both hypotheses load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses) and mathematically needed, compiled: GL₂ in characteristic 2 is reductive but not a torus (tori are linearly reductive, GL₂ there is not), so the theorem forces its k̄-points to be non-solvable, and 𝔾ₐ has commutative points but is not a torus, so it is not reductive; compiled the converse (every torus, split or not, is reductive with solvable geometric points), so the hypotheses are satisfiable and the theorem is one half of an iff; specialised to the split rank-3 torus; pinned Mathlib has no reductive groups; the file elaborates in well under 1 s.

Defines the Bochner average A(y) = |G|⁻¹ Σ_{g∈G} ρ(g)⁻¹ c(g·y) of a map c : X → F, for a finite group G acting on a set X and a continuous linear representation ρ of G on a topological 𝕜-module F. Lean ↔ maths: the body is `⅟(Fintype.card G : 𝕜) • ∑ g : G, ρ g⁻¹ (c (g • y))`; `Fintype.card G` is |G| cast into 𝕜, `⅟` is the inverse supplied by the hypothesis `[Invertible (Fintype.card G : 𝕜)]` (|G| invertible in the scalars), `ρ g⁻¹` is the continuous linear map ρ(g⁻¹) = ρ(g)⁻¹ because a `ContRepresentation` is a monoid hom G → (F →L[𝕜] F), and `g • y` is the given action on X; this is exactly the formula A(y) = |G|⁻¹ Σ_g L_g⁻¹ c(g·y) of TauCetiRoadmap Orbifolds O2.1 (dd4b28f1) with L = ρ, and it is the nonlinear analogue of Maschke averaging. Lean subtlety: `⅟` is the Invertible-instance inverse, not `⁻¹`, so there is no 0⁻¹ = 0 junk: when the characteristic of 𝕜 divides |G| no instance exists and the definition does not apply at all; over ℝ or ℂ the instance is found automatically (`invertibleOfPos`). Checks (Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): its equivariance (`bochnerAverage_smul`) and fixed-point value (`bochnerAverage_apply_of_forall_smul_eq`) are proved; a compiled probe with ℤˣ = {±1} acting on ℝ by multiplication, χ = the identity chart and σ = `TauCeti.isotropyRepresentation` runs it through `exists_equivariant_chart`; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate (Mathlib's `Representation.averageMap` and `LinearMap.equivariantProjection` average linear maps only).

At a common fixed point x (`hx : ∀ g, g • x = x`), A(x) = |G|⁻¹ Σ_g ρ(g) c(x) = `ρ.toRepresentation.averageMap (c x)`: Mathlib's `Representation.averageMap` is the averaging projection onto the invariants, equal to `⅟|G| • ∑ g, ρ g` (Tau Ceti's `Representation.averageMap_apply`), `ρ.toRepresentation` is ρ viewed as a plain linear representation, and the sum of ρ(g⁻¹) is reindexed by g ↦ g⁻¹. It gives e(x) = 0 in `exists_equivariant_chart`, where c = χ − χ x vanishes at x.

`bochnerAverage ρ c ∘ f = fun w => ⅟(Fintype.card G : 𝕜) • ∑ g, ρ g⁻¹ (c (g • f w))`: the Bochner average pulled back along f : Y → X, written as an explicit function of w ∈ Y (the pointwise unfolding, used to differentiate A ∘ χ.symm).

`bochnerAverage ρ c y = ⅟(Fintype.card G : 𝕜) • ∑ g, ρ g⁻¹ (c (g • y))`: the defining equation A(y) = |G|⁻¹ Σ_g ρ(g)⁻¹ c(g·y) of the Bochner average, stated as a lemma because the module system does not expose the definition's body; proved by unfolding (`rw [bochnerAverage]`).

If c is already equivariant, `hc : ∀ g y, c (g • y) = ρ g (c y)`, then `bochnerAverage ρ c = c` as functions X → F: averaging fixes equivariant maps, since each summand ρ(g)⁻¹ c(g·y) equals c(y) and the average of |G| copies of a vector is that vector (`Fintype.invOf_card_smul_sum_const`).

Equivariance of the Bochner average: `bochnerAverage ρ c (h • y) = ρ h (bochnerAverage ρ c y)`, i.e. A(h·y) = ρ(h)A(y) for every h ∈ G and y ∈ X, with no hypothesis on c (no continuity or differentiability). The proof reindexes the sum by g ↦ gh (`Equiv.mulRight h`), the computation 'A(h·y) = L_h A(y)' of TauCetiRoadmap Orbifolds O2.1 (dd4b28f1). Lean subtlety: none beyond `⅟|G|` being a genuine inverse (Invertible instance).

If each w ↦ c(g·f(w)) is C^n at z (`ContDiffAt 𝕜 n`, with n : WithTop ℕ∞ covering finite n, ∞ and analytic ω), then so is A ∘ f: finite sums, continuous linear maps and constant scalings preserve C^n.
If each w ↦ c(g·f(w)) is C^n on s ⊆ E (`ContDiffOn 𝕜 n _ s`), then so is A ∘ f: finite sums, continuous linear maps and constant scalings preserve C^n on a set.

If each w ↦ c(g·f(w)) is continuous on s ⊆ Y, then A ∘ f is continuous on s (`ContinuousOn (bochnerAverage ρ c ∘ f) s`): a constant multiple (`[ContinuousConstSMul 𝕜 F]`) of a finite sum of the continuous linear maps ρ(g⁻¹) applied to continuous functions.
If each w ↦ c(g·f(w)) is continuous on Y, then A ∘ f is continuous: the s = univ case of `continuousOn_bochnerAverage_comp`.

The same as `hasStrictFDerivAt_bochnerAverage_comp` for ordinary Fréchet derivatives: if each w ↦ c(g·f(w)) has derivative D g at z then A ∘ f has derivative |G|⁻¹ Σ_g ρ(g⁻¹) ∘ D g there (`HasFDerivAt` is a predicate, no fderiv junk).
The `HasFDerivAt` version: if each w ↦ c(g·f(w)) has derivative ρ(g) ∘ D₀ at z, then A ∘ f has derivative D₀ at z, since |G|⁻¹ Σ_g ρ(g⁻¹)ρ(g)D₀ = D₀.

If each w ↦ c(g·f(w)) has strict Fréchet derivative D g at z (`HasStrictFDerivAt _ (D g) z`), then A ∘ f has strict derivative |G|⁻¹ Σ_g ρ(g⁻¹) ∘ D g at z, written `⅟(Fintype.card G : 𝕜) • ∑ g, (ρ g⁻¹).comp (D g)` — the sum rule and the chain rule for the continuous linear maps ρ(g⁻¹). Lean subtlety: `HasStrictFDerivAt` is a genuine predicate (no `fderiv` = 0 junk); X needs no topology since only the composites are differentiated.

If the strict derivative of each w ↦ c(g·f(w)) at z is ρ(g) ∘ D₀ (`(ρ g).comp D₀`) for one fixed D₀, then A ∘ f has strict derivative D₀ at z, because |G|⁻¹ Σ_g ρ(g⁻¹)ρ(g)D₀ = D₀. With D₀ = id and ρ the derivative representation this is the step 'dA_x = id' of TauCetiRoadmap Orbifolds O2.1 (dd4b28f1); it is used in `exists_equivariant_chart` and in Manifold/GroupAction/Linearization.lean.

On its domain the Bochner chart is the Bochner average: given an open partial homeomorphism Θ : E → F that agrees with A ∘ χ⁻¹ on its source (`hΘ : EqOn Θ (ρ.bochnerAverage c ∘ χ.symm) Θ.source`) and y in the source of `(χ.trans Θ).restrInvariant G` — Θ ∘ χ restricted to the largest G-invariant open part of its domain, source ∩ ⋂_g (g•·)⁻¹(source) — one has `(χ.trans Θ).restrInvariant G y = ρ.bochnerAverage c y`, as Θ(χ y) = A(χ⁻¹(χ y)) = A(y). Lean subtlety: the coercion of an open partial homeomorphism is a total function with junk values off its source; the statement evaluates it only at y in the source.

Claim: the Bochner chart intertwines the action with ρ, e(g·y) = ρ(g)e(y), for every g ∈ G and every y in its domain. Lean ↔ maths: e is `(χ.trans Θ).restrInvariant G`, the composite Θ ∘ χ restricted by `OpenPartialHomeomorph.restrInvariant` to the largest G-invariant open subset of its domain (source ∩ ⋂_g (g•·)⁻¹ source); `hΘ : EqOn Θ (ρ.bochnerAverage c ∘ χ.symm) Θ.source` says Θ is a chart of the Bochner average A(y) = |G|⁻¹ Σ_g ρ(g)⁻¹ c(g·y) read in the coordinates of χ (in the application Θ is the inverse-function-theorem chart of A ∘ χ⁻¹); `hy` puts y in the invariant domain, so g·y is there too (`smul_mem_restrInvariant_source`); the conclusion `e (g • y) = ρ g (e y)` is the identity d_y h ∘ φ = φ ∘ h of Isaev, Proper group actions in complex geometry, arXiv:1501.07656, Thm 3.1 (Bochner's linearization), holding on one G-invariant neighbourhood for all g at once. This lemma is the equivariance step, not the whole theorem: the chart's existence with x in its domain, e(x) = 0 and derivative the identity is `OpenPartialHomeomorph.exists_equivariant_chart`, and 'g acts trivially near x iff its derivative is 1' is `OpenPartialHomeomorph.map_eq_one_iff_mem_germKernel`. Lean subtlety: the chart's coercion is total with junk values off its source, and the statement would be vacuous for an empty source — but both sides are evaluated only inside the invariant source, and `exists_equivariant_chart` shows the fixed point lies in it; `⅟|G|` in A is the Invertible-instance inverse (no 0⁻¹ junk; |G| must be invertible in 𝕜, automatic over ℝ and ℂ). Source and checks (Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): TauCetiRoadmap Orbifolds O2.1 (dd4b28f1) prescribes this construction (A(h·y) = L_h A(y), then the inverse function theorem and an invariant shrink); a compiled probe with ℤˣ = {±1} acting on ℝ by multiplication, χ = the identity chart and σ = `TauCeti.isotropyRepresentation` obtains through `exists_equivariant_chart` a chart with e(−y) = −e(y); the four equivariance lemmas also compile with no norm or field structure (RT-20261104-0ec3d4, MINOR generality); axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

The inverse of the Bochner chart intertwines ρ with the action: e⁻¹(ρ(g)w) = g·e⁻¹(w) for w in the target (`((χ.trans Θ).restrInvariant G).symm (ρ g w) = g • ((χ.trans Θ).restrInvariant G).symm w`). Lean subtlety: `.symm` is a total function with junk values off the target; both w and ρ(g)w lie in the target (`map_mem_bochnerChart_target`), so no junk is used.

Smoothness of the inverse chart: at w in the target of the Bochner chart e, if A ∘ χ⁻¹ is C^n and has an invertible derivative D' (`HasFDerivAt … (D' : E →L[𝕜] F)` with D' : E ≃L[𝕜] F) at the corresponding point χ(e⁻¹ w), then χ ∘ e⁻¹ (the inverse read in χ-coordinates) is C^n at w — Mathlib's inverse-function-theorem lemma `OpenPartialHomeomorph.contDiffAt_symm` applied to χ⁻¹ followed by e, which agrees with A ∘ χ⁻¹ near χ(e⁻¹ w). Lean subtlety: no `fderiv` junk is involved (derivatives are hypotheses given as `HasFDerivAt`); `[CompleteSpace E]` is the inverse-function-theorem hypothesis.

If each w ↦ c(g·χ⁻¹(w)) is C^n on s ⊆ E, then the Bochner chart read in χ-coordinates, e ∘ χ⁻¹, is C^n on s ∩ (χ⁻¹)⁻¹(domain of e): there it coincides with A ∘ χ⁻¹ (`bochnerChart_apply`), which is C^n by `contDiffOn_bochnerAverage_comp`. Lean subtlety: χ.symm is a total function; the preimage condition keeps exactly the points it sends into the chart's domain, where `bochnerChart_apply` applies whatever value χ.symm takes.

Claim: Bochner linearization for a finite group G of order invertible in 𝕜 — near a common fixed point x there is a chart e with x in its domain, e(x) = 0, G-invariant domain inside that of χ, derivative the identity at x in χ-coordinates, and e(g·y) = σ(g)e(y). Lean ↔ maths: `χ : OpenPartialHomeomorph X E` is a chart (homeomorphism between open sets) of X with values in a complete normed space E (`[CompleteSpace E]`, needed by the inverse function theorem); `hxχ` and `hx` say x lies in the chart and is fixed by all of G; `hσ : ∀ g, HasStrictFDerivAt (χ ∘ (g • ·) ∘ χ.symm) (σ g) (χ x)` says each g, read in χ-coordinates, is strictly differentiable at the fixed point with derivative σ(g) — strict derivatives are unique, so σ is forced to be the derivative representation, and `TauCeti.isotropyRepresentation` with `hasStrictFDerivAt_conj_smul_isotropyRepresentation` builds it from the differentiability alone, so asking for σ as a representation moves no content into the hypotheses; in the conclusion `∀ g, ∀ y ∈ e.source, g • y ∈ e.source ∧ e (g • y) = σ g (e y)` is one G-invariant domain on which e ∘ g = σ(g) ∘ e, the identity d_y h ∘ φ = φ ∘ h of Isaev, Proper group actions in complex geometry, arXiv:1501.07656, Thm 3.1 (Bochner's linearization) for a finite group, and `HasStrictFDerivAt (e ∘ χ.symm) (ContinuousLinearMap.id 𝕜 E) (χ x)` says e is tangent to χ at x. Scope: the hypotheses are weaker than the textbook's (strict differentiability at x only, implied by C¹ over ℝ or ℂ) and so is the conclusion — e is a homeomorphism with derivative the identity at x, not claimed to be a diffeomorphism; the C^n chart is `TauCeti.exists_equivariant_contMDiff_chart` (Manifold/GroupAction/Linearization.lean), with this file's `contDiffOn_bochnerChart_comp_symm` and `contDiffAt_comp_bochnerChart_symm`; no faithfulness is assumed. Lean subtlety: `⅟|G|` comes from `[Invertible (Fintype.card G : 𝕜)]` (automatic over ℝ, ℂ; a real restriction in characteristic p dividing |G|), not from `⁻¹`; the coercions of χ, χ.symm and e are total functions with junk values off their sources and targets, but e is evaluated only on its source and the derivative only near χ x, inside the open χ.target; no `fderiv` junk (`HasStrictFDerivAt` is a predicate). Source and checks (Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): TauCetiRoadmap Orbifolds O2.1 (dd4b28f1) prescribes exactly this construction (c = χ − χ x, A = |G|⁻¹ Σ L_g⁻¹ c(g·), inverse function theorem, invariant shrink); a compiled probe with ℤˣ = {±1} acting on ℝ by multiplication, χ = the identity chart and σ = `TauCeti.isotropyRepresentation` yields e with 0 ∈ e.source, e 0 = 0 and e(−y) = −e(y); lean_minimal_hypotheses finds χ, hxχ, hx, σ, hσ all load-bearing; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Claim: over ℝ in finite dimensions, a chart e centred at x (e(x) = 0) with G-invariant domain in which G acts linearly through σ can be shrunk, inside any neighbourhood s of x, to a chart e' with the same underlying map onto an invariant ball {v | Σ_g ‖σ(g)v‖² < c}, c > 0, with G-invariant preconnected domain. Lean ↔ maths: `σ : Representation ℝ G E` is a linear representation (automatically continuous as `[FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`); `he` is equivariance on the invariant domain and `hs : s ∈ 𝓝 x` the neighbourhood; the conclusion gives `0 < c`, `x ∈ e'.source`, `⇑e' = ⇑e` (so e' is a restriction of e), `e'.source ⊆ e.source ∩ s`, `e'.target = σ.sumOfConjugatesInnerSublevel c` — by definition {v | sumOfConjugatesForm σ ⟪·,·⟫ v v < c}, and that form on the diagonal is Σ_g ‖σ g v‖² (`sumOfConjugatesForm_inner_apply_self`), an open convex σ-invariant neighbourhood of 0 —, `IsPreconnected e'.source`, and equivariance on e'.source. This is the step 'average an inner product to obtain an invariant ball and the equivariant chart' of TauCetiRoadmap Orbifolds O2.1 (dd4b28f1). Lean subtlety: the sublevel set is empty for c ≤ 0, excluded by `0 < c`; chart coercions are total but are used only on their sources and targets. Checks (Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): lean_minimal_hypotheses finds e, σ, hxe, hex, he, hs all load-bearing; consumed by Manifold/GroupAction/GermKernel.lean and Linearization.lean; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

If A ∘ χ⁻¹ has an invertible strict derivative D at z ∈ χ.target (`hA`, with D : E ≃L[𝕜] F a continuous linear isomorphism), then the Bochner chart built from the inverse-function-theorem chart `hA.toOpenPartialHomeomorph`, read in χ-coordinates (e ∘ χ⁻¹), has the same strict derivative D at z: near z it agrees with A ∘ χ⁻¹, because χ ∘ χ⁻¹ = id near z (`χ.eventually_right_inverse`) and `restrInvariant` does not change the underlying function. Lean subtlety: χ.symm is total with junk values off χ.target, but strict differentiability only sees a neighbourhood of z inside the open target; `[CompleteSpace E]` is the inverse-function-theorem hypothesis.

Claim: in the setting of `exists_equivariant_chart`, an element g of G acts as the identity on some neighbourhood of the fixed point x if and only if its derivative σ(g) there, in χ-coordinates, is the identity — both directions are proved. Lean ↔ maths: `σ g = 1` is equality with the identity in `E →L[𝕜] E`; `TauCeti.MulAction.germKernel G x` is the subgroup {g | ∀ᶠ y in 𝓝 x, g • y = y} (`mem_germKernel` is Iff.rfl), i.e. g fixes every point of some neighbourhood of x, which may depend on g — exactly 'g acts trivially near x'; the hypotheses are those of `exists_equivariant_chart`, and σ is forced to be the derivative representation by uniqueness of strict derivatives. The forward direction uses the equivariant chart (e(g·y) = σ(g)e(y) = e(y) and e is injective on its source); the converse holds because χ ∘ g ∘ χ⁻¹ = id near χ x, so its derivative is 1. This is the statement 'the derivative representation detects the ineffective kernel' of TauCetiRoadmap Orbifolds O2.1 (dd4b28f1). Lean subtlety: the forward direction genuinely needs `[Invertible (Fintype.card G : 𝕜)]` (over 𝔽_p((t)), z ↦ z/(1+z) on the open unit ball generates a ℤ/p-action with derivative 1 at 0 that is not the identity near 0) and uses `[CompleteSpace E]` for the inverse function theorem; no `fderiv` junk (σ g is a strict derivative by hypothesis). Checks (Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): a compiled probe with ℤˣ = {±1} acting on ℝ by multiplication, χ = the identity chart and σ = `TauCeti.isotropyRepresentation` derives (−1) ∉ germKernel ℤˣ 0 from σ(−1) = −1 ≠ 1; all explicit hypotheses load-bearing; consumers (GroupAction/FaceKernel.lean, Manifold/GroupAction GermKernel, Linearization, TangentRepresentation) use it as the iff; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

The target of the Bochner chart is ρ-invariant: w in the target of `(χ.trans Θ).restrInvariant G` implies `ρ g w` is in it, since w = e(y) for y in the G-invariant source and ρ(g)e(y) = e(g·y) (`bochnerChart_smul`).

If each conjugated map χ ∘ (g • ·) ∘ χ⁻¹ has some strict derivative L g at χ x, then the isotropy representation's value at g is that strict derivative: `HasStrictFDerivAt (χ ∘ (g • ·) ∘ χ.symm) (isotropyRepresentation … g) (χ x)`, since fderiv equals the (unique) derivative L g. It supplies the hypothesis hσ of `exists_equivariant_chart` with σ = `TauCeti.isotropyRepresentation`, as that theorem's docstring says.

Defines the derivative (isotropy) representation of G at a common fixed point x in the coordinates of a chart χ: g ↦ D(χ ∘ g ∘ χ⁻¹)(χ x). Lean ↔ maths: the body is `.ofMonoidHom` of `g ↦ fderiv 𝕜 (χ ∘ (g • ·) ∘ χ.symm) (χ x)`, the Fréchet derivative at χ x of g read in the chart — the linear part d_x h of Isaev, Proper group actions in complex geometry, arXiv:1501.07656, Thm 3.1 (Bochner's linearization), transported to E by χ, and the L_g = d(g)_x of TauCetiRoadmap Orbifolds O2.1 (dd4b28f1); `hxχ : x ∈ χ.source` puts x in the chart, `hx : ∀ g, g • x = x` makes x a common fixed point (so χ x is fixed by every conjugate), `hd` assumes each conjugate differentiable at χ x; `map_one'` is D(id) = 1 and `map_mul'` is the chain rule at the fixed point (the conjugates of gh and of g ∘ h agree near χ x, `conj_mul_smul_eventuallyEq`), so this is a genuine monoid hom G → (E →L[𝕜] E), a `ContRepresentation`. Lean subtlety: `fderiv` is 0 at non-differentiable points, which would make the 'representation' junk (map_one' would fail) — `hd` excludes this, so every value is the true derivative; the proofs hxχ, hx, hd are arguments of the definition and, by proof irrelevance, any proofs give the same representation. Checks (Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): a compiled probe (ℤˣ = {±1} acting on ℝ by multiplication, χ = the identity chart) computes σ(−1) = −1, the derivative of y ↦ −y, and feeds it to `exists_equivariant_chart` and `map_eq_one_iff_mem_germKernel`; [Group G] can be weakened to [Monoid G] (RT-20261104-d682f3, MINOR generality).

`isotropyRepresentation hxχ hx hd g = fderiv 𝕜 (χ ∘ (g • ·) ∘ χ.symm) (χ x)`: the representation at g is the derivative at χ x of g read in the chart; true by rfl. Lean subtlety: `fderiv` is 0 at non-differentiable points, excluded here by the hypothesis `hd`.

(1) The free components: the residual components neither reachable from the component of the source nor reaching the component of the sink, with the induced order. (2) `{C : f.ResidualComponent // ¬f.residualComponent s ≤ C ∧ ¬C ≤ f.residualComponent t}` with the subtype partial order; `¬[s] ≤ C` says C is not a successor of the source's component and `¬C ≤ [t]` that C is not a predecessor of the sink's (by `residualComponent_le_residualComponent`, not positively residually reachable from s / not reaching t). This is Picard–Queyranne's reduced relation after eliminating the component of t with all its predecessors and the component of s with all its successors. (3) Lean subtlety: the components of s and t themselves are excluded by reflexivity of ≤, as intended. (4) Picard–Queyranne, Tech. Rep. EP-R-79-15 (École Polytechnique de Montréal, 1979), p. 6; TauCetiRoadmap GraphConnectivityAndFlows §4.4. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: on the roadmap example the free components are exactly those of a and b (the file's example), and on s→a→b→t (capacities 2,1,2, flow 1) the type is empty (compiled).

The free components contained in S ⊓ T (the intersection of the two minimum cuts) are the intersection of those contained in S and in T. Lean subtlety: ⊓ in `(UpperSet _)ᵒᵈ` is ⊔ in the reverse-ordered `UpperSet`, whose carrier is the intersection (`map_inf, ofDual_inf, UpperSet.coe_sup`). Cf. Picard–Queyranne, Tech. Rep. EP-R-79-15 (École Polytechnique de Montréal, 1979), Corollary 3.

The free components contained in S ⊔ T (the union of the two minimum cuts: ⊔ in the sublattice `minimizers` is ∪ of finsets) are the union of those contained in S and in T. Lean subtlety: the isomorphism takes ⊔ to ⊔ in `(UpperSet _)ᵒᵈ`, which is ⊓ in the reverse-ordered `UpperSet`, whose carrier is the union — the proof is exactly `map_sup, ofDual_sup, UpperSet.coe_inf`. Cf. Picard–Queyranne, Tech. Rep. EP-R-79-15 (École Polytechnique de Montréal, 1979), Corollary 3.

For a maximum assignment with s ≠ t, `Disjoint (Set.Ici [s]) (Set.Iic [t])`: no residual component is both reachable from the source's component and reaches the sink's; by `Set.Ici_disjoint_Iic` this is `¬[s] ≤ [t]`, i.e. there is no augmenting walk from s to t (`IsMaximum.not_positiveReachable`). Lean subtlety: `hst` is needed, since at s = t both sets contain [s].

(1) For a maximum assignment between distinct terminals, the minimum cut is unique exactly when no residual component is free. (2) `∃! S, TerminalCut.IsMinimum (cutBound lo hi) {s} {t} S` says exactly one vertex set S with s ∈ S, t ∉ S minimises the cut bound; `IsEmpty f.FreeComponent` says every residual component is reachable from the component of s or reaches that of t. The proof reduces it, through `residualComponent_le_residualComponent` and surjectivity of `residualComponent`, to `existsUnique_isMinimum_iff` (every vertex is positively residually reachable from s or reaches t). (3) Lean subtlety: both hypotheses matter and are present — at s = t there is no minimum cut, so the left side is false while the right can hold; without maximality (zero flow on s→a, a→t, s→t, unit capacities) nothing is free yet {s} and {s,a} are both minimum. Uniqueness is of the `Finset`, with no `sInf` or junk value. (4) Immediate from Picard–Queyranne, Tech. Rep. EP-R-79-15 (École Polytechnique de Montréal, 1979), p. 6 (every closure of the reduced relation gives a minimum cut, so there is one cut iff the reduced relation is empty). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: compiled both directions on concrete networks — the roadmap example gives `¬∃!` from a free component, and s→a→b→t (capacities 2,1,2, flow 1) gives `∃!` from `IsEmpty FreeComponent`.

A free component C lies in the upper set attached to a minimum cut S iff every vertex v with `f.residualComponent v = C.1` lies in S, i.e. the forward map is 'the free components contained in S'; it holds by `Iff.rfl`, so it is the definition of the map (`ofDual` only strips the order dual).

Vertex-membership formula: v lies in the minimum cut attached to an upper set U iff `[s] ≤ [v]` (v is forced onto the source side) or [v] is free and belongs to U — Picard–Queyranne's 'a closure of the reduced relation, plus S and all its successors' (Picard–Queyranne, Tech. Rep. EP-R-79-15 (École Polytechnique de Montréal, 1979), p. 6). Lean subtlety: `ofDual U` is the upper set itself, the dual only fixing the order.

For a maximum f with s ≠ t and any minimum cut S (`TerminalCut.IsMinimum (cutBound lo hi) {s} {t} S`), every vertex v with `[s] ≤ [v]` (positively residually reachable from s) lies in S: the vertices forced onto every source side, Picard–Queyranne's 'S and all its successors must belong to a closure containing S' (Picard–Queyranne, Tech. Rep. EP-R-79-15 (École Polytechnique de Montréal, 1979), p. 6).

(1) The Picard–Queyranne theorem: for a maximum s–t assignment f with s ≠ t, the minimum s–t cuts ordered by inclusion are order-isomorphic to the upper sets (closures) of the poset of free strongly connected components of the positive residual graph, ordered by inclusion. (2) The domain `minimizers (isSubmodular_cutBound lo hi _) {s} {t}` is the sublattice of `Finset V` of source sides S with `TerminalCut.IsMinimum (cutBound lo hi) {s} {t} S`, i.e. s ∈ S, t ∉ S and S minimises (`IsMinOn`) `cutBound lo hi S = arrowSum hi S Sᶜ − arrowSum lo Sᶜ S` (upper bounds out minus lower bounds in; for lo = 0 the capacity c(S, S̄)) over all such sets, with the order of `Finset` inclusion; `hf : f.IsMaximum` is `IsMaxOn val univ f` (value maximal among all bounded s–t assignments) and `hst : s ≠ t` is distinct terminals. In the codomain, `f.FreeComponent` is the subtype of `Quiver.StronglyConnectedComponent` for the quiver whose arrows v → w are residual arrows (`ResidualHom Q v w = Q v w ⊕ Q w v`) of strictly positive `residualCapacity` (hi e − f e forward, f e − lo e backward), ordered by C ≤ D iff a path runs from C to D (`mk_le_mk`), restricted to the C with `¬[s] ≤ C ∧ ¬C ≤ [t]`: exactly Picard–Queyranne's reduced relation after deleting the component of s with its successors and the component of t with its predecessors. `UpperSet` = sets of components closed under passing to a reachable component = their closures. The forward map sends S to the free components all of whose vertices lie in S (`mem_minimizersOrderIso_iff`, by `Iff.rfl`); the inverse sends U to the vertices reachable from s or lying in a component of U (`mem_minimizersOrderIso_symm_iff`). (3) Lean subtlety: Mathlib orders `UpperSet` by REVERSE inclusion, hence the `ᵒᵈ`; I compiled `(S : Finset V) ⊆ T ↔ ↑(ofDual (e S)) ⊆ ↑(ofDual (e T))`, so the isomorphism is inclusion-to-inclusion (and `toDual ⊤` is the EMPTY upper set). The residual quiver uses `PositiveHom`, so saturated, empty or zero-capacity arcs contribute no residual arrow, matching Picard–Queyranne's strict inequalities f_ij < c_ij, f_ji > 0. `minimizers` is defined by `IsMinOn`, not `sInf`, so there is no junk value; at s = t it would be empty, which `hst` excludes (compiled: no minimum cut exists when s = t, while upper sets always exist). Coefficients are any linearly ordered abelian group (ℤ, ℚ, ℝ; not ℕ or ℝ≥0) and negative bounds are allowed; the submodularity proof inside `minimizers` is a Prop, so irrelevant. (4) Picard–Queyranne, Tech. Rep. EP-R-79-15 (École Polytechnique de Montréal, 1979), Theorem 1 (a cut is minimum iff S is a closure for R containing s and not t, where iRj iff f_ij < c_ij on an arc (i,j) or f_ji > 0 on an arc (j,i)) and p. 6 (shrink strong components, remove the sink component with its predecessors and the source component with its successors; closures of the rest give the minimum cuts), and TauCetiRoadmap GraphConnectivityAndFlows §4.4, state it this way. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: compiled specialisations — on the roadmap four-vertex network the inverse sends the principal upper set of [b] to {s,b}; on s→a→b→t (capacities 2,1,2, one unit of flow) no component is free and the inverse sends the only upper set to {s,a}; `Nat.card` of the minimum cuts equals `Nat.card` of the upper sets; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.

The minimum cut attached to `toDual ⊥` is `largest hsub _`, the greatest minimum cut under inclusion. Lean subtlety: ⊥ in the reverse-ordered `UpperSet` is the FULL upper set (carrier univ), so the full upper set gives the largest cut (the vertices from which t is not residually reachable); `largest` is a `Classical.choose` of an `IsGreatest` witness, unique by `largest_eq_iff`.

The minimum cut attached to `toDual ⊤` is `smallest hsub _`, the least minimum cut under inclusion. Lean subtlety: ⊤ in Mathlib's reverse-ordered `UpperSet` is the EMPTY upper set (`UpperSet.coe_top`), so this says the empty upper set gives the smallest cut (the vertices residually reachable from s); `hsub` is any proof of submodularity (a Prop, so irrelevant), and `smallest` is a `Classical.choose` of an `IsLeast` witness, which is unique (`smallest_eq_iff`).

For a maximum f with s ≠ t and any minimum cut S, no vertex v with `[v] ≤ [t]` (from which t is positively residually reachable) lies in S: the vertices forced off every source side, Picard–Queyranne's eliminated predecessors of the sink component (Picard–Queyranne, Tech. Rep. EP-R-79-15 (École Polytechnique de Montréal, 1979), p. 6).

For a vertex v whose component is free (`h`), that component lies in the upper set of a minimum cut S iff v ∈ S: a minimum cut is closed under positive residual reachability, so one vertex of a strong component in S puts the whole component in S.

(1) The residual components of f: the strongly connected components of the residual graph of f restricted to arrows of positive residual capacity, partially ordered by reachability. (2) The body is `@Quiver.StronglyConnectedComponent V ⟨PositiveHom (residualCapacity lo hi f.toFun)⟩`: Mathlib's quotient of V by mutual path-reachability for the quiver whose arrows v → w are `{e : Q v w ⊕ Q w v // 0 < residualCapacity lo hi f.toFun e}` — forward copies with room hi e − f e > 0 and reverse copies with f e − lo e > 0, i.e. the residual graph G_f — and the order is Tau Ceti's `Quiver.StronglyConnectedComponent.instPartialOrder` (C ≤ D iff a path runs from C to D). (3) Lean subtlety: the quiver structure is passed as a local instance, so the type depends on f; arrows of zero residual capacity are dropped (`PositiveHom`), as in Picard–Queyranne's strict relation. (4) Picard–Queyranne, Tech. Rep. EP-R-79-15 (École Polytechnique de Montréal, 1979), relation (1) of Theorem 1 and p. 6 (shrinking the strong components). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: witnessed on the roadmap example and on s→a→b→t (compiled).

`f.residualComponent v` is `Quiver.StronglyConnectedComponent.mk v` for the positive residual quiver, the strong component containing v; it is characterised by `residualComponent_le_residualComponent` (≤ iff positive residual reachability), `residualComponent_eq_residualComponent` (= iff mutual reachability) and `residualComponent_surjective`. Lean subtlety: the def is not exposed to importing modules, so downstream proofs go through these lemmas instead of unfolding it.

Two vertices have the same residual component iff each is positively residually reachable from the other — mutual reachability, the defining relation of a strong component; it follows from the order lemma by antisymmetry.

`f.residualComponent v ≤ f.residualComponent w ↔ PositiveReachable (residualCapacity lo hi f.toFun) v w`: the component of v is below that of w exactly when some walk from v to w uses only residual arrows of positive capacity — the reachability order on strong components, from Mathlib's path quiver via `positiveReachable_iff_nonempty_arrowWalk`.

`Function.Surjective f.residualComponent`: every residual component contains a vertex, i.e. the quotient map from vertices to strong components is onto (Mathlib's `Quiver.StronglyConnectedComponent` is a quotient; `mk_surjective`).

For a maximum ordinary flow, the free components inside the intersection S ⊓ T of two minimum cuts are the intersection of those inside each. Lean subtlety: ⊓ in `(UpperSet _)ᵒᵈ` is ⊔ in `UpperSet`, whose carrier is the intersection.

For a maximum ordinary flow, the free components inside the union S ⊔ T of two minimum cuts are the union of those inside each. Lean subtlety: ⊔ in `(UpperSet _)ᵒᵈ` is ⊓ in the reverse-ordered `UpperSet`, whose carrier is the union.

For a maximum ordinary flow between distinct terminals, `∃! S, IsMinimum (fun S ↦ arrowSum cap S Sᶜ) {s} {t} S` (exactly one source side S ∋ s, ∌ t of minimum outgoing capacity) iff `IsEmpty f.FreeComponent` (every residual component is reachable from s's or reaches t's); it is the bounded-flow corollary at lower bound 0 after rewriting `cutBound 0 cap` to the outgoing capacity. Lean subtlety: `hst` and `hf` are both needed (at s = t there is no cut; for a non-maximum flow the right side can hold with several minimum cuts), and residual arrows of zero capacity are excluded. Immediate from Picard–Queyranne, Tech. Rep. EP-R-79-15 (École Polytechnique de Montréal, 1979), p. 6. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: specialised to s→a→b→t (capacities 2,1,2, one unit of flow), where no component is free, to get the unique minimum cut {s,a} (compiled).

For a maximum ordinary flow, v lies in the minimum cut attached to an upper set U iff v's residual component is reachable from the source's or is free and in U — Picard–Queyranne's description of every minimum cut (Picard–Queyranne, Tech. Rep. EP-R-79-15 (École Polytechnique de Montréal, 1979), p. 6); the bounded-flow formula at lower bound 0.

(1) The Picard–Queyranne isomorphism for ordinary flows: for a maximum s–t flow f (0 ≤ f ≤ cap) with s ≠ t, the minimum cuts under inclusion are order-isomorphic to the upper sets of the free residual components under inclusion. (2) `Flow cap s t` is a `BoundedFlow 0 cap s t` of nonnegative value and `Flow.IsMaximum` is maximality among such flows (the same as bounded maximality, `Flow.isMaximum_toBoundedFlow`); the domain is `minimizers` of the set function `S ↦ arrowSum cap S Sᶜ`, the capacity of the arcs leaving S (Picard–Queyranne's c(S, S̄)), over source sides s ∈ S, t ∉ S ordered by ⊆; `f.FreeComponent` is the bounded-flow notion at lower bound 0, so the residual arrows are i→j with f_ij < c_ij and j→i with f_ij > 0, exactly Picard–Queyranne's relation R, and free means neither reachable from the component of s nor reaching that of t. The definition transports `BoundedFlow.IsMaximum.minimizersOrderIso` along `cutBound 0 cap = fun S ↦ arrowSum cap S Sᶜ` (`cutBound_zero_left`), so it is the same map (forward: free components inside S; inverse: vertices reachable from s plus the vertices of the chosen components). (3) Lean subtlety: the codomain is `(UpperSet _)ᵒᵈ` because Mathlib orders upper sets by reverse inclusion, so both sides are ordered by inclusion; arcs with zero residual capacity are absent (`PositiveHom`); `cap` lives in a linearly ordered abelian group, so ℕ- or ℝ≥0-capacities are handled by casting to ℤ or ℝ, and nonnegativity of cap comes from the flow itself; `hst` rules out the empty `minimizers` at s = t. (4) Picard–Queyranne, Tech. Rep. EP-R-79-15 (École Polytechnique de Montréal, 1979), Theorem 1 and p. 6, state it for positive capacities in exactly this form. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: compiled the roadmap example through this isomorphism (the inverse of the principal upper set of [b] is {s,b}) and a unique-cut instance (s→a→b→t, capacities 2,1,2: the only upper set goes to {s,a}); standard axioms.

For a maximum ordinary flow, `toDual ⊥` — the FULL upper set in the reverse-ordered `UpperSet` — corresponds to `largest hsub _`, the greatest minimum cut for the outgoing capacity; proved through the bounded-flow statement at lower bound 0 and `mem_largest_iff`.

For a maximum ordinary flow, `toDual ⊤` — the EMPTY upper set, since Mathlib's `UpperSet` is reverse-ordered — corresponds to `smallest hsub _`, the least minimum cut for the outgoing capacity; proved by reducing to the bounded-flow statement at lower bound 0 through the membership characterisations `mem_smallest_iff`.

For a maximum ordinary flow and a vertex v whose residual component is free, that component lies in the upper set of a minimum cut S (for the outgoing capacity) iff v ∈ S; it is the bounded-flow lemma at lower bound 0.

Correctly stated: over R, the automorph attached to the norm-one element x + yω is !![x + y(D − b)/2, −cy; ay, x + y(D + b)/2]. Lean ↔ mathematics: `x` and `y` are `.re` and `.im` of z in R[ω] (ω² − Dω + (D² − D)/4 = 0); the matrix is x·1 + y·M with M = !![(D − b)/2, −c; a, (D + b)/2], the integral matrix of trace D and determinant (D² − D)/4 by which ω acts, whose form Q_M = M₁₀x² + (M₁₁ − M₀₀)xy − M₀₁y² is f. With t = 2x + Dy (the trace of x + yω) and u = y the entries are ((t − bu)/2, −cu; au, (t + bu)/2), O'Sullivan's Gq(t, u) (arXiv:2408.14405v3, eq. (8.1)). Lean subtlety: `((D - f.b) / 2 : ℤ)` and `((D + f.b) / 2 : ℤ)` are Int divisions cast to R; they are exact, not rounded, because D − b = b² − b − 4ac is even (`two_mul_ediv_two_of_discrim_eq` gives 2·((D − b)/2) = D − b). Checks compiled at 5f78b5307b: over ℤ, z = −5 + 2ω at D = 8 gives !![3, 4; 2, 3] for x² − 2y², and z = 1 + ω at D = 0 gives !![1, 0; 1, 1] for x².

Correctly stated: the automorph attached to the norm-one unit x + y√D of ℤ[(D + √D)/2] is !![x − by, −2cy; 2ay, x + by]. Lean ↔ mathematics: `(stabilizerEquivNormOneUnits hf hfD).symm u` is the inverse isomorphism at the unit u, coerced to SL(2, ℤ) and then to an integer matrix, whose entries `.map (Int.cast : ℤ → ℚ)` reads in ℚ; `x` and `y` are `.re` and `.im` of u viewed in `QuadraticAlgebra ℚ D 0`, so u = x + y√D with rational x, y (an order element m + n(D + √D)/2 has x = m + nD/2, y = n/2, half-integers). Writing t = 2x and u = 2y, the matrix is ((t − bu)/2, −cu; au, (t + bu)/2), and norm one means t² − Du² = 4: this is O'Sullivan's Gq(t, u), and his map Gq(t, u) ↦ (t + u√D)/2 runs in the same direction as this inverse. Lean subtlety: the identity is deliberately stated after casting to ℚ, because x and y are half-integers; over ℚ there is no division rounding, and the integer matrix is recovered since `Int.cast` is injective. The integral-entry companion `coe_stabilizerEquivUnitary_symm_apply` instead uses the Int divisions (D ± b)/2, which are exact because D ≡ b mod 2. Source: O'Sullivan, Topographs for binary quadratic forms and class numbers, arXiv:2408.14405v3, Prop. 8.1 (citing Landau Thm. 202 and Buell Thm. 3.9) and Cor. 8.2, eq. (8.1). Checks compiled at 5f78b5307b: for f = x² − 2y² (D = 8) the unit 3 + √8 (x = 3, y = 1) gives !![3, 4; 2, 3], which fixes f under the file's action while its transpose does not; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: naturality in the coefficient ring; a ring homomorphism φ : R → S maps the automorph attached to z entrywise to the automorph attached to the element w with coordinates φ(re z), φ(im z). Lean ↔ mathematics: `SpecialLinearGroup.map φ` applies φ to each entry; `hre` and `him` say w = φ(z) coordinatewise (w is passed explicitly because Mathlib's `QuadraticAlgebra.mapRingHom φ` lands in `QuadraticAlgebra S (φ n) (φ D)`, not syntactically the target's parameters (n : S), (D : S)); `hR`, `hS` supply the two isomorphisms. Lean subtlety: `hS` is needed separately (2 regular in R does not give it in S, e.g. ℤ → ZMod 2, where no isomorphism exists); nothing holds vacuously, since w is determined by `hre`, `him`. Checks: follows entrywise from `coe_stabilizerEquivUnitary_symm_apply`; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: for a primitive integral binary quadratic form f = ax² + bxy + cy² of discriminant D, the group of proper automorphs of f in SL₂(ℤ) is isomorphic as a group to the norm-one units of the quadratic order ℤ[(D + √D)/2]. Lean ↔ mathematics: `stabilizer SL(2, ℤ) f` is the stabiliser for the instance `MulAction SL(2, R) (BinaryQuadraticForm R)`, whose action is `γ • f = f ∘ γ⁻¹` (`eval_smul`: (γ • f)(x, y) = f(sx − qy, −rx + py) for γ = !![p, q; r, s]); since f ∘ γ⁻¹ = f iff f ∘ γ = f, it is exactly {γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ) : f(px + qy, rx + sy) = f(x, y)}, the classical proper automorph group with column substitution (the transposed convention would give a different subgroup: compiled, !![3, 4; 2, 3] fixes x² − 2y² and its transpose does not). `f.IsPrimitive` is `f.content = 1` with `content = Int.gcd a (Int.gcd b c)`; `hfD : f.discrim = D` with `discrim = b² − 4ac`. `QuadraticOrder.normOneUnits D _` is by definition the kernel of `Algebra.normUnits ℤ` on the units of `QuadraticOrder.toSubalgebra D _`, the ℤ-subalgebra of `QuadraticAlgebra ℚ D 0` = ℚ[√D] (ω² = D) that is the range of `QuadraticOrder.lift`, i.e. generated by `generator D = ⟨D/2, 1/2⟩ = (D + √D)/2` (`toSubalgebra_eq_adjoin`), with ℤ-basis 1, (D + √D)/2 of discriminant D (`discr_basis`); its ℤ-algebra norm is x² − Dy² (`QuadraticOrder.norm_coe`). `≃*` is a `MulEquiv`, a group isomorphism and not just a bijection, and the map is pinned down by `map_stabilizerEquivNormOneUnits_symm_apply` (x + y√D ↦ !![x − by, −2cy; 2ay, x + by]). D ≡ 0, 1 mod 4 is not assumed but derived from `hfD` (`discrim_emod_four_eq_zero_or_one`), and D may be a square or 0: ℚ[√D] is only a ring (split, resp. ℚ[ε]/ε²), never asserted to be a field. Lean subtlety: the integral model behind the proof uses the Int division (D − D²)/4, exact because D ≡ 0, 1 mod 4 (`QuadraticOrder.parameter_discr`); the parameter D is free but fixed by `hfD`, and the congruence proof inside the type is a Prop, so it does not matter which proof is used. No junk value is involved: square and zero discriminants are genuinely covered, not degenerate. Source: O'Sullivan, Topographs for binary quadratic forms and class numbers, arXiv:2408.14405v3, Prop. 8.1 (citing Landau Thm. 202 and Buell Thm. 3.9) and Cor. 8.2: for primitive q of non-square discriminant D, Aut(q) = {M ∈ SL(2, ℤ) : q(αx + βy, γx + δy) = q} = {((t − bu)/2, −cu; au, (t + bu)/2) : t² − Du² = 4}, with Gq(t, u) ↦ (t + u√D)/2 an injective homomorphism; Cor. 8.2 gives Aut(q) = {±I} for D a nonzero square and Aut(q)/{±I} ≅ ℤ for D = 0. Red-team checks compiled at 5f78b5307b: Nat.card (stabilizer SL(2, ℤ) (x² + y²)) = 4 via this equivalence and `card_normOneUnits_of_neg`; Nat.card = 2 for xy (D = 1) and x² + 3xy (D = 9), as Cor. 8.2 says; primitivity cannot be dropped (no such MulEquiv exists for 2x² + 2y², D = −16: 4 automorphs, 2 norm-one units); D = 0 handled (1 + ω ↦ !![1, 0; 1, 1]); axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: for a primitive integral binary quadratic form f of discriminant D and a commutative ring R in which 2 is not a zero divisor, the automorphs of f in SL₂(R) form a group isomorphic to the norm-one elements of R ⊗ 𝒪_D = R[ω]/(ω² − Dω + (D² − D)/4). Lean ↔ mathematics: `stabilizer SL(2, R) (f.map (Int.castRingHom R))` is the stabiliser of f with coefficients read in R, for the action `γ • f = f ∘ γ⁻¹` (`eval_smul`), i.e. {γ ∈ SL₂(R) : f(px + qy, rx + sy) = f(x, y)}. `QuadraticAlgebra R n D` with n = ((D − D²)/4 : ℤ) read in R is R[ω] with ω² = n + Dω, i.e. ω² − Dω + (D² − D)/4 = 0; for R = ℤ it is ℤ[(D + √D)/2], since `QuadraticOrder.lift` sends ω to (D + √D)/2 injectively. `unitary` is {z : star z * z = 1 ∧ z * star z = 1}, which Mathlib's `QuadraticAlgebra.norm_eq_one_iff_mem_unitary` identifies with {z : norm z = 1}, where `norm_def` gives norm(x + yω) = x² + Dxy − ny². `IsLeftRegular (2 : R)` says multiplication by 2 is injective, i.e. 2 is a non-zero-divisor of the commutative ring R. `≃*` is a group isomorphism; its inverse is given by `coe_stabilizerEquivUnitary_symm_apply`. Lean subtlety: n = (D − D²)/4 is an Int division cast to R, exact because D ≡ 0, 1 mod 4 (derived from `hfD`). For the zero ring, 2 = 0 is vacuously left regular and both groups are trivial, so the statement is still right. The hypothesis on 2 cannot be dropped: compiled over ZMod 2 for f = xy (D = 1), the swap !![0, 1; 1, 0] is an automorph different from 1, but the only norm-one element of 𝔽₂[ω]/(ω² − ω) is 1, so no such MulEquiv exists, as the module docstring says. Source: for R = ℤ it specialises to `stabilizerEquivNormOneUnits`, i.e. O'Sullivan, Topographs for binary quadratic forms and class numbers, arXiv:2408.14405v3, Prop. 8.1 (citing Landau Thm. 202 and Buell Thm. 3.9) and Cor. 8.2. Checks compiled at 5f78b5307b: over ℤ the inverse sends −5 + 2ω (= 3 + √8, D = 8) to !![3, 4; 2, 3] = O'Sullivan's Gq(6, 2), an automorph of x² − 2y², and 1 + ω (D = 0) to !![1, 0; 1, 1] for x²; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Correctly defined: `IsSymmetricCocycleCoeff n b` says a sequence b₀, b₁, … in an abelian group satisfies b_{n−i} = b_i for i ≤ n (field `symm`), and C(i + j, i)·b_{i+j} = C(j + k, j)·b_i for all i, j, k ≥ 1 with i + j + k = n (field `rel`). Lean ↔ maths: read b_a as the coefficient m_{a, n−a} of XᵃYⁿ⁻ᵃ in a degree-n cocycle. Then `symm` is m_{a,b} = m_{b,a}, and `rel` is Lurie's relation C(i + j, j)·m_{i+j,k} = C(j + k, j)·m_{i,j+k}: C(i + j, i) = C(i + j, j), b_{i+j} = m_{i+j,k} because n − (i + j) = k, and b_i = m_{i,j+k}. `•` is ℕ-scalar multiplication. The definition omits Lurie's boundary conditions m_{0,n} = m_{n,0} = 0, so b_0 = b_n is left free. Every consumer concludes only about 0 < i < n (`exists_eq_nsmul`), and for polynomial cocycles the boundary coefficients are shown to vanish separately (`IsAddCocycle₂.coeff_single_one_eq_zero`). Lean subtlety: `n - i` is truncated subtraction, but `symm` quantifies only over i ≤ n and `rel` only over i + j ≤ n, so it never truncates. Values b_a with a > n are unconstrained and never used. Source: Lurie, Chromatic Homotopy Theory, Lecture 3, Lemma 2, with N = n. Checks compiled: a witness (the C_4 coefficients 0, 2, 3, 2, 0 satisfy it) and two non-witnesses (the symmetric sequence 1, 1, 0, 1, 1 in degree 4 fails `rel` at (1, 1, 2) because 2·0 ≠ 3·1, and an asymmetric sequence in degree 3 fails `symm`).

Correctly stated: for every abelian group M and every solution b of the degree-n coefficient equations, there is r ∈ M with b_i = (C(n, i)/d_n)·r for all 0 < i < n. This is the surjectivity half of Lurie's Lecture 3, Proposition 6: λ′ : M → F(M), m ↦ (C(N, i)/d)·m, is an isomorphism for every abelian group M. Lean ↔ maths: `IsSymmetricCocycleCoeff n b` is Lurie's F(M) without its boundary terms, and the conclusion constrains only 0 < i < n, where those terms play no role. `(n.choose i / lazardGcd n) • r` is the ℕ-multiple (C(n, i)/d_n)·r, where `lazardGcd n` is d_n: p for n = pᵏ and 1 otherwise, for n ≥ 2. Lean subtlety: `/` is ℕ-division, exact because d_n divides n.choose i (`lazardGcd_dvd_choose`). For n < 2 there is no index 0 < i < n, so the statement is vacuous there and the proof takes r = 0, as intended. Axioms are only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

`map`: if b solves the degree-n coefficient equations in M, then i ↦ φ (b i) solves them in N for every additive homomorphism `φ : M →+ N`. The equations are ℤ-linear, and `map_nsmul` carries the ℕ-multiples C(i + j, i) • b_{i+j} through φ.
`sub`: the termwise difference i ↦ b i − b' i of two solutions of the degree-n coefficient equations is again a solution. Both equations are linear (`nsmul_sub`).

Correctly stated: for every commutative ring R and every n ≥ 2, a polynomial f(X, Y) over R that is homogeneous of degree n, symmetric and an additive 2-cocycle is r·C_n for exactly one r ∈ R, where C_n = ((X + Y)ⁿ − Xⁿ − Yⁿ)/d_n is the Lazard cocycle. Lean ↔ maths, piece by piece: `f : MvPolynomial (Fin 2) R` is a polynomial in X = `X 0` and Y = `X 1`. `f.IsHomogeneous n` (Mathlib) says every monomial with nonzero coefficient has total degree n. `f.IsSymmetric` (Mathlib) is `rename e f = f` for every permutation e of `Fin 2`, i.e. f(Y, X) = f(X, Y). `f.IsAddCocycle₂` unfolds (`isAddCocycle₂_iff`) to `aeval ![X 0, X 1] f + aeval ![X 0 + X 1, X 2] f = aeval ![X 0, X 1 + X 2] f + aeval ![X 1, X 2] f` in R[X, Y, Z], which is f(X, Y) + f(X + Y, Z) = f(X, Y + Z) + f(Y, Z). `lazardCocycle n R` is by definition the sum over `Icc 1 (n - 1)` of `monomial (XⁱYⁿ⁻ⁱ) ((n.choose i / lazardGcd n : ℕ) : R)`. Here `lazardGcd n` is the gcd of the n.choose i with 0 < i < n, and `lazardGcd_eq_minFac_of_isPrimePow` and `lazardGcd_eq_one_of_not_isPrimePow` identify it with p when n = pᵏ (k ≥ 1) and with 1 otherwise. Values checked by `decide`: d_2 = 2, d_4 = 2, d_6 = 1, d_8 = 2, d_9 = 3, d_12 = 1. `lazardGcd_nsmul_lazardCocycle` gives d_n • C_n = (X + Y)ⁿ − Xⁿ − Yⁿ. `r • g` is `C r * g`, and `∃! r` is existence together with uniqueness. Lean subtlety: the division in C_n is the natural-number division `n.choose i / lazardGcd n`, done in ℕ before the cast to R. It is exact because d_n divides each n.choose i (`lazardGcd_dvd_choose`), so it gives the integer coefficients of C_n, not a division in R that could be junk where p is not invertible. Compiled checks: over ZMod 3, (X + Y)³ − X³ − Y³ = 0 but C_3 ≠ 0; over ZMod 2, the integer coefficients 2, 3, 2 of C_4 make C_4 = X²Y². `2 ≤ n` is needed because `lazardGcd` of the empty range is 0 and the empty sum makes C_0 = C_1 = 0. Compiled: uniqueness fails at n = 1 (0 = 0 • C_1 = 1 • C_1), and existence fails at n = 0 (the constant 1 is a homogeneous symmetric cocycle of degree 0, while C_0 = 0). The truncated `n - i` in exponents is only taken for i ≤ n. Source: Lurie, Chromatic Homotopy Theory (Harvard 2010), Lecture 3, Lemma 2, Corollary 5 and Proposition 6. For every abelian group M, m ↦ (C(N, i)/d)·m is a bijection from M onto the symmetric solutions of the coefficient equations of a degree-N cocycle, with d = p for N = pᶠ and 1 otherwise. The polynomial identity f(X, Y) + f(X + Y, Z) = f(X, Y + Z) + f(Y, Z) is those equations coefficientwise (`isSymmetricCocycleCoeff_coeff`), so the Lean statement is that bijection with coefficients in the ring R. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: specialised over ZMod 2 at n = 4, where X²Y² meets all three hypotheses and the unique r the theorem returns is 1 (compiled); lean_minimal_hypotheses: hn, hh, hs and hf all load-bearing; the hypotheses are satisfied by C_n itself, so they are not contradictory; axioms are only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: over any commutative ring R, a polynomial f(X, Y) that is homogeneous of degree n ≠ 0, symmetric and an additive 2-cocycle is r·C_n for some r ∈ R (existence part of Lazard's lemma). Lean ↔ maths: `f.IsHomogeneous n` is homogeneity of total degree n, `f.IsSymmetric` is f(Y, X) = f(X, Y) (invariance under `rename` by every permutation of `Fin 2`), and `f.IsAddCocycle₂` is f(X, Y) + f(X + Y, Z) = f(X, Y + Z) + f(Y, Z) via the four `aeval` substitutions. `lazardCocycle n R` has the integer coefficient `n.choose i / lazardGcd n` at XⁱYⁿ⁻ⁱ for 0 < i < n and 0 elsewhere (`coeff_lazardCocycle`), and `∃ r, f = r • lazardCocycle n R` says f = r·C_n. Lean subtlety: the division by d_n is exact ℕ-division before the cast into R, not division in R. At n = 1, `lazardGcd 1` is the gcd of an empty set, which is 0, and C_1 is the empty sum 0, so the statement says every degree-1 homogeneous symmetric cocycle is 0. That junk value is the correct one: aX + bY satisfies the cocycle identity only if a = b = 0. n = 0 is excluded by `hn` and must be: the constant 1 is a degree-0 symmetric cocycle while C_0 = 0 (compiled). The proof takes the coefficients of Xⁿ and Yⁿ to vanish from the cocycle identity (`IsAddCocycle₂.coeff_single_one_eq_zero`) and symmetry, and the others from `IsSymmetricCocycleCoeff.exists_eq_nsmul`.
