name: The Schoenflies theorem
text: every Jordan curve in the plane is the image of the unit circle under a homeomorphism of ℂ carrying the open disc onto its inside, and on the 2-sphere a homeomorphism carries a great circle onto any Jordan curve (Moise, *Geometric Topology in Dimensions 2 and 3*).

name: The sharp isoperimetric inequality
text: every set E ⊆ ℝⁿ of finite volume satisfies P(E)ⁿ ≥ nⁿ ωₙ |E|ⁿ⁻¹ with no boundedness or regularity assumed and balls attaining the bound, extending the planar, relative and convex-body cases announced earlier (Maggi, *Sets of Finite Perimeter and Geometric Variational Problems*, Ch. 14).

name: The Hilbert class field is the maximal unramified abelian extension
text: the Hilbert class field of a number field K is unramified everywhere, and a finite abelian extension of K lies in it exactly when it is unramified at every finite and infinite place (Neukirch, *Algebraic Number Theory*, VI.6).

name: Conjugacy of Cartan subalgebras
text: in a semisimple Lie algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, any two Cartan subalgebras are conjugate under the group of inner automorphisms (Humphreys, *Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory*, §16.4).

name: The Godement resolution
text: every sheaf F on a topological space embeds in the flasque sheaf ∏ₓ (iₓ)_* Fₓ, and iterating on the cokernels gives a functorial flasque resolution of F, exact for sheaves of modules or abelian groups (Godement, *Topologie algébrique et théorie des faisceaux*, II.4.3).

name: The quotient of an affine scheme by a finite locally free equivalence relation
text: for an equivalence relation R ⇉ X on an affine scheme with R → X finite locally free, the quotient X/R is an affine scheme, X → X/R is finite locally free, and it represents the fppf quotient sheaf (SGA 3, Exp. V, Thm 4.1).

name: Kronecker's theorem for linear flows on tori
text: a line t ↦ θ + tν in the torus (ℝ/pℤ)ⁿ is dense exactly when ν is nonresonant, that is, no nonzero integer vector k has Σ kᵢνᵢ = 0 (Arnold, *Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics*, §51).

name: Weyl's equidistribution theorem for linear flows
text: along a nonresonant line on the unit torus, the time averages T⁻¹ ∫₀ᵀ f(θ + tν) dt of every continuous function f converge to the integral of f over the torus (Arnold, *Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics*, §51).

name: Landen's transformation for the complete integral of the second kind
text: now for E(k): E(2√k/(1 + k)) = (2E(k) − (1 − k²)K(k))/(1 + k), with the descending form E(k) = (1 + k′)E((1 − k′)/(1 + k′)) − k′K(k), extending the K(k) transformation announced earlier (DLMF §19.8(ii)).

name: Perfectoid fields
text: a complete non-archimedean field is perfectoid exactly when it is not discretely valued, ‖p‖ < 1 and Frobenius is surjective on 𝒪_K/p; ℂ_p is one and ℚ_p is not (Scholze, *Perfectoid spaces*, Def. 3.1).

name: Cartesian fibrations of simplicial sets
text: an inner fibration p : X → S in which every edge of S ending at p(y) lifts to a p-Cartesian edge ending at y, the ∞-categorical Grothendieck fibrations, stable under base change and composition (Lurie, *Higher Topos Theory*, Def. 2.4.2.1).

## What it says
The Schoenflies theorem in the plane: every Jordan curve $C \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is the image of the unit circle under a homeomorphism of the whole plane, which also carries the open unit disc onto the inside of $C$ and the closed unit disc onto the inside together with $C$.

- `{C : Set ℂ}`: a subset $C$ of the plane.
- `(hC : IsJordanCurve C)`: $C$ is a Jordan curve, that is, homeomorphic to the circle (`TauCeti.IsJordanCurve C` is `Nonempty (C ≃ₜ Circle)`).
- The conclusion: there is a homeomorphism $e$ of $\mathbb{C}$ onto itself (`ℂ ≃ₜ ℂ`) with $e(S^1) = C$, $e(D) = \operatorname{filledHull}(C) \setminus C$ and $e(\bar D) = \operatorname{filledHull}(C)$, where $S^1$, $D$, $\bar D$ are `sphere 0 1`, `ball 0 1`, `closedBall 0 1`.

`TauCeti.filledHull C` is the set of points whose connected component in the complement of $C$ is bounded; so `filledHull C \ C` is the bounded complementary component, the inside of $C$, and `filledHull C` is its closure. This is the theorem as Moise states it for the plane: the pair $(\mathbb{R}^2, C)$ is homeomorphic to $(\mathbb{R}^2, S^1)$.

## References and tests
- A. Schoenflies, *Beiträge zur Theorie der Punktmengen. III*, Math. Ann. 62 (1906), 286–328.
- E. E. Moise, *Geometric Topology in Dimensions 2 and 3*, Springer GTM 47 (1977), for the planar Schoenflies theorem.
- Ch. Pommerenke, *Boundary Behaviour of Conformal Maps*, Springer (1992), Chapter 2, for Carathéodory's theorem, from which the result is derived.
- Roadmap: [GeometricTopology, Layer 2, locally flat embeddings](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/GeometricTopology/README.md#L327), target `schoenflies-theorem`.
- `TauCeti.IsJordanCurve.exists_homeomorph_image_sphere_of_mem` — the stronger form it is read off from: the homeomorphism can send $0$ to any prescribed point of the inside.
- `TauCeti.IsJordanCurve.exists_homeomorph_image_inner_eq_zero` — the version on the 2-sphere, derived from this one by stereographic projection; it exercises the planar theorem at infinity.

## Lean subtleties
- `ℂ ≃ₜ ℂ` is a homeomorphism of the plane: only the topology of $\mathbb{C}$ is used, not its complex structure.
- `IsJordanCurve C` is a proposition, the existence of a homeomorphism with the circle; the theorem chooses nothing, it asserts that some $e$ exists.
- `filledHull C` is defined by boundedness of components of the complement; the inside is nonempty (`TauCeti.IsJordanCurve.nonempty_filledHull_sdiff`), so no degenerate case arises.

## What it says
The sharp isoperimetric inequality in a Euclidean space of dimension $n \ge 1$: every Lebesgue-measurable set $s$ of finite positive volume satisfies $n^n \omega_n |s|^{n-1} \le P(s)^n$, with $\omega_n$ the volume of the unit ball and $P(s)$ the perimeter of $s$ in the whole space.

- `{E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] [MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E]`: a finite-dimensional real inner product space; `volume` is its Lebesgue measure, giving an orthonormal unit cube volume $1$.
- `{s : Set E} (hs : NullMeasurableSet s volume)`: a Lebesgue-measurable set.
- `(hμs : volume s ≠ ⊤)`: finite volume; `(hn : finrank ℝ E ≠ 0)`: $n = \dim E \ge 1$; `(hs0 : volume s ≠ 0)`: positive volume.
- The conclusion, in the extended nonnegative reals: $n^n \omega_n |s|^{n-1} \le P(s)^n$, where `perimeter volume ⊤ s` is `TauCeti.perimeter`, the total variation of the indicator of $s$ on the whole space `⊤`, the supremum of $\int_s \operatorname{div}\varphi$ over test vector fields with $\|\varphi\| \le 1$.

This is the isoperimetric inequality for sets of finite perimeter in its sharp form (Maggi, Chapters 13–14), with no boundedness, connectedness or regularity hypothesis. Unlike the textbook statement, the perimeter may be infinite, and the equality case, that only balls attain equality, is not included.

## References and tests
- F. Maggi, *Sets of Finite Perimeter and Geometric Variational Problems*, Chapters 13–14.
- R. J. Gardner, *The Brunn–Minkowski inequality*, Section 5.
- Roadmap: [Isoperimetry, I4 — Sharp Euclidean perimeter inequality and ball rigidity](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/Isoperimetry/README.md#L225), target `sharp-perimeter-inequality` (partial: the rigidity half is not here).
- `TauCeti.perimeter_ball_pow` — balls attain equality: $P(B)^n = n^n \omega_n |B|^{n-1}$, so the constant is sharp.
- `ConvexBody.finrank_pow_mul_volume_ball_mul_volume_pow_le_perimeter_pow` — the same inequality for convex bodies of positive volume, proved separately from Brunn–Minkowski; this theorem recovers it.
- `MeasureTheory.NullMeasurableSet.mul_volume_real_rpow_mul_le_perimeter_toReal` — the real-valued form $n\,\omega_n^{1/n} |s|^{1-1/n} \le P(s)$ for sets of finite perimeter.

## Lean subtleties
- All quantities live in `ℝ≥0∞`: a set of infinite perimeter satisfies the inequality trivially. Finite volume cannot be dropped: the complement of a ball has finite perimeter.
- `finrank ℝ E - 1` is truncated subtraction on `ℕ`; `hn` makes it the honest $n - 1$.
- `⊤` is the whole space as an open set, so this is the full perimeter, not a relative one.

## What it says
The Hilbert class field of a number field $K$ is its maximal unramified abelian extension: a finite abelian extension $L/K$ lies in it exactly when $L/K$ is unramified at every finite prime and at every infinite place.

- `{K : Type} [Field K] [NumberField K]`, `{L : Type} [Field L] [NumberField L] [Algebra K L]`: number fields $K \subseteq L$.
- `[IsAbelianGalois K L]`: $L/K$ is Galois with abelian Galois group.
- `(ι : L →ₐ[K] SeparableClosure K)`: a $K$-embedding of $L$ into a fixed separable closure $K^s$; `ι.fieldRange` is its image, an intermediate field of $K^s/K$.
- The conclusion: `ι.fieldRange ≤ hilbertClassField K`, the image of $L$ is contained in the Hilbert class field, if and only if every nonzero prime $w$ of $\mathcal{O}_L$ (`HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 L)`) is unramified over $\mathcal{O}_K$ (`Algebra.IsUnramifiedAt (𝓞 K) w.asIdeal`) and every infinite place of $L$ is unramified over $K$ (`IsUnramifiedAtInfinitePlaces K L`: no real place of $K$ becomes complex).

`TauCeti.ClassFieldTheory.hilbertClassField K` is the ray class field of the trivial modulus, so the theorem is `isAdmissibleModulus_iff_le_rayClassField` combined with the fact that the trivial modulus is admissible exactly for everywhere unramified extensions. With the Artin isomorphism $\mathrm{Cl}(K) \cong \mathrm{Gal}(H/K)$ this is the standard characterisation (Neukirch, Chapter VI, §6), "unramified" meaning at finite and infinite places, as there.

## References and tests
- J. Neukirch, *Algebraic Number Theory*, Chapter VI, §6.
- J. S. Milne, *Class Field Theory*, Chapter V.
- Roadmap: [ClassFieldTheory, Layer 13: norm theorems and class fields](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/ClassFieldTheory/README.md#L1834), target `hilbert-class-field-maximal-unramified`.
- `TauCeti.ClassFieldTheory.isUnramifiedAt_hilbertClassField` — the forward direction applied to $H$ itself: every prime of $H$ is unramified over $\mathcal{O}_K$.
- `TauCeti.ClassFieldTheory.isUnramifiedAtInfinitePlaces_hilbertClassField` — likewise $H/K$ is unramified at the infinite places.
- `TauCeti.ClassFieldTheory.fieldRange_le_narrowHilbertClassField_iff` — the narrow companion: without the infinite-place condition the field becomes the narrow Hilbert class field.
- `TauCeti.ClassFieldTheory.hilbertClassArtinEquiv` — $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathcal{O}_K) \cong \mathrm{Gal}(H/K)$, the other half of the usual description.

## Lean subtleties
- `Algebra.IsUnramifiedAt (𝓞 K) w.asIdeal` says the localisation of $\mathcal{O}_L$ at $w$ is formally unramified over $\mathcal{O}_K$: ramification index $1$ with separable residue extension.
- `IsUnramifiedAtInfinitePlaces K L` compares the multiplicity of each infinite place of $L$ with that of its restriction to $K$; a complex place over a real place is ramified.
- `ι` is injective, being a homomorphism of fields; the theorem is about the subfield $\iota(L)$ of $K^s$, since `hilbertClassField K` is an intermediate field of $K^s/K$.

## What it says
Conjugacy of Cartan subalgebras: in a finite-dimensional Lie algebra with nondegenerate Killing form over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, any two Cartan subalgebras are conjugate under the group of inner automorphisms.

- `{K L : Type*} [Field K] [LieRing L] [LieAlgebra K L]`: a Lie algebra $L$ over a field $K$.
- `[CharZero K] [IsAlgClosed K]`: $K$ has characteristic zero and is algebraically closed.
- `[LieAlgebra ℚ L]`: a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space structure on $L$, needed to form the exponentials $\exp(\operatorname{ad} x)$; any $K$-Lie algebra in characteristic zero has one.
- `[FiniteDimensional K L] [LieAlgebra.IsKilling K L]`: $L$ is finite-dimensional with nondegenerate Killing form, which in characteristic zero is the semisimple case.
- `(H H' : LieSubalgebra K L) [H.IsCartanSubalgebra] [H'.IsCartanSubalgebra]`: two Cartan subalgebras, nilpotent and self-normalising.
- The conclusion: there is $g$ in `TauCeti.intLieAlgebra K L`, the subgroup $\mathrm{Int}(L)$ of $\mathrm{GL}(L)$ generated by the $\exp(\operatorname{ad} x)$ with $\operatorname{ad} x$ nilpotent, whose automorphism `intLieAlgebraLieEquiv g` of $L$ maps $H$ onto $H'$ (`H.map … = H'`).

This is Chevalley's conjugacy theorem in the form of Serre, Chapter III, and Bourbaki, Chapter VII, §3, proved by the density argument: the conjugates of a Cartan subalgebra contain a nonempty principal open set. The literature states it for every finite-dimensional Lie algebra in characteristic zero over an algebraically closed field; this statement assumes a nondegenerate Killing form, and uses the group generated by all nilpotent $\exp(\operatorname{ad} x)$, as the standard form does.

## References and tests
- J.-P. Serre, *Complex Semisimple Lie Algebras*, Springer, 1987, Chapter III.
- N. Bourbaki, *Lie Groups and Lie Algebras*, Chapters 7–9, Chapter VII, §3.

None.

## Lean subtleties
- The hypotheses in square brackets are typeclasses, found by Lean automatically; `[LieAlgebra ℚ L]` is one of them and must be supplied, although it is determined by the $K$-structure.
- `IsKilling` is Mathlib's name for "the Killing form is nondegenerate", not standard terminology; in characteristic zero it is semisimplicity, by Cartan's criterion.
- `intLieAlgebra K L` is a subgroup of the general linear group of $L$ as a $K$-vector space; `intLieAlgebraLieEquiv g` repackages its element as a Lie algebra automorphism, and `.toLieHom` as a homomorphism so that `H.map` applies.

## What it says
The KAK decomposition of $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ and $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$: every matrix of determinant one is $U\,\mathrm{diag}(d)\,V$ with $U$, $V$ special orthogonal (over $\mathbb{R}$) or special unitary (over $\mathbb{C}$) and $d$ positive, decreasing and of product one, and the diagonal $d$ is unique.

- `{𝕜 : Type*} [RCLike 𝕜]`: the scalar field is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
- `{n : ℕ}`, `(g : SpecialLinearGroup (Fin n) 𝕜)`: an $n \times n$ matrix of determinant $1$, indexed by `Fin n` $= \{0, \dots, n-1\}$.
- The conclusion, `∃! d : Fin n → ℝ, …`: there is exactly one real vector $d$ such that all $d_i > 0$, $d$ is non-increasing (`Antitone d`), $\prod_i d_i = 1$, and there exist $U$, $V$ in `specialUnitaryGroup (Fin n) 𝕜`, the unitary matrices of determinant $1$, with $g = U \,\mathrm{diag}(d)\, V$ as matrices.

This is the Cartan decomposition $G = K \overline{A^+} K$ (Knapp, Chapter VII) in the matrix model $G = \mathrm{SL}_n$, $K = \mathrm{SO}(n)$ or $\mathrm{SU}(n)$, $A$ the positive diagonal matrices of determinant one, the closed positive Weyl chamber being the decreasing diagonals; uniqueness of the chamber element is the "unique up to the Weyl group" clause. Equivalently it is the singular value decomposition (Horn–Johnson, Section 2.6) restricted to determinant one. The statement for a general real reductive group is not here.

## References and tests
- A. W. Knapp, *Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction*, second edition, Chapter VII.
- R. A. Horn and C. R. Johnson, *Matrix Analysis*, second edition, Section 2.6.
- Roadmap: [RepresentationTheory/LieGroups, Layer 9, restricted roots and the KAK decomposition](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/RepresentationTheory/LieGroups/README.md#L458), target `kak-decomposition-sl-n`.

- `Matrix.exists_specialUnitary_mul_mul_specialUnitary_iff_singularValues_eq_and_det_eq` — two square matrices lie in the same two-sided special unitary orbit exactly when their singular values and determinants agree.

## Lean subtleties
- `∃!` asserts uniqueness of $d$ only; $U$ and $V$ are not unique, and repeated singular values are allowed.
- `Antitone d` means $i \le j \Rightarrow d_j \le d_i$ on `Fin n`: largest singular value first.
- Over $\mathbb{R}$, `specialUnitaryGroup` is the special orthogonal group, the star of a real matrix being its transpose.
- `(d i : 𝕜)` and `(g : Matrix …)` are coercions: the real $d_i$ viewed in $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and the group element as a matrix.

## What it says
Kronecker's theorem for linear flows on tori: the line $t \mapsto \theta + t\nu$ in the torus $(\mathbb{R}/p\mathbb{Z})^\iota$ is dense if and only if its velocity $\nu$ is nonresonant, that is, $\sum_i k_i \nu_i \ne 0$ for every nonzero integer vector $k$.

- `{ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]`: a finite index set, the coordinates of the torus.
- `{p : ℝ} (hp : p ≠ 0)`: a nonzero period; `AddCircle p` is $\mathbb{R}/p\mathbb{Z}$.
- `(θ ν : ι → ℝ)`: the starting point and the velocity, as real vectors.
- The conclusion: `DenseRange (fun t ↦ fun i ↦ ((θ i + ν i * t : ℝ) : AddCircle p))`, the image of $\mathbb{R}$ under $t \mapsto (\theta_i + \nu_i t \bmod p)_i$ is dense in $\prod_i \mathbb{R}/p\mathbb{Z}$, if and only if `∀ k : ι → ℤ, ∑ i, (k i : ℝ) * ν i = 0 → k = 0`.

This is the dynamical form of Kronecker's theorem, the minimality criterion for linear flows on the torus (Arnold, Section 51), stated in both directions and for an arbitrary period $p$ rather than only $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$.

- V. I. Arnold, *Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics*, second edition, GTM 60, Springer, 1989, Section 51.

- `TauCeti.closure_range_oscillatorActionAngle_eq_iff` — the application it was made for: the orbit of finitely many uncoupled harmonic oscillators, in action–angle coordinates, is dense in its invariant torus exactly when the frequencies are nonresonant. This is the theorem with $p = 2\pi$, so it checks a period other than $1$.

## Lean subtleties
- `AddCircle p` is $\mathbb{R}/p\mathbb{Z}$ for any real $p \ne 0$; a negative $p$ gives the same group as $|p|$. The hypothesis `hp` excludes `AddCircle 0`, which is $\mathbb{R}$ itself.
- The double coercion `((… : ℝ) : AddCircle p)` forms the real number $\theta_i + \nu_i t$ and reduces it modulo $p$.
- `ι → AddCircle p` carries the product topology, and `DenseRange` says the closure of the range is everything.
- `k = 0` means $k$ is the zero function. When `ι` is empty both sides hold: the torus is a point and the only integer vector is $0$.

## What it says
Weyl's equidistribution theorem for linear flows: along a nonresonant line in the unit torus, the time averages of a continuous function converge to its space average.

- `{d : Type*} [Fintype d]`: a finite index set; `UnitAddTorus d` is the torus $(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^d$, the functions from `d` to `UnitAddCircle` $= \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$.
- `{ν : d → ℝ} (hν : ∀ k : d → ℤ, ∑ i, (k i : ℝ) * ν i = 0 → k = 0)`: the velocity $\nu$ is nonresonant, no nonzero integer vector is orthogonal to it.
- `(θ : d → ℝ)`: the starting point of the line.
- `(f : C(UnitAddTorus d, ℂ))`: a continuous complex-valued function on the torus.
- The conclusion: as $T \to +\infty$ (`atTop` on `ℝ`), $T^{-1} \int_0^T f(\theta + t\nu)\,dt$ tends to $\int f$, the integral of $f$ against `volume` on the torus, which has total mass $1$ and so is the space average.

This is the continuous-time Weyl theorem, as in Arnold, Section 51, for a single line and every continuous $f$; the proof is Weyl's, computing the averages on the characters $e^{2\pi i \langle n, x\rangle}$ and extending by uniform density of trigonometric polynomials.

- `∫ t in 0..T` is the interval integral and `T⁻¹ •` the scalar multiple; Lean sets $0^{-1} = 0$, irrelevant for the limit as $T \to +\infty$.

## What it says
The coarea formula for maps with surjective derivative: for $f : E \to F$ differentiable with surjective derivative at every point of a Lebesgue-measurable set $s$, integrating the $(\dim E - \dim F)$-dimensional Hausdorff measures of the fibres $s \cap f^{-1}(y)$ over $y \in F$ equals the integral over $s$ of the coarea Jacobian $J f(x) = \sqrt{\det(Df(x)\,Df(x)^*)}$.

- `{E F : Type*}`, with typeclasses `[InnerProductSpace ℝ _] [FiniteDimensional ℝ _] [BorelSpace _]`: finite-dimensional real inner product spaces with Lebesgue measure `volume`.
- `{f : E → F} {s : Set E}` with `(hs : NullMeasurableSet s)`: a map and a Lebesgue-measurable set.
- `(hd : ∀ x ∈ s, DifferentiableAt ℝ f x)`, `(hsurj : ∀ x ∈ s, Surjective (fderiv ℝ f x))`: on $s$, $f$ is differentiable with derivative onto $F$.
- The conclusion: $\int_F \mathcal{H}^{n-m}(s \cap f^{-1}\{y\})\,dy = \int_s \operatorname{normDet}((Df(x))^*)\,dx$, where `μHE[k]` is Mathlib's normalised $k$-dimensional Hausdorff measure on $E$ and `LinearMap.normDet` of the adjoint $Df(x)^* : F \to E$ is $\sqrt{\det(Df\,Df^*)}$.

This is the regular part of the coarea formula of Federer, §3.2, and Evans–Gariepy, §3.4 (the case $Jf > 0$ of §3.4.3). The textbook statement is for Lipschitz $f$ and includes the critical set $\{Jf = 0\}$; here Lipschitz is replaced by pointwise differentiability on $s$, the critical set is excluded by hypothesis, and the weighted and real-valued forms are absent.

## What it says
The Godement resolution of a sheaf, as a functor: to a sheaf $F$ on $X$ with values in $C$ it assigns the cochain complex $G^0(F) \to G^1(F) \to G^2(F) \to \cdots$ built by iterating the canonical embedding of a sheaf into the product of its stalks.

- `(C : Type*) [Category.{u} C] [Abelian C] [HasColimits C] [HasProducts.{u} C]`: an abelian category with colimits and products indexed by the points of $X$.
- `(X : TopCat.{u})`: a topological space; `[HasSheafify (Opens.grothendieckTopology X) C]` makes `X.Sheaf C` abelian.
- The value: a functor `X.Sheaf C ⥤ CochainComplex (X.Sheaf C) ℕ`, defined as `(toGodement C X).resolution`, the resolution `CategoryTheory.NatTrans.resolution` of the natural monomorphism `toGodement C X : F ⟶ G(F)`. Writing $G(F) = \prod_x (i_x)_* F_x$ for the Godement sheaf (`TauCeti.Topology.godement`), the terms are $G^n(F) = G(Z^n F)$ with $Z^0 F = F$ and $Z^{n+1} F = \operatorname{coker}(Z^n F \to G(Z^n F))$, and the differential $G(Z^n F) \to G(Z^{n+1} F)$ is the cokernel projection followed by the canonical embedding of the cokernel.

This is Godement's canonical resolution (Godement, Chapter II, §4.3) in his iterated-cokernel form; the Stacks Project (Section 20.30) and the roadmap paragraph present the same flasque resolution in cosimplicial form, $f_* f^* F \to f_* f^* f_* f^* F \to \cdots$ for $f$ the identity from $X$ with the discrete topology.

## What it says
For sheaves valued in an abelian concrete category with the usual stalk hypotheses, such as modules over a ring or abelian groups, the Godement resolution of $F$ is a resolution of $F$: the augmentation from $F$ in degree $0$ is a quasi-isomorphism, so $0 \to F \to G^0(F) \to G^1(F) \to \cdots$ is exact.

- `(C : Type*) [Category.{u} C] [Abelian C] [HasColimits C] [HasProducts.{u} C]`, `(X : TopCat.{u})`, `[HasSheafify … C]`: as for `TauCeti.Topology.godementResolution`.
- `[ConcreteCategory.{u} C FC]` with `[PreservesFilteredColimits (forget C)] [HasLimits C] [PreservesLimits (forget C)] [(forget C).ReflectsIsomorphisms]`: $C$ is concrete and its forgetful functor to sets preserves filtered colimits and limits and reflects isomorphisms, so that stalks are computed on underlying sets and detect monomorphisms.
- `(F : X.Sheaf C)`: a sheaf.
- The conclusion: `QuasiIso ((toGodementResolution C X).app F)`, the morphism of cochain complexes from `single₀ F`, $F$ in degree $0$ and $0$ elsewhere, to the Godement complex induces isomorphisms on all cohomology objects.

This is the statement that the Godement complex resolves $F$ (Godement, Chapter II, §4.3; Stacks, Section 20.30). It is the general fact that iterating a natural monomorphism on cokernels gives a resolution, applied to `toGodement C X`, whose components are monomorphisms because a section is determined by its germs; the concrete-category hypotheses are what that monomorphism needs.

## What it says
A *marked simplicial set*: a simplicial set with a distinguished set of edges, the marked ones, containing every degenerate edge. Three fields:

- `toSSet : SSet.{u}`: the underlying simplicial set $X$; `u` is the universe of its sets of simplices.
- `marked : Set (toSSet _⦋1⦌)`: a set of edges of $X$, `toSSet _⦋1⦌` being its set of $1$-simplices.
- `σ_mem_marked`: for every vertex $x$, the degenerate edge $s_0 x$ (`toSSet.σ 0 x`) is marked.

The file makes these the objects of a category: a morphism `Hom X Y` is a map of simplicial sets sending marked edges to marked edges. This is Lurie's Definition 3.1.0.1, a pair $(X, \mathcal{E})$ with $\mathcal{E}$ a set of edges containing the degenerate ones, with the same morphisms. The extreme markings $X^\flat$ and $X^\sharp$ of that definition are `flat` and `sharp`.

## What it says
For simplicial sets $X$, $S$ and a map `p : X ⟶ S`, the class says that $p$ is a Cartesian fibration, in two parts.

- `extends InnerFibration p`: $p$ is an inner fibration, Mathlib's class for the right lifting property against the inner horn inclusions $\Lambda^n_i \to \Delta^n$, $0 < i < n$.
- `exists_isCartesian_lift`: for every vertex $y$ of $X$, vertex $s$ of $S$ and edge $e : s \to p(y)$ of $S$ (`Edge s (p.app _ y)`), there are a vertex $x$ and an edge $f : x \to y$ of $X$ which is $p$-Cartesian (`f.IsCartesian p`, the slice trivial-fibration test) with image $e$: `(f.map p).edge = e.edge`.

This is Lurie's Definition 2.4.2.1: an inner fibration along which every edge of the base with a prescribed lift of its target lifts to a Cartesian edge. The lemmas `of_isPullback` and `comp` are Proposition 2.4.2.3. The coCartesian dual, with a prescribed source, is not defined here.

## What it says
For simplicial sets $X$, $S$, vertices `x y : X _⦋0⦌`, an edge `f : Edge x y` (a $1$-simplex with source $x$ and target $y$) and a map `p : X ⟶ S`, the proposition `f.IsCartesian p` says that $f$ is $p$-Cartesian. Its value is

`(monomorphisms SSet.{u}).rlp (slice.restrictionMap (stdSimplex.δ 0) p (yonedaEquiv.symm f.edge))`,

that is: the map of slices
$$X_{/f} \longrightarrow X_{/y} \times_{S_{/p(y)}} S_{/p(f)}$$
has the right lifting property against every monomorphism, so is a trivial fibration. Here `yonedaEquiv.symm f.edge : Δ[1] ⟶ X` is the edge as a map from the standard $1$-simplex, `stdSimplex.δ 0 : Δ[0] ⟶ Δ[1]` its target vertex, and `slice.restrictionMap` restricts a cone over $f$ to a cone over $y$ and pushes it forward along $p$.

This is Lurie's Definition 2.4.1.1, with one difference: Lurie states it for an inner fibration $p$, whereas the predicate is defined here for every map $p$; the inner-fibration hypothesis enters in `SSet.CartesianFibration`.

## What it says
For $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d)$ with $d$ squarefree, the negative Pell equation $x^2 - d y^2 = -1$ has an integer solution if and only if $\mathcal{O}_K$ has a unit of norm $-1$.

- `{K : Type*} [Field K] [NumberField K]`: a number field.
- `{θ : 𝓞 K} {d : ℤ}`: an algebraic integer $\theta$ of $K$ and an integer $d$.
- `hmin : minpoly ℤ θ = X ^ 2 - C d`: the minimal polynomial of $\theta$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ is $X^2 - d$.
- `hgen : Algebra.adjoin ℚ {(θ : K)} = ⊤`: $K = \mathbb{Q}(\theta)$, so $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d)$.
- `hsf : Squarefree d`.
- Conclusion: integers $x, y$ with $x^2 - d y^2 = -1$ exist iff some unit $u$ of $\mathcal{O}_K$ has field norm $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(u) = -1$.

This is the classical comparison. Solutions are the units of norm $-1$ of the order $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d]$; for $d \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ a unit of $\mathcal{O}_K$ may have half-integral coordinates, as $(1 + \sqrt 5)/2$ does, and its cube then lies in the order. No sign of $d$ is assumed; for negative $d$ both sides are false.

## What it says
Over a right Noetherian ring $A$, a left module $M$ with a finite projective presentation and $\operatorname{Ext}^i(\operatorname{Tr} M, A) = 0$ for $1 \le i \le k$ is a $k$-th syzygy of finitely generated projective modules.

- `{A : Type u} [Ring A]`: a ring, not necessarily commutative; `P₀ P₁ M` with `[AddCommGroup] [Module A]`: left $A$-modules; `p`, `π`: $A$-linear maps.
- `[HasExt.{w} (ModuleCat.{u} Aᵐᵒᵖ)]`: right $A$-modules have Ext groups in universe `w`, Mathlib's assumption for `Ext`.
- `[IsNoetherianRing Aᵐᵒᵖ]`: $A$ is right Noetherian.
- `[Module.Finite A P₀] [Module.Projective A P₀]`, and the same for $P_1$: finitely generated projective.
- `hexact : Function.Exact p π`, `hπ : Function.Surjective π`: $P_1 \to P_0 \to M \to 0$ is exact.
- `(k : ℕ)` and `hext`: for $0 < i \le k$ every element of $\operatorname{Ext}^i(\operatorname{Tr} M, A)$ is zero, where `AuslanderReitenTranspose p` is the cokernel of $\operatorname{Hom}_A(P_0, A) \to \operatorname{Hom}_A(P_1, A)$, a right module.
- Conclusion: `ModuleCat.of A M` is a $k$-th syzygy for the property "finitely generated projective": $k$ short exact sequences $0 \to M \to Q_1 \to M_1 \to 0$, $0 \to M_1 \to Q_2 \to M_2 \to 0$, … with every $Q_i$ finitely generated projective, which splice to an exact $0 \to M \to Q_1 \to \cdots \to Q_k$.

This is Auslander and Bridger's theorem that $k$-torsionfree modules are $k$-th syzygies, $k$-torsionfree being defined through the transpose. The ring is only assumed right Noetherian; the converse implication is not part of the statement.

## What it says
Two unnormalized Markov traces on the Temperley–Lieb tower are equal.

- `{R : Type*} [CommSemiring R] {δ : R}`: a commutative semiring of scalars and a loop parameter $\delta \in R$.
- `{tr tr' : ∀ n : ℕ, TemperleyLieb R δ n →ₗ[R] R}`: two families, indexed by the number of strands $n$, of $R$-linear forms on the Temperley–Lieb algebra $TL_n(R, \delta)$, presented by generators $e_0, \dots, e_{n-2}$ with $e_i^2 = \delta e_i$, $e_i e_{i \pm 1} e_i = e_i$ and far commutation.
- `htr`, `htr'`: both are Markov traces (`IsMarkovTrace`): $tr_n(1) = \delta^n$, $tr_n(xy) = tr_n(yx)$, $tr_{n+2}(\iota x) = \delta\, tr_{n+1}(x)$ and $tr_{n+2}(\iota x \cdot e_n) = tr_{n+1}(x)$, $\iota$ adding a straight strand.
- Conclusion: `tr = tr'`.

This is the uniqueness of the Markov trace on the Temperley–Lieb tower, as in Jones' *Index for subfactors*: on $n + 2$ strands every element is a combination of $\iota a$ and $\iota a \cdot e_n \cdot \iota b$ (`span_strandIncl_union_strandIncl_mul_e_last_mul_eq_top`), whose traces are determined one level down. It holds over every commutative semiring and every $\delta$, with no invertibility; it is the uniqueness half of the roadmap's existence-and-uniqueness headline. Existence is not asserted here.

## What it says
The predicate that a family of linear forms on the Temperley–Lieb tower is an unnormalized Markov trace.

- `(R : Type*) [CommSemiring R] (δ : R)`: scalars and the loop parameter $\delta$.
- `(tr : ∀ n : ℕ, TemperleyLieb R δ n →ₗ[R] R)`: for every number of strands $n$, an $R$-linear form $tr_n$ on $TL_n(R, \delta)$, presented by generators $e_0, \dots, e_{n-2}$ with $e_i^2 = \delta e_i$, $e_i e_{i\pm1} e_i = e_i$ and far commutation.

Four fields:

- `map_one`: $tr_n(1) = \delta^n$;
- `map_mul_comm`: $tr_n(xy) = tr_n(yx)$;
- `map_strandIncl`: $tr_{n+2}(\iota x) = \delta\, tr_{n+1}(x)$ for $x \in TL_{n+1}$, $\iota$ = `strandIncl` adding a straight strand on the right;
- `map_strandIncl_mul_e_last`: $tr_{n+2}(\iota x \cdot e_n) = tr_{n+1}(x)$, the Markov property, $e_n$ = `e δ (Fin.last n)` the last generator on $n + 2$ strands.

This is Jones' Markov trace on the tower $TL_1 \subset TL_2 \subset \cdots$, division-free: the identity on $n$ strands has trace $\delta^n$ ($n$ loops), and capping the last strand with $e_n$ removes it. With $E_i = e_i/\delta$ and the normalised trace $\delta^{-n} tr_n$, the last field is the usual $\operatorname{Tr}(x E_n) = \delta^{-2}\operatorname{Tr}(x)$.

## What it says
A *perfectoid field* at $p$: a complete, ultrametric, nontrivially normed field which is a perfectoid Tate ring at $p$.

- `(p : ℕ)`: a natural number; primality is not part of the class, and is assumed as `[Fact p.Prime]` by the results needing it.
- `(K : Type*) [NontriviallyNormedField K]`: a field with a multiplicative norm which is not trivial: some $x$ has $\|x\| > 1$.
- `[IsUltrametricDist K]`: $\|x + y\| \le \max(\|x\|, \|y\|)$; `[CompleteSpace K]`: complete.
- The single parent field, `extends IsPerfectoidTateRing p K`: for the Tate structure `IsTateRing.of_nontriviallyNormedField` (ring of definition the closed unit ball $K^\circ$, pseudouniformisers the $\varpi$ with $0 < \|\varpi\| < 1$), $K^\circ$ is bounded and some pseudouniformiser $\varpi$ has $\varpi^p \mid p$ in $K^\circ$ with Frobenius $K^\circ/\varpi \to K^\circ/\varpi^p$ bijective.

This is Scholze's definition in *Étale cohomology of diamonds*: a perfectoid Tate ring which is a nonarchimedean field. His definition in *Perfectoid spaces* (not discretely valued, $\|p\| < 1$, Frobenius surjective on $K^\circ/p$) is the theorem `isPerfectoidField_iff`. The norm is real-valued, so the valuation has rank one, as in both sources.

## What it says
Scholze's characterisation: a complete ultrametric nontrivially normed field $K$ is perfectoid at a prime $p$ exactly when

1. its norms accumulate at $1$: for every real $\varepsilon > 1$ there is $x \in K$ with $1 < \|x\| < \varepsilon$, so $K$ is not discretely valued;
2. $\|p\| < 1$, that is, $K$ has residue characteristic $p$;
3. the $p$-th power map on $K^\circ/p$ is surjective, where `ModP (powerBoundedSubring K) p` is the quotient of the closed unit ball $K^\circ$ by the ideal $(p)$.

- `{p : ℕ} [Fact p.Prime]`: a prime, primality carried as a typeclass fact.
- `{K : Type*} [NontriviallyNormedField K] [IsUltrametricDist K] [CompleteSpace K]`: a complete field with a nontrivial ultrametric real norm.
- Conclusion: `IsPerfectoidField p K ↔ (i) ∧ (ii) ∧ (iii)`.

This is Proposition 3.8 of *Étale cohomology of diamonds*: the Tate-ring definition of a perfectoid field (`IsPerfectoidField`) agrees with *Perfectoid spaces*, Definition 3.1, a complete nonarchimedean field of residue characteristic $p$, not discretely valued, with Frobenius surjective on $\mathcal{O}_K/p$. Condition (i) cannot be dropped: $\mathbb{Q}_p$ satisfies (ii) and (iii).

## What it says
The Seifert genus $g(K)$ of a smooth knot $K$ in a sphere: the least genus of a Seifert surface bounded by $K$.

- `{E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]`, `{n : ℕ} [Fact (finrank ℝ E = n + 1)]`: a real inner product space $E$ of dimension $n + 1$ (the dimension is a typeclass hypothesis), so `sphere (0 : E) 1` is $S^n$; the classical case is $n = 3$.
- `(K : SmoothCircleEmbedding (𝓡 n) (sphere (0 : E) 1))`: a smooth embedding of the unit circle into $S^n$, a parametrized smooth knot.
- The value, in `ℕ∞` $= \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$: `⨅ S : SeifertSurface K, (S.genus : ℕ∞)`, the infimum over all Seifert surfaces $S$ of $K$ of their genus.

This is the genus of a knot as in Lickorish, Chapter 2, the least genus of a Seifert surface, with two differences: the knot may lie in $S^n$ for any $n$, and the value $\infty$ is allowed when $K$ bounds no Seifert surface, since Seifert's existence theorem is not proved in the library.

## What it says
A Seifert surface for a smooth knot $K$ in a sphere $S^n$: a compact, connected, orientable smooth surface with boundary, smoothly embedded in $S^n$ with boundary exactly the knot.

- `{E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]`, `{n : ℕ} [Fact (finrank ℝ E = n + 1)]`: a real inner product space $E$ of dimension $n + 1$; `sphere (0 : E) 1` is $S^n$.
- `(K : SmoothCircleEmbedding (𝓡 n) (sphere (0 : E) 1))`: a smooth embedding of the unit circle into $S^n$, the knot.

Its fields:

- `carrier : Type`: the surface $S$.
- `[chartedSpace : ChartedSpace (EuclideanHalfSpace 2) carrier]`, `[isManifold : IsManifold (𝓡∂ 2) ∞ carrier]`: $S$ is a smooth surface with boundary, charted on the closed half-plane.
- `[compactSpace]`, `[connectedSpace]`, `[orientable : Orientable (𝓡∂ 2) carrier]`: $S$ is compact, connected and orientable.
- `toFun : carrier → sphere (0 : E) 1`, `isSmoothEmbedding : IsSmoothEmbedding (𝓡∂ 2) (𝓡 n) ∞ toFun`: a map $\Phi : S \to S^n$, a $C^\infty$ immersion and topological embedding.
- `image_boundary : toFun '' (𝓡∂ 2).boundary carrier = range K`: $\Phi$ carries the boundary of $S$ onto the image of $K$.

This is the Seifert surface of Lickorish, Chapter 2, and Rolfsen, Chapter 5, with the knot in $S^n$ for any $n$, the surface smooth rather than piecewise linear, and orientable rather than oriented.

## What it says
Nondegenerate $2$-elementary finite quadratic modules are classified by their order, their Gauss-sum invariant and whether their quadratic form takes values in $\tfrac12\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$.

- `{A B : FiniteQuadraticModule}`: finite abelian groups with a quadratic map $q : A \to \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ whose polar form $q(x+y) - q(x) - q(y)$ is the stored symmetric pairing $b$.
- `(hA : A.IsNondegenerate) (hB : B.IsNondegenerate)`: the adjoint $A \to \mathrm{Hom}(A, \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$ of $b$ is bijective.
- `(h2A : ∀ x : A, 2 • x = 0) (h2B : …)`: every element is killed by $2$, so $A \cong (\mathbb{Z}/2)^a$.
- The conclusion: an isometry $A \cong B$ exists (`Nonempty (Isometry A B)`, an additive isomorphism preserving $q$) if and only if $|A| = |B|$ (`Nat.card`), the Gauss-sum invariants agree (`gaussSign`, the $k \in \mathbb{Z}/8$ with $\sum_{x \in A} e^{2\pi i q(x)} = \sqrt{|A|}\, e^{2\pi i k/8}$), and $q(x) + q(x) = 0$ for all $x \in A$ exactly when the same holds in $B$.

This is the classification of $2$-elementary finite quadratic forms by $a$, the Gauss sign and Nikulin's invariant $\delta$, the arithmetic half of his treatment of $2$-elementary lattices in §3.6. The library's $q$ is $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$-valued, half of Nikulin's $\mathbb{Q}/2\mathbb{Z}$-valued form, so the generator $q_\theta^{(2)}(2)$ takes $\theta/4$ and the condition $\delta = 0$ reads $q(x) \in \tfrac12\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$.

## What it says
Landen's descending transformation of the complete elliptic integral of the second kind.

- `{k : ℝ} (hk : k ^ 2 < 1)`: a real modulus $k$ with $k^2 < 1$, that is $-1 < k < 1$.
- The conclusion: with $k' = \sqrt{1 - k^2}$ and $k_1 = (1 - k')/(1 + k')$,
  $$E(k) = (1 + k')\,E(k_1) - k'\,K(k),$$
  where `legendreEc k` is $E(k) = \int_0^{\pi/2} (1 - k^2 \sin^2\theta)^{1/2}\,d\theta$ and `legendreK k` is $K(k) = \int_0^{\pi/2} (1 - k^2 \sin^2\theta)^{-1/2}\,d\theta$.

This is the descending Landen transformation for $E$ as in DLMF §19.8(ii), with the same normalisation ($k$ is the modulus, not the parameter $m = k^2$). The library states it for all $k$ with $k^2 < 1$, including $k = 0$ and negative $k$, since $E$ and $K$ are even in $k$; the roadmap asks for $0 \le k < 1$.

## What it says
Landen's ascending transformation of the complete elliptic integral of the second kind.

- `{k : ℝ} (hk₀ : 0 ≤ k) (hk₁ : k < 1)`: a real modulus $0 \le k < 1$.
- The conclusion:

## What it says
The universal enveloping algebra of the Lie algebra of a finite-dimensional real Lie group acts faithfully on the smooth functions on the group.

Here $\mathfrak{g}$ is `LeftInvariantDerivation I G`, Mathlib's Lie algebra of $G$: the left-invariant derivations of the algebra $C^\infty(G)$ of smooth real functions (`C^∞⟮I, G; ℝ⟯`), with the commutator bracket. `envelopingAction I G` is the algebra homomorphism $U(\mathfrak{g}) \to \mathrm{End}_\mathbb{R}(C^\infty(G))$ given by the universal property from $X \mapsto (f \mapsto Xf)$, under which $X_1 \cdots X_n$ acts by applying $X_n, \dots, X_1$ in turn. This is the injectivity half of Helgason, Chapter II, §4, Theorem 4.3, which identifies $U(\mathfrak{g})$ with the left-invariant differential operators on $G$. The library's statement is for the action on $C^\infty(G)$; the identification with all left-invariant differential operators is not part of it, as the library has no notion of differential operator.

## What it says

Over any field, the Brauer algebra $B_k(\delta)$ is semisimple as soon as the loop value $\delta$ is transcendental over $\mathbb{Z}$.

- `{K : Type*} [Field K]`: a type $K$ with a field structure, found by typeclass search; nothing is assumed about its characteristic.

The proof goes through the discriminant `TauCeti.BrauerAlgebra.discr k`, one integer polynomial whose value at $\delta$ is the Gram determinant of the regular trace form in the diagram basis: the algebra is semisimple wherever it does not vanish, and the polynomial is nonzero because $B_k(k)$ is semisimple over $\mathbb{Q}$. This is the generic semisimplicity of Brauer and Brown in its weakest form: Wenzl locates the exceptional $\delta$ among the integers, whereas here only the roots of one integer polynomial are excluded, so nothing is said about algebraic values.

## What it says
A finite-dimensional algebra over a field of characteristic zero is semisimple exactly when its regular trace form is nondegenerate: Dickson's trace-form criterion.

- `{K A : Type*} [Field K] [Ring A] [Algebra K A]`: a field $K$ and an associative unital ring $A$, not necessarily commutative, that is a $K$-algebra; all found by typeclass search.
- `[FiniteDimensional K A]`: $A$ is finite-dimensional over $K$.
- `[CharZero K]`: $K$ has characteristic zero.
- The conclusion: `IsSemisimpleRing A`, Mathlib's class saying $A$ is a semisimple module over itself, holds if and only if `Algebra.regularTraceForm K A` is nondegenerate. The regular trace form is $(x, y) \mapsto \operatorname{tr}_K(z \mapsto xyz)$, the trace of left multiplication by $xy$; `Nondegenerate` means separating on both sides: $x = 0$ whenever $\operatorname{tr}(L_{xy}) = 0$ for all $y$, and symmetrically.

This is the criterion as the literature states it in characteristic zero. The direction from nondegeneracy to semisimplicity holds over every field (`TauCeti.isSemisimpleRing_of_nondegenerate_regularTraceForm`); the converse (`TauCeti.nondegenerate_regularTraceForm`) is where characteristic zero enters, since an idempotent operator of trace $0$ must then be $0$. Mathlib's `Algebra.traceForm` is the same form for commutative $A$; the regular trace form needs no commutativity.

Cauchy's formula on an annulus: for $r < |w - c| < R$, $f(w)$ is $\frac{1}{2\pi i}$ times the outer circle integral of $f(z)/(z - w)$ minus the inner one.

- `{s : Set ℂ} (hs : s.Countable)`: a countable exceptional set.
- `(hw : w ∈ ball c R \ closedBall c r)`: $r < |w - c| < R$, so $r < R$ is not needed separately.
- `(hc : ContinuousOn f (closedBall c R \ ball c r))`: $f$ is continuous on the closed annulus $r \le |z - c| \le R$.

This is the two-circle Cauchy formula that begins the Laurent expansion, as in Conway, with the generality of Mathlib's disc formula: vector-valued, differentiability off a countable set, the evaluation point allowed in that set. Nothing is assumed inside the inner circle, so essential singularities at $c$ are allowed.

## What it says
Any two pivotal structures on a finite semisimple rigid linear monoidal category over an algebraically closed field differ by exactly one character of the universal grading group.

- `{C : Type u} [Category.{v} C] [Abelian C] [MonoidalCategory C] [RigidCategory C] [MonoidalPreadditive C] [Linear k C] [MonoidalLinear k C]`: an abelian, rigid, $k$-linear monoidal category with bilinear tensor product; `u`, `v` are universe levels.

- `A ⊗[K] L` and `A ⊗[K] M` carry the base-changed bracket and action; $A = K$ returns the hypothesis.

## What it says
Given a presented group $G = \langle \alpha \mid R \rangle$, a subgroup $K \le G$, a free basis of the preimage $\tilde K$ of $K$ in the free group $F(\alpha)$, and coset representatives $T$, the transversal-conjugated relators rewritten in that basis present $K$: the kernel-identification step of the Reidemeister–Schreier theorem.

- `{α β : Type*}`: alphabets of generators.
- `{R : Set (FreeGroup α)}`: relators; `PresentedGroup R` is $F(\alpha)/\langle\langle R \rangle\rangle$ and `PresentedGroup.mk R` the quotient map.
- `(K : Subgroup (PresentedGroup R))`.
- `(e : FreeGroup β ≃* K.comap (PresentedGroup.mk R))`: an isomorphism from the free group on $\beta$ onto the preimage $\tilde K$ of $K$: a free basis of $\tilde K$ indexed by $\beta$.
- `(T : Set (FreeGroup α))`, `(hT : ∀ g, ∃ h : K.comap (PresentedGroup.mk R), ∃ t ∈ T, (h : FreeGroup α) * t = g)`: every element of $F(\alpha)$ is $h t$ with $h \in \tilde K$, $t \in T$, so $T$ meets every right coset $\tilde K g$.
- The value: an isomorphism `PresentedGroup (PresentedGroup.subgroupRelators R (K.comap (PresentedGroup.mk R)) e T) ≃* K`, the relators being the $w \in F(\beta)$ with $e(w) = t r t^{-1}$, $t \in T$, $r \in R$. It sends the class of $w$ to the class of $e(w)$ (`coe_presentationEquiv_mk`); its inverse rewrites $h \in \tilde K$ as $e^{-1}(h)$ (`presentationEquiv_symm_mk`).

This is the Reidemeister–Schreier presentation of a subgroup, as in Johnson's Chapter 9, with the Schreier construction left out: the free basis and the representatives are inputs, and the rewriting process is the abstract inverse $e^{-1}$. Nothing is assumed about $K$.

## References and tests
- D. L. Johnson, *Presentations of Groups*, second edition, Chapter 9.

## Lean subtleties
- `≃*` is a group isomorphism; `Subgroup.comap f K` is the preimage $f^{-1}(K)$; the definition is `noncomputable`, assembled from quotient-by-kernel isomorphisms rather than an algorithm.
- Relators are conjugated as $t r t^{-1}$, matching the factorization $g = h t$ (right cosets of $\tilde K$).
- `hT` does not require $T$ to be a transversal: representatives may repeat a coset, and $1 \in T$ is not required.
- The general form for any $H \ge \langle\langle R \rangle\rangle$ is `PresentedGroup.subgroupPresentationEquiv`; here $H = \tilde K$, whose image is $K$ since `PresentedGroup.mk R` is surjective.

## What it says
Finite $\pi_1$-sensitive Hofer–Zehnder capacity of $W$ forces a closed characteristic contractible in $W$ on some level in every interval $(a, b)$ of levels of an energy function with compact sublevel inside $W$: the dense-levels Hofer–Zehnder existence theorem.

- `[FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`, `[IsManifold I ∞ M]`: $M$ is a finite-dimensional $C^\infty$ manifold, boundary and corners allowed.
- `(hσ : σ.IsNondegenerate)`: the two-form $\sigma$ is nondegenerate on every tangent space; closedness is not assumed.
- `(hF : ContMDiff I 𝓘(ℝ) ∞ F)`: $F : M \to \mathbb{R}$ is smooth; `(hab : a < b)`.
- `(hcpt : IsCompact {x | F x ≤ b})`, `(hW : … ⊆ interior W)`, `(hM : … ⊆ I.interior M)`: the sublevel $\{F \le b\}$ is compact and lies in the interior of $W$ and away from the boundary of $M$.
- `(ha : ∃ x, F x < a)`, `(hb : ∃ x ∈ interior W, b < F x)`: $F$ goes below $a$ somewhere and above $b$ in the interior of $W$.
- `(hcap : σ.contractibleHZCapacity W < ⊤)`: the capacity $c^\circ_{HZ}(W)$, the supremum in $[0, \infty]$ of the maxima of the admissible Hamiltonians (`IsContractibleHZAdmissible`: no nonconstant periodic orbit of period $\le 1$ contractible in $W$), is finite.
- The conclusion: some $s \in (a, b)$ satisfies `σ.HasContractibleClosedCharacteristic W F s`: a nonconstant $T$-periodic orbit of $X_F$, $T > 0$, lies in $F^{-1}(s)$ with loop $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z} \to W$ nullhomotopic in $W$.

This is the step of Hofer and Zehnder's argument turning finite capacity into closed characteristics on a dense set of levels, here for the $\pi_1$-sensitive capacity. The almost-every-level refinement (Struwe; Proposition 6.3 of the roadmap's source) is not stated.

- `⊤` in `ℝ≥0∞` is $+\infty$; `Ioo a b` is the open interval; `interior W` is the interior in $M$ and `I.interior M` the set of points off the boundary of $M$.
- $X_F$ is `σ.hamiltonianVectorField F`, the inverse flat map of $\sigma$ applied to $dF$; nondegeneracy keeps that map invertible.

## What it says
Metrics of positive scalar curvature agreeing on the neck of a connected sum glue to one on $M \# N$: the gluing step of the Gromov–Lawson and Schoen–Yau construction.

- `[InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`, `[T2Space M] [IsManifold I ∞ M]`, likewise for `N`: Hausdorff smooth manifolds modelled on a Euclidean space $E$.
- `{e₁ : E → M} {e₂ : E → N}`: the coordinate balls of `TauCeti.ConnectedSum e₁ e₂`, which removes $e_1(0)$, $e_2(0)$ and glues $e_1(v)$ to $e_2(v/\|v\|^2)$.
- `{g₁ g₂}`: smooth metrics.
- `(h₁ : IsOpenEmbedding e₁)`, `(d₁ : IsLocalDiffeomorph 𝓘(ℝ, E) I ∞ e₁)`, `h₂`, `d₂`: open embeddings and smooth local diffeomorphisms.
- `(hg : ∀ v, a < ‖v‖ → ‖v‖ < b → ∀ ξ ζ, …)`: on the neck $a < \|v\| < b$, $g_1(de_1\,\xi, de_1\,\zeta) = g_2(d(e_2 \circ \operatorname{inv})\,\xi, d(e_2 \circ \operatorname{inv})\,\zeta)$, $\operatorname{inv}$ the unit-sphere inversion: the gluing map is a neck isometry.
- `(hg₁ : g₁.HasPositiveScalarCurvature) (hg₂ : g₂.HasPositiveScalarCurvature)`, `(ha : 0 ≤ a) (hab : a < b)`: both scalar curvatures are positive.
- The conclusion: the glued metric `g₁.connectedSum g₂ h₁ h₂ d₁ d₂ hg ha hab`, $g_1$ on $M$ outside $e_1(\bar B(0, a))$ and $g_2$ on $N$ outside $e_2(\bar B(0, b^{-1}))$, has positive scalar curvature.

In Gromov–Lawson and Schoen–Yau the theorem is that $M \# N$ carries positive scalar curvature when $M$ and $N$ do, in dimension $\ge 3$; the work there is deforming each metric into a torpedo with a cylindrical neck; this is only the final gluing, with no dimension restriction. Cylindrical necks satisfy `hg` (`inner_mfderiv_inversion_eq_of_cylinder`).

## What it says
The sharp isoperimetric inequality in a Euclidean space of dimension $n \ge 1$: every Lebesgue-measurable set $s$ of finite positive volume satisfies $n^n \omega_n |s|^{n-1} \le P(s)^n$, with $\omega_n$ the volume of the unit ball and $P(s)$ the perimeter of $s$ in the whole space.

- `{E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] [MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E]`: a finite-dimensional real inner product space; `volume` is its Lebesgue measure, giving an orthonormal unit cube volume $1$.
- `{s : Set E} (hs : NullMeasurableSet s volume)`: a Lebesgue-measurable set.
- `(hμs : volume s ≠ ⊤)`: finite volume; `(hn : finrank ℝ E ≠ 0)`: $n = \dim E \ge 1$; `(hs0 : volume s ≠ 0)`: positive volume.
- The conclusion, in the extended nonnegative reals: $n^n \omega_n |s|^{n-1} \le P(s)^n$, where `perimeter volume ⊤ s` is `TauCeti.perimeter`, the total variation of the indicator of $s$ on the whole space `⊤`, the supremum of $\int_s \operatorname{div}\varphi$ over test vector fields with $\|\varphi\| \le 1$.

This is the isoperimetric inequality for sets of finite perimeter in its sharp form (Maggi, Chapters 13–14), with no boundedness, connectedness or regularity hypothesis. Unlike the textbook statement, the perimeter may be infinite, and the equality case, that only balls attain equality, is not included.

## References and tests
- F. Maggi, *Sets of Finite Perimeter and Geometric Variational Problems*, Chapters 13–14.
- R. J. Gardner, *The Brunn–Minkowski inequality*, Section 5.
- Roadmap: [Isoperimetry, I4 — Sharp Euclidean perimeter inequality and ball rigidity](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/Isoperimetry/README.md#L225), target `sharp-perimeter-inequality` (partial: the rigidity half is not here).
- `TauCeti.perimeter_ball_pow` — balls attain equality: $P(B)^n = n^n \omega_n |B|^{n-1}$, so the constant is sharp.
- `ConvexBody.finrank_pow_mul_volume_ball_mul_volume_pow_le_perimeter_pow` — the same inequality for convex bodies of positive volume, proved separately from Brunn–Minkowski; this theorem recovers it.
- `MeasureTheory.NullMeasurableSet.mul_volume_real_rpow_mul_le_perimeter_toReal` — the real-valued form $n\,\omega_n^{1/n} |s|^{1-1/n} \le P(s)$ for sets of finite perimeter.

## Lean subtleties
- All quantities live in `ℝ≥0∞`: a set of infinite perimeter satisfies the inequality trivially. Finite volume cannot be dropped: the complement of a ball has finite perimeter.
- `finrank ℝ E - 1` is truncated subtraction on `ℕ`; `hn` makes it the honest $n - 1$.
- Positive volume (`hs0`) matters only in dimension $n = 1$. There `volume s ^ (n - 1)` is `volume s ^ 0`, which is $1$ even for a null set, since $0^0 = 1$ in `ℝ≥0∞`, while a null set has perimeter $0$: the left side would be $\omega_1 = 2$ and the right side $0$. In dimension $n \ge 2$ a null set makes the left side $0$ and the inequality trivial.
- `⊤` is the whole space as an open set, so this is the full perimeter, not a relative one.

## What it says
A finite-dimensional Lie group with the left-invariant Riemannian metric determined by an inner product on its Lie algebra is complete for the distance of that metric.

- `{E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`, `{H} [TopologicalSpace H]`, `{I : ModelWithCorners ℝ E H}`: a finite-dimensional real model space.
- `{G : Type*} [TopologicalSpace G] [T2Space G] [ChartedSpace H G] [Group G] [IsManifold I 1 G] [LieGroup I ∞ G]`: a Hausdorff $C^\infty$ Lie group modelled on $I$. `IsManifold I 1 G`, that the charts of $G$ form a $C^1$ atlas, is a hypothesis of its own: `LieGroup I ∞ G` only says that multiplication and inversion are smooth, and both the metric and the distance below ask for the atlas.
- `{m : ℕ∞ω} (hm : m + 1 ≤ ∞)`: a smoothness exponent for the metric, any natural number or $\infty$ (only the analytic $\omega$ is excluded).
- `(b : TangentSpace I (1 : G) →L[ℝ] TangentSpace I (1 : G) →L[ℝ] ℝ)` with `hsymm`, `hpos`: a continuous, symmetric, positive-definite bilinear form on the tangent space at $1$, an inner product on $\mathfrak{g}$.
- The conclusion installs by `letI` the Riemannian structure `leftInvariantMetric hm b hsymm hpos`, $\langle v, w\rangle_x = b(dL_{x^{-1}}v, dL_{x^{-1}}w)$, then the extended metric `EMetricSpace.ofRiemannianMetric I G`, whose distance is the infimum of lengths of paths, and asserts `CompleteSpace G` for it.

This is the completeness of left-invariant metrics, obtained as in Lee, Chapter 6, from homogeneity: left translations act transitively by isometries, and a finite-dimensional homogeneous Riemannian manifold is complete. No compactness or connectedness is assumed.

## References and tests
- J. M. Lee, *Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds*, 2nd ed., GTM 176, Chapter 3 (invariant metrics on Lie groups) and Chapter 6 (homogeneous manifolds are complete).
- J. Milnor, *Curvatures of left invariant metrics on Lie groups*, Advances in Math. 21 (1976).
- Roadmap [RiemannianGeometry, R1, the Lie-group paragraph](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/RiemannianGeometry/README.md#L241); PR #25135.

Tests: None. The theorem instantiates `TauCeti.completeSpace_ofRiemannianMetric_of_inner_mulInvariantVectorField` for the constructed metric.

## Lean subtleties
- `TangentSpace I (1 : G)` is a copy of $E$; `→L[ℝ]` is a continuous linear map, automatic in finite dimension.
- The `letI`/`haveI` lines put the instances inside the statement: the conclusion is about the distance of this metric, not a metric $G$ already carries. The topology of `EMetricSpace.ofRiemannianMetric` is by construction that of $G$; it needs $G$ regular, which a Hausdorff topological group is, and the statement derives the topological group structure from `LieGroup I ∞ G`.
- The distance takes values in $[0, \infty]$; points in different path components are at distance $\infty$, which is why no connectedness is needed.
- $m + 1 \le \infty$ holds for $m = \infty$, since $\infty + 1 = \infty$ in `ℕ∞ω`.

## What it says
Over a field of characteristic zero, the Brauer algebra $B_k(\delta)$ fails to be semisimple for only finitely many loop values $\delta$.

- `(k : ℕ)`: the number of strands, explicit.
- `(K : Type*) [Field K] [CharZero K]`: a type $K$ with a field structure of characteristic zero, both found by typeclass search; `CharZero K` says the natural numbers embed in $K$.
- The conclusion: the set $\{\delta \in K \mid B_k(\delta) \text{ not semisimple}\}$ is finite (`Set.Finite`). Here `BrauerAlgebra K δ k` is the free $K$-module on the Brauer diagrams on $k$ strands, two diagrams multiplying to $\delta^c$ times their stack when $c$ closed loops are left in the middle, and `IsSemisimpleRing` is Mathlib's class: semisimple as a module over itself.

In characteristic zero $B_k(\delta)$ is semisimple exactly when the discriminant `TauCeti.BrauerAlgebra.discr k`, an integer polynomial, does not vanish at $\delta$ (`TauCeti.BrauerAlgebra.isSemisimpleRing_iff_aeval_discr_ne_zero`); the polynomial is nonzero, so it has finitely many roots. This is the generic semisimplicity of Brown and Wenzl. Wenzl says more: in characteristic zero the exceptional values are integers in an explicit range. This statement bounds the exceptional set without locating it. Characteristic zero enters through the embedding of $\mathbb{Z}$ in $K$: it keeps the discriminant a nonzero polynomial with coefficients in $K$, so that only the direction "discriminant nonzero, hence semisimple" of the criterion is needed, the one that holds over every field (`TauCeti.BrauerAlgebra.isSemisimpleRing_of_aeval_discr_ne_zero`).

## References and tests
- W. P. Brown, *An algebra related to the orthogonal group*, Michigan Math. J. 3 (1955); H. Wenzl, *On the structure of Brauer's centralizer algebras*, Ann. of Math. 128 (1988): references of the module and of the discriminant module.
- Roadmap target: [RepresentationTheory/SchurWeyl, Layer 9, "Semisimplicity of `B_k(δ)`"](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/RepresentationTheory/SchurWeyl/README.md#L468). The explicit range $|\delta| \ge 2k - 2$ and the symplectic value $\delta = -2l$ asked there are not decided here.

Tests: None.

## Lean subtleties
- `CharZero K` is a typeclass hypothesis. It makes the cast $\mathbb{Z} \to K$ injective, so the discriminant, nonzero in $\mathbb{Z}[X]$, is still nonzero in $K[X]$ and has finitely many roots there. It cannot be dropped: in characteristic $p \le k$ the group algebra $K[S_k]$ is a quotient of $B_k(\delta)$, by killing the diagrams with a horizontal arc, and is not semisimple by Maschke's theorem, so no $B_k(\delta)$ is semisimple and the set is all of $K$, infinite when $K$ is. The converse of the trace-form criterion, semisimple hence discriminant nonzero, also needs characteristic zero: the trace-form module notes that in characteristic $p$ the regular trace form of the $p \times p$ matrix algebra vanishes although the algebra is simple. That direction is not used here.
- For $k \le 1$ there is a single diagram, $B_k(\delta) = K$ is semisimple for every $\delta$, and the finite set is empty. The theorem does not say which $\delta$, if any, are exceptional for larger $k$.
- `k` and `K` are explicit arguments, since neither can be read off a hypothesis.

## What it says
A finite-dimensional algebra over a field of characteristic zero is semisimple exactly when its regular trace form is nondegenerate: Dickson's trace-form criterion.

- `{K A : Type*} [Field K] [Ring A] [Algebra K A]`: a field $K$ and an associative unital ring $A$, not necessarily commutative, that is a $K$-algebra; all found by typeclass search.
- `[FiniteDimensional K A]`: $A$ is finite-dimensional over $K$.
- `[CharZero K]`: $K$ has characteristic zero.
- The conclusion: `IsSemisimpleRing A`, Mathlib's class saying $A$ is a semisimple module over itself, holds if and only if `Algebra.regularTraceForm K A` is nondegenerate. The regular trace form is $(x, y) \mapsto \operatorname{tr}_K(z \mapsto xyz)$, the trace of left multiplication by $xy$; `Nondegenerate` is Mathlib's one-sided condition: $x = 0$ whenever $\operatorname{tr}(L_{xy}) = 0$ for all $y$. Since the form is symmetric, this is the same as the two-sided condition of the literature.

This is the criterion as the literature states it in characteristic zero. The direction from nondegeneracy to semisimplicity holds over every field (`TauCeti.isSemisimpleRing_of_nondegenerate_regularTraceForm`); the converse (`TauCeti.nondegenerate_regularTraceForm`) is where characteristic zero enters, since an idempotent operator of trace $0$ must then be $0$. Mathlib's `Algebra.traceForm` is the same form for commutative $A$; the regular trace form needs no commutativity.

## References and tests
- C. W. Curtis and I. Reiner, *Representation theory of finite groups and associative algebras*, Interscience (1962), §26.
- R. S. Pierce, *Associative algebras*, GTM 88, Springer (1982), §10.2.
- Roadmap target: [RepresentationTheory/SchurWeyl, Layer 9, "Semisimplicity of `B_k(δ)`"](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/RepresentationTheory/SchurWeyl/README.md#L468), for which this criterion is the tool.
- `TauCeti.BrauerAlgebra.isSemisimpleRing_iff_aeval_discr_ne_zero` — the criterion specialised to the Brauer algebra $B_k(\delta)$: through `LinearMap.BilinForm.nondegenerate_iff_det_ne_zero`, nondegeneracy becomes the nonvanishing of the Gram determinant in the diagram basis, an integer polynomial in $\delta$.

The specialisation exercises the criterion on a family of noncommutative algebras whose semisimplicity is then read off a single determinant.

## Lean subtleties
- `LinearMap.BilinForm.Nondegenerate B` asks only that $B(x, y) = 0$ for all $y$ forces $x = 0$; Mathlib has no separate right-sided condition. The regular trace form is symmetric, $\operatorname{tr}(L_x L_y) = \operatorname{tr}(L_y L_x)$, so the left and right conditions coincide, and in finite dimension each is the nonvanishing of the Gram determinant.
- `CharZero K` is a typeclass; the module docstring records the failure of the converse in characteristic $p$ for the $p \times p$ matrix algebra, whose regular trace form is $p \cdot \operatorname{tr}(xy) = 0$.
- The zero algebra is allowed: it is semisimple, and the zero form on the zero module is nondegenerate.
- `[Algebra K A]` makes $K$ act through the centre of $A$.

- `{e₁ : E → M} {e₂ : E → N}`: the coordinate balls of `TauCeti.ConnectedSum e₁ e₂`, which removes $e_1(0)$, $e_2(0)$ and glues $e_1(v)$ to $e_2(v/\|v\|^2)$.
- `{g₁ g₂}`: smooth metrics.
- `(h₁ : IsOpenEmbedding e₁)`, `(d₁ : IsLocalDiffeomorph 𝓘(ℝ, E) I ∞ e₁)`, `h₂`, `d₂`: open embeddings and smooth local diffeomorphisms.
- `(hg : ∀ v, a < ‖v‖ → ‖v‖ < b → ∀ ξ ζ, …)`: on the neck $a < \|v\| < b$, $g_1(de_1\,\xi, de_1\,\zeta) = g_2(d(e_2 \circ \operatorname{inv})\,\xi, d(e_2 \circ \operatorname{inv})\,\zeta)$, $\operatorname{inv}$ the unit-sphere inversion: the gluing map is a neck isometry.
- `(hg₁ : g₁.HasPositiveScalarCurvature) (hg₂ : g₂.HasPositiveScalarCurvature)`: both scalar curvatures are positive at every point.
- `(ha : 0 ≤ a) (hab : a < b)`: the neck radii satisfy $0 \le a < b$, so the annulus $a < \|v\| < b$ on which `hg` is asked is nonempty and misses $0$.
- The conclusion: the glued metric `g₁.connectedSum g₂ h₁ h₂ d₁ d₂ hg ha hab`, $g_1$ on $M$ outside $e_1(\bar B(0, a))$ and $g_2$ on $N$ outside $e_2(\bar B(0, b^{-1}))$, has positive scalar curvature.

In Gromov–Lawson and Schoen–Yau the theorem is that $M \# N$ carries positive scalar curvature when $M$ and $N$ do, in dimension $\ge 3$; the work there is deforming each metric into a torpedo with a cylindrical neck; this is only the final gluing, with no dimension restriction. Cylindrical necks satisfy `hg` (`inner_mfderiv_inversion_eq_of_cylinder`). No dimension restriction is needed because the glued metric is, near every point of $M \# N$, isometric to $g_1$ near a point of $M$ or to $g_2$ near a point of $N$: its scalar curvature at each point is a value of the scalar curvature of $g_1$ or of $g_2$ (`range_scalarCurvature_connectedSum_subset`), hence positive.

## Lean subtleties
- The statement begins with `letI`/`haveI` installing the connected sum's manifold instances, those `g₁.connectedSum g₂ …` is defined with.
- `inversion 0 1` is Mathlib's `EuclideanGeometry.inversion`, $v \mapsto v/\|v\|^2$; at $v = 0$ it is $0$ by the convention $x/0 = 0$, but $a \ge 0$ keeps $0$ off the neck; $a = 0$ is allowed, and then only the point $e_1(0)$ is cut out of $M$.
- `HasPositiveScalarCurvature` is `∀ x, 0 < g.scalarCurvature x`, for the Levi-Civita connection of $g$.

Correctly stated: if T is antisymmetric in its first pair, R has no zero divisors and 2 ≠ 0, then T(x,y,y,x) = 0 whenever x and y are linearly dependent. Lean ↔ mathematics: `T x y y x` is the value k(x,y) of the curried quadrilinear form. `h₁` is antisymmetry in the first pair only; antisymmetry in the last pair and the Bianchi identity are neither needed nor assumed. `hxy : ¬LinearIndependent R ![x, y]` says that s x + t y = 0 for some s, t not both 0 (`LinearIndependent.pair_iff`). `[NoZeroDivisors R]` and `(2 : R) ≠ 0` give T(a,a,c,d) = 0 from 2T(a,a,c,d) = 0, and then force k = 0 from s²k = t²k = 0. Lean subtlety: dependence is of the family `![x, y]`, so x = y, or a torsion x (s x = 0 with s ≠ 0), counts as dependent. Both correctly give 0, and M need not be torsion-free. Checks at 5f78b5307b: the hypothesis `2 ≠ 0` is necessary. Compiled counterexample: on 𝔽₂ the form abcd satisfies h₁, the pair (1,1) is dependent, and T(1,1,1,1) = 1. All three explicit hypotheses are load-bearing, and the only axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: two quadrilinear forms that are antisymmetric in each pair, satisfy the first Bianchi identity and have T₁(x,y,y,x) = T₂(x,y,y,x) for all x, y are equal whenever multiplication by 6 is injective on R. Lean ↔ mathematics: `T₁ T₂ : M →ₗ[R] M →ₗ[R] M →ₗ[R] M →ₗ[R] R` are curried quadrilinear forms. `h₁ h₂ h₃` and their primed copies are the two antisymmetries and the Bianchi identity for each form. `hT : ∀ x y, T₁ x y y x = T₂ x y y x` is agreement of all the values k(x,y), with no independence condition. `IsLeftRegular (6 : R)` says that a ↦ 6a is injective, i.e. 6 is a non-zero-divisor; this holds in ℤ, in any ℚ-algebra and in any domain of characteristic ≠ 2, 3. The conclusion `T₁ = T₂` is equality of the forms, obtained by `ext` and cancelling 6 in the polarization identity. Lean subtlety: `IsLeftRegular` is left cancellation, and since R is commutative it just means non-zero-divisor. This is weaker than `IsUnit 6` or `Invertible 6`, so the theorem covers ℤ-valued forms too. Checks at 5f78b5307b: the regularity hypothesis cannot be dropped. Compiled counterexamples: over 𝔽₃, det on 𝔽₃⁴ (every value T(x,y,y,x) is 0 but det ≠ 0); over 𝔽₂, an explicit nonzero form on 𝔽₂³ whose values T(x,y,y,x) are all 0. Every explicit hypothesis is load-bearing, and the only axioms are propext and Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: two curvature-type quadrilinear forms that agree on the values T(x,y,y,x) for every linearly independent pair are equal. This holds over any commutative domain with 6 ≠ 0 and any module over it. Lean ↔ mathematics: `T₁ T₂ : M →ₗ[R] M →ₗ[R] M →ₗ[R] M →ₗ[R] R` are curried R-quadrilinear forms, so `T x y z w` is T(x,y,z,w). `h₁`/`h₂` (and `h₁'`/`h₂'`) are antisymmetry in the first and in the last pair of arguments. `h₃`/`h₃'` is the first Bianchi identity T(x,y,z,w)+T(y,z,x,w)+T(z,x,y,w)=0. These are the symmetries of an algebraic curvature tensor, except that pair symmetry is not assumed, so the theorem assumes less than the textbook. `hT` asks for agreement only when `LinearIndependent R ![x, y]` holds, i.e. when no relation sx+ty=0 with (s,t)≠(0,0) exists; over a field these pairs are exactly the bases of the 2-planes. With an inner product, the sectional curvature of span{x,y} is T(x,y,y,x)/(|x|²|y|²−⟨x,y⟩²), and the denominator is the same nonzero number for T₁ and T₂, so `hT` says K₁(σ)=K₂(σ) for every plane σ. `[NoZeroDivisors R]` together with `(6 : R) ≠ 0` says R is a domain of characteristic ≠ 2, 3 (ℝ, ℚ, ℤ, …). The conclusion `T₁ = T₂` is equality of the forms. Lean subtlety: `![x, y]` is a family indexed by `Fin 2`, so x = y counts as dependent, which is correct. `NoZeroDivisors` alone would allow the zero ring, but `6 ≠ 0` excludes it. The sign convention does not matter: under `h₂`, T(x,y,y,x) = −T(x,y,x,y), so agreement of the numerators T(x,y,y,x) (Lee's convention) is the same as agreement of R(X,Y,X,Y). No division and no junk value is involved. The inner product never enters, since the theorem is purely algebraic. The Riemannian corollary R(w,u)v = κ(⟨u,v⟩w − ⟨w,v⟩u) is proved downstream in Curvature/Polarization.lean, not in this file. Source: the sectional-curvature lemma in §2 of D. Chua's notes of Cambridge Part III Riemannian Geometry states the real-vector-space case (assuming pair symmetry, with K = R(X,Y,X,Y)/|X∧Y|²), and this theorem implies that statement in full. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the hypothesis 6 ≠ 0 cannot be dropped. Compiled counterexamples: det on 𝔽₃⁴ (characteristic 3: it has both antisymmetries, its Bianchi sum is 3·det = 0, det(x,y,y,x) = 0, and det ≠ 0), and an explicit nonzero form on 𝔽₂³ (characteristic 2). A compiled torsion edge case: over ℤ on the module ZMod 2 no pair is independent, and the theorem correctly yields T = 0. The hypotheses are jointly satisfiable (the zero form over ℚ), all 8 explicit hypotheses are load-bearing, and the only axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. The theorem is consumed over ℝ by `CovariantDerivative.IsMetricCompatible.riemannCurvatureTensor_eq_of_forall_linearIndependent`, and through it by the constant-curvature characterization.

Correctly stated: for a quadrilinear form T antisymmetric in each argument pair and satisfying the first Bianchi identity, 6·T(x,y,z,w) equals an explicit signed sum of fourteen values k(a,b) = T(a,b,b,a). This holds over every commutative ring. Lean ↔ mathematics: `T : M →ₗ[R] M →ₗ[R] M →ₗ[R] M →ₗ[R] R` is a curried quadrilinear form, with `T x y z w` = T(x,y,z,w). `h₁` and `h₂` are antisymmetry in the first and in the last pair, and `h₃` is the first Bianchi identity (cyclic in the first three arguments, the last fixed). The left side `6 * T x y z w` is 6·T(x,y,z,w), where `6` is the numeral in R. Every term on the right has the shape `T a b b a`, i.e. k(a,b). I checked the fourteen terms and their signs one by one against the module docstring's formula 6T = k(x+w,y+z) − k(x+z,y+w) − k(x,y+z) − k(w,y+z) + k(x,y+w) + k(z,y+w) − k(x+w,y) + k(x+z,y) − k(x+w,z) + k(x+z,w) + k(w,y) − k(z,y) + k(x,z) − k(x,w). Lean subtlety: the statement is about 6·T and does not divide by 6. The identity holds in every commutative ring, including characteristics 2 and 3, where 6·T = 0 and the identity says nothing about T; the compiled det-on-𝔽₃⁴ example shows that T is then genuinely not determined by the values k. Recovering T requires cancelling 6, which `LinearMap.eq_of_cyclic_eq_zero` does. Checks at 5f78b5307b: `lean_minimal_hypotheses` finds h₁, h₂ and h₃ all used. The only axioms are propext and Quot.sound. Mathlib has no curvature-tensor material, and `LinearMap.BilinForm.ext_of_isSymm` is only the bilinear analogue.

(1) For every finite set s of positions in a linear order, the number of noncrossing partitions of s is C_{|s|}. (2) `NoncrossingPartition s` is `{P : Finpartition s // P.IsNoncrossing}`: set partitions of s into nonempty blocks with no a < b < c < d where a, c lie in one block and b, d in another distinct block. `Fintype.card` counts this finite subtype, `#s` is |s|, and `catalan` is Mathlib's C_0 = 1, C_{n+1} = Σ C_i C_{n−i}. The noncrossing condition only uses the order, so this is the order-invariant form of |NC(n)| = C_n, and `card_fin_eq_catalan` is its instance s = univ in Fin n. The proof is strong induction on #s: the first-block recurrence `card_eq_sum_card_mul_card`, re-indexed over x ∈ s by rank, is `catalan_succ`. (3) Lean subtlety: s = ∅ is included and gives 1 = `catalan 0` through the unique partition with no blocks, the standard convention. No hypotheses and no junk value are involved. (4) Wikipedia's Catalan number article states that C_n counts the noncrossing partitions of {1,…,n}. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: #eval values for |s| ≤ 4 and a `decide +kernel` check at |s| = 3 agree with the statement. Axioms are standard.

(1) For a nonempty finite set s in a linear order, |NC(s)| = Σ_{x∈s} |NC(s_{<x})|·|NC(s_{>x})|: the noncrossing partitions are counted by the point x where the block of the first position ends. (2) `{y ∈ s | y < x}` and `{y ∈ s | x < y}` are the positions of s before and after x. x ranges over all of s, because the block of min s can end at any point. On each fibre, P ↦ (P restricted before x, P restricted after x) is a bijection (x is adjoined back to the block of min s). The statement is `sum_mul_prod_eq_sum_mul_sum` at G = F = 1 in ℕ, and by size it is the Catalan recurrence. (3) `hs : s.Nonempty` is needed: for s = ∅ the left side is 1 and the right side is an empty sum, 0. `lean_minimal_hypotheses` reports it load-bearing. (4) This is the recurrence by the block containing the first position named in the FreeProbability roadmap (F2). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the hypothesis is load-bearing, the n ≤ 4 counts 1, 1, 2, 5, 14 (#eval) satisfy it, and the axioms are standard.

(1) For every n ≥ 0 the number of noncrossing set partitions of the n ordered points 0 < 1 < … < n−1 is the Catalan number C_n. (2) `univ : Finset (Fin n)` is the set {0,…,n−1} with its usual order. `Finpartition univ` is Mathlib's finite partition: a finset `parts` of nonempty (`bot_notMem`), pairwise disjoint (`supIndep`) blocks whose union is the whole set (`sup_parts`), i.e. a set partition into nonempty blocks. `NoncrossingPartition s` is by definition (an abbrev) the subtype `{P : Finpartition s // P.IsNoncrossing}`, and `Finpartition.IsNoncrossing P` says that for blocks B, C ∈ P.parts and a ∈ B, b ∈ C, c ∈ B, d ∈ C with a < b < c < d we get B = C, which is exactly "no two distinct blocks cross". `Fintype.card` counts this finite subtype; the instance is `Subtype.fintype Finpartition.IsNoncrossing` over Mathlib's `Fintype (Finpartition s)`, and `Fintype.card` does not depend on which instance is used. `catalan` is Mathlib's C_0 = 1, C_{n+1} = Σ_{i≤n} C_i C_{n−i}. With `succ_mul_catalan_eq_centralBinom` the theorem gives (n+1)·|NC(n)| = binom(2n, n) (compiled). The proof is `card_eq_catalan` (strong induction on the first-block recurrence) at s = univ, with `card_univ` and `Fintype.card_fin`. (3) Lean subtlety: n = 0 is included. `Fin 0` is empty and the only partition of ∅ has no blocks, so it is vacuously noncrossing and the count is 1 = `catalan 0`, which is the standard convention NC(0) = {∅}. Only `<` on `Fin n` is used, so `Fin` wrap-around arithmetic plays no role. The count is a `Fintype.card` of a genuine finite subtype, not a `Nat.card` that could be a junk 0. (4) Wikipedia's Catalan number article states that C_n is the number of noncrossing partitions of {1,…,n}, and its Noncrossing partition article defines crossing as two blocks interleaved a x b y. The FreeProbability roadmap (F2) asks for exactly this carrier, predicate and `card NC(n) = catalan n`. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: an independent #eval of the subtype's cardinality gives 1, 1, 2, 5, 14 for n = 0..4 against Bell numbers 1, 1, 2, 5, 15 for all partitions, the one excluded partition at n = 4 being {0,2}|{1,3}. `decide +kernel` proves the n = 3 count is 5 without using the theorem. The predicate rejects the crossing partition {0,2}|{1,3} of Fin 4 and accepts the nested {0,3}|{1,2} (both compiled). Specialisations to n = 0, 3, 4, 5 give 1, 5, 14, 42. Axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound only.

(1) A finite set of 2n positions in a linear order has exactly C_n noncrossing pair partitions. (2) `{P : NoncrossingPartition s // P.1.IsPairing}` is the set of noncrossing partitions of s all of whose blocks have size 2 (`IsPairing` unfolds to `∀ B ∈ P.parts, #B = 2`), counted by `Fintype.card`. `hn : #s = 2 * n` says |s| = 2n, and `catalan n` is Mathlib's C_n. The proof is strong induction on n through `card_isPairing_eq_sum`, with odd sizes contributing 0 by `card_isPairing_eq_zero`. (3) Lean subtlety: n = 0 (s = ∅) is included. The partition with no blocks is vacuously a pairing, so the count is 1 = `catalan 0`, the standard convention. The proof's helper `g i = if Even i then catalan (i / 2) else 0` uses ℕ division only on even i, and its truncated subtractions `2k − (2j+1)` occur only with 2j+1 ≤ 2k. (4) Wikipedia's Catalan number article states that C_n is the number of noncrossing partitions of {1,…,2n} in which every block has size 2. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: on Fin 4 the #eval count is 2 = `catalan 2` (out of 3 pairings), `hn` is load-bearing, and the axioms are standard.

(1) For nonempty s with first position m, |NC₂(s)| = Σ_{x∈s, m<x} |NC₂(s ∩ (m,x))|·|NC₂(s_{>x})|. In a noncrossing pairing, m is paired with some x > m, and the rest is a noncrossing pairing of the points strictly between m and x together with one of the points after x. (2) `{P : NoncrossingPartition s // P.1.IsPairing}` is NC₂(s), the noncrossing partitions all of whose blocks have exactly two elements (`Finpartition.IsPairing P` unfolds to `∀ B ∈ P.parts, #B = 2`). `{y ∈ s | s.min' hs < y ∧ y < x}` is s ∩ (m, x), `{y ∈ s | x < y}` is s ∩ (x, ∞), and `∑ x ∈ s with s.min' hs < x` runs over the possible partners x of m. (3) For a one-point s the sum is empty and the count is 0, which is right because a singleton has no pairing. `hs` is load-bearing. (4) Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: on Fin 4 the right side is 1·1 (x = 1) + 0 (x = 2) + 1·1 (x = 3) = 2, matching the #eval count of 2 noncrossing pairings out of 3 pairings. Axioms are standard.

(1) A finite set of odd size has no noncrossing pair partition: `Fintype.card {P : NoncrossingPartition s // P.1.IsPairing} = 0` under `Odd #s`, where `IsPairing` says every block has two elements. (2) The proof uses `IsPairing.even_card`: a pairing of s has |s| = 2·#blocks. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: `hs` is load-bearing (s = ∅ has one pairing). Axioms are standard.

(1) The 2n ordered points of Fin (2n) have C_n noncrossing pair partitions. (2) `univ : Finset (Fin (2 * n))` is {0,…,2n−1} with its usual order, and the subtype `{P : NoncrossingPartition univ // P.1.IsPairing}` is NC₂(2n), the noncrossing partitions with all blocks of size 2. The statement is `card_isPairing_eq_catalan` with #univ = 2n (`card_univ`, `Fintype.card_fin`). (3) Lean subtlety: n = 0 gives Fin 0, whose one empty partition is a pairing, matching `catalan 0` = 1.
