(1) The weighted first-block recurrence. Let s be nonempty with first position m, and give the block of m the weight G and every other block the weight F, with values in a commutative semiring. Then Σ_{P∈NC(s)} G(block of m)·Π_{B∌m} F(B) = Σ_{x∈s} (Σ_{L∈NC(s_{<x})} G({x} ∪ block of m in L)·Π_{B∈L, B∌m} F(B))·(Σ_{R∈NC(s_{>x})} Π_{B∈R} F(B)). (2) `s.min' hs` is the least element m of s and `P.1.part m` is the block of P containing m. `∏ B ∈ P.1.parts with m ∉ B, F B` is the product over the other blocks, and `insert x (L.1.part m)` is the block of m in L with x adjoined. x runs over s as the last element of the block of m, and the inner sums run over the finite sets NC(s_{<x}) and NC(s_{>x}). (3) Lean subtlety: when x = m, `{y ∈ s | y < m}` is empty and its unique partition has no blocks, so `L.1.part m = ∅` (Mathlib's `Finpartition.part` is ∅ off the underlying set) and `insert m ∅ = {m}`. That term counts the partitions in which m is a singleton, as it should. `CommSemiring M` is what a product over a finset needs. (4) Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: at G = F = 1 in ℕ it gives `card_eq_sum_card_mul_card`, `hs` and the weights are load-bearing, and the axioms are standard. It is consumed by Narayana.lean (Narayana numbers) and PowerSeries.lean (moment–cumulant functional equation).

(1) Weight each block of size two by v and every other block by 0. Then the total weight of NC(s) is v^{|s|/2}·C_{|s|/2} if |s| is even and 0 if it is odd. (2) `∏ B ∈ P.1.parts, (if #B = 2 then v else 0)` is the product over the blocks of P of v·[|B| = 2]. By `prod_ite_zero` and `IsPairing.card_eq_two_mul` it equals v^{|s|/2} when P is a pairing and 0 otherwise. The sum over `NoncrossingPartition s` is the sum over NC(s), so the total is v^{|s|/2}·|NC₂(s)|, and `card_isPairing_eq_catalan` and `card_isPairing_eq_zero` give the two cases. `(catalan (#s / 2) : M)` is the natural-number cast into M. (3) Lean subtlety: `#s / 2` is ℕ division, used only in the `Even #s` branch, where it is exact. At s = ∅ both sides are 1: the empty product, and v^0 = 1 even for v = 0 (`0 ^ 0 = 1`), matching the zeroth moment 1. A block of size ≠ 2 contributes the factor 0 through the `if`. (4) This is the moment formula of a semicircular element of variance v, whose only nonzero free cumulant is κ₂ = v, as the docstring says. It is consumed by FreeProbability/Semicircular/Basic.lean. Correctly stated: `IsPerfectoidTateRing p R` is Fontaine's notion as defined in Scholze, Étale cohomology of diamonds, Definition 3.1: a complete Tate ring that is uniform and has a pseudo-uniformizer ϖ with ϖ^p | p in R° and Frobenius Φ : R°/ϖ → R°/ϖ^p, x ↦ x^p, an isomorphism. The ring: `[CommRing R] [UniformSpace R] [IsUniformAddGroup R] [IsTopologicalRing R]` make R a commutative topological ring whose uniformity is the additive one (Mathlib's `IsUniformAddGroup.rightUniformSpace_eq`), so `[CompleteSpace R] [T2Space R]` is 'complete' in Huber's sense, i.e. complete and separated. `[IsTateRing R]` is a Huber ring (a `PairOfDefinition`: an open subring R₀ with a finitely generated ideal I inducing the I-adic topology on R₀) with a topologically nilpotent unit, and Tau Ceti's `isTateRing_iff_exists_isOpen_isBounded` shows this is exactly Scholze's 'contains an open and bounded subring and a topologically nilpotent unit'. `powerBoundedSubring R` is R°: by `mem_powerBoundedSubring` its members are the `IsPowerBounded` elements, those whose set of powers is bounded, where `IsBounded S` is Huber's boundedness (every neighbourhood U of 0 has a neighbourhood V of 0 with V·S ⊆ U), not a metric bornology. Field (a), `IsBounded (powerBoundedSubring R : Set R)`, is Scholze's 'uniform, i.e. R° ⊂ R is bounded'. Field (b): `ϖ : powerBoundedSubring R` with `IsPseudoUniformizer (ϖ : R)` (by `isPseudoUniformizer_iff`, a unit of R whose powers tend to 0, Mathlib's `IsTopologicallyNilpotent`) is a pseudo-uniformizer; Scholze notes such a ϖ automatically lies in R° (Tau Ceti `IsPowerBounded.of_isTopologicallyNilpotent`), so taking ϖ in R° loses nothing. `ϖ ^ p ∣ (p : powerBoundedSubring R)` is divisibility inside the subring R°, exactly 'ϖ^p | p in R°'. `∀ x, ∃ y, ϖ ^ p ∣ x - y ^ p` is surjectivity of Φ and `∀ y, ϖ ^ p ∣ y ^ p → ϖ ∣ y` is triviality of its kernel; for prime p, `isPerfectoidTateRing_iff` proves the class equivalent to `IsUniform R ∧ ∃ ϖ, IsPseudoUniformizer ϖ ∧ ∃ h : ϖ ^ p ∣ p, Function.Bijective (frobeniusModPow p h)`, where `frobeniusModPow_mk` shows `frobeniusModPow p h` is the ring map R°/(ϖ) → R°/(ϖ^p), [x] ↦ [x^p], so Definition 3.1 is recovered word for word. Lean subtlety: `p : ℕ` is not required to be prime in the class (Scholze fixes a prime p throughout §3). At p = 0 or p = 1 the class forces R to be the zero ring (compiled: ϖ becomes a unit of R°, so 1 = (uϖ)^n → 0); at composite p it is not the literature notion, and every result in the file that needs Φ to be a ring map assumes `[Fact p.Prime]` (or `[NeZero p]` where that suffices). The divisibility is taken in R°, not in R, where it would be automatic since ϖ is a unit of R. `(p : powerBoundedSubring R)` is the natural-number cast, which is 0 in characteristic p, where the condition is vacuous, as in Scholze's Proposition 3.5. The zero ring satisfies the class (`isPerfectoidTateRing_of_subsingleton`), as it satisfies Definition 3.1. Source: Scholze, Étale cohomology of diamonds, Definition 3.1 and Remarks 3.2–3.3 (read in the arXiv text). Correctly stated: in a perfectoid Tate ring every element of R° is a p-th power modulo p, i.e. Frobenius on R°/p is surjective. `(p : powerBoundedSubring R) ∣ x - y ^ p` says x ≡ y^p mod pR°. Correctly stated definition: a null chain of U is a sequence of crosscuts, each disjoint from the next, whose cut-off domains decrease and whose chordal diameters tend to 0. Lean ↔ mathematics: the four fields say exactly this: `exists_isCrosscut` — each `C n` is `range γ` for a path with `γ.IsCrosscut U` (γ injective, γ 0 and γ 1 in `frontier U`, γ maps the open interval (0,1) into U), i.e. the closure of an open Jordan arc in U meeting ∂U in its two endpoints; `disjoint_succ` — `Disjoint (C n) (C (n + 1))`, and as C n is already closed this is condition (i) C̄_n ∩ C̄_{n+1} = ∅; `nullChainDomain_succ_subset` — D_{n+1} ⊆ D_n for D_n = `nullChainDomain U C n`, the component of U \ C n containing C (n+1) (`IsNullChain.nullChainDomain_eq_connectedComponentIn`); `eventually_chordal_lt` — for every ε > 0, eventually every pair z, w ∈ C n has chordal distance < ε, i.e. diam# C n → 0. The source's condition (ii), C_n separates C_0 from C_{n+1}, is replaced by nesting: `IsNullChain.separatesIn` derives (ii) from the fields and `isNullChain_iff_separatesIn` proves the two definitions agree on a preconnected open U. Lean subtlety: crosscut endpoints are finite and distinct (narrower than sources allowing an endpoint at ∞ or a = b; the module docstring states the finite-endpoint restriction and that endpoints are distinct); only consecutive crosscuts must be disjoint, as in (i); the chordal formula lacks the factor 2 (sphere of diameter 1), harmless for → 0; U is not assumed open, connected or simply connected (theorems add `IsOpen U` where they need it). Source and checks: Carmona-Fedorovskiy, Carathéodory Sets in the Plane (EMS Memoirs 14, 2024), Ch. 2, Def. 2.2; Rempe-Gillen, On prime ends and local connectivity (arXiv:math/0309022), Sec. 2-3; Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: a path `Path x x` is never a crosscut (compiled), so degenerate crosscuts are excluded; the radial chord chains of the disc satisfy it (`isNullChain_unitDiscRadialChain`), so it is satisfiable; nesting and separation agree on domains (proved).
The domains of a null chain decrease: `Antitone (nullChainDomain U C)` follows from the field D_{n+1} ⊆ D_n.
For open U and compact K ⊆ U, eventually C n ∩ K = ∅: the crosscuts of a null chain leave every compact subset of the domain.
For bounded U the Euclidean diameters also tend to 0: for every ε > 0, eventually ‖z - w‖ < ε for all z, w ∈ C n.
For a null chain the decreasing domains form an antitone basis of its filter (`HasAntitoneBasis`).
The next crosscut lies, inside U, in the current domain: C (n+1) ∩ U ⊆ `nullChainDomain U C n`.
Inside U every later crosscut lies in the first domain: C (n+1) ∩ U ⊆ `nullChainDomain U C 0`.
Each crosscut C n of a null chain is compact, being the range of a path.
The part C n ∩ U of each crosscut inside U (the open arc when U is open) is connected and nonempty (`IsConnected` includes nonemptiness).

Every domain of a null chain is nonempty.
For open U no domain of a null chain lies in a compact K ⊆ U: the domains reach the boundary.
For a null chain the n-th domain is the component of U \ C n containing any point of C (n+1) ∩ U, the standard definition of the domain cut off by C n.

For a null chain, the crosscut C (n+1) separates each point of C 0 ∩ U from each point of C (n+2) ∩ U: `γ.SeparatesIn U z w` for any path γ with range C (n+1) is condition (ii) of Carmona-Fedorovskiy, Carathéodory Sets in the Plane (EMS Memoirs 14, 2024), Ch. 2, Def. 2.2 for k = n+1 ≥ 1 (z, w off the cut and in different components of U \ C (n+1)); no openness of U is needed.

Correctly stated definition: chains C and C' are equivalent when every domain of either contains a domain of the other. Lean ↔ mathematics: the body is `(∀ m, ∃ n, nullChainDomain U C' n ⊆ nullChainDomain U C m) ∧ ∀ m, ∃ n, nullChainDomain U C n ⊆ nullChainDomain U C' m`, i.e. for every m some D'_n ⊆ D_m and some D_n ⊆ D'_m, which is the relation of Ferreira-Jové, Boundary behaviour of universal covering maps (arXiv:2409.01070), Sec. 2.1 (for every large m there is n with N_n ⊂ N'_m and N'_n ⊂ N_m) and, for nested chains, Rempe-Gillen's condition that the crosscuts of each chain eventually lie in every cut-off domain of the other; for null chains it is equality of the generated filters (`nullChainEquivalent_iff_nullChainFilter_eq`). Lean subtlety: it is defined for arbitrary sequences, not only null chains (harmless: `nullChainSetoid` restricts it to null chains); 'every m' and 'every large m' agree because the domains of a null chain decrease. Checks: Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity proved (`equivalence_nullChainEquivalent`).
Every sequence is equivalent to itself.
Equivalence of chains is symmetric (the two conjuncts swap).
Equivalence of chains is transitive: containments compose.

Correctly stated definition: a prime end of U is an equivalence class of null chains of U. Lean ↔ mathematics: `PrimeEnd U` is by definition `Quotient (nullChainSetoid U)`, the quotient of the subtype `{C : ℕ → Set ℂ // IsNullChain U C}` by the setoid whose relation is `NullChainEquivalent U` on the underlying sequences; so an element is a class of sequences C 0, C 1, … with `IsNullChain U C` (each C n the closed range of a crosscut — an injective path with both endpoints on `frontier U` and its open parameter interval in U —, consecutive C n disjoint, the domains `nullChainDomain U C n` = component of U \ C n containing C (n+1) decreasing, chordal diameters → 0), two chains being identified when each domain of either contains a domain of the other; `PrimeEnd.mk_eq_mk_iff` states exactly this. Lean subtlety: (a) it is a `Quotient` by a `Setoid` whose transitivity is proved (`NullChainEquivalent.trans`), not a `Quot` by an unproved relation, so equal classes really are equivalent chains; (b) no hypothesis on U: the type exists for every U ⊆ ℂ, and for U = ℂ, ℂ \ {0} and ∅ it is empty (compiled: frontier ℂ = ∅, and a crosscut needs two distinct frontier points), while for non-domains it has no classical meaning; (c) crosscuts have finite, distinct endpoints, so the chains are narrower than in sources whose crosscuts may end at ∞ (the module docstring says so) or may have coincident endpoints a = b (Ferreira-Jové Def. 2.3, in the disc); Rempe-Gillen's convention (closed Jordan arcs, distinct endpoints) is Lean's; that every classical prime end of an arbitrary simply connected domain has such a representative is not proved in Lean (it is for the disc: `unitDiscPrimeEnd_bijective`); (d) the chordal distance is written ‖z - w‖ / √((1 + ‖z‖^2)(1 + ‖w‖^2)), the sphere of diameter 1 (no factor 2), irrelevant for diameters → 0, and the √ argument is ≥ 1 so no `Real.sqrt` junk; diameters are expressed pairwise, not via `Metric.diam`, so there is no diam-of-unbounded-set = 0 junk; (e) `nullChainDomain` is a union over all z ∈ C (n+1) of `connectedComponentIn (U \ C n) z`, which Mathlib sets to ∅ when z ∉ U \ C n, so the endpoints of C (n+1) contribute nothing, as intended. Source and checks: Carmona-Fedorovskiy, Carathéodory Sets in the Plane (EMS Memoirs 14, 2024), Ch. 2, Def. 2.2 (null chain: disjoint consecutive closures, separation, spherical diameter → 0) and Rempe-Gillen, On prime ends and local connectivity (arXiv:math/0309022), Sec. 2-3 (nested cut-off domains, eventual containment) state the same; Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: emptiness for ℂ, ℂ \ {0}, ∅ compiled; the disc's prime ends are in bijection with the circle (`unitDiscPrimeEnd_bijective`, compiled as a witness); no Classical.choose, Metric.diam or sInf in the construction; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.
The filter of a prime end, the lift of C ↦ `nullChainFilter U C`, well defined because equivalent null chains have equal filters.

A prime end is determined by its filter: `domainFilter p = domainFilter q → p = q`, where `(mk C hC).domainFilter = nullChainFilter U C` (`domainFilter_mk`) is the filter generated by the domains of any representing chain; with the well-definedness of `domainFilter` this identifies prime ends with the filters ⨅ₙ 𝓟(Dₙ) of null chains.
The filter of a prime end of U lives on U: `p.domainFilter ≤ 𝓟 U`.
The filter of the prime end of a chain is the chain's filter: `(mk C hC).domainFilter = nullChainFilter U C`.
Every prime end is `mk C hC` for some null chain C.
For open U the filter of a prime end has a basis consisting of its open members, the domains of any representing chain being open.
A function on null chains that is constant on equivalence classes descends to prime ends (`Quotient.lift`).
The lifted function evaluates on `mk C hC` as on the chain: `lift f hf (mk C hC) = f C hC`.
The prime end represented by a null chain: the class `Quotient.mk` of ⟨C, hC⟩.
Two null chains represent the same prime end iff they are equivalent: `mk C hC = mk C' hC' ↔ NullChainEquivalent U C C'` (`Quotient.eq` for the setoid).
The filter of every prime end is proper (instance `NeBot`).
For open U and compact K ⊆ U, K is not in the filter of any prime end: prime ends live at the boundary.
The chordal distance ‖z - w‖ / √((1 + ‖z‖^2)(1 + ‖w‖^2)) is at most ‖z - w‖, because the square root is at least 1.
`Equivalence (NullChainEquivalent U)`: the relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive on all sequences, so the prime-end quotient is by a genuine equivalence relation.

Correctly stated: on a preconnected open U, a sequence of closed crosscut ranges with consecutive ones disjoint and chordal diameters → 0 is an `IsNullChain` (nested domains) exactly when it satisfies Pommerenke's separation condition. Lean ↔ mathematics: `hUo : IsOpen U` and `hUc : IsPreconnected U` make U a domain (or empty); `hcut`, `hdisj`, `hdiam` are 'each C n is a crosscut', condition (i) and condition (iii); the right side `∀ n γ, range γ = C (n + 1) → ∀ z ∈ C 0 ∩ U, ∀ w ∈ C (n + 2) ∩ U, γ.SeparatesIn U z w` is (ii) 'C_k separates C_0 and C_{k+1} for k ≥ 1' with k = n+1, where `Path.SeparatesIn U z w` means z, w ∈ U \ range γ lie in different `connectedComponentIn`s and C 0 ∩ U is the open arc of C_0. Lean subtlety: the separation is quantified over every path with range C (n+1), harmless since `SeparatesIn` depends only on the range; the source assumes U simply connected, which this equivalence does not need. Source and checks: Carmona-Fedorovskiy, Carathéodory Sets in the Plane (EMS Memoirs 14, 2024), Ch. 2, Def. 2.2 is the right-hand definition; Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: lean_minimal_hypotheses finds all five hypotheses load-bearing; axioms standard.
z ∈ `nullChainDomain U C n` iff z lies in the component of U \ C n of some point of C (n+1): the unfolding of the union defining the domain.
For ‖z‖, ‖w‖ ≤ R, ‖z - w‖ ≤ (1 + R^2) times the chordal distance, because the square root is at most 1 + R^2; for R < 0 the hypotheses cannot hold, so nothing is claimed there.
For ‖z‖, ‖w‖ ≤ R, chordal distance < ε / (1 + R^2) forces ‖z - w‖ < ε; the division is by 1 + R^2 > 0, so no division-by-zero junk.

Correctly stated definition: the n-th domain of a sequence of cuts, the union of the components of U \ C n that meet C (n+1). Lean ↔ mathematics: the body `⋃ z ∈ C (n + 1), connectedComponentIn (U \ C n) z` is that union; for a null chain it is the single component of U \ C n containing C (n+1) ∩ U (`IsNullChain.nullChainDomain_eq_connectedComponentIn`), which on a simply connected domain is the side of C n away from C 0, the role played by Rempe-Gillen's U_{C_n} (the component of U \ C_n not containing a fixed base point). Lean subtlety: `connectedComponentIn F z = ∅` when z ∉ F (Mathlib `connectedComponentIn_eq_empty`), so the endpoints of C (n+1), which lie outside U, and any point of C (n+1) on C n contribute nothing; that is what makes the union the intended component. If C (n+1) ∩ U is preconnected and C (n+1) misses C n, the n-th domain is the single component of U \ C n through any z ∈ C (n+1) ∩ U; the disjointness hypothesis is stronger than the proof needs (recorded separately), which does not affect correctness.
The n-th domain avoids the n-th cut: `nullChainDomain U C n ⊆ U \ C n`, since each `connectedComponentIn (U \ C n) z` lies in U \ C n.
The n-th domain lies in U: `nullChainDomain U C n ⊆ U`.

On a preconnected open U, for closed crosscut ranges with consecutive ones disjoint, the separation condition (ii) implies D_{n+1} ⊆ D_n for every n, where D_n = `nullChainDomain U C n`; the hypotheses are those of `isNullChain_iff_separatesIn` minus the diameter condition, each load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses), and the two-components theorem for crosscuts is not used.
The definitional unfolding (`Iff.rfl`) of `NullChainEquivalent` as mutual cofinal containment of domains.

For null chains C and C', `NullChainEquivalent U C C'` iff `nullChainFilter U C = nullChainFilter U C'`, where `nullChainFilter U C = ⨅ n, 𝓟 (nullChainDomain U C n)` is the filter generated by the domains; since the domains form an antitone basis, `≤` in both directions is mutual cofinal containment.
The filter `⨅ n, 𝓟 (nullChainDomain U C n)` generated by the domains of a sequence of cuts; for a null chain the domains form an antitone basis of it.
The filter of a sequence of cuts lives on U: `nullChainFilter U C ≤ 𝓟 U`, as the domains lie in U.

The setoid on `{C // IsNullChain U C}` whose relation is `NullChainEquivalent U` on the underlying sequences (`Setoid.comap Subtype.val`), with the equivalence proof `equivalence_nullChainEquivalent`: the setoid of null chains up to equivalence.

Correctly stated: this is Schur's theorem for ℓ¹. Over ℝ or ℂ and for any index set ι, a sequence in ℓ¹(ι) that converges weakly to y converges to y in norm; the Lean statement allows any countably generated filter, which includes sequences. Lean ↔ mathematics: `lp (fun _ : ι ↦ 𝕜) 1` is Mathlib's ℓ¹(ι, 𝕜). It consists of the functions ι → 𝕜 with Σ‖f i‖ summable (`Memℓp f 1`), and its norm is Σᵢ ‖f i‖ (`lp.hasSum_norm_one`). `[RCLike 𝕜]` means 𝕜 = ℝ or ℂ. ι is an arbitrary type, so uncountable index sets are covered: the audit compiled the theorem at ι = ℝ, 𝕜 = ℂ. `toWeakSpace 𝕜 E` is the identity map (`LinearEquiv.refl`) into `WeakSpace 𝕜 E`, which is E itself with the weak topology σ(E, E*). Mathlib defines it as `WeakBilin (topDualPairing 𝕜 E).flip`, and the audit compiled by `rfl` that its topology is `TopologicalSpace.induced (fun x f ↦ f x)` of the product topology on `StrongDual 𝕜 E → 𝕜`. `StrongDual 𝕜 E = E →L[𝕜] 𝕜` contains every norm-continuous linear functional: all of (ℓ¹)* ≅ ℓ^∞, not just coordinate functionals or pairings with finitely supported sequences. So the hypothesis `hx` says exactly that f(x n) → f(y) for every f ∈ (ℓ¹)*: `TauCeti.tendsto_toWeakSpace_iff_forall_eval_tendsto` is that iff, and the audit derived the textbook form `(∀ f : StrongDual 𝕜 (lp _ 1), Tendsto (fun n ↦ f (x n)) atTop (𝓝 (f y))) → Tendsto (fun n ↦ ‖x n - y‖) atTop (𝓝 0)` from the theorem. Correctly stated: along a countably generated filter, in particular for sequences, a family in ℓ¹(ι) over ℝ or ℂ converges weakly to y if and only if it converges to y in norm. Whitehead's first lemma, correctly stated: for a finite-dimensional Lie algebra L with nondegenerate Killing form over a field K of characteristic 0 and a finite-dimensional L-module M, every derivation D : L → M is inner, D(x) = x·m for some m ∈ M, i.e. H¹(L, M) = 0. Lean ↔ mathematics: `LieDerivation K L M` is a K-linear map D : L → M with the axiom `leibniz'`: D⁅a, b⁆ = ⁅a, D b⁆ − ⁅b, D a⁆, which is Weibel's Definition 7.4.3 of a derivation g → M (D([x,y]) = x(Dy) − y(Dx)), i.e. a Chevalley–Eilenberg 1-cocycle; `LieDerivation.inner K L M m` is by definition `(LieModule.toEnd K L M).flip m`, the map x ↦ ⁅x, m⁆ (`inner_apply_apply`), which is Weibel's inner derivation D_m(x) = xm (Example 7.4.4); the conclusion `∃ m, inner K L M m = D` is equality of derivations, i.e. D(x) = ⁅x, m⁆ for all x (`LieDerivation.ext`), so Der(L, M) = Der_inn(L, M), which is H¹(L, M) = 0 by Weibel's Theorem 7.4.7. Hypotheses: `[Field K] [CharZero K]` is a field of characteristic 0 (not assumed algebraically closed, as in Weibel); `[LieAlgebra.IsKilling K L]` is by definition `LieIdeal.killingCompl K L ⊤ = ⊥`, i.e. the radical {x | κ(y, x) = 0 for all y} of the Killing form `killingForm K L x y = trace(ad x ∘ ad y)` is zero — nondegeneracy — and together with `[FiniteDimensional K L]` and characteristic 0 this is exactly semisimplicity (Cartan's criterion, Weibel 7.8.4; in Mathlib both directions: `LieAlgebra.IsKilling.instSemisimple` and `LieAlgebra.HasTrivialRadical.instIsKilling`); `[LieRingModule L M] [LieModule K L M] [FiniteDimensional K M]` is a finite-dimensional representation x ↦ ⁅x, ·⁆ of L. Lean subtlety: `inner` is x ↦ ⁅x, m⁆, which for M = L is −ad m, whereas Mathlib's adjoint-case theorem `LieDerivation.IsKilling.exists_eq_ad` uses `ad x = ⁅x, ·⁆` — the witnesses differ by a sign, harmless for an existence statement; Mathlib's `killingForm` is a trace and `LinearMap.trace` is 0 on a module without a finite basis, a junk case that `[FiniteDimensional K L]` rules out; the zero Lie algebra satisfies `IsKilling` and the statement is then trivially true. Source: Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra, Cor. 7.8.10 (p. 245: g semisimple over a field of characteristic 0, M any finite-dimensional g-module ⇒ H¹(g, M) = 0, every derivation g → M is inner), with Def. 7.4.3, Ex. 7.4.4, Thm. 7.4.7 and Cartan's criterion 7.8.4 (read in the text). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only; with `[LieAlgebra.IsSemisimple K L]` in place of `IsKilling` it applies by instance search (compiled); specialised to sl₂(ℚ) acting on itself it gives that every derivation of sl₂(ℚ) is inner (compiled; sl₂(ℚ) is nonzero and `IsKilling` is inferred), and at M = L it agrees with Mathlib's `exists_eq_ad`, which is the only case Mathlib has; the hypothesis is needed: for the 1-dimensional abelian L = K acting on itself, id is a derivation that is not inner, and the lemma (via its cochain form) forces ¬ IsKilling K K (compiled).

Whitehead's second lemma, correctly stated: for a finite-dimensional Lie algebra L with nondegenerate Killing form over a field K of characteristic 0 and a finite-dimensional L-module M, every Chevalley–Eilenberg 2-cocycle is a coboundary, i.e. H²(L, M) = 0. Right side: `inertiaSubgroup K` is by definition the subgroup of `Field.absoluteGaloisGroup K` (literally `AlgebraicClosure K ≃ₐ[K] AlgebraicClosure K`) fixing the maximal unramified extension (generated by the roots of X^{q^f} − X), and `inertiaSubgroup_le_fixingSubgroup_iff` shows a finite separable subextension is unramified exactly when inertia fixes it, so it is the usual I_K; `W.tateModuleGaloisRepresentation ℓ` is the ℤ_ℓ-linear action on `TateModule ℓ (W⁄(AlgebraicClosure K)).toAffine.Point`, the compatible families (x_n) with x_n ∈ E[ℓ^n](K^alg) and ℓ·x_{n+1} = x_n, i.e. lim E[ℓ^n] (not one finite level), σ acting on coordinates level by level; `= 1` is the identity endomorphism, and `∀ σ ∈ inertiaSubgroup K` restricts this to inertia, not all of G_K. Claim: for every curve γ continuous on [a, b] with values in a finite-dimensional real inner product space V, the length of γ on [a, b] equals ∫_V N(y) dH¹(y), where N(y) = #{t ∈ [a, b] : γ(t) = y} ∈ {0, 1, …, ∞} is Banach's indicatrix; both sides may be ∞. Lean subtlety: (i) `∫⁻` of a function not proved measurable is Mathlib's lower integral (the supremum over measurable simple functions below it), and the file never proves y ↦ N(y) measurable; but N is Borel, being the increasing limit of the counts over half-open dyadic subintervals, whose images are σ-compact, so the lower integral is the honest integral. (ii) `encard` gives ⊤, not 0 as `Set.ncard` would, on an infinite fibre: pauses count correctly, and a constant curve has fibre ⊤ over one μH[1]-null point, so both sides are 0 (compiled). (iii) For a > b, `Icc a b = ∅` and both sides are 0 (compiled). (iv) There is no `toReal` junk: a non-rectifiable continuous curve gets ∞ = ∞. Source and checks: Warner, 'Analysis 101: Curves and Length' (arXiv 2311.16418), §2, Notation 12 and Theorem 13, states ℓ(C) = ∫ N(f;−) dH¹ for a continuous f : [a, b] → ℝ^M, with N(f; x) the number (finite or infinite) of parameters over x and ℓ the partition supremum of Definition 7. That is exactly this statement. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound; specialisations compiled (the identity on [0, 1] in ℝ gives length 1, the Lebesgue length; t ↦ |t| on [−1, 1] gives 2 through its 2-point fibres over (0, 1]; a constant curve gives 0; an empty interval gives 0); continuity is load-bearing; the hypotheses are satisfiable. The formula also holds in every extended metric space (MINOR generality finding RT-20261104-3a1345, proved in a compiled probe), so the stated version is a correct special case.

Claim: for γ Lipschitz on [a, b] (`LipschitzOnWith K γ (Icc a b)`: K-Lipschitz on the closed interval, values outside irrelevant) with values in a finite-dimensional real inner product space, the length `eVariationOn γ (Icc a b)` (the [0, ∞]-valued supremum over partitions of Σ ‖γ(tᵢ₊₁) − γ(tᵢ)‖) equals `∫⁻ y, ↑(Icc a b ∩ γ ⁻¹' {y}).encard ∂μHE[1]`, the H¹-integral of the number of parameters over y. `encard` is ⊤ on infinite fibres, cast to ∞, and `μHE[1] = μH[1]` is H¹ normalised to agree with length (`Measure.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_one`, `hausdorffMeasure_real`). It is the Lipschitz case of Banach's indicatrix formula (Warner, arXiv 2311.16418, §2 Theorem 13, for continuous curves in ℝ^M); here it comes from the area formula and `AbsolutelyContinuousOnInterval.eVariationOn_eq_lintegral_enorm_deriv`. Claim (weighted area formula for curves): for γ Lipschitz on [a, b] with values in a finite-dimensional real inner product space and any measurable weight g : ℝ → [0, ∞], ∫_{[a,b]} |γ'(t)| g(t) dt = ∫_V Σ_{t ∈ [a,b], γ(t) = y} g(t) dH¹(y). Both happen only on a Lebesgue-null set (Rademacher's theorem in the interior, two endpoints), and the proof rewrites the integrand only for a.e. t ∈ (a, b) (`setLIntegral_congr_fun_ae` with `ae_ne a`, `ae_ne b`), so the left side is the classical ∫|γ'| g. The `tsum` has no non-summable junk in ℝ≥0∞. For a > b both sides are 0. Checks: standard axioms; both hypotheses are load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses); at g ≡ 1 it gives the Lipschitz indicatrix formula, which underlies the continuous theorem whose specialisations compiled.

Correctly stated: over an algebraically closed field, let i : Y → X be an immersion whose image lies in the orbit of x, and let e assign to each k-point g of G an automorphism of Y with i ∘ e(g) = translation(g) ∘ i. Then the e(g) act transitively on the closed points of Y. Lean to mathematics: `[IsImmersion i]` is an immersion of schemes; `hrange : Set.range i ⊆ orbit G x` is the containment; `he` is the intertwining square in the category of schemes; `closedPoints Y` is the set of closed points. It holds because X is Jacobson (finite type over k), so the immersion sends closed points to closed points of the orbit, translations are transitive on those, and i is injective. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: i, hrange, e, he, hy and hz are all needed (lean_minimal_hypotheses); consumers Orbit/Scheme.lean, Orbit/Smooth.lean and Orbit/Translation.lean.

Correctly stated: over an algebraically closed field, for a group scheme G acting on X with G and X locally of finite type, any two closed points p and q of the orbit of x satisfy q = g·p for some k-point g of G. Lean to mathematics: `(translation X g).hom.left` is the automorphism of X given by acting with g (by definition `(toUnit X ≫ g) • 𝟙 X`, the action map restricted to {g} × X), and `p ∈ orbit G x ∩ closedPoints X.left` says p is a closed point of the orbit. By `orbit_inter_closedPoints`, p = g•x and q = h•x, so h·g⁻¹ works. The `[IsAlgClosed k]` hypothesis is in the signature. The docstring omits it (RT-20261104-469164), and over ℝ the claim fails, but the declaration itself is right. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: both explicit hypotheses are needed (lean_minimal_hypotheses).

Correctly stated: over an algebraically closed field (hypotheses as in `isLocallyClosed_orbit`), the boundary closure(O) ∖ O of the orbit O of a rational point is closed. Lean to mathematics: `orbitBoundary G x` is by definition `orbitClosure G x \ orbit G x`, which is closure(O) ∖ O. A locally closed set has open coborder, i.e. (closure(O) ∖ O)ᶜ is open (Mathlib `IsLocallyClosed.isOpen_coborder`). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: for the trivial action the boundary is ∅ (compiled); consumer GroupAction/ClosedOrbit.lean (closed-orbit existence).

Correctly stated: for a monoid scheme G over any base S that is locally of finite type over S with quasi-compact underlying space, acting on a quasi-compact, locally Noetherian S-scheme X, the orbit of a section x is a constructible subset of X. Lean to mathematics: `[MonObj G]` in `Over S` (cartesian under fibre product over S) is a monoid scheme over S, so the statement covers group schemes; `[ModObj G X]` is an action satisfying the unit and associativity laws; `x : 𝟙_ (Over S) ⟶ X` is a section of X → S; `orbit G x` is the image of the orbit morphism g ↦ g•x; `IsConstructible` is Mathlib's Boolean algebra generated by retrocompact opens, which on the Noetherian space X is the usual 'finite union of locally closed sets'. This is Chevalley's theorem (Mathlib `Scheme.Hom.isConstructible_image`, Stacks 054J) applied to the orbit morphism. That morphism is locally of finite type because its composite with X → S is G → S; on a locally Noetherian target this means locally of finite presentation, and quasi-compact G with quasi-separated X gives quasi-compactness. Lean subtlety: `[CompactSpace G.left]` asks for quasi-compactness of the scheme G rather than of G → S. Here the two agree, because G → S factors through the quasi-compact X. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the hypotheses are satisfiable (trivial group scheme over Spec k, compiled); it is the input to `isLocallyClosed_orbit`.

Correctly stated: over an algebraically closed field k, for a finite-type group scheme G acting on a finite-type k-scheme X and a k-rational point x, the orbit G·x is locally closed in X (the closed orbit lemma). Lean to mathematics: `Over (Spec (.of k))` is the category of k-schemes, cartesian monoidal by fibre product over Spec k with unit `𝟙_` = Spec k (`(𝟙_ (Over S)).hom = 𝟙 S` holds by rfl, checked), so `[GrpObj G]` is a group scheme over k and `x : 𝟙_ ⟶ X` is a section of X → Spec k, i.e. a k-point; `[ModObj G X]` is Mathlib's action class whose fields `one_smul` and `mul_smul` are exactly the unit and associativity diagrams μ(e,x) = x, μ(gh,x) = μ(g,μ(h,x)) of Platonov–Rapinchuk–Rapinchuk §2.4.5 (an action, not just a morphism); `[LocallyOfFiniteType G.hom]` with `[CompactSpace G.left]` is 'G of finite type over k' (the base is a point, so quasi-compactness of G → Spec k is compactness of G), likewise for X; `orbit G x` is by definition `Set.range (orbitMap G x).left`, the image of the orbit morphism g ↦ g•x (`orbitMap G x = 𝟙 G • (toUnit G ≫ x)`, the action map applied to (g, x)); `IsLocallyClosed s` is Mathlib's ∃ U open, Z closed, s = U ∩ Z, equivalent to 'open in its closure' (`isLocallyClosed_iff_isOpen_preimage_val_closure`, and `isOpen_orbitClosure_preimage_orbit` in this file). Lean subtlety: `orbit G x` is a set of scheme points that includes non-closed (generic) points, not the set G(k)·x of k-points that the classical sources use. This is harmless and in fact stronger: `orbit_inter_closedPoints` shows its closed points are exactly the translates g•x by g ∈ G(k), and X is Jacobson, so intersecting with the closed points gives the classical orbit as a locally closed subset of X(k). No junk values are involved. The group structure is essential: a monoid action such as (s,t)·(a,b) = (sa, stb) on 𝔸² has orbit {a ≠ 0} ∪ {(0,0)} through (1,1), which is not locally closed (by hand). Quasi-compactness of G is essential too: the constant group ℤ translating 𝔸¹ in characteristic 0 has orbit ℤ (by hand). `[IsAlgClosed k]` is stronger than the statement needs (base change to k̄, recorded as needs-human RT-20261104-945b07), but the docstring states it. Source: Platonov–Rapinchuk–Rapinchuk, Algebraic Groups and Number Theory I (2023), Prop. 2.48 (Closed Orbit Lemma, citing Borel §1.8): each orbit is open in its closure; it works with varieties over an algebraically closed field, and the Lean version also covers non-reduced G and arbitrary finite-type X. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the hypotheses are jointly satisfiable (the trivial group scheme Spec k acting on itself; `isLocallyClosed_orbit` and `topologicalKrullDim_orbitBoundary_lt` apply, compiled); under the trivial action the orbit is the single point underlying x and its boundary is empty, and under the regular action the orbit of the identity section is all of G (all compiled); no declaration in the module takes over 0.2 s (profiler).

Correctly stated: over an algebraically closed field (hypotheses as in `isLocallyClosed_orbit`), the orbit of a rational point is open in its closure. Lean to mathematics: `orbitClosure G x` is by definition `closure (orbit G x)`, and `(Subtype.val : orbitClosure G x → X.left) ⁻¹' orbit G x` is the orbit seen inside its closure with the subspace topology. So `IsOpen` of it is literally 'open in its closure', the wording of Platonov–Rapinchuk–Rapinchuk (2023) Prop. 2.48. It is `isLocallyClosed_orbit` read through Mathlib's `isLocallyClosed_iff_isOpen_preimage_val_closure`, and it has no consumer (RT-20261104-9013d9).

Correctly stated: over an algebraically closed field, for G and X locally of finite type, a k-rational point y of X lies in the orbit of the k-point x exactly when y = g•x for some k-point g of G. Lean to mathematics: `y.left a` is the point of X underlying y (`a` runs over the one-point space Spec k); `orbit G x` is the image of g ↦ g•x; `g : 𝟙_ ⟶ G` is a k-point of G and `g • x` is Mathlib's action of global points on global points (Spec k → G ×_k X → X), so the right-hand side says y ∈ G(k)·x. The forward direction is the Nullstellensatz step, which uses `[IsAlgClosed k]`: a k-point in the image of a finite-type morphism lifts to a k-point (`Scheme.Hom.exists_comp_eq_iff_mem_range`). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: instantiating at x = y with g = 1 recovers x ∈ orbit (that is how `topologicalKrullDim_orbitBoundary_lt` uses it); consumer GroupAction/ClosedOrbit.lean.

Correctly stated: over an algebraically closed field, with G and X locally of finite type, the closed points of the orbit of x are exactly the points g•x for g ∈ G(k). Lean to mathematics: `closedPoints X.left` is the set of closed points of the underlying space. `Set.range (g • x).left` is the single point underlying the k-point g•x (Spec k is a point), so `⋃ g : 𝟙_ ⟶ G, …` is the classical orbit G(k)·x as a set of closed points. This identifies the scheme-theoretic orbit (all points of the image) with the classical one at the level of closed points. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: for the trivial action both sides are {x} (orbit computed as the point, compiled); consumer GroupAction/ClosedOrbit.lean.

Correctly stated: over an algebraically closed field, for a finite-type group scheme G acting on a finite-type X and a rational point x, the boundary closure(O) ∖ O of the orbit O has strictly smaller dimension than O. Lean to mathematics: `orbitBoundary G x` is by definition `closure (orbit G x) \ orbit G x`; `topologicalKrullDim` of a set is Mathlib's Krull dimension of the subspace (the supremum of lengths of chains of irreducible closed subsets), which for subsets of a finite-type k-scheme is the usual dimension; `<` is strict in `WithBot ℕ∞`. The hypotheses read as in `isLocallyClosed_orbit`: group scheme, action with unit and associativity laws, finite type, k-point. Lean subtlety: dimensions live in `WithBot ℕ∞`, and the empty set has dimension ⊥ = −∞ (`topologicalKrullDim (∅ : Set T) = ⊥` compiled). So when the orbit is closed the statement reads ⊥ < dim O, which is the intended 'empty boundary' case: O contains x, so dim O ≥ 0 and nothing holds vacuously. Under the trivial action the boundary is empty (compiled). There is no ⊤ junk value either, since finite type gives finite dimension (the proof uses `topologicalKrullDim_ne_top_of_locallyOfFiniteType`). Source: Platonov–Rapinchuk–Rapinchuk (2023) Prop. 2.48 says the boundary of an orbit 'is a union of orbits of strictly lower dimension'. The Lean statement is the set form of that: the boundary is translation-invariant (`image_translation_orbitBoundary`), so it is a union of orbits, and dim(boundary) < dim O says each of them is smaller. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the hypotheses are jointly satisfiable and the conclusion holds at the trivial group scheme acting on itself (compiled); consumer GroupAction/ClosedOrbit.lean (orbits of minimal dimension are closed).

Correctly stated: over an algebraically closed field (hypotheses as in `isLocallyClosed_orbit`), the closure of the orbit O has the same dimension as O. Lean to mathematics: `topologicalKrullDim` of a set is the Krull dimension of the subspace (the supremum of lengths of chains of irreducible closed subsets), and `orbitClosure G x = closure (orbit G x)`. Equality holds because O is open and dense in its closure, and in a finite-type k-scheme every irreducible component of the closure meets O in a dense open subset of the same dimension. Values lie in `WithBot ℕ∞` and are finite here. It is a one-line specialisation of `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.topologicalKrullDim_closure_of_isLocallyClosed` with no consumer (RT-20261104-cd68e7).

Correctly stated: for every finite index type σ and every complete non-archimedean normed field K, the Tate algebra K⟨X_i : i ∈ σ⟩ of restricted power series is a unique factorisation domain. Lean ↔ mathematics: `Tate σ` is local notation for `MvPowerSeries.IsRestricted.subring (R := K) (fun _ : σ ↦ 1)`, Mathlib's subring of `MvPowerSeries σ K` cut out by `IsRestricted c f := Tendsto (fun t ↦ ‖coeff t f‖ * t.prod (c · ^ ·)) cofinite (𝓝 0)`. With c ≡ 1 the product is 1, so membership says exactly that ‖c_ν‖ → 0 as the multi-index ν leaves every finite set, i.e. as |ν| → ∞. That is Bosch's Definition 2 read through his Lemma 1. We compiled `f ∈ Tate K σ ↔ Tendsto (fun t ↦ ‖coeff t f‖) cofinite (𝓝 0)`, and that the geometric series Σ Xⁿ is not a member. So the instance is about the restricted subring and not about all of K[[X]], which would be a different theorem. `[NormedField K] [IsUltrametricDist K] [CompleteSpace K]` say that K is a field with an absolute value obeying the strong triangle inequality (non-archimedean) and that K is complete. `[Finite σ]` means finitely many variables, n = card σ, with n = 0 allowed. In pinned Mathlib, `UniqueFactorizationMonoid` extends `IsCancelMulZero` and asks for well-founded strict divisibility together with irreducible ⇔ prime. Together with the subring's `Nontrivial` this gives `IsDomain (Tate K σ)` (compiled). The textbook UFD properties follow: `UniqueFactorizationMonoid.exists_prime_factors` (every nonzero element is associated to a product of primes) and `UniqueFactorizationMonoid.factors_unique` (two factorisations into irreducibles agree up to order and associates) both compile at `Tate K σ`. The monoid structure the instance uses is the subring's `CommRing` one, which the instance matches under with_reducible_and_instances, so there is no diamond. Lean subtlety: the absolute value need not be nontrivial. For the trivial absolute value, 'coefficients → 0' means only finitely many coefficients are nonzero, so `Tate σ` is the polynomial ring K[X_i], which is still a UFD. The statement is therefore more general than Bosch's, who assumes non-trivial absolute values, and is not wrong there. For σ empty, `σ →₀ ℕ` is a single point, the cofinite filter is ⊥ and the restriction condition is vacuous. That is correct, because a series in no variables is a constant, and the proof's base case is the ring isomorphism K ≃ `Tate ∅`. `UniqueFactorizationMonoid` is not literally 'domain with unique factorisation', but it is equivalent to that, as above. No junk values (division by zero, ℕ subtraction) occur. Source and checks: Bosch, Lectures on Formal and Rigid Geometry (Münster preprint, April 2008), §1.2, Definition 2, Lemma 1 and Proposition 14 ('T_n is factorial and, hence, normal'), for K complete non-archimedean. The Lean proof follows Bosch's: induction on the number of variables, Gauss's lemma, Weierstrass preparation, and the isomorphism T_{n-1}[ζ]/(ω) ≅ T_n/(ω). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the instance is found at ℚ_[p] with Fin 0 and Fin 2, so the hypotheses are consistent. `IsIntegrallyClosed` (Mathlib's `UniqueFactorizationMonoid.instIsIntegrallyClosed`) is inferred with only this module imported. `Algebra.HasGoingDown (Tate K σ) S` is inferred for every domain S that is integral and faithful over it, which bears out the module docstring. Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. There is no duplicate in Mathlib or elsewhere in Tau Ceti; the Huber completed-Tate-algebra instance transports this one.

Correctly stated: for polynomials f, g over a ring with a real additive valuation, the Newton polygon of fg is the Minkowski sum of the Newton polygons of f and g. Lean ↔ mathematics: `v : AddValuation R (WithTop ℝ)` is a map v : R → ℝ ∪ {∞} with v(0) = ∞, v(1) = 0, v(xy) = v(x) + v(y) and v(x + y) ≥ min(v x, v y), a genuine rank-one valuation even on a ring with zero divisors (xy = 0 forces v(x) = ∞ or v(y) = ∞, so any term lost in fg had height ∞ anyway); `f.newtonPolygon v` is by `Polynomial.newtonPolygon_def` the `lowerConvexEnvelope` of the coefficient heights n ↦ v(f.coeff n), and by `Polynomial.isLowerConvexEnvelope_newtonPolygon` the greatest convex minorant of the points (n, v(aₙ)) (height ∞ = no point), recorded by its values at the integers n : ℕ, which determine the polygon because its vertices are integral; `TauCeti.minkowskiSum h g n` is by `minkowskiSum_def` the min-convolution min over i + j = n (`Finset.antidiagonal n`) of h(i) + g(j), and for two convex polygons with integral vertices this is the height at n of the Minkowski sum of the polygons (y ↦ h(y) + g(n − y) is convex piecewise linear with integral break points, so the real infimal convolution is attained at an integer split); the `=` is equality of functions ℕ → WithTop ℝ, i.e. at every index, including the ∞ values outside the polygons' domains. There are no hypotheses: no field, no f, g ≠ 0, no commutativity. Lean subtlety: in `WithTop ℝ`, ⊤ + x = ⊤, and this is what makes the degenerate case right: if f = 0, or every coefficient of f has valuation ∞, then `newtonPolygon_eq_top_iff` gives the empty polygon ⊤, `top_minkowskiSum` gives ⊤ on the right, and fg also has the empty polygon (a Minkowski sum with the empty set is empty); the ⊤ fallback of `lowerConvexEnvelope` for heights with no affine lower bound never arises, since polynomial heights are always admissible (`isAdmissible_addValuation_coeff`). Source: K. S. Kedlaya, *Newton polygons* (MIT 18.787 notes, fall 2007) §2: for P, Q ∈ F[T] the slope multiset of PQ is the union of those of P and Q, via Proposition 1, v_r(PQ) = v_r(P) + v_r(Q) with v_r(Σ PᵢTⁱ) = minᵢ {v(Pᵢ) + ri} (Kedlaya plots (−i, v(Pᵢ)), so his r is −σ here); the Lean statement is the more general any-ring form. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only; compiled over ℚ₂ with the 2-adic valuation that ((X − 2)(X − 1/2)).newtonPolygon v 1 = min(1 + 0, 0 + (−1)) = −1, agreeing with the independently computed valuation −1 of the middle coefficient −5/2, and that (X − 1)(X + 1) = X² − 1 has polygon value 0 at index 1 although its middle coefficient vanishes (the lost term is interpolated by the hull, not a counterexample).

Correctly stated: if only 0 has infinite valuation, f ≠ 0 and g divides f, then every finite Newton slope of g is a finite slope of f, counted with multiplicity. Lean ↔ mathematics: `hv : ∀ x, v x = ⊤ → x = 0` says the valuation has trivial support (as for any valuation on a field or division ring); `g ∣ f` is ∃ h, f = g * h; `≤` on `Multiset ℝ` is sub-multiset inclusion counting multiplicities; `newtonSlopes` is the multiset of finite slopes (`Polynomial.newtonSlopes_def`). It is the corollary of `Polynomial.newtonSlopes_mul`: f = gh with g, h ≠ 0 gives slopes(f) = slopes(g) + slopes(h). Lean subtlety: over a noncommutative ring `g ∣ f` means a left factor, f = g * h; `f ≠ 0` is needed, since 0 is divisible by everything and has no finite slopes. The hypotheses are stronger than necessary (f.newtonPolygon v ≠ ⊤ alone suffices; recorded as a MINOR generality finding), which does not make the statement as given wrong. Source: the multiplicativity in K. S. Kedlaya, *Newton polygons* (MIT 18.787 notes, fall 2007) §2. Checks: the weaker-hypothesis form compiled in a module probe; axioms standard.

Correctly stated: if f and g each have a coefficient of finite valuation, the multiset of finite Newton slopes of fg is the multiset union of those of f and g. Lean ↔ mathematics: `f.newtonSlopes v` is by `Polynomial.newtonSlopes_def` the image under `unitSlope (f.newtonPolygon v)` (the increment NP(n+1) − NP(n)) of the finite unit edges, i.e. every slope of the Newton polygon counted with multiplicity equal to the width of its segment, the infinite slopes coming from a factor Xᵏ being left out (hence 'finite'); `+` on `Multiset ℝ` is union with multiplicities; the hypotheses `f.newtonPolygon v ≠ ⊤` and `g.newtonPolygon v ≠ ⊤` say, by `Polynomial.newtonPolygon_eq_top_iff`, that some coefficient of each factor has finite valuation; over a field, or whenever only 0 has valuation ∞, this is just f ≠ 0 and g ≠ 0 (`Polynomial.newtonPolygon_ne_top_of_ne_zero`). A slope m corresponds to roots of valuation −m (Kedlaya's notes have the opposite sign because they plot at −i). Lean subtlety: the hypotheses are genuinely needed: compiled over ℚ₂, 0 · (X − 2) has no finite slopes while the slopes of 0 plus those of X − 2 are {−1}; `unitSlope` reads `untop₀` (∞ ↦ 0, a junk value), but `newtonSlopes` only evaluates it on finite edges, where both endpoint heights are real. Source: K. S. Kedlaya, *Newton polygons* (MIT 18.787 notes, fall 2007) §2: 'the slope multiset of PQ is the union of the slope multisets of P and Q' (his multiset also lists +∞ for the missing low-degree terms; removing those on both sides gives this statement). Checks: compiled specialisation over ℚ₂ with the 2-adic valuation, ((X − 2)(X − 2⁻¹)).newtonSlopes v = {−1, 1}, i.e. root valuations 1 and −1; axioms standard.

Correctly stated: for every real σ, the supporting value min over n of v(cₙ) − σn of the coefficient heights of fg is the sum of those of f and g (additively, multiplicativity of the Gauss norm at every radius). Lean ↔ mathematics: `supportingValue a σ` is by `supportingValue_def` the infimum ⨅ n, a(n) − σn in `EReal`, i.e. the y-intercept of the supporting line of slope σ, which for a polynomial is a minimum over the finitely many finite heights; `fun n => v ((f * g).coeff n)` are the coefficient heights of fg; there are no hypotheses. This is Kedlaya's Proposition 1 in the untwisted case, v_r(PQ) = v_r(P) + v_r(Q) with v_r = minᵢ {v(Pᵢ) + ri}, at r = −σ. Lean subtlety: `EReal` addition has ⊤ + ⊥ = ⊥ (checked), which would spoil the identity if a supporting value were −∞; for polynomials it never is (`supportingValue_ne_bot_of_finite`, used in the proof), and if all heights of a factor are ∞ (e.g. it is 0) both sides are ⊤, as the docstring says, because ⊤ + x = ⊤ for x ≠ ⊥; the cast n : ℕ → ℝ in σ * n is harmless. Source: K. S. Kedlaya, *Newton polygons* (MIT 18.787 notes, fall 2007) §2, Proposition 1. Checks: axioms standard; follows from `Polynomial.newtonPolygon_mul` and the supporting values of a Minkowski sum.

Correctly stated: with i and j the greatest contact indices (`IsGreatest` = member and maximal) of supporting lines of a common slope σ for the heights of f and g, the coefficient of fg at i + j has valuation v(aᵢ) + v(bⱼ), by the mirror of Kedlaya's smallest-minimiser argument.

Correctly stated: with i and j the least contact indices (`IsLeast` = member and minimal) of supporting lines of a common slope σ for the heights of f and g, the coefficient of fg at i + j has valuation v(aᵢ) + v(bⱼ). This is the step in Kedlaya's proof of Proposition 1 (K. S. Kedlaya, *Newton polygons* (MIT 18.787 notes, fall 2007) §2: 'let i₀ and j₀ be the smallest values of i and j which minimize ri + v(Pᵢ) and rj + v(Qⱼ)').

Correctly stated: if lines of slope σ support the heights of f and g (`IsSupportingLine`: c + σn ≤ v(aₙ) and d + σn ≤ v(bₙ) for all n), touch them at i and j (`supportingFace`: v(aᵢ) = c + σi, v(bⱼ) = d + σj), and every other split p + q = i + j has a point strictly above its line, then the coefficient of fg at i + j has valuation v(aᵢ) + v(bⱼ): the unique dominant term of Σ_{p+q=i+j} a_p b_q (`AddValuation.map_add_eq_of_lt_left`). The strictness hypothesis is satisfiable: the `_of_isLeast` version derives it from minimal contacts.

Correctly stated: the n-th coefficient cₙ = Σ_{i+j=n} aᵢbⱼ of fg has valuation at least min over i + j = n of v(aᵢ) + v(bⱼ), which is `minkowskiSum` of the two height sequences at n (`minkowskiSum_def`); this is the ultrametric inequality together with v(ab) = v(a) + v(b) (`AddValuation.map_le_sum`, `AddValuation.map_mul`).

Correctly stated: for power series with admissible coefficient heights, the Minkowski sum of their Newton polygons lies pointwise below the Newton polygon of the product. `IsAdmissible a` is ∃ c m, ∀ n, c + mn ≤ a n (an affine lower bound), `≤` on ℕ → WithTop ℝ is pointwise, and `minkowskiSum` is the min-convolution over i + j = n. Lean subtlety: without admissibility `PowerSeries.newtonPolygon` is the ⊤ fallback and the left side would be ⊤, so the hypotheses exclude exactly that junk case (e.g. f = ∑ p^(−n²)Xⁿ and its inverse, whose product 1 has a nonempty polygon).

Correctly stated: for power series f, g whose coefficient heights touch a supporting line of every real slope, the Newton polygon of fg is the Minkowski sum of the Newton polygons of f and g. Lean ↔ mathematics: the hypothesis `∀ σ, ∃ c i, IsSupportingLine (fun n => v (coeff n f)) σ c ∧ i ∈ supportingFace (fun n => v (coeff n f)) σ c` says, by `isSupportingLine_iff_forall` and `mem_supportingFace`, that for every slope σ the line y = c + σx lies on or below every point (n, v(aₙ)) and passes through one of them, i.e. the infimum defining the supporting value is attained at every slope; `PowerSeries.newtonPolygon` is the greatest convex minorant of the heights (`PowerSeries.newtonPolygon_def`) and `minkowskiSum` the min-convolution over i + j = n, which for convex sequences with integral vertices is the Minkowski sum of the polygons. The contact hypotheses hold for polynomials with nonempty polygons and for nonzero entire series, as the docstring says. Lean subtlety: `PowerSeries.newtonPolygon` is the `lowerConvexEnvelope`, which returns ⊤ (the empty polygon) when the heights have no affine lower bound; the contact hypotheses force admissibility (`IsSupportingLine.isAdmissible`), so that fallback never enters. Checks: the docstring's counterexample without contact compiled over ℚ₂: (∑ Xⁿ)(1 − X) = 1 has polygon ⊤ at index 2 while the Minkowski sum of the factors' polygons is ≤ 0 there, so the hypotheses are needed; axioms standard.

Correctly stated: if lines of a common slope σ support and touch the coefficient heights of f and g, then the infimum over n of v(cₙ) − σn for fg is the sum of the same infima for f and g. Lean ↔ mathematics: `supportingValue` is the `EReal` infimum ⨅ n, a(n) − σn (`supportingValue_def`); `IsSupportingLine h σ c` is ∀ n, c + σn ≤ h n and `i ∈ supportingFace h σ c` is h i = c + σi, so the hypotheses say the infima for f and g are c and d, attained at i and j; the conclusion is Kedlaya's Proposition 1, v_r(PQ) = v_r(P) + v_r(Q) at r = −σ, for power series under attainment. Lean subtlety: all values here are real (c, d, c + d), so `EReal`'s ⊤ + ⊥ = ⊥ is not involved; without attainment the identity can fail (for ∑ Xⁿ at σ > 0 the value is ⊥). Checks: axioms standard; the hypotheses are met by every polynomial with a nonempty polygon.

Correctly stated: if lines of slope σ support and touch the coefficient heights of f and of g, the supporting value at σ of the Newton polygon of fg is the sum of those of the polygons of f and g. Lean ↔ mathematics: `supportingValue a σ` is ⨅ n, a(n) − σn in `EReal` (`supportingValue_def`), the intercept of the supporting line of slope σ; `IsSupportingLine h σ c` means c + σn ≤ h(n) for all n and `i ∈ supportingFace h σ c` means h(i) = c + σi, so the factors attain supporting values c and d; a Newton polygon has the same supporting values as its heights (`PowerSeries.supportingValue_newtonPolygon`). Lean subtlety: a power series polygon is the ⊤ fallback for heights with no affine lower bound; the contacts give admissibility of the heights of f, g and fg, and all values are real (c, d, c + d), so neither the fallback nor `EReal`'s ⊤ + ⊥ = ⊥ enters. Source: K. S. Kedlaya, *Newton polygons* (MIT 18.787 notes, fall 2007) §2, Proposition 1 (polynomial case). Checks: axioms standard.

Correctly stated: let E, H, Z be linear endomorphisms of a K-vector space with EZ - ZE = H and HE - EH = 2E, and suppose k + 1 ≠ 0 in K. Then H - k maps ker E ∩ im E^k into ker E ∩ im E^(k+1). Lean to maths: `E * Z - Z * E = H` and `H * E - E * H = 2 • E` are commutators in the ring `Module.End K V`, where multiplication is composition and `2 • E` is E + E. `LinearMap.ker E ⊓ LinearMap.range (E ^ k)` is ker E ∩ im E^k. `H c - (k : K) • c` is (H - k)c. `[NeZero ((k + 1 : ℕ) : K)]` states k + 1 ≠ 0 in K. There is no finiteness, nilpotence or characteristic assumption. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: I re-derived it by hand from [E^(k+1), Z] = (k+1) E^k (H + k) and H E^k = E^k (H + 2k); these are the file's imported `f_mul_e_pow_succ` and `h_mul_e_pow`. lean_minimal_hypotheses finds both relations load-bearing. exact? finds no Mathlib duplicate.

Correctly stated: let E be a nilpotent endomorphism of a vector space over a field of characteristic 0, and suppose EZ - ZE = H and HE - EH = 2E for some Z. Then every eigenvalue of H on ker E is a natural number. No finite-dimensionality is assumed. Lean to maths: `IsNilpotent E` says E^m = 0 for some m. `E * Z - Z * E = H` and `H * E - E * H = 2 • E` are commutators in `Module.End K V`. `hc : E c = 0`, `hc0 : c ≠ 0` and `hHc : H c = a • c` say c is an eigenvector of H in ker E with eigenvalue a. The conclusion `∃ n : ℕ, a = n` says a lies in the image of ℕ → K, a map that is injective by `[CharZero K]`. Lean subtlety: `IsNilpotent` asks for one exponent for the whole space, and it cannot be weakened to local nilpotence. A red-team probe compiled a counterexample: on ℚ[X], E = d/dx kills each polynomial after some number of steps, but no power of E is zero. With Z = -X^2 d/dx - 2X and H = -2X d/dx - 2, both relations hold, E 1 = 0 and H 1 = -2·1, and -2 is not a natural number. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: lean_minimal_hypotheses finds all six hypotheses load-bearing. It has a consumer, `disjoint_range_ker` in RangeKer.lean. Mathlib has no duplicate: `IsSl2Triple.HasPrimitiveVectorWith.exists_nat` assumes a full triple acting on a Noetherian torsion-free module.

Correctly stated: assume the same operator hypotheses (E nilpotent, EZ - ZE = H, HE - EH = 2E, characteristic 0). Then for every a ∈ K that is not a natural number, H - a maps ker E onto ker E: each w ∈ ker E equals (H - a)c for some c ∈ ker E. Lean to maths: `ha : ∀ n : ℕ, a ≠ n` says a avoids the image of ℕ in K. `hw : w ∈ LinearMap.ker E` says Ew = 0. The conclusion `∃ c ∈ LinearMap.ker E, H c - a • c = w` is surjectivity of H - a restricted to ker E. Lean subtlety: `IsNilpotent E` asks for one exponent for the whole space, as in `exists_eq_natCast_of_apply_eq_smul`; the descending induction starts from that exponent. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: this is the existence step of Morozov's lemma, used with a = -2 in `existsUnique_lie_eq_and_lie_eq_neg_two_nsmul`. lean_minimal_hypotheses finds all hypotheses load-bearing. exact? finds no Mathlib duplicate.

Correctly stated: this is Morozov's lemma with uniqueness. Over a field K of characteristic 0, let e, h be elements of any Lie algebra L (no finiteness assumed) with ad e nilpotent, [h, e] = 2e, h in [e, L] and h nonzero. Then exactly one f makes (h, e, f) an sl2-triple. Lean to maths: `[Field K] [CharZero K] [LieRing L] [LieAlgebra K L]` is a Lie algebra over a characteristic-zero field, with no `FiniteDimensional` or Killing-form assumption anywhere. `LieAlgebra.ad K L e` is the K-linear map x ↦ ⁅e, x⁆ (`LieAlgebra.ad_apply`), and `IsNilpotent (ad K L e)` says that some power (ad e)^n is the zero map. `hhe : ⁅h, e⁆ = 2 • e` is [h, e] = 2e. `hh : h ∈ LinearMap.range (ad K L e)` unfolds to: there is z with ⁅e, z⁆ = h, i.e. h ∈ [e, L]. `h0 : h ≠ 0` is h nonzero. The conclusion `∃! f, IsSl2Triple h e f` is existence of f together with f' = f for every other f' satisfying the predicate. Mathlib's structure `IsSl2Triple h e f` (Mathlib/Algebra/Lie/Sl2.lean) has exactly four fields: h ≠ 0, ⁅e, f⁆ = h, ⁅h, e⁆ = 2 • e and ⁅h, f⁆ = -(2 • f). Since h ≠ 0 and [h, e] = 2e are hypotheses, the conclusion says precisely that a unique f has [e, f] = h and [h, f] = -2f, which are the standard sl2 relations. Lean subtlety: (i) `2 • e` and `2 • f` are natural-number multiples (e + e). They equal (2 : K) • e by `Nat.cast_smul_eq_nsmul`, so the relations mean what they say. (ii) `IsNilpotent` asks for one exponent that works on all of L. In infinite dimension this is strictly stronger than local nilpotence, and the theorem needs the stronger form. A red-team probe compiled the counterexample: on ℚ[X], take E = d/dx (each polynomial is killed by some power of E, but no power of E is zero), Z = -X^2 d/dx - 2X and H = [E, Z] = -2X d/dx - 2. Both commutator relations hold, and the constant 1 lies in ker E with H-eigenvalue -2. A vector of exactly this kind would make f non-unique. (iii) h0 appears only because Mathlib's `IsSl2Triple` includes h ≠ 0. Under the other hypotheses h = 0 holds iff e = 0 (compiled). Nothing in the statement takes a Lean default value: there is no division, no truncated subtraction and no cardinality. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the hypotheses are satisfiable and the result specialises correctly in gl2(ℚ). With e = E12 and h = diag(1, -1), the theorem's unique f is E21, even though gl2 has a nonzero centre. It also holds in the infinite-dimensional loop algebra gl2(ℚ[X]) over ℚ, where ¬ Module.Finite ℚ ℚ[X] and X·1 commutes with e, so the centralizer of e is infinite-dimensional; f is again E21. All of this was compiled. lean_minimal_hypotheses finds all four explicit hypotheses load-bearing. simp_all, grind and aesop derive no False from the hypotheses. The only axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. exact?, loogle and leansearch find no Mathlib duplicate. I checked the proof idea independently. Two solutions differ by a vector of ker(ad e) with ad h-eigenvalue -2. On ker E ∩ im E^k the operator ad h - k maps into ker E ∩ im E^(k+1), and this filtration reaches 0 at the nilpotency exponent, so every eigenvalue of ad h on ker E is a natural number.

Correctly stated: this is the bracket form of Morozov's lemma. Over a field of characteristic 0, if ad e is nilpotent, [h, e] = 2e and h ∈ [e, L], then exactly one f satisfies [e, f] = h and [h, f] = -2f. L is any Lie algebra (no finiteness), and h = 0 is allowed. Lean to maths: `IsNilpotent (ad K L e)` says some power of x ↦ ⁅e, x⁆ is the zero map. `⁅h, e⁆ = 2 • e` is [h, e] = 2e. `h ∈ LinearMap.range (ad K L e)` says there is z with ⁅e, z⁆ = h, i.e. h ∈ [e, L]. `∃! f : L, ⁅e, f⁆ = h ∧ ⁅h, f⁆ = -(2 • f)` gives a solution f of both relations and says every f' solving them equals f. Lean subtlety: (i) `2 • f` is the natural-number multiple f + f, which equals (2 : K) • f. (ii) `IsNilpotent` is nilpotence with one exponent for all of L. This is stronger than local nilpotence in infinite dimension, and the result needs it (see the compiled d/dx probe on the named companion). (iii) At h = 0 the hypothesis ⁅0, e⁆ = 2 • e forces e = 0 in characteristic 0, and the unique f is then 0 (both compiled). So the allowed h = 0 case holds but is only the zero pair. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: [CharZero K] is necessary. Over ZMod 2, in the abelian Lie algebra ZMod 2, the pair h = 0, e = 1 meets all three hypotheses, yet both f = 0 and f = 1 solve the equations (compiled). lean_minimal_hypotheses finds all explicit hypotheses load-bearing. The named theorem `existsUnique_isSl2Triple_of_isNilpotent_ad` is this one plus h ≠ 0, in one line. The only axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: if ad e is nilpotent, [h, e] = 2e and h ∈ [e, L], then every eigenvalue of ad h on the centralizer of e is a natural number. Lean to maths: `hc : ⁅e, c⁆ = 0` puts c in the centralizer ker(ad e). `hc0 : c ≠ 0` and `hhc : ⁅h, c⁆ = a • c` make c an eigenvector of ad h with eigenvalue a ∈ K. The conclusion `∃ n : ℕ, a = n` says a is the image of a natural number in K. `IsNilpotent (ad K L e)`, `⁅h, e⁆ = 2 • e` and `h ∈ LinearMap.range (ad K L e)` mean the same as in Morozov's lemma above. Lean subtlety: (i) `(n : K)` is the cast ℕ → K. It is injective only because of `[CharZero K]`; in characteristic p every element of the prime field is such a cast. (ii) `IsNilpotent` asks for one exponent for all of L, and that is needed. The compiled d/dx probe on ℚ[X] (E locally but not uniformly nilpotent) has eigenvalue -2 on ker E. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: this is the operator lemma `TauCeti.Sl2.exists_eq_natCast_of_apply_eq_smul` applied to E = ad e, H = ad h and Z = ad z, where h = ⁅e, z⁆. lean_minimal_hypotheses finds all six explicit hypotheses load-bearing. Mathlib has no duplicate: its `IsSl2Triple.HasPrimitiveVectorWith.exists_nat` needs a full triple acting on a Noetherian module.

Correctly stated: assume [h, e] = 2e, h ∈ [e, L], and k + 1 ≠ 0 in K. Then ad h - k maps the k-th step ker(ad e) ∩ im((ad e)^k) of the centralizer filtration into the (k+1)-st step. Lean to maths: `LinearMap.ker (ad K L e) ⊓ LinearMap.range (ad K L e ^ k)` is the centralizer intersected with the image of (ad e)^k; ⊓ of submodules is intersection. `⁅h, c⁆ - (k : K) • c` is (ad h - k)(c). `[NeZero ((k + 1 : ℕ) : K)]` states k + 1 ≠ 0 in K. No nilpotence and no characteristic is assumed. Lean subtlety: the side condition k + 1 ≠ 0 is passed as a `NeZero` instance. In characteristic 0 it is found automatically, as at its consumer in JacobsonMorozov.lean. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: this is `TauCeti.Sl2.apply_sub_smul_mem_ker_inf_range_pow_succ` for E = ad e, H = ad h and Z = ad z. I re-derived the identity [E^(k+1), Z] = (k+1) E^k (H + k), which gives (H - k) E^k y = (k+1)^(-1) E^(k+1) Z y whenever E^(k+1) y = 0. lean_minimal_hypotheses finds all hypotheses load-bearing.

Correctly stated: the Cantor function is differentiable with derivative 0 at Lebesgue-almost every real number. Lean ↔ maths: `∀ᵐ x, P x` with no measure named means `∀ᵐ x ∂volume`, i.e. {x | ¬P x} is Lebesgue-null (compiled: the declaration is accepted at type `∀ᵐ x ∂(volume : Measure ℝ), …`). `HasDerivAt cantorFunction 0 x` says (C(x+h) − C(x))/h → 0 as h → 0, so it asserts both that C is differentiable at x and that the derivative is 0. The proof is the standard one: the exceptional set lies inside Mathlib's `cantorSet`, which is Lebesgue-null (`TauCeti.volume_cantorSet`), and off that set C is locally constant. Lean subtlety: `deriv f x = 0` holds by a junk value at every point where f is not differentiable, so 'deriv = 0 a.e.' would hold for wrong reasons (it is true even of a nowhere-differentiable function). This declaration asserts `HasDerivAt` instead, which fails at non-differentiable points, so the a.e. qualifier carries real content: C is not differentiable at the Cantor point 0, where C(3⁻ⁿ)/3⁻ⁿ = (3/2)ⁿ. The weaker `deriv` form follows from it (compiled). Source and checks: the TauCetiRoadmap GeometricMeasureTheory acceptance example asks for C' = 0 a.e. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: standard axioms only.

Correct definition of the Cantor–Lebesgue function C : ℝ → ℝ. Lean ↔ maths: the body is `sSup (dyadic '' {s | ternary s ≤ x})` (public form `cantorFunction_eq_sSup`), where for a code `s : ℕ → Bool`, `ternary s` is `(cantorSetEquivNatToBool.symm s : ℝ) = Real.ofDigits (fun i ↦ cond (s i) 2 0)`, the Cantor point 0.(2s₀)(2s₁)…₃ (Mathlib's `Real.ofDigits d` is Σ dᵢ·b^-(i+1)), and `dyadic s = Real.ofDigits (fun i ↦ cond (s i) 1 0)` is 0.s₀s₁…₂. Every point of Mathlib's `cantorSet` has such a code (private `range_ternary`), so C(x) = sup{C(c) : c in the Cantor set, c ≤ x}. That is the standard digit map Σ aᵢ3^-(i+1) ↦ Σ (aᵢ/2)2^-(i+1) (aᵢ ∈ {0,2}) on the Cantor set, extended constantly on the removed intervals, by 0 on the left and by 1 on the right. The private `dyadic_le_dyadic_of_ternary_le` (0/2 ternary codes are ordered lexicographically) makes the sup at a Cantor point equal to its own dyadic value. The binary non-uniqueness causes no clash: 1/3 = 0.0222…₃ and 2/3 = 0.2000…₃ both go to 1/2. Lean subtlety: for x < 0 the set of codes is empty, and `sSup ∅ = 0` in ℝ gives the value. That junk value is exactly the standard extension C = 0 on (-∞, 0), as the docstring says. The image is always bounded above by 1 (`Real.ofDigits_le_one`), so `sSup` never takes its unbounded-set junk value. Source and checks: the TauCetiRoadmap GeometricMeasureTheory acceptance example asks for exactly this: C on [0,1] built from the ternary Cantor-set/dyadic-value construction with Mathlib's Cantor set, and extended constantly outside. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b compiled these value tests: C(1/3) = 1/2 (code 0111…), C(1/4) = 1/3 (1/4 = 0.0202…₃ ↦ 0.0101…₂), C(0) = 0, C(1) = 1, and by simp C(x) = 0 for x < 0 and C(2) = 1. Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

The dyadic-value description: at the Cantor point 0.(2s₀)(2s₁)…₃, C takes the value 0.s₀s₁…₂. Lean ↔ maths: by Mathlib's definition, `cantorSetEquivNatToBool.symm s` is the point `Real.ofDigits (fun i ↦ cond (s i) 2 0)` of `cantorSet`, coerced to ℝ. The right side `Real.ofDigits (fun i ↦ cond (s i) (1 : Fin 2) 0)` is Σ sᵢ2^-(i+1). The equivalence is a bijection onto `cantorSet`, so ranging over all `s : ℕ → Bool` covers every Cantor point. This is the standard formula f(Σ aᵢ3^-(i+1)) = Σ (aᵢ/2)2^-(i+1). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: at s = 0111… and s = 0101… it gives the compiled values C(1/3) = 1/2 and C(1/4) = 1/3.

States the definition with the private helpers written out: `cantorFunction x` is the `sSup` of the base-2 values `Real.ofDigits (fun i ↦ cond (s i) 1 0)` over the codes `s` whose Cantor point `cantorSetEquivNatToBool.symm s` (= `Real.ofDigits (fun i ↦ cond (s i) 2 0)`) is ≤ x. It is proved by `rfl`, so it is the definition itself. Lean subtlety: for x < 0 the set is empty, and `sSup ∅ = 0` gives the intended value 0.

`cantorFunction =ᶠ[𝓝 x] fun _ ↦ cantorFunction x` says that, for every x ∉ `cantorSet`, C equals the constant C(x) on a neighbourhood of x. So C is locally constant on the open complement of the Cantor set, which includes x < 0 and x > 1. The reason: a small ball around x contains no Cantor point, so the set of codes defining C does not change on it.
C(x) ≤ 1 for every real x: every `Real.ofDigits` value is ≤ 1 (`Real.ofDigits_le_one`), and `Real.sSup_le` with 0 ≤ 1 also handles the empty set.

0 ≤ C(x) for every real x: each base-2 value `Real.ofDigits` is ≥ 0, and `Real.sSup_nonneg` also covers the empty set. Lean subtlety: for x < 0 the bound comes from the junk value `sSup ∅ = 0`, which is also the true value there.

For x in Mathlib's `cantorSet`, C(x) is the base-2 number whose digits are the Mathlib code `cantorSetEquivNatToBool ⟨x, hx⟩` of x, that is, the 0/2 ternary digits of x halved. It is `cantorFunction_cantorSetEquivNatToBool_symm` after the equivalence's inverse law, so it is the same standard formula, stated pointwise on the Cantor set.
C(x) = 0 for every x ≤ 0. This is the standard constant extension to the left, from monotonicity, C(0) = 0 and C ≥ 0. The hypothesis is needed, since C(1) = 1.
C(x) = 1 for every x ≥ 1. This is the standard constant extension to the right, from monotonicity, C(1) = 1 and C ≤ 1. The hypothesis is needed, since C(0) = 0.
C(1) = 1: 1 = 0.222…₃ is the Cantor point of the all-true code, whose dyadic value is 0.111…₂ = 1 (Mathlib's `Real.ofDigits_const_last_eq_one`, the identity 0.(b−1)(b−1)… = 1).
C(0) = 0: 0 is the Cantor point of the all-false code, whose dyadic value is 0 (`Real.ofDigits_const_zero`).

Correct definition: C packaged as a Mathlib `StieltjesFunction ℝ`, i.e. a monotone right-continuous function ℝ → ℝ. The fields are `toFun := cantorFunction`, monotonicity from `monotone_cantorFunction`, and right-continuity from continuity. Its `StieltjesFunction.measure` is the Lebesgue–Stieltjes (Cantor) measure dC, with dC((a,b]) = C(b) − C(a). Since C is continuous, no right-limit modification is needed (unlike `Monotone.stieltjesFunction`), so the underlying function is C itself (`coe_cantorStieltjesFunction`, by `rfl`). Lean subtlety: none; the structure fields are proofs, so there is no free data. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the measure has total mass 1 and gives [0,1] mass 1 (both compiled).

`cantorStieltjesFunction.measure cantorSetᶜ = 0`: dC is concentrated on the Cantor set, which is the roadmap's 'supported on the Cantor set'. Each x off the Cantor set has a neighbourhood (x−ε/2, x+ε/2] on which C is constant, so that interval has dC-mass C(x+ε/2) − C(x−ε/2) = 0. Mathlib's `measure_null_of_locally_null` (using second countability) then makes the whole complement null.
The underlying function of `cantorStieltjesFunction` is `cantorFunction` (by `rfl`), so its Stieltjes measure is built from C itself.

`Continuous cantorFunction` is continuity on all of ℝ in the usual topology. The proof is the standard argument that a monotone map onto an interval has no jumps: Mathlib's `Monotone.continuous_of_surjective`, applied to C as a map onto `Icc 0 1`.

Correctly stated: the total variation of C over the whole real line is 1. Lean ↔ maths: `eVariationOn cantorFunction univ` is Mathlib's [0,∞]-valued total variation, the supremum over all finite increasing sequences u₀ ≤ … ≤ uₙ of the sums Σ edist(C uᵢ₊₁, C uᵢ). So `= 1` says that C has bounded variation on ℝ with V(C) = 1. Since C is monotone, each sequence contributes C(uₙ) − C(u₀) ≤ 1 − 0, and the interval [0,1] alone already gives 1. Lean subtlety: the equation is in ℝ≥0∞ (`eVariationOn` itself, not its `toReal`), so it cannot hold through the junk value `ENNReal.toReal ∞ = 0`. Source and checks: the TauCetiRoadmap GeometricMeasureTheory acceptance example asks for variation one. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: standard axioms only.

`eVariationOn cantorFunction (Icc 0 1) = 1`: the total variation of C on [0,1] is 1 = C(1) − C(0), as for any monotone function (`MonotoneOn.eVariationOn_eq`). Mathlib's `eVariationOn f s` is the supremum, over finite increasing sequences in s, of the sums Σ|f(uᵢ₊₁) − f(uᵢ)|, valued in [0,∞]. Lean subtlety: the equation holds in ℝ≥0∞, with no `toReal`, so the junk value `ENNReal.toReal ∞ = 0` is not involved.

`HasDerivAt cantorFunction 0 x` for x ∉ `cantorSet`: C is genuinely differentiable at x with derivative 0. This follows from local constancy (`HasDerivAt.congr_of_eventuallyEq` with a constant function). Lean subtlety: the statement uses `HasDerivAt`, which asserts that the derivative exists, not the junk-prone `deriv … = 0`.

`cantorFunction '' cantorSet = Icc 0 1`: C maps Mathlib's ternary Cantor set onto [0,1]. Every y in [0,1] has a base-2 expansion (Mathlib's `Real.ofDigits_SurjOn`), and C sends the Cantor point with the doubled digits to y. The other inclusion is 0 ≤ C ≤ 1.
C is Borel measurable (`Measurable` for the Borel σ-algebra on ℝ); this follows from continuity.

`Monotone cantorFunction` means x ≤ y → C(x) ≤ C(y) on all of ℝ (Mathlib's `Monotone` is non-strict). This is the standard non-decreasing property, and it holds because the set of codes in the supremum grows with x.

Correctly stated: the Cantor measure dC and Lebesgue measure are mutually singular. Lean ↔ maths: `μ ⟂ₘ ν` is Mathlib's `Measure.MutuallySingular`, which unfolds to: there is a measurable s with μ s = 0 and ν sᶜ = 0 (`Iff.rfl` compiles). Here `cantorStieltjesFunction.measure` is dC and `volume` is Lebesgue measure on ℝ. The witness s is the complement of Mathlib's `cantorSet`, which is open and hence measurable. dC(s) = 0 is `cantorStieltjesFunction_measure_compl_cantorSet`, and volume(cantorSet) = 0 is `TauCeti.volume_cantorSet`. The file also has the instances `IsProbabilityMeasure cantorStieltjesFunction.measure` (total mass C(+∞) − C(−∞) = 1 − 0, via the limits at ±∞) and `NullSingletonClass` (points are null because C is continuous). Together these give the roadmap's 'singular continuous probability measure supported on the Cantor set'. Lean subtlety: `NullSingletonClass` (formerly Mathlib's `NoAtoms`) only says that singletons are null; for a finite Borel measure on ℝ this is the usual 'atomless/continuous'. The pinned-Mathlib trap that `Measure.map` along a non-measurable map is a Dirac mass does not arise, since no pushforward is used. Source and checks: the TauCetiRoadmap GeometricMeasureTheory acceptance example. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: compiled dC(univ) = 1 and dC([0,1]) = 1; standard axioms only.

Correctly stated: C is not absolutely continuous on [0,1]. Lean ↔ maths: `AbsolutelyContinuousOnInterval f a b` is Mathlib's absolute continuity on `uIcc a b`, which is [0,1] here. Mathlib proves it equivalent (`absolutelyContinuousOnInterval_iff`) to the textbook ε-δ definition: for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that every finite family of disjoint intervals (aᵢ,bᵢ] in [a,b] with total length < δ has Σ|f(bᵢ) − f(aᵢ)| < ε. The declaration is the negation of that. The proof: Mathlib's fundamental theorem of calculus for AC functions (`AbsolutelyContinuousOnInterval.integral_deriv_eq_sub`) would give ∫₀¹ C' = C(1) − C(0) = 1, but C' = 0 a.e. Lean subtlety: the proof integrates `deriv cantorFunction`, which takes the junk value 0 at non-differentiable points. It only uses `deriv = 0` a.e., though, and gets that from `ae_hasDerivAt_cantorFunction` (genuine derivatives), so no junk value enters the statement. The negation is not vacuous, because the notion is satisfiable: `AbsolutelyContinuousOnInterval id 0 1` compiles via `LipschitzOnWith.absolutelyContinuousOnInterval`. Source and checks: the TauCetiRoadmap GeometricMeasureTheory README calls C the named singular BV example and the input to a non-AC example. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: standard axioms only.
`range cantorFunction = Icc 0 1`: the values of C on all of ℝ are exactly [0,1]. The inclusion ⊆ is 0 ≤ C ≤ 1, and ⊇ already holds on the Cantor set.

`(e : R ≃+* S) → IsNagata R → IsNagata S`: being Nagata is invariant under ring isomorphisms, with R and S in independent universes (compiled at R : Type u, S : Type v); the proof is `of_finite` along the surjective ring map `e`.

Correctly stated: this is Stacks Definition 10.162.1 (032R), a ring R is Nagata if R is Noetherian and R/𝔭 is N-2 (Japanese) for every prime ideal 𝔭. Lean ↔ mathematics: `class IsNagata R extends IsNoetherianRing R` makes Noetherianity part of the definition (the parent `toIsNoetherian : IsNoetherian R R` is the ascending chain condition on ideals); the single field `isJapanese_quotient (p : Ideal R) [p.IsPrime] : IsJapanese (R ⧸ p)` quantifies over every prime ideal p, and `R ⧸ p` is Mathlib's quotient ring by p (`Ideal.Quotient`), a domain by the instance `Ideal.Quotient.isDomain`; `IsJapanese` (TauCeti.RingTheory.Japanese) is N-2, not merely N-1: its field asks, for EVERY field `L` with `[Algebra (FractionRing R) L]`, a compatible `[IsScalarTower R (FractionRing R) L]` and `[FiniteDimensional (FractionRing R) L]`, that `Module.Finite R (integralClosure R L)` hold, i.e. the integral closure of the domain in every finite extension of its fraction field is a finite module, inseparable extensions included, which is Stacks Definition 10.161.1 (032F); taking L = FractionRing gives N-1 as a special case. A probe proved `IsNagata R ↔ IsNoetherianRing R ∧ ∀ p [p.IsPrime], IsJapanese (R ⧸ p)` directly from the constructor and projections. Lean subtlety: `IsJapanese` quantifies only over extensions `L` in the universe of the domain; `R ⧸ p` lives in R's universe and every finite extension of its fraction field has an isomorphic copy there, so nothing is lost (`IsJapanese.finite_integralClosure` restates it for any model and universe); the zero ring has no prime ideals and is Noetherian, so it is Nagata, as in Stacks. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: witnesses compiled for ℤ, ℤ_[p], ℤ ⧸ I, ℤ_(p), ℚ, 𝓞 K for a number field K, every field, ZMod 1 and ZMod 6; non-witness compiled: `¬ IsNoetherianRing R → ¬ IsNagata R` (Examples/RingTheory/UniversallyJapanese.lean proves `¬ IsNagata (ℕ → ZMod 2)`); no Mathlib or other Tau Ceti definition of Nagata rings (git grep, loogle, leansearch, leanfinder); axioms standard. No Noetherian non-Japanese domain (such as the DVR of Stacks Example 10.162.17) exists in Mathlib or Tau Ceti, so the Japanese clause has no compiled non-witness.

`[IsDomain R] [IsNagata R] : IsJapanese R`: a Nagata domain is Japanese (N-2); it is the defining clause at the prime 𝔭 = (0), transported along `RingEquiv.quotientBot R : R ⧸ ⊥ ≃+* R`. `[IsDomain R]` is needed for `IsJapanese R` even to typecheck, and it excludes the zero ring.
`IsNagata (Localization M)` for R Nagata and any submonoid M: `of_isLocalization` at Mathlib's model `Localization M`. Compiled at `Localization.AtPrime p` for a prime p of ℤ.
