Every field k is Nagata (`IsNagata k`, an instance): a field is Noetherian, its only prime is (0), and k/(0) ≅ k is Japanese. Compiled by `inferInstance`; Stacks Proposition 10.162.16 (0335) lists fields among the Nagata rings.

Correctly stated: if R is Nagata and S is a commutative R-algebra that is finitely generated as an R-module, then S is Nagata; this is the finite case of Stacks Lemma 10.162.5 (032T), which allows any quasi-finite R → S. Lean ↔ mathematics: `[Algebra R S]` is the ring map R → S, `[Module.Finite R S]` says S is a finite R-module (the map is finite), `[IsNagata R]` is the hypothesis and `IsNagata S` the conclusion, with R and S in independent universes; R → S need not be injective, so quotients are covered. Lean subtlety: none needed; the zero algebra is finite and Nagata, correctly. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: specialised to `IsNagata (𝓞 K)` for a number field K (finite over ℤ) and to `ℤ ⧸ I`; hypotheses consistent (witnessed); axioms standard.

`[IsDomain R] [IsNoetherianRing R] [Ring.KrullDimLE 1 R] [IsJapanese R] : IsNagata R`: a Noetherian Japanese domain of Krull dimension at most one is Nagata. The quotient by (0) is R itself, and a nonzero prime is maximal when `krullDim (PrimeSpectrum R) ≤ 1` (`Ideal.IsPrime.isMaximal_of_ne_bot`), so the other prime quotients are fields; `Ring.KrullDimLE 1 R` includes dimension 0. Compiled at ℤ and ℤ_[p]; Noetherianity cannot be dropped since it is part of being Nagata.

If R is Nagata and S is a localization of R at a submonoid M (`[IsLocalization M S]`, for any model S, not only `Localization M`), then S is Nagata: Stacks Lemma 10.162.6 (032U). Compiled at ℚ as the localization of ℤ at `nonZeroDivisors ℤ`.

`[IsNoetherianRing R] [Ring.KrullDimLE 0 R] : IsNagata R`: a Noetherian ring of Krull dimension at most zero is Nagata. `Ring.KrullDimLE 0 R` is Mathlib's `Order.KrullDimLE 0 (PrimeSpectrum R)`, i.e. `krullDim (PrimeSpectrum R) ≤ 0` in `WithBot ℕ∞`, so every prime is maximal and each R/𝔭 is a field, which is Japanese. Lean subtlety: the zero ring has Krull dimension ⊥ ≤ 0, so it is covered, and it is Nagata (no primes), as the docstring says. Compiled at ZMod 1 and at ZMod 6 (Artinian, not a domain).

If `Ideal.span t = ⊤` (the elements of t generate the unit ideal) and `Localization.Away f`, Mathlib's R_f = R[1/f], is Nagata for every f ∈ t, then R is Nagata: Stacks Lemma 10.162.7 (032V), with t any set rather than finitely many f_i (1 is a finite combination, so this is equivalent). lean_minimal_hypotheses: `ht` and `H` are both load-bearing. Compiled at t = {1} and at t = {2, 3} ⊆ ℤ. Lean subtlety: for nilpotent f, `Localization.Away f` is the zero ring, which is Nagata; harmless.

`IsNagata (R ⧸ I)` for every ideal I of a Nagata ring R: quotients of Nagata rings are Nagata, `R ⧸ I` being Mathlib's quotient ring; the proof is `of_finite` along the surjection R → R ⧸ I. Compiled at `IsNagata (ℤ ⧸ I)` by `inferInstance`.

Correctly stated: a Noetherian domain of Krull dimension at most one is Nagata if and only if it is Japanese (N-2). Lean ↔ mathematics: `[IsDomain R]` is 'domain' (it excludes the zero ring), `[IsNoetherianRing R]` is Noetherian, and `[Ring.KrullDimLE 1 R]` unfolds to `Order.KrullDimLE 1 (PrimeSpectrum R)`, i.e. `krullDim (PrimeSpectrum R) ≤ 1`, so fields (dimension 0; `IsNagata k ↔ IsJapanese k` compiled) and discrete valuation rings and Dedekind domains (dimension 1, by Mathlib instances) are all covered; `IsNagata` is Stacks Definition 10.162.1 (032R) and `IsJapanese` is N-2, the integral closure being finite in every finite extension of the fraction field (Stacks Definition 10.161.1 (032F)). The forward direction is the defining clause at 𝔭 = (0) (`IsNagata.isJapanese`); the backward direction holds because every nonzero prime is maximal, so the other prime quotients are fields. Lean subtlety: `krullDim` takes values in `WithBot ℕ∞`, and `≤ 1` (a coerced natural number) also admits 0 and ⊥, the latter being the zero ring, excluded here by `IsDomain`; the dimension bound sits in a typeclass binder, so the theorem applies only where Lean finds `Ring.KrullDimLE 1 R`, as the docstring says. Source: Stacks Example 10.162.17 (09E1) states exactly this for discrete valuation rings, and the Lean theorem specialises to it (compiled under `[IsDiscreteValuationRing R]`). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: hypotheses consistent (ℤ satisfies all of them), backward direction compiled at ℤ, axioms standard.

For t with `Ideal.span t = ⊤`, `IsNagata R ↔ ∀ f ∈ t, IsNagata (Localization.Away f)`: being Nagata is local on Spec R. The forward direction is Stacks Lemma 10.162.6 (032U) (localizations, via the `localization` instance), the backward one Lemma 10.162.7 (032V) (`of_span_eq_top`).

Correctly stated: the measure with bounded moment sequence b has Amice transform Σ bₙ Tⁿ, `PowerSeries.mk b` being the power series with n-th coefficient b n; it follows from `mahlerMomentsEquiv_apply` and `apply_symm_apply`. Check: over ℚ_p, b = `lp.single ∞ 0 1` gives the Dirac mass at 0 (compiled).

Correctly stated: over a Tate ring the moments (μ(x choose n))ₙ of every measure are bounded: `BddAbove (Set.range fun n ↦ ‖μ.amiceTransform.coeff n‖)` says the moment norms have an upper bound. `TauCeti.NormedRing.IsTate R` (a unit ϖ with 0 < ‖ϖ‖ < 1 and ‖ϖx‖ = ‖ϖ‖‖x‖) makes the continuous functional μ uniformly bounded (`IsTate.bound_of_continuous`, rescaling into a shell by powers of ϖ), and `norm_coeff_amiceTransform_le` then bounds each moment. Lean subtlety: `D(ℤ_[p], R)` requires only continuity, not boundedness; this lemma is where the Tate hypothesis turns one into the other.

Correctly stated: for a measure μ on ℤ_p and f ∈ C(ℤ_p, R), μ(f) = Σₙ aₙ(f)·bₙ, with aₙ(f) = Δⁿf(0) the Mahler coefficients of f and bₙ = μ(x choose n) the moments, as an unconditionally convergent series. Lean ↔ mathematics: `mahlerEquiv R f n` is by definition (`mahlerEquiv_apply`, rfl) `Δ_[1]^[n] f 0`, the n-th Mahler coefficient; `μ.amiceTransform.coeff n` is `μ ((mahler n) • 1)` (`coeff_amiceTransform`), the n-th moment; `HasSum g a` says Σ g converges unconditionally to a. The hypotheses (complete, ultrametric, contractive ℤ_p-action) are those of Mathlib's Mahler theorem `hasSum_mahler`, and the statement is its image under the continuous linear map μ. Lean subtlety: `HasSum` rather than `∑'` is used, so convergence is asserted and the statement cannot hold through the junk value 0 of a non-summable `tsum`. Source: Colmez, Fonctions d'une variable p-adique (author's PDF), Th. I.2.3 (Mahler) and the formula ∫ f μ = Σ bₙ aₙ(f) of the proof of Th. II.2.2. Check: at the Dirac mass at x over ℚ_p it compiles to Mahler's formula f(x) = Σ Δⁿf(0) (x choose n).

Correctly stated: over a complete ultrametric commutative normed ring R with a contractive ℤ_p-algebra structure and a multiplicative pseudo-uniformiser, sending a measure μ on ℤ_p to its moment sequence (μ(x ↦ (x choose n)))ₙ is an R-linear bijection from the measures onto the bounded sequences. Lean ↔ mathematics: `D(ℤ_[p], R)` is Mathlib's `AbstractMeasure ℤ_[p] R R`, by definition the continuous R-linear maps `C(ℤ_[p], R) →L[R] R`; ℤ_p is compact, so the topology on `C(ℤ_[p], R)` is the sup-norm topology and these are exactly the measures D_0(ℤ_p, R), the topological dual of C^0 (boundedness is not built in). `lp (fun _ : ℕ ↦ R) ∞` is ℓ^∞(ℕ, R): membership is `BddAbove` of the norms and the norm is their supremum. `≃ₗ[R]` is an R-linear equivalence. The body is `toCLMEquiv` (the identity of the type synonym), then precomposition with the inverse of the Mahler isometry `C(ℤ_[p], R) ≅ C₀(ℕ, R)`, f ↦ (Δⁿf(0))ₙ (Mathlib's `PadicInt.mahlerEquiv`, made R-linear), then the inverse of `linearCombinationEquiv R R : ℓ^∞ ≅ (C₀(ℕ, R) →L[R] R)`, which reads off u ↦ (u(eₙ))ₙ; so μ goes to (μ(mahlerTerm 1 n))ₙ, and `mahlerMomentsEquiv_apply` proves the n-th entry is `μ.amiceTransform.coeff n` = μ(`mahler n` • 1), where `mahler n x = Ring.choose x n` is the binomial polynomial extending n.choose. Hypotheses: `IsUltrametricDist R` and `CompleteSpace R` (complete ultrametric), `IsBoundedSMul ℤ_[p] R` (‖a • r‖ ≤ ‖a‖‖r‖), and `TauCeti.NormedRing.IsTate R` (a unit ϖ with 0 < ‖ϖ‖ < 1 and ‖ϖx‖ = ‖ϖ‖‖x‖), which makes every continuous functional bounded (`IsTate.bound_of_continuous`). Lean subtlety: the equivalence is only linear, not a bundled isometry, because Mathlib gives `AbstractMeasure` no norm; the isometry is the separate theorem `ringOpNorm_toCLMEquiv_eq_norm_mahlerMomentsEquiv` for the scoped ring operator norm. `IsTate` excludes R = ℤ_[p] (all units of ℤ_p have norm 1; `¬ IsTate ℤ_[p]` compiles), so the integral case is not an instance of this definition but is Mathlib's `AbstractMeasure.amiceTransformEquiv`; every complete nontrivially normed field such as ℚ_p or ℂ_p is an instance. Source: Colmez, Fonctions d'une variable p-adique (author's PDF), Prop. II.3.1 with r = 0 and §II.3.2 (for a closed subfield L of ℂ_p, μ ↦ A_μ is an isometry from the measures onto the power series with bounded coefficients); this is its generalisation to Tate coefficient rings. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: the hypotheses are jointly satisfied by ℚ_[p]; the moments of the Dirac mass at x compile to `Ring.choose x n`; the inverse sends `lp.single ∞ 0 1` to the Dirac mass at 0; no duplicate in pinned Mathlib 1b1ccf4b, current Mathlib master (only R = ℤ_p; the general case is a TODO there) or Tau Ceti; standard axioms only.

Correctly stated: the n-th term of the moment sequence `mahlerMomentsEquiv p R μ` is the n-th coefficient of the Amice transform of μ, i.e. μ(x ↦ (x choose n)·1) by Mathlib's `coeff_amiceTransform`; this pins `mahlerMomentsEquiv` down as the moment map. The `@[simp]` attribute is not redundant (`simp [-mahlerMomentsEquiv_apply]` fails on the statement).

Correctly stated: the measure with bounded moment sequence b integrates f to Σₙ Δⁿf(0)·bₙ (`mahlerEquiv R f n` is Δⁿf(0)), the formula ∫ f μ = Σ bₙ aₙ(f) of Colmez, Fonctions d'une variable p-adique (author's PDF), proof of Th. II.2.2. Lean subtlety: `∑'` is 0 for a non-summable family, but this series converges (aₙ(f) → 0, b bounded, R complete ultrametric) and the statement is derived from the `HasSum` lemma, so the right side is the genuine sum.

Correctly stated: over a Tate ring, a power series F ∈ R⟦X⟧ is the Amice transform of a measure on ℤ_p iff its coefficients are bounded. Lean ↔ mathematics: `LinearMap.range (amiceTransform …)` is the image of Mathlib's Amice transform μ ↦ Σ μ(x choose n) Tⁿ; `BddAbove (Set.range fun n ↦ ‖F.coeff n‖)` is boundedness of the coefficient norms, so the right side is E+ = R+_0, 'l'espace R+_0 des séries à coefficients bornés' (Colmez, Fonctions d'une variable p-adique (author's PDF), §II.1). Forward is `bddAbove_norm_coeff_amiceTransform`, backward is `mahlerMomentsEquiv.symm`. Lean subtlety: none in the statement (both sides are propositions about genuine objects, no junk value); note `IsTate` excludes ℤ_[p], where every power series is an Amice transform (Mathlib's `amiceTransformEquiv`). Source: Colmez, Fonctions d'une variable p-adique (author's PDF), Prop. II.3.1 with r = 0 and §II.3.2. Checks: the file's compiled example shows Σ p⁻ⁿ Tⁿ is not in the range over ℚ_p, and Σ Tⁿ is (compiled).

Correctly stated: if every moment μ(x choose n) (`μ.amiceTransform.coeff n`) has norm ≤ C, then ‖μ f‖ ≤ C‖f‖ for every continuous f, where `‖f‖` is the sup norm on `C(ℤ_[p], R)` (compact domain). The proof is the ultrametric estimate ‖Σ aₙ(f) bₙ‖ ≤ supₙ ‖aₙ(f)‖‖bₙ‖ ≤ ‖f‖·C of the Mahler expansion, using only submultiplicativity of the norm (no multiplicative norm) and that the Mahler map preserves the sup norm; C ≥ 0 is forced by `hC 0`, and `hC` is load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses).

Correctly stated: if ‖μ f‖ ≤ C‖f‖ for all continuous f, then each moment μ(x choose n) (`μ.amiceTransform.coeff n`) has norm ≤ C: evaluate the bound at `mahlerTerm 1 n` = (x ↦ (x choose n)·1), whose sup norm is ‖1‖ (`norm_mahlerTerm`). Lean subtlety: `[NormOneClass R]` (‖1‖ = 1) is genuinely needed, since without it the bound is only C‖1‖; it holds automatically over Tate rings. The lemma also carries an unused ultrametric instance, which only narrows its scope.

Correctly stated: over a complete ultrametric nontrivially normed field K with a contractive ℤ_p-algebra structure (ℚ_p, ℂ_p, any closed subfield of ℂ_p), the operator norm of a measure equals supₙ ‖μ(x choose n)‖, which is Colmez, Fonctions d'une variable p-adique (author's PDF), Prop. II.3.1 with r = 0 (v'_{D_0}(μ) = inf v_p(bₙ)). Here `‖toCLMEquiv μ‖` is Mathlib's own `ContinuousLinearMap.opNorm` (the scope is closed; `rfl` against `opNorm` compiles) and the proof transports the Tate-ring version by `ringOpNorm_eq_opNorm`, K being Tate by the instance for nontrivially normed fields. Lean subtlety: a real `⨆` of an unbounded family is 0, excluded because the moments are bounded (`bddAbove_norm_coeff_amiceTransform`). Check: for the Dirac mass at 0 over ℚ_p both sides compute to 1 (compiled).

Correctly stated: over such a field K, ‖μ‖ ≤ C iff every moment μ(x choose n) has norm ≤ C, with `‖toCLMEquiv μ‖` Mathlib's operator norm; it is the sup formula with `ciSup_le_iff` on the bounded moments. For C < 0 both sides are false (norms are nonnegative), so no sign hypothesis is needed.

Correctly stated: over a Tate ring the operator norm of a measure equals supₙ ‖μ(x choose n)‖. Lean ↔ mathematics: `‖toCLMEquiv μ‖` is, under `open scoped TauCeti.RingOpNorm`, `ContinuousLinearMap.ringOpNorm`, by definition sInf {c ≥ 0 | ∀ x, ‖μ x‖ ≤ c‖x‖}, Mathlib's operator-norm formula without the field assumption, i.e. the least Lipschitz constant sup ‖μ f‖/‖f‖, which is Colmez's valuation v'_{D_0}(μ) = inf (v_p(μ f) − v(f)); `⨆ n, ‖μ.amiceTransform.coeff n‖` is the real supremum of the moment norms. The two inequalities are `norm_apply_le_of_forall_norm_coeff_le` and `norm_coeff_amiceTransform_le`, which use only submultiplicativity, ‖1‖ = 1 and the ultrametric inequality, so the equality is exact even when the norm of R is not multiplicative. Lean subtlety: both sides have junk values (ringOpNorm is sInf ∅ = 0 when no uniform bound exists; a real `⨆` of an unbounded family is 0) and neither occurs: `IsTate` supplies the uniform bound and `bddAbove_norm_coeff_amiceTransform` the bounded moments. Source: Colmez, Fonctions d'une variable p-adique (author's PDF), Prop. II.3.1 with r = 0, for field coefficients.

Correctly stated: Mahler duality is isometric: the operator norm of μ equals the ℓ^∞ norm of its moment sequence. The right side is the `lp ∞` norm of `mahlerMomentsEquiv p R μ`, the supremum ⨆ n ‖bₙ‖ (`lp.norm_eq_ciSup`); the left side is `ContinuousLinearMap.ringOpNorm` (the least uniform bound) under the scope `TauCeti.RingOpNorm`. With `mahlerMomentsEquiv` this is the isometry of Colmez, Fonctions d'une variable p-adique (author's PDF), Prop. II.3.1 with r = 0, for Tate coefficient rings. Lean subtlety: the isometry is a norm equation, not a bundled `≃ₗᵢ`, because Mathlib's `AbstractMeasure` carries no norm; the scoped norm is the ring operator norm, which agrees with Mathlib's operator norm over fields (`ringOpNorm_eq_opNorm`).

Correctly stated: for every finite simple graph G and commutative ring k, the Artin (generalised braid) group of G acts on the homotopy category of graded modules over the zigzag algebra Z of G, the generator σᵢ acting by tensoring with the two-term complex Bᵢ = [Pᵢ ⊗_k eᵢZ → Z]. Lean ↔ mathematics: `ArtinGroup G.coxeterMatrix` is the `PresentedGroup` on the vertices with, for each pair (i, i'), the relator equating the two alternating words of length `M i i'`, and `G.coxeterMatrix` has 1 on the diagonal (empty relator), 3 on edges and 2 on non-edges (`coxeterMatrix_apply_of_adj`, `coxeterMatrix_apply_of_not_adj`), so it is exactly Huerfano–Khovanov's Br(Γ): σₐσ_bσₐ = σ_bσₐσ_b when a, b are joined by an edge and σₐσ_b = σ_bσₐ otherwise. `zigzagAlgebra k G` is HK's A(Γ) (paths of length ≤ 2 in the doubled graph modulo the zigzag relations), built as a product over connected components with the dual numbers k[x]/x² on a one-vertex component, graded by path length with x in degree 2 (`zigzagAlgebraInternalGrading`, ℤ-indexed, zero in negative degrees); `GradedModuleCat (…).piece` is the category of graded left Z-modules with degree-0 Z-linear maps, and `HomotopyCategory _ (ComplexShape.up ℤ)` is the homotopy category of unbounded cochain complexes of them. `AutoequivalenceClass C` is the opposite of the unit group of the monoid `Skeleton (C ⥤ C)` (product = composition), i.e. the group of natural-isomorphism classes of autoequivalences of C: the product of the classes of F and G is the class of F ∘ G (`toAutoequivalenceClass_trans`), and two equivalences have the same class iff their functors are naturally isomorphic (`toAutoequivalenceClass_eq_iff`). A monoid hom out of a presented group is the same as values on the generators satisfying the relators, so with `zigzagBraidArtinAction_gen` (σᵢ ↦ class of `zigzagBraidAutoequivalence k G i`, whose functor is `bimoduleModuleTensorHomotopy … (zigzagBraidComplex k G i)`, tensoring with Bᵢ, and whose inverse tensors with Bᵢ') the declaration says exactly HK Prop. 7: each Σᵢ is invertible, ΣᵢΣⱼΣᵢ ≅ ΣⱼΣᵢΣⱼ for adjacent i, j and ΣᵢΣⱼ ≅ ΣⱼΣᵢ otherwise. Lean subtlety: 'acts' here is a weak action in the sense of Khovanov–Seidel Def. 2.6 (a homomorphism to isomorphism classes of functors, with no coherent choice of the isomorphisms F_gF_h ≅ F_gh), which is what HK and KS mean by an action; only generators (and, via `map_inv`, their inverses) get a specified representative functor; nontriviality and faithfulness are not asserted (for k the zero ring the category is trivial and the statement holds trivially, as it should); module carriers live in universe `max u w`. Source: Huerfano–Khovanov, A category for the adjoint representation, §4.6, Prop. 7 and the remark that tensoring with (35) 'also define[s] a braid group action in various homotopy categories'; HK §3 assumes Γ connected, Lean also covers disconnected graphs through the product algebra; Khovanov–Seidel, Quivers, Floer cohomology and braid group actions, Prop. 2.4, Thm 2.5, Def. 2.6 and Prop. 2.7 for type A (their A_m is graded differently). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only; compiled that the homomorphism with `_gen` yields σᵢ⋙σⱼ⋙σᵢ ≅ σⱼ⋙σᵢ⋙σⱼ for adjacent and σᵢ⋙σⱼ ≅ σⱼ⋙σᵢ for distinct nonadjacent vertices, that σᵢ⁻¹ goes to the class whose functor tensors with Bᵢ', that a class is 1 iff its functor is ≅ 𝟭, and that for the one-vertex graph the Artin generator has infinite order and Z ≅ `DualNumber k`; nontriviality of the image of σᵢ is not proved in Lean (Tau Ceti's K₀ computation gives the Euler class of Bᵢ ⊗ Pᵢ as −q²[Pᵢ]).

Correctly stated: the standard generator σᵢ is sent to the natural-isomorphism class of tensoring with the braid complex Bᵢ. Lean: `zigzagBraidArtinAction k G (ArtinGroup.gen G.coxeterMatrix i) = (zigzagBraidAutoequivalence k G i).toAutoequivalenceClass`, and `zigzagBraidAutoequivalence_functor` identifies that equivalence's functor with M ↦ Bᵢ ⊗_Z M on the homotopy category; this is what pins the homomorphism down to the braid action (Khovanov–Seidel: 'to σᵢ associate the complex Rᵢ'). Proved by the generic `SimpleGraph.artinAutoequivalenceAction_gen`; with `map_inv` and `Equivalence.toAutoequivalenceClass_symm` it also gives σᵢ⁻¹ ↦ the class of tensoring with Bᵢ' (compiled at 5f78b5307b).

Correctly stated: for a vertex i, tensoring over Z with the braid complex Bᵢ is an autoequivalence σᵢ of the homotopy category of graded Z-modules, with inverse tensoring with the inverse complex Bᵢ'. Lean ↔ mathematics: the type `HomotopyCategory (GradedModuleCat …) c ≌ HomotopyCategory (GradedModuleCat …) c` is a self-equivalence of the homotopy category of unbounded cochain complexes of graded Z-modules; the body is `GradedModuleCat.bimoduleModuleTensorHomotopyEquivalence` at K = `zigzagBraidComplex k G i` (Bᵢ = [Pᵢ ⊗_k eᵢZ → Z], the multiplication map, in cohomological degrees −1, 0, no internal shift) and K' = `zigzagBraidInverseComplex k G i` (Bᵢ' = [Z → (Pᵢ ⊗_k eᵢZ){−2}], the Casimir coevaluation, degrees 0, 1), with the homotopy equivalences Bᵢ ⊗_Z Bᵢ' ≃ Z and Bᵢ' ⊗_Z Bᵢ ≃ Z (`inverseForward`, `inverseReverse` of `zigzagBraidComplexRelations`) giving the unit and counit; its functor and inverse are pinned by `zigzagBraidAutoequivalence_functor` and `_inverse`. Lean subtlety: the internal shift is M{d}_p = M_{p−d}, so {−2} makes the degree-2 coevaluation a degree-0 map (Khovanov–Seidel write {−1} for the same map in their halved grading); carriers live in universe `max u w`. Source: Khovanov–Seidel §2d and Prop. 2.4 (Rᵢ, Rᵢ' with A_m in degree 0, RᵢRᵢ' ≅ Id ≅ Rᵢ'Rᵢ); Huerfano–Khovanov (34)–(35) and Prop. 7 ('Σₐ are invertible'). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: standard axioms only; equivalence data come from the two compiled homotopy equivalences.

Correctly stated: for adjacent vertices i, j, applying σᵢ, σⱼ, σᵢ in turn is naturally isomorphic to applying σⱼ, σᵢ, σⱼ in turn (Khovanov–Seidel Thm 2.5 (2.9), Huerfano–Khovanov Prop. 7). Lean: `(σᵢ.trans (σⱼ.trans σᵢ)).functor` is σᵢ ⋙ (σⱼ ⋙ σᵢ); `h : G.Adj i j` is 'joined by an edge', the Coxeter entry 3; the isomorphism is the homotopy equivalence of triple tensor products of braid complexes (`zigzagBraidComplexAdjacentHomotopyEquiv`, used at `h.symm`) pushed through the action and conjugated by associators. Lean subtlety: composites are bracketed as `Equivalence.trans` brackets them and no strict associativity is assumed; the iso is data, and only its existence enters `zigzagBraidArtinAction`. Checks at 5f78b5307b: standard axioms; compiled that the action recovers this isomorphism class.

Correctly stated: for distinct vertices i, j not joined by an edge, applying σᵢ then σⱼ is naturally isomorphic to applying σⱼ then σᵢ (Khovanov–Seidel Thm 2.5 (2.10), Huerfano–Khovanov Prop. 7). Lean: `((σᵢ).trans σⱼ).functor` is σᵢ.functor ⋙ σⱼ.functor (σᵢ first); `hij : i ≠ j` and `hadj : ¬ G.Adj i j` say distinct and non-adjacent, the Coxeter entry 2; the isomorphism is the homotopy equivalence Bⱼ ⊗_Z Bᵢ ≃ Bᵢ ⊗_Z Bⱼ (`zigzagBraidComplexTensorCommHomotopyEquiv`) pushed through the action, conjugated by the associator T(K₁ ⊗ K₂) ≅ T(K₂) ⋙ T(K₁). Lean subtlety: `i ≠ j` is not needed mathematically (for i = j both sides coincide) but matches the Artin presentation's interface; the iso is data, and only its existence enters `zigzagBraidArtinAction`. Checks at 5f78b5307b: standard axioms; compiled that the action recovers this isomorphism class.

Correctly stated: `(zigzagBraidAutoequivalence k G i).functor` is `(bimoduleModuleTensorHomotopy Γ Γ).obj [Bᵢ]`, the functor M ↦ Bᵢ ⊗_Z M (totalised balanced tensor product, on homotopy classes), so σᵢ is literally tensoring with Bᵢ as in Huerfano–Khovanov (34) and Khovanov–Seidel's Rᵢ(M) = Rᵢ ⊗ M; it is the generic `bimoduleModuleTensorHomotopyEquivalence_functor`, which holds by rfl.

Correctly stated: the inverse functor of σᵢ is `(bimoduleModuleTensorHomotopy Γ Γ).obj [Bᵢ']`, tensoring with the inverse complex Bᵢ' = [Z → (Pᵢ ⊗_k eᵢZ){−2}], as Khovanov–Seidel's Rᵢ' = Rᵢ⁻¹ (Prop. 2.4); it is the generic `bimoduleModuleTensorHomotopyEquivalence_inverse`, which holds by rfl.

Any automaton with output `M : DFAO (Fin k) σ Δ` with `[Finite σ]`, σ in any universe, computes a k-automatic sequence, namely n ↦ `M.output (M.eval ((Nat.digits k n).map (Fin.ofNat k)))`: the converse of the definition with finiteness weakened from `Fintype` to `Finite` and the universe freed, proved by relabelling σ ≃ Fin m (`DFAO.reindex`, which preserves every output by `output_eval_reindex`). Lean subtlety: this is what makes the universe-0 restriction `σ : Type` in `IsAutomatic` harmless. Axioms standard; used for every automatic witness in the file and in Kernel.lean.

Correctly stated: `IsAutomatic k a` says the sequence a : ℕ → Δ is k-automatic, i.e. some automaton with finitely many states reading the base-k digits of n outputs a(n). Lean ↔ mathematics: the body is `∃ (σ : Type) (_ : Fintype σ) (M : DFAO (Fin k) σ Δ), ∀ n, a n = M.output (M.eval ((Nat.digits k n).map (Fin.ofNat k)))`; `TauCeti.DFAO (Fin k) σ Δ` is a triple (step : σ → Fin k → σ, start, output : σ → Δ), i.e. a k-DFAO (Q, Σ_k, δ, q₀, Δ, τ) with input alphabet Fin k = {0,…,k−1}, and `Fintype σ` is the finiteness of Q (it is enforced: a compiled probe shows the finite-valued sequence n ↦ [n = 2^(2^L) for some L] is NOT 2-automatic, by pigeonhole on the states reached after i zeros, so the definition is not satisfied by every finite-valued sequence); `M.eval w` is `List.foldl M.step M.start w`, i.e. δ(q₀, w) reading w from its head, and `Nat.digits k n` lists the base-k digits of n least significant first with no zero at the end and `Nat.digits k 0 = []`, so the body says a(n) = τ(δ(q₀, reverse of the canonical base-k expansion of n)) for every n, with a(0) = τ(q₀) (checked: 6 is read as [0,1,1]). This is Bridy's reverse-reading convention on canonical expansions; Bridy §2.1 cites Allouche–Shallit Thm 5.2.3 for forward and reverse reading giving the same class and Thm 5.2.1 for the leading-zero question, so for k ≥ 2 this is the classical class with one convention fixed (and documented in the docstring). The output set Δ is arbitrary where the sources take it finite; nothing changes, since `IsAutomatic.finite_range` forces a finite range. Lean subtlety: `Fin.ofNat k d` is d mod k, harmless because base-k digits are < k for k ≥ 2 (`Nat.digits_lt_base`); `[NeZero k]` excludes k = 0, where `Nat.digits 0 n = [n]` is junk; k = 1 is admitted and means unary input (`Nat.digits 1 n` is n ones, sent to n copies of 0 : Fin 1), so `IsAutomatic 1 a` is exactly 'a is eventually periodic' (compiled: IsAutomatic 1 a gives N and p > 0 with a(n+p) = a(n) for n ≥ N; the converse is `isAutomatic_of_eventually_periodic`), a non-standard but documented extension (the module docstring says so; Wikipedia's 'Automatic sequence' notes k-automatic is normally defined for k ≥ 2 and 1-automatic sequences are ultimately periodic), and every downstream theorem that needs the classical notion assumes 2 ≤ k (`isAutomatic_iff_finite_kernel`, `isAutomatic_pow_iff`) or uses the base `Fintype.card K` ≥ 2 of a finite field (the Christol files); σ lives in `Type` (universe 0), no loss because `DFAO.isAutomatic` relabels any finite state type by Fin m. Checks (red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): compiled witnesses Thue–Morse t(n) = s₂(n) mod 2 is 2-automatic via the two-state DFAO s ↦ s + d on ZMod 2 (values 0,1,1,0,1,0,0,1 by decide), parity, and a preperiod-5 period-3 sequence in bases 7 and 10; non-witnesses the identity (file) and the 2^(2^L) indicator (compiled); axioms propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound; no Mathlib notion of automatic sequence or DFAO (git grep, leansearch, leanfinder, loogle).

A k-automatic sequence takes only finitely many values: `(Set.range a).Finite`, since each value a(n) is τ(q) for one of the finitely many states q (`Set.finite_range M.output`). This is why the definition may allow an arbitrary output type Δ where the sources take Δ finite; the file uses it to show the identity sequence is not automatic.

If a is k-automatic then so is n ↦ f(a n) for every map f : Δ → Δ' (closure under codings / changes of output alphabet): the same automaton with output f ∘ τ (`DFAO.mapOutput`); the Lean conclusion `IsAutomatic k fun n ↦ f (a n)` is exactly that sequence, with no hypothesis on f. Compiled in an example mapping n mod 5 to [n mod 5 = 1] in base 3.

If a and b are k-automatic (same base) then so is the paired sequence n ↦ (a n, b n) with values in Δ × Δ': the product automaton on the finite state set σ × τ with output (τ_a, τ_b) (`DFAO.prod`); the Lean conclusion `IsAutomatic k fun n ↦ (a n, b n)` is exactly that pairing. Compiled example: pairing n mod 2 with [n mod 5 = 1] in base 3. (Naming only: Mathlib would call this `prodMk`, recorded separately.)

The constant sequence n ↦ c is k-automatic for every base k ≠ 0, computed by the one-state automaton on `Unit` with output c; the Lean statement `IsAutomatic k fun _ ↦ c` is exactly that, with no hypothesis on c or Δ.

`IsAutomatic k a ↔ ∃ (σ : Type) (_ : Fintype σ) (M : DFAO (Fin k) σ Δ), ∀ n, a n = M.output (M.eval ((Nat.digits k n).map (Fin.ofNat k)))`: the unfolding of the definition, proved by `Iff.rfl`, so it says exactly what `IsAutomatic` means; it is the intro/elim rule importing modules need because the module system does not expose the body of `IsAutomatic` (used in AutomaticSequence/Kernel.lean).

Correctly stated: every eventually periodic sequence is k-automatic, in every base. Lean ↔ mathematics: the hypotheses `hp : 0 < p` and `h : ∀ n, N ≤ n → a (n + p) = a n` say that a has period p > 0 from the preperiod N on, i.e. a is ultimately periodic; the base k is implicit with only `[NeZero k]`, so the conclusion `IsAutomatic k a` holds for every k ≠ 0, in particular every k ≥ 2, and Δ is an arbitrary type; `IsAutomatic` is the reverse-reading k-DFAO notion (see its yes). The automaton keeps (min(value read so far, N), value mod p) and (min(place value k^i, N), k^i mod p), finite data compatible with + and × by a digit, from which a(n) is read off. Lean subtlety: `hp` is essential — with p = 0 the hypothesis `a (n + 0) = a n` holds for every sequence, and the identity is not automatic (compiled), and `lean_minimal_hypotheses` reports both hp and h load-bearing; hp also supplies `NeZero p` so that `ZMod p` is finite (for p = 0, `ZMod 0 = ℤ`); digits are fed through `Fin.ofNat k` (mod k), faithful since they are < k for k ≥ 2, and k = 1 (unary input) is handled by a separate counter automaton; the read-off uses `(x.2 - N).val` with subtraction in `ZMod p`, i.e. the residue (n − N) mod p, so no truncated ℕ subtraction is involved. Checks (red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): specialised at a preperiod-5, period-3 sequence in bases 7 and 10 (compiled), at parity and n mod 3 (file), and used by Christol.lean; axioms propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound; proof 10 lines, no declaration of the file over 1 s (profiler).

Says: if g is complex-differentiable at x then ∂̄g(x) = 0, the Cauchy–Riemann equations in Wirtinger form. Lean ↔ maths: `DifferentiableAt ℂ g x` is complex Fréchet differentiability at x (holomorphy at the point); the proof replaces the real derivative by the complex derivative with scalars restricted (`fderiv_restrictScalars`), and complex-linearity makes Dv + i·D(iv) = Dv − Dv = 0; `= 0` is equality with the zero conjugate-linear map, i.e. for every direction v. Lean subtlety: the hypothesis implies real differentiability, so no `fderiv` junk value is involved; the converse is not claimed here and would be false without real differentiability (compiled: g z = ‖z‖ at 0 has ∂̄g = 0 by the junk convention but is not complex-differentiable); its correct form, with `DifferentiableAt ℝ g x`, is `differentiableAt_iff_conjWirtingerDeriv_eq_zero` in Wirtinger/Holomorphic.lean. Source and checks: the Wikipedia article 'Wirtinger derivatives' states that ∂f/∂z̄ = 0 is the complex form of the Cauchy–Riemann equations; red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the hypothesis is needed (compiled: ∂̄ of z ↦ conj z is not 0); standard axioms.

Says: if g is complex-differentiable at x then ∂g(x) is its complex derivative, `wirtingerDeriv g x = fderiv ℂ g x` as continuous complex-linear maps V → W. Lean ↔ maths: `fderiv ℂ g x` is the complex Fréchet derivative and `DifferentiableAt ℂ g x` complex differentiability; when Dg(x) is complex-linear, ½(Dv − i·D(iv)) = ½(Dv + Dv) = Dv. Lean subtlety: the hypothesis is essential, not only a guard against junk: without it `fderiv ℂ g x` is the junk 0 while ∂g need not be (compiled: g z = z + conj z has ∂g = id but `fderiv ℂ g x = 0`). Source and checks: the Wikipedia article 'Wirtinger derivatives' notes ∂f/∂z = df/dz for complex-differentiable f; red-team audit at 5f78b5307b specialised it to ∂(z ↦ z²)(x)(1) = 2x (compiled).

Says: as a function, ∂̄g(x) equals `complexAntilinearPart J J' F` with F = `(fderiv ℝ g x : V →ₗ[ℝ] W)` the real derivative and J, J' = `DistribSMul.toLinearMap ℝ _ I` multiplication by i on V and W; `complexAntilinearPart J J' F` is by definition ½(F + J'∘F∘J) (`complexAntilinearPart_apply`), so ∂̄g(x) is the complex-antilinear part of the real derivative. Lean subtlety: at non-differentiable points both sides are 0 (fderiv junk), so the equation is unconditional. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: signs compared against `complexAntilinearPart_apply` (½(F v + J'(F(J v)))).

Says: as a function, ∂g(x) equals `complexLinearPart J J' F` with F = `(fderiv ℝ g x : V →ₗ[ℝ] W)` (the real derivative as a plain real-linear map) and J = `DistribSMul.toLinearMap ℝ V I`, J' = `DistribSMul.toLinearMap ℝ W I` (multiplication by i on V and on W, as real-linear maps); `complexLinearPart J J' F` is by definition ½(F − J'∘F∘J) (`complexLinearPart_apply`), so this is 'the Wirtinger derivative is the complex-linear part of the real derivative' in the almost-complex-structure language of TauCeti.LinearAlgebra.Complex.LinearPart, where `complexLinearPart_isComplexLinear` shows that part commutes with the structures; `⇑` is the underlying function. Lean subtlety: at non-differentiable points both sides are 0 (fderiv junk), so the equation is unconditional. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: signs compared against `complexLinearPart_apply` (½(F v − J'(F(J v)))).

Says: `conjWirtingerDeriv g x` is the conjugate Wirtinger derivative ∂̄g(x), the continuous conjugate-linear map v ↦ ½(Dg(x)v + i·Dg(x)(iv)), the complex-antilinear part of the real derivative; on a coordinate vector e_j it is ∂g/∂z̄_j = ½(∂g/∂x_j + i·∂g/∂y_j). Lean ↔ maths: `fderiv ℝ g x` is the real derivative Dg(x) (V and W viewed as real spaces by restriction of scalars); the body is `(2 : ℂ)⁻¹ • (fderiv ℝ g x v + I • fderiv ℝ g x (I • v))`; the type `V →L⋆[ℂ] W` is Mathlib notation for continuous maps semilinear over complex conjugation `starRingEnd ℂ`, i.e. f(c·v) = c̄·f(v), which is exactly antilinearity; `coe_conjWirtingerDeriv_eq_complexAntilinearPart` identifies it with ½(F + J∘F∘J). The sign is the right one: for complex-linear F the bracket F v + i·F(iv) = F v + i·i·F v vanishes. Lean subtlety: like `fderiv` it is 0 where g is not real-differentiable (compiled: g z = ‖z‖ at 0 has ∂̄g = 0 although g is not complex-differentiable there), so ∂̄g(x) = 0 alone does not imply holomorphy; the file never claims that, and the converse in Wirtinger/Holomorphic.lean assumes `DifferentiableAt ℝ g x`. Source and checks: matches ∂/∂z̄_j = ½(∂/∂x_j + i·∂/∂y_j) in the Wikipedia article 'Wirtinger derivatives'; red-team audit at 5f78b5307b compiled ∂̄(z ↦ z) = 0, ∂̄(z ↦ conj z)(x)v = conj v, ∂̄(z ↦ z·conj z)(x)v = x·conj v (so ∂̄|z|² = z dz̄), and that ∂̄ of conj is not 0; standard axioms only.

Says ∂̄g(x)v = ½(Dg(x)v + i·Dg(x)(iv)) with `fderiv ℝ g x` the real derivative Dg(x): the definition unfolded (proved by `rfl`). Lean subtlety: `fderiv ℝ g x` is 0 where g is not real-differentiable, and the identity holds there too (both sides 0). Used in the red-team value tests at 5f78b5307b (∂̄ of z ↦ z is 0, ∂̄ of conj is conj).

Says: for f : ℂ → W, ∂̄f(x)v = conj(v)·∂̄f(x)(1), i.e. in one variable ∂̄f(x) is v ↦ v̄·∂f/∂z̄ with ∂f/∂z̄ = `conjWirtingerDeriv f x 1`; it is antilinearity (`map_smulₛₗ` over conjugation) applied to v = v·1, so it holds for every f.

Says: for f : ℂ → W, ∂̄f(x) = 0 as a conjugate-linear map iff the single number ∂f/∂z̄(x) = `conjWirtingerDeriv f x 1` is 0, because ∂̄f(x)v = v̄·∂̄f(x)(1); it holds for every f (pure linear algebra), and with Wirtinger/Holomorphic.lean it gives the one-equation Cauchy–Riemann criterion for real-differentiable f.

Says: for a real-valued f on V, viewed in ℂ as `fun y ↦ (f y : ℂ)` (the real embedding ℝ → ℂ), ∂̄f(x)v = conj(∂f(x)v): the real derivative takes real values, so the conjugate of ½(Dv − i·D(iv)) is ½(Dv + i·D(iv)). Lean subtlety: at points where f is not real-differentiable both sides are `fderiv`'s junk 0, so the identity is unconditional and holds there trivially. Source and checks: the real-valued case of Lemma 4 of the Wikipedia article 'Wirtinger derivatives' (conj(∂f/∂z_i) = ∂f̄/∂z̄_i with f̄ = f); red-team audit at 5f78b5307b instantiated it at f = |z|² (compiled), where ∂ = conj(x)·v and ∂̄ = x·conj v.

Says: for f : ℂ → W, Df(x)v = v·∂f/∂z + conj(v)·∂f/∂z̄, with `fderiv ℝ f x` the real derivative, ∂f/∂z = `wirtingerDeriv f x 1` and ∂f/∂z̄ = `conjWirtingerDeriv f x 1`: the one-variable formula df = f_z dz + f_z̄ dz̄ (dz(v) = v, dz̄(v) = v̄). Lean subtlety: as its docstring says, it holds without differentiability because at non-differentiable points every term is `fderiv`'s junk 0. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: it is the sum decomposition plus the two one-variable lemmas; consistent with the compiled |z|² computation D(z·z̄)(x)v = x·v̄ + x̄·v.

Says: for a map g : V → W between complex normed spaces and a point x, `wirtingerDeriv g x` is the Wirtinger derivative ∂g(x), the continuous complex-linear map v ↦ ½(Dg(x)v − i·Dg(x)(iv)), i.e. the complex-linear part of the real derivative; on a complex coordinate vector e_j it is ∂g/∂z_j = ½(∂g/∂x_j − i·∂g/∂y_j). Lean ↔ maths: `fderiv ℝ g x : V →L[ℝ] W` is the real Fréchet derivative Dg(x), with V and W regarded as real normed spaces by restriction of scalars (the instance is `NormedSpace.complexToReal`, checked by `rfl`); the body is literally `(2 : ℂ)⁻¹ • (fderiv ℝ g x v - I • fderiv ℝ g x (I • v))`, and since Dg(x)(e_j) = ∂g/∂x_j and Dg(x)(i·e_j) = ∂g/∂y_j this is the coordinate formula; the type `V →L[ℂ] W` records that the result is complex-linear and continuous (the file proves complex homogeneity by splitting c = Re c + i·Im c), and `coe_wirtingerDeriv_eq_complexLinearPart` identifies it with ½(F − J∘F∘J) for F = Dg(x) and J = multiplication by i. Lean subtlety: `fderiv` is 0 at points where g is not real-differentiable, so ∂g(x) = 0 there too (compiled: g z = ‖z‖ at 0 gives `wirtingerDeriv _ 0 = 0`); this is a totality convention, not a claim, and no theorem in the file uses it to conclude anything about holomorphy: the results concluding ∂̄g = 0 or ∂g = complex derivative assume `DifferentiableAt ℂ g x`, and the converse (Wirtinger/Holomorphic.lean) assumes `DifferentiableAt ℝ g x`; `(2 : ℂ)⁻¹` is the genuine ½ (no division by zero). Source and checks: the formula ∂/∂z_j = ½(∂/∂x_j − i·∂/∂y_j) is the one in the Wikipedia article 'Wirtinger derivatives'; red-team audit at 5f78b5307b compiled the value tests ∂(z ↦ z) = id, ∂(z ↦ conj z) = 0, ∂(z ↦ z·conj z)(x)v = conj(x)·v (so ∂|z|² = z̄ dz) and ∂(z ↦ z²)(x)(1) = 2x; Mathlib has no Wirtinger derivative (only the one-variable Cauchy–Riemann criterion `differentiableAt_complex_iff_differentiableAt_real`); standard axioms only.

Says ∂g(x)v + ∂̄g(x)v = Dg(x)v for every v, with `fderiv ℝ g x` the real derivative: the real derivative is the sum of its complex-linear and complex-antilinear parts (½(Dv − i·D(iv)) + ½(Dv + i·D(iv)) = Dv), the decomposition dg = ∂g + ∂̄g. Lean subtlety: it needs no differentiability hypothesis because at points where g is not real-differentiable all three terms are `fderiv`'s junk 0; as an identity this is harmless. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: no hypotheses to drop; consumed by the converse Cauchy–Riemann criterion in Wirtinger/Holomorphic.lean.

Says ∂g(x)v = ½(Dg(x)v − i·Dg(x)(iv)) with `fderiv ℝ g x` the real derivative Dg(x): the definition unfolded (proved by `rfl`), the formula consumers rewrite with. Lean subtlety: `fderiv ℝ g x` is 0 where g is not real-differentiable, and the identity holds there too (both sides 0). Used in the red-team value tests at 5f78b5307b (∂ of z ↦ z is the identity, ∂ of conj is 0).

Says: for f : ℂ → W, ∂f(x)v = v·∂f(x)(1), i.e. in one variable ∂f(x) is multiplication by the number ∂f/∂z = `wirtingerDeriv f x 1`; it is complex-linearity of ∂f(x) applied to v = v·1, so it holds for every f (at non-differentiable points both sides are the junk 0).

Correctly stated: the underlying simplicial set of a simplicial abelian group is a Kan complex. Lean vs mathematics: `G : SimplicialObject AddCommGrpCat.{u}` is a functor Δᵒᵖ → Ab, a simplicial abelian group; `G ⋙ forget AddCommGrpCat` is its underlying simplicial set; the proof gives each `(G ⋙ forget AddCommGrpCat).obj n` the additive group of `G.obj n` and gets additivity of every simplicial operator from `map_add (G.map f).hom`, then applies `SSet.kanComplex_of_addGroup`; `SSet.KanComplex` is fibrancy against all horn inclusions. Lean subtlety: a Prop-valued instance matched on the literal form `G ⋙ forget AddCommGrpCat`; it is not subsumed by the `GrpCat` instance, since an object of `AddCommGrpCat` is additive and not syntactically a `GrpCat` object. Source: Goerss–Jardine Lemma I.3.4 and May Theorem 17.1, for the special case of abelian groups. Checks at 5f78b5307b: `inferInstance` finds it for an arbitrary `SimplicialObject AddCommGrpCat.{0}` (compiled); axioms standard.

Correctly stated: the underlying simplicial set of a simplicial group is a Kan complex. Lean vs mathematics: `G : SimplicialObject GrpCat.{u}` is a functor Δᵒᵖ → Grp, a simplicial group in Goerss–Jardine's sense; `G ⋙ forget GrpCat` is its composite with the forgetful functor to sets, i.e. its underlying simplicial set; `SSet.KanComplex` is fibrancy against all horn inclusions Λ[n+1,i] ↪ Δ[n+1]; the proof gives `(G ⋙ forget GrpCat).obj n` the group structure of `G.obj n` and gets the homomorphism hypothesis from `map_mul (G.map f).hom`, so it is `SSet.kanComplex_of_group` for the bundled object. Lean subtlety: a Prop-valued instance (no data, so no diamond risk), found by instance search for the literal form `G ⋙ forget GrpCat` (other presentations of the underlying simplicial set must be rewritten to it); groups in `GrpCat.{u}` give a simplicial set in `SSet.{u}`. Source: Goerss–Jardine Lemma I.3.4 states exactly this. Checks at 5f78b5307b: `inferInstance` finds it for an arbitrary `SimplicialObject GrpCat.{0}` and for the constant simplicial group `(Functor.const _).obj H`, and `SSet.KanComplex.hornFilling` then fills Λ[1,0], Λ[2,2] and every Λ[n+1,i] (compiled).

Correctly stated: the underlying simplicial set of a simplicial module over any ring is a Kan complex. Lean vs mathematics: `G : SimplicialObject (ModuleCat.{u} R)` with `[Ring R]` is a functor Δᵒᵖ → R-Mod, a simplicial R-module; `G ⋙ forget (ModuleCat R)` is its underlying simplicial set; only the additive group of each `G.obj n` is used, with additivity of the simplicial operators from `map_add (G.map f).hom` (linear maps are additive), via `SSet.kanComplex_of_addGroup`; `SSet.KanComplex` is fibrancy against all horn inclusions. Lean subtlety: R may live in any universe and the modules in `ModuleCat.{u} R`; the instance matches the literal form `G ⋙ forget (ModuleCat R)`, not the composite through `forget₂ (ModuleCat R) AddCommGrpCat`; its consumers (the Dold–Kan simplicial sets in `DoldKan/Cochain`, `DoldKan/SimplexChainMap/Module`, `KanComplex/MooreComplex`, and the DG mapping spaces in `CategoryTheory/DG/Simplicial`) rewrite to that form and call `infer_instance`. Source: Goerss–Jardine Lemma I.3.4 and May Theorem 17.1, since a simplicial R-module is in particular a simplicial group. Checks at 5f78b5307b: `inferInstance` finds it for an arbitrary `SimplicialObject (ModuleCat.{0} R)` over an arbitrary ring R (compiled); axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.

Correctly stated: Moore's theorem in additive notation, that a simplicial set whose sets of n-simplices are additive groups, with every simplicial operator additive, is a Kan complex. Lean vs mathematics: `[∀ n, AddGroup (X.obj n)]` is an additive group structure on X_n in every degree (commutativity is not required); `hX : X.map f (x + y) = X.map f x + X.map f y` for every morphism f of `SimplexCategoryᵒᵖ` says every face, degeneracy and composite is additive, hence a homomorphism of additive groups, so X is the underlying simplicial set of a simplicial additive group; `X.KanComplex` is Mathlib's fibrancy against every horn inclusion `Λ[n + 1, i].ι`, n ≥ 0, i : Fin (n + 2), i.e. every horn, inner or outer, of every dimension ≥ 1 extends to a simplex. Lean subtlety: the proof transports to `kanComplex_of_group` through the type synonym `Multiplicative (X.obj n)`, whose `*` is definitionally `+`, and passes `hX` by that defeq; this affects only the proof, the statement itself is purely additive. Sources: Goerss–Jardine Lemma I.3.4 and May Theorem 17.1 (stated for groups, written additively here). Checks at 5f78b5307b: it is the route by which this file's `SimplicialObject AddCommGrpCat` and `SimplicialObject (ModuleCat R)` instances are proved, and instance search finds both for arbitrary simplicial objects (compiled); axioms standard.

Correctly stated: this is Moore's theorem, that a simplicial set whose sets of n-simplices are groups, with every simplicial operator a group homomorphism (i.e. the underlying simplicial set of a simplicial group), is a Kan complex. Lean vs mathematics: `X : SSet.{u}` is a simplicial set, a functor Δᵒᵖ → Type u; `[∀ n, Group (X.obj n)]` is a group structure on X_n for every object n of `SimplexCategoryᵒᵖ`, i.e. in every degree; `hX : ∀ ⦃m n⦄ (f : m ⟶ n) x y, X.map f (x * y) = X.map f x * X.map f y` says every simplicial operator `X.map f` (every face δ_i, every degeneracy σ_j and every composite) is multiplicative, hence a group homomorphism, so the data are exactly a functor Δᵒᵖ → Grp with underlying simplicial set X, which is Goerss–Jardine's simplicial group and May's group complex ("G_n is a group and the face and degeneracy operators are homomorphisms"); the conclusion `X.KanComplex` is Mathlib's `SSet.KanComplex`, by definition `IsFibrant X` for the Quillen fibrations `J.rlp`, where `J` is the family of all horn inclusions `Λ[n + 1, i].ι : Λ[n + 1, i] ⟶ Δ[n + 1]` (n ≥ 0, i : Fin (n + 2)), so it says every horn Λ^n_k → X, n ≥ 1, 0 ≤ k ≤ n, extends along the inclusion to Δ^n → X (Goerss–Jardine's K1); by Mathlib's `KanComplex.iff` this is the same as: every compatible family of n-simplices on the faces j ≠ i (compatibility d_i y_j = d_{j-1} y_i, i < j) is the family of faces of one (n+1)-simplex (Goerss–Jardine's K2). Lean subtlety: the group structures are typeclass data indexed by the objects of `SimplexCategoryᵒᵖ`, and `hX` constrains exactly those instances; `hX` asks only for multiplicativity, which for groups already forces preservation of 1 and of inverses (the proof derives `σ_one` and `δ_inv` with `MonoidHom.mk'`), so no homomorphism axiom is missing; `KanComplex` has Mathlib's scoped Quillen fibration structure built into the abbreviation, and its `Λ[n + 1, i]` indexing starts in dimension 1 with i ranging over all of `Fin (n + 2)`, so outer horns and the 1-dimensional horns (a single vertex, filled in the proof by its degenerate edge) are included; X lives in `SSet.{u}` and the groups in `Type u`, with no further universe restriction. Sources: Goerss–Jardine, Simplicial Homotopy Theory, Lemma I.3.4 (Moore), "The underlying simplicial set of any simplicial group H is fibrant", with a simplicial group defined as a functor Δᵒᵖ → Grp; May, Simplicial Objects in Algebraic Topology, Theorem 17.1, "Every group complex G is a Kan complex". Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: compiled the unbundled form on the constant simplicial set on ℤ (as `Multiplicative ℤ`) with `hX` by `rfl`; instance search derives the Kan property of every `SimplicialObject GrpCat`, `SimplicialObject AddCommGrpCat`, `SimplicialObject (ModuleCat R)` and of the constant simplicial group; specialised `SSet.KanComplex.hornFilling` to the outer horns Λ[1,0] and Λ[2,2] and to a general Λ[n+1,i]; checked `KanComplex S ↔ IsFibrant S` by `Iff.rfl` and every `Λ[n + 1, i].ι ∈ J` by `horn_ι_mem_J`; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only; no Mathlib duplicate at the pin 1b1ccf4b (loogle, leansearch, leanfinder, git grep for KanComplex and simplicial group) and none elsewhere in Tau Ceti; the file elaborates in about 3 s.

Correctly stated: a Borel k-subgroup, i.e. one with B_{k̄} a Borel subgroup of G_{k̄} (which is how `IsBorel` is defined), is parabolic. The proof unfolds both predicates to the geometric fibre and applies the algebraically closed case. Compiled witness: the upper-triangular Borel of GL₂ over ℚ.

Correctly stated: over an algebraically closed field every Borel subgroup is parabolic (Milne iAG Ex. 18.20, Thm 18.12(a)). In Lean a Borel ideal I is minimal among smooth, geometrically connected, geometrically solvable Hopf ideals. It is smooth because it is a candidate, and it contains a Borel, namely itself (`I ≤ I`). Compiled witness: the upper-triangular Borel of GL₂.

Correctly stated: a closed subgroup P of a finite-type affine group G over an arbitrary field k is parabolic iff P_{k̄} is a smooth closed subgroup of G_{k̄} that contains a Borel subgroup of G_{k̄}. Lean ↔ mathematics: `H : CommHopfAlgCat k` with `[Algebra.FiniteType k H]` is O(G) for an affine k-group of finite type, and `I : HopfIdeal k H` is the ideal of P. The body base-changes both to K = `AlgebraicClosure k`. `FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat.baseChange` gives K ⊗[k] H = O(G_{k̄}). `CommHopfAlgCat.baseChangeHopfIdeal I` is the kernel of K⊗H → K⊗(H/I), i.e. the ideal generated by 1⊗I, which cuts out P_{k̄}. The body then asks `IsParabolicOverAlgClosed K H' I'`: P_{k̄} is smooth and contains a Borel subgroup of G_{k̄}, i.e. a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup. By `isParabolic_iff`, smoothness can equivalently be tested over k (faithfully flat descent). Lean subtlety: the `IsAlgClosed` conjunct of `IsParabolicOverAlgClosed` holds automatically for `AlgebraicClosure k` (Mathlib instance). The Hopf-ideal order is contravariant (`I' ≤ J` means P_{k̄} ⊇ B). The Borel subgroup need only exist over k̄, not over k; that is correct, since Milne remarks that a parabolic subgroup need not contain a Borel k-subgroup. Smoothness is required, so non-reduced thickenings are excluded, matching Milne's "subgroup variety" and Conrad Def. 5.2.1. The algebraic closure is Mathlib's canonical one; any other is isomorphic, though invariance under that choice is not formalised. Source: Milne, Algebraic Groups (iAG v2.00), Def. 18.63 (a parabolic subgroup is a subgroup variety with G/P complete, a property that can be tested after field extension), with Thm 18.21 over k̄; Conrad, Reductive group schemes (Luminy notes), Def. 5.2.1. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: witnesses over ℚ compiled (GL₂ itself via `isParabolic_bot_iff`, and its upper-triangular Borel via `IsBorel.isParabolic`). Non-witness over every field compiled: the trivial subgroup `augmentation` of GL₂ is not `IsParabolic`. A downstream file proves all weight parabolics of GL_N parabolic over every field. There is no duplicate predicate in Mathlib (which has only the unrelated parabolic 2×2 matrices) or in Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated: over any field, parabolicity transports along a Hopf-algebra isomorphism `e : H ≅ L`, where the ideal e⁻¹(J) of H cuts out the corresponding subgroup. The proof base-changes e to the algebraic closure and uses `baseChangeHopfIdeal_comapOfIso`.
Correctly stated: two-sided isomorphism invariance of `IsParabolic` over an arbitrary field. For `e : H ≅ L`, the ideal e⁻¹(J) is parabolic in H iff J is parabolic in L.

Correctly stated: over any field, conjugating a parabolic subgroup P by a k-rational point g gives a parabolic subgroup. Here g lies in `WithConv (H →ₐ[k] k)`, the convolution group of k-points, and `I.conjugate g` is the ideal of gPg⁻¹ (the inverse image under the coordinate automorphism of x ↦ gxg⁻¹).

Correctly stated: the base change P_{k̄} of a parabolic subgroup contains a Borel subgroup of G_{k̄}. In Lean there is J in O(G_{k̄}) with `IsBorelOverAlgClosed (AlgebraicClosure k) … J` and `baseChangeHopfIdeal I ≤ J`; in the contravariant order this says P_{k̄} contains the subgroup cut out by J. The Borel lives over k̄, not over k, as it must (Milne iAG 18.63).

Correctly stated: over any field, suppose Q (ideal J) is smooth over k (`Algebra.Smooth k (H ⧸ J)`) and contains a parabolic P (`J ≤ I` in the contravariant order). Then Q is parabolic: base change is monotone (`baseChangeHopfIdeal_mono`), and smoothness passes to k̄.

Correctly stated: a parabolic subgroup over k is smooth over k. `smoothCommHopfAlgProperty k (CommHopfAlgCat.quotient H I)` is `Algebra.Smooth k (H ⧸ I)`, and it follows from smoothness of the geometric fibre by faithfully flat descent along k → k̄ (`smoothCommHopfAlgProperty_quotient_baseChange_iff`).

Correctly stated: over an algebraically closed field k, a closed subgroup P of a finite-type affine group G is parabolic exactly when P is smooth and contains a Borel subgroup of G. Lean ↔ mathematics: `H : FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat k` is the coordinate ring O(G) of an affine k-group G of finite type, and a `HopfIdeal k H` is an ideal I with Δ(I) ⊆ I⊗H + H⊗I, ε(I) = 0 and S(I) ⊆ I, i.e. the ideal of the closed subgroup scheme P = Spec(H/I); the body is `IsAlgClosed k ∧ smoothCommHopfAlgProperty k (FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat.quotient H I).obj ∧ ∃ J, IsBorelOverAlgClosed k H J ∧ I ≤ J`. `smoothCommHopfAlgProperty k A` is by definition `Algebra.Smooth k A`, so the middle conjunct says P is smooth (a subgroup variety). `IsBorelOverAlgClosed k H J` is `IsAlgClosed k ∧ Minimal (IsBorelCandidate k H) J`, where `IsBorelCandidate` asks that H/J be smooth, geometrically connected (Spec((H/J)⊗K) connected for every field K) and have a solvable group of k̄-points; a minimal such ideal cuts out a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup, i.e. a Borel subgroup B (Milne Def. 18.10). Finally `I ≤ J` says P ⊇ B, because a larger ideal cuts out a smaller subgroup. Lean subtlety: the order on Hopf ideals is contravariant (`I ≤ J` means the subgroup of I contains that of J; ⊥ is G itself). `IsAlgClosed k` is a conjunct, not a hypothesis, so the predicate is simply false over a non-closed field (compiled: false for every ideal of O(GL₂) over ℚ); the general-field notion is `IsParabolic`. Smoothness is imposed explicitly, so a non-reduced subgroup scheme that contains a Borel (possible in characteristic p) is not parabolic. This is the convention of Milne ("subgroup variety") and of Conrad Def. 5.2.1 (P smooth). G itself need not be smooth or connected: its Borels then lie in (G_red)°, and for smooth G the definition agrees with "G/P complete" (Conrad: parabolicity does not require connectedness). A Hopf ideal is never ⊤, since ε vanishes on it, so there is no empty-subgroup junk case. Source: Milne, Algebraic Groups (iAG v2.00), Def. 18.19 with Thm 18.21 (a subgroup variety is parabolic iff it contains a Borel subgroup); Conrad, Reductive group schemes (Luminy notes), §1.1, citing Borel 11.2 Cor. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: witnesses compiled (GL₂ itself and its upper-triangular Borel are parabolic over any algebraically closed field). Non-witness compiled: the trivial subgroup (`augmentation`) of GL₂ is not parabolic. When the whole group is a Borel candidate (smooth, connected, solvable), every parabolic ideal equals ⊥, as in Milne Cor. 18.22. A downstream file proves all weight parabolics of GL_N parabolic.

Correctly stated: let `e : H ≅ L` be a Hopf-algebra isomorphism of coordinate rings, i.e. a group isomorphism Spec L ≅ Spec H. The ideal `J.comapOfSurjective (toBialgHom e.hom) _` = e⁻¹(J) ⊆ H cuts out the subgroup of Spec H that corresponds to Spec(L/J), and parabolicity transports along e. So the notion is invariant under isomorphism of the ambient group.
Correctly stated: the two-sided version. For `e : H ≅ L`, the pulled-back ideal e⁻¹(J) is parabolic in H iff J is parabolic in L, so parabolicity is invariant under isomorphism of the ambient group.

Correctly stated: conjugating a parabolic subgroup by a rational point keeps it parabolic. Here `g : WithConv (H →ₐ[k] k)` is a k-point of G, with convolution as the group law. `I.conjugate g` is the inverse image of I under the coordinate automorphism of x ↦ gxg⁻¹, i.e. the ideal of gPg⁻¹.

Correctly stated: over an algebraically closed field, if P is parabolic and B is any Borel subgroup, some rational point g conjugates P to a subgroup containing B. Lean ↔ mathematics: `hI : IsParabolicOverAlgClosed k (FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat.of k H) I` says P = Spec(H/I) is smooth and contains a Borel subgroup. `hJ : IsBorelOverAlgClosed … J` says J cuts out a Borel subgroup B, i.e. a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup. The conclusion `∃ g : WithConv (H →ₐ[k] k), I.conjugate g ≤ J` says gPg⁻¹ ⊇ B for some k-point g: `I.conjugate g` is the ideal of gPg⁻¹, and `≤` is the contravariant order. The proof uses Tau Ceti's Borel conjugacy theorem `IsBorelOverAlgClosed.exists_conjugate_eq` (any two Borels are G(k)-conjugate, even when the ambient group is not smooth or connected), which is proved, not assumed. Lean subtlety: `H : Type u` lies in the universe of k, inherited from the conjugacy theorem, which is stated for `FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat.{u, u}`. "Conjugate" means conjugate by a k-rational point, and over algebraically closed k these are all of G(k), as in Milne Thm 18.12(b). Source: Milne, Algebraic Groups (iAG v2.00), Thm 18.12(b) and Thm 18.21. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: axioms only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. Both hypotheses are load-bearing and jointly satisfiable (GL₂ with its upper-triangular Borel, compiled).

Correctly stated: a parabolic subgroup contains a Borel subgroup. In Lean there is J with `IsBorelOverAlgClosed k H J` (J is minimal among Hopf ideals with smooth, geometrically connected, geometrically solvable quotient, so it cuts out a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup) and `I ≤ J`. In the contravariant Hopf-ideal order that inequality says Spec(H/I) ⊇ Spec(H/J).

Correctly stated: projection of the first conjunct. A parabolic subgroup in the algebraically closed formulation exists only when `IsAlgClosed k` holds, because the predicate carries that as a conjunct.

Correctly stated: suppose P (ideal I) is parabolic and Q (ideal J) is a smooth closed subgroup with `J ≤ I`, i.e. Q ⊇ P in the contravariant order. Then Q is parabolic, since a Borel inside P lies in Q (the overgroup direction of Milne iAG Thm 18.21). Smoothness of Q (`Algebra.Smooth k (H ⧸ J)`) is a genuine hypothesis in this smooth convention, and lean_minimal_hypotheses finds all three hypotheses load-bearing.

Correctly stated: a parabolic subgroup P = Spec(H/I) is smooth. `smoothCommHopfAlgProperty k (FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat.quotient H I).obj` is by definition `Algebra.Smooth k (H ⧸ I)`, and this is the projection of the second conjunct.

Correctly stated: the whole group G, cut out by the zero Hopf ideal ⊥, is parabolic in itself iff k is algebraically closed and G is smooth (`Algebra.Smooth k H`, via H ⧸ ⊥ ≅ H). The backward direction uses existence of a Borel subgroup (`exists_minimal_isBorelCandidate`), which G contains since ⊥ ≤ J for every J. Lean subtlety: `IsAlgClosed k` appears on the right because the predicate carries it as a conjunct. The lemma is stated only for coordinate algebras in the universe of k (`FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat.{u, u}`); this is inherited from the Borel-existence theorem and harmless for concrete groups. In the smooth convention a non-smooth G (e.g. μ_p in characteristic p) is not parabolic in itself. Compiled: GL₂ over an algebraically closed field.

Correctly stated: P is parabolic iff its conjugate gPg⁻¹ by a rational point g (`I.conjugate g`, with g in the convolution group of k-points) is parabolic. This is the two-sided form of `IsParabolicOverAlgClosed.conjugate`, obtained via g⁻¹.

Correctly stated: this is the unfolding lemma (`Iff.rfl`) of `IsParabolicOverAlgClosed k H I` into its three conjuncts. They are: k is algebraically closed; `Algebra.Smooth k (H ⧸ I)`, i.e. P = Spec(H/I) is smooth; and some Borel ideal J satisfies `I ≤ J`, i.e. P contains the Borel subgroup cut out by J (the Hopf-ideal order is contravariant). The definition is not exposed outside its module, so this lemma is its public interface.

Correctly stated: over an algebraically closed field, fix one Borel subgroup B. Then a closed subgroup P is parabolic iff it is smooth and some G(k)-conjugate of P contains B. Lean ↔ mathematics: `hJ : IsBorelOverAlgClosed k (FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat.of k H) J` fixes the Borel subgroup B = Spec(H/J): J is minimal among Hopf ideals whose quotient is smooth, geometrically connected and has solvable k̄-points, so B is a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup. The left side `IsParabolicOverAlgClosed … I` says that P = Spec(H/I) is smooth and contains some Borel subgroup. The right side is `smoothCommHopfAlgProperty k (quotient … I).obj` together with `∃ g : WithConv (H →ₐ[k] k), I.conjugate g ≤ J`. The first part is by definition `Algebra.Smooth k (H ⧸ I)`, i.e. P is smooth. In the second part g ranges over k-points with convolution product, `I.conjugate g` is the ideal of gPg⁻¹, and `≤` is reverse inclusion of subgroups, so gPg⁻¹ ⊇ B. The forward direction is the Borel conjugacy theorem, proved in Tau Ceti (`IsBorelOverAlgClosed.exists_conjugate_eq`); the backward direction holds because g⁻¹Bg is a Borel subgroup inside P. Lean subtlety: algebraic closedness of k is not a separate hypothesis. It is extracted from `hJ`, because the Borel predicate carries `IsAlgClosed k` as a conjunct; over a non-closed field no such J exists, and the statement is then vacuous. `H : Type u` must lie in k's universe (inherited from the conjugacy theorem). Conjugation is by rational points, as in Milne. Source: Milne, Algebraic Groups (iAG v2.00), Thm 18.12(b) and Thm 18.21; Conrad, Reductive group schemes (Luminy notes), §1.1 (Thm 1.1.8 and the paragraph on parabolic subgroups). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: specialised to GL₂ with its upper-triangular Borel (compiles). Non-witness: the trivial subgroup of GL₂ is not parabolic. hJ is load-bearing, and the axioms are standard.

Correctly stated: over any field, the whole group G (zero Hopf ideal ⊥) is parabolic in itself iff G is smooth (`Algebra.Smooth k H`). The backward direction base-changes, uses that ⊥ base-changes to ⊥, and uses that G_{k̄} has a Borel subgroup. Lean subtlety: the lemma is stated only for H in the universe of k (`CommHopfAlgCat.{u} k`), inherited from Borel existence (`exists_minimal_isBorelCandidate`). In the smooth convention a non-smooth G is not parabolic in itself. Compiled: `IsParabolic ℚ (coordinateHopfAlgebra ℚ 2) ⊥`.
Correctly stated: over any field, gPg⁻¹ (`I.conjugate g`) is parabolic iff P is, for every k-rational point g. This is the two-sided form, obtained via g⁻¹.

Correctly stated: P is parabolic iff P is smooth over k and P_{k̄} contains a Borel subgroup of G_{k̄}. Lean ↔ mathematics: the left side is `IsParabolic k H I`. The right side is `smoothCommHopfAlgProperty k (CommHopfAlgCat.quotient H I)` together with `∃ J : HopfIdeal K H'.obj, IsBorelOverAlgClosed K H' J ∧ I' ≤ J`. The first part is by definition `Algebra.Smooth k (H ⧸ I)`, i.e. smoothness over the ground field. In the second, K = `AlgebraicClosure k`, H' = K ⊗ H = O(G_{k̄}), I' is the ideal of P_{k̄} generated by 1 ⊗ I, J is a Borel subgroup of G_{k̄}, and `I' ≤ J` means P_{k̄} ⊇ B. The nontrivial content is descent of smoothness along the faithfully flat extension k → k̄ (`smoothCommHopfAlgProperty_quotient_baseChange_iff`), so imperfect fields are handled correctly. Lean subtlety: the statement uses `let` binders, which are definitional abbreviations. It is `@[simp]`, so simp unfolds `IsParabolic` into this form (checked: `simp at h` works). `IsAlgClosed K` is supplied by Mathlib's instance for `AlgebraicClosure k`. Source: Milne, Algebraic Groups (iAG v2.00), Def. 18.63 with Thm 18.21; Conrad, Reductive group schemes (Luminy notes), Def. 5.2.1. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the witnesses and non-witness compiled for `IsParabolic` (GL₂ over ℚ) apply here too; axioms are standard.

Correctly stated: the unfolding lemma (`Iff.rfl`). `IsParabolic k H I` is `IsParabolicOverAlgClosed` applied to the base change K ⊗ H (= O(G_{k̄})) and to `baseChangeHopfIdeal I` (the ideal of P_{k̄}), with K = `AlgebraicClosure k`. It is the public interface of the unexposed definition. Lean subtlety: the statement's `let` binders are definitional abbreviations.

Correctly stated: for a basis b of a finite free A-algebra B and any field K that is an A-algebra, the image of the discriminant of b in K is nonzero iff the fibre K ⊗_A B is étale over K. Lean ↔ mathematics: `b : Module.Basis ι A B` with `[Fintype ι]` is a finite A-basis of B, which is what makes B finite free; `Algebra.discr A b` unfolds (`Algebra.discr_def`) to the determinant of `Algebra.traceMatrix A b`, whose (i, j) entry is `Algebra.trace A B (b i * b j)` (`traceMatrix_apply`, `traceForm_apply`), i.e. det(Tr_{B/A}(b_i b_j)); `algebraMap A K` is the structure map A → K (for instance A → κ(𝔭)), so the left side says the discriminant does not vanish at the point Spec K → Spec A; `K ⊗[A] B` with its K-algebra structure from the left factor is the fibre algebra, and `Algebra.Etale` is Mathlib's étale (formally étale plus finitely presented). The proof base-changes b to the basis 1 ⊗ b_i of K ⊗_A B, whose discriminant is the image of disc(b), and applies the field case `etale_iff_traceForm_nondegenerate`. Lean subtlety: `[DecidableEq ι]` is only bookkeeping for the determinant; in a field `≠ 0` is the same as being a unit, so this is the pointwise form of the unit criterion. Source and checks: the fibre step in the proof of Stacks, Lemma 49.3.1 (0BJF) (the trace pairing commutes with base change). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b, compiled: for every number field K the generic fibre ℚ ⊗_ℤ 𝓞_K is étale over ℚ, from `NumberField.discr_ne_zero`; consumed at residue fields by TauCeti/RingTheory/Etale/Purity.lean.

Correctly stated: for commutative rings A and B with B a finite free A-algebra and b a basis, B is étale over A iff the discriminant det(Tr_{B/A}(b_i b_j)) is a unit of A. Lean ↔ mathematics: `[CommRing A] [CommRing B] [Algebra A B]` impose no condition on the base (not local, not Noetherian); `b : Module.Basis ι A B` with `[Fintype ι]` says B is free of finite rank |ι| over A, which is the whole of "finite free" (a finite basis gives `Module.Free` and `Module.Finite`); `Algebra.discr A b` unfolds by `Algebra.discr_def` to `(Algebra.traceMatrix A b).det`, and `traceMatrix_apply` and `traceForm_apply` give its entries as `Algebra.trace A B (b i * b j)`, the trace of multiplication by b_i b_j, so this is the matrix of Stacks' trace pairing Q_π in the basis b and `Algebra.discr A b` is det(Q_π) there; `IsUnit` in A means it lies in no maximal ideal, i.e. the discriminant D_π = V(det Q_π) ⊂ Spec A, which Stacks (Section 49.3, 0BVH) defines as the zero scheme of det(Q_π), is empty; `Algebra.Etale A B` is Mathlib's étale class (`FormallyEtale` plus `FinitePresentation`), whose docstring cites Stacks 00UR for the equivalence with the standard definition. So the statement is 0BJF for a finite free π: π is étale iff D_π = ∅. The left side does not mention b, so the criterion is independent of the chosen basis. Lean subtlety: Mathlib's `Algebra.trace` is defined as 0 when B is not finite free, which the basis b rules out, so the traces are the genuine ones; `[DecidableEq ι]` is only needed to define `Matrix.det`; ι empty forces B = 0, and then `Algebra.discr` is the determinant of the empty matrix, 1, a unit, matching the fact that the zero ring is étale (compiled); A = 0 makes both sides trivially true. Stacks assumes finite locally free; the Lean hypothesis is a global basis, as its docstring's "finite free" says, so a finite projective non-free algebra is outside it. Source and checks: Stacks, Lemma 49.3.1 (0BJF), with the discriminant of Section 49.3 (0BVH). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b, compiled specialisations: for every number field K ≠ ℚ, `¬ Algebra.Etale ℤ (𝓞 K)` follows from this theorem with Mathlib's `RingOfIntegers.basis K` and `NumberField.abs_discr_gt_two` (|disc| > 2, so not ±1), which is the classical fact that ℚ has no everywhere-unramified extension and covers ℤ[i] (disc −4) and ℤ[√2] (disc 8); `Algebra.Etale ℤ (𝓞 ℚ)` from `NumberField.discr_rat`; the empty basis and the one-element basis of ℤ over ℤ. The instance hypotheses are satisfiable (these witnesses), axioms are propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound, and Mathlib has no duplicate (loogle `Algebra.Etale _ _ ↔ IsUnit (Algebra.discr _ _)` is empty; leansearch and leanfinder return only field-extension lemmas such as `Algebra.discr_isUnit_of_basis`).

Correctly stated: a finite-dimensional commutative algebra B over a field K (not necessarily a field) is étale iff its trace form (x, y) ↦ Tr_{B/K}(xy) is nondegenerate. Lean ↔ mathematics: `[Field K] [CommRing B] [Algebra K B]` make B a commutative K-algebra and `[FiniteDimensional K B]` (= `Module.Finite K B`) says dim_K B < ∞; `Algebra.Etale K B` is Mathlib's étale class (formally étale plus finitely presented), which over a field is equivalent, by Mathlib's `Algebra.Etale.iff_exists_algEquiv_prod`, to B ≅ a finite product of finite separable field extensions of K, the usual meaning of an étale K-algebra; `Algebra.traceForm K B` is by definition `compr₂ (lmul K B) (trace K B)`, so `traceForm_apply` gives `traceForm K B x y = Algebra.trace K B (x * y)` with `Algebra.trace K B z` the trace of multiplication by z on B, i.e. Stacks' trace pairing Q_{B/K}; `LinearMap.BilinForm.Nondegenerate` is `SeparatingLeft ∧ SeparatingRight` (no nonzero x pairs to 0 with every y, on either side), which for this symmetric form on a finite-dimensional space is the usual nondegeneracy, equivalently a nonzero Gram determinant in any basis (`LinearMap.BilinForm.nondegenerate_iff_det_ne_zero`). Lean subtlety: Mathlib's `Algebra.trace` is defined to be 0 when B has no finite basis; `[FiniteDimensional K B]` rules that out, so the trace here is the genuine one. B = 0 (the zero ring) is allowed: it is étale (empty product) and the form on the zero space is nondegenerate, so the statement is consistent there. Source and checks: the fibre case in the proof of Stacks, Lemma 49.3.1 (0BJF), which states exactly this for a finite k-algebra and Q_{A/k}. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b, compiled: for B a field the theorem combined with Mathlib's `traceForm_nondegenerate_tfae` (0BIL) gives `Algebra.Etale K L ↔ Algebra.IsSeparable K L`, so an inseparable finite extension is not étale; a non-field case, (Fin 2 → K) étale hence nondegenerate trace form; `[Field K]` cannot be weakened to a domain (for a number field K ≠ ℚ the ℤ-trace form of 𝓞_K is nondegenerate, discriminant ≠ 0, yet 𝓞_K is not étale over ℤ); the file's dual-numbers example is the non-étale case; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; no Mathlib duplicate (Mathlib has only the field-extension case).

Correctly stated: if B is a finite free A-algebra with a basis b whose discriminant det(Tr_{B/A}(b_i b_j)) is a unit of A, then B is étale over A. Lean ↔ mathematics: `b : Module.Basis ι A B` with `[Fintype ι]` is the finite basis (finite free); `hb : IsUnit (Algebra.discr A b)` says that determinant (`Algebra.discr_def`, entries `Algebra.trace A B (b i * b j)`) is invertible in A; `Algebra.Etale A B` is Mathlib's étale (formally étale plus finitely presented). This is the ⇐ half of Stacks, Lemma 49.3.1 (0BJF) for a free algebra. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: `hb` is needed (the dual numbers over a field have a basis, discriminant 0, and are not étale, the file's example); compiled `Algebra.Etale ℤ ℤ` from the one-element basis, whose discriminant is Tr(1) = 1.

Correctly stated: for a basis b of a finite free A-algebra B and any commutative A-algebra A', the discriminant of b becomes a unit in A' iff the base change A' ⊗_A B is étale over A'. Lean ↔ mathematics: `A'` with `[CommRing A'] [Algebra A A']` is an arbitrary base change and `algebraMap A A'` its structure map; `A' ⊗[A] B`, with its A'-algebra structure from the left factor, is the base change of B and is free over A' with basis `Algebra.TensorProduct.basis A' b` (the elements 1 ⊗ b_i), whose discriminant is the image of `Algebra.discr A b` (`TauCeti.Algebra.discr_basis_baseChange`); so this is `etale_iff_isUnit_discr` for the base-changed basis, i.e. the discriminant locus D_π commutes with base change. Lean subtlety: A' = 0 is allowed, and there both sides hold (every element of the zero ring is a unit, and the zero algebra is étale). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the localization form `isUnit_discr_localization_iff` is its instance at A' = A_𝔭; two-line proof by rewriting with the main theorem.

Correctly stated: for a prime 𝔭 of A and a basis b of a finite free A-algebra B, the discriminant of b is a unit in A_𝔭 iff B_𝔭 is étale over A_𝔭, i.e. 𝔭 lies outside the discriminant locus exactly when B is étale over the local ring at 𝔭. Lean ↔ mathematics: `p : Ideal A` with `[p.IsPrime]` is the prime 𝔭; `Localization.AtPrime p` is A_𝔭, the localization at the complement of 𝔭; `algebraMap A (Localization.AtPrime p)` is a ↦ a/1; `Localization.AtPrime p ⊗[A] B` is B_𝔭 as an A_𝔭-algebra; `Algebra.discr A b` is det(Tr_{B/A}(b_i b_j)). Lean subtlety: `[p.IsPrime]` is what makes `Localization.AtPrime p` the local ring A_𝔭, and in it a/1 is a unit iff a ∉ 𝔭 (Mathlib's `IsLocalization.AtPrime.isUnit_to_map_iff`), so the left side reads disc(b) ∉ 𝔭. This is the localization form requested in TauCetiRoadmap/LocalPurity §0.2; its proof is `isUnit_algebraMap_discr_iff_etale_baseChange` at A' = A_𝔭.

A topological group isomorphism e : G ≃ₜ* H (a bicontinuous multiplicative equivalence) carries Φ(G) onto Φ(H): `(profiniteFrattini G).map e = profiniteFrattini H`. One inclusion is `map_profiniteFrattini_le` for e, the other is the same lemma for e.symm. Checked as a simp lemma: without it `simp` makes no progress on the left-hand side, so that side is in simp normal form, and with it `simp` closes the goal.

f(Φ(G)) ≤ Φ(H) (`Subgroup.map f`) for a continuous surjective homomorphism f. This is Ribes–Zalesskii Prop. 2.8.2(b) ('if ρ : G → H is an epimorphism of profinite groups, then ρ(Φ(G)) ≤ Φ(H)'), stated here for arbitrary topological groups. Surjectivity is required: the preimage of a maximal subgroup along a non-surjective map need not be maximal.

For a continuous (`hf`) and surjective (`hsurj`) homomorphism f : G →* H, Φ(G) ≤ f⁻¹(Φ(H)) (`Subgroup.comap f`). The preimage of a maximal open subgroup of H is open by continuity and maximal by surjectivity (`Subgroup.isCoatom_comap_of_surjective`). That is the argument of Ribes–Zalesskii Prop. 2.8.2(b), and the statement is the topological analogue of Mathlib's `frattini_le_comap_frattini_of_surjective`.

Correctly stated: Φ(G) consists of non-generators. If H is a closed subgroup of a profinite group G with HΦ(G) = G, then H = G. Lean ↔ maths: 'profinite' is the three classes `[IsTopologicalGroup G] [CompactSpace G] [TotallyDisconnectedSpace G]`. Hausdorffness follows (`inferInstance` finds `T2Space G`, checked), so this is R–Z's compact Hausdorff totally disconnected group. `hH : IsClosed (H : Set G)` is 'H ≤_c G'. `H ⊔ profiniteFrattini G = ⊤` says the join in the subgroup lattice, i.e. the abstract subgroup generated by H and Φ(G), is all of G. Since Φ(G) is normal that join is the product HΦ(G), so the hypothesis is R–Z's HΦ(G) = G. The conclusion `H = ⊤` is H = G. Lean subtlety: `⊔` is the abstract join, not its closure. That is exactly R–Z's hypothesis HΦ(G) = G, and for closed H it makes no difference, because HΦ(G) is a product of two compact sets and so is already closed. The closedness of H is necessary (in ℤ_p the dense proper subgroup ℤ has ℤ + pℤ_p = ℤ_p), and lean_minimal_hypotheses finds `hH` load-bearing. Compactness and total disconnectedness are necessary too: the circle and ℚ_p both have Φ = ⊤. Source: Ribes–Zalesskii, Profinite Groups (2nd ed., 2010), Corollary 2.8.5 ('Let G be a profinite group, H ≤_c G … In particular, if HΦ(G) = G, then H = G'). Checks: no Mathlib replacement (`exact?` fails, and Mathlib's `frattini_nongenerating` concerns the abstract Frattini subgroup under `IsCoatomic (Subgroup G)`); axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

`IsClosed (Φ(G) : Set G)` whenever left and right translations are continuous (`SeparatelyContinuousMul G`, weaker than being a topological group). An open subgroup is closed, since its complement is a union of open cosets (`Subgroup.isClosed_of_isOpen`), and an intersection of closed sets is closed. As an instance it makes `G ⧸ profiniteFrattini G` Hausdorff, which is R–Z's profinite Frattini quotient (§2.8).

Φ(G) is topologically characteristic. `IsTopCharacteristic G N` unfolds (checked with `#print`) to `∀ φ : ContinuousAut G, N.map φ = N`: every continuous automorphism maps Φ(G) onto itself. This is the remark in Ribes–Zalesskii §2.8, p. 53 ('Plainly Φ(G) is a characteristic subgroup of G, that is, for every continuous automorphism ψ of G, ψ(Φ(G)) = Φ(G)'), here for every topological group.

x ∈ Φ(G) iff x lies in every subgroup M that is open (`IsOpen ↑M`) and maximal (`IsCoatom M`): Φ(G) is the intersection of the maximal open subgroups, as in Ribes–Zalesskii §2.8. Follows from `Subgroup.mem_iInf`.

Correct definition: Φ(G), the intersection of the maximal open subgroups of G. Lean ↔ maths: the body is `⨅ (M : Subgroup G) (_ : IsOpen (M : Set G)) (_ : IsCoatom M), M`. That is the infimum in the subgroup lattice, which is intersection (`Subgroup.mem_iInf`; see `mem_profiniteFrattini_iff`), taken over the subgroups M that are open (`IsOpen ↑M`) and maximal (`IsCoatom M`: M ≠ ⊤ and no subgroup lies strictly between M and ⊤). `IsCoatom` asks for maximality among all subgroups, while Ribes–Zalesskii say maximal among open subgroups. For a topological group the two agree, because a subgroup containing an open subgroup is open; a red-team probe compiles the equivalence from `Subgroup.isOpen_mono`. R–Z also note that a maximal closed subgroup of a profinite group is open, so using closed subgroups would give the same intersection. Lean subtlety: the empty infimum is `⊤`. When there are no maximal open subgroups (the trivial group, or a connected group such as ℝ), `profiniteFrattini G = ⊤`. For the trivial group this is R–Z's Φ(1) = 1 = G. For a nontrivial profinite group it cannot happen (`profiniteFrattini_ne_top`). The definition is stated for any topological group, and only the profinite case is claimed to be R–Z's Φ. Source: Ribes–Zalesskii, Profinite Groups (2nd ed., 2010), §2.8, p. 53 ('Define the Frattini subgroup Φ(G) of G to be the intersection of all its maximal open subgroups'). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b, all compiled: with the discrete topology it is Mathlib's abstract `frattini` (`profiniteFrattini_eq_frattini`); `frattini G ≤ profiniteFrattini G` in every topology; `profiniteFrattini Unit = ⊤`; on `Multiplicative ℤ_[p]` it is pℤ_p (via `IsProP.proPFrattini_eq_profiniteFrattini`), as used in the ℤ_p specialisation of the lifting theorem. It is not a duplicate: Mathlib has only the abstract `frattini`, and Tau Ceti's `proPFrattini p G` (the intersection of the index-p open normal subgroups) is a different subgroup that equals this one only for pro-p groups (ProP/MaximalSubgroup).

`profiniteFrattini G` equals its defining infimum, taken over the subgroups that are open (`IsOpen ↑M`) and maximal (`IsCoatom M`). It is the unfolding lemma for the unexposed body, proved by `rw [profiniteFrattini]`.

With the discrete topology (`[DiscreteTopology G]`), Φ(G) is Mathlib's abstract `frattini G`, which is `Order.radical`: the intersection of all coatoms (maximal subgroups) of `Subgroup G`.
