Every subgroup is open (`isOpen_discrete`), so the openness condition disappears. For a finite group this is the classical Frattini subgroup, and R–Z's definition reduces to it. Lean subtlety: both sides use the empty-infimum convention, so they are both `⊤` for a group with no maximal subgroups (e.g. ℚ) and agree there too.
Φ(G) ≤ M for every subgroup M that is open (`IsOpen ↑M`) and maximal (`IsCoatom M`): an intersection lies inside each of the sets it intersects.

For a nontrivial (`[Nontrivial G]`) profinite group (a compact, totally disconnected topological group), Φ(G) ≠ G (`≠ ⊤`). This is Ribes–Zalesskii §2.8, p. 53: 'if G is a nontrivial profinite group, then one always has Φ(G) < G'. The proof applies the non-generator property to the closed trivial subgroup. It shows that the empty-infimum value `⊤` occurs exactly for the trivial group.

Φ(G) is normal (`Subgroup.Normal`) whenever translations are continuous (`SeparatelyContinuousMul G`). Conjugation by any g is then a continuous automorphism, which fixes Φ(G) by `isTopCharacteristic_profiniteFrattini`. Together with `isClosed_profiniteFrattini` this gives the Hausdorff topological quotient G ⧸ Φ(G) used in `topologicalClosure_closure_eq_top_iff_quotient_profiniteFrattini`.

Correctly stated: for a Frattini cover f : G → K, a subset s topologically generates G iff f(s) topologically generates K. Lean ↔ maths: G is profinite via `[IsTopologicalGroup G] [CompactSpace G] [TotallyDisconnectedSpace G]` (T2 follows). K is a Hausdorff topological group (`[IsTopologicalGroup K] [T2Space K]`), and it is automatically profinite as a compact Hausdorff quotient of G, so the statement covers R–Z's epimorphisms of profinite groups. `hf : Continuous f`, `hsurj : Function.Surjective f` and `hker : f.ker ≤ profiniteFrattini G` together are R–Z's definition of a Frattini cover: a continuous epimorphism whose kernel lies in Φ, where Φ is the intersection of the maximal open subgroups. `(Subgroup.closure s).topologicalClosure = ⊤` says the closure of the abstract subgroup generated by s is all of G, which is R–Z's 'X generates G' (§2.4: 'the abstract subgroup ⟨X⟩ of G generated by X is dense in G'). `f '' s` is the image set. Lean subtlety: 'generates' means the closure of the abstract subgroup, on both sides, and no junk values are involved. `T2Space K` is essential. If K = ℤ/2 has the indiscrete topology and f is the identity, every subset of K generates a dense subgroup and the lifting fails; a red-team probe compiles this counterexample. Source: Ribes–Zalesskii, Profinite Groups (2nd ed., 2010), Corollary 2.8.5 and the proof of Lemma 2.8.6 (generation of G is detected on G/Φ(G)), with the Frattini-cover definition after Lemma 2.8.15. Checks: each explicit hypothesis is load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses), and `hsurj` is genuinely needed for the forward direction; no Mathlib replacement (`exact?`, loogle, leansearch, leanfinder); axioms are standard.

Correctly stated: a subset s of a profinite group G topologically generates G iff its image topologically generates the Frattini quotient G/Φ(G). Lean ↔ maths: `QuotientGroup.mk' (profiniteFrattini G)` is the quotient map G → G ⧸ Φ(G). The quotient carries the quotient topology and is a Hausdorff topological group, because Φ(G) is normal (`profiniteFrattini_normal`) and closed (`isClosed_profiniteFrattini`). Generation means 'the closure of the abstract subgroup generated is ⊤', as in R–Z §2.4. The statement is the previous iff applied to the quotient map, whose kernel is Φ(G) (`QuotientGroup.ker_mk'`). Lean subtlety: `G ⧸ profiniteFrattini G` is Hausdorff only because the closedness of Φ(G) is an instance. Instance search finds it here, so the target really is R–Z's profinite Frattini quotient. Source: Ribes–Zalesskii, Profinite Groups (2nd ed., 2010), proof of Lemma 2.8.6 ('G = ⟨X, Φ(G)⟩ = ⟨X⟩Φ(G) = ⟨X⟩ by Corollary 2.8.5', with ψ : G → G/Φ(G) the canonical epimorphism). Checks: no hypotheses beyond profiniteness; axioms are standard.

Correctly stated: along a Frattini cover f : G → K of profinite groups, every lift of a topologically generating family of K topologically generates G, for any index type. Lean ↔ maths: `[IsTopologicalGroup G] [CompactSpace G] [TotallyDisconnectedSpace G]` make G profinite, and `inferInstance` finds `T2Space G` (checked). K is a Hausdorff topological group, hence profinite as a continuous image of G. `hf`, `hsurj` and `hker : f.ker ≤ profiniteFrattini G` are R–Z's Frattini cover, a continuous epimorphism with Ker(f) ≤ Φ(G), where `profiniteFrattini` is the intersection of the maximal open subgroups (R–Z p. 53). `g : ι → G` is the lift and `f ∘ g : ι → K` is the family it lifts. Quantifying over every g that satisfies `hg` therefore covers every lift of every generating family. `(Subgroup.closure (Set.range (f ∘ g))).topologicalClosure = ⊤` and `(Subgroup.closure (Set.range g)).topologicalClosure = ⊤` say that the abstract subgroup generated by the family is dense, which is R–Z's 'generates' (§2.4). Lean subtlety: generation is topological (a dense abstract subgroup) on both sides, as in R–Z, and no junk values are involved. The empty family is handled correctly: `hg` then forces K = 1, so G = Φ(G), so G = 1 by `profiniteFrattini_ne_top`. `T2Space K` is load-bearing. A compiled counterexample takes K = ℤ/2 with the indiscrete topology, f = id and the empty family: it satisfies every other hypothesis and fails the conclusion. Source: Ribes–Zalesskii, Profinite Groups (2nd ed., 2010), §2.8: the definition of Frattini cover after Lemma 2.8.15, Corollary 2.8.5, and the proof of Lemma 2.8.6. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b, all compiled: (i) at G = ℤ_p (`Multiplicative ℤ_[p]`), K = ℤ/p and f = reduction mod p, it gives that every u with u mod p ≠ 0 topologically generates ℤ_p; ker f ≤ Φ is discharged via `IsProP.proPFrattini_eq_profiniteFrattini`; (ii) for finite discrete groups it gives the classical finite statement with Mathlib's `frattini`; (iii) the axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. The hypothesis `hsurj` can be dropped, since it follows from compactness, `T2Space K` and `hg` (MINOR RT-20261104-5187c1); this does not affect correctness.

Correctly stated: this is the direction 'completely continuous ⇒ row compact' over a complete ultrametric Tate normed ring. From `hu : u.IsCompletelyContinuous` (for every ε > 0, a continuous v with range in a finitely generated submodule and ‖u x − v x‖ ≤ ε‖x‖) and `hclosed` (all finitely generated submodules of C₀(I, R) are closed), it concludes `u.IsRowCompact` (bounded entries, and row norms → 0 along the cofinite filter on the output index). This is the half of Serre §3 Prop. 4 saying that the rows of a limit of finite-rank maps decay, with closedness of finitely generated submodules standing in for finite-dimensionality. `hu` cannot be dropped: otherwise every map, including the identity of C₀(ℕ, ℚ_p), would be row compact, which `not_isRowCompact_id` refutes (compiled). `hclosed` makes the approximants' range submodules complete for the open mapping theorem.

Correctly stated: over a complete non-archimedean field with a nontrivial absolute value, a continuous linear map u : c₀(J) → c₀(I) is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank maps exactly when its matrix has sup_j |a_ij| → 0 as the output index i → ∞ (Serre, Publ. Math. IHÉS 12 (1962), §3, Proposition 4 and its Corollaire). Lean ↔ mathematics: `[NontriviallyNormedField K] [IsUltrametricDist K] [CompleteSpace K]` is a complete field with an absolute value that is not trivial (some |x| > 1) and satisfies |x + y| ≤ max(|x|, |y|). This is exactly Serre's standing hypothesis in §1: "K désigne un corps valué complet, non archimédien … On suppose en outre que K n'est pas discret, c'est-à-dire que G ≠ {1}". Here "non discret" means a nontrivial value group, not a discrete valuation. Serre assumes a discrete valuation only for particular results (Propositions 1, 2, 9, 13, 15), and not for Proposition 4, so the Lean hypotheses are Serre's own rather than a generalisation of them. `C₀(J, K)` with `[DiscreteTopology J]` is Mathlib's `ZeroAtInftyContinuousMap`. On a discrete space the cocompact filter is the cofinite one, so the elements are the families with x_j → 0 along the cofinite filter, under the sup norm: Serre's c(J), for an index type of any cardinality. `u.matrixCoeff i j = u (single j 1) i` puts the output index first, `rowNorm i = ⨆ j, ‖matrixCoeff i j‖`, and `IsRowCompact` is "entries bounded ∧ `Tendsto rowNorm cofinite (𝓝 0)`" along the output index type I. Serre, with target c(J), instead writes u(e_i) = (n_ij)_{j∈J} with the source index first, and sets r_j(u) = |w_j| = sup_i |n_ij| for the target index j. So Lean's `rowNorm i` (I the target) is Serre's r_j(u) with the letters renamed, and the decay is along the target index in both, with no transposition. `IsCompletelyContinuous u` says that for every ε > 0 some continuous v whose range lies in a finitely generated submodule has ‖u x − v x‖ ≤ ε‖x‖ for all x. I compiled its equivalence with `u ∈ closure {v | FiniteDimensional K (range v)}` for Mathlib's operator norm, which is Serre's definition, "adhérent dans L(E,F) au sous-espace des applications linéaires continues de rang fini": a uniform limit, not a strong one. `↔` gives both directions. Lean subtlety: `rowNorm` is a real `⨆`, which Mathlib sets to 0 for an unbounded family (and for J empty, where 0 is the right value). The bounded-entries clause of `IsRowCompact` stops that junk value from making an operator row compact, and over a field the bound is automatic (|a_ij| ≤ ‖u‖). For finite I the cofinite filter is ⊥, so every u is row compact (compiled). That is the correct answer, because a map into the finite-dimensional C₀(I, K) has finite rank. Checks (red-team audit at 5f78b5307b, all compiled over ℚ_p): the identity of C₀(ℕ, ℚ_p) is not row compact (`not_isRowCompact_id`), so the theorem says it is not completely continuous. That agrees with `isCompletelyContinuous_id_iff` (complete continuity of the identity means finite generation). The rank-one map x ↦ (Σ_j x_j)·e₀ has matrix a_ij = [i = 0], and every one of its columns has an entry of norm 1. It is row compact and of finite rank, and the theorem returns 'completely continuous'; a column-wise (transposed) condition would wrongly reject it. diag(pⁿ) is covered by `isCompletelyContinuous_diagonalCLM_iff`. The statement is also re-derived independently as `isRowCompact_iff_hasCompactoidImage.trans hasCompactoidImage_iff_isCompletelyContinuous` (neither file imports this one). Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: over a complete ultrametric Tate normed ring R (`[NormedRing R] [IsUltrametricDist R] [CompleteSpace R] [TauCeti.NormedRing.IsTate R]`, i.e. R has a topologically nilpotent unit, as in the Banach–Tate setting of Johansson–Newton §2.1), assume `hclosed`: every finitely generated R-submodule of C₀(I, R) is closed. Then a continuous R-linear u : C₀(J, R) → C₀(I, R) satisfies `IsRowCompact` (bounded entries, and row norms sup_j ‖u(e_j)(i)‖ → 0 along the cofinite filter on the output index) exactly when it satisfies `IsCompletelyContinuous` (uniformly ε-approximable by continuous maps whose range lies in a finitely generated submodule, which is how 'finite rank' reads over a ring). `hclosed` is satisfiable: it holds over every complete nontrivially normed field by `Submodule.closed_of_finiteDimensional`, compiled at ℚ_p, and this file uses it that way for Serre's field case (§3 Prop. 4, Corollaire). lean_minimal_hypotheses marks it load-bearing. Lean subtlety: the real `⨆` in `rowNorm` is 0 for an unbounded row. `IsRowCompact` includes the entry bound, which holds automatically over Tate scalars, so the statement does not use that junk value. Axioms: standard.

Correctly stated: over a complete ultrametric Tate normed ring, suppose the range of u : C₀(J, R) →L[R] C₀(I, R) lies in a submodule L (`(u : _ →ₗ[R] _).range ≤ L`) that is finitely generated (`L.FG`) and closed (`IsClosed (L : Set C₀(I, R))`). Then u is row compact: its entries are bounded and its row norms sup_j ‖u(e_j)(i)‖ tend to 0 along the cofinite filter on the output index. I compiled it on the rank-one map x ↦ (Σ_j x_j)·e₀ over ℚ_p with L = span{e₀}, and it gives row compactness as expected. lean_minimal_hypotheses marks all three hypotheses load-bearing.

Correctly stated: let Q be a measurable, convex, symmetric subset of a finite-dimensional real inner product space E that dominates the Gaussian measure on symmetric convex sets (∫_A e^{−π‖x‖²} dx ≤ vol(A ∩ Q) for every measurable convex A = −A); then every central section V ∩ Q by a linear subspace V has (dim V)-dimensional volume at least one. Lean ↔ mathematics: `E` with `[InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]` and its Borel σ-algebra is a Euclidean space, whose `volume` is the orthonormal-basis Lebesgue measure (so the Gaussian has total mass 1); `hQ`, `hQc`, `hQneg` are measurability of Q, `Convex ℝ Q` and Q = −Q; `hgauss` is the domination hypothesis, `∫⁻ x in A, ENNReal.ofReal (Real.exp (-π * ‖x‖ ^ 2))` being the Gaussian measure of A; `((↑) : V → E) ⁻¹' Q` is the preimage of Q under the inclusion of V, i.e. V ∩ Q as a subset of V; `volume` on `↥V` is the inner-product Lebesgue measure of V (`measureSpaceOfInnerProductSpace`; by `rfl` the Haar measure of `stdOrthonormalBasis ℝ V`), not the ambient measure of V, which would be 0 for V ≠ E. Lean subtlety: the inequality is in ℝ≥0∞ with no `toReal`; an infinite-volume section would satisfy it, but then the volume really is ≥ 1; `hgauss` excludes degenerate Q (Q = ∅ fails it at A = univ, whose Gaussian measure is 1), so the statement is not vacuous. Source: this is the slicing step of Vaaler's proof of Theorem 1, Pacific J. Math. 83 (1979), §3, 548–549 (read), which thickens P_K by a slab H_ε of width ε along an orthonormal basis of its orthogonal complement, applies the peakedness Lemma 5 to it and lets ε → 0+; the file applies `hgauss` to the ε-slab around V the same way, replacing Vaaler's dominated-convergence step by Brunn's principle (every parallel slice is at most the central one). Checks (Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b (Lean v4.36.0-rc2, Mathlib 1b1ccf4b08)): `hgauss` and convexity are needed (Q = {0} satisfies the other hypotheses, and so does Q = B \ V for B a product of unit-volume balls, since V is null in E; both have slice volume 0); the hypotheses are satisfiable (the product-of-balls theorem in this file supplies `hgauss`); axioms standard.

Correctly stated: if B_i is a closed ball of volume one in a finite-dimensional real inner product space α_i (finitely many i), then every central section V ∩ ∏ B_i of the product by a real linear subspace V of the orthogonal sum ⊕ α_i has (dim V)-dimensional volume at least one (Vaaler's theorem for products of balls). Lean ↔ mathematics: `[Fintype ι]`, `[∀ i, InnerProductSpace ℝ (α i)]`, `[∀ i, FiniteDimensional ℝ (α i)]` and the Borel σ-algebras say the factors are finitely many Euclidean spaces ℝ^{n_i}; `hρ : ∀ i, volume (closedBall (0 : α i) (ρ i)) = 1` says the closed ball of radius ρ_i about 0 has volume one for α_i's inner-product Lebesgue measure (Mathlib's `volume` on such a space is the orthonormal-basis Haar measure); `PiLp 2 α` is ∏ α_i with the ℓ² norm, i.e. the orthogonal direct sum ℝ^N, N = Σ n_i; `{x : V | ∀ i, ‖(x : PiLp 2 α) i‖ ≤ ρ i}` is V ∩ ∏ B_i regarded inside V; `volume` on the subtype `↥V` is `measureSpaceOfInnerProductSpace` for the inherited inner product (by `rfl` the Haar measure of `stdOrthonormalBasis ℝ V`), the intrinsic Lebesgue measure of V; `1 ≤ …` is the bound. Lean subtlety: the inequality is in ℝ≥0∞, but the slice is bounded and so of finite volume, so it is not met by ∞; `closedBall 0 r` is empty for r < 0, so `hρ` forces ρ_i ≥ 0 (ρ_i > 0 when α_i ≠ 0); zero-dimensional factors are allowed — their only ball is {0}, of (Dirac) volume one, and their constraint is vacuous — a harmless extension of Vaaler's positive n_j; and the product is the ℓ² `PiLp 2 α` (the plain `∀ i, α i` has the sup norm and no inner product), so the measure on V is the Euclidean one. Source: Vaaler, Pacific J. Math. 83 (1979), Theorem 1 and its Corollary, 543–544 (read): for Q_N = S_{n_1} × ⋯ × S_{n_J}, S_n the closed ball of volume one in ℝ^n, and every K-dimensional subspace P_K of ℝ^N, μ_K(Q_N ∩ P_K) ≥ 1, μ_K the K-dimensional Lebesgue measure (the Corollary takes an orthonormal basis of P_K). Checks (Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b (Lean v4.36.0-rc2, Mathlib 1b1ccf4b08)): `hρ` is needed (with ρ = 0 the section is {0}, of volume 0 in any V ≠ 0) and is satisfiable (`TauCeti.exists_volume_closedBall_eq_one`; the cube corollary uses ρ_i = 1/2); the measure on V checked by `rfl`; the cube corollary's values at V = ⊥, V = ⊤ and the diagonal of ℝ² compiled; axioms standard. The hypothesis could be weakened to `1 ≤ volume …` (a recorded MINOR generality finding); that does not affect correctness.

Correctly stated: every central section of the unit polydisc {z ∈ ℂ^n : |z_i| ≤ 1 for all i} by a complex linear subspace V of complex dimension k has real 2k-dimensional volume at least π^k. Lean ↔ mathematics: `EuclideanSpace ℂ ι` is ℂ^n (n = #ι) with the Hermitian ℓ² structure; `V : Submodule ℂ (EuclideanSpace ℂ ι)` is a complex subspace and `V.restrictScalars ℝ` the same set viewed as a real subspace; the real inner product used for the volume is that of `PiLp 2` with factors `instInnerProductSpaceRealComplex` (checked with pp.explicit), ⟨z, w⟩_ℝ = Σ_i Re(conj z_i · w_i), i.e. the Euclidean structure of ℂ^n = ℝ^{2n}; `volume` on `↥(V.restrictScalars ℝ)` is `measureSpaceOfInnerProductSpace` for it (by `rfl` the Haar measure of `stdOrthonormalBasis ℝ`), the intrinsic 2k-dimensional Lebesgue measure; `‖(x : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) i‖ ≤ 1` is |z_i| ≤ 1; `finrank ℂ V` is k; `ENNReal.ofReal π ^ finrank ℂ V` is π^k. Lean subtlety: the inequality is in ℝ≥0∞ with no `toReal`, and the section is bounded, hence of finite volume; the exponent is the complex dimension while the measure is real (the file proves finrank ℝ (V.restrictScalars ℝ) = 2 · finrank ℂ V); Mathlib also has `InnerProductSpace.rclikeToReal` on `EuclideanSpace ℂ ι`, not definitionally equal to the instance in this statement, but typeclass inference picks the same instance as the statement (`#synth InnerProductSpace ℝ (EuclideanSpace ℂ (Fin 3))` gives `PiLp.innerProductSpace` with `instInnerProductSpaceRealComplex` factors), so callers meet the same measure. Derivation from the source: Vaaler, Pacific J. Math. 83 (1979), Corollary, 544 (read), with all n_j = 2 gives every real section of the product of discs of area one volume ≥ 1; the polydisc is that product dilated by √π, and a 2k-dimensional volume scales by (√π)^{2k} = π^k, which is how the file proves it. Checks (Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b (Lean v4.36.0-rc2, Mathlib 1b1ccf4b08)): the measure on V checked by `rfl`; no hypotheses beyond `[Fintype ι]`; axioms standard.

Correctly stated: every central section V ∩ [−1, 1]^n of the cube by a k-dimensional linear subspace V of ℝ^n has k-dimensional volume at least 2^k (Vaaler's cube-slicing theorem). Lean ↔ mathematics: `EuclideanSpace ℝ ι` is by definition `PiLp 2 (fun _ ↦ ℝ)`, i.e. ℝ^n (n = #ι, finite by `[Fintype ι]`) with the Euclidean ℓ² norm and inner product; `V : Submodule ℝ (EuclideanSpace ℝ ι)` is an arbitrary real linear subspace, of any dimension including 0 and n; `{x : V | ∀ i, |(x : EuclideanSpace ℝ ι) i| ≤ 1}` is the set of points of V whose coordinates all lie in [−1, 1], i.e. V ∩ [−1, 1]^n regarded as a subset of V; `volume` on the right is the measure of the subtype `↥V`, Mathlib's `measureSpaceOfInnerProductSpace` for the inner product V inherits from ℝ^n — the red team checked `(volume : Measure V) = (stdOrthonormalBasis ℝ V).toBasis.addHaar` by `rfl`, and `OrthonormalBasis.volume_parallelepiped` gives the parallelepiped of every orthonormal basis of V volume one, so this is the basis-independent intrinsic k-dimensional Lebesgue measure of V, not a measure tied to some choice of coordinates; `finrank ℝ V` is k = dim V (the honest dimension, V being finite-dimensional); the conclusion `2 ^ finrank ℝ V ≤ volume …` is 2^k ≤ vol_k(V ∩ [−1, 1]^n). Lean subtlety: the inequality lives in ℝ≥0∞, where ∞ satisfies every lower bound, and no `toReal` is involved; the red team compiled that this slice has finite volume for every V (it lies in the ball of radius √n of V), so the bound is genuine; also the ambient space is `EuclideanSpace ℝ ι` (ℓ²), not `ι → ℝ` (sup norm, no inner product), so the measure on V is the Euclidean one, as it must be. Source: Vaaler, Pacific J. Math. 83 (1979), 543–544 (read): for C_N = [−1/2, 1/2]^N and a K-dimensional subspace P_K, μ_K(C_N ∩ P_K) ≥ 1 (the Corollary to Theorem 1 with all n_j = 1), which is this statement after dilating by 2, since a k-dimensional volume scales by 2^k. Checks (Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b (Lean v4.36.0-rc2, Mathlib 1b1ccf4b08)): compiled k = 0 (V = ⊥: the slice is all of V and has volume 1 = 2^0), V = ⊤ (slice volume exactly 2^n = 2^finrank, so the constant is sharp) and the diagonal line of ℝ² (slice volume computed in Lean as exactly 2√2 ≥ 2); no hypotheses besides `[Fintype ι]`; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: if B = ∏ B_i is a product of closed balls of volume one in finite-dimensional real inner product spaces α_i, then the Gaussian measure ∫_A e^{−π|x|²} dx of every measurable convex set A ⊆ ∏ α_i with −A = A is at most vol(A ∩ B) (the peakedness lemma behind Vaaler's theorem). Lean ↔ mathematics: `hρ` says each `closedBall (0 : α i) (ρ i)` has volume one for α_i's inner-product Lebesgue measure; `A : Set (∀ i, α i)` with `MeasurableSet A`, `Convex ℝ A` and `∀ x ∈ A, -x ∈ A` is a measurable, convex, symmetric set; on `∀ i, α i` Mathlib's `volume` is `Measure.pi` of the factor volumes, i.e. Lebesgue measure on ℝ^N, N = Σ dim α_i; the integrand `∏ i, ENNReal.ofReal (Real.exp (-π * ‖x i‖ ^ 2))` equals exp(−π Σ_i ‖x_i‖²) = e^{−π|x|²} for the Euclidean norm of the orthogonal sum (the file rewrites it so with `PiLp.norm_sq_eq_of_L2` and `Real.exp_sum`), so `∫⁻ x in A, …` is the standard Gaussian measure of A; `univ.pi fun i ↦ closedBall 0 (ρ i)` is ∏ B_i, and the right side is vol(A ∩ B). Lean subtlety: the domain is the plain product `∀ i, α i`, whose norm is the sup norm, but only the coordinate norms ‖x i‖ and the product measure appear, so nothing depends on it; `ENNReal.ofReal` of the positive real e^{−π‖x_i‖²} is that real; the inequality is in ℝ≥0∞ with both sides finite (the Gaussian measure is at most 1). Source: Vaaler, Pacific J. Math. 83 (1979), Lemma 5, 547 (read): the indicator of Q_N = S_{n_1} × ⋯ × S_{n_J} is more peaked than exp(−π|x|²), i.e. ∫_U e^{−π|x|²} dx ≤ μ(U ∩ Q_N) for closed convex symmetric U; the Lean statement drops closedness (any measurable U), a mild generalisation. Checks (Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b (Lean v4.36.0-rc2, Mathlib 1b1ccf4b08)): all four hypotheses are load-bearing (`lean_minimal_hypotheses`), and convexity and symmetry are needed mathematically (a small ball far from the origin has positive Gaussian measure and misses B); the hypotheses are satisfiable (radii from `TauCeti.exists_volume_closedBall_eq_one`); axioms standard. `hρ` could be weakened to `1 ≤ volume …` (a recorded MINOR generality finding); that does not affect correctness.

A monic polynomial has a nonempty polygon for any valuation, since its leading coefficient has valuation v(1) = 0. Lean subtlety: the zero ring, where 0 is monic, carries no `AddValuation` (v 1 = 0 ≠ ∞ = v 0), so no degenerate case arises.
If v x = ∞ only for x = 0, the finite unit edges of the polygon are those with natTrailingDegree f ≤ n < natDegree f; for f = 0 both sides are empty (`Set.Ico 0 0`).
A monomial c·Xᵏ (a constant when k = 0) has no finite unit edges: its polygon is one point or empty; this holds for every valuation and every c.
If the end coefficients have finite valuation, the unit edges [n, n+1] with both polygon heights finite (`finiteEdges`) are exactly those with natTrailingDegree f ≤ n < natDegree f (`Set.Ico`).
{n | v(aₙ) ≠ ∞} is finite: a polynomial has only finitely many coefficient points, all within its support.

`IsAdmissible fun n => v (f.coeff n)`: the coefficient heights of a polynomial admit a real affine lower bound (∃ c m, c + m·n ≤ v(aₙ) for all n), because they are ∞ beyond the degree and only finitely many are finite; so the fallback of `lowerConvexEnvelope` never applies to polynomials.
The polygon of a polynomial is a convex height sequence (`IsConvexSeq`: finite on an integer interval with nondecreasing increments).

Correctly stated. (1) The Newton polygon of every polynomial is the greatest convex minorant of its coefficient heights. (2) `IsLowerConvexEnvelope (fun n => v (f.coeff n)) (f.newtonPolygon v)` unfolds to three fields: `IsConvexSeq` (finite on an integer interval, nondecreasing increments), `≤` the heights pointwise (on or below every point (n, v(aₙ))), and `greatest`: above every convex sequence below the heights; equivalently `IsGreatest {g | IsConvexSeq g ∧ g ≤ a}` (`isLowerConvexEnvelope_iff_isGreatest`). On ℕ this is the lower convex hull of the points read at the integers. No hypothesis on f or v. (3) Lean subtlety: no admissibility hypothesis is needed because polynomial heights are ∞ beyond the degree (`isAdmissible_addValuation_coeff`), so the `else ⊤` fallback is never used; zero coefficients (and, over a non-domain, nonzero ones of valuation ∞) have height ∞ and constrain nothing. (4) Sources: Kedlaya, MIT 18.787 notes 'Newton polygons' §1 (the lower convex hull of {(−i, v(Pᵢ)) : Pᵢ ≠ 0}, i.e. the intersection of the closed half-planes above nonvertical lines lying below all the points; he plots at −i, so Tau Ceti's polygon is his reflected by x ↦ −x and slopes change sign); TauCetiRoadmap NewtonPolygons README (Conventions 1, 3, 4; §§0.1, 2.1). Red-team checks: the 2-adic witness was computed through this lemma and uniqueness of envelopes (compiled over ℚ_[2] with the real 2-adic valuation (`Padic.addValuation` composed with ℤ → ℝ): 1 + 8X² has polygon (0, 3/2, 3, ∞, …), so the missing X-coefficient imposes no constraint and the gap is crossed on the chord; and for any v with v 2 = 1, 1 + 4X + X² has polygon value 0 at index 1 although the point there has height 2, so the polygon is the envelope, not the point heights; (0, ∞, 0, …) and (0, 2, 0, …) are refuted as `IsConvexSeq`); axioms standard.
Every `IsConvexSeq H` with H n ≤ v(aₙ) for all n lies below `f.newtonPolygon v` pointwise: the polygon dominates every convex minorant of the points.

If v x = ∞ only for x = 0, the polygon has deg f − ord₀ f finite unit edges (roadmap Convention 4: d − a finite unit slopes). Lean subtlety: the ℕ subtraction never truncates since natTrailingDegree ≤ natDegree; f = 0 gives 0 = 0.

Correctly stated. (1) For a polynomial f = Σ aₙXⁿ over a ring R and a real additive valuation v, `f.newtonPolygon v` is the Newton polygon of f as the height function n ↦ height over the abscissa n ∈ ℝ ∪ {∞}. (2) `v : AddValuation R (WithTop ℝ)` is Mathlib's additive valuation with values in ℝ ∪ {∞} (v 0 = ∞, v 1 = 0, v(xy) = v x + v y, v(x + y) ≥ min(v x, v y); the ord_p orientation, larger value = smaller absolute value). The body is `lowerConvexEnvelope fun n => v (f.coeff n)`: the heights v(aₙ) encode the points (n, v(aₙ)), with height ∞ (no point) where aₙ = 0. Polynomial heights are ∞ beyond the degree, hence `IsAdmissible` (`isAdmissible_addValuation_coeff`), so `lowerConvexEnvelope` is the pointwise supremum of all g ≤ heights with `IsConvexSeq g`, where `IsConvexSeq g` means the finite domain {n | g n ≠ ⊤} is order-connected (an integer interval) and the increments g(n+1) − g(n) are nondecreasing on consecutive finite indices, i.e. g is a discrete convex function with value ∞ outside an interval (the restriction to ℕ of a convex piecewise-linear function); that is the greatest convex minorant, the lower boundary of the convex hull of the points read at the integers (`Polynomial.isLowerConvexEnvelope_newtonPolygon`). Its finite domain is [natTrailingDegree f, natDegree f] when the end coefficients have finite valuation (`newtonPolygon_ne_top_iff_of_ne_top`), and interior gaps are crossed on chords. (3) Lean subtlety: the `else ⊤` fallback of `lowerConvexEnvelope` is never taken for a polynomial; the zero polynomial gets the empty polygon ⊤ (roadmap Convention 4, not a junk value); v may be ∞ at a nonzero element when R is not a domain, and such a coefficient is dropped like a zero one. (4) Sources: Kedlaya, MIT 18.787 notes 'Newton polygons' §1 (the lower convex hull of {(−i, v(Pᵢ)) : Pᵢ ≠ 0}, i.e. the intersection of the closed half-planes above nonvertical lines lying below all the points; he plots at −i, so Tau Ceti's polygon is his reflected by x ↦ −x and slopes change sign); TauCetiRoadmap NewtonPolygons README (Conventions 1, 3, 4; §§0.1, 2.1). New red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: compiled over ℚ_[2] with the real 2-adic valuation (`Padic.addValuation` composed with ℤ → ℝ): 1 + 8X² has polygon (0, 3/2, 3, ∞, …), so the missing X-coefficient imposes no constraint and the gap is crossed on the chord; and for any v with v 2 = 1, 1 + 4X + X² has polygon value 0 at index 1 although the point there has height 2, so the polygon is the envelope, not the point heights; (0, ∞, 0, …) and (0, 2, 0, …) are refuted as `IsConvexSeq`; axioms standard.
`(C c * f).newtonPolygon v n = v c + f.newtonPolygon v n`: multiplying by the constant c translates the polygon by v(c) (`coeff_C_mul`). Lean subtlety: v c = ∞ makes both sides ⊤.
The polygon of Xᵏ·f at n is that of f at n − k for k ≤ n and ∞ for n < k: multiplication by Xᵏ shifts the polygon k places right. Lean subtlety: truncated `n - k` is used only under `k ≤ n`.
The polygon at abscissa 0 is v(a₀), the height of the constant term, which is ∞ when a₀ = 0 (consistent with the polygon starting at the order of vanishing).

The power-series polygon of the coercion `(f : R⟦X⟧)` equals the polynomial polygon of f: both are the envelope of the same heights, as `coeff_coe` gives the same coefficients; so the two definitions agree.

(1) Substituting cX for X shears the polygon: P(f(cX))(n) = P(f)(n) + n·v(c). (2) `f.comp (C c * X)` is f(cX), with coefficients aₙcⁿ (`comp_C_mul_X_coeff`) of valuation v(aₙ) + n·v(c), so the points and hence the greatest convex minorant move by the linear function n ↦ n·v(c); the sign is right. `n • v c` is n-fold addition in `WithTop ℝ`. (3) Lean subtlety: `n • ⊤` is 0 at n = 0 and ∞ elsewhere; the hypothesis `hc : v c ≠ ⊤` is stated but not needed for polynomials (finding RT-20261104-9bfd8e: when v c = ∞ both sides are (v(a₀), ∞, ∞, …), compiled in a module probe), so the statement is correct, only less general than it could be. (4) TauCetiRoadmap NewtonPolygons README (Conventions 1, 3, 4; §§0.1, 2.1) (§2.1).
`f.newtonPolygon v = lowerConvexEnvelope fun n => v (f.coeff n)`: the defining equation of the polynomial Newton polygon, proved by `rfl`; needed because the module system does not expose the body.
For n ≥ natDegree f the polygon at n equals v(aₙ): the leading coefficient's height at the degree, and ∞ = ∞ beyond it.

The polygon of f is ⊤ (empty) iff every coefficient has valuation ∞. Lean subtlety: over a field this means f = 0 (`AddValuation.top_iff`), but over a non-domain v can be ∞ at nonzero coefficients, which is why the criterion is stated through v rather than f = 0.

The polygon is ∞ at every n below the order of vanishing at 0 (`natTrailingDegree f`): nothing to the left of the first nonzero coefficient. Lean subtlety: natTrailingDegree 0 = 0, so it is vacuous for f = 0.
The polygon is ∞ at every n > natDegree f: nothing to the right of the leading coefficient.
`f.newtonPolygon v n ≤ v (f.coeff n)` for every n: the polygon lies on or below every coefficient point; no hypothesis is needed since polynomial heights are admissible.
If w(φ x) = v(x) for all x, the polygon of `f.map φ` under w equals that of f under v: the coefficients φ(aₙ) have the same heights (`coeff_map`).

If w(φ x) = c·v(x) for a real c > 0 (`(v x).map (c * ·)`, ∞ kept), the polygon of `f.map φ` is c times that of f, as scaling heights by a positive factor scales the greatest convex minorant; e.g. X ↦ X^q on Laurent-series coefficients multiplies orders by q. Lean subtlety: `WithTop.map` fixes ∞.
The polygon at natDegree f equals v(leadingCoeff f): it ends at the point of the leading coefficient. Lean subtlety: for f = 0, natDegree 0 = 0 and leadingCoeff 0 = 0, both sides ∞.

The polygon at natTrailingDegree f equals v(trailingCoeff f): it begins at the point of the lowest nonzero coefficient. Lean subtlety: for f = 0, natTrailingDegree 0 = 0 and trailingCoeff 0 = 0, so both sides are ∞.

If v x = ∞ only for x = 0 (over a division ring this is `AddValuation.top_iff`) and f ≠ 0, the finite domain of the polygon is [natTrailingDegree f, natDegree f]. Both hypotheses are needed: for f = 0 the domain is empty while the right side holds at n = 0; and without the condition on v an end coefficient may have valuation ∞ (e.g. 1 + 2X over ℤ/4ℤ with v = 0 on units and ∞ on {0, 2}: domain {0}, degree 1).

If the trailing and leading coefficients have finite valuation, the polygon is finite at n exactly when natTrailingDegree f ≤ n ≤ natDegree f: its finite domain is [ord₀ f, deg f], gap indices included. Lean subtlety: the two hypotheses exclude f = 0 (v 0 = ∞) and, over a non-domain, end coefficients of infinite valuation, where the domain would be smaller.
If v x = ∞ only for x = 0, every nonzero polynomial has a nonempty polygon (≠ ⊤), since its leading coefficient has finite height.
The polygon of −f equals that of f, because v(−x) = v(x) (`AddValuation.map_neg`).

If natDegree f ≤ N, the polygon of `reflect N f` (coefficients aₙ ↦ a_{N−n}) at n is that of f at N − n for n ≤ N and ∞ beyond: the polygon is mirrored in x ↦ N − x. Lean subtlety: truncated `N - n` is used only under n ≤ N; the degree hypothesis is needed because Mathlib's `reflect N` (via `revAt`) leaves coefficients above N in place.

With d = natDegree f, the polygon of `f.reverse` (= `reflect d f`, i.e. X^d·f(1/X)) at n is that of f at d − n for n ≤ d and ∞ beyond: reversal mirrors the polygon. Lean subtlety: truncated `d - n` only under n ≤ d; for f = 0 both sides are ⊤.

`(c • f).newtonPolygon v n = v c + f.newtonPolygon v n`: scalar multiplication translates the polygon vertically by v(c), as c·aₙ has valuation v(c) + v(aₙ). Lean subtlety: v c = ∞ makes both sides ⊤.
The zero polynomial has the empty polygon ⊤, as roadmap Convention 4 prescribes.

`supportingValue (f.newtonPolygon v) = supportingValue (fun n => v (f.coeff n))`, where `supportingValue a σ = ⨅ n, a n − σ·n ∈ EReal` is the intercept of the lowest line of slope σ under the points (Kedlaya's v_r with r = −σ in his reflected convention): the polygon and its points have the same supporting lines. Lean subtlety: values in `EReal`, ⊤ on both sides for the zero polynomial.

`IsConvexSeq (f.newtonPolygon v)`: the polygon of any power series is a convex height sequence (finite on an integer interval, nondecreasing increments). Lean subtlety: for inadmissible heights it holds because the all-∞ fallback is trivially convex, as the docstring says.

(1) If some real line lies below the coefficient points of a power series, its Newton polygon is their greatest convex minorant. (2) `IsAdmissible fun n => v (coeff n f)` is ∃ c m : ℝ, c + m·n ≤ v(aₙ) for all n (a nonvertical line below all points; by the roadmap, f restricted at some positive radius); `IsLowerConvexEnvelope a h` bundles `IsConvexSeq h` (finite on an integer interval, nondecreasing increments), `h ≤ a` pointwise, and h ≥ every convex g ≤ a, i.e. `IsGreatest {g | IsConvexSeq g ∧ g ≤ a} h` (`isLowerConvexEnvelope_iff_isGreatest`), the lower convex hull of the points read at the integers. (3) Lean subtlety: the hypothesis is needed, since without it the definition returns the ⊤ fallback, which lies above the finite points (compiled: over a field with v 2 = 1 the series ∑ (2⁻¹)^(n²) Xⁿ has heights −n², is not `IsAdmissible`, and its `newtonPolygon` is ⊤ although no coefficient vanishes). (4) TauCetiRoadmap NewtonPolygons README (Conventions 1, 3, 4; §§0.1, 2.1); Kedlaya, MIT 18.787 notes 'Newton polygons' §1 (the lower convex hull of {(−i, v(Pᵢ)) : Pᵢ ≠ 0}, i.e. the intersection of the closed half-planes above nonvertical lines lying below all the points; he plots at −i, so Tau Ceti's polygon is his reflected by x ↦ −x and slopes change sign).

Any `IsConvexSeq H` with H n ≤ v(aₙ) for all n satisfies H ≤ `f.newtonPolygon v` pointwise: the polygon dominates every convex minorant of the points. No admissibility is needed, because a convex minorant itself forces an affine lower bound.

Correctly stated. (1) For a power series f = Σ aₙXⁿ over a ring R and a real additive valuation v, `f.newtonPolygon v` is the Newton polygon of f, recorded as its height function n ↦ (height of the polygon over the abscissa n) ∈ ℝ ∪ {∞}; since every vertex has integer abscissa, nothing is lost. (2) `v : AddValuation R (WithTop ℝ)` is Mathlib's additive valuation with values in ℝ ∪ {∞} (v 0 = ∞, v 1 = 0, v(xy) = v x + v y, v(x + y) ≥ min(v x, v y); the ord_p orientation, larger value = smaller absolute value). The body is `lowerConvexEnvelope fun n => v (coeff n f)`: the sequence n ↦ v(aₙ) encodes the points (n, v(aₙ)), height ∞ (no point) where aₙ = 0. `lowerConvexEnvelope a` is, when `IsAdmissible a` (∃ c m : ℝ, c + m·n ≤ a n for all n: some nonvertical line lies below all the points), the pointwise supremum of all sequences g ≤ a with `IsConvexSeq g`, where `IsConvexSeq g` means the finite domain {n | g n ≠ ⊤} is order-connected (an integer interval) and the increments g(n+1) − g(n) are nondecreasing on consecutive finite indices, i.e. g is a discrete convex function with value ∞ outside an interval (the restriction to ℕ of a convex piecewise-linear function). So it is the greatest convex minorant of the points, which is the lower boundary of their convex hull read at the integers; `PowerSeries.isLowerConvexEnvelope_newtonPolygon` proves exactly this characterisation, and points of height ∞ constrain nothing. (3) Lean subtlety: `WithTop ℝ` has no −∞, so when no line lies below the points (e.g. v(aₙ) = −n², radius of convergence 0, where the classical polygon is vertical) the definition returns the all-∞ fallback ⊤ through an explicit `if IsAdmissible … else ⊤`, as its docstring says; this fallback coincides with the polygon of the zero series, so `f.newtonPolygon v = ⊤` does not imply f = 0 for power series, and every geometric statement about power series in the file assumes admissibility. The admissible branch takes `⨆` over a nonempty family in the conditionally complete order `WithTop ℝ`, so it is a genuine least upper bound (`isLUB_lowerConvexEnvelope`), not a junk `sSup ∅`. Also, v may be ∞ at a nonzero element (R need not be a domain); such coefficients are dropped like zero ones. (4) Sources: Kedlaya, MIT 18.787 notes 'Newton polygons' §1 (the lower convex hull of {(−i, v(Pᵢ)) : Pᵢ ≠ 0}, i.e. the intersection of the closed half-planes above nonvertical lines lying below all the points; he plots at −i, so Tau Ceti's polygon is his reflected by x ↦ −x and slopes change sign); TauCetiRoadmap NewtonPolygons README (Conventions 1, 3, 4; §§0.1, 2.1), which prescribe this total envelope with the all-∞ fallback. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: compiled: over a field with v 2 = 1 the series ∑ (2⁻¹)^(n²) Xⁿ has heights −n², is not `IsAdmissible`, and its `newtonPolygon` is ⊤ although no coefficient vanishes; the polynomial witnesses below apply through `Polynomial.newtonPolygon_coe`; no Newton polygon in pinned Mathlib (grep, leansearch, leanfinder, loogle) and no second construction in Tau Ceti; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

`(C c * f).newtonPolygon v n = v c + f.newtonPolygon v n`: multiplying by the constant series c translates the polygon by v(c), as `coeff_C_mul` gives coefficients c·aₙ. Lean subtlety: v c = ∞ gives ⊤ on both sides.

The polygon of Xᵏ·f at n is that of f at n − k when k ≤ n and ∞ when n < k: multiplying by Xᵏ shifts the polygon k places to the right. Lean subtlety: `n - k` is truncated ℕ subtraction but is only used under `k ≤ n`.

`f.newtonPolygon v = lowerConvexEnvelope fun n => v (coeff n f)`: the defining equation (the polygon is the lower convex envelope of the coefficient heights), proved by `rfl`; it is needed because the module system does not expose the body.

For admissible heights and ord(f) = n, the polygon at n is v(aₙ): it starts at the point of the first nonzero coefficient. Lean subtlety: admissibility is needed (the fallback is ⊤ while v(aₙ) may be finite, e.g. ∑ (2⁻¹)^(n²) Xⁿ at n = 0).
If n < ord(f) (`PowerSeries.order` in ℕ∞, with n cast), the polygon is ∞ at n: there is no polygon before the first nonzero coefficient; it holds with no admissibility hypothesis.

For admissible heights, `f.newtonPolygon v n ≤ v (coeff n f)`: the polygon lies on or below every coefficient point. Lean subtlety: admissibility is needed, since the ⊤ fallback of an inadmissible series lies above its finite points (checked on ∑ (2⁻¹)^(n²) Xⁿ).

If φ : R →+* S satisfies w(φ x) = v(x) for all x (φ preserves the valuations), the polygon of `map φ f` under w equals that of f under v, since the coefficients φ(aₙ) have the same heights (`coeff_map`).

If w(φ x) = c·v(x) for a real c > 0 (written `(v x).map (c * ·)`: multiply the finite value by c, keep ∞), the polygon of `map φ f` is c times that of f: scaling all heights by a positive factor scales the greatest convex minorant. Lean subtlety: `WithTop.map (c * ·)` fixes ∞; for an inadmissible f both sides are the ⊤ fallback.
The polygon of −f equals that of f, because v(−x) = v(x) (`AddValuation.map_neg`) gives the same heights.

(1) Substituting cX for X shears the polygon by the linear function n ↦ n·v(c): P(f(cX))(n) = P(f)(n) + n·v(c). (2) `rescale c f` is Mathlib's substitution X ↦ cX on R⟦X⟧, with coefficients cⁿaₙ (`coeff_rescale`), of valuation v(aₙ) + n·v(c); so every point moves up by n·v(c), and the greatest convex minorant moves by the same linear function (`lowerConvexEnvelope_add_nsmul`); the sign is right (larger v(c) lifts later points, slopes increase by v(c)). `n • v c` is n-fold addition in `WithTop ℝ`; `[CommRing R]` because Mathlib's `rescale` needs commutativity. (3) Lean subtlety: `hc : v c ≠ ⊤` is genuinely needed for power series, because `n • ⊤` is 0 at n = 0 and ∞ for n ≥ 1, which is not linear: compiled, for ∑ (2⁻¹)^(n²) Xⁿ over a field with v 2 = 1 and c = 0 the left side at 0 is v 1 = 0 while the right side is the fallback ⊤. (4) TauCetiRoadmap NewtonPolygons README (Conventions 1, 3, 4; §§0.1, 2.1) (§2.1: substitution X ↦ cX for c ≠ 0).

`(c • f).newtonPolygon v n = v c + f.newtonPolygon v n`: multiplying by a scalar translates the polygon vertically by v(c), since c·aₙ has valuation v(c) + v(aₙ). Lean subtlety: if v c = ∞ both sides are ⊤ (∞ + x = ∞); for an inadmissible f both sides are the ⊤ fallback, so the identity holds there consistently.
The zero series has polygon ⊤, the all-∞ (empty) polygon, as roadmap Convention 4 prescribes.

For admissible heights, `supportingValue (f.newtonPolygon v) = supportingValue (fun n => v (coeff n f))`, where `supportingValue a σ = ⨅ n, a n − σ·n` in `EReal` is the intercept of the lowest line of slope σ under the points (Kedlaya's v_r(P) = minᵢ{v(Pᵢ) + r i} with r = −σ in his reflected convention): the polygon and its points have the same supporting lines. Lean subtlety: values lie in `EReal`; admissibility is needed, since an inadmissible sequence has supporting value ⊥ at every slope while the ⊤ fallback has ⊤.

‖T‖ ≤ πₚ(T) for every bounded T and every 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞, as an inequality in [0,∞] (`‖T‖ₑ` is the operator norm as an extended real; πₚ(T) may be ∞): the one-vector family (v) has image norm ‖T v‖ and weak norm ‖v‖ (`weakLpNorm_single`), so ‖T v‖ ≤ πₚ(T)‖v‖ (`opENorm_le_bound`). Lean subtlety: the comparison is in ℝ≥0∞ with no toReal, so it is correct (and trivial) when πₚ(T) = ∞. Checks: specialising the inclusion theorem at q = ∞ gives the same bound (compiled); the audit also showed it holds over any nontrivially normed field (a generality note, not a correctness issue).

For every n and family x₁..xₙ in E, ‖(T xᵢ)ᵢ‖_p / w_p(x) ≤ πₚ(T): `WithLp.toLp p (fun i ↦ T (x i))` is the vector (T xᵢ) in `PiLp p` with its ℓᵖ norm (the sup norm at p = ∞), `‖·‖ₑ` is that norm in [0,∞], and `ENNReal.ofReal (weakLpNorm p x)` is the weak ℓᵖ norm sup_{‖f‖≤1}‖(f xᵢ)ᵢ‖_p; `T.summingENorm p` is by definition the supremum of exactly these ratios, so this is 'each term is below the supremum' (`le_iSup₂`). Lean subtlety: division is in ℝ≥0∞, so a family of zero weak norm with non-null image contributes ∞ and 0/0 = 0 — the convention the gauge is built on.

Over ℝ or ℂ, for every finite index type ι and x : ι → E, ‖(T xᵢ)ᵢ‖_p ≤ πₚ(T) · w_p(x) in [0,∞]: the defining inequality with the optimal constant, for any finite index set (reduced to Fin n by `Fintype.equivFin`, both norms being invariant under reindexing). Lean subtlety: ∞ · 0 = 0 in ℝ≥0∞, so when πₚ(T) = ∞ and w_p(x) = 0 the right side is 0; the proof covers this with `norm_toLp_eq_zero_of_weakLpNorm_eq_zero` (the image is then null), which is why this version needs RCLike while `enorm_toLp_le_summingENorm_mul_of_ne_top` assumes finiteness instead.

If πₚ(T) < ∞ then for every finite index type ι and x : ι → E, ‖(T xᵢ)ᵢ‖_p ≤ πₚ(T)·w_p(x), the defining inequality with the optimal constant; `T.summingENorm p ≠ ∞` is finiteness of πₚ(T), and `[Fintype ι]` allows any finite index set, reduced to `Fin n` via `Fintype.equivFin` because both norms are reindexing-invariant (`PiLp.norm_toLp_comp_equiv`, `weakLpNorm_comp_equiv`). Lean subtlety: ∞·0 = 0 in ℝ≥0∞, so without `hT` the inequality fails when w_p(x) = 0 but the image is non-null, which really happens over general fields (compiled: over ℚ the dual of ℝ is trivial and the version without `hT` is refuted); `hT` is load-bearing, and this is why the lemma is distinct from the RCLike `enorm_toLp_le_summingENorm_mul`.

Over ℝ or ℂ, T ↦ πₚ(T) ∈ [0,∞] is lower semicontinuous on E →L[𝕜] F for the operator-norm topology (Mathlib's `LowerSemicontinuous`: for every y < πₚ(T), y < πₚ(S) for all S near T), the input for completeness of Πₚ. Each ratio T ↦ ‖(T xᵢ)ᵢ‖ₑ / c is continuous for c ≠ 0 and identically 0 for c = 0, and a supremum of lower semicontinuous functions is lower semicontinuous (`lowerSemicontinuous_iSup`). Lean subtlety: for c = 0 the ℝ≥0∞ quotient would be ∞ on a non-null image; over ℝ, ℂ the image is null (`norm_toLp_eq_zero_of_weakLpNorm_eq_zero`), so the ratio vanishes identically (the audit also found the statement holds over any nontrivially normed field — a generality note).

Over ℝ or ℂ, if a finite family x has weak ℓᵖ norm `weakLpNorm p x = 0`, its image (T xᵢ)ᵢ has ℓᵖ norm 0: each ‖xᵢ‖ ≤ weakLpNorm p x (`norm_le_weakLpNorm`, which uses Hahn–Banach), so ‖T xᵢ‖ ≤ ‖T‖‖xᵢ‖ = 0. This is why the ratio defining πₚ never meets a/0 = ∞ over these fields. `[RCLike 𝕜]` is genuinely needed: the audit compiled that the continuous ℚ-dual of ℝ is trivial, so over ℚ every family in ℝ has weak norm 0 while id does not kill it.

For T of finite p-summing norm and every finite family, ‖(T xᵢ)ᵢ‖_p ≤ πₚ(T)·w_p(x) in ℝ: `(T.summingENorm p).toReal` is πₚ(T) as a real number and `weakLpNorm p x` the real weak ℓᵖ norm, so this is the textbook defining inequality. Lean subtlety: `ENNReal.toReal ∞ = 0` would collapse the right side to 0; `hT : T.summingENorm p ≠ ∞` excludes that, and the ℚ/ℝ probe shows the statement is false without it.

(1) `T.summingENorm p` is the absolutely p-summing norm πₚ(T) ∈ [0,∞] of a bounded operator T : E → F: the least C with (∑‖T xᵢ‖ᵖ)^{1/p} ≤ C·sup_{‖f‖≤1}(∑|f(xᵢ)|ᵖ)^{1/p} for all finite families (xᵢ), and ∞ when no such C exists — the definition requested in the Tau Ceti roadmap BanachSpaceTheory B6. (2) The body is the supremum over n : ℕ and families x : Fin n → E of ‖WithLp.toLp p (fun i ↦ T (x i))‖ₑ / ENNReal.ofReal (weakLpNorm p x). `WithLp.toLp p` places (T xᵢ)ᵢ in Mathlib's `PiLp p`, whose norm is (∑‖T xᵢ‖^p)^{1/p} for finite p and maxᵢ‖T xᵢ‖ for p = ∞ (`PiLp.norm_eq_ciSup`); `‖·‖ₑ` is that norm as an element of [0,∞]; `weakLpNorm p x` (TauCeti/Analysis/Normed/Lp/Weak.lean) is the operator norm of the dual-evaluation map f ↦ (f(xᵢ))ᵢ from the continuous dual `StrongDual 𝕜 E` into `PiLp p`, i.e. the supremum over the dual unit ball of ‖(f(xᵢ))ᵢ‖_p (`weakLpNorm_le_iff`, `weakLpNorm_eq_sSup`). By homogeneity the supremum of these ratios is the least admissible constant (`summingENorm_le_ofReal_iff`), and arbitrary finite index types add nothing (`enorm_toLp_le_summingENorm_mul`). `(p : ℝ≥0∞) [Fact (1 ≤ p)]` is the range 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞, excluding the quasi-norm exponents p < 1. (3) Lean subtlety: the ratio is division in ℝ≥0∞, where a/0 = ∞ for a ≠ 0 and 0/0 = 0. Over ℝ or ℂ a family of zero weak norm has null image (`norm_toLp_eq_zero_of_weakLpNorm_eq_zero`, Hahn–Banach), so only 0/0 = 0 occurs and no spurious ∞ arises; the value ∞ for a non-summing operator is the honest 'no constant' value, not a junk real. Over a general nontrivially normed field with trivial dual (e.g. 𝕜 = ℚ, E = ℝ) the gauge is ∞ on every nonzero operator, as the defining inequality dictates and the docstring says. At p = ∞ the PiLp sup-norm convention is used, not an exponent 1/∞ (which with `ENNReal.rpow` would give the junk x⁰ = 1). `ENNReal.ofReal` is exact on the nonnegative weak norm; the empty family contributes 0/0 = 0. (4) Checks (compiled): witness πₚ(id_ℝ) = 1 for every p; non-witness π₁(id) ≥ 2 > 1 = ‖id‖ on ℓ^∞_2 = (Fin 2 → ℝ) with the family (e₀, e₁) (weak ℓ¹ norm ≤ 1, strong ℓ¹ norm 2), so the gauge is not the operator norm; the identity of ℓ^∞(ℕ) is not 1-summing. Mathlib has no summing operators (git grep).
Subadditivity πₚ(S+T) ≤ πₚ(S) + πₚ(T) in [0,∞], infinite values included: on each family the ℓᵖ triangle inequality `enorm_add_le` for (S xᵢ + T xᵢ)ᵢ, then `ENNReal.add_div` and the two suprema.

The two-sided ideal inequality πₚ(A∘T∘B) ≤ ‖A‖·πₚ(T)·‖B‖, read as (‖A‖ₑ·πₚ(T))·‖B‖ₑ in [0,∞], by chaining `summingENorm_comp_left_le` and `summingENorm_comp_right_le`. Lean subtlety: the 0·∞ = 0 cases are exactly those of the two one-sided lemmas, each true there.

For bounded A : F → G, πₚ(A∘T) ≤ ‖A‖·πₚ(T), where `A ∘L T` is composition and `‖A‖ₑ` the operator norm in [0,∞]: on each family ‖(A T xᵢ)ᵢ‖_p ≤ ‖A‖‖(T xᵢ)ᵢ‖_p (`PiLp.norm_toLp_comp_le`). Lean subtlety: if ‖A‖ = 0 and πₚ(T) = ∞ the bound reads ≤ 0·∞ = 0, still correct because A∘T then kills every vector.

For bounded B : E → F, πₚ(T∘B) ≤ πₚ(T)·‖B‖, using w_p(Bx) ≤ ‖B‖·w_p(x) (`weakLpNorm_comp_le`) and the defining inequality for T. Lean subtlety: when πₚ(T) = ∞ and ‖B‖ = 0 the right side is ∞·0 = 0 in ℝ≥0∞; the case split at L224–231 (reachable, e.g. T = id : ℝ →L[ℚ] ℝ, B = 0) proves ‖T∘B‖ = 0 and hence πₚ(T∘B) = 0, so the statement keeps its meaning.

`T.summingENorm p` equals, by definition (`rfl`), the supremum over n and x : Fin n → E of ‖(T xᵢ)ᵢ‖_p / weakLpNorm p x in [0,∞]; it is the unfolding equation importing modules need, since the definition is not exposed.

For a normed (separated) target F, πₚ(T) = 0 iff T = 0: ⇐ is `summingENorm_zero`, ⇒ follows from ‖T‖ ≤ πₚ(T) (`enorm_le_summingENorm`) and `opENorm_eq_zero_iff`. `[NormedAddCommGroup F]` is the separation that turns ‖T‖ = 0 into T = 0; for seminormed F only ‖T‖ = 0 would follow.

An operator of operator (semi)norm 0 — possible since E and F are only seminormed — has πₚ(T) = 0: by `summingENorm_le_ofReal_iff` with C = 0, since ‖T xᵢ‖ ≤ ‖T‖‖xᵢ‖ = 0 on every family. The hypothesis `‖T‖ = 0` is needed (id : ℝ →L[ℚ] ℝ has πₚ = ∞).

For a finite C ∈ [0,∞), πₚ(T) ≤ C iff ‖(T xᵢ)ᵢ‖_p ≤ C · weakLpNorm p x for every n and x : Fin n → E, computed in [0,∞] (`‖·‖ₑ`, `ENNReal.ofReal`). Lean subtlety: `hC : C ≠ ∞` is needed because ∞ · 0 = 0 in ℝ≥0∞ — with C = ∞ the right side would force a null image on families of zero weak norm, which fails over fields with trivial dual; `lean_minimal_hypotheses` reports `hC` load-bearing.

For real C ≥ 0, πₚ(T) ≤ C iff (∑‖T xᵢ‖ᵖ)^{1/p} ≤ C · w_p(x) for every n and x : Fin n → E, with `‖WithLp.toLp p (fun i ↦ T (x i))‖` the real ℓᵖ norm of the image family (max at p = ∞) and `weakLpNorm p x` the weak ℓᵖ norm; so πₚ(T) is exactly the least constant of the defining inequality of roadmap B6. Lean subtlety: `ENNReal.ofReal C = 0` for negative C, and the iff then fails (T = 0, C = −1, a family of positive weak norm), so `hC : 0 ≤ C` is needed — load-bearing by `lean_minimal_hypotheses`.

(1) Inclusion theorem for summing operators: over ℝ or ℂ, for 1 ≤ p ≤ q ≤ ∞, π_q(T) ≤ πₚ(T) for every bounded T, so every absolutely p-summing operator is absolutely q-summing with no larger summing norm. (2) `T.summingENorm q` and `T.summingENorm p` are π_q(T), πₚ(T) ∈ [0,∞] (supremum of ℓ^q- resp. ℓᵖ-norm of the image over the weak norm, PiLp sup norm at ∞); `[Fact (1 ≤ p)]`, `[Fact (1 ≤ q)]` and `hpq : p ≤ q` (order of ℝ≥0∞, so q = ∞ is allowed) are the hypotheses 1 ≤ p ≤ q; `[RCLike 𝕜]` is real or complex scalars; T : E →L[𝕜] F is any bounded operator between seminormed spaces — no completeness, which the finite-family inequality does not need. The conclusion is an inequality in [0,∞]: trivially true when πₚ(T) = ∞, and for p-summing T it gives π_q(T) ≤ πₚ(T) < ∞, the full claim including the norm bound. The proof splits off q = ∞ (via ‖T‖ ≤ πₚ), p = q and πₚ(T) = ∞, then applies the p-summing inequality to the reweighted family cᵢxᵢ, cᵢ = ‖T xᵢ‖^{(Q−P)/P}, with Hölder for weak norms (`weakLpNorm_smul_le`, 1/P = 1/s + 1/Q). (3) Lean subtlety: the real-exponent step uses `p.toReal`, `q.toReal`, which would be 0 at ∞ (`ENNReal.toReal ∞ = 0`); q = ∞ is split off first, so p < q < ∞ gives 0 < P < Q, and πₚ(T) is converted with `ENNReal.ofReal_toReal` only after the case πₚ(T) = ∞ is disposed of, so no toReal junk supplies the inequality. (4) Checks: `hpq` is load-bearing (`lean_minimal_hypotheses`) and the direction is right — without it the statement is false, since π₁(id) ≥ 2 > 1 = π_∞(id) on ℓ^∞_2 (compiled); specialising q = ∞ recovers ‖T‖ ≤ πₚ(T) (compiled); axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; roadmap BanachSpaceTheory B6 asks for exactly 'inclusion π_q(T) ≤ π_p(T) for p ≤ q'.
πₚ(−T) = πₚ(T), the case c = −1 of `summingENorm_smul`; the simp lemma is not redundant.

Absolute homogeneity πₚ(cT) = |c|·πₚ(T) in [0,∞] for every scalar c, where `‖c‖ₑ` is |c| as an extended real: ‖c‖ₑ is pulled out of each ratio and through the supremum (`ENNReal.mul_iSup`). Lean subtlety: at c = 0 with πₚ(T) = ∞ the right side is 0·∞ = 0, matching πₚ(0) = 0.

Over ℝ or ℂ, the rank-one operator x ↦ f(x)·y (`f.smulRight y`, f in the continuous dual `StrongDual 𝕜 E`, y ∈ F) has πₚ = ‖f‖‖y‖ for every 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞, as an equality in [0,∞]: ≤ by `summingENorm_smulRight_le` (‖(f(xᵢ)y)ᵢ‖_p = ‖(f(xᵢ))ᵢ‖_p‖y‖ ≤ w_p(x)‖f‖‖y‖), ≥ by ‖f.smulRight y‖ = ‖f‖‖y‖ (`norm_smulRight_apply`) and ‖T‖ ≤ πₚ(T). Check: f = id, y = 1 gives πₚ(id_ℝ) = 1 (compiled).

The rank-one operator x ↦ f(x)·y (`f.smulRight y`, f in `StrongDual 𝕜 E`, the continuous dual) has πₚ ≤ ‖f‖‖y‖ over any nontrivially normed field: on each family ‖(f(xᵢ)y)ᵢ‖_p = ‖(f xᵢ)ᵢ‖_p‖y‖ ≤ w_p(x)‖f‖‖y‖ by `norm_eval_le_weakLpNorm`, the defining bound of the weak norm. Check: f = id, y = 1 gives πₚ(id_ℝ) ≤ 1 (compiled).

(1) At exponent ∞ the summing norm is the operator norm: π_∞(T) = ‖T‖ over ℝ or ℂ. (2) `T.summingENorm ∞` is the supremum of maxᵢ‖T xᵢ‖ / w_∞(x), since the `PiLp ∞` norm is the sup norm; `weakLpNorm_top` identifies the weak ∞-norm of a finite family with its strong norm maxᵢ‖xᵢ‖ (by Hahn–Banach, hence RCLike), so each ratio is ≤ ‖T‖ (`PiLp.norm_toLp_comp_le`), and ≥ is `enorm_le_summingENorm`; `‖T‖ₑ` is ‖T‖ as a finite extended real, and `Fact (1 ≤ ∞)` is Mathlib's instance. (3) Lean subtlety: p = ∞ goes through Mathlib's PiLp sup-norm convention, not an exponent 1/∞ (which with `ENNReal.rpow` would be the junk x⁰ = 1), and the equality is in ℝ≥0∞ with no toReal. (4) Checks: π_∞(id_ℝ) = 1 (compiled); together with the inclusion theorem this is the endpoint case of roadmap B6's 'π_q(T) ≤ π_p(T) for p ≤ q'.
πₚ(0) = 0 for the zero operator `(0 : E →L[𝕜] F)`, from `summingENorm_eq_zero_of_norm_eq_zero` with ‖0‖ = 0; the simp lemma is not redundant (`simp [-summingENorm_zero]` makes no progress).

(1) `AbsolutelySumming 𝕜 p E F` is Πₚ(E,F), the space of absolutely p-summing operators E → F with the p-summing norm. (2) It abbreviates `(summingGauge 𝕜 p E F).Carrier`: pairs of a bounded operator T : E →L[𝕜] F and a proof that πₚ(T) < ∞, a separate type rather than a subtype of `E →L[𝕜] F` so that it does not inherit the operator norm; for normed F the carrier gets the norm ‖T‖ = πₚ(T) (`norm_def`) and the linear structure of the operators, the inclusion `OperatorGauge.Carrier.toContinuousLinearMapL` has norm ≤ 1 because πₚ dominates the operator norm, and the `CompleteSpace` instance makes it a Banach space when F is complete — the 'separate normed type synonym Π_p(E,F) carrying the π_p norm, with a contractive forgetful inclusion' of roadmap B6. For 1 ≤ p ≤ q, the identity on operators as a bounded linear map Πₚ(E,F) → Π_q(E,F): `hpq : p ≤ q` and `[Fact (1 ≤ q)]` encode the exponent condition; it is `LinearMap.mkContinuous` of T ↦ `mk'` T, membership from `absolutelySummingOperators_le_of_exponent_le`, bound 1 from π_q ≤ πₚ (`summingENorm_le_summingENorm_of_exponent_le`). The underlying operator of `precomp p F B T` is `T ∘L B`, by definition; left side in simp normal form.

(1) `absolutelySummingOperators 𝕜 p E F` is the space of absolutely p-summing operators E → F as a 𝕜-submodule of the bounded operators `E →L[𝕜] F` (roadmap B6: 'bundle the operators satisfying this finite-family inequality as an underlying submodule of E →L[𝕜] F'). (2) Its carrier is {T | T.summingENorm p < ∞}, finiteness of πₚ(T), which by `mem_absolutelySummingOperators_iff` is exactly 'some C ≥ 0 has ‖(T xᵢ)ᵢ‖_p ≤ C·w_p(x) for all finite families'; closure under +, 0 and scalar multiplication comes from subadditivity, πₚ(0) = 0 and absolute homogeneity of the gauge.
