(4) Checks (compiled): rank-one operators and id_ℝ are members; the identity of ℓ^∞(ℕ) = `lp (fun _ : ℕ ↦ ℝ) ∞` is not, via the 1-summing iff and the series ∑ eₙ/(n+1), which is unconditionally summable (tails of sup norm ≤ 1/(N+1)) but not absolutely summable.

Over ℝ or ℂ, for 1 ≤ p ≤ q (in ℝ≥0∞, q = ∞ allowed), the submodule of absolutely p-summing operators is contained in that of absolutely q-summing ones (`≤` of submodules of E →L[𝕜] F): immediate from π_q(T) ≤ πₚ(T) < ∞ (`summingENorm_le_summingENorm_of_exponent_le`); `hpq` is load-bearing.

If T : E → F is absolutely p-summing and A : F → G is bounded, then A∘T is absolutely p-summing: membership in `absolutelySummingOperators 𝕜 p E F` means πₚ < ∞ (`mem_absolutelySummingOperators`, `Iff.rfl`), and πₚ(A∘T) ≤ ‖A‖·πₚ(T) < ∞ (`summingENorm_comp_left_le`, `ENNReal.mul_lt_top`).
If T : F → G is absolutely p-summing and B : E → F is bounded, then T∘B is absolutely p-summing (membership means πₚ < ∞), since πₚ(T∘B) ≤ πₚ(T)·‖B‖ < ∞ (`summingENorm_comp_right_le`).

The submodule of operators of finite gauge for `summingGauge` (`OperatorGauge.finiteSubmodule`, the T with g T < ∞) equals `absolutelySummingOperators 𝕜 p E F` = {T | πₚ(T) < ∞}: the operators of finite summing gauge are exactly the absolutely p-summing ones. Proved by extensionality and the two membership lemmas; left side in simp normal form.

The map T ↦ πₚ(T) ∈ [0,∞] (the coercion of `summingGauge 𝕜 p E F` to a function) is lower semicontinuous on `E →L[𝕜] F` with the operator-norm topology, i.e. πₚ(T) ≤ liminf πₚ(Tₙ) whenever Tₙ → T in operator norm; it is `ContinuousLinearMap.lowerSemicontinuous_summingENorm` restated for the gauge (definitionally) and is the input to completeness of Πₚ.
T ∈ `absolutelySummingOperators 𝕜 p E F` iff πₚ(T) < ∞ in ℝ≥0∞; it holds by definition (`Iff.rfl`) and is the simp unfolding of membership.

T is absolutely p-summing iff some real C ≥ 0 satisfies (∑‖T xᵢ‖ᵖ)^{1/p} ≤ C·w_p(x) for every n and x : Fin n → E — the definition of roadmap B6 — where `‖WithLp.toLp p (fun i ↦ T (x i))‖` is the ℓᵖ norm of the image (max at p = ∞) and `weakLpNorm p x` the weak ℓᵖ norm. Lean subtlety: the forward direction takes C = (πₚ(T)).toReal, which is legitimate because πₚ(T) < ∞ there (the junk toReal ∞ = 0 is excluded).

(1) A bounded operator T : E → F on a Banach space E over ℝ or ℂ is absolutely 1-summing iff it maps every unconditionally convergent series in E to an absolutely convergent series in F. (2) `T ∈ absolutelySummingOperators 𝕜 1 E F` is π₁(T) < ∞, i.e. ∑‖T xᵢ‖ ≤ C·sup_{‖f‖≤1}∑|f(xᵢ)| for all finite families (`mem_absolutelySummingOperators_iff` at p = 1). For `x : ℕ → E`, `Summable x` is unconditional convergence of the series: Mathlib's `Summable` uses the default `SummationFilter.unconditional`, convergence of the net of finite partial sums ∑_{i∈s} xᵢ over all finsets s (in a Banach space, convergence of every rearrangement), not of the ordered partial sums. `Summable fun n ↦ ‖T (x n)‖` is summability of a nonnegative real series, ∑‖T xₙ‖ < ∞, i.e. absolute convergence. `[CompleteSpace E]` says E is a Banach space and `[RCLike 𝕜]` that 𝕜 is ℝ or ℂ; F needs no completeness, a harmless strengthening since the conclusion concerns real norms. (3) Lean subtlety: the unconditional reading of `Summable` is essential — with ordered partial sums the statement would fail already for T = id_ℝ (the alternating harmonic series converges, but not absolutely); the audit compiled ¬ Summable (fun n ↦ (−1)ⁿ/(n+1)) in ℝ, confirming `Summable` is the unconditional notion. The ⇐ direction concatenates blocks yᵏ with ∑ᵢ‖T yᵏᵢ‖ = 1 and weak ℓ¹ norm ≤ 2⁻ᵏ into a family over a countably infinite sigma type and re-indexes it by ℕ through a `Denumerable` equivalence (summability is invariant, `Equiv.summable_iff`), so quantifying over ℕ-indexed sequences only loses nothing. (4) Checks: specialisation T = id_ℝ (π₁ = 1) gives 'every summable real sequence is absolutely summable' (compiled); the identity of ℓ^∞(ℕ) is shown not 1-summing from the iff and ∑ eₙ/(n+1) (compiled); the hypotheses are satisfiable (E = ℝ); axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; roadmap BanachSpaceTheory B6 asks for 'for p = 1, the characterization by taking unconditionally convergent series to absolutely convergent series'. The audit found `[CompleteSpace E]` can be dropped (a generality note; the statement as given is correct).

Every rank-one operator x ↦ f(x)·y with f in the continuous dual E* and y ∈ F is absolutely p-summing, i.e. lies in the submodule of operators of finite πₚ, because πₚ ≤ ‖f‖‖y‖ < ∞ (`summingENorm_smulRight_le`).

Over ℝ or ℂ, an absolutely 1-summing T sends every unconditionally summable family (xᵢ)_{i∈ι}, ι arbitrary, to an absolutely summable one, ∑ᵢ‖T xᵢ‖ < ∞. `Summable x` is Mathlib's unconditional summability (default `SummationFilter.unconditional`: the net of finite partial sums converges) and `Summable fun i ↦ ‖T (x i)‖` for nonnegative reals is ∑‖T xᵢ‖ < ∞; the proof bounds every finite partial sum by π₁(T)·C, where C bounds the weak ℓ¹ norms of all finite subfamilies (`Summable.exists_forall_weakLpNorm_one_le`, Banach–Steinhaus on the complete dual). Lean subtlety: the constant is (π₁(T)).toReal, valid because hT gives π₁(T) < ∞; neither E nor F needs completeness.

(1) `summingGauge 𝕜 p E F` is the absolutely p-summing norm πₚ packaged as an operator gauge on `E →L[𝕜] F`. (2) Its function is T ↦ `ContinuousLinearMap.summingENorm p T`, the supremum over finite families of ‖(T xᵢ)ᵢ‖_p / w_p(x), which is πₚ(T) ∈ [0,∞] with value ∞ exactly on non-summing operators; `OperatorGauge` (OperatorIdeal/Carrier.lean) is the structure of [0,∞]-valued functions on bounded operators that are subadditive, absolutely homogeneous and dominate the operator norm, and its three fields are `summingENorm_add_le` (triangle inequality), `summingENorm_smul` (πₚ(cT) = |c|πₚ(T)) and `enorm_le_summingENorm` (‖T‖ ≤ πₚ(T)). (3) Lean subtlety: the gauge lives in ℝ≥0∞, so a non-summing operator gets ∞ rather than a junk real value; the ℝ≥0∞ division conventions inside `summingENorm` are discussed with that definition. (4) Checks (compiled): `summingGauge 𝕜 ∞ E F T = ‖T‖ₑ`, the rank-one operator `f.smulRight y` has gauge ‖f‖‖y‖, and ‖T‖ₑ ≤ summingGauge T; Mathlib has no summing operators, and the other Tau Ceti gauges (nuclear, integral, Hilbert-space families) are different gauges.
The gauge `summingGauge 𝕜 p E F` evaluated at a bounded operator T is the extended p-summing norm `T.summingENorm p` = πₚ(T) ∈ [0,∞]; it holds by definition and its left side is in simp normal form.

Correctly defined: a finite partition P of a finite set s of positions in a linear order is noncrossing iff there are no a < b < c < d with a, c in one part and b, d in a different part. Lean ↔ maths: `Finpartition s` is Mathlib's partition of s into nonempty (`⊥ ∉ parts`), pairwise disjoint (`SupIndep`) finsets covering s (`parts.sup id = s`), i.e. a partition of S = s whose blocks are `P.parts`; the body `∀ B ∈ P.parts, ∀ C ∈ P.parts, ∀ a ∈ B, ∀ b ∈ C, ∀ c ∈ B, ∀ d ∈ C, a < b → b < c → c < d → B = C` says that whenever p1 = a and p2 = c share the block B, q1 = b and q2 = d share the block C, and p1 < q1 < p2 < q2, the two blocks are the same, i.e. p1 ∼ q1 — exactly the negation of Nica–Speicher's 'crossing' (there exist p1 < q1 < p2 < q2 with p1 ∼ p2, p2 ≁ q1, q1 ∼ q2). For s = univ : Finset (Fin n) this is NC(n). Lean subtlety: positions in `Fin n` are 0, …, n−1 rather than 1, …, n (an order isomorphism, harmless); blocks are nonempty by `Finpartition`'s `⊥ ∉ parts`, matching non-void blocks; for s = ∅ the only partition (no parts) is vacuously noncrossing, the usual NC(0) convention; the body is not exposed to importing modules, which use `isNoncrossing_iff`. Source: Nica–Speicher, Lectures on the Combinatorics of Free Probability, Definitions 9.1 (stated for an arbitrary finite totally ordered set S, as here); R. Speicher, Free Probability Theory lecture notes, arXiv:1908.08125, Definition 2.2(3). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: non-witness — the crossing partition {0,2}|{1,3} of Fin 4 is proved not noncrossing; witnesses — singletons, one part, pair partitions and the nested partition {1,2}|{0,3} are noncrossing; |NC(3)| = 5 and |NC(4)| = 14 via `card_eq_catalan`; standard axioms only.

If P is noncrossing and every part B of P carries a noncrossing partition `Q B hB` of B, then `P.bind Q` (Mathlib: the partition of s whose parts are all the parts of all the `Q B`) is noncrossing — refining the blocks of a noncrossing partition by noncrossing partitions stays noncrossing.

A noncrossing partition of a nonempty s has a part B containing every z ∈ s that lies strictly between two elements of B, i.e. a block that is an interval of s; for s = {1, …, n} this is the 'at least one block V ∈ π is an interval' of Nica–Speicher Remarks 9.2(2). `hs : s.Nonempty` is needed (∅ has no parts).

A noncrossing partition of a nonempty s has a part that is a singleton (`#B = 1`) or contains x < y with no position of s strictly between them (`∀ z ∈ s, z ≤ x ∨ y ≤ z`); the two smallest elements of an interval block (`exists_interval_mem_parts`) are such x, y.

For noncrossing P and positions i ≤ j of s with no position of s strictly between them (`hadj : ∀ z ∈ s, z ≤ i ∨ j ≤ z`), there is a noncrossing Q ≥ P whose part through i is `P.part i ∪ P.part j`: merging the blocks through two adjacent positions keeps a partition noncrossing. As the docstring's second clause says, the statement fixes only Q's part through i (the witness built is the merge itself). Lean subtlety: `hij : i ≤ j` matters — for j < i, `hadj` would hold vacuously.

If P is a noncrossing partition of t and i ∉ t (`Disjoint t {i}`) with t ∪ {i} = s, then `P.extend …` (Mathlib: P with the extra part {i}) is a noncrossing partition of s, since a one-element block cannot take part in a crossing; `({i} : Finset α) ≠ ⊥` is the always-true side condition `Finpartition.extend` asks of a new part.

If P and Q are noncrossing, so is `P ⊓ Q`, Mathlib's meet of finite partitions, whose parts are the nonempty intersections B ∩ C of a part of P and a part of Q (`Finpartition.parts_inf`) — formula (9.16) in the proof of Nica–Speicher Proposition 9.17; this is the closure of NC(s) under meets that the lattice uses.

For noncrossing P ≤ Q, let m and M be the first and last positions of the P-part through m (`hmin`, `hM`, `hmax`) and t the first position after M of the Q-part through m (`ht`, `hMt`, `htmin`); then every b in the P-part of any a with m ≤ a < t satisfies m ≤ b < t, i.e. the positions of s in [m, t) form a union of parts of P, as the docstring says. Lean subtlety: `P.part a = ∅` for a ∉ s, so `hb : b ∈ P.part a` already forces a ∈ s and nothing is claimed vacuously; the hypothesis `hm : m ∈ s` is redundant (it follows from `hM`; MINOR finding), which removes no case.

In a noncrossing partition, a < b < c < d with a ∼ c (`P.part a = P.part c`) and b ∼ d (`P.part b = P.part d`) give a ∼ b (`P.part a = P.part b`), so all four lie in one block. Lean subtlety: `P.part x = ∅` off s, so `ha : a ∈ s` and `hb : b ∈ s` are genuinely needed (without them a, c ∉ s would satisfy `P.part a = P.part c = ∅`); c, d ∈ s then follow from the two equalities.

For t ⊆ s, `P.restrict hts` (Mathlib: the nonempty B ∩ t for B ∈ P.parts) is a noncrossing partition of t when P is noncrossing: π|W ∈ NC(W) in Nica–Speicher Notations 9.3(2). Lean subtlety: t = ∅ is allowed (the restriction is then the empty partition), where Nica–Speicher take W nonempty; the statement is still true there.

`(⊥ : Finpartition s).IsNoncrossing`: Mathlib's ⊥ is the partition into singletons (`parts_bot : parts = s.map singleton`), the 0_n of Nica–Speicher Definitions 9.14(2), and it is noncrossing because a crossing needs two distinct elements in one block.

`P.IsNoncrossing ↔ ∀ B ∈ P.parts, ∀ C ∈ P.parts, ∀ a ∈ B, ∀ b ∈ C, ∀ c ∈ B, ∀ d ∈ C, a < b → b < c → c < d → B = C` restates the definition of `IsNoncrossing` word for word (proof `Iff.rfl`); it is how importing modules see the definition, whose body the module system does not expose.

Noncrossing in terms of `P.part x`, the part of P containing x: P is noncrossing iff for all a, b ∈ s, c ∈ P.part a, d ∈ P.part b with a < b < c < d we have `P.part a = P.part b` — i.e. a ∼ c, b ∼ d and a < b < c < d force a ∼ b, Nica–Speicher's Definitions 9.1(3) phrased through the block of each point; both directions are proved. Lean subtlety: `P.part x` is ∅ for x ∉ s, which is why a and b are required to lie in s; c and d then lie in s automatically.

`pairPartition s i j hij` (Tau Ceti: the partition of s with the part {i, j} and singletons elsewhere, `mem_parts_pairPartition`) is noncrossing, since a crossing needs two blocks with at least two elements each. Lean subtlety: i = j is allowed, where it is the partition into singletons.

If C ⊆ s is nonempty and contains every position of s between two of its elements (`hconv`), then `splitPartition s C` (Tau Ceti: the two parts C and s \ C, `parts_splitPartition`) is noncrossing; red-team probe: {1,2}|{0,3} on Fin 4 is noncrossing by this lemma (hconv by `decide`), while for the non-convex C = {0,2} the split {0,2}|{1,3} is proved crossing, so `hconv` is needed.

`(⊤ : Finpartition s).IsNoncrossing`: Mathlib's ⊤ is the partition with the single part s (`parts_top`; no parts when s = ∅), the 1_n of Nica–Speicher Definitions 9.14(2); with at most one part, any two parts coincide.

Correctly defined: `NoncrossingPartition s` is the type `{P : Finpartition s // P.IsNoncrossing}` of noncrossing partitions of s, NC(S) of Nica–Speicher Definitions 9.1(4) with S = s, and NC(n) for s = univ : Finset (Fin n). Lean ↔ maths: being an abbrev of a subtype, its order is `Subtype.partialOrder`, so P ≤ Q iff P.1 ≤ Q.1 in Mathlib's `Finpartition` order, which is 'every part of P is contained in some part of Q' (checked as `Iff.rfl`) — Nica–Speicher's reversed refinement order of Definitions 9.14 (finer is smaller), with ⊥ the singletons (checked `rfl` against `s.map singleton`) and ⊤ the one-part partition. Lean subtlety: Fin n is 0-indexed (order-isomorphic to {1, …, n}); NC(0), for s = ∅ or an empty type such as Fin 0, has exactly one element, the partition with no parts (the file's `Unique` instances, checked for Fin 0); positions may lie in any linear order, as in Nica–Speicher's 'finite totally ordered set S'. Source: Nica–Speicher, Lectures on the Combinatorics of Free Probability, Definitions 9.1 and 9.14. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: order direction `Iff.rfl`; |NC(3)| = 5 and |NC(4)| = 14 via `card_eq_catalan`; no other construction of noncrossing partitions in Mathlib or Tau Ceti (Tau Ceti's `IsNoncrossingMatching` is the permutation encoding of perfect matchings).
⊥ = ⊤ in NC(s) iff #s ≤ 1: the partitions 0 and 1 coincide exactly when s has at most one element (both are the empty partition for s = ∅, both are {s} for a singleton).
If s has more than one element (`1 < #s`), then ⊥ ≠ ⊤ in NC(s): the singleton partition has #s parts and the one-part partition has 1.
`↑(⊥ : NoncrossingPartition s) = ⊥` (`rfl`): the least noncrossing partition is Mathlib's partition into singletons, 0_n.

`↑(P ⊓ Q) = ↑P ⊓ ↑Q` (`rfl`): the meet in NC(s) is the meet of the underlying partitions, as Nica–Speicher Remark 9.19 notes ('π ∧ σ is the same, no matter whether the meet is considered in NC(n) or in P(n)').
`↑(⊤ : NoncrossingPartition s) = ⊤` (`rfl`): the greatest noncrossing partition is Mathlib's one-part partition, 1_n (no parts when s = ∅).
If s = ∅, every noncrossing partition of s equals ⊥: the empty set has only the partition with no parts, so NC(∅) is one point (consistent with Mathlib's `Unique (Finpartition ⊥)`).

Every noncrossing partition of {i, j} is ⊥ or ⊤: a set with at most two elements has only the singleton partition and the one-block partition. Lean subtlety: `{i, j}` with i = j is the one-element set {i}, where ⊥ = ⊤; the statement covers it.

Correctly stated: the noncrossing partitions of s, ordered by refinement, form a lattice whose meet is the common refinement and whose join is the least noncrossing common coarsening (Nica–Speicher Proposition 9.17). Lean ↔ maths: this is a `Lattice (NoncrossingPartition s)` whose order is the subtype's (`toPartialOrder = Subtype.partialOrder _`, checked by `with_reducible_and_instances rfl`), so P ≤ Q iff each part of P lies in a part of Q (Nica–Speicher Definitions 9.14); `inf P Q := ⟨P.1 ⊓ Q.1, _⟩` is Mathlib's meet of finite partitions, with parts the nonempty B ∩ C (`Finpartition.parts_inf`), formula (9.16) of the proof of Proposition 9.17; `sup P Q` is `Finset.inf id` over all R : Finpartition s with R noncrossing, P ≤ R and Q ≤ R, i.e. ⋀{τ ∈ NC(s) | π ≤ τ, σ ≤ τ}, the join of Nica–Speicher Remarks 9.16(2) and of Speicher's Proposition 3.18, and the fields `le_sup_left`, `le_sup_right`, `sup_le` prove it is the least noncrossing upper bound (`IsLUB {P, Q} (P ⊔ Q)`, checked). It is not the join among all partitions: red-team probe in NC(4) on Fin 4 with π = {0,2}|{1}|{3} and σ = {0}|{1,3}|{2} proves π ⊔ σ = ⊤ (one block), while the crossing partition {0,2}|{1,3} ≠ ⊤ is a common upper bound among all partitions — Nica–Speicher Remark 9.19's example {1,3}|{2}|{4} ∨ {1}|{2,4}|{3} = 1_4, whose join in P(4) is {1,3}|{2,4}. The bounds come from a separate `BoundedOrder` instance with ⊥ the singletons and ⊤ the one-part partition (`coe_bot`, `coe_top`). Lean subtlety: the join is an iterated meet `Finset.inf` over a finite filtered set; `Finset.inf` of an empty set would be ⊤, but the set always contains ⊤ (noncrossing and above everything), so no junk value enters, and the result is noncrossing by `Finset.inf_induction` from `isNoncrossing_top` and `IsNoncrossing.inf`; the `open Classical in` and `noncomputable` affect only computability, not the value (both unneeded, NIT finding); for s = ∅ the lattice has a single element (⊥ = ⊤), the NC(0) convention; Mathlib's `Finpartition s` has no join of its own (no `Max` instance, checked), so no competing ⊔ exists. Source: Nica–Speicher, Lectures on the Combinatorics of Free Probability, Definitions 9.14–9.15, Remarks 9.16(2), Proposition 9.17 and Remark 9.19; R. Speicher, Free Probability Theory lecture notes, arXiv:1908.08125, Proposition 3.18 and Remark 3.19. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the NC(4) join example above compiled; order diamond `rfl`; |NC(3)| = 5, |NC(4)| = 14; NC(0) has one element; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.
The parts of the image of π under `singletonPartEquiv` are the parts of π with {i} removed (`π.1.1.parts.erase {i}`).
The parts of the preimage of τ under `singletonPartEquiv` are the parts of τ with {i} added (`insert {i} τ.1.parts`).

A bijection between the noncrossing partitions of s having {i} as a part and NC(s \ {i}) (`s.erase i`): the forward map restricts to s.erase i (deleting the part {i}), the inverse adds the part {i} back (`Finpartition.extend`), and both composites are proved to be identities; `hi : i ∈ s` is what makes s.erase i ∪ {i} = s.

For positions i ≤ j of s with no position of s strictly between them (`hadj`), a noncrossing x satisfies `x ⊔ ⟨pairPartition s i j hij, _⟩ = ⊤` — the NC join (the `instLattice` join) of x with the partition whose only non-singleton block is {i, j} is the one-block partition — iff the blocks of x through i and j cover s (`x.1.part i ∪ x.1.part j = s`). Lean subtlety: `hle : i ≤ j` is essential — for j < i `hadj` holds vacuously, and the equivalence then fails for non-adjacent positions (in NC(4), {0,2}|{1}|{3} joined with the pair block {1,3} is the one-block partition, red-team probe, while the blocks through 1 and 3 are {1} and {3}).
As a finset, all of NC({i, j}) is {⊥, ⊤} (a one-element finset when i = j, where ⊥ = ⊤).

Correctly stated: if α < ω₁ is a level at which back-and-forth equivalence of tuples of the countable structure M has stabilised, the Scott sentence of M at level α holds in a countable structure N exactly when N ≅ M (relational countable language). Lean ↔ maths: `scottSentenceAt M α` is by definition (`scottSentenceAt_def`) `scottFormula Fin.elim0 α ⊓ iInfAlong (…) (fun p => ((scottFormula p.2 α).imp (scottFormula p.2 (α + 1))).alls)`, i.e. Φ_{∅,α} ∧ ⋀_{ā ∈ M^{<ω}} ∀v(Φ_{ā,α}(v) → Φ_{ā,α+1}(v)), a countable conjunction coded into ℕ whose unused codes carry ⊤ (harmless by `realize_iInfAlong`); `scottFormula a α` is characterised by `realize_scottFormula_iff_bfEquiv` as α-back-and-forth equivalence with a; `hα : α < ω₁` keeps the level countable; `hs : SelfStabilizesCompletely M α` says that for every n and all a, b ∈ M^n, a ∼_α b ↔ a ∼_{α+1} b, Marker's Γ_α = Γ_{α+1}, so α may be any stabilising level, not only the least; `[Countable N]` and `Nonempty (M ≃[L] N)` are a countable test structure and an isomorphism. Lean subtlety: both hypotheses are load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses): hα because the recursion assigns the junk value ⊤ at uncountable limit stages, hs because M satisfies its sentence at level α only when α is stabilising (`realize_scottSentenceAt_self`); the ordinal universe o is independent of the universes of M and N. Source: Marker, Lectures on Infinitary Model Theory (UIC lecture notes, Fall 2013), §2.2, Lemma 2.15 (claim 1) and Theorem 2.19. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms standard; hα and hs are jointly satisfiable for every countable M (`selfStabilizationOrdinal_lt_omega_one`, `selfStabilizesCompletely_selfStabilizationOrdinal`, compiled).

Correctly stated: in a countable relational language, the canonical Scott sentence of a countable structure M holds in a countable structure N exactly when N ≅ M. Lean ↔ maths: `scottSentence M` is by definition (`scottSentence_def`) `scottSentenceAt M (selfStabilizationOrdinal M)`, the conjunction of the Scott formula of the empty tuple at level α with the universally closed implications φ_{ā,α} → φ_{ā,α+1} over all finite tuples ā of M (a countable conjunction coded into ℕ), at the least α where back-and-forth equivalence of tuples of M stabilises, i.e. Marker's Scott sentence Φ^M at the Scott rank; `SentenceInf.Realize … N` is Tarskian satisfaction of an ℕ-branching (L_{ω₁ω}) sentence; `[L.IsRelational]` and `[Countable (Σ k, L.Relations k)]` give a countable relational vocabulary; `[Countable M]`, `[Countable N]` countable structures; `Nonempty (M ≃[L] N)` a Mathlib isomorphism (bijection preserving relations both ways). The proof is the textbook pair: a model of the sentence is potentially isomorphic to M (`potentialIso_of_realize_scottSentence`, any cardinality), potential isomorphism of countable structures is isomorphism (`countable_potentialIso_iff_iso`, back and forth), and isomorphic copies satisfy it. Lean subtlety: `[L.IsRelational]` is needed for this particular sentence, whose atomic diagram tests only equalities and relations among tuple positions and would ignore function symbols; `[Countable N]` cannot be dropped (for instance ℝ satisfies the Scott sentence of (ℚ, <), being ∞ω-equivalent to it); M and N may live in different universes; the recursion's junk value ⊤ at uncountable limits is never reached since the level is < ω₁. Source: Marker, Lectures on Infinitary Model Theory (UIC lecture notes, Fall 2013), §2.2, Theorem 2.19 and the definition of Φ^M before it. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms standard; specialised to ℕ in the empty language (holds in ℤ, fails in Fin 5).

Correctly stated: for a countable relational language L, every countable L-structure M has an L_{ω₁ω} sentence σ true in M such that a countable L-structure N satisfies σ exactly when N ≅ M (Scott's isomorphism theorem, relational case). Lean ↔ maths: `L.Sentenceω` unfolds (by `rfl`, checked) to `L.BoundedFormulaInf ℕ Empty 0`, the inductive syntax with falsum, equality and relation atoms over Mathlib terms, implication, ∀ over the last bound slot, and `iSup`/`iInf` over families indexed by ℕ only, so conjunctions and disjunctions are countable and every subformula has finitely many variables (free variables in `Empty`, bound slots `Fin n`): this is L_{ω₁ω}, not L_{∞ω}; `SentenceInf.Realize σ N` is Tarskian satisfaction (`BoundedFormulaInf.Realize`: ∀ ranges over the carrier, `iInf`/`iSup` are ∀ i/∃ i over ℕ, checked by `Iff.rfl`); `[L.IsRelational]` says L has no function symbols and `[Countable (Σ k, L.Relations k)]` that it has countably many relation symbols of all arities (nullary included), so L is a countable relational vocabulary; `[Countable M]` and `[Countable N]` are countability of the two structures (finite and empty ones included); `Nonempty (M ≃[L] N)` is the existence of a Mathlib `FirstOrder.Language.Equiv`, a bijection preserving every relation in both directions, i.e. an isomorphism. The sentence is built syntactically, not defined as 'isomorphic to M': the proof's witness is `scottSentence M`, made by ordinal recursion (`scottFormula`: the atomic diagram at 0, the forth-and-back clauses ⋀_x ∃ φ_{ax} and ∀ ⋁_x φ_{ax} at successors, ⋀_{β<α} at countable limits) at the least level where back-and-forth equivalence of tuples of M stabilises (proved < ω₁), which is Marker's Φ^M = Φ_{∅,α} ∧ ⋀_ā ∀v(Φ_{ā,α}(v) → Φ_{ā,α+1}(v)) at the Scott rank α (Tau Ceti also keeps the previous level at successors, which only matters for empty structures with nullary relations). Lean subtlety: (i) universes: `N : Type w'` with w' a universe parameter of the theorem, so formally it says 'for each universe w' there is a σ'; the docstring's 'in any universe' is still right because the witness `scottSentence M` does not depend on w' (`realize_scottSentence_iff` states it for that one sentence), and L, M and N may live in unrelated universes; (ii) the recursion puts the junk value ⊤ at uncountable limit stages, never reached because the level used is < ω₁ (`selfStabilizationOrdinal_lt_omega_one`); (iii) `selfStabilizationOrdinal` is an `sInf`, but of a nonempty set (`exists_selfStabilizesCompletely`), so no `sInf ∅ = 0` junk; (iv) `[L.IsRelational]` is a real restriction compared with Scott's theorem for arbitrary countable vocabularies, recorded as a MINOR generality finding (the general form follows through Tau Ceti's graph translation), not a misstatement, since its docstring says 'relational'. Source: Marker, Lectures on Infinitary Model Theory (UIC lecture notes, Fall 2013), §2.2, Theorem 2.19 and the remark before it ('If τ is a countable vocabulary and M is countable τ-structure, then Φ^M ∈ L_{ω₁,ω}'); Harrison-Trainor, arXiv:2011.03923, Definition 1.2 and Theorem 2.2. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only; specialised to the empty language, the σ for Fin 2 holds in Bool and fails in Fin 3, and the Scott sentence of ℕ holds in ℤ and fails in Fin 5; M in Type 1 against N in Type 0 compiles; the hypotheses are jointly satisfiable; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate (Karp's countable theorem and the finite-structure version are different statements).

(1) `OrbitCategory D n` is Keller's orbit category D/[n] of a category D with an integral shift: the objects of D, and (for D preadditive with additive shift functors) Hom(X, Y) = ⨁_{j∈ℤ} Hom_D(X, Y[nj]) with the natural composition. (2) The structure is only the object wrapper (field `obj : D`), so its objects are exactly those of D; the morphisms are given by the file's `Category` instance, whose hom type is `OrbitCategory.Hom X Y = DirectSum ℤ (fun j ↦ ShiftedHom X.obj Y.obj (n * j))`, where Mathlib's `ShiftedHom X Y m` is by definition X ⟶ Y⟦m⟧ and `DirectSum` is the finitely supported sum (`Π₀`), so this is ⊕_j Hom(X, F^j Y) for F = [n] — the direct sum, not the product (compiled: `(X ⟶ Y) = Π₀ j, ShiftedHom X.obj Y.obj (n * j)` by rfl, and every morphism is the finite sum of its homogeneous components); composition sends f : X → Y[ni] and g : Y → Z[nj] to Mathlib's `ShiftedHom.comp f g` = f ≫ g⟦n*i⟧' ≫ (Z[nj][ni] ≅ Z[n(i+j)]) in degree i + j, i.e. F^i(g) ∘ f, extended bilinearly; the identity is 𝟙 in degree 0; addition is componentwise; and associativity and the unit laws are proved (induction on homogeneous pieces plus `ShiftedHom.comp_assoc`), not assumed. (3) Lean subtlety: the degree-0 identity is `ShiftedHom.mk₀ (n * 0) _ (𝟙 X)` because `n * 0` is only propositionally 0 (mk₀ composes with the canonical iso X ≅ X⟦n*0⟧), which is harmless; n = 0 and negative n are allowed and give the intended categories — D/[0] is Keller's D/id with Hom = ⨁_ℤ Hom(X, Y⟦0⟧), which keeps the degrees apart (compiled: a nonzero degree-1 piece is not a degree-0 piece), not D itself, and D/[−n] is D/[n] reindexed by j ↦ −j; the type depends on D's `Category` instance but not on the shift, which is found by instance resolution. (4) Keller, On triangulated orbit categories, Doc. Math. 10 (2005), §1 (arXiv math/0503240v4, read) defines T/F with the same objects as T and morphisms ⊕_{n∈ℤ} Hom_T(X, F^n Y) with composition 'in the natural way'; here F = [n], for preadditive D (slightly more general than Keller's additive T). red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: instances synthesize for cochain complexes of abelian groups (n = 2, 0, −3) and for the homotopy category; identity/composition and degree addition compiled; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.

`OrbitCategory.Hom X Y` is the orbit hom group ⨁_{j∈ℤ} Hom_D(X, Y⟦n*j⟧): its body is `DirectSum ℤ (fun j ↦ ShiftedHom X.obj Y.obj (n * j))`, Mathlib's finitely supported direct sum of the groups `ShiftedHom X Y m` = (X ⟶ Y⟦m⟧), so a morphism is a finite family of homogeneous pieces (direct sum, not product), and it is the hom type of the orbit category (`(X ⟶ Y) = Hom X Y` by rfl). Lean subtlety: it needs only `[Preadditive D]` and `[HasShift D ℤ]` (the group structure of the summands); additivity of the shift functors enters only through composition. Keller, On triangulated orbit categories, Doc. Math. 10 (2005), §1 (arXiv math/0503240v4, read): Hom_{T/F}(X, Y) = ⊕_n Hom_T(X, F^n Y).

`homOf i : ShiftedHom X Y (n * i) →+ (⟨X⟩ ⟶ ⟨Y⟩)` is the inclusion of the degree-i summand Hom_D(X, Y⟦n*i⟧) into the orbit hom group, as an additive map: `homOf_def` shows it is `DirectSum.of _ i`, the canonical summand inclusion, which is injective (compiled from `DirectSum.of_injective`).

The degree-adding composition law on homogeneous pieces: `homOf i f ≫ homOf j g = homOf (i + j) (f.comp g _)`, where Mathlib's `ShiftedHom.comp f g` = f ≫ g⟦n*i⟧' ≫ (Z⟦n*j⟧⟦n*i⟧ ≅ Z⟦n*(i+j)⟧) (the inverse of `shiftFunctorAdd'`) is F^i(g) ∘ f — a compiled unfolding confirms exactly this formula, with the shift applied to the second map by the degree of the first, the 'natural' composition of Keller (2005) §1. Lean subtlety: it is `@[simp low]` so that the degree-0 forms fire first and avoid indices like 0 + j; this affects only simp, not the statement.

For f : X → Y⟦n*i⟧, g : Y → Z⟦n*j⟧ and any k with `h : i + j = k`, the orbit composite `homOf i f ≫ homOf j g` is the degree-k piece `homOf k (f.comp g _)`, where Mathlib's `ShiftedHom.comp f g` = f ≫ g⟦n*i⟧' ≫ (Z⟦n*j⟧⟦n*i⟧ ≅ Z⟦n*k⟧) is F^i(g) ∘ f for F = [n]: homogeneous pieces compose by the natural composition, adding degrees. Lean subtlety: the free index k with `h : i + j = k` avoids transporting along an index that is only propositionally the one needed (e.g. 0 + j versus j).

Postcomposing a degree-i piece f : X → Y⟦n*i⟧ with the degree-0 piece of g : Y → Z gives the degree-i piece f ≫ g⟦n*i⟧', i.e. F^i(g) ∘ f — the natural composition, with g shifted into f's degree (`ShiftedHom.comp_mk₀`).
`homOf i = DirectSum.of (fun j ↦ ShiftedHom X Y (n * j)) i`: the homogeneous inclusion is the canonical inclusion of the i-th summand of the direct sum (rfl; it exports the otherwise unexposed body).

A homogeneous piece f : X → Y⟦n*i⟧ of degree i equals π(f) followed by the shift isomorphism π(Y⟦n*i⟧) ≅ π(Y): `homOf i f = projection.map f ≫ (shiftIso Y (n * i) i rfl).hom`, so orbit morphisms are generated by projected morphisms and the shift isomorphisms.

Precomposing a degree-j piece g : Y → Z⟦n*j⟧ with the degree-0 piece of f : X → Y gives the degree-j piece f ≫ g: projected morphisms of D act on orbit morphisms by ordinary composition (`ShiftedHom.mk₀_comp`).

A property of morphisms X ⟶ Y of D/[n] that holds for 0 and for every homogeneous piece `homOf i g`, and is closed under addition, holds for every morphism — direct-sum induction (`DirectSum.induction_on`: every element of ⨁ is a finite sum of homogeneous pieces) stated for orbit hom groups.

The identity of ⟨X⟩ in D/[n] is the degree-0 piece `homOf 0 (ShiftedHom.mk₀ (n * 0) _ (𝟙 X))`, i.e. 𝟙_X viewed in Hom(X, X⟦n*0⟧) ≅ Hom(X, X). Lean subtlety: `ShiftedHom.mk₀` composes with the canonical iso X ≅ X⟦n*0⟧ because n * 0 is only propositionally 0.

(1) Uniqueness up to isomorphism in Keller's universal property: an additive F : D/[n] → E with e : π ⋙ F ≅ G compatible with the periodicity isomorphisms is isomorphic to `lift G φ`, with components given by e. (2) `[F.Additive]` is additivity of F, `e : projection ⋙ F ≅ G` says F restricts to G along π, and `he` says F(periodicity_X) ≫ e_X = e_{X⟦n⟧} ≫ φ_X, i.e. e is an isomorphism of periodic functors (π ⋙ F, F(periodicity)) ≅ (G, φ); the conclusion is `NatIso.ofComponents` with components `e.app X.obj` (π is the identity on objects), naturality being checked on homogeneous pieces by writing `homOf i f = π(f) ≫ shiftIso_i` and showing via `periodicityZPow_unique` that the transported shift isomorphisms are exactly the powers φ^i. (3) Lean subtlety: `isoLift_hom_app` is stated at objects `⟨X⟩` because e is indexed by objects of D; at a general orbit object the component is `e.app X.obj` by rfl. (4) Keller, On triangulated orbit categories, Doc. Math. 10 (2005), §1 (arXiv math/0503240v4, read) calls π 2-universal; this is the 1-categorical uniqueness part (the 2-cell part is not formalised, see the module-docstring finding). red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: `he` is necessary (compiled: any iso F ≅ lift G φ with components e forces `he`, and dropping it would make all periodicity isos of G equal); the hypotheses are satisfiable (F = lift G φ, e = projectionCompLift, compiled); a hand counterexample (a multiplicative, non-additive F on End = ℤ[t, t⁻¹], not compiled) shows `F.Additive` is needed; the specialisation F = 𝟭 gives 𝟭 ≅ lift π periodicity (compiled); axioms standard.
The component of `isoLift F e he` at the orbit object ⟨X⟩ is `e.hom.app X`: the isomorphism is e on components (rfl).
The component of the inverse of `isoLift F e he` at ⟨X⟩ is `e.inv.app X` (rfl).

(1) `lift G φ` is Keller's descent of an additive functor G : D → E (E preadditive) equipped with φ : [n] ⋙ G ≅ G to a functor D/[n] → E. (2) On objects it is X ↦ `G.obj X.obj` (the orbit objects are those of D); on morphisms it is `liftMap G φ X Y`, which sends a degree-i piece f : X → Y⟦n*i⟧ of Hom(X, Y) = ⨁_j Hom(X, Y⟦n*j⟧) to G(f) followed by `Iso.periodicityZPow φ i` at Y, the i-th power φ^i : G∘[n*i] ≅ G of φ (built from φ⁻¹ for i < 0), extended additively; `Functor.Additive G` is the textbook additivity hypothesis, functoriality is proved from the cocycle law `periodicityZPow_add_hom_app` and naturality of φ^i, and identities from `periodicityZPow_zero`. (3) Lean subtlety: identities of D/[n] are degree-0 pieces `ShiftedHom.mk₀ (n * 0) _ (𝟙 X)` because n * 0 is only propositionally 0, and φ^0 is correspondingly G of `shiftFunctorZero' (n * 0)`, so the two cancel; `(lift G φ).obj X` agrees with `G.obj X.obj` only by unfolding `lift`, which makes simp leave trivial goals (an API inconvenience, not a change of meaning); n = 0 (Keller's T/F for F ≅ id) and negative n are handled uniformly. (4) Keller, On triangulated orbit categories, Doc. Math. 10 (2005), §1 (arXiv math/0503240v4, read) states that π : T → T/F with π∘F ≅ π is 2-universal among such functors; this functor is the existence half. red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: degree 1 maps to G.map f ≫ G.map eqToHom ≫ φ.hom.app Y, degree −1 uses φ⁻¹, `periodicity.inv.app X` maps to `φ.inv.app X`, and the descent of the projection along its own periodicity is isomorphic to the identity and fixes every morphism (all compiled); Preadditive E and G.Additive are needed for it to elaborate; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.

(1) Descent commutes with postcomposition: for an additive H : E → E', lift G φ ⋙ H ≅ lift (G ⋙ H) φ_H, where φ_H is the image of φ under H. (2) The periodicity isomorphism of G ⋙ H is `(Functor.associator _ _ _).symm ≪≫ Functor.isoWhiskerRight φ H` : [n] ⋙ (G ⋙ H) ≅ ([n] ⋙ G) ⋙ H ≅ G ⋙ H, whose X-component is H(φ_X) (checked by simp); the isomorphism is `isoLift` applied to F = lift G φ ⋙ H with an e of identity components, `he` reducing to `lift_map_periodicity_hom_app`; `[H.Additive]` is needed both for lift G φ ⋙ H to be additive and for `lift (G ⋙ H)` to exist (without it the statement does not elaborate). (3) Lean subtlety: the identity components are typed at objects of lift G φ ⋙ H, equal to H.obj (G.obj X) only by unfolding (documented term chaining). (4) A consequence of the universal property (not stated in Keller's text); the specialisation H = 𝟭 compiles; axioms standard.
The component of `liftCompIso G φ H` at ⟨X⟩ is the identity of H(G(X)) (rfl).
The component of the inverse of `liftCompIso G φ H` at ⟨X⟩ is the identity of H(G(X)) (rfl).

`liftMap G φ X Y` is the additive map from the orbit hom group ⨁_i Hom_D(X, Y⟦n*i⟧) to Hom_E(G X, G Y) sending a degree-i piece f : X → Y⟦n*i⟧ to G(f) followed by the i-th power of φ at Y. Correctly stated: this is the Hasse product formula. For a regular quadratic form Q over a number field K, the product of its finite Hasse signs s_v(Q) over all finite places and of its real Hasse signs over the real places is 1. Lean ↔ mathematics: `Q : QuadraticForm K V` lives on a finite-dimensional space (`[FiniteDimensional K V]`). `hQ : Q.Nondegenerate` is Mathlib's `QuadraticMap.Nondegenerate` (zero radical, and polar radical of rank ≤ 1), which in characteristic 0 is regularity of the polar form. `Q.globalInvariants hQ` records the rank, the discriminant class, `finiteHasse` and `realPositiveIndex`. Here `finiteHasse v` is the local Hasse invariant of the class of Q ⊗ K_v, i.e. ∏_{i<j} (a_i,a_j)_v for any diagonalization over K_v. `hasseProduct` is by definition `(∏ᶠ v, finiteHasse v) * ∏ w, realHasse w`, where `realHasse w = (−1)^C(q_w, 2)` and q_w = n − p_w is the negative index at w. This is the Hasse sign ∏_{i<j} (a_i,a_j)_w of p⟨1⟩ ⊥ q⟨−1⟩ over ℝ; `globalInvariants_realHasse_eq_prod_hilbertSymbol` proves it equals ∏_{i<j} (a_i,a_j)_w for any diagonalization over K. The conclusion `= 1` is the product formula. The proof diagonalizes Q ≅ ⟨a_1,…,a_n⟩ over K and applies `hilbertSymbol_productFormula` to each pair i < j. Lean subtlety: `finprod` returns the junk value 1 on an infinite support, but `finiteHasse` has finite support (`hasFiniteMulSupport_finiteHasse`). A compiled probe shows that for ⟨−1,−1⟩ over ℚ, whose real Hasse sign is −1, the theorem forces ∏ᶠ_v s_v = −1, so the junk value is not what makes it true. The truncated ℕ subtraction n − p_w in `realNegativeIndex` is harmless because p_w ≤ n (`realPositiveIndex_add_realNegativeIndex_eq_finrank`). Rank 0 (V = 0) gives empty products, correctly 1. K is restricted to `Type`. The Hasse convention is ∏_{i<j}, and the real sign uses the same convention. Source: it follows pair by pair from Milne, Class Field Theory v4.03, V Example 5.4. Red-team checks: axioms are standard. `@[simp]` fires (`by simp` closes it for a variable form). The non-vacuity probe above compiles.

Correctly stated: the system of local invariants of every regular quadratic form of positive rank over a number field is admissible. Lean ↔ mathematics: `(Q.globalInvariants hQ).IsAdmissible` is the structure of exact conditions. (i) 1 ≤ rank. (ii) At each real place, p_w ≤ n and the image of the discriminant d in ℝˣ/ℝˣ² is (−1)^(n − p_w). (iii) The finite Hasse signs are trivial at all but finitely many places (`Function.HasFiniteMulSupport`). (iv) In rank 1 every s_v = 1, and in rank 2 s_v = 1 wherever d_v is the class of −1. (v) `hasseProduct = 1`. `hn : 1 ≤ Module.finrank K V` is positive rank, and `hQ : Q.Nondegenerate` is regularity, as in characteristic 0. The theorem combines `isAdmissible_globalInvariants_iff` (every condition except (i) and (v) holds for every regular form) with the Hasse product formula. Lean subtlety: `realNegativeIndex` uses the truncated ℕ subtraction n − p_w; this is safe because p_w ≤ n is itself part of the proof. `Module.finrank` would be 0 for an infinite-dimensional space, but `[FiniteDimensional K V]` rules that out. `hn` is genuinely needed: a compiled probe shows that the system of a rank-0 form is not admissible, because `one_le_rank` fails. The `finprod` in `hasseProduct` has finite support, as noted for `globalInvariants_hasseProduct_eq_one`. K is restricted to `Type`. Red-team checks: axioms are standard. A compiled witness at the hyperbolic plane ⟨1,−1⟩ over ℚ is `isAdmissible_globalInvariants _ _ (by simp)`, and the probe showing `hn` is needed also compiles.

Correctly stated: Hilbert's product formula over ℚ: for a, b ∈ ℚˣ, ∏_ℓ (a,b)_ℓ · (a,b)_∞ = 1, with the local symbols computed in ℚ_ℓ and ℝ. Lean ↔ mathematics: `Nat.Primes` indexes the primes ℓ. `Units.map (algebraMap ℚ ℚ_[ℓ]).toMonoidHom a` is a viewed in Mathlib's ℓ-adic numbers ℚ_ℓ, and `algebraMap ℚ ℝ` is the inclusion, the unique real place. `hilbertSymbol x y` is +1 exactly when y = u² − x·w² is solvable in the field concerned, which is the classical Hilbert symbol (z² = x u² + y w² has a nontrivial solution). `a b : ℚˣ` are the nonzero rationals. Lean subtlety: the product over primes is a `finprod`, which returns the junk value 1 on an infinite support. Its support is finite: it is transported from `hasFiniteMulSupport_hilbertSymbol_unitAtFinitePlace` along `Rat.HeightOneSpectrum.primesEquiv`. As a compiled check, ∏ᶠ_ℓ (−1,−1)_ℓ computed independently is −1 (`finprod_eq_single` at ℓ = 2), the genuine finite product. Source: Milne, Class Field Theory v4.03, III Aside 4.2, eq. (34), records exactly this ∏_{p≤∞} (a,b)_p = 1. Red-team checks: axioms are standard. The theorem is derived from the number-field formula, rewriting the finite places of ℚ as primes and the real place as ℝ. A compiled specialisation at (−1,−1) uses independent local values: −1 at 2 (`hilbertSymbol_neg_one_neg_one_padicTwo`), 1 at odd ℓ (`TauCeti.Padic.hilbertSymbol_intCast_intCast_eq_one`), and −1 at ∞ (no real solution to −1 = x² + y²). The product is 1, and the theorem forces the 2-adic part to be −1.

Correctly stated: this is Hilbert's product formula for every number field K: for a, b ∈ Kˣ, ∏_{v finite} (a,b)_v · ∏_{w real} (a,b)_w = 1. Lean ↔ mathematics: `a b : Kˣ` are the nonzero elements of K (units of the field, not of 𝓞_K), and `[NumberField K]` says K is a number field. `hilbertSymbol x y : ℤˣ` is by definition `if ∃ u w, y = u² − x·w² then 1 else −1`, i.e. +1 exactly when y is a norm from F(√x), the split case included; for nonzero x, y this is the standard condition that z² = x·u² + y·w² has a nontrivial solution (Milne III §4, p. 111, states this equivalence over ℚ_p). `HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K)` is the set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K, i.e. the finite places, and `v.unitAtFinitePlace` is `Units.map` of the algebra map K → `v.adicCompletion K`, so the first factor is (a,b)_v computed in the completion K_v. `{w : InfinitePlace K // w.IsReal}` lists each real place once (`InfinitePlace` identifies conjugate embeddings). `unitAtRealPlace w` is `Units.map (embedding_of_isReal w.2)`, so the second factor is the real symbol, which `hilbertSymbol_real` shows is −1 exactly when both images are negative. The complex places are left out correctly: every complex number is a square, so their symbols are 1 (the proof checks that the complex invariants vanish). Lean subtlety: the finite product is a `finprod` (∏ᶠ), which returns the junk value 1 when its support is infinite. Here the support is finite: `hasFiniteMulSupport_hilbertSymbol_unitAtFinitePlace` proves it, and the proof rewrites ∏ᶠ as a `Finset` product over `finiteHilbertSupport`. A compiled probe shows the theorem forces ∏ᶠ_ℓ (−1,−1)_ℓ = −1 over ℚ, so it cannot hold through the junk value. Also: K is restricted to `Type` (universe 0), inherited from `ClassFieldTheory.hilbertProductFormula`; every number field has an isomorphic copy there. The real-place product uses a classical `Fintype` instance, which is harmless because every `Fintype` instance gives the same product. Source: Milne, Class Field Theory v4.03, V Example 5.4 (∏_v (a,b)_v = 1 over every number field; see also III Remark 4.8). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms are only propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound, so no sorry anywhere in the class-field-theory closure, and the idele-class H¹ input is now a theorem, not a hypothesis. The statement has no hypotheses beyond a and b. A compiled ℚ specialisation at (a,b) = (−1,−1) computes each local value independently (−1 at 2 by `hilbertSymbol_neg_one_neg_one_padicTwo`, 1 at every odd ℓ, −1 at ∞), and their product is 1, as the theorem says. The general statement also instantiates at K = ℚ.

Correctly stated: for a number field K, a Brauer class of K whose localizations at all places vanish is zero, i.e. Br K → ⨁_v Br K_v is injective (Albert–Brauer–Hasse–Noether). Lean ↔ mathematics: `Br K` is by definition `continuousCohomology 2 (unitsRep K)`, Mathlib's continuous H² of the absolute Galois group `Field.absoluteGaloisGroup K` with coefficients the units of `SeparableClosure K` (discrete, acted on through restriction to the separable closure), i.e. the Galois cohomology H²(Gal(K̄/K), K̄ˣ) that Milne writes H²(·/K) and identifies with Br(K); every class is inflated from some H²(Gal(L/K), Lˣ) with L/K finite Galois (`exists_relBrInfl_eq`). `brLocalization K` sends x to the pair whose component at a finite place v is `brBaseChange K (v.adicCompletion K) x` and at an infinite place w is `brBaseChange K w.Completion x` (`brLocalization_fst_apply`, `brLocalization_snd_apply`), and `brBaseChange K L` is the pullback along G_L → G_K and (Kˢ)ˣ → (Lˢ)ˣ induced by a K-embedding of separable closures, independent of that embedding (`brBaseChange_apply`): the restriction map x ↦ x_v of Galois cohomology. The places: `HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K)` is the set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K, i.e. the finite places, with Mathlib's completion `v.adicCompletion K` = K_v; `InfinitePlace K` is Mathlib's type of archimedean places, real and complex, with completion `w.Completion` ≅ ℝ or ℂ. So every place occurs. The codomain `(Π₀ v, Br K_v) × ((w : InfinitePlace K) → Br K_w)` is the direct sum over all places: `Π₀` is the finitely supported families, and there are finitely many infinite places. That the localizations of x are finitely supported is a theorem (`hasFiniteSupport_finiteInvAt`) used to define `brLocalization`, not an assumption. `Function.Injective` of the additive map `brLocalization K` is equivalent to: x = 0 whenever every `brBaseChange K K_v x` is 0. I compiled this kernel form from the theorem. Lean subtlety: `Br K` is the cohomological Brauer group, not Mathlib's central-simple-algebra `BrauerGroup K`. Tau Ceti does not formalize Br(K) ≅ H², so 'a central simple algebra split at every completion is split' is the classical reading, not what is proved. K ranges over `Type` (universe 0); this is harmless, since every number field is isomorphic to one there. `brBaseChange` uses an embedding of separable closures chosen by `IsSepClosed.lift` (choice), but the map is proved independent of the choice. The component at a complex place lies in Br ℂ = 0 (`brCompletion_eq_zero_of_isComplex`), as in Milne. No junk values are involved. Source: Milne, Class Field Theory v4.03, VII §7 (H²(·/K) = Br(K); Theorem 7.1: H²(L/K) → ⨁_v H²(L_v/K_v) is injective for every Galois L/K, possibly infinite) and VIII Theorem 4.2 (0 → Br(K) → ⨁_v Br(K_v) → ℚ/ℤ → 0 is exact; this is exactness at Br(K)). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound only. The only hypotheses are `[Field K] [NumberField K]`, with no hypothesis class: the result is derived from the vanishing of idele-class H¹ (`subsingleton_h1_globalFormation`, from the second inequality). It specialises to K = ℚ. Non-vacuity: I compiled a class x ∈ Br ℚ with nonzero localization at a finite place and at the real place, with real invariant 1/2 (via `exists_br_of_sum_eq_zero`), so Br ℚ ≠ 0 and the archimedean summand is really there. Mathlib has no such result; it has only the CSA definition `BrauerGroup`.

Correctly stated: for a number field K and every x ∈ Br K, the local invariants inv_v(x_v) ∈ ℚ/ℤ sum to zero over all places v. Lean ↔ mathematics: `Br K` = `continuousCohomology 2 (unitsRep K)` = H²(Gal(K̄/K), K̄ˣ) = Br(K). `brLocalization K x` is the family of localizations x_v = `brBaseChange K K_v x` (restriction in Galois cohomology), finitely supported over the finite places `HeightOneSpectrum (𝓞 K)` (`Π₀`) and over all of `InfinitePlace K`, as for `brLocalization_injective`. `sumLocalInv K` is by definition `AddMonoidHom.coprod (DFinsupp.sumAddHom fun v ↦ invMap (v.adicCompletion K)) (∑ w, infiniteInvMap w ∘ eval w)`: the sum of inv_v over the finite support at the finite places plus the sum over the finitely many infinite places. Hence `sumLocalInv K (brLocalization K x) = ∑_{v ∈ S} finiteInvAt K v x + ∑_w infiniteInvAt K w x` for every finite S ⊇ `brauerSupport K x` (`sumLocalInv_brLocalization`); I compiled this textbook form with S = `brauerSupport K x`. The target `AddCircle (1 : ℚ)` = ℚ/1ℤ is ℚ/ℤ. `invMap K_v : Br K_v ≃+ ℚ/ℤ` is Tau Ceti's local invariant of the nonarchimedean local field K_v, whose local-field structure comes from the v-adic valuation `Valued.v` of Mathlib's completion. It is an isomorphism, normalized by arithmetic Frobenius: on an unramified layer of degree n the class of a has invariant v(a)/n (`unramifiedInv`). Milne's inv_K is likewise defined by evaluation at the Frobenius (III Theorem 1.7). `infiniteInvMap w` is 1/2 on the nonzero class at a real place (`infiniteInvMap_apply_of_isReal`, Br ℝ ≅ ½ℤ/ℤ) and 0 at a complex place, which is Milne's inv_v at the archimedean places. The conclusion `= 0` says Σ_v inv_v(x_v) ≡ 0 mod ℤ. Lean subtlety: the 'sum over all places' is a genuine finite sum (`DFinsupp.sumAddHom` over a finitely supported family plus a sum over the finite type `InfinitePlace K`), not a `tsum` or `finsum` that could be a junk 0. `infiniteInvMap` is a classical `if w.IsReal then … else 0`, and the 0 branch is the correct value because Br K_w = 0 at a complex place. A global change of sign convention for inv at the finite places would not change the statement, since 1/2 = −1/2 at the real places. `Br K` is cohomological, not Mathlib's CSA `BrauerGroup`, so the reading 'the local invariants of a central simple algebra sum to 0' is the classical translation. K ranges over `Type`. Source: Milne, Class Field Theory v4.03, VII Theorem 8.1(b) (Σ inv_v(α) = 0 for α ∈ H²(L/K), L/K finite Galois) and Lemma 8.6, and VIII Theorem 4.2 (Σ : ⨁_v Br(K_v) → ℚ/ℤ, (β_v) ↦ Σ inv_v(β_v), with 0 → Br(K) → ⨁ Br(K_v) → ℚ/ℤ → 0 exact; this theorem is the image ⊆ kernel half in the middle). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound only. The only hypotheses are `[Field K] [NumberField K]`, and the proof uses no reciprocity hypothesis: it goes through the Hasse principle and the product formula for local Artin symbols on cyclic cyclotomic extensions. It specialises to K = ℚ. I compiled the consequence that no global class has exactly one nonzero local component at a finite place (via `sumLocalInv_single`). A class of Br ℚ with invariants 1/2 at a finite place and 1/2 at the real place exists, so the statement is not vacuous. `simp` makes no progress on the left side without this lemma, so its `@[simp]` form is normal.

Correctly stated: at a generic q, in a finite-dimensional U_q(sl₂)-module on which the Casimir element Ω has the single generalized eigenvalue c = casimirScalar(εq^m), E kills the generalized K-weight space of weight εq^m. Lean ↔ mathematics: `casimir q` is FE + ((q − q⁻¹)²)⁻¹ • (qK + q⁻¹K⁻¹), the quantum Casimir; `casimirScalar q μ` is (qμ + q⁻¹μ⁻¹)/(q − q⁻¹)², the scalar by which Ω acts on a highest-weight vector of weight μ (`casimir_smul_of_e_smul_eq_zero`); `casimirBlock q V c` is the maximal generalized eigenspace of Ω at c, a U_q-submodule since Ω is central (`mem_casimirBlock_iff`), so `= ⊤` says Ω − c is locally nilpotent, hence nilpotent, on V; the conclusion is `e q • w = 0` for every `w ∈ genWeightSpace q V (ε * q ^ m)` (the generalized K-eigenspace at εq^m). Lean subtlety: `casimirScalar` uses Lean's `/` and `⁻¹`, which would give junk 0 at q = ±1 or μ = 0; here q − q⁻¹ ≠ 0 (q generic) and μ = ±q^m ≠ 0, so the scalar is the honest one; finite-dimensionality is load-bearing although the docstring omits it (RT-20261105-e7f1ee). Checks (red team, 5f78b5307b): the hypothesis `casimirBlock … = ⊤` holds non-trivially on the ladder module L_m^ε (compiled), where the lemma specialises to E = 0 on the top weight space.

Correctly stated: at a generic q, if E kills the generalized K-weight space W of weight εq^m (ε = ±1), then F^r is injective on W for every r ≤ m. Lean ↔ mathematics: `genWeightSpace q V (ε * q ^ m)` is the generalized eigenspace of K at εq^m, `hE` says E = 0 on it, and from `hr : r ≤ m`, `hw : w ∈ W` and `hf : f q ^ r • w = 0` it concludes `w = 0`, which is injectivity of F^r restricted to W; no finite-dimensionality is assumed or needed. Lean subtlety: `(ε : ℂ)` is the double cast ℤˣ → ℤ → ℂ, i.e. ±1. Checks (red team, 5f78b5307b): `hr` is needed (F^(m+1) kills W by the next lemma); specialised (compiled) to the ladder module L_m^ε it gives F^m v₀ ≠ 0, the known length m + 1 of the lowering string; it holds with E w = 0 for the single w (RT-20261105-9371be).

Correctly stated: at a generic q, in a finite-dimensional U_q(sl₂)-module, if E kills the generalized K-weight space W of weight εq^m (ε = ±1), then F^(m+1) kills W. Lean ↔ mathematics: `genWeightSpace q V (ε * q ^ m)` is the generalized eigenspace of K at εq^m (`maxGenEigenspace` of the action of `k q`), `hE` says E acts by 0 on it, `[FiniteDimensional ℂ V]` is dim V < ∞, and the conclusion `f q ^ (m + 1) • w = 0` for each `w` in it is F^(m+1)W = 0. Lean subtlety: `(ε : ℂ)` is the cast of a unit of ℤ, so ±1. Checks (red team, 5f78b5307b): finite-dimensionality is used to get some F^N w = 0, and the exponent is lowered step by step using r ≠ m and the distinct powers of q; the hypotheses are satisfiable non-trivially (on L_m^ε, compiled); it even holds with E w = 0 for the single w (RT-20261105-9371be, a generality improvement, not a correctness problem).

Correctly stated: at a generic q, in a finite-dimensional U_q(sl₂)-module, if E kills the generalized K-weight space of weight εq^m (ε = ±1), then that generalized weight space is the honest weight space, i.e. K acts on it by the scalar εq^m. Lean ↔ mathematics: `genWeightSpace q V μ` is by definition `(Algebra.lsmul ℂ ℂ V (k q)).maxGenEigenspace μ`, the vectors killed by some power of K − μ (`mem_genWeightSpace_iff`), and `weightSpace q V μ` is the eigenspace of K at μ (`mem_weightSpace_iff : v ∈ weightSpace q V μ ↔ k q • v = μ • v`); both are ℂ-subspaces, so the equation says ker(K − εq^m)^∞ = ker(K − εq^m) on V without assuming K diagonalizable; `hq : IsGenericQuantumParameter q` is q ≠ 0 and not a root of unity, and `hE` says E w = 0 for every w in the generalized weight space. Lean subtlety: `(ε : ℂ)` is the double cast ℤˣ → ℤ → ℂ, which is ±1; no division or junk value enters the statement. Checks (red team, 5f78b5307b): specialised (compiled) to the ladder module L_m^ε with hE discharged by `e_smul_eq_zero_of_casimirBlock_eq_top`; the inclusion weightSpace ≤ genWeightSpace is the trivial half, and the proof's use of hq (distinct powers of q) and finite-dimensionality (F eventually kills every vector) matches the commutator argument of roadmap QuantumGroups Q8 item 3.

Correctly stated: for q ∈ ℂ nonzero and not a root of unity, every finite-dimensional U_q(sl₂)-module is semisimple. Lean ↔ mathematics: `UqSl2 q` is by definition `RingQuot (UqSl2.Rel q)`, the free ℂ-algebra on E, F, K, K⁻¹ modulo KK⁻¹ = K⁻¹K = 1, KE = q²EK, KF = q⁻²FK and EF − FE = (q − q⁻¹)⁻¹ • (K − K⁻¹), exactly the presentation of U_q(sl₂) in Virelizier §2.3; `IsGenericQuantumParameter q` unfolds to `q ≠ 0 ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → q ^ n ≠ 1`, i.e. q ∈ ℂ× is not a root of unity (so q = ±1, i, primitive cube roots, … are all excluded); the module is an arbitrary `[Module (UqSl2 q) V]` together with `[Module ℂ V] [IsScalarTower ℂ (UqSl2 q) V]`, which only says that the ℂ-structure is the restriction of the U_q-action along `algebraMap` (every U_q-module carries such a structure, compiled via `Module.compHom`), and `[FiniteDimensional ℂ V]` is dim_ℂ V < ∞; no condition on K appears (no type-1, positivity or diagonalizability assumption), so modules where K has eigenvalues −q^n, or a priori non-trivial Jordan blocks, are covered; `IsSemisimpleModule (UqSl2 q) V` is Mathlib's class extending `ComplementedLattice (Submodule (UqSl2 q) V)`: every submodule has a complementary submodule, equivalently V is the sum of its simple submodules (`sSup_simples_eq_top_iff_isSemisimpleModule`). Lean subtlety: the defining relation inverts q − q⁻¹ with Lean's `⁻¹`, and 0⁻¹ = 0, so at q = ±1 `UqSl2 q` is the commutative algebra ℂ[E, F, K^{±1}] and at q = 0 the relations force E = F = 0, neither being the quantum group; the hypothesis excludes all three (q ≠ 0 is its first conjunct, q² ≠ 1 its n = 2 case), so here q − q⁻¹ ≠ 0 and the relation is the honest EF − FE = (K − K⁻¹)/(q − q⁻¹); V is in an arbitrary universe and the zero module is included (trivially semisimple). Source and checks: Virelizier, Quantum groups, Theorem 3.13 proves this for finite-dimensional type-1 modules (category F) with q not a root of unity; the Lean statement is the full signed version required by roadmap QuantumGroups Q8 (q ≠ 0, q^r ≠ 1 for r > 0; item 3, every finite-dimensional U_q module is semisimple). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only; applied (compiled) to the trivial module L_0^+, the 2-dimensional simple L_1^+, the type −1 module L_3^− and L_1^+ × L_2^− (on L_2^− K acts on v₀ by −q², compiled); the hypothesis is satisfiable (q = 2 is generic, compiled) and load-bearing: at q = 1 (ℂ² with E a nonzero nilpotent, F = 0, K = 1) and at q = i, where q² = −1 ≠ 1 so the relation is the genuine quantum-group one (ℂ² with K = diag(1, −1), E = e₁₂, F = 0), there are 2-dimensional non-semisimple modules (both compiled), so 'not a root of unity' cannot be weakened to q² ≠ 1.

Correctly stated: for a flat morphism f : X → Y of locally Noetherian schemes and x ∈ X, codim(x in X) = codim(f x in Y) + codim(x in its fibre), i.e. dim 𝒪_{X,x} = dim 𝒪_{Y,f x} + dim 𝒪_{X_{f x},x}, the dimension formula. Lean ↔ mathematics: `[IsLocallyNoetherian X] [IsLocallyNoetherian Y]` are Mathlib's locally Noetherian schemes (Γ(U) Noetherian on affine opens) and `[Flat f]` is Mathlib's flat morphism (flat ring maps on affine charts, equivalently on stalks). Mathlib orders the points of a scheme by `a ≤ b ↔ b ⤳ a` (checked: `x ≤ y ↔ y ⤳ x` is `Iff.rfl`), so the generic point is the top and `Order.coheight x` is the supremum of the lengths of chains x < x₁ < … < xₙ of strict generizations of x; Mathlib's `ringKrullDim_stalk_eq_coheight` says this is dim 𝒪_{X,x}, the codimension of x, and likewise for `coheight (f x)` in Y. `f ⁻¹' {f x}` is the set-theoretic fibre with the order restricted from X (`Subtype.preorder`), which is the fibre's own specialisation order (compiled from `IsInducing.subtypeVal.specializes_iff`), and `⟨x, rfl⟩` is x as a point of it; Mathlib's `Scheme.Hom.fiberHomeo : f.fiber y ≃ₜ f ⁻¹' {y}` identifies this space with the scheme-theoretic fibre X ×_Y Spec κ(y). Putting these together I compiled, from this theorem in five rewrites, `ringKrullDim (X.presheaf.stalk x) = ringKrullDim (Y.presheaf.stalk (f x)) + ringKrullDim ((f.fiber (f x)).presheaf.stalk (f.asFiber x))`, the textbook form with Mathlib's own fibre scheme. Lean subtlety: the direction of the order — with Mathlib's convention codimension is `coheight` (chains going up to generizations), not `height` (which would be the dimension of the closure of x); the equation is in ℕ∞, where ⊤ absorbs, so there is no truncated subtraction (all three terms are finite here anyway, local Noetherian rings having finite dimension); and the fibre term is the coheight inside the subspace f⁻¹{f x}, not inside X. Source: Stacks Tag 00ON (Lemma 10.112.7): for a map R → S of Noetherian rings with going down (e.g. flat) and a prime q over p, dim S_q = dim R_p + dim S_q/pS_q; on affine charts this is the statement, S_q/pS_q being the local ring of the fibre at x. Checks (red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): compiled specialisations — identity (fibre term 0) and Spec ℤ[X] → Spec ℤ at a maximal ideal containing 2, where the three coheights are 2 = 1 + 1 and the theorem forces the fibre term to be 1; hypotheses satisfiable (no False); no explicit hypotheses beyond f and x; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; the same proof goes through under the weaker `GeneralizingMap f` (going down), recorded as a generality note.

Correctly stated: a flat, surjective, locally quasi-finite morphism f : X → Y has dim X = dim Y. Lean ↔ mathematics: `topologicalKrullDim` is the Krull dimension of the underlying space (`WithBot ℕ∞`); `[Flat f] [Surjective f]` give dim Y ≤ dim X by `topologicalKrullDim_le_of_flat_of_surjective`, and `[LocallyQuasiFinite f]` (Mathlib: locally of finite type with discrete fibres) gives dim X ≤ dim Y by the Tau Ceti lemma `Scheme.Hom.topologicalKrullDim_le`, a strict specialisation never staying inside a discrete fibre; `le_antisymm` gives the equality. The docstring's 'finite faithfully flat covers' is covered: `IsFinite f → LocallyQuasiFinite f` is a Mathlib instance (compiled) and faithfully flat means flat and surjective. Lean subtlety: values in `WithBot ℕ∞` (⊥ empty, ⊤ infinite-dimensional), and the equality is the intended one in all cases; the name lists only flat and surjective, but the statement needs and carries `LocallyQuasiFinite` (without it 𝔸¹_ℚ → Spec ℚ has dims 1 ≠ 0, compiled), recorded as a naming note. Checks (red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): hypotheses met by the identity of Spec ℚ (compiled); axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: if f : X → Y is flat and surjective, then dim Y ≤ dim X. Lean ↔ mathematics: `topologicalKrullDim` is the Krull dimension of the underlying topological space (supremum of lengths of chains of irreducible closed subsets) in `WithBot ℕ∞`, the usual dimension of a scheme; `[Flat f]` and `[Surjective f]` are Mathlib's flat and surjective morphisms. The proof is the textbook one: flat morphisms are generalizing (Mathlib `Flat.generalizingMap`, going down), and the Tau Ceti lemma `GeneralizingMap.topologicalKrullDim_le_of_surjective` shows a continuous surjective generalizing map from a T₀ space to a quasi-sober T₀ space (a scheme is both) cannot increase dimension, since chains of generizations below f x lift to X. Lean subtlety: `topologicalKrullDim` is ⊥ for the empty space and ⊤ for an infinite-dimensional one; surjectivity makes Y empty when X is, and ⊤ on the right makes the inequality trivially true, so each case is the intended statement. Checks (red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): no Noetherian hypothesis is needed and none is assumed; no Mathlib duplicate (loogle, leansearch, leanfinder, grep of the pinned Mathlib); axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: for f flat, surjective and locally quasi-finite, if every nonempty open of X has dimension d then every nonempty open of Y has dimension d. Lean ↔ mathematics: `U : Y.Opens` with `[Nonempty U]` is a nonempty open of Y and `topologicalKrullDim U` is the dimension of the open subscheme `U.toScheme`, whose space is the open subspace U (elaborated term checked); `hd` says every nonempty open of X has dimension d. The proof restricts f to f⁻¹U → U, still flat, surjective and locally quasi-finite, so dim f⁻¹U = dim U by `topologicalKrullDim_eq_of_flat_of_surjective`, and f⁻¹U is nonempty by surjectivity, so its dimension is d. Lean subtlety: d ranges over `WithBot ℕ∞`; d = ⊥ would force X, hence Y, empty, and the conclusion is then vacuous, which is the right reading; `[Nonempty U]` excludes the empty open, whose dimension is ⊥. Checks (red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; name omits the essential locally-quasi-finite hypothesis (naming note).

Correctly stated: in Spec A, the codimension of a point x of the closed set V(I), measured inside V(I), is the height of the prime x/I of A/I. Lean ↔ mathematics: `{y : Spec A | I ≤ y.asIdeal}` is V(I), the primes containing I, made a type whose order is the order of the scheme `Spec A` restricted to it (`Subtype.preorder`); Mathlib orders the points of a scheme by `a ≤ b ↔ b ⤳ a` (b specialises to a, i.e. b.asIdeal ⊆ a.asIdeal), so `coheight ⟨x, hx⟩` is the supremum of the lengths of chains of strict generizations of x that stay in V(I), i.e. of chains of primes I ⊆ p₀ ⊊ … ⊊ pₙ = x; `hx : I ≤ x.asIdeal` says x ∈ V(I); `x.asIdeal.map (Ideal.Quotient.mk I)` is the image x/I of x in A/I (prime because I ⊆ x) and `Ideal.height` is the usual height (supremum of lengths of chains of primes below it); primes of A/I below x/I correspond to primes of A between I and x, so the two sides are the same number. Lean subtlety: the scheme order is reverse inclusion of primes (Mathlib's `PrimeSpectrum` order is inclusion), which is why codimension is `coheight` here and not `height`; both sides are in ℕ∞, so nothing is truncated. Checks (red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): compiled specialisation I = x gives coheight 0 = height of the zero ideal of the domain A/x; the statement also has a 7-line proof from Mathlib's order isomorphism `Ideal.primeSpectrumQuotientOrderIsoZeroLocus : PrimeSpectrum (A ⧸ I) ≃o zeroLocus I`, which is exactly the correspondence above (module probe); axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Correct definition: f is a maximum bounded s–t assignment when every bounded s–t assignment for the same bounds has value at most f's. Lean ↔ maths: `BoundedFlow lo hi s t` is an arrow function `toFun` with lo e ≤ f e ≤ hi e on every arrow (`mem_Icc : toFun ∈ Set.Icc lo hi`, pointwise order) and `excessAt toFun v = 0` (inflow minus outflow) at every v ≠ s, t; `f.val` is `excessAt f.toFun t`, the net inflow at t, which equals the net outflow at s (`excessAt_source`); the body `IsMaxOn val Set.univ f` unfolds by `isMaximum_iff` (Mathlib's `isMaxOn_univ_iff`) to ∀ g, g.val ≤ f.val, so 'maximum' means value-maximal among all feasible assignments, not maximal for some order on assignments. Lean subtlety: the body is not exposed, so users go through `isMaximum_iff`; under a mere preorder 'every g ≤ f' is stronger than 'no g > f', but every main result of the file is over a linear order, where they agree; if lo e > hi e on some arrow the type is empty and the predicate is never instantiated. With lo = 0 this is Schrijver's 'maximum s–t flow ... of maximum value' (Combinatorial Optimization Vol. A, §10.1, p. 149). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: witnessed on a 3-vertex network: a value-1 flow proved maximum via `Flow.tfae_isMaximum`, which `Flow.isMaximum_toBoundedFlow` transfers to this predicate.

For s ≠ t, a maximum bounded s–t assignment attains the cut bound `cutBound lo hi S` (hi on arrows leaving S minus lo on arrows entering S) of some S with s ∈ S, t ∉ S; with weak duality this is max-flow = min-cut-bound with lower bounds. The (1) ⇒ (3) part of `tfae_isMaximum`; for s = t no such S exists, so `hst` is needed.

For s ≠ t, a maximum bounded s–t assignment has no augmenting walk (t is not positively reachable from s in its residual network): otherwise `exists_val_lt_of_positiveReachable` gives g with f.val < g.val ≤ f.val. The (1) ⇒ (2) step of `tfae_isMaximum`.
Two maximum bounded s–t assignments have the same value: each value is at most the other by `isMaximum_iff`, and `le_antisymm` in the partial order K gives equality (the maximum value is unique).

Correct definition: f is minimum when every bounded s–t assignment for the same bounds has value at least f.val; the body `IsMinOn val Set.univ f` unfolds by `isMinimum_iff` (Mathlib's `isMinOn_univ_iff`) to ∀ g, f.val ≤ g.val, with `val` the net inflow at t and, as the docstring says, no sign condition. This is the minimum-flow problem with lower and upper bounds, exchanged with maximality by swapping the terminals (`isMaximum_swap`).

For s ≠ t, a minimum bounded s–t assignment has value −cutBound lo hi Sᶜ = (lo on arrows leaving S) − (hi on arrows entering S) for some S with s ∈ S, t ∉ S — the min-flow max-cut theorem — obtained from `IsMaximum.exists_val_eq_cutBound` for `f.swap` with S the complement of the t-side set and `val_swap`. Lean subtlety: the docstring ('attains a lower cut bound') omits s ≠ t and the separation condition, both carried by the statement (finding RT-20261105-47289f).
Two minimum bounded s–t assignments have the same value: each value is at most the other by `isMinimum_iff`, and `le_antisymm` in the partial order K gives equality.

If s ≠ t and t is positively reachable from s in the residual network of f, some bounded s–t assignment has strictly larger value: the proof extracts an augmenting path (`positiveReachable_iff_exists_isPath`), takes its bottleneck q > 0 (the least residual capacity on it) and updates f by q along it (`update` by a `walkFlow`), which raises the value by q; forward copies raise and reverse copies lower their arrows. This is the augmentation step in Schrijver's proof of Theorem 10.3 (p. 150). `hst` is necessary: for s = t the empty walk makes t reachable while every value is 0.

`f.IsMaximum ↔ ∀ g : BoundedFlow lo hi s t, g.val ≤ f.val`: f is maximum exactly when every bounded s–t assignment for the same bounds has value at most f.val; it is Mathlib's `isMaxOn_univ_iff` applied to the definition.

For s ≠ t, a bounded s–t assignment is maximum iff the sink is not positively reachable from the source in its residual network (`residualCapacity lo hi f.toFun`: forward copies hi e − f e, reverse copies f e − lo e), i.e. it has no augmenting walk; the (1) ⇔ (2) part of `tfae_isMaximum`. `hst` is needed: at s = t every assignment is maximum yet s reaches itself.

For coinciding terminals (`hst : s = t`) every bounded assignment is maximum: all values are 0 (`val_eq_zero_of_eq`: the total excess of any arrow function is 0 and conservation holds at every vertex other than s), so g.val ≤ f.val reads 0 ≤ 0. This is the degenerate case excluded by the `s ≠ t` hypothesis of `tfae_isMaximum`.

If s ∈ S, t ∉ S and f.val = cutBound lo hi S, then f is maximum: `cutBound lo hi S` is by definition `arrowSum hi S Sᶜ − arrowSum lo Sᶜ S` (upper bounds on arrows leaving S minus lower bounds on arrows entering S), and weak duality `val_le_cutBound` bounds every bounded s–t value by it. For lo = 0 this is Schrijver's Theorem 10.2 (Combinatorial Optimization Vol. A, p. 149), the (3) ⇒ (1) step of the augmenting-path criterion.

`f.swap.IsMaximum ↔ f.IsMinimum`: `swap` views the same arrow function as a t–s assignment (`swap_toFun`), whose value, the net inflow at the new sink s, is −f.val (`val_swap`); swap is a bijection (`swap_swap`), so maximizing the t–s value over all assignments is minimizing the s–t value.
`f.IsMinimum ↔ ∀ g, f.val ≤ g.val`: minimum means every feasible assignment has value at least f's; Mathlib's `isMinOn_univ_iff` applied to the definition.

For s ≠ t, a bounded s–t assignment f is minimum iff the source s is not positively reachable from the sink t in its residual network: minimizing the s–t value is maximizing the t–s value of `f.swap` (`isMaximum_swap`), whose residual network is that of the same arrow function (`swap_toFun`), so this is `isMaximum_iff_not_positiveReachable` with the terminals exchanged. Lean subtlety: the docstring omits the hypothesis s ≠ t, which the statement carries and needs (at s = t every assignment is minimum while t reaches s trivially; finding RT-20261105-47289f).
For s = t every bounded assignment has value 0 (`val_eq_zero_of_eq`), so every one is minimum (0 ≤ 0).

If s ∈ S, t ∉ S and f.val = −cutBound lo hi Sᶜ, then f is minimum: −cutBound lo hi Sᶜ = arrowSum lo S Sᶜ − arrowSum hi Sᶜ S (lower bounds on arrows leaving S minus upper bounds on arrows entering S) is a lower bound for the value of every bounded s–t assignment (`neg_cutBound_compl_le_val`, weak duality from below), so attaining it forces minimality. Lean subtlety: the docstring's 'attaining a lower cut bound' does not say that S must contain s but not t, which the statement requires (`hs`, `ht`; finding RT-20261105-47289f).
`f.swap.IsMinimum ↔ f.IsMaximum`: the companion of `isMaximum_swap`, applied to `f.swap` and simplified by `swap_swap`.

Correctly stated augmenting-path optimality criterion with lower bounds: for a bounded s–t assignment f with s ≠ t, (1) f is maximum, (2) f has no augmenting walk, (3) f.val equals the cut bound of some vertex set containing s but not t, are equivalent. Lean ↔ maths: the network is a finite vertex type `V` (`[Fintype V]`) with finite arrow sets `Q v w` (`[∀ v w, Fintype (Q v w)]`, so parallel arrows and loops are allowed) and coefficients in a linearly ordered abelian group `K` (`[AddCommGroup K] [LinearOrder K] [IsOrderedAddMonoid K]`: ℤ, ℚ, ℝ, …); `BoundedFlow lo hi s t` is an arrow function `toFun` with lo e ≤ f e ≤ hi e on every arrow (`mem_Icc : toFun ∈ Set.Icc lo hi`, pointwise order) and `excessAt toFun v = 0` (inflow minus outflow) at every v ≠ s, t; `f.val` is `excessAt f.toFun t`, the net inflow at t, which equals the net outflow at s (`excessAt_source`); `List.TFAE [P₁, P₂, P₃]` means the three are pairwise equivalent. P₁ `f.IsMaximum` is ∀ g, g.val ≤ f.val (`isMaximum_iff`). P₂ `¬PositiveReachable (residualCapacity lo hi f.toFun) s t`: the residual network gives each arrow e a forward copy of capacity hi e − f e and a reverse copy of capacity f e − lo e, and positive reachability is a walk s → t through residual arrows of positive capacity, so P₂ says Schrijver's residual graph D_f, with A_f = {a | f(a) < c(a)} ∪ {a⁻¹ | f(a) > d(a)} ((10.9), d = lo, c = hi), has no s–t path. P₃ `∃ S, s ∈ S ∧ t ∉ S ∧ f.val = cutBound lo hi S` with `cutBound lo hi S = arrowSum hi S Sᶜ − arrowSum lo Sᶜ S` (upper bounds leaving S minus lower bounds entering S). Lean subtlety: `PositiveReachable` is reflexive (the empty walk), so `hst : s ≠ t` is essential — at s = t every assignment is maximum while s reaches itself and no S separates s from s (compiled); a walk may repeat vertices but contains a path (`positiveReachable_iff_exists_isPath`), so 'walk' or 'path' gives the same P₂; if lo e > hi e on some arrow there is no assignment and the statement is vacuous; only abelian-group operations and finite sums occur, so no junk values. Source: Schrijver, Combinatorial Optimization Vol. A, Ch. 10 (checked): Theorem 10.2 (weak duality, P₃ ⇒ P₁), Corollary 10.2a (P₂ ⇒ P₃, U = vertices reachable in D_f) and the augmentation in the proof of Theorem 10.3 (P₁ ⇒ P₂), stated there for lo = 0 and real capacities; here lower bounds are arbitrary and K any linearly ordered abelian group. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; `hst` load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses, and the compiled s = t counterexample); instantiated with lo = 0 through `Flow.tfae_isMaximum` on two concrete networks.

Without an augmenting walk, f.val equals the cut bound of U = the vertices positively reachable from s in the residual network. Lean ↔ maths: `residualCapacity lo hi f.toFun` gives each arrow e a forward copy `Sum.inl e` of capacity hi e − f e and a reverse copy `Sum.inr e` of capacity f e − lo e (residual arrow family `ResidualHom Q v w = Q v w ⊕ Q w v`); `PositiveReachable c s v` says some walk from s to v uses only residual arrows of positive capacity; `univ.filter (PositiveReachable … s)` is U, containing s (empty walk) and not t (hypothesis). Since no positive residual arrow leaves U, the residual cut gap `cutBound_sub_val` vanishes. For lo = 0 this is Schrijver's Corollary 10.2a (Combinatorial Optimization Vol. A, p. 150). Lean subtlety: the set is built under `open Classical in`, so the statement's `Finset.filter` uses classical decidability; harmless, though a consumer holding another decidability instance must convert.

Correct definition of one augmentation step: `f.AugmentsTo g` holds when some walk p from s to t in the residual arrow family `ResidualHom Q` (forward copies `Sum.inl e`, reverse copies `Sum.inr e`) traverses at least one arrow (`p.arrows ≠ []`), no arrow twice (`p.arrows.Nodup`), has positive residual capacity `residualCapacity 0 cap f.toFun` on every arrow, and g = `f.augmentBottleneck p hp hne`, which raises each forward arrow and lowers each reverse arrow of p by the bottleneck (least residual capacity on p). This is Schrijver's step (10.12), 'f := f + εχ_P, where ε is as large as possible so as to maintain 0 ≤ f ≤ c' (Combinatorial Optimization Vol. A, p. 151). Lean subtlety: p is a trail, not necessarily a path, and may use both copies of one arrow (which cancel); this is more permissive than Schrijver's s–t path, but every augmenting path is such a trail and each step still raises the value by the bottleneck (`AugmentsTo.val_lt`).

If the capacities and the values of f all lie in an additive subgroup H of K (e.g. the multiples of d), so do the values of any g one augmentation step away: the bottleneck is one of the residual capacities cap e − f e or f e, all in H (`augmentBottleneck_mem`). This is the integrality step behind Schrijver's Corollary 10.3a (integrity theorem, p. 151).

For s ≠ t an augmentation step strictly increases the value: the new value is f.val plus the bottleneck (`val_augmentBottleneck`), which is positive because every residual capacity on the walk is (`val_lt_val_augmentBottleneck`). `hst` is needed: for s = t a residual closed walk leaves the value unchanged.

Correct definition: an ordinary s–t flow f is maximum when every ordinary s–t flow for the same capacities has value at most f.val (`Flow.isMaximum_iff`, Mathlib's `isMaxOn_univ_iff`). Lean ↔ maths: `Flow cap s t` extends `BoundedFlow 0 cap s t`, so 0 ≤ f e ≤ cap e on every arrow and inflow equals outflow at every v ≠ s, t, plus `excessAt_sink_nonneg : 0 ≤ excessAt toFun t`; `g.val` is the net inflow at t, equal to Schrijver's value(f) = f(δ^out(s)) − f(δ^in(s)) ((10.2)). Lean subtlety: the value ≥ 0 clause is not in Schrijver's (10.1); it does not change which flows are maximum, since for nonnegative capacities the zero flow has value 0, and `isMaximum_toBoundedFlow` shows maximality among these flows equals maximality among all `BoundedFlow 0 cap s t` (Schrijver's flows of any value). Matches Schrijver, Combinatorial Optimization Vol. A, §10.1, p. 149 ('an s–t flow under c, of maximum value').

For s ≠ t, a maximum ordinary flow saturates a cut: f.val = `arrowSum cap S Sᶜ`, the total capacity of the arrows from S to its complement, for some S with s ∈ S, t ∉ S; with weak duality this is the max-flow min-cut theorem (Schrijver, Theorem 10.3, p. 150). Compiled on s→a→t with capacities 2, 1: the value-1 flow and S = {s, a}.
