Augmenting f by the bottleneck along a nonempty residual s–t trail with positive residual capacity on every arrow is an augmentation step: it is the defining witness of `AugmentsTo`.
Unfolds `f.AugmentsTo g` to its defining existential (a nonempty residual s–t trail of positive residual capacities whose bottleneck augmentation is g); `Iff.rfl`.
`f.IsMaximum ↔ ∀ g : Flow cap s t, g.val ≤ f.val`: every ordinary s–t flow for the same capacities has value at most f's; Mathlib's `isMaxOn_univ_iff` applied to the definition.

For s ≠ t, an ordinary flow is maximum iff no augmentation step starts from it: a step strictly raises the value (`AugmentsTo.val_lt`), and conversely an augmenting walk contains a path whose bottleneck augmentation is a step, so `isMaximum_iff_not_positiveReachable` applies. This is the stopping rule of the Ford–Fulkerson algorithm (Schrijver p. 151: 'If no such path exists, the flow f is maximum, by Corollary 10.2a').

For s ≠ t, an ordinary s–t flow is maximum iff it has no augmenting walk, i.e. t is not reachable from s through residual arrows of positive capacity in `residualCapacity 0 cap f.toFun` (forward copies cap e − f e, reverse copies f e); Schrijver's Corollary 10.2a with the augmentation in the proof of Theorem 10.3 (Combinatorial Optimization Vol. A, p. 150). The (1) ⇔ (2) part of `Flow.tfae_isMaximum`; `hst` is needed.

Over a linear order, an ordinary flow is maximum among ordinary flows iff it is maximum among all bounded assignments with lower bound 0 (Schrijver's flows, whose value may be negative): an assignment of value larger than f.val ≥ 0 has nonnegative value, so it is itself an ordinary flow. This is what makes the nonnegative-value clause of `Flow` harmless. Lean subtlety: the argument needs comparability of values, hence `[LinearOrder K]`, which the statement assumes.

Correctly stated augmenting-path theorem: for an ordinary s–t flow f with s ≠ t, (1) f is maximum, (2) f has no augmenting walk, (3) f.val equals the capacity of the arrows leaving some vertex set containing s but not t, are equivalent. Lean ↔ maths: the network is a finite vertex type `V` (`[Fintype V]`) with finite arrow sets `Q v w` (`[∀ v w, Fintype (Q v w)]`, so parallel arrows and loops are allowed) and coefficients in a linearly ordered abelian group `K` (`[AddCommGroup K] [LinearOrder K] [IsOrderedAddMonoid K]`: ℤ, ℚ, ℝ, …), with capacities `cap : Assignment Q K`; `Flow cap s t` is an arrow function with 0 ≤ f e ≤ cap e (`mem_Icc : toFun ∈ Set.Icc 0 cap`), `excessAt` (inflow minus outflow) zero at every v ≠ s, t, and nonnegative value; `f.val` = `excessAt f.toFun t`, the net inflow at t = net outflow at s (Schrijver's value(f), (10.2)); `List.TFAE [P₁, P₂, P₃]` means the three are pairwise equivalent. P₁ `f.IsMaximum` is ∀ g, g.val ≤ f.val (`Flow.isMaximum_iff`): value-maximal among all flows for the same cap, s, t. P₂ `¬PositiveReachable (residualCapacity 0 cap f.toFun) s t`: `residualCapacity 0 cap f` gives each arrow e a forward residual copy `Sum.inl e` of capacity cap e − f e and a reverse copy `Sum.inr e` of capacity f e − 0, and `PositiveReachable c s t` asks for a walk from s to t through residual arrows of positive capacity, so P₂ says Schrijver's residual graph D_f (A_f = {a | f(a) < c(a)} ∪ {a⁻¹ | f(a) > 0}, (10.9) with d = 0) has no s–t path — reverse arcs included (compiled: with unit capacities on 0→1, 0→2, 1→2, 1→3, 2→3, the flow along 0→1→2→3 is shown non-maximum by the theorem through the walk 0→2, reverse of 1→2, 1→3). P₃ `∃ S, s ∈ S ∧ t ∉ S ∧ f.val = arrowSum cap S Sᶜ`: `arrowSum cap S Sᶜ` = Σ_{v∈S} Σ_{w∉S} Σ_{e : Q v w} cap e is the capacity c(δ^out(S)) of the s–t cut (parallel arrows counted separately, loops never). Lean subtlety: `PositiveReachable` is reflexive (the empty walk), so `hst : s ≠ t` is essential — at s = t every flow is maximum while s reaches itself and no S separates s from s (compiled counterexample); the walk in P₂ may repeat vertices but always contains a path (`positiveReachable_iff_exists_isPath`), so 'augmenting walk' and 'augmenting path' give the same P₂; the clause value ≥ 0 in `Flow` is not in Schrijver's definition but does not change maximality (`isMaximum_toBoundedFlow`), and `BoundedFlow.tfae_isMaximum` with lo = 0 covers flows of any sign; capacities are not required nonnegative, and if some cap e < 0 no flow exists and the statement is vacuous; `[DecidableEq V]` only serves to form Sᶜ; only abelian-group operations and finite sums appear, so no junk values; existence of a maximum flow is not claimed here (ShortestAugmentation.lean proves it). Source: Schrijver, Combinatorial Optimization Vol. A, Ch. 10 (checked): Theorem 10.2 (value(f) ≤ c(δ^out(U)), giving P₃ ⇒ P₁), Corollary 10.2a (no s–t path in D_f ⇒ value(f) = c(δ^out(U)) for U the vertices reachable from s, giving P₂ ⇒ P₃) and the augmentation in the proof of Theorem 10.3 (P₁ ⇒ P₂). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: specialised to s→a→t with capacities 2, 1 over ℤ — the value-1 flow proved maximum via P₃ with S = {s, a}, hence every flow has value ≤ 1, and the zero flow proved non-maximum via the augmenting walk s→a→t; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; `hst` load-bearing.

Correctly stated: let μ, ν ∈ P₂(E), with μ absolutely continuous and neither endpoint of internal energy −∞. Then some constant-speed W₂-geodesic γ from μ to ν carries the internal energy convexly: 𝓤(γ_t) ≤ (1−t)𝓤(μ) + t𝓤(ν) for t ∈ [0,1]. This is McCann's theorem in Wasserstein space. Lean ↔ mathematics: `WassersteinSpace 2 E` is the space of probability measures with finite second moment, with the W₂ distance. `IsGeodesicSegment γ μ ν` says γ(0) = μ, γ(1) = ν and dist(γ s, γ t) = |s − t|·W₂(μ, ν) on [0,1], i.e. a constant-speed minimizing geodesic. `ConvexAlong 0 φ γ` unfolds to φ(γ t) ≤ (1−t)φ(γ 0) + tφ(γ 1) − 0 for all t ∈ [0,1], the m = 0 case of m-convexity along a curve. `hμ` is μ ≪ ρ with ρ a Haar measure. `h₀` and `h₁` exclude energy −∞ at the endpoints. `hU0`, `hc` and `ha` are McCann's condition (A1). The ∃γ form is the usual notion of geodesic convexity, as in `TauCeti.GeodesicallyConvex`. Geodesics out of an absolutely continuous law are unique on [0,1] (`TauCeti.WassersteinSpace.eqOn_of_isGeodesicSegment_of_absolutelyContinuous`), so this is convexity along the displacement interpolation, as the docstring says. The proof takes γ = ((1−t)·id + t∇u)₊μ for the Brenier map ∇u. Lean subtlety: ν need not be absolutely continuous, because `internalEnergy` charges its singular part at U'(∞). For superlinear U (U'(∞) = +∞), a singular ν therefore has energy ⊤ and the inequality is trivial. `ConvexAlong` reads γ only on [0,1]. `EReal` arithmetic (⊥ + ⊤ = ⊥) is why the ⊥ exclusions are needed. For the Boltzmann entropy on P₂ they hold automatically (`TauCeti.WassersteinSpace.boltzmannEntropy_ne_bot`, given exp(−a·d(x, x₀)²) integrable against ρ). Source: McCann, Adv. Math. 128 (1997), Theorem 2.2, with absolutely continuous endpoints and the displacement interpolation of the Brenier map. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: the proof applies `internalEnergy_map_smul_add_smul_gradient_le` directly to the Brenier map. That theorem was audited here and specialised to dilations and to U(r) = r log r, both compiled. Every explicit hypothesis is used, and the axioms are standard. [Nontrivial E] is removable (recorded as a minor generality point).

Correctly stated: the internal energy of the endpoint ν = (∇F)₊μ is ∫_D g dρ. Here r = dμ/dρ, and g equals det H · U(r/det H) where det H ≠ 0 and L·r where det H = 0. L is the recession constant U'(∞), or any real number when μ gives no mass to {det H = 0}. The reason: ∇F collapses the degenerate set to a Lebesgue-null set, which carries νˢ. `internalEnergy` charges νˢ at U'(∞), so the degenerate set contributes U'(∞)·μ(det H = 0) = ∫_{det H = 0} L·r dρ. Lean ↔ mathematics: `internalEnergy U ρ ν` is ∫ U(dν/dρ) dρ + `recessionConstant U`·νˢ(E). `hL : recessionConstant U = ↑L ∨ μ {x | (H x).det = 0} = 0` reads: L is U'(∞) and U'(∞) is a real number, or the degenerate set is μ-null. If U'(∞) = ±∞ and the degenerate set has mass, this theorem does not apply; the main theorem handles that case separately, where the energy is ⊤. `if (H x).det = 0 then L * r x else (H x).det * U (r x / (H x).det)` is the piecewise integrand, and `indicator` restricts it to D. `hH`, `hf`, `hbot`, `hμ` and `hμD` are as in `internalEnergy_map_smul_add_smul_gradient`, now with μ σ-finite. Lean subtlety: the explicit `if` avoids division by zero. Without it, r/0 = 0 would turn det H · U(r/det H) into 0 on the degenerate set. `Measure.map` along ∇F is a genuine pushforward because `gradient` is always measurable, so no Dirac junk arises. ν may fail to be σ-finite (f = 0 sends ρ to ∞·δ₀), but it is s-finite, so Mathlib's Lebesgue decomposition exists and νˢ is not a junk zero. The singular term is `EReal.toENNReal (recessionConstant U)` times νˢ(E), computed in ℝ≥0∞ where 0·∞ = 0, so U'(∞) = 0 removes even an infinite singular mass, as it should. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: specialised at f = (a/2)‖x‖² (det H = aⁿ ≠ 0, so the second disjunct of hL holds with L = 0) and μ uniform on the unit ball K. It gives ρ(K)·aⁿU(a⁻ⁿ), the direct value for the dilate by a; compiled. Every explicit hypothesis is used in the proof, and the axioms are standard.

Correctly stated: for 0 ≤ t < 1, the internal energy of μₜ = ((1−t)·id + t∇F)₊μ equals ∫_D Jₜ·U(r/Jₜ) dρ. Here r = dμ/dρ, D is the interior of dom f, and Jₜ = det((1−t)I + tH), where H is the Alexandrov Hessian of f. This is McCann's change-of-variables identity (15) in the proof of his Theorem 2.2 (Adv. Math. 128, 1997). Lean ↔ mathematics: `internalEnergy U ρ ν` is ∫ U(dν/dρ) dρ + U'(∞)·νˢ(E). For t < 1 the interpolant is absolutely continuous, so the singular term vanishes. `potentialEnergy V ρ` is the extended-real ∫ V dρ: positive part minus negative part, and ⊤ when the positive part diverges. Here V is `(interior {x | f x ≠ ⊤}).indicator (fun x => Jₜ x * U (r x / Jₜ x))`, the integrand on D and 0 off D. `((1 - t) • ContinuousLinearMap.id ℝ E + t • H x).det` is det((1−t)I + tH(x)). `hH` says that, for ρ-almost every x in D, H(x) is a first-order expansion of the subdifferential at x: ‖y′ − y − H(x)(x′ − x)‖ ≤ ε‖x′ − x‖ for every subgradient y′ at every x′ near x. That is Alexandrov's second derivative. It exists almost everywhere (`TauCeti.exists_mongeAmpereMeasure_eq_singularPart_add_withDensity`), and it is unique at each such x because subgradients exist at every point of the open set D. `hU0 : U 0 = 0` is needed because points off D, and points outside the image, carry density 0. `[SFinite μ]`, `hμ` and `hμD` are the hypotheses on the source. Lean subtlety: `x / 0 = 0` could matter in `r x / Jₜ x`, but for almost every x in D the matrix H(x) is positive semidefinite, so Jₜ > 0 there for t < 1 and no division by zero occurs where it matters. The junk values of `gradient` and `EReal.toReal` off D are μ-null effects, as in the main theorem. `ENNReal.toReal ∞ = 0` matters only for an s-finite μ with infinite density; the intended case is a σ-finite μ, whose density is finite almost everywhere. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: specialised at f = (a/2)‖x‖², where H = aI and Jₜ = ((1−t)+ta)ⁿ, with μ uniform on the unit ball K. It gives ρ(K)·λⁿU(λ⁻ⁿ) for the dilate by λ = (1−t)+ta, which matches the direct computation (density λ⁻ⁿ on λK); compiled. Every explicit hypothesis is used in the proof, and the axioms are standard.

Correctly stated: this is McCann's displacement convexity of the internal energy: if μ is absolutely continuous, σ-finite and carried by the interior D of the domain of a convex f, then along μₜ = ((1−t)·id + t∇F)₊μ one has 𝓤(μₜ) ≤ (1−t)𝓤(μ) + t𝓤((∇F)₊μ) for every t ∈ [0,1]. Lean ↔ mathematics: E is a finite-dimensional real inner product space of dimension n = `finrank ℝ E` ≥ 1 (`[FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`, `[Nontrivial E]`), and `ρ` with `[ρ.IsAddHaarMeasure]` is Lebesgue measure up to a constant factor. `internalEnergy U ρ ν` is by definition ∫ U(dν/dρ) dρ + U'(∞)·νˢ(E), where dν/dρ is `ν.rnDeriv ρ` read through `ENNReal.toReal`, νˢ is `ν.singularPart ρ` and U'(∞) is `recessionConstant U` = limsup_{s→∞} U(s)/s in `EReal`. Positive and negative parts are summed separately. `hU0 : U 0 = 0` together with `hc`/`ha`, which say `ConvexOn`/`AntitoneOn` on `Ioi 0` of s ↦ s^n · U((s^n)⁻¹), is exactly McCann's condition (A1). The probe checked that `U (s ^ n)⁻¹` parses as U applied to s^(−n). `hf : Convex ℝ {p : E × ℝ | f p.1 ≤ p.2}` says that f : E → [−∞, ∞] has a convex epigraph, and `hbot` that f never takes the value −∞. F = `fun x' => (f x').toReal` is the real representative of f, and `∇` is Mathlib's `gradient`, the Riesz dual of `fderiv`. `hμ : μ ≪ ρ`, `[SigmaFinite μ]` and `hμD` (μ-almost every point lies in the interior of dom f) are the hypotheses on the source. Brenier's theorem supplies exactly these, as the Wasserstein corollary in this file shows. `Measure.map T μ` is the pushforward T₊μ, and the conclusion is the displayed inequality in `EReal` with coefficients `((1 - t : ℝ) : EReal)` and `(t : EReal)`. `h₀` and `h₁` (neither endpoint energy is ⊥) are needed. In `EReal`, ⊥ + ⊤ = ⊥, so a source of energy −∞ together with a target of energy +∞ would otherwise force 𝓤(μₜ) = −∞. Lean subtlety: (i) `gradient` is 0 wherever F is not differentiable, and `EReal.toReal ⊤ = 0` outside dom f. Neither matters here: F is differentiable ρ-almost everywhere on the open set D, and μ ≪ ρ is carried by D, so ∇F is the true gradient μ-almost everywhere. (ii) In pinned Mathlib 1b1ccf4b, `Measure.map` along a map that is not a.e.-measurable is a Dirac mass (`Measure.map_of_not_aemeasurable_of_ne_zero`). The gradient of any function is measurable (`TauCeti.measurable_gradient`), so both pushforwards here are genuine. (iii) `ENNReal.toReal ∞ = 0`. This is harmless: a σ-finite μ has an almost-everywhere finite density. The target (∇F)₊μ may fail to be σ-finite (f = 0 sends ρ to ∞·δ₀), but it is s-finite, so Mathlib's Lebesgue decomposition exists and its singular part is charged at U'(∞) instead of becoming a junk 0. (iv) The energy is ⊤ as soon as its positive part diverges (∞ − ∞ is read as +∞). Also `((1 - t : ℝ) : EReal) * ⊤ = ⊤` for t < 1, while `0 * ⊤ = 0` at the endpoints t = 0, 1. (v) U is real-valued, so McCann's densities A taking the value +∞ are not covered, and the values of U on (−∞, 0) are never used. Source: R. J. McCann, A convexity principle for interacting gases, Adv. Math. 128 (1997), Theorem 2.2 with condition (A1) on p. 162. McCann states it for absolutely continuous probability endpoints and the Brenier map. The Lean statement is that inequality for any convex f and any σ-finite μ, and it allows a singular target. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b, all compiled: specialised at f = (a/2)‖x‖² and μ = ρ restricted to the unit ball K. The file's own formulas give ρ(K)·λⁿU(λ⁻ⁿ) for the dilate by λ, which matches the hand computation (density λ⁻ⁿ on λK), and the theorem reduces exactly to φ((1−t)+ta) ≤ (1−t)φ(1) + tφ(a) with φ(s) = sⁿU(s⁻ⁿ), i.e. McCann's condition itself. Specialised to U(r) = r log r (the Boltzmann entropy). All hypotheses hold together with μ = ρ ≠ 0. lean_minimal_hypotheses: all 10 explicit hypotheses are load-bearing. By a hand computation, U 0 = 0 is also mathematically necessary: U = 1 at 0 and 0 elsewhere satisfies the McCann condition but breaks the conclusion in ℝ² along x ↦ diag(1+t, 1−t/2) applied to ρ restricted to the complement of a unit square. Axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. [Nontrivial E] is removable (the n = 0 case is trivial; recorded as a minor generality point).

`coeff (single 1 n) F.toPowerSeries = if n = 1 then 1 else 0`: the coefficient of Yⁿ in a formal group law F(X, Y) is 1 for n = 1 and 0 otherwise, i.e. F(0, Y) = Y coefficientwise, via Mathlib's `FormalGroup.zeroX_eq_X`; Ravenel's Definition A2.1.1(i) has F(0, x) = x.

`coeff (single 0 n) F.toPowerSeries = if n = 1 then 1 else 0`: the coefficient of Xⁿ (the exponent vector `single 0 n`, n on X and 0 on Y) in a formal group law F(X, Y) is 1 for n = 1 and 0 otherwise, which is F(X, 0) = X read coefficientwise; the proof rewrites with Mathlib's `FormalGroup.Xzero_eq_X` (F(X, 0) = X), and F(x, 0) = x is Ravenel's Definition A2.1.1(i). Placement finding recorded separately (general fact in the Lazard file); the statement itself is correct.

Correctly defined: the Lazard ring L = ℤ[aᵢⱼ | i, j ≥ 1] / I with I = `LazardRing.relations`, the ideal of associativity and commutativity coefficients of X + Y + Σ aᵢⱼ XⁱYʲ. Lean ↔ maths: the body is literally `MvPolynomial (ℕ+ × ℕ+) ℤ ⧸ LazardRing.relations`, and its `CommRing` instance is the quotient ring structure (`inferInstanceAs`); the universal property that makes it the Lazard ring is proved as `LazardRing.lift : {F : FormalGroup R // F.IsComm} ≃ (LazardRing →+* R)`, where Mathlib's `FormalGroup R` (zero constant term, coefficient 1 at X and at Y, F(F(X, Y), Z) = F(X, F(Y, Z)); Mathlib derives F(X, 0) = X and F(0, Y) = Y) together with `IsComm` (F(X, Y) = F(Y, X)) is exactly Ravenel's Definition A2.1.1 (i)–(iii). Lean subtlety: indexing the generators by `ℕ+ × ℕ+` leaves out the coefficients fixed by the unit axiom, which Ravenel instead kills by relations a₁₀ − 1, a₀₁ − 1, aᵢ₀, a₀ᵢ; both presentations give the same ring because `lazardSeries` hard-codes X + Y and no pure powers. `LazardRing : Type` lives in universe 0, while the coefficient ring R in `lift` may live in any universe. Source: Ravenel, Complex Cobordism and Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres (author's online edition), Appendix A2.1, Definition A2.1.1 and Theorem A2.1.8 with its proof. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b, compiled: L is not the zero ring (it maps to ℤ, classifying X + Y), the class of a₁₁ is nonzero, a₁₂ = a₂₁ holds in L; standard axioms only.
As a function, `gradedLift F` is `lift F`; by `rfl`.
The formal group law attached to a graded homomorphism φ : L →+*ᵍ A is the base change `formalGroup.map φ.toRingHom` of the universal law; by `rfl`.
`(lift.symm φ).1 = formalGroup.map φ`: the formal group law attached to φ : L → R is Σ φ(āᵢⱼ) XⁱYʲ, the universal law with φ applied to every coefficient; by `rfl`.
For i, j ≥ 1, the coefficient of XⁱYʲ (`single 0 i + single 1 j`) in the universal formal group law is the class `mk (X (i, j))` of the generator aᵢⱼ.

The coefficient of X^(d 0) Y^(d 1) in the universal law lies in L of degree 2(d 0 + d 1 − 1) (`d.degree` is the total degree d 0 + d 1): for i, j ≥ 1 it is āᵢⱼ of degree 2(i + j − 1). Lean subtlety: `d.degree - 1` truncates to 0 at d = 0, where the coefficient is 0 and lies in every degree, and the coefficients of X and Y are 1 ∈ L₀, so the truncation is harmless.

Correctly defined: the homological degree |aᵢⱼ| = 2(i + j − 1) of the generator aᵢⱼ. Lean: the body is `2 * ((ij.1 : ℕ) + ij.2 - 1)` with i, j ∈ ℕ+ cast to ℕ. Lean subtlety: ℕ subtraction truncates, but i + j ≥ 2 for positive i, j, so i + j − 1 is never truncated. Source: Ravenel, Complex Cobordism and Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres (author's online edition), Appendix A2.1, p. 354 (grading |aᵢⱼ| = 2(i + j − 1), under which F(x, y) is homogeneous of degree −2 when |x| = |y| = −2).
`degree (i, j) = 2 * (i + j - 1)`: the degree of aᵢⱼ unfolded, by `rfl`; no truncation since i + j ≥ 2.

Correctly defined: the universal formal group law X + Y + Σ āᵢⱼ XⁱYʲ over L, where āᵢⱼ = `mk (MvPolynomial.X (i, j))` is the class of the variable aᵢⱼ. Lean ↔ maths: `toPowerSeries := lazardSeries fun ij ↦ mk (MvPolynomial.X ij)` is that series; the constant-term and linear-coefficient fields hold by the shape of `lazardSeries`, and the associativity field comes from `relations_le_ker_iff` applied to `ker_mk`, i.e. the quotient map kills every associativity coefficient; commutativity is the separate instance `formalGroup.IsComm`. Lean subtlety: none beyond `lazardSeries`'s (its `Nat.toPNat'` branch never sees 0); associativity is not computed but holds because every associativity coefficient is in the kernel of `mk`. Source: Ravenel, Complex Cobordism and Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres (author's online edition), Appendix A2.1, Theorem A2.1.8 (F(x, y) = Σ aᵢⱼ xⁱyʲ over L). Checks at 5f78b5307b: its base change along `lift F` is F (`map_lift`); compiled tests with X + Y and X + Y + XY.
`formalGroup.toPowerSeries = lazardSeries fun ij ↦ mk (MvPolynomial.X ij)`: the universal law is the series X + Y + Σ āᵢⱼ XⁱYʲ, by `rfl`.

Correctly stated (the graded universal property): for a commutative ring A graded by 𝒜 : ℕ → σ, graded ring homomorphisms L →+*ᵍ A correspond bijectively to commutative formal group laws over A whose coefficient of each X^(d 0) Y^(d 1) lies in 𝒜 (2(d 0 + d 1 − 1)), i.e. with aᵢⱼ ∈ 𝒜 (2(i + j − 1)). Lean ↔ maths: `grading →+*ᵍ 𝒜` is Mathlib's `GradedRingHom`, a ring homomorphism f with x ∈ Lₙ → f x ∈ 𝒜 n; the domain is the subtype of `FormalGroup A` satisfying `IsComm` and the degree condition on every coefficient; `toFun` is `lift F` with `map_mem` from `lift_mem_iff (.id ℕ)`, `invFun φ` is `formalGroup.map φ.toRingHom`, and both round trips are proved (`GradedRingHom.ext` for one), so this is the restriction of the bijection `lift` to graded maps and graded laws. Lean subtlety: `d.degree - 1` truncates at d = 0, harmless since that coefficient is 0; the target grading is ℕ-indexed (homological), the cohomological version being `lift_mem_iff` with e = −(inclusion) into ℤ. Source: Ravenel, Complex Cobordism and Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres (author's online edition), Appendix A2.1, p. 354 (the grading |aᵢⱼ| = 2(i + j − 1) on L). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b, compiled: over ℤ with the trivial grading (everything in degree 0), X + Y satisfies the condition and `gradedLift.symm (gradedLift ⟨X + Y, …⟩)` returns it, while X + Y + XY violates it (a₁₁ = 1 would need degree 2) and indeed `lift` of X + Y + XY sends a₁₁ ∈ L₂ to 1 ∉ 𝒜 2; the subtype condition is exactly what `GradedRingHom.map_mem` needs.

Correctly defined: Lₙ is the image in L of the polynomials in the aᵢⱼ homogeneous of weight n for |aᵢⱼ| = 2(i + j − 1). Lean ↔ maths: the body `GradedAlgebra.quotientPiece (weightedHomogeneousSubmodule ℤ degree) relations n` is by definition the image `(𝒜 n).map mk` of the weight-n piece under the quotient map (`quotientPiece_def`; characterised by `mem_grading_iff`); `isInternal_grading` proves L = ⨁ₙ Lₙ, using that the relations are homogeneous. Lean subtlety: indexed by ℕ, odd degrees are the zero submodule. Source: Ravenel, Complex Cobordism and Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres (author's online edition), Appendix A2.1, p. 354 (the grading |aᵢⱼ| = 2(i + j − 1) on L).

Two ring maps φ, ψ : L → R with `formalGroup.map φ = formalGroup.map ψ` (the same base change of the universal law) are equal: the uniqueness half of Ravenel's Theorem A2.1.8; checked that it forces an endomorphism of L fixing the universal law to be the identity.

Correctly stated: with aᵢⱼ in degree 2(i + j − 1), the ideal of Lazard relations in ℤ[aᵢⱼ] is homogeneous. Lean ↔ maths: `MvPolynomial.weightedHomogeneousSubmodule ℤ degree` is the grading of ℤ[aᵢⱼ] whose weight-n piece is spanned by the monomials Π aᵢⱼ^eᵢⱼ with Σ eᵢⱼ · 2(i + j − 1) = n (made a `GradedAlgebra` by the local instance `MvPolynomial.weightedGradedAlgebra`), and `Ideal.IsHomogeneous 𝒜 I` says every homogeneous component of every element of I lies in I, i.e. I is generated by homogeneous elements. The proof rescales the universal law by T² over L[T] and reads off the coefficient of Tⁿ, which is the degree-n component. Lean subtlety: the grading is indexed by ℕ, so the odd-degree pieces are zero rather than absent. Source: Ravenel, Complex Cobordism and Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres (author's online edition), Appendix A2.1, p. 354, which grades L by |aᵢⱼ| = 2(i + j − 1) and notes F(x, y) is then homogeneous of degree −2 for |x| = |y| = −2, the reason the relations are homogeneous.

`DirectSum.IsInternal grading`: the canonical map ⨁ₙ Lₙ → L is a bijection, i.e. L is the internal direct sum of its graded pieces; this needs (and uses) the homogeneity of the relations, `isHomogeneous_relations`.
`RingHom.ker mk = relations`: the kernel of the quotient map ℤ[aᵢⱼ] → L is exactly the ideal of Lazard relations; it is `Ideal.mk_ker`.

Correctly stated (the universal property of the Lazard ring): commutative one-dimensional formal group laws over any commutative ring R correspond bijectively to ring homomorphisms θ : L → R, the law attached to θ being Σ θ(aᵢⱼ) XⁱYʲ. Lean ↔ maths: `{F : FormalGroup R // F.IsComm}` is the set of commutative formal group laws over R (Mathlib's `FormalGroup`: constant term 0, coefficient 1 at X and Y, F(F(X, Y), Z) = F(X, F(Y, Z)); `IsComm`: F(X, Y) = F(Y, X)), `LazardRing →+* R` is the set of ring homomorphisms, and `≃` is an explicit bijection with both round trips proved: `toFun` sends F to the map āᵢⱼ ↦ coefficient of XⁱYʲ in F (`lift_mk_X`) and `invFun` sends θ to `formalGroup.map θ`, the universal law with θ applied to every coefficient (`coe_lift_symm`); so `map_lift` is existence (every F is θ_* of the universal law) and `hom_ext` is uniqueness of θ, while `lift_map` gives naturality in R. Lean subtlety: R ranges over every universe (`Type*`) while L : Type; `IsComm` is a Prop-valued class carried inside the subtype, so the subtype adds no data; Mathlib's `FormalGroup` does not include the formal inverse, which is harmless because it exists automatically (Ravenel, Proposition A2.1.2). Source: Ravenel, Complex Cobordism and Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres (author's online edition), Appendix A2.1, Theorem A2.1.8 (for any formal group law G over any commutative ring R there is a unique θ : L → R with G(x, y) = Σ θ(aᵢⱼ) xⁱyʲ), whose formal group laws are commutative by Definition A2.1.1(ii). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b, compiled: the additive law X + Y is classified by the map killing every aᵢⱼ, and `lift.symm` of such a map is `FormalGroup.𝔾ₐ`; the multiplicative law X + Y + XY sends a₁₁ ↦ 1 and every other aᵢⱼ ↦ 0; `lift` elaborates for R in an arbitrary universe; standard axioms only.
On ℤ[aᵢⱼ], `(lift F).comp mk` is the evaluation homomorphism `MvPolynomial.aeval` sending each aᵢⱼ to the coefficient of XⁱYʲ in F.
Naturality in the coefficient ring: for a commutative formal group law F over R and g : R →+* S, the homomorphism classifying `F.map g` (g applied to every coefficient) is `g.comp (lift F)`.

Correctly stated (the graded universal property, pointwise): let A be graded by 𝒜 over a commutative monoid ι and e : ℕ →+ ι; the homomorphism classifying a commutative formal group law F over A maps each Lₙ into 𝒜 (e n) exactly when the coefficient of every monomial X^(d 0) Y^(d 1) in F lies in 𝒜 (e (2(d 0 + d 1 − 1))). Lean ↔ maths: `grading n` is Lₙ, `lift F` the classifying map, and the left side `∀ n x, x ∈ grading n → lift F x ∈ 𝒜 (e n)` says `lift F` is graded after regrading along e (e = id for homological, e = −(inclusion) into ℤ for cohomological degrees); `𝒜 : ι → σ` with `[SetLike σ A] [AddSubgroupClass σ A] [SetLike.GradedMonoid 𝒜]` is a family of additive subgroups with 1 ∈ 𝒜 0 and 𝒜 i · 𝒜 j ⊆ 𝒜 (i + j), no direct-sum decomposition required; `d.degree` is the total degree d 0 + d 1, and quantifying over every monomial d is equivalent to asking aᵢⱼ ∈ 𝒜 (e (2(i + j − 1))) for i, j ≥ 1, since the other coefficients are 0 or 1 (that equivalence compiled, as the docstring says). Lean subtlety: `d.degree - 1` truncates to 0 at d = 0, where the coefficient is 0 ∈ 𝒜 (e 0); at d = X, Y the condition is 1 ∈ 𝒜 (e 0), supplied by `GradedMonoid`; `AddSubgroupClass` is genuinely needed — with additive submonoids the equivalence fails (compiled counterexample over ℤ with 𝒜 0 = ℕ, all other pieces 0, F = X + Y: the right side holds but −1 ∈ L₀ maps to −1 ∉ 𝒜 0). Source: Ravenel, Complex Cobordism and Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres (author's online edition), Appendix A2.1, p. 354 (|aᵢⱼ| = 2(i + j − 1), with F(x, y) homogeneous of degree −2 when |x| = |y| = −2, i.e. this statement for ι = ℤ). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: `lean_minimal_hypotheses` needs `e` and `F`; the generality finding (`AddMonoid ι` suffices) is recorded separately and does not affect correctness.
`lift F (mk (X ij)) = coeff (single 0 i + single 1 j) F`: the homomorphism classifying F sends the class of aᵢⱼ to the coefficient of XⁱYʲ in F, as Ravenel's θ does.

`formalGroup.map (lift F) = F.1`: pushing the universal law forward along the homomorphism classifying F gives back F, so every commutative formal group law is a base change of the universal one (existence in Ravenel's Theorem A2.1.8).
x ∈ Lₙ iff x is the class `mk p` of a polynomial p that is weighted-homogeneous of degree n (`IsWeightedHomogeneous degree p n`) — the definition of the quotient grading as an image.
The quotient map ℤ[aᵢⱼ] → L: its body is `Ideal.Quotient.mk relations`.
The class of a weight-n homogeneous polynomial in the aᵢⱼ lies in Lₙ.
`Function.Surjective mk`: every element of L is the class of a polynomial in the aᵢⱼ; it is `Ideal.Quotient.mk_surjective`.

Correctly defined: the ideal of ℤ[aᵢⱼ | i, j ≥ 1] generated by every coefficient of G(G(X, Y), Z) − G(X, G(Y, Z)) and of G(X, Y) − G(Y, X), where G = X + Y + Σ aᵢⱼ XⁱYʲ is the generic series. Lean ↔ maths: `MvPolynomial (ℕ+ × ℕ+) ℤ` is the polynomial ring ℤ[aᵢⱼ] on generators indexed by pairs of positive integers; the generic series is `lazardSeries MvPolynomial.X`, whose coefficient of XⁱYʲ is the variable aᵢⱼ; `genericSeries.subst ![genericSeries.subst ![X 0, X 1], X 2]` is G(G(X, Y), Z) in the three variables X 0, X 1, X 2 (the same substitution Mathlib's `FormalGroup.assoc` uses) and `genericSeries.subst ![X 1, X 0]` is G(Y, X); `Ideal.span (Set.range fun d ↦ coeff d …)` is the ideal generated by the coefficients at every monomial d, not only up to some degree. The coefficient of XⁱYʲ in G(X, Y) − G(Y, X) is aᵢⱼ − aⱼᵢ, so the commutativity part is Ravenel's relations aᵢⱼ − aⱼᵢ. Lean subtlety: `MvPowerSeries.subst` is defined through an evaluation that gives a junk value on inadmissible substitutions; here every substituted series has zero constant term (`constantCoeff_lazardSeries`), so the substitutions are genuine compositions, and the private `relations_le_ker_iff` proves that a ring map kills this ideal exactly when the pushed-forward series satisfies Mathlib's associativity and commutativity identities. Source: Ravenel, Complex Cobordism and Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres (author's online edition), Appendix A2.1, proof of Theorem A2.1.8 (L = ℤ[aᵢⱼ]/I with I generated by the unit relations, aᵢⱼ − aⱼᵢ and all coefficients bᵢⱼₖ of F(F(x, y), z) − F(x, F(y, z))); here the unit relations are built into the generic series instead. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b, compiled: a₁₂ − a₂₁ ∈ relations, a₁₁ ∉ relations (the multiplicative law sends it to 1); standard axioms only.
The underlying ring homomorphism of `gradedLift F` is `lift F`, the ungraded classifying map; by `rfl`.
For i, j ≥ 1 (`i j : ℕ+`, cast to ℕ), the coefficient of XⁱYʲ (exponent vector `single 0 i + single 1 j`) in X + Y + Σ aᵢⱼ XⁱYʲ is aᵢⱼ.

The coefficient of X^(d 0) Y^(d 1) in `lazardSeries a` is a_{d 0, d 1} when both exponents are positive, 1 at X and Y, and 0 otherwise: the defining formula, by `MvPowerSeries.coeff_apply`; `Nat.toPNat'` is only applied to nonzero exponents.
The coefficient of Yⁿ (`single 1 n`) in X + Y + Σ aᵢⱼ XⁱYʲ is 1 for n = 1 and 0 otherwise.
The coefficient of Xⁿ (`single 0 n`) in X + Y + Σ aᵢⱼ XⁱYʲ is 1 for n = 1 and 0 otherwise: no mixed term contributes to a pure power of X.
`constantCoeff (lazardSeries a) = 0`: the series X + Y + Σ aᵢⱼ XⁱYʲ has no constant term, the condition that makes substituting it into another series legitimate.

Correctly defined: for a family a : ℕ+ × ℕ+ → A, the power series X + Y + Σ_{i,j≥1} aᵢⱼ XⁱYʲ in two variables. Lean ↔ maths: an `MvPowerSeries (Fin 2) A` is a function from exponent vectors d = (d 0, d 1) to coefficients; the body returns aᵢⱼ with i = d 0, j = d 1 when both exponents are nonzero, 1 at the two monomials X and Y (`d 0 + d 1 = 1`), and 0 at the constant term and at the pure powers Xⁿ, Yⁿ (n ≥ 2), which is exactly the shape that F(X, 0) = X and F(0, Y) = Y force on a formal group law (Ravenel, Definition A2.1.1(i)). Lean subtlety: `Nat.toPNat'` sends 0 to 1 (a junk value), but it is only evaluated in the branch where both exponents are nonzero, so it never fires; the index type ℕ+ × ℕ+ makes i, j ≥ 1 part of the type. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b, compiled: `lazardSeries 0` is the additive law X + Y and the family with a₁₁ = 1 and all other aᵢⱼ = 0 is the multiplicative law X + Y + XY; every formal group law is `lazardSeries` of its own coefficients (`lazardSeries_coeff_toPowerSeries`).

Every formal group law F(X, Y) over a commutative ring equals X + Y + Σ_{i,j≥1} aᵢⱼ XⁱYʲ with aᵢⱼ its own coefficient of XⁱYʲ (`coeff (single 0 i + single 1 j)`): the content is that the constant term, the pure powers Xⁿ, Yⁿ (n ≥ 2) vanish and X, Y have coefficient 1, which the proof takes from F(X, 0) = X and F(0, Y) = Y (`FormalGroup.coeff_single_zero`, `coeff_single_one`); checked by specialising to X + Y and X + Y + XY.
`map φ (lazardSeries a) = lazardSeries (φ ∘ a)`: applying a ring homomorphism φ to every coefficient (`MvPowerSeries.map`) of X + Y + Σ aᵢⱼ XⁱYʲ gives X + Y + Σ φ(aᵢⱼ) XⁱYʲ, since φ fixes 0 and 1.

A linear isometry `f : E →ₗᵢ[𝕜] F` (𝕜-linear with ‖f x‖ = ‖x‖) gives `FinitelyRepresentable 𝕜 E F`: on each finite-dimensional S ⊆ E the restriction `f.toContinuousLinearMap.comp S.subtypeL` has ‖T x‖ = ‖x‖, so it meets the 1 ± ε bounds for every ε > 0 — a space is finitely representable in any space containing an isometric copy of it.

If `f : F →ₗᵢ[𝕜] E` is a linear isometry with `DenseRange f` (F is isometric to a dense subspace of E) then `FinitelyRepresentable 𝕜 E F`: the inclusion of a finite-dimensional S ⊆ E is approximated within ε in operator norm by `f ∘ U` for some `U : S →L[𝕜] F` (`ContinuousLinearMap.denseRange_comp`), so ‖x‖ − ε‖x‖ ≤ ‖U x‖ ≤ ‖x‖ + ε‖x‖. Lean subtlety: the field assumptions `[NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] [CompleteSpace 𝕜]` (ℝ, ℂ, ℚ_p, …) are genuinely needed and not a restriction of the classical real/complex case — over the incomplete field ℚ, ℝ is not finitely representable in its dense subspace ℚ (by Dirichlet approximation of √2, no ℚ-linear map from span_ℚ{1, √2} to ℚ is almost isometric); both explicit hypotheses are load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses).

Correctly defined: `FinitelyRepresentable 𝕜 E F` says E is finitely representable in F, i.e. every finite-dimensional subspace of E sits linearly inside F with norm distortion as close to 1 as we like. Lean ↔ maths: the body is `∀ S : Submodule 𝕜 E, FiniteDimensional 𝕜 S → ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ T : S →L[𝕜] F, ∀ x : S, (1 - ε) * ‖x‖ ≤ ‖T x‖ ∧ ‖T x‖ ≤ (1 + ε) * ‖x‖`; `S : Submodule 𝕜 E` with `FiniteDimensional 𝕜 S` is an arbitrary finite-dimensional linear subspace E₀ ⊆ E, `‖x‖` for `x : S` is the norm of x in E (the subspace carries the restricted norm), `S →L[𝕜] F` is a bounded 𝕜-linear map E₀ → F, and the order ∀E₀ ∀ε ∃T lets T depend on both E₀ and ε (not one T for all ε). For ε < 1 the lower bound makes T injective with ‖T⁻¹‖ ≤ (1−ε)⁻¹ on T(E₀), so T is an isomorphism onto a subspace F₀ = T(E₀) with ‖T‖‖T⁻¹‖ ≤ (1+ε)/(1−ε); conversely over ℝ or ℂ an isomorphism with ‖T‖‖T⁻¹‖ < 1+ε, rescaled so that ‖T⁻¹‖ = 1, satisfies the two-sided bounds, and the file proves this equivalence (`TauCeti.finitelyRepresentable_iff_banachMazurDist_lt`), which is the form of Albiac–Kalton, Topics in Banach Space Theory, Def. 11.1.1 (as quoted verbatim in Rueda Zoca, arXiv:2207.08717, §2: for every finite-dimensional subspace E₀ of X and ε > 0 a subspace F₀ of Y and a linear continuous bijection T : E₀ → F₀ with ‖T‖‖T⁻¹‖ ≤ 1 + ε). Lean subtlety: for ε ≥ 1 the lower bound (1−ε)‖x‖ ≤ ‖T x‖ is vacuous (T = 0 satisfies the bounds), which is harmless because the definition demands every ε > 0, so small ε are always required; and the definition is stated over any `NormedField 𝕜`, where (e.g. for ℚ_p) the two-sided form is strictly stronger than the Banach–Mazur form since scalars of arbitrary norm are not available for rescaling — the implementation notes say so, and the classical notion (real or complex Banach spaces) is the case where they agree; completeness of E, F is not assumed, which is harmless since F and its completion are interchangeable (`TauCeti.finitelyRepresentable_completion_iff`). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: witness — ℝ is finitely representable in every nonzero real normed space (via `LinearIsometry.toSpanSingleton`), compiled; non-witnesses compiled — ℝ is not finitely representable in the zero space, and ℓ∞² (sup norm on `Fin 2 → ℝ`) is not finitely representable in any real inner product space (parallelogram law at ε = 1/10); no Mathlib or other Tau Ceti definition of the notion; the roadmap B7 asks for exactly this small-distortion definition.

The elimination rule: from `h : FinitelyRepresentable 𝕜 E F`, a subspace `S` with `[FiniteDimensional 𝕜 S]` and `0 < ε` it gives `T : S →L[𝕜] F` with (1−ε)‖x‖ ≤ ‖T x‖ ≤ (1+ε)‖x‖ for every x ∈ S, which is the definition applied to S and ε (finite-dimensionality passed as an instance instead of an explicit hypothesis).
`FinitelyRepresentable 𝕜 E E`: every normed space is finitely representable in itself, by the identity isometry (`LinearIsometry.id.finitelyRepresentable`); reflexivity of the relation.

If E is finitely representable in F then so is every subspace `S : Submodule 𝕜 E` (with the restricted norm, no finite-dimensionality assumed): `S.subtypeₗᵢ` is an isometric embedding S → E, so S is finitely representable in E (`LinearIsometry.finitelyRepresentable`), then transitivity.

Transitivity with the hypotheses the right way round: `FinitelyRepresentable 𝕜 E F` and `FinitelyRepresentable 𝕜 F G` give `FinitelyRepresentable 𝕜 E G`. The proof embeds a finite-dimensional S ⊆ E into F by T with distortion 1 ± δ, then the finite-dimensional range `LinearMap.range T` into G by U, and uses `U ∘ T.rangeRestrict`; with δ = min(ε, 1)/3, (1+δ)² ≤ 1+ε and (1−δ)² ≥ 1−ε. Red-team: the real specialisation compiles; axioms are propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

`FinitelyRepresentable 𝕜 (UniformSpace.Completion E) E`: the completion Ê of a normed space is finitely representable in E. `UniformSpace.Completion E` is Mathlib's completion with its normed-space structure, and E sits in it isometrically with dense range via `UniformSpace.Completion.toComplₗᵢ` (`denseRange_coe`), so this is `LinearIsometry.finitelyRepresentable_of_denseRange` for that embedding, under the same complete nontrivially normed field 𝕜.

`FinitelyRepresentable 𝕜 E (UniformSpace.Completion F) ↔ FinitelyRepresentable 𝕜 E F`: E is finitely representable in the completion F̂ iff it is in F. ← composes with the isometric embedding F → F̂ (`toComplₗᵢ.finitelyRepresentable`) by transitivity; → composes with `finitelyRepresentable_completion` (F̂ is finitely representable in F). Red-team: the complex specialisation with E = F (E and Ê each finitely representable in the other) compiles.

The unfolding of `FinitelyRepresentable 𝕜 E F` (proved by `Iff.rfl`): it holds iff each finite-dimensional `S : Submodule 𝕜 E` and each real ε > 0 admit a continuous linear `T : S →L[𝕜] F` with (1−ε)‖x‖ ≤ ‖T x‖ ≤ (1+ε)‖x‖ for all x ∈ S, the definition verbatim; it is the public way to unfold it (used by `TauCeti.finitelyRepresentable_doubleDual`).

Correctly stated: over ℝ or ℂ, E is finitely representable in F iff for every finite-dimensional subspace E₀ ⊆ E and every ε > 0 some subspace F₀ ⊆ F is isomorphic to E₀ at Banach–Mazur distance d(E₀, F₀) < 1 + ε — the classical definition, Albiac–Kalton, Topics in Banach Space Theory, Def. 11.1.1 (as quoted verbatim in Rueda Zoca, arXiv:2207.08717, §2: for every finite-dimensional subspace E₀ of X and ε > 0 a subspace F₀ of Y and a linear continuous bijection T : E₀ → F₀ with ‖T‖‖T⁻¹‖ ≤ 1 + ε). Lean ↔ maths: `[RCLike 𝕜]` means 𝕜 = ℝ or ℂ; the left side is the file's two-sided definition; on the right, `G : Submodule 𝕜 F` is F₀ with the restricted norm, `Nonempty (S ≃L[𝕜] G)` says a linear homeomorphism E₀ ≅ F₀ exists, and `banachMazurDist 𝕜 S G` is by definition `⨅ T : S ≃L[𝕜] G, ‖T‖ * ‖T.symm‖`, i.e. inf ‖T‖‖T⁻¹‖; by `banachMazurDist_lt_iff`, when an isomorphism exists d < r iff some T has ‖T‖‖T⁻¹‖ < r, so the right side reads ∀E₀ ∀ε ∃F₀ ∃T with ‖T‖‖T⁻¹‖ < 1 + ε, equivalent to Albiac–Kalton's ≤ 1 + ε because ε is arbitrary. The proof: → takes δ = ε/(ε+3), so the 1 ± δ embedding has ‖T‖‖T⁻¹‖ ≤ (1+δ)/(1−δ) < 1+ε; ← rescales T by the scalar ‖T⁻¹‖ ∈ ℝ ⊆ 𝕜, giving ‖x‖ ≤ ‖T′x‖ ≤ (1+ε)‖x‖. Lean subtlety: `banachMazurDist` is an infimum in ℝ, which takes the junk value 0 (`Real.iInf_of_isEmpty`) when there is no isomorphism, so without the `Nonempty (S ≃L[𝕜] G)` conjunct the right side would hold vacuously; the conjunct is there and excludes this — compiled: for E = ℝ and F the zero space the guarded right side is false (as is the left side), while the unguarded `∃ G, banachMazurDist ℝ ⊤ G < 1 + 1` is true by the junk value; the zero subspace S = 0 satisfies both sides (distance 0, T = 0), consistently. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; the definition's witness and non-witness tests compile; the hypothesis RCLike could be weakened to a complete densely normed field (recorded MINOR, not a correctness issue: the docstring claims only ℝ or ℂ).

It suffices to check the definition for 0 < ε < 1: if every finite-dimensional `S : Submodule 𝕜 E` and every ε with `0 < ε` and `ε < 1` admit `T : S →L[𝕜] F` with the bounds (1−ε)‖x‖ ≤ ‖T x‖ ≤ (1+ε)‖x‖, then `FinitelyRepresentable 𝕜 E F`; correct because the bounds for min(ε, 1/2) imply those for ε, the interval [1−ε, 1+ε] growing with ε.

Correctly stated: for m = n + 2 ≥ 2 and X (m−1)-connected at x, the Hurewicz map π_m(X, x) → H_m(X; ℤ), [p] ↦ p_*[I^m], is a bijection. Lean ↔ mathematics: the function is `a ↦ (hurewicz (ModuleCat.of ℤ ℤ) (n + 1) a).hom 1`, where `HomotopyGroup.hurewicz R k` is the Hurewicz map in degree k + 1 (so index n + 1 is degree n + 2), defined on a representative p by `GenLoop.hurewicz`: the generator of H_{n+2}(I^{n+2}, ∂I^{n+2}; ℤ) ≅ ℤ pushed forward along p : (I^{n+2}, ∂I^{n+2}) → (X, {x}) and read in H_{n+2}(X; ℤ) through the quotient isomorphism H_{n+2}(X) ≅ H_{n+2}(X, {x}) (Hatcher's h([f]) = f_*(α), pp. 369–370); `.hom 1` evaluates the ℤ-linear map ℤ → H_{n+2}(X; ℤ) at 1, giving the class itself; `Function.Bijective` is injective and surjective; hX is (n+1)-connectedness exactly as in `hurewiczAddEquiv` (k = 0 is path-connectedness via `TauCeti.pathConnectedSpace_iff_subsingleton_homotopyGroup_zero`, k = 1 simple connectivity; compiled). Lean subtlety: the index shift (`hurewicz R k` lives in degree k + 1) is bookkeeping only; X : Type is universe 0 only (MINOR generality finding); the statement concerns the underlying function, homomorphy being `HomotopyGroup.hurewicz_mul`; the fixed generator determines h up to a global sign, irrelevant for bijectivity; no junk values are involved (natural-number indices, no subtraction or division). Source: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 4.32 with the Hurewicz map of pp. 369–370 and Theorem 4.37 for A the basepoint. Checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; hX load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses) and satisfiable (the point and S^{n+2}, compiled); the proof composes the cubical Hurewicz equivalence with multiplication by a universal unit, and the relative Hurewicz theorem (Hurewicz/Relative.lean) consumes it.

Correctly stated: there is one sign ε = ±1 such that for every space X, point x and class a ∈ π_{n+2}(X, x), the Hurewicz class of a is ε times its cubical Hurewicz class transported to simplicial singular homology. Lean ↔ mathematics: `ℤˣ` is the unit group {1, −1} of ℤ, and `∃ ε, ∀ X x a` puts the sign before the space, so it is universal (independent of X, x and a), as the docstring says; `(hurewicz (ModuleCat.of ℤ ℤ) (n + 1) a).hom 1` is the Hurewicz class p_*[I^{n+2}] in degree n + 2; `cubicalHurewicz ℤ (n + 1) a` is the class of the loop, viewed as a singular (n+2)-cube, in normalized cubical homology, and `(singularCubicalHomologyIso ℤ (TopCat.of X) (n + 2)).inv` is the inverse of the natural cubical–simplicial comparison isomorphism, so both sides lie in H_{n+2}(X; ℤ); `•` is the ℤ-scalar multiplication on that group. Lean subtlety: X ranges only over Type (universe 0), so 'every space' means every space of the lowest universe (MINOR generality finding); no connectivity hypothesis is needed, correctly, since both maps are defined for all spaces and are natural. Checks at 5f78b5307b: not true for a trivial reason — on S^{n+2} the left side at the tautological loop is a generator of H_{n+2}(S^{n+2}; ℤ) ≅ ℤ (`isIso_hurewicz_sphereGenLoop`, compiled), so it is nonzero; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; the proof reduces to the sphere through naturality of both maps and `GenLoop.map_toSphere_sphereGenLoop`, as the module docstring explains.

Correctly stated: this is the Hurewicz theorem with the Hurewicz map itself as the isomorphism — for m ≥ 2 and X (m−1)-connected at x, h : π_m(X, x) → H_m(X; ℤ) is an isomorphism of groups. Lean ↔ mathematics: the degree is written m = n + 2 with n : ℕ, which ranges over exactly m = 2, 3, …, so m = 1 (where h is only abelianisation) is excluded by the shape of the statement; `HomotopyGroup (Fin (n + 2)) X x` is Mathlib's π_{n+2}(X, x), classes of maps of the cube I^{n+2} sending its boundary to x, with the concatenation group law (`HomotopyGroup.mul_spec`), and `Additive` only renames that group law (abelian, as n + 2 ≥ 2) as +; the hypothesis `hX : ∀ k < n + 2, Subsingleton (HomotopyGroup (Fin k) X x)` says π_k(X, x) has at most one element for k = 0, …, n + 1, and as every π_k contains the constant class this is triviality, i.e. X is (n+1)-connected in Hatcher's sense (p. 346: π_i = 0 for i ≤ n + 1, 0-connected meaning path-connected): for k = 0, `HomotopyGroup (Fin 0) X x` is π₀ (the cube I⁰ is a point with empty boundary) and `TauCeti.pathConnectedSpace_iff_subsingleton_homotopyGroup_zero` turns its triviality into path-connectedness, and k = 1 is simple connectivity (a compiled probe derives `PathConnectedSpace X ∧ Subsingleton (π_ 1 X x)` from hX); the target `((singularHomologyFunctor (ModuleCat ℤ) (n + 2)).obj ℤ).obj X` is Mathlib's unreduced singular homology H_{n+2}(X; ℤ), definitionally the homology of `TauCeti.singularChains ℤ` (checked by `rfl`); `≃+` is an isomorphism of additive groups, and `hurewiczAddEquiv_apply` fixes its forward map as `hurewiczHom` evaluated at 1 ∈ ℤ, i.e. `GenLoop.hurewicz`: [p] ↦ j⁻¹(p_*(α)) with α the generator `singularHomologyCubeBoundaryPairIso` of H_{n+2}(I^{n+2}, ∂I^{n+2}; ℤ) ≅ ℤ, p_* induced by p : (I^{n+2}, ∂I^{n+2}) → (X, {x}), and j : H_{n+2}(X) ≅ H_{n+2}(X, {x}) the quotient isomorphism — Hatcher's h([f]) = f_*(α) (pp. 369–370) with the cube modulo its boundary in place of the disk or sphere. Lean subtlety: X : Type is universe 0 only (the ℤ-coefficient chain complexes live over TopCat.{0}); every space met in practice lives there, and this is recorded as a MINOR generality finding, not a correctness issue; `Subsingleton` rather than '= 0' is harmless because π_k is never empty; Mathlib defines the group law on π_m through a classically chosen coordinate (`HomotopyGroup.group`), but `mul_spec` shows it is concatenation in any coordinate, and the order of concatenation is irrelevant in an abelian group; `hurewiczHom` is morphism-valued (ℤ ⟶ H) and evaluation at 1 is the identification Hom(ℤ, A) = A; α is one specific generator (through explicit cube and disk homeomorphisms), and the other choice changes the map by the global sign −1, which does not affect bijectivity; reduced and unreduced homology agree in degree n + 2 ≥ 1. Source: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 4.32 (if X is (n−1)-connected, n ≥ 2, then π_n(X) ≈ H_n(X)), the definition of h on pp. 369–370, and Theorem 4.37, which makes h itself the isomorphism and 'includes the absolute form of the theorem by taking A to be the basepoint'; every part of hX is needed (S² ⊔ S² has π₂ = ℤ but H₂ = ℤ²; a nontrivial π₁-action puts [γ][f] − [f] in ker h, Hatcher p. 370; spheres have nonzero homotopy above their dimension with zero homology there, Hatcher p. 367). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only; hX satisfiable (compiled for the one-point space and for S^{n+2} via `subsingleton_homotopyGroup_sphere_of_lt`) and the statement non-vacuous: composed with `reducedSingularHomologySphereIso` it gives a compiled π_{n+2}(S^{n+2}) ≃+ ℤ, whose value on the tautological loop is that loop's Hurewicz class, a generator (`isIso_hurewicz_sphereGenLoop`); the specialisation n = 0 gives π₂(X) ≃+ H₂(X; ℤ) for path-connected, simply connected X (compiled); hX load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses); no Mathlib counterpart (the pinned Mathlib has no Hurewicz theorem: git grep, leansearch, leanfinder, loogle).

Correctly stated: the forward map of `hurewiczAddEquiv hX` sends a to `(hurewiczHom (ModuleCat.of ℤ ℤ) (n + 1) a).hom 1`, the Hurewicz homomorphism in degree n + 2 evaluated at 1 ∈ ℤ, i.e. [p] ↦ p_*[I^{n+2}] in H_{n+2}(X; ℤ); it is what makes the equivalence the Hurewicz isomorphism rather than an arbitrary one. Checked: holds by `AddEquiv.ofBijective_apply`; with it `simp` proves `hurewiczAddEquiv hX a = (hurewicz (ModuleCat.of ℤ ℤ) (n + 1) a.toMul).hom 1` (compiled).

(1) Claim: on a Hausdorff smooth manifold M modelled on a finite-dimensional real space, with boundary or corners allowed, a C^r differential form φ of positive degree k+1 (r ≥ 1, r = ∞ allowed) with values in a Banach space F that is closed on a neighbourhood of x is, on some neighbourhood U of x, the exterior derivative dψ of a C^r k-form ψ defined on all of M: the Poincaré lemma in its local (germ) form. (2) Lean ↔ mathematics: `RoughForm I M F (k + 1)` is by definition (an abbrev) the type of dependent functions y ↦ continuous alternating (k+1)-linear map T_yM → F, i.e. an arbitrary F-valued (k+1)-form with no regularity; `IsSmoothForm I r φ` unfolds (`isSmoothForm_def`, proved by Iff.rfl) to `ContMDiff` of order r of the section y ↦ (y, φ y) into the total space of the alternating bundle, whose charts are Mathlib's alternating-map bundle charts built from the tangent-bundle trivialisations, so it says φ is a C^r section; `mextDeriv φ y` is by definition (`mextDeriv_def`) Mathlib's flat `extDerivWithin` of the chart expression `φ.inChartAt y` (φ pulled back along the inverse of the preferred extended chart at y) within `range I`, at the chart point of y, which is the coordinate definition of d with derivatives taken inside the model half-space or quadrant at boundary and corner points, and over a vector space `mextDeriv_eq_extDeriv` identifies it with Mathlib's `extDeriv`, for which `extDeriv_apply` gives dω(v₀,…,v_k) = Σᵢ (−1)^i D(ω(…v̂ᵢ…))(vᵢ). Hypotheses: `hr : 1 ≤ r` with `r : ℕ∞` means r ∈ {1, 2, …, ∞}; `hφ` is 'φ is C^r'; `hclosed : ∀ᶠ y in 𝓝 x, mextDeriv φ y = 0` is 'dφ = 0 on a neighbourhood of x'; `[IsManifold I ∞ M]` is a smooth atlas; `[FiniteDimensional ℝ E]` and `[T2Space M]` are finite dimension and Hausdorffness, used only to get a smooth bump function; `[CompleteSpace F]` is completeness of the coefficients, which is needed (the docstring's c₀₀-valued smooth 1-form on ℝ has no local primitive). Conclusion: `∃ U ∈ 𝓝 x, ∃ ψ : RoughForm I M F k, IsSmoothForm I r ψ ∧ ∀ y ∈ U, mextDeriv ψ y = φ y` says there are a neighbourhood U of x and a C^r k-form ψ on all of M with dψ = φ on U. U depends on φ, so this is the germ statement (every closed germ of positive degree is exact), not the statement with one neighbourhood for all closed forms; the germ form is what its consumers (local primitives, path integrals, H¹ of simply connected M) use. (3) Lean subtlety: `mextDeriv` is total, and through `fderivWithin` it returns 0 wherever the chart expression is not differentiable. So for a merely continuous φ (r = 0) the closedness hypothesis could hold vacuously while the conclusion fails: take g(x)dy on ℝ² with g continuous and nowhere differentiable; then mextDeriv is identically 0, but a ψ with dψ = g(x)dy near a point where g ≠ 0 would force ∂ₓψ = 0 and ∂ᵧψ = g(x), so g would be locally constant. `hr : 1 ≤ r` excludes this. With it, mextDeriv φ and mextDeriv ψ are both genuine derivatives (φ and ψ are C^r, r ≥ 1), independent of the chart by `IsSmoothForm.inChartAt_mextDeriv_eq`. The normalisation of d (Mathlib uses no 1/(k+1) factor) does not matter, since rescaling d degree by degree does not change which forms are exact. `r : ℕ∞` leaves out the analytic order ω. (4) It matches the Tau Ceti roadmap's DifferentialGeometry item 6.2, which asks for exactly this manifold corollary `exists_mextDeriv_eq_nhds` of the relative flat lemma, with complete coefficients and the c₀₀ caveat. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b, all compiled: specialised to the closed form dx on ℝ, the conclusion yields g : ℝ → ℝ differentiable with g' = 1 near 0, so it cannot be met by junk values; over 𝓘(ℝ, E) it gives the flat statement for Mathlib's `extDeriv`; it applies at every point of the half-plane 𝓡∂ 2 and of [0,1]×[0,1] (boundary and corners). `lean_minimal_hypotheses` finds hr, hφ and hclosed all load-bearing. There is no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate (Mathlib has only the convex 1-form flat case). Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Relational structures whose empty tuples are back-and-forth equivalent at level ω are elementarily equivalent `M ≅[L] N`. `BFEquiv ω 0 Fin.elim0 Fin.elim0` is equivalence at every finite level (the limit clause), first-order sentences have finite quantifier rank (`qrank_toInf_lt_omega0`), so the previous theorem gives agreement on each `toInf φ`, and `Sentence.realize_toInf` transfers this to first-order truth. Lean subtlety: ω is taken in an arbitrary ordinal universe `o` and the carrier used is `PUnit`; only the true direction is claimed (the converse fails for infinite languages).

Tuples that are back-and-forth equivalent at level α satisfy the same infinitary formulas of quantifier rank ≤ α, at any carrier. `BFEquiv α n a b` is the ordinal EF relation (level 0: same atomic type; α+1: level α plus forth and back into level α; limits: all lower levels); `φ.qrank` is 0 on atoms, max on `imp`, successor under ∀ and the supremum over infinitary branches, the usual quantifier rank. Lean subtlety: `qrank` takes values in `Ordinal.{uκ}` and α in `Ordinal.{o}`, so the hypothesis compares them after `Ordinal.lift` to a common universe; lifting is an order embedding, so it says exactly qrank φ ≤ α.

`InfEquivAt κ M N` says that M and N satisfy the same L_{∞ω} sentences whose infinitary conjunctions and disjunctions are indexed by κ, i.e. agreement on all sentences with big connectives of size at most |κ|. Lean ↔ maths: the body is `∀ φ : L.SentenceInf κ, φ.Realize M ↔ φ.Realize N`; `L.SentenceInf κ` is `BoundedFormulaInf L κ Empty 0`, the inductive type with `falsum`, term equations, relation atoms, `imp`, `all` (∀ over the last bound slot) and `iSup`/`iInf` over families `κ → formula`, so it is the set of L_{∞ω} sentences whose big connectives are indexed by κ; families of any size ≤ |κ| are expressed by padding with ⊤/⊥ along an `IndexCoding` (`iInfAlong`/`iSupAlong`, `realize_iInfAlong : … ↔ ∀ i, …`); `Realize` is Tarski semantics (`iInf` = ∀ i, `iSup` = ∃ i, `all` = ∀ y in the structure) under the empty valuations. Lean subtlety: one carrier per formula, in its own universe `uκ` independent of the universes of M and N, so this is the bounded fragment, not full L_{∞ω}-equivalence (that is `InfEquivW`, which quantifies over carriers outside the syntax); structures may be empty in Mathlib, and then `∃ x, ⊤` separates an empty from a nonempty structure, as it should. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: compiled `¬ InfEquivAt κ Empty Unit` (empty language) for every κ, including an empty carrier; compiled that two empty structures differing only on a nullary relation are separated at every κ by the atomic sentence; compiled (relational L) that for encodable structures `InfEquivAt ℕ M N ↔ InfEquivW M N`.

Agreement on the κ-carried infinitary sentences, for any κ and any language, implies elementary equivalence `M ≅[L] N` (Mathlib's: the same first-order sentences hold). Each first-order `L.Sentence` embeds as `BoundedFormula.toInf φ` at every carrier and `Sentence.realize_toInf` says the embedding preserves truth, so L_{ωω} ⊆ L_{∞ω}. Lean subtlety: `toInf` uses only the primitive `falsum`/`equal`/`rel`/`imp`/`all`, so this holds even for an empty carrier, and no relational hypothesis is needed.

Agreement at one carrier into which both structures are coded already gives full L_{∞ω}-equivalence (relational L): `InfEquivAt κ M N` with `IndexCoding M κ`, `IndexCoding N κ` implies `InfEquivW M N`, by Karp's converse (`InfEquivAt.potentialIso`) followed by the forward direction at every carrier. Lean subtlety: it carries `[L.IsRelational]` from the section although the docstring does not say so (recorded as a docs nit).

Agreement at carrier κ gives agreement at every carrier ι with an `IndexCoding ι κ` (an injection ι → κ with a left-inverse decoder, i.e. |ι| ≤ |κ|): sentences with smaller connectives are among those with larger ones (L_{λω} ⊆ L_{μω} for λ ≤ μ). The proof sends an ι-sentence φ to `BoundedFormulaInf.reindex c φ` and uses `realize_reindex` (reindexing preserves meaning). Lean subtlety: the coding is data with a decoder rather than a bare injection; classically every injection has such a decoder, so nothing is lost.

Karp's theorem, converse direction: relational structures that are both coded into κ and agree on the κ-carried L_{∞ω} sentences are potentially isomorphic. `cM : IndexCoding M κ` and `cN : IndexCoding N κ` say |M|, |N| ≤ |κ|, so conjunctions over the elements of M and of N are κ-carried sentences; the proof takes S = the pairs of tuples that agree on every κ-carried formula and checks it is a tuple back-and-forth system (forth with `cN`, back with `cM`), hence a potential isomorphism (`PotentialIso M N` is ∃ S, a nonempty set of `FGEquiv M N` (isomorphisms between finitely generated substructures, which in a relational language are finite) such that every f ∈ S extends within S to a g whose domain contains any given m ∈ M, and to one whose range contains any given n ∈ N (`f ≤ g` = g extends f); this is the partial-isomorphism relation A ≅_p B (SEP uses arbitrary substructures; restricting such a family to its finite sub-maps gives an FG family with the same extension property, so the notions agree)). Lean subtlety: both codings are used (forth needs a conjunction of size |N|, back one of size |M|); the carrier's universe is independent of those of M and N. Source: Bell, 'Infinitary Logic', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, §2 (direction A ≡_{∞ω} B ⇒ A ≅_p B).

`InfEquivW M N` is L_{∞ω}-equivalence M ≡_{∞ω} N: M and N satisfy the same infinitary sentences, with conjunctions and disjunctions of any size available in the universe of M ⊕ N. Lean ↔ maths: the body is `∀ κ : Type (max w w'), InfEquivAt κ M N` (M : Type w, N : Type w'); since `InfEquivAt κ` covers every sentence whose connectives have size ≤ |κ| (padding along `IndexCoding`), this is agreement on every sentence whose connectives are bounded by a cardinal of `Type (max w w')`, in particular by |M ⊕ N|, which is the size Karp's converse needs. Lean subtlety (universes, the key point): real L_{∞ω} is a proper class with conjunctions of arbitrary set size, which no single Lean universe captures; here the carriers range over `Type (max w w')`, the universe of M ⊕ N itself, not a smaller universe, so M ⊕ N is an admissible carrier; and `InfEquivW.infEquivAt` (relational L) proves that `InfEquivW` already gives agreement at carriers in every universe, so the definition is equivalent to unrestricted ≡_{∞ω}, not weaker; the quantification over carriers is outside the syntax (each sentence has one carrier). Sources: Bell, 'Infinitary Logic', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, §2 (A ≡_{∞ω} B); TauCetiRoadmap Completed/InfinitaryLogic README (Standing hypotheses, 'Carriers (Karp)'; Layer 1) (full equivalence quantifies over carriers outside the syntax). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: compiled `InfEquivW ℚ ℝ` for the orders and agreement at the carrier `ULift.{3} (Set ℝ)` (a universe above both structures); compiled `¬ InfEquivW Empty Unit`; checked by `Iff.rfl` that for `M : Type`, `N : Type 1` it quantifies over `Type 1`.

Full equivalence, stated with carriers in the universe of M ⊕ N, gives agreement at carriers in any universe uμ (relational L): `InfEquivW M N → InfEquivAt μ M N` for `μ : Type uμ`, via `karp_theorem` (InfEquivW ⇒ PotentialIso ⇒ agreement at every carrier). This shows `InfEquivW` is not weaker than unrestricted L_{∞ω}-equivalence. Lean subtlety: universe uμ is arbitrary, including universes above those of M and N; the relational hypothesis comes from the section.

Pairs (a,b) of a tuple back-and-forth system satisfy the same infinitary formulas at every carrier κ. `IsTupleBFSystem S` is the standard back-and-forth set of pairs of equal-length finite tuples: it contains the empty pair, every pair has the same atomic type (`SameAtomicType`: the same equalities and relations among positions, nullary relations included), and it has forth and back extensions within S; the conclusion is `φ.Realize v a ↔ φ.Realize w b` for every `φ : L.BoundedFormulaInf κ Empty n` (the valuations of the empty set of free variables are vacuous). Lean subtlety: in a relational language every term is a variable (`Term.exists_eq_var_inr_of_isRelational`), which is why atomic type decides the atomic formulas.

Karp's theorem, forward direction: potentially isomorphic relational structures satisfy the same κ-carried L_{∞ω} sentences, for every carrier κ in any universe. `PotentialIso M N` is ∃ S, a nonempty set of `FGEquiv M N` (isomorphisms between finitely generated substructures, which in a relational language are finite) such that every f ∈ S extends within S to a g whose domain contains any given m ∈ M, and to one whose range contains any given n ∈ N (`f ≤ g` = g extends f); this is the partial-isomorphism relation A ≅_p B (SEP uses arbitrary substructures; restricting such a family to its finite sub-maps gives an FG family with the same extension property, so the notions agree); `[L.IsRelational]` means no function or constant symbols; `InfEquivAt κ M N` is agreement on κ-carried sentences. Lean subtlety: the carrier universe `uκ` is free, so this gives agreement at arbitrarily large carriers. Source: Bell, 'Infinitary Logic', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, §2 (Karp's partial isomorphism theorem, direction A ≅_p B ⇒ A ≡_{∞ω} B, there for any similar structures; here for relational ones).

For countable relational structures: M and N satisfy the same L_{ω₁ω} sentences iff they are isomorphic. Lean ↔ maths: `InfEquivAt ℕ M N` is agreement on sentences whose big connectives are indexed by ℕ, i.e. countable conjunctions and disjunctions: exactly L_{ω₁ω} (finite families via padding); `Nonempty (M ≃[L] N)` is the existence of an L-isomorphism; `[Countable M] [Countable N]` code both structures into ℕ (`IndexCoding.ofEncodable`), so `karp_theorem_at` at carrier ℕ turns agreement into potential isomorphism, and the countable back-and-forth (`countable_potentialIso_iff_iso`) turns that into isomorphism. Lean subtlety: no countability of the language is assumed (the converse conjoins over elements, not symbols); the countability of both structures is needed: `InfEquivW ℚ ℝ` (compiled) gives `InfEquivAt ℕ ℚ ℝ` while ℚ ≄ ℝ. Source: TauCetiRoadmap Completed/InfinitaryLogic README (Standing hypotheses, 'Carriers (Karp)'; Layer 1) (Layer 1 countable corollary). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: consumed by `not_infEquivAt_nat_int_sumLex_int` (ℤ vs ℤ ⊕ₗ ℤ); axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

The forth step of Karp's converse: if a ∈ Mⁿ and b ∈ Nⁿ satisfy the same κ-carried formulas (`hab`, over all `L.BoundedFormulaInf κ Empty n`) and N is coded into κ (`cN : IndexCoding N κ`, |N| ≤ |κ|), then each x ∈ M has a y ∈ N with the extended tuples `Fin.snoc a x`, `Fin.snoc b y` again satisfying the same κ-carried formulas. The proof is Karp's: otherwise choose for every y a formula ψ_y true at (a,x) and false at (b,y); then ∃z ⋀_{y∈N} ψ_y (the conjunction is `iInfAlong cN ψ`, κ-carried because of the coding) holds at a but not at b. Lean subtlety: the separating formulas are picked by classical choice (`by_contra`, `choose`); no relational hypothesis is needed; the coding of N is load-bearing (`lean_minimal_hypotheses`).

`InfEquivAt κ M N ↔ ∀ φ : L.SentenceInf κ, φ.Realize M ↔ φ.Realize N`: the unfolding of the definition (whose body is not exposed to importing modules), by `Iff.rfl`; it is the API downstream files use to apply the definition.

Agreement at κ is agreement of `φ.Realize Empty.elim Fin.elim0` for all `φ : L.BoundedFormulaInf κ Empty 0`, i.e. sentences read as bounded formulas with no free variables (`Empty.elim`) and no bound slots (`Fin.elim0`), via `SentenceInf.realize_def`/`FormulaInf.realize_def`. Lean subtlety: `Fin 0 → M` has exactly one element even when M is empty, so the `default` valuation used by `SentenceInf.Realize` equals `Fin.elim0` and nothing is lost.
`InfEquivW M N ↔ ∀ κ : Type (max w w'), InfEquivAt κ M N`: the unfolding of the unexposed definition, by `Iff.rfl`; full equivalence is agreement at every carrier in the universe of M ⊕ N.

Karp's theorem: relational structures M, N of arbitrary cardinality are potentially isomorphic iff they are L_{∞ω}-equivalent; no countability. Lean ↔ maths: the statement is `PotentialIso M N ↔ InfEquivW M N` under `[L.IsRelational]` (no function or constant symbols), with M : Type w, N : Type w' in independent universes and no other hypothesis; `PotentialIso M N` is ∃ S, a nonempty set of `FGEquiv M N` (isomorphisms between finitely generated substructures, which in a relational language are finite) such that every f ∈ S extends within S to a g whose domain contains any given m ∈ M, and to one whose range contains any given n ∈ N (`f ≤ g` = g extends f); this is the partial-isomorphism relation A ≅_p B (SEP uses arbitrary substructures; restricting such a family to its finite sub-maps gives an FG family with the same extension property, so the notions agree); `InfEquivW M N` is `∀ κ : Type (max w w'), InfEquivAt κ M N`, agreement on all sentences whose big connectives are indexed by a carrier in the universe of M ⊕ N (`L.SentenceInf κ` is `BoundedFormulaInf L κ Empty 0`, the inductive type with `falsum`, term equations, relation atoms, `imp`, `all` (∀ over the last bound slot) and `iSup`/`iInf` over families `κ → formula`, so it is the set of L_{∞ω} sentences whose big connectives are indexed by κ; families of any size ≤ |κ| are expressed by padding with ⊤/⊥ along an `IndexCoding` (`iInfAlong`/`iSupAlong`, `realize_iInfAlong : … ↔ ∀ i, …`); `Realize` is Tarski semantics (`iInf` = ∀ i, `iSup` = ∃ i, `all` = ∀ y in the structure) under the empty valuations). Lean subtlety: universes are the whole point: L_{∞ω} is a proper class, and here the carriers range over `Type (max w w')`, which contains M ⊕ N (the carrier the converse uses, with conjunctions over the elements of both structures), not a smaller universe; and `InfEquivW.infEquivAt` derives agreement at carriers in every universe, so the right side is equivalent to unrestricted ≡_{∞ω} and is not weaker; relational only, as the docstring and the roadmap's standing hypotheses say (SEP states it for all similar structures); no junk values (both sides are propositions). Sources: Bell, 'Infinitary Logic', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, §2 (Karp's partial isomorphism theorem A ≡_{∞ω} B ⇔ A ≅_p B, with the same back-and-forth family); TauCetiRoadmap Completed/InfinitaryLogic README (Standing hypotheses, 'Carriers (Karp)'; Layer 1). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: compiled `InfEquivW ℚ ℝ` (orders; not isomorphic, ℝ uncountable) and agreement at the carrier `ULift.{3} (Set ℝ)`; compiled that isomorphic `M : Type`, `N : Type 2` are `InfEquivW`; compiled that two empty structures differing on a nullary relation are not potentially isomorphic, read off `karp_theorem.1` and the atomic sentence; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; the file elaborates in about 1 s.

Karp's theorem at a common carrier: for relational L and codings of M and N into κ, M and N are potentially isomorphic iff they satisfy the same κ-carried L_{∞ω} sentences. `PotentialIso M N ↔ InfEquivAt κ M N` with `cM : IndexCoding M κ`, `cN : IndexCoding N κ` (|M|, |N| ≤ |κ|); `PotentialIso M N` is ∃ S, a nonempty set of `FGEquiv M N` (isomorphisms between finitely generated substructures, which in a relational language are finite) such that every f ∈ S extends within S to a g whose domain contains any given m ∈ M, and to one whose range contains any given n ∈ N (`f ≤ g` = g extends f); this is the partial-isomorphism relation A ≅_p B (SEP uses arbitrary substructures; restricting such a family to its finite sub-maps gives an FG family with the same extension property, so the notions agree); `InfEquivAt κ` is agreement on sentences whose big connectives have size ≤ |κ|. Lean subtlety: the codings are what makes the separating conjunctions expressible at κ; with κ := M ⊕ N and the sum codings they always exist (compiled), so the hypotheses are never contradictory. Sources: Bell, 'Infinitary Logic', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, §2; TauCetiRoadmap Completed/InfinitaryLogic README (Standing hypotheses, 'Carriers (Karp)'; Layer 1) (common-carrier headline). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: no False from the hypotheses (sum codings); axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

For T between Banach spaces and a continuous linear `W : F →L[𝕜] G` into a Hausdorff topological 𝕜-module: `↑W ∘ₗ T` is continuous iff `T.separatingSpace ≤ ker ↑W`, i.e. iff W vanishes on S(T). ⇒ is `separatingSpace_le_ker_of_continuous_comp` (needs `[T2Space G]`); ⇐ factors W ∘ T as `liftQL W` ∘ (mkQ ∘ T) and uses `continuous_mkQ_comp`. With W = N.mkQL for a closed N it says S(T) is the smallest closed subspace modulo which T is continuous, as the module docstring states.

Correctly stated: a linear map T : E → F between Banach spaces is continuous iff S(T) = {0}. Lean ↔ maths: `E`, `F` are `NormedAddCommGroup` + `NormedSpace 𝕜` + `CompleteSpace` over a `NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜` (covering ℝ, ℂ and complete nonarchimedean fields), i.e. Banach spaces; `T : E →ₗ[𝕜] F` is an arbitrary linear map, not assumed bounded; `Continuous T` is continuity for the norm topologies; `T.separatingSpace = ⊥` says S(T) is the zero submodule. ⇒ is `separatingSpace_eq_bot_of_continuous` (normed spaces are Hausdorff); ⇐ turns S(T) = 0 into a closed graph (`isClosed_graph_iff_separatingSpace_eq_bot`) and applies Mathlib's closed graph theorem `LinearMap.continuous_of_isClosed_graph`. Lean subtlety: none — no junk values; completeness is exactly what ⇐ needs (standard example, not compiled: d/dx on C¹[0,1] with the sup norm has closed graph, hence S = 0, yet is unbounded). Source: Grønbæk, Proc. Edinburgh Math. Soc. 25 (1982), p. 35: 'By the closed graph theorem T is continuous if and only if S(T) = (0)' for T between Banach algebras; Bosch, García, Gilsdorf, Gómez-Wulschner, Vera, arXiv:2003.14164, Props. 2.2–2.3 in seminorm form. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; specialised to the identity of ℝ (gives ⊥); the compiled ℓ¹ witness (S(T) = ℝ for f ↦ Σ n·f(n) on finitely supported sequences) confirms S can be nonzero, its discontinuity following from the forward direction; consumed by AutomaticContinuity/Commutative, SeparatingIdeal/Semisimple and Derivation.

For T between Banach spaces, `Continuous (T.separatingSpace.mkQ ∘ₗ T)`: T becomes continuous after passing to F ⧸ S(T). The quotient is Banach because S(T) is closed (`isClosed_separatingSpace` supplies the `IsClosed` instance inside the proof), the composite has closed graph (`isClosed_graph_mkQ_comp`), and the closed graph theorem applies. Lean subtlety: on `F ⧸ T.separatingSpace` the quotient topology and the quotient-norm topology agree up to reducible defeq (compiled `with_reducible_and_instances rfl`), so `Continuous` here means continuity into the quotient topology and there is no instance diamond.

Correctly stated: Sinclair's stability lemma, with exact intertwining weakened to intertwining up to continuous errors — for Banach E, F, a linear T : E → F and continuous linear R n on E, S n on F with each S n T − T R n continuous, the closures of S₀⋯S_{n−1}(S(T)) are eventually constant. Lean ↔ maths: `R : ℕ → E →L[𝕜] E` and `S : ℕ → F →L[𝕜] F` are bounded operators; `hRS : ∀ n, Continuous (↑(S n) ∘ₗ T - T ∘ₗ ↑(R n))` says S_n T − T R_n is continuous (exact intertwining is the case where the difference is 0 — compiled); `V` with `hV0 : V 0 = id` and `hV : V (n + 1) = (V n).comp (S n)` is forced to be V n = S 0 ∘ S 1 ∘ ⋯ ∘ S (n−1), with S 0 outermost as in Sinclair's R₁⋯R_n (such V exists for every S — compiled); `(T.separatingSpace.map ↑(V n)).topologicalClosure` is closure(V_n 𝔊(T)); `Filter.EventuallyConst … atTop` is ∃ N, ∀ n ≥ N, equality with the N-th term (`Filter.eventuallyConst_atTop`). Source: Sinclair, Automatic Continuity of Linear Operators, Lemma 1.6 (p. 11), as quoted in Bosch, García, Gilsdorf, Gómez-Wulschner, Vera, arXiv:2003.14164, Introduction: X, Y Banach, (T_n), (R_n) continuous operators on X, Y, S linear with S T_n = R_n S ⇒ ∃ N ∀ n ≥ N, closure(R₁⋯R_n 𝔊) = closure(R₁⋯R_N 𝔊); the Lean statement implies it with the letters renamed (Lean's R ↔ Sinclair's T_n, Lean's S ↔ Sinclair's R_n), and that specialisation compiles in the ∃ N, ∀ n ≥ N form. Lean subtlety: V is specified by recursion equations rather than defined, but they determine it uniquely, so nothing is hidden in the hypotheses; indexing from 0 adds the term V 0 = id (closure 𝔊(T) = 𝔊(T)), harmless for eventual constancy. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; hRS, hV0 and hV all load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses); consumed by `LinearMap.isSeparatingIdeal_separatingSpace` in SeparatingIdeal/Basic.

For T between Banach spaces and a closed subspace N (`[IsClosed (N : Set F)]`) with `¬ T.separatingSpace ≤ N`: for every δ > 0 and every real c there is x with ‖x‖ ≤ δ and c ≤ ‖N.mkQ (T x)‖ — modulo N, T sends arbitrarily small vectors to arbitrarily large ones (the contrapositive of 'q_N ∘ T bounded near 0 ⇒ continuous ⇒ q_N kills S(T)'). Lean subtlety: ‖N.mkQ y‖ is the quotient norm inf over n ∈ N of ‖y + n‖, and the `IsClosed` hypothesis is needed — for a dense proper N the quotient seminorm vanishes identically and the conclusion fails for c > 0; `0 < δ` is needed too (δ = 0 forces x = 0). The statement also holds without completeness (compiled).

`IsClosed (T.graph : Set (E × F)) ↔ T.separatingSpace = ⊥`: T has closed graph in the product topology iff its separating space is the zero submodule `⊥`. No Hausdorff assumption is needed: in a non-Hausdorff F neither side holds (closure{0} ⊆ S(T) and the graph is not closed). Combined with the closed graph theorem it gives the Banach continuity criterion.

`IsClosed ((T.separatingSpace.mkQ ∘ₗ T).graph)` in E × (F ⧸ S(T)): composing T with the quotient map by its separating space gives a map with closed graph, for arbitrary topological modules. `F ⧸ T.separatingSpace` carries the quotient topology; the proof pulls back along the open quotient map id × mkQ, under which the graph's preimage is closure(graph T) (by `mem_closure_graph_iff`).

`IsClosed (T.separatingSpace : Set F)`: the separating space is a closed subset of F, for any linear map between topological modules (no completeness or Hausdorff assumption): it is the preimage of the closed set closure(graph T) under the continuous map y ↦ (0, y). Same as Bosch, García, Gilsdorf, Gómez-Wulschner, Vera, arXiv:2003.14164, Corollary 2.1 ('G(T) is a σ-closed subspace of Y').

`T.separatingSpace.map ↑U ≤ (↑U ∘ₗ T).separatingSpace` for a continuous linear `U : F →L[R] G`: U(S(T)) ⊆ S(U ∘ T), because T x → y along x → 0 gives U(T x) → U y; `Submodule.map` is the image submodule and `↑U` the underlying linear map. Bosch, García, Gilsdorf, Gómez-Wulschner, Vera, arXiv:2003.14164, Prop. 4.3 states the same inclusion in seminorm form.

For continuous linear `U : F →L[R] G`, `V : E →L[R] D` and a linear `T' : D →ₗ[R] G` with `↑U ∘ₗ T - T' ∘ₗ ↑V` continuous: U(S(T)) ⊆ S(T'), by U(S(T)) ⊆ S(U ∘ T) = S(T' ∘ V) ⊆ S(T'). With T' = T this is the step showing that a map whose commutators with module actions are continuous has an invariant separating space, as used in SeparatingIdeal/Basic and Derivation.

`(x, y) ∈ closure (T.graph) ↔ y - T x ∈ T.separatingSpace`: the closure of the graph is the graph thickened vertically by S(T), i.e. {(x, T x + s) : s ∈ S(T)}; proved by subtracting (x, T x), which lies in the closed submodule closure(graph T) — with the correct order y − T x.

For first-countable E and F: y ∈ S(T) iff there is `x : ℕ → E` with `Tendsto x atTop (𝓝 0)` and `Tendsto (T ∘ x) atTop (𝓝 y)`, i.e. xₙ → 0 and T xₙ → y — the classical sequential definition (Grønbæk, Proc. Edinburgh Math. Soc. 25 (1982), p. 35; Sinclair's, quoted in Bosch, García, Gilsdorf, Gómez-Wulschner, Vera, arXiv:2003.14164). `[FirstCountableTopology E] [FirstCountableTopology F]` makes E × F first countable, so closure points are sequential limits (`mem_closure_iff_seq_limit`); it is needed only for ⇒, and normed spaces satisfy it. Red-team: used to prove S(T) = ℝ for the unbounded functional f ↦ Σ n·f(n) on finitely supported ℓ¹ (compiled).

`y ∈ T.separatingSpace ↔ MapClusterPt y (𝓝 0) T`: `MapClusterPt y (𝓝 0) T` means y is a cluster point of the filter `map T (𝓝 0)`, i.e. every neighbourhood V of y meets T(U) for every neighbourhood U of 0 — exactly (0, y) ∈ closure(graph T) through the product neighbourhood basis; this is the filter/net form of 'limits of T x as x → 0', valid without any countability.

`y ∈ T.separatingSpace ↔ ((0 : E), y) ∈ closure (T.graph : Set (E × F))`: y is in the separating space iff (0, y) lies in the closure of the graph of T in the product topology E × F — the defining property, obtained by unfolding `Submodule.comap` along `LinearMap.inr` (y ↦ (0, y)) and `Submodule.topologicalClosure_coe` (the closure submodule has the set closure as carrier).

Correctly defined: for a linear map T : E → F of topological R-modules, S(T) = {y ∈ F : (0, y) ∈ closure of the graph of T}, the separating space. Lean ↔ maths: the body `T.graph.topologicalClosure.comap (LinearMap.inr R E F)` takes `LinearMap.graph T` = {(x, T x)} ⊆ E × F, closes it in the product topology (`Submodule.topologicalClosure`, whose carrier is the set closure by `Submodule.topologicalClosure_coe`; the topology on `E × F` is the product instance), and pulls it back along `LinearMap.inr R E F : y ↦ (0, y)`, so membership is exactly `((0 : E), y) ∈ closure T.graph` (`mem_separatingSpace_iff_mem_closure`); being a `Submodule R F` records that S(T) is a linear subspace. In first-countable (e.g. normed) spaces this is the classical sequential definition, y ∈ S(T) iff some xₙ → 0 has T xₙ → y (`mem_separatingSpace_iff_exists_seq`, under `[FirstCountableTopology E] [FirstCountableTopology F]`), as in Grønbæk, Proc. Edinburgh Math.
