It is R²/4 at R = 1 (Wikipedia), not the variance 1 of the radius-2 law.

(1) A `ProjValMeasure X H` is a projection-valued measure on the measurable sets of a measurable space X, acting on a complex Hilbert space H. (2) The field `proj B hB : H →L[ℂ] H` assigns a bounded operator P(B) to each set B together with a proof `hB : MeasurableSet B`, so P lives on the σ-algebra only; `proj_univ` is P(X) = I (`ContinuousLinearMap.id`); `proj_inter` is P(B₁)P(B₂) = P(B₁ ∩ B₂), where `*` on `H →L[ℂ] H` is composition; `diag ξ : Measure X` with `diag_finite` (`IsFiniteMeasure`, i.e. diag ξ X < ∞) and `inner_proj` (⟪ξ, P(B)ξ⟫ = (diag ξ B).toReal) says that for every ξ the map B ↦ ⟨P(B)ξ, ξ⟩ is a finite, nonnegative, countably additive measure μ_ξ. These fields are equivalent to the textbook axioms (each P(B) an orthogonal projection, P(∅) = 0, P(X) = I, P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F), and P(⋃Eₙ)v = Σ P(Eₙ)v for disjoint Eₙ and every vector v): the file derives P(∅) = 0 (`proj_empty`), `IsStarProjection` (Mathlib's idempotent-and-self-adjoint, i.e. orthogonal projection) for every P(B), and strong — vector-wise, not operator-norm — countable additivity as a `HasSum` (`hasSum_proj_of_pairwise_disjoint`); conversely I compiled a constructor that takes exactly the textbook axioms (additivity as the strong limit of natural-order partial sums) and builds a `ProjValMeasure` with diag ξ := `Measure.ofMeasurable` (B ↦ ofReal re⟪ξ, P(B)ξ⟫), so the structure is neither stronger nor weaker than the standard notion, and `diag` adds no freedom (`ext` recovers it from `proj`). (3) Lean subtlety: `ENNReal.toReal ∞ = 0`, so `inner_proj` alone would not pin down diag (diag 0 could be an infinite measure); `diag_finite` excludes that. The measurability proof is an argument of `proj`, so there is no junk value on non-measurable sets, and `proj_congr` shows the value does not depend on which proof is given; Mathlib's `Measure` also assigns values to non-measurable sets (its outer-measure extension), but those are determined by the measurable-set values, which are all `inner_proj` constrains. The axiomatisation needs ℂ: over ℝ, real diagonal matrix elements would not force self-adjointness. Mathlib's inner product is conjugate-linear in the first slot; the diagonal values are real, so slot order is immaterial. For empty X, X = ∅ forces I = 0, i.e. H = 0, as the mathematics demands. (4) Source: the four-condition definition in Wikipedia's 'Projection-valued measure' article (orthogonal projections, π(∅) = 0, π(X) = I, π(⋃Eⱼ)v = Σⱼ π(Eⱼ)v, π(E₁∩E₂) = π(E₁)π(E₂); scalar measures μ_ξ(E) = ⟨π(E)ξ|ξ⟩). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: witness — the Dirac PVM P(B) = 1_B(a)·I with diag ξ = ‖ξ‖²·δ_a compiles, and any PVM with those projections has that diag (via `ext`); the one-point space gives P(univ) = I, P(∅) = 0; non-witness — on Bool, Q(B) = I iff B = univ (multiplicative, Q(∅) = 0, Q(X) = I, not additive) is provably not a `ProjValMeasure`; the converse constructor compiles; axioms of `hasSum_proj_of_pairwise_disjoint` and `ext`: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.
μ_ξ(X) = ‖ξ‖² stated with `Measure.real` (`μ.real s` is by definition `(μ s).toReal`), Mathlib's real-valued form of a finite measure's value.

μ_ξ(X) = ‖ξ‖ₑ² in ℝ≥0∞, where `‖ξ‖ₑ` is the norm as an extended nonnegative real: the total mass of the scalar measure is ‖ξ‖², so μ_ξ is a probability measure for unit ξ; it follows from the real version by `ENNReal.ofReal_toReal` (finite mass) and `ofReal_norm`.
The total mass of μ_ξ is ‖ξ‖² (as a real number): the case B = X of `norm_sq_proj_apply`, with P(X) = I. Lean subtlety: stated through `toReal`, harmless as μ_ξ is finite.

Extensionality: two PVMs with P(B) = Q(B) for every measurable B are equal, because μ_ξ(B) is read off from ⟪ξ, P(B)ξ⟫ on measurable sets and a measure is determined there (`Measure.ext`), so the `diag` field is not free data. Lean subtlety: the recovery goes through `ENNReal.toReal`, injective only on finite values; both measures are finite (`measure_ne_top`).
P = Q iff P.diag ξ = Q.diag ξ for every ξ: one direction is rewriting, the other is `ext_of_diag`.
Two PVMs with the same scalar measures μ_ξ for every ξ are equal: equal diagonals ⟪ξ, P(B)ξ⟫ = ⟪ξ, Q(B)ξ⟫ force P(B) = Q(B) by complex polarization, and the remaining fields are propositions.

(1) Unconditional strong countable additivity: for pairwise disjoint measurable sets Bₙ and every vector ξ, the series Σₙ P(Bₙ)ξ converges unconditionally in H with sum P(⋃ₙ Bₙ)ξ. (2) `HasSum g a` means the finite partial sums Σ_{n∈s} g n tend to a as the finite set s ⊆ ℕ grows (filter `atTop` on `Finset ℕ`), i.e. unconditional convergence, stronger than the natural-order limit; g n = P(Bₙ)ξ is a vector, so this is strong (vector-wise) additivity, not norm convergence of operator sums; `hf` and `hdisj` encode measurability and pairwise disjointness (f i ∩ f j = ∅ for i ≠ j); the sum `P.proj (⋃ n, f n) (MeasurableSet.iUnion hf) ξ` is P(⋃Bₙ)ξ. Unconditional convergence is the true statement because the vectors P(Bₙ)ξ are mutually orthogonal with Σ‖P(Bₙ)ξ‖² = Σ μ_ξ(Bₙ) = μ_ξ(⋃Bₙ) < ∞, which is how the proof gets summability (`OrthogonalFamily`). (3) Lean subtlety: the statement is a `HasSum`, not a `tsum` equation, so the `tsum = 0` junk value for non-summable families plays no role; `toReal` appears in the summability step and is legitimate because μ_ξ is finite. (4) Condition 3 of the definition in Wikipedia's 'Projection-valued measure' article (π(⋃Eⱼ)v = Σⱼ π(Eⱼ)v), in its unconditional form. Checks at 5f78b5307b: hf and hdisj load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses); specialised to the Dirac PVM P(B) = 1_B(a)·I; my converse constructor shows these laws, with natural-order additivity, give back the structure; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

⟪P(B)ξ, ξ⟫ = μ_ξ(B) as a complex number: the defining identity `inner_proj` with P(B) moved to the conjugate-linear first slot; the right side `((P.diag ξ) B).toReal` is real, so conjugation (`inner_conj_symm`, `Complex.conj_ofReal`) leaves it unchanged. Lean subtlety: `toReal` sends ∞ to 0, excluded because μ_ξ is finite.
⟪ψ, P(B)ξ⟫ = ⟪P(B)ψ, P(B)ξ⟫ for all ψ, ξ, a property of every orthogonal projection: by self-adjointness and idempotence, ⟪Pψ, Pξ⟫ = ⟪ψ, P²ξ⟫ = ⟪ψ, Pξ⟫.

Each scalar measure μ_ξ = `P.diag ξ` is finite: `IsFiniteMeasure μ` means μ X < ∞, and the instance is exactly the structure's `diag_finite` field, registered so typeclass search finds it (the mass is ‖ξ‖² by `diag_univ`).

Each P(B) is a positive operator: Mathlib's `IsPositive` for `H →L[ℂ] H` is self-adjoint with re⟪Tx, x⟫ ≥ 0, and here re⟪P(B)ξ, ξ⟫ = μ_ξ(B) ≥ 0; Mathlib's `IsPositive.of_isStarProjection` gives the same for any orthogonal projection.

Each P(B) is self-adjoint: for `T : H →L[ℂ] H`, `IsSelfAdjoint T` means `star T = T` with `star` the Hilbert-space adjoint; here ⟪ξ, P(B)ξ⟫ = μ_ξ(B) is real for every ξ, so P(B)* and P(B) have the same diagonal and coincide by complex polarization. Lean subtlety: the argument needs scalars ℂ (over ℝ a real diagonal says nothing), and the adjoint needs `[CompleteSpace H]`, which is part of H being a Hilbert space.

Each P(B) is an orthogonal projection, the first textbook axiom: Mathlib's `IsStarProjection p` is the structure with fields `IsIdempotentElem p` and `IsSelfAdjoint p` (p² = p and p* = p, where for `H →L[ℂ] H` the star is the Hilbert adjoint, `star_eq_adjoint`), which on a Hilbert space is exactly an orthogonal projection; it is assembled from `proj_idem` and `isSelfAdjoint_proj`.

‖P(B)ξ‖ ≤ ‖ξ‖, i.e. every P(B) is a contraction: ‖P(B)ξ‖² = μ_ξ(B) ≤ μ_ξ(X) = ‖ξ‖² by monotonicity of the measure. Lean subtlety: `toReal` is monotone only on finite values, supplied by the finiteness of μ_ξ.

‖P(B)ξ‖² = μ_ξ(B) as a real number, the standard identity μ_ξ(B) = ⟨P(B)ξ, ξ⟩ = ‖P(B)ξ‖²: ‖Pξ‖² = re⟪Pξ, Pξ⟫ = re⟪ξ, Pξ⟫ for an orthogonal projection, and `inner_proj` evaluates the last. Lean subtlety: `toReal` would turn ∞ into 0; μ_ξ is finite, so the real number is the measure.
P(B)(P(B)v) = P(B)v for every vector v: idempotence (`proj_idem`) applied to a vector.

P(Bᶜ) = I − P(B) (`ContinuousLinearMap.id ℂ H` is I): apply `proj_union` to the disjoint sets B, Bᶜ, whose union is X, and use P(X) = I; the measurability of Bᶜ is the canonical proof `hB.compl`, irrelevant by proof irrelevance.

If B₁ = B₂ then P(B₁) = P(B₂) whichever measurability proofs h₁, h₂ are supplied: `proj` takes the proof of `MeasurableSet B` as an argument, and proof irrelevance makes the value depend on the set alone.

P(∅) = 0, the textbook axiom: the diagonal matrix elements ⟪ξ, P(∅)ξ⟫ = μ_ξ(∅) = 0 vanish for every ξ, and a complex-linear operator with vanishing diagonal is zero (complex polarization, `eq_of_diagonal`).
P(B)P(B) = P(B), i.e. each P(B) is idempotent (`*` on `H →L[ℂ] H` is composition): the case B₁ = B₂ = B of `proj_inter`, since B ∩ B = B.
P(B)P(C) = P(C)P(B): projections of a PVM commute, since both products equal P(B ∩ C) by `proj_inter` and B ∩ C = C ∩ B.
For measurable B ⊆ C, P(B)P(C) = P(B): by `proj_inter` the product is P(B ∩ C) = P(B).
For measurable B ⊆ C, P(C)P(B) = P(B): the left version combined with commutativity (`proj_mul_comm`).
If B and C are disjoint (`Disjoint B C`, i.e. B ∩ C = ∅) then P(B)P(C) = 0, so their ranges are orthogonal: P(B)P(C) = P(B ∩ C) = P(∅) = 0.
B ⊆ C implies range P(B) ⊆ range P(C): `(P.proj B hB).range ≤ (P.proj C hC).range` compares the ranges of the underlying linear maps as submodules, and P(B) = P(C)P(B) maps into range P(C).

Finite additivity: for disjoint measurable B₁, B₂, P(B₁ ∪ B₂) = P(B₁) + P(B₂); proved on diagonals by additivity of μ_ξ (`measure_union`) and complex polarization. Lean subtlety: `toReal` of a sum is the sum of the `toReal`s only for finite values, supplied by the finiteness of μ_ξ (`measure_ne_top`).

(1) Strong countable additivity in the natural order: for pairwise disjoint measurable sets Bₙ and every vector ξ, the partial sums Σ_{k<n} P(B_k)ξ converge in H to P(⋃ₙ Bₙ)ξ, the textbook P(⋃Bₙ) = s-lim Σ P(Bₙ). (2) `hf : ∀ n, MeasurableSet (f n)` makes each Bₙ = f n measurable, which `proj` requires; `hdisj : Pairwise (Disjoint on f)` says f i ∩ f j = ∅ for i ≠ j; `∑ k < n` sums over `Finset.Iio n` = {0, …, n−1}, and the operator sum is then applied to ξ; `Tendsto (·) atTop (𝓝 v)` is convergence of that sequence of vectors to v in the norm of H, i.e. strong (pointwise) convergence of the operators at ξ, not operator-norm convergence, which fails in general; the limit `P.proj (⋃ k, f k) (MeasurableSet.iUnion hf) ξ` is P(⋃Bₙ)ξ. (3) Lean subtlety: the union's measurability proof is the canonical `MeasurableSet.iUnion hf`, irrelevant by proof irrelevance; the proof computes with ℝ≥0∞ masses and `toReal`, legitimate because μ_ξ is finite (the `toReal ∞ = 0` case never arises); no other junk value is involved. (4) Matches condition 3 of the definition in Wikipedia's 'Projection-valued measure' article (π(⋃Eⱼ)v = Σⱼ π(Eⱼ)v). Checks at 5f78b5307b: hf and hdisj load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses); the natural-order limit is also implied by the unconditional `hasSum_proj_of_pairwise_disjoint`; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

For an equivariant *-homomorphism π : A → B (`Hom α γ`: a nonunital star-algebra map with π(α_t a) = γ_t(π a)) and a functional ψ on A with `hψ : ∀ x, ψ x = φ (π x)` (ψ = φ ∘ π), F is a KMS function of (a, b) for ψ if and only if it is one of (π a, π b) for φ: the analytic fields do not mention the algebra, and the boundary values agree because ψ(a α_t(b)) = φ(π a · γ_t(π b)) by multiplicativity and equivariance.

Defines when F : ℂ → ℂ is a KMS function at inverse temperature β for a functional φ and a pair a, b: the strip function of the KMS condition. Lean ↔ maths: `α : CStarAction (Multiplicative ℝ) A` is a homomorphism t ↦ α_t (α_t = `α (Multiplicative.ofAdd t)`, ℝ written multiplicatively so α_{s+t} = α_s ∘ α_t) into the *-automorphisms of the C*-algebra A with norm-continuous orbits, i.e. a C*-dynamical system; `φ : A →L[ℂ] ℂ` is any continuous linear functional; `im ⁻¹' uIcc 0 β` is the closed horizontal strip of z with Im z between 0 and β and `im ⁻¹' uIoo 0 β` its interior. The five fields say: F is continuous on the closed strip (`continuousOn`); complex-differentiable on the open strip (`differentiableOn`; on an open set this is holomorphy); its image of the closed strip is bounded (`isBounded_image`); F(t) = φ(a α_t(b)) for real t (`apply_ofReal`); and F(t + iβ) = φ(α_t(b) a) (`apply_ofReal_add_mul_I`). This is exactly the F_{a,b} of the strip form of the KMS condition, including the boundedness that makes F unique and the order of the two products. Lean subtlety: `uIcc`/`uIoo` are unordered intervals, so for β < 0 the strip is β ≤ Im z ≤ 0 (the correct side) and for β = 0 `uIoo 0 0 = ∅`, holomorphy is vacuous and the closed strip is the real line; F is unconstrained off the closed strip, which is harmless since only its values there are used and they are unique (`IsKMSFunction.eqOn`). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the constant F = ψ(ab) satisfies all five fields for the trivial action on a commutative C*-algebra (compiled); the side of the strip and the sign of β are pinned by the compiled Gibbs test (for K = diag(0,1) and τ_t = e^(itK)·e^(−itK), Tr(e^(−K)·)/Tr(e^(−K)) is 1-KMS and Tr(e^(K)·)/Tr(e^(K)) is not); axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

For a KMS function F and an entire analytic b (`α.IsEntireAnalytic b`: t ↦ α_t(b) is the restriction of an entire A-valued function, whose value at z is `α.entireExtension b z` = α_z(b)), F z = φ(a α_z(b)) at every z of the closed strip: both sides are continuous on the closed strip, holomorphic inside and agree on ℝ, so `eqOn_of_apply_ofReal` applies. Lean subtlety: `entireExtension` is defined to be 0 off the entire analytic elements; the hypothesis `hb` excludes that branch.

If the pair a, b has a KMS function and b is entire analytic, then φ(a α_{t+iβ}(b)) = φ(α_t(b) a) for every real t (`α.entireExtension b (t + β * I)` is α_{t+iβ}(b)): the upper boundary value of F, rewritten through `apply_eq_apply_mul_entireExtension`. Lean subtlety: the junk value 0 of `entireExtension` off entire analytic elements is excluded by `hb`.

Uniqueness of KMS functions: two KMS functions F, G of the same functional and pair agree on the closed strip, `EqOn F G (im ⁻¹' uIcc 0 β)`; it is `eqOn_of_apply_ofReal` applied to G's continuity, holomorphy and lower boundary values.

If F is a KMS function for (φ, a, b) and G is continuous on the closed strip `im ⁻¹' uIcc 0 β`, holomorphic on the open strip `im ⁻¹' uIoo 0 β` and has the same real-axis values G(t) = φ(a α_t(b)), then `EqOn F G (im ⁻¹' uIcc 0 β)`, i.e. F = G on the closed strip: the identity theorem across the real edge, proved by Schwarz reflection (`eqOn_zero_im_preimage_uIcc_of_zero_on_real_axis`). G needs no boundedness, so this is slightly more general than uniqueness of KMS functions; at β = 0 it says F = G on ℝ, which the boundary values give directly.

A KMS function satisfies ‖F z‖ ≤ ‖φ‖ ‖a‖ ‖b‖ at every z of the closed strip (`hz : z ∈ im ⁻¹' uIcc 0 β`): on both boundary lines |φ(a α_t b)|, |φ(α_t(b) a)| ≤ ‖φ‖ ‖a‖ ‖b‖ because each α_t is isometric, and the Phragmén–Lindelöf principle for a horizontal strip (`PhragmenLindelof.horizontal_strip`, which is where the boundedness field is used) carries the bound to the interior; at β = 0 the strip is the real line and only the boundary bound is needed. For a state (‖φ‖ = 1) it is the bound |F(z)| ≤ ‖a‖ ‖b‖ that accompanies the strip form of the KMS condition.

If F is a KMS function for the pair (a, b) and G one for (a, c), then z ↦ F z − G z is one for (a, b − c): continuity, holomorphy and boundedness pass to differences, and both boundary values are linear in the second coefficient (φ(a α_t(b − c)) = φ(a α_t b) − φ(a α_t c) by `mul_sub`, and likewise with `sub_mul`).

Defines the β-KMS states of a C*-dynamical system: the states ω such that for every pair a, b the correlation t ↦ ω(a α_t(b)) extends to a bounded continuous function on the closed strip between Im z = 0 and Im z = β, holomorphic inside, whose values on Im z = β are ω(α_t(b) a). Lean ↔ maths: `[NonUnitalCStarAlgebra A]` is a complex C*-algebra, possibly without unit; `[PartialOrder A] [StarOrderedRing A]` force ≤ to be the C*-order (`StarOrderedRing` says the nonnegative elements are exactly the finite sums of elements s*s and that a ≤ b iff b − a is one of them), so `ω : A →P[ℂ] ℂ` is a continuous linear functional that is positive for that order, with values compared in Mathlib's scoped `ComplexOrder` on ℂ (0 ≤ z iff z is real and ≥ 0) — a positive functional; `norm_eq_one : ‖(ω : A →L[ℂ] ℂ)‖ = 1` makes it a state in the sense right for nonunital algebras (for unital A it amounts to ω(1) = 1). `α : CStarAction (Multiplicative ℝ) A` is a homomorphism t ↦ α_t = `α (Multiplicative.ofAdd t)` into *-automorphisms with norm-continuous orbits, a strongly continuous one-parameter automorphism group. `exists_isKMSFunction a b : ∃ F, α.IsKMSFunction β ω a b F` asks, for every a, b, for an F continuous on `im ⁻¹' uIcc 0 β`, holomorphic on `im ⁻¹' uIoo 0 β`, bounded on the closed strip, with F(t) = ω(a α_t(b)) and F(t + iβ) = ω(α_t(b) a): the strip form of the KMS condition. Lean subtlety: `uIcc 0 β` and `uIoo 0 β` are unordered intervals, so β < 0 puts the strip below the real axis, and at β = 0 the open strip is empty, holomorphy is vacuous and the condition becomes ω(ab) = ω(ba): the 0-KMS states are all tracial states and no α-invariance is imposed (`isKMSState_zero_iff`; some authors add invariance to the definition at β = 0 — the module docstring states this choice, and for β ≠ 0 invariance is the theorem `IsKMSState.apply_action`); `StarOrderedRing A` appears in no field but pins the order that 'positive' refers to; the definition does not use `entireExtension`, so its junk value 0 plays no role here. Source: the analytic form ω(ab) = ω(b α_{iβ}(a)) for all analytic a, b, as stated in arXiv:1810.01828 eq. (1.1) (which cites Bratteli–Robinson), is this condition with a and b swapped. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b, all compiled: (i) the analytic definition transcribed in Lean — ‖ω‖ = 1 and ω(a α_{iβ}(b)) = ω(b a) for all a, b in some norm-dense α-invariant *-subalgebra of entire analytic elements — is equivalent to `IsKMSState` (via `isKMSState_iff_of_dense` and `dense_entireAnalytic`), so the strip definition is the analytic one; (ii) sign test: for K = diag(0,1) and τ_t = e^(itK)·e^(−itK), the Gibbs state Tr(e^(−K)·)/Tr(e^(−K)) is 1-KMS (`isKMSState_gibbsState`) while Tr(e^(K)·)/Tr(e^(K)) is not, so β has the physical sign (e^(−βH) is the β-KMS state); (iii) witnesses: every state of a commutative C*-algebra, and the identity state of ℂ, is β-KMS for the trivial action, built from the definition with a constant F; (iv) non-witness: the rotation of the circle has no 1-KMS state (`isKMSState_rotation_iff`); axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Invariance of KMS states: for β ≠ 0 (`hβ : β ≠ 0`), every β-KMS state satisfies ω(α_t(a)) = ω(a) for every t (`t : Multiplicative ℝ`, a real number written multiplicatively, so `α t` is α_t) and every a ∈ A, with no unit assumed; it follows from `apply_entireExtension` at real times and density of the entire analytic elements. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: hβ is necessary — the evaluation state at 1 on C(S¹) is a 0-KMS state of the rotation (`isKMSState_zero_ofClass_evalStarAlgHom`) that is not invariant (`exists_ofClass_evalStarAlgHom_rotation_ne`), compiled as one example; axioms standard. Lean subtlety: none beyond the `Multiplicative ℝ` encoding of time.

For β ≠ 0 (`hβ`), a β-KMS state is invariant in complex time on entire analytic elements: ω(α_z(b)) = ω(b) for every z ∈ ℂ (`α.entireExtension b z` = α_z(b)). The proof shows z ↦ ω(α_z(b)) is entire with period iβ, hence bounded and constant by Liouville. hβ is necessary: evaluation states on C(S¹) are 0-KMS for the rotation but not invariant (compiled). Lean subtlety: `entireExtension` is 0 off entire analytic elements; `hb` excludes that branch.

Analytic form of the KMS condition: for a β-KMS state ω, every a and every entire analytic b, ω(a α_{iβ}(b)) = ω(b a), where `α.entireExtension b (β * I)` is α_{iβ}(b), the value at iβ of the entire extension of t ↦ α_t(b); it is the upper boundary value of the KMS function at t = 0. arXiv:1810.01828 eq. (1.1) writes the same identity as ω(ab) = ω(b α_{iβ}(a)) for analytic a, b (a and b swapped). Lean subtlety: `entireExtension` is 0 off the entire analytic elements, which `hb` excludes (without it the identity would read ω(0) = ω(ba)).

Pullback of KMS states: for an equivariant *-homomorphism π : A → B (`Hom α γ`) and a β-KMS state ω of (B, γ), the positive functional ω ∘ π (`ω.comp (.ofClass π)`) is a β-KMS state of (A, α) provided it has norm one (`hnorm`). The norm hypothesis is the state condition itself and can fail (for π = 0, ω ∘ π = 0), which the docstring states ('as soon as it has norm one'); the KMS functions transfer by `Hom.isKMSFunction_iff`.

For a surjective equivariant *-homomorphism π (`hπ : Function.Surjective π`), e.g. the quotient map by a closed invariant ideal, ω ∘ π is a β-KMS state whenever ω is: pulling a positive functional back along a surjective *-homomorphism preserves its norm (`opNorm_comp_ofClass_of_surjective`, via approximate units), so the norm hypothesis of `IsKMSState.comp` holds.

Restriction of KMS states: for a closed (`[IsClosed (S : Set A)]`) α-invariant (`hS : IsInvariant …`) star subalgebra S, so that S is a C*-algebra with the restricted dynamics `hS.restrict`, the restriction of a β-KMS state ω to S (ω composed with the inclusion `hS.subtypeHom`) is a β-KMS state of the restricted dynamics provided it has norm one (`hωS`), which is needed since the restriction of a state can have smaller norm; it is `IsKMSState.comp` at the inclusion.

For entire analytic b, the function z ↦ φ(a α_z(b)) is a KMS function of the pair a, b exactly when φ(a α_{t+iβ}(b)) = φ(α_t(b) a) for all real t: continuity and holomorphy hold because z ↦ α_z(b) is entire, boundedness on the closed strip because α_z(b) is bounded on horizontal strips of bounded width (`isBounded_image_im_preimage`), and the lower boundary value because α_t(b) agrees with the extension on ℝ, so only the upper boundary value is a condition. `hb` excludes the junk value of `entireExtension`.

For a surjective equivariant *-homomorphism π : A → B, the pullback ω ∘ π is a β-KMS state of (A, α) if and only if ω is a β-KMS state of (B, γ): ← is `comp_of_surjective`; → writes every pair of B as (π a, π b) using surjectivity and uses norm preservation, so `hπ` is needed for that direction.

The 0-KMS states are exactly the tracial states: for every dynamics α, `α.IsKMSState 0 ω ↔ ‖(ω : A →L[ℂ] ℂ)‖ = 1 ∧ ∀ a b, ω (a * b) = ω (b * a)`; since ω : A →P[ℂ] ℂ is a positive functional, the right side says ω is a state with ω(ab) = ω(ba), a tracial state. Forward, the two boundary values at t = 0 give ω(ab) = ω(ba); backward, z ↦ ω(a α_{Re z}(b)) is a KMS function because the strip is the real line, the open strip is empty and α_t(b) a can be traded for a α_t(b) by traciality. Lean subtlety: at β = 0 `uIoo 0 0 = ∅`, so the holomorphy field is vacuous and the definition imposes no α-invariance; some authors add invariance to the definition of 0-KMS states, and the module docstring says this file does not (the circle rotation has 0-KMS evaluation states that are not invariant, compiled). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: consistent with the Gibbs state at β = 0 being the normalised trace Tr(·)/n (`gibbsState_zero_apply`), the unique tracial state of Mₙ(ℂ); axioms standard.

On a commutative C*-algebra B (`NonUnitalCommCStarAlgebra B`, with the C*-order), for every dynamics γ, a positive functional ψ is a 0-KMS state exactly when ‖ψ‖ = 1: every state is 0-KMS, because ψ(ab) = ψ(ba) holds automatically (`isKMSState_zero_iff` with `mul_comm`). The restriction to β = 0 is genuine: the rotation action on C(S¹) has no β-KMS states for β ≠ 0 (`isKMSState_rotation_iff`).

Claim: a finite-dimensional basic algebra A over an algebraically closed field k is a bound quiver algebra: some surjective k-algebra map kQ → A from the path algebra of a finite quiver has admissible kernel, so A ≅ kQ/I with I admissible. Lean to mathematics: `IsBasic A` is by definition `IsSemisimpleRing (A ⧸ Ring.jacobson A) ∧ IsReduced (A ⧸ Ring.jacobson A)`, and `isBasic_iff_pi_divisionRing` shows this says A/rad A is a finite product of division rings, i.e. no Wedderburn block of size > 1 (no repeated indecomposable projective), which over an algebraically closed field is A/rad A ≅ k × ⋯ × k, the standard notion of a basic algebra; `Quiver.{0} Q`, `Finite Q` and `∀ i j : Q, Finite (i ⟶ j)` give a finite quiver; `F : pathAlgebra k Q →ₐ[k] A` is a k-algebra homomorphism from kQ (the free k-module on paths with the concatenation product); `Function.Surjective F` and `IsAdmissibleIdeal (RingHom.ker F.toRingHom)` say F is onto and its kernel I satisfies R_Q^N ⊆ I ⊆ R_Q² for the arrow ideal R_Q (the span of the paths of positive length), and by the first isomorphism theorem (`Ideal.quotientKerAlgEquivOfSurjective`) this is exactly A ≅ kQ/I with I admissible. Lean subtlety: `RingHom.ker` is a Mathlib left `Ideal`; its two-sidedness instance, which `IsAdmissibleIdeal` takes as an argument, is found automatically. Only some finite quiver is asserted, as the docstring says, not its identification with the ordinary (Ext-)quiver of A, which the roadmap lists as a separate target. No connectedness is assumed. The zero algebra is basic and is presented by the empty quiver. The universes of k and A are independent. Source and checks: the Tau Ceti roadmap (QuiverRepresentations README, Layer 3) states it in this form. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only; instantiated at A = k; the textbook form `∃ Q I, IsAdmissibleIdeal I ∧ Nonempty (A ≃ₐ[k] pathAlgebra k Q ⧸ I)` follows in one line (compiled); conversely the conclusion implies `FiniteDimensional k A ∧ IsBasic A` (compiled), so neither hypothesis can be dropped; and `[IsAlgClosed k]` is load-bearing: compiled proof that the basic 2-dimensional ℝ-algebra ℂ has no such presentation over ℝ.

Claim: with the same data over a field k, if J is a nilpotent two-sided ideal containing every arrow value (`harrows : f a ∈ J`), every vertex idempotent is nonzero (`hne`), and for all i, j the classes of the arrows i ⟶ j in A/J² are k-linearly independent (`hind`), then the kernel of `liftAlgHomOfArrows k e he f hl hr : kQ → A` is admissible, `IsAdmissibleIdeal` meaning R_Q^N ⊆ ker ⊆ R_Q² for the arrow ideal R_Q (span of the paths of positive length). Mathematically: arrows in the nilpotent J kill every path of length ≥ N (lower bound), and the vertices (nonzero orthogonal idempotents outside J) and the arrows (independent within each corner, hence across corners by orthogonality) stay independent modulo J², so kQ/R_Q² injects into A/J² and ker ⊆ R_Q² (upper bound). Lean subtlety: `IsNilpotent J` is nilpotence in the monoid of ideals (J^n = ⊥); `hne` cannot be dropped, since a zero vertex idempotent would put a trivial path in the kernel and an admissible ideal contains none. Checks (red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): lean_minimal_hypotheses finds hJ, hne, harrows and hind all load-bearing; it is applied in the basic presentation theorem at J = Ring.jacobson A; it reduces to the general `AlgHom.isAdmissibleIdeal_ker` (Kernel.lean) plus the per-corner independence argument; Mathlib has no path algebras, so no duplicate.

Claim: for a nilpotent two-sided ideal J of A, a complete family of orthogonal idempotents `e : Q → A` (`CompleteOrthogonalIdempotents e`: e_i e_j = δ_ij e_i and Σ e_i = 1) and corner elements f a ∈ e_j A e_i for the arrows a : i ⟶ j (`hl`, `hr`), the algebra map `liftAlgHomOfArrows k e he f hl hr : kQ → A` (vertex i ↦ e i, arrow a ↦ f a by its evaluation lemmas) is surjective provided `hquot`, the classes of the e_i span A/J over k, and `hlayer`, for every x ∈ J the class of e_j x e_i in A/J² lies in the k-span of the classes of the arrows i ⟶ j, i.e. the arrows span the (j, i)-corner of J/J². This is the standard 'onto modulo J and onto the first layer J/J² implies onto' argument for nilpotent J. Lean subtlety: `J ^ 2` is a power of a Mathlib left ideal, which for the two-sided J (`[J.IsTwoSided]`) is the usual J²; `hlayer` asks only that the corner be contained in the span (the arrows need not lie in J), so the theorem is if anything stronger than its docstring's 'span'. Checks (red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): lean_minimal_hypotheses finds hJ, hquot and hlayer all load-bearing; it is applied in the basic presentation theorem at J = Ring.jacobson A, so its hypotheses are jointly satisfiable (e.g. A = k); it specialises the general `AlgHom.surjective_of_nilpotent_ideal`, adding the corner decomposition x = Σ e_j x e_i; Mathlib has no path algebras, so no duplicate.

Claim: every finite-dimensional algebra A over an algebraically closed field k is Morita equivalent to a bound quiver algebra kQ/I, with Q a finite quiver and I an admissible ideal. Lean to mathematics: `∃ (Q : Type) (_ : Quiver.{0} Q) (_ : Finite Q) (_ : ∀ i j : Q, Finite (i ⟶ j))` is a quiver with finitely many vertices and finitely many arrows between any two vertices, i.e. a finite quiver; `pathAlgebra k Q` is by definition the free k-module `Quiver.TotalPath Q →₀ k` on all paths, multiplied by concatenation (0 on non-composable pairs) with unit the sum of the trivial paths, i.e. kQ; `I : Ideal (pathAlgebra k Q)` together with `I.IsTwoSided` is a two-sided ideal (Mathlib's `Ideal` alone means a left ideal); `IsAdmissibleIdeal I` is the structure `∃ N, arrowIdeal k Q ^ N ≤ I` and `I ≤ arrowIdeal k Q ^ 2`, where `arrowIdeal k Q` is the span of the paths of positive length (`arrowIdeal_eq_span_arrows`: the ideal generated by the arrows) and `mem_arrowIdeal_pow` identifies its n-th power with the span of the paths of length ≥ n, so this is R_Q^N ⊆ I ⊆ R_Q²; `IsMoritaEquivalent k A B` is Mathlib's `Nonempty (MoritaEquivalence k A B)`, a k-linear equivalence of categories `ModuleCat A ≌ ModuleCat B`, which is Morita equivalence (equivalence of module categories), not isomorphism; `[FiniteDimensional k A]` and `[IsAlgClosed k]` are the textbook hypotheses. Lean subtlety: `k` and `A` are bound in one universe `u` (`(k A : Type u)`, an artifact of Mathlib's universe-monomorphic `IsMoritaEquivalent.trans`), so the docstring's 'every' covers only same-universe pairs; mathematically nothing is lost, and a universe-polymorphic version compiles from existing API (recorded as MINOR RT-20261105-dbf77c). The module categories are `ModuleCat.{u}`, modules in A's universe, Mathlib's standard encoding. The exponent N is not required to be ≥ 2, which is harmless: R^N ⊆ I gives R^max(N,2) ⊆ I. The path product is 'later factor first', which at most replaces Q by its opposite quiver and does not matter for an existence statement. The zero algebra is covered by the empty quiver (kQ = 0). Source and checks: the Tau Ceti roadmap (QuiverRepresentations README, Layer 3, 'Gabriel's presentation theorem') asks for exactly this statement. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only; instantiated at the non-basic M₂(k); compiled proof that a nontrivial algebra is never Morita equivalent to a subsingleton ring, so the empty quiver with I = ⊤ cannot witness the statement for A ≠ 0; `IsAdmissibleIdeal` witness (x²) and non-witnesses (0) and (x) on the one-loop quiver k[x], compiled.

Correctly stated: every maximal ideal M of the Tate algebra K⟨X_i : i ∈ σ⟩ (σ finite, K complete nonarchimedean) has height #σ. Lean ↔ mathematics: `M : Ideal (IsRestricted.subring (fun _ : σ ↦ 1))` with `[M.IsMaximal]` is a maximal ideal of the Tate algebra (carrier as in `ringKrullDim_isRestricted_subring`); `Ideal.height M : ℕ∞` is Mathlib's height, the infimum over minimal primes over M of their prime heights, which for a prime ideal is `Order.height` of M in `PrimeSpectrum`, the supremum of lengths of strict chains of primes ending at M; the right side is n = `Nat.card σ` cast into ℕ∞, so the equation says the longest chain of primes below M has length exactly n. Lean subtlety: `Ideal.height` is valued in ℕ∞, so a priori it could be ⊤, and the equation excludes that; `Nat.card σ = 0` for infinite σ, excluded by `[Finite σ]`; at n = 0 the Tate algebra is K, whose only maximal ideal ⊥ has height 0, matching (checked); the lemma is `@[simp]` and fires on any maximal ideal of the Tate algebra (checked: `simp` proves height 2 at n = 2). Source: Bosch, Lectures on Formal and Rigid Geometry (2014), §2.2, Proposition 17: 'Every maximal ideal m ⊂ T_n is of height n'. Checks: specialised over ℚ_2 at n = 2 (every maximal ideal has height 2, by simp) and n = 0 (height 0); axioms standard; no Mathlib duplicate.

Correctly stated: the Tate algebra K⟨X_i : i ∈ σ⟩ in finitely many variables over a complete nonarchimedean field has finite Krull dimension. Lean ↔ mathematics: `FiniteRingKrullDim R` is Mathlib's abbreviation for `FiniteDimensionalOrder (PrimeSpectrum R)`, a longest chain of prime ideals exists, i.e. R is nonzero and its Krull dimension is a natural number; the carrier `IsRestricted.subring (fun _ : σ ↦ 1)` is the Tate algebra as in `ringKrullDim_isRestricted_subring`, from which the instance is derived by `FiniteRingKrullDim.of_ringKrullDim_eq_natCast`. Lean subtlety: the class excludes both ⊥ (zero ring) and ⊤, and both are excluded here because the dimension equals the natural number #σ; it is a Prop-valued instance, so no instance diamond can arise. Checks: `inferInstance` finds it on the Tate algebra over ℚ_2 in four variables; axioms standard. (Its name is recorded separately as a naming issue; the statement is right.)

Correctly stated: a commutative ring A that is integral over an injectively embedded Tate algebra K⟨X_i : i ∈ σ⟩ (σ finite, K complete nonarchimedean) has Krull dimension #σ. Lean ↔ mathematics: `[Algebra (Tate σ) A]` is the structure map T → A; `[Algebra.IsIntegral (Tate σ) A]` says every element of A is a root of a monic polynomial over T; `[FaithfulSMul (Tate σ) A]` says distinct elements of T act differently on A, which for an algebra is equivalent to injectivity of `algebraMap` (`faithfulSMul_iff_algebraMap_injective`), the 'injectively embedded'; the conclusion `ringKrullDim A = Nat.card σ` is dim A = n as in `ringKrullDim_isRestricted_subring`, combined with the fact that an injective integral extension preserves Krull dimension (`TauCeti.ringKrullDim_eq_of_isIntegral_of_faithfulSMul`: incomparability for ≤, lying over and going up for ≥). Lean subtlety: `FaithfulSMul` rules out the zero ring A, where `ringKrullDim` would be ⊥ (checked: it implies `Nontrivial A`); both hypotheses are needed (T ⧸ (X_1) is integral over T but not faithful and has dimension n − 1; T in more variables is faithful but not integral); the structure map need not be a K-algebra map, which only makes the statement more general; `[Finite σ]` excludes the junk `Nat.card σ = 0`. Source: Bosch, Lectures on Formal and Rigid Geometry (2014), §2.2, Corollary 11: for a finite monomorphism T_d → T_n/a, 'the Krull dimension of T_n/a coincides with the one of T_d', which equals d by Proposition 17, so d is uniquely determined. Checks: specialised at A = T (dimension 2 for two variables over ℚ_2); a probe derives from it that two finite injective maps T_d → A and T_e → A force d = e; axioms standard; used by `TauCeti.IsAffinoidAlgebra.exists_ringKrullDim_eq_finite_injective`.

Correctly stated: for a complete nonarchimedean field K and finitely many variables σ, the Tate algebra K⟨X_i : i ∈ σ⟩ has Krull dimension #σ. Lean ↔ mathematics: `IsRestricted.subring (R := K) (fun _ : σ ↦ 1)` is Mathlib's subring of `MvPowerSeries σ K` of the series f with `‖coeff t f‖ * ∏ 1 ^ t_i → 0` along the cofinite filter on multi-indices t : σ →₀ ℕ, i.e. |c_ν| → 0 as |ν| → ∞ (a set of multi-indices is finite iff bounded), which is exactly T_n = K⟨ζ_1, …, ζ_n⟩; `[NormedField K] [IsUltrametricDist K] [CompleteSpace K]` say K is a field with a non-archimedean absolute value under which it is complete; `[Finite σ]` and `Nat.card σ` are the finite set of variables and its size n; `ringKrullDim R` is by definition `Order.krullDim (PrimeSpectrum R)`, the supremum of lengths of strict chains of prime ideals, valued in `WithBot ℕ∞`, and the right side is the natural number n cast into `WithBot ℕ∞` (equal to `((n : ℕ∞) : WithBot ℕ∞)` by `WithBot.coe_natCast`), so the equation says every chain of primes has length ≤ n and one has length n. Lean subtlety: `Nat.card σ = 0` for infinite σ, so `[Finite σ]` is what rules out a junk right side; `ringKrullDim` would be ⊥ for the zero ring and ⊤ for unbounded chains, and the equation pins it to a finite natural (checked: ≠ ⊥, ≠ ⊤ at n = 3); the norm may be trivial (Bosch assumes a non-trivial absolute value), where restricted series are exactly the finitely supported ones and the Tate algebra is the polynomial ring K[X_1, …, X_n], again of dimension n, so this is a genuine generalisation, not a degenerate case. Source: Bosch, Lectures on Formal and Rigid Geometry (LNM 2105, 2014), §2.2, Definition 2 (T_n = K⟨ζ_1, …, ζ_n⟩ is the K-algebra of power series with lim_{|ν|→∞} |c_ν| = 0, and T_0 = K) and Proposition 17, 'In particular, the Krull dimension of T_n is n'. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only; specialised over ℚ_2 at n = 0, 1, 3 (dimension 0, 1, 3; n = 1 gives ≠ 2); over ℚ with the trivial absolute value (WithAbs, shown ultrametric and complete) restricted series are finitely supported and the theorem gives dimension 2 in two variables; hypotheses satisfiable (no False); no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate (loogle, leansearch, leanfinder, git grep).

Correctly stated: for any discrete index type ι and real or complex scalars, ℓ¹(ι) is isometrically isomorphic to the continuous dual of c₀(ι) via a ↦ (f ↦ Σᵢ aᵢfᵢ). Lean ↔ maths: `lp (fun _ : ι ↦ 𝕜) 1` is Mathlib's ℓ¹(ι, 𝕜), the families with Σ‖aᵢ‖ < ∞ normed by Σ‖aᵢ‖ (`lp.norm_eq_tsum_rpow` at p = 1); `C₀(ι, 𝕜)` is Mathlib's `ZeroAtInftyContinuousMap` on ι with `[DiscreteTopology ι]`, where compact sets are finite, so vanishing at infinity means fᵢ → 0 along the cofinite filter (`tendsto_cofinite`, `mkOfDiscrete`), and its norm is the sup norm ⨆ᵢ‖fᵢ‖ (`norm_eq_iSup_norm`), so it is c₀(ι); `StrongDual 𝕜 C₀(ι, 𝕜)` is `C₀(ι, 𝕜) →L[𝕜] 𝕜` with the operator norm, the Banach dual; `≃ₗᵢ[𝕜]` (`LinearIsometryEquiv`) is a 𝕜-linear norm-preserving bijection, i.e. an isometric isomorphism; the map itself is pinned down by `dualEquiv_apply` (a ↦ (f ↦ ∑' i, a i * f i), bilinear, with no conjugation over ℂ) and its inverse by `dualEquiv_symm_apply` (Λ ↦ (Λ eᵢ)ᵢ with eᵢ = `single i 1`); `[RCLike 𝕜]` means 𝕜 = ℝ or ℂ; ι is any type at all (no countability or nonemptiness assumption), given the discrete topology. Lean subtlety: the pairing is a `tsum`, which Lean sets to 0 for a non-summable family, but here ‖aᵢfᵢ‖ ≤ ‖f‖‖aᵢ‖ with Σ‖aᵢ‖ < ∞, so the series converges absolutely (a `Summable` and a `HasSum` probe compile), and the forward map is Mathlib's Hölder pairing `lp.dualPairing 1 ∞` restricted along the isometry `toLpInfty`, so no junk value enters; the inverse comes from `LinearIsometryEquiv.ofSurjective` (made with choice) and the def is built in tactic mode, but the inverse is unique and both directions are fixed by the two formula lemmas. Source: the TauCetiRoadmap BanachSpaceTheory README (at dd4b28f) asks for exactly this identification c₀* = ℓ¹, with `C₀(ℕ,𝕜)` for c₀, `lp` for ℓ¹ and the series pairing through `lp.dualPairing`; Wikipedia's 'Sequence space' states 'The dual of c₀ is ℓ¹'. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b (compiled): ι = ℕ gives ‖f ↦ f 0‖ = 1; ι = Fin 2 gives ‖f ↦ f 0 + f 1‖ = 2, the ℓ¹ norm of (1,1); `dualEquiv ℝ ℕ (lp.single 1 0 1) = evalCLM ℝ 0`; it instantiates at ℝ with the discrete topology (uncountable) and at ι = Empty; axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound only; pinned Mathlib 1b1ccf4b has no c₀ dual (grep, loogle, leansearch, leanfinder).

Correctly stated: the forward duality map is the series pairing, `dualEquiv 𝕜 ι a f = ∑' i, a i * f i`, i.e. a ∈ ℓ¹ acts on f ∈ c₀ by Σᵢ aᵢfᵢ, bilinearly with no conjugation over ℂ. Lean subtlety: `∑'` is 0 for a non-summable family, but ‖aᵢfᵢ‖ ≤ ‖f‖‖aᵢ‖ with Σ‖aᵢ‖ < ∞, so the series converges absolutely and the tsum is its true sum; Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b a `Summable` probe and the `HasSum` form compile.
Correctly stated: the functional of a ∈ ℓ¹ takes the value aᵢ z on the coordinate vector z·eᵢ (`single i z`), i.e. Σⱼ aⱼ (z eᵢ)ⱼ = aᵢ z.

Correctly stated: the inverse duality sends a functional Λ to its coordinate family; the i-th entry of `(dualEquiv 𝕜 ι).symm Λ` ∈ ℓ¹ is Λ(eᵢ) with eᵢ = `single i 1`. This pins down uniquely the inverse that `dualEquiv` builds with choice.

Correctly stated: under the duality, the coordinate evaluation δᵢ : f ↦ f(i) (`evalCLM 𝕜 i`) corresponds to the unit vector eᵢ of ℓ¹ (`lp.single 1 i 1`, 1 at i and 0 elsewhere); Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: `dualEquiv ℝ ℕ (lp.single 1 0 1) = evalCLM ℝ 0` compiles.

Correctly stated: every continuous linear functional Λ on c₀(ι) is given by its coordinate series Λ(f) = Σᵢ Λ(eᵢ) fᵢ, convergent unconditionally. In Lean, `single i 1` is the unit vector eᵢ, and `HasSum g s` asserts that the sums of g over finite subsets converge to s, which gives both convergence and the value (not a junk-prone `tsum`); it is Λ applied to the coordinate expansion f = Σᵢ fᵢ eᵢ (`hasSum_smul_single_one`) via `HasSum.mapL`. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: three consumers (Krein–Šmulian, Dual/NullSequence, WeaklyCompact/ZeroAtInfty).

Correctly stated: every continuous linear functional Λ on c₀(ι), over ℝ or ℂ and for any discrete index type ι, has norm ‖Λ‖ = Σᵢ |Λ(eᵢ)|. Lean ↔ maths: `‖Λ‖` is the operator norm on `StrongDual 𝕜 C₀(ι, 𝕜)`, the supremum of |Λ f| over the sup-norm unit ball of c₀(ι); `single i 1` is the i-th unit vector eᵢ (1 at i, 0 elsewhere); `∑' i, ‖Λ (single i 1)‖` is the unconditional sum over the arbitrary type ι; the proof transports Λ through the norm-preserving `(dualEquiv 𝕜 ι).symm`, whose coordinates are Λ(eᵢ) (`dualEquiv_symm_apply`), and uses the ℓ¹ norm formula `lp.norm_eq_tsum_rpow`. Lean subtlety: `∑'` is 0 for a non-summable family, which would make this identity false for any nonzero Λ; here the family is summable for every Λ (`summable_norm_apply_single_one`, from finite partial sums ≤ ‖Λ‖), so the tsum is the true sum; the real power ‖·‖^(1:ℝ) from the ℓᵖ norm formula at p = 1 simplifies to ‖·‖. Source: Wikipedia's 'Sequence space' states 'The dual of c₀ is ℓ¹', and this is the norm half of that identification. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b (compiled): ι = ℕ, Λ = (f ↦ f 0) gives ‖Λ‖ = 1 = Σ|Λ(eᵢ)|; ι = Fin 2, Λ = (f ↦ f 0 + f 1) gives ‖Λ‖ = 2; ι = Empty gives ‖Λ‖ = 0.

Correctly stated: for a functional Λ on c₀(ι) over ℝ or ℂ and any finite set s ⊆ ι, Σ_{i∈s} |Λ(eᵢ)| ≤ ‖Λ‖. In Lean, `∑ i ∈ s` is a finite (Finset) sum, `single i 1` is eᵢ and `‖Λ‖` is the operator norm; `[RCLike 𝕜]` is needed, because the proof tests Λ against g = Σ_{i∈s} uᵢ eᵢ with unimodular phases uᵢ = conj(Λ eᵢ)/|Λ eᵢ| (sup norm ≤ 1). Lean subtlety: x/0 = 0 in Lean, so when Λ(eᵢ) = 0 the phase uᵢ is 0, not undefined; that coordinate then contributes 0 = |Λ(eᵢ)|, and the proof handles it by a case split.

Correctly stated: for every functional Λ on c₀(ι) over ℝ or ℂ, the family (|Λ(eᵢ)|)ᵢ is summable (unconditionally, over any index type), i.e. (Λ(eᵢ))ᵢ ∈ ℓ¹; it follows from the uniform bound ‖Λ‖ on finite partial sums via `summable_of_sum_le`. It is what keeps the `tsum` in `norm_eq_tsum_norm_apply_single_one` from being the junk value 0.

Correctly stated: for any topological space α, the inclusion C₀(α, E) ↪ ℓ∞(α, E), f ↦ (f x)ₓ, is a 𝕜-linear isometry. Lean ↔ maths: `lp (fun _ : α ↦ E) ∞` is Mathlib's ℓ∞(α, E), the bounded families normed by ⨆ₓ‖f x‖ (`lp.norm_eq_ciSup`); the map sends f to its underlying function, bounded by ‖f‖ (`norm_coe_le_norm`); `→ₗᵢ[𝕜]` (`LinearIsometry`) means 𝕜-linear with ‖toLpInfty f‖ = ‖f‖, which holds because the C₀ norm is the sup norm ⨆ₓ‖f x‖ (`norm_eq_iSup_norm`); `[NormedRing 𝕜] [Module 𝕜 E] [IsBoundedSMul 𝕜 E]` are exactly what Mathlib needs to make ℓ∞ a 𝕜-module. Lean subtlety: the ℓ∞ norm is a real `⨆`, which Lean sets to 0 for an empty or unbounded range; an empty α gives 0 = 0 on both sides and the family is bounded by construction, so the convention does no harm. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: `toLpInfty_apply` holds by `rfl`; Mathlib has only `lpBCFₗᵢ` (for discrete α) and no bundled linear `toBCF`, so it is not a duplicate.
Correctly stated: the inclusion `toLpInfty 𝕜` of C₀(α, E) into ℓ∞ does not change values, `toLpInfty 𝕜 f x = f x` for every x, i.e. the ℓ∞ family is f itself; it holds by `rfl`.

Brunn's concavity principle in its classical form: for a convex set s in an n-dimensional real inner product space E and a unit vector e, if every hyperplane section orthogonal to e has finite (n−1)-volume, then t ↦ |s ∩ {⟪e, x⟫ = t}|^{1/(n−1)} is concave on ⟪e, s⟫ = {⟪e, x⟫ : x ∈ s}. Lean ↔ mathematics: `{y : (ℝ ∙ e)ᗮ | (y : E) + t • e ∈ s}` is the section at height t translated into the hyperplane e⊥ = `(ℝ ∙ e)ᗮ`, so its `volume` (Mathlib's inner-product-space volume on that subspace, its (n−1)-dimensional Lebesgue measure; instance checked) is |K ∩ (θ⊥ + tθ)|_{n−1}; `volume.real` is `toReal`; `((Module.finrank ℝ E - 1 : ℕ) : ℝ)⁻¹` is 1/(n−1); `(fun x ↦ ⟪e, x⟫) '' s` is the set of heights with nonempty section; `ConcaveOn ℝ D f` is convexity of D plus a·f(x) + b·f(y) ≤ f(a x + b y) for convex weights; `hfin` is finiteness of every section. Lean subtlety: `ENNReal.toReal ∞ = 0`, and `hfin` stops an infinite section from reading as 0 (it is needed, as for fibres: a convex set with one finite section and infinite sections beside it breaks concavity); `finrank - 1` is truncated subtraction, harmless since a unit vector forces n ≥ 1, and for n = 1 the exponent `(0 : ℝ)⁻¹ = 0` makes the function the constant 1. Source: Livshyts, MATH-8803 lecture notes on concentration of measure and convexity (Georgia Tech, Fall 2023, version of July 16, 2024), §3.5, Definition 3.4 and Theorem 3.3, p. 32: A_{θ,K}^{1/(n−1)} is concave on its support for a convex body K; the Lean statement is stronger (convex sets with finite sections, and all heights with nonempty section, which contain the support). Checks: reduces by a proved reparametrisation (private `convex_hyperplaneFibers`, `fst_image_hyperplaneFibers`) to the fibre theorem, whose triangle specialisation and `hfin`-necessity counterexample compiled; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Brunn's concavity principle: for a convex set s in P × F, F a real inner product space of finite dimension d, all of whose fibres have finite volume, p ↦ |s_p|^{1/d} (the d-th root of the d-volume of the fibre over p) is concave on the projection of s. Lean ↔ mathematics: `Convex ℝ s` is convexity of s for the product vector-space structure, with P any real vector space (`[AddCommGroup P] [Module ℝ P]`; concavity only uses segments, so no topology is needed); `Prod.mk p ⁻¹' s` is the fibre s_p = {y ∈ F | (p, y) ∈ s}; `Prod.fst '' s` is the projection of s to P, i.e. exactly the set of p with nonempty fibre; `volume` on F is Mathlib's `measureSpaceOfInnerProductSpace`, the Haar measure giving an orthonormal-basis cube volume 1, i.e. Lebesgue measure on F (`InnerProductSpace.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_eq_volume` identifies it with d-dimensional Hausdorff measure); `volume.real A` is `(volume A).toReal` (`measureReal_def`); `Module.finrank ℝ F` is d, so `(d : ℝ)⁻¹` is the exponent 1/d and `^` is the real power, the d-th root; `hfin : ∀ p, volume (Prod.mk p ⁻¹' s) ≠ ∞` says every fibre has finite volume (outside the projection fibres are empty, so this only constrains the projection); `ConcaveOn ℝ D f` unfolds to: D is convex and a·f(x) + b·f(y) ≤ f(a•x + b•y) for x, y ∈ D, a, b ≥ 0, a + b = 1 — Brunn's inequality |s_{λp+(1−λ)q}|^{1/d} ≥ λ|s_p|^{1/d} + (1−λ)|s_q|^{1/d}. Lean subtlety: `ENNReal.toReal ∞ = 0`, so without `hfin` an infinite fibre would read as volume 0; the hypothesis is genuinely needed — the convex set ({0} × [0,1]) ∪ ((0,1] × ℝ) ⊂ ℝ × ℝ has f(0) = 1 and f = 0 on (0,1], not concave (compiled) — and with `hfin` toReal is faithful. Lean subtlety: in dimension d = 0, `(0 : ℝ)⁻¹ = 0` and x^0 = 1 (`Real.rpow`), so the 'd-th root' is the constant 1 and the statement is trivially true, as the module docstring says; for d ≥ 1 it is the real theorem. The base of the real power is a nonnegative volume, so the negative-base convention of `Real.rpow` never enters. Source: Livshyts, MATH-8803 lecture notes on concentration of measure and convexity (Georgia Tech, Fall 2023, version of July 16, 2024), §3.5, Theorem 3.3 and Remark 3.5, p. 32: for a convex body K and a k-dimensional subspace H, y ↦ |K ∩ (H + y)|^{1/k} is concave on its support in H⊥; the Lean statement implies this (take P = H⊥, F = H) and is stronger — any convex set with finite-volume fibres, and concavity on the whole projection, which contains the support and also the nonempty zero-volume fibres. The proof is the one in the notes: fibre inclusion plus Brunn–Minkowski in F. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: specialised to the triangle {(p, y) | 0 ≤ y ≤ p ≤ 1} ⊂ ℝ × ℝ it yields concavity of p ↦ p on [0, 1] (compiled); the counterexample above shows `hfin` is needed; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate (Mathlib has no Brunn–Minkowski; Tau Ceti's `Convex.logConcave_measure_preimage_prodMk` is the weaker log-concave form).

For a convex set s in a finite-dimensional real inner product space and a unit vector e, if every section orthogonal to e has finite volume, the section volume t ↦ |s ∩ {⟪e, x⟫ = t}|_{n−1} is continuous on the interior of the interval ⟪e, s⟫. Lean ↔ mathematics: `volume.real {y : (ℝ ∙ e)ᗮ | (y : E) + t • e ∈ s}` is the (n−1)-dimensional Lebesgue volume of the section at height t, translated into e⊥, as a real number; `interior ((fun x ↦ ⟪e, x⟫) '' s)` is the interior of the set of heights of s; `hfin` is finiteness of every section. Lean subtlety: `ENNReal.toReal ∞ = 0`; `hfin` makes the real value the volume (the conclusion in fact holds without `hfin`, MINOR finding RT-20261105-6f9fd4). It is the fibre-continuity theorem transported along (t, y) ↦ y + t e. Checks: the `hfin`-free version compiled; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

If every fibre of a convex set s ⊆ P × F has finite volume (P a finite-dimensional real normed space, F a finite-dimensional real inner product space), the fibre volume p ↦ |s_p| is continuous on the interior of the projection of s. Lean ↔ mathematics: `ContinuousOn f (interior (Prod.fst '' s))` is continuity of f restricted to the interior, in P's norm topology, of the projection; `volume.real (Prod.mk p ⁻¹' s)` is `(volume _).toReal` of the fibre {y | (p, y) ∈ s}, with `volume` Lebesgue measure on F; `hfin` is finiteness of every fibre volume. Lean subtlety: `ENNReal.toReal ∞ = 0`; with `hfin` the real value is the true volume (the conclusion in fact stays true without `hfin`, recorded as MINOR generality finding RT-20261105-7fbcad: if one interior fibre is infinite then all are, and the constant 0 is continuous); in dimension 0 every fibre over the projection is all of F and the function is constant (the proof's first branch). Proof: Brunn's principle gives concavity of |s_p|^{1/d} on the projection, Mathlib's `ConcaveOn.continuousOn_interior` gives continuity on the interior of a finite-dimensional convex set, and the d-th power recovers |s_p| (`Real.rpow_inv_natCast_pow`). Checks: the `hfin`-free strengthening compiled; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

For a bounded Borel convex set s in a finite-dimensional real inner product space, a unit vector e and a height c interior to ⟪e, s⟫, V(c) = |{x ∈ s : ⟪e, x⟫ ≤ c}| is differentiable at c with V′(c) = |s ∩ {⟪e, x⟫ = c}|_{n−1}. Lean ↔ mathematics: `HasDerivAt f f' c` says f has derivative f′ at c; `{x ∈ s | ⟪e, x⟫ ≤ c}` is the part of s below the hyperplane; the derivative `volume.real {y : (ℝ ∙ e)ᗮ | (y : E) + c • e ∈ s}` is the (n−1)-volume of the section at c, translated into e⊥; `hsb : Bornology.IsBounded s` is boundedness, `hsm : MeasurableSet s` Borel measurability (E carries its Borel σ-algebra), `he : ‖e‖ = 1` the unit normal, `hc : c ∈ interior ((fun x ↦ ⟪e, x⟫) '' s)` the interior height. Lean subtlety: `volume.real` is `toReal` and `ENNReal.toReal ∞ = 0`, which would matter for an unbounded set (a downward cone has infinite volume below every height, so V ≡ 0 while its sections are positive); boundedness makes every volume finite, so V and the derivative are the true volumes. Proof: Cavalieri (`volume_sep_inner_mem_eq_setLIntegral`) writes V(c′) as ∫_a^{c′} of the section volume near c, Brunn's principle gives continuity of the section volume at the interior height c, and the fundamental theorem of calculus (`intervalIntegral.integral_hasDerivAt_right`) gives V′(c). Checks: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; whole file elaborates in under 4 s.

Brunn's principle for hyperplane sections, extended-real form: for convex s in an n-dimensional real inner product space E, a unit vector e, heights t, u at which the section is nonempty and convex weights a, b: a·|s_t|^{1/(n−1)} + b·|s_u|^{1/(n−1)} ≤ |s_{a t + b u}|^{1/(n−1)}. Lean ↔ mathematics: s_t = `{y : (ℝ ∙ e)ᗮ | (y : E) + t • e ∈ s}` is the section of s by the hyperplane ⟪e, x⟫ = t, translated into e⊥; `volume` on the subspace `(ℝ ∙ e)ᗮ` is Mathlib's inner-product-space volume of that (n−1)-dimensional space, i.e. its Lebesgue measure (checked with pp.explicit that the instance is `measureSpaceOfInnerProductSpace`, not a comap of E's volume, which would vanish on a hyperplane); `ht : t ∈ (fun x ↦ ⟪e, x⟫) '' s` says the section at t is nonempty (for unit e, by the file's private lemma `fst_image_hyperplaneFibers`); `he : ‖e‖ = 1` is the unit normal; `((Module.finrank ℝ E - 1 : ℕ) : ℝ)⁻¹` is 1/(n−1). Lean subtlety: `finrank ℝ E - 1` is truncated natural subtraction, harmless because a unit vector forces n ≥ 1; for n = 1 the exponent is `(0 : ℝ)⁻¹ = 0` and every power is 1, so the claim is a + b ≤ 1. Volumes are in [0, ∞] with 0·∞ = 0, so infinite sections are allowed. Source: Livshyts, MATH-8803 lecture notes on concentration of measure and convexity (Georgia Tech, Fall 2023, version of July 16, 2024), §3.5, Definition 3.4 and Theorem 3.3, p. 32 (A_{θ,K}(t) = |K ∩ (θ⊥ + tθ)|_{n−1}), stated there for convex bodies; the Lean form covers every convex set. Checks: derived from the fibre version by the reparametrisation (t, y) ↦ y + t e and `Submodule.finrank_orthogonal_span_singleton_eq_finrank_sub_one`; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Brunn's inequality in extended-real form: for convex s ⊆ P × F (F a d-dimensional real inner product space), points p, q with nonempty fibres and weights a, b ≥ 0 with a + b = 1, a·|s_p|^{1/d} + b·|s_q|^{1/d} ≤ |s_{a p + b q}|^{1/d}, fibre volumes allowed to be infinite. Lean ↔ mathematics: `Prod.mk p ⁻¹' s` is the fibre {y | (p, y) ∈ s}; `hp hq : (Prod.mk _ ⁻¹' s).Nonempty` say p and q lie in the projection; `volume` is Lebesgue measure on F (`measureSpaceOfInnerProductSpace`) with values in [0, ∞]; `ENNReal.ofReal a` is the weight a in [0, ∞]; `^ (Module.finrank ℝ F : ℝ)⁻¹` is the extended-real power 1/d; `ha hb hab` are the convex weights. Lean subtlety: arithmetic is in ℝ≥0∞, where ∞^{1/d} = ∞ for d ≥ 1 and 0·∞ = 0, so an infinite fibre at p with a > 0 forces an infinite middle fibre — the correct extended reading; in dimension d = 0 the exponent is `(0 : ℝ)⁻¹ = 0`, every power is 1 and the claim is a + b ≤ 1 (the proof's first branch). Nonemptiness cannot be dropped: for d ≥ 1 and s = {q} × F the fibre at p ≠ q is empty (0^{1/d} = 0), the fibre at q is all of F, and the middle fibre is empty, so the left side is ∞ and the right side 0. Source: the displayed chain of inequalities in the proof of Theorem 3.3 in Livshyts, MATH-8803 lecture notes on concentration of measure and convexity (Georgia Tech, Fall 2023, version of July 16, 2024), §3.5, p. 32, proved the same way here (fibre inclusion `Convex.smul_preimage_prodMk_add_smul_preimage_prodMk_subset` plus weighted Brunn–Minkowski `TauCeti.mul_volume_rpow_add_mul_volume_rpow_le`); no measurability hypothesis is needed because convex fibres are null-measurable (`Convex.nullMeasurableSet`). Checks: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

For sets K, L in a real inner product space, a vector e and reals a, b, s, t: a·K_s + b·L_t ⊆ (a·K + b·L)_{a s + b t}, where X_u = `{y : (ℝ ∙ e)ᗮ | (y : E) + u • e ∈ X}` is the section of X by the hyperplane e⊥ + u e, translated into e⊥ (`(ℝ ∙ e)ᗮ` is the orthogonal complement of the line through e), and `•`, `+` on sets are pointwise dilation and Minkowski sum. It is the identity a(y + s e) + b(z + t e) = (a y + b z) + (a s + b t) e, so no sign or convexity condition is needed, matching the arbitrary reals in the statement; it is the two-set form of inclusion (7) in the proof of Theorem 3.3 in Livshyts, MATH-8803 lecture notes on concentration of measure and convexity (Georgia Tech, Fall 2023, version of July 16, 2024), p. 32.

Multiplicative Brunn–Minkowski for sections: for Borel sets K, L in a finite-dimensional real inner product space, a vector e, θ ∈ (0, 1) and heights s, t: |K_s|^{1−θ}·|L_t|^θ ≤ |((1−θ)K + θL)_{(1−θ)s + θt}|. Lean ↔ mathematics: X_u = `{y : (ℝ ∙ e)ᗮ | (y : E) + u • e ∈ X}` is the section of X by the hyperplane e⊥ + u e, translated into e⊥, and `volume` is the Lebesgue measure of the subspace `(ℝ ∙ e)ᗮ`; `(1 - θ) • K + θ • L` is the pointwise Minkowski combination, measured by outer measure (no measurability of it is assumed); `hK hL : MeasurableSet` are Borel measurability; `hθ₀ hθ₁` are 0 < θ < 1; powers are in [0, ∞]. Lean subtlety: in ℝ≥0∞, x^0 = 1 (also for x = 0) and 0·∞ = 0; θ must be strict, since at θ = 0 with L = ∅ the right side is the section of 1•K + 0•∅ = ∅ (volume 0) while the left side is |K_s|. Source: Livshyts, MATH-8803 lecture notes on concentration of measure and convexity (Georgia Tech, Fall 2023, version of July 16, 2024), §3.1, inequality (6), p. 25 (|λK + (1−λ)L| ≥ |K|^λ|L|^{1−λ} for Borel sets), applied in the hyperplane to the sections together with the inclusion `TauCeti.smul_hyperplaneSection_add_smul_hyperplaneSection_subset`. Checks: `lean_minimal_hypotheses` reports hK, hL, hθ₀, hθ₁ load-bearing; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Correctly stated: this is the transformation T with T(E) ~ GEV(m, s, ξ) when E is a rate-one exponential variable. Lean ↔ maths: the body is `if ξ = 0 then m - s * Real.log e else m + s * (Real.exp (-ξ * Real.log e) - 1) / ξ`; for e > 0, `Real.exp (-ξ * Real.log e)` is e^(-ξ) (`generalizedExtremeValueMap_eq_rpow`, via `Real.rpow_def_of_pos`), so T(e) = m + s(e^(-ξ) - 1)/ξ for ξ ≠ 0 and T(e) = m - s log e for ξ = 0, which is the ξ → 0 limit since (e^(-ξ) - 1)/ξ → -log e. It is the right map because, for s > 0 and ξ ≠ 0, P(T(E) ≤ x) = P(E ≥ (1 + ξ(x - m)/s)^(-1/ξ)) = exp(-(1 + ξ(x - m)/s)^(-1/ξ)) on the support, which Cdf.lean proves as `cdf_generalizedExtremeValueMeasure_eq`. Lean subtlety: dividing by ξ would give junk at ξ = 0 (`x / 0 = 0`; the unbranched cdf would have -1/0 = 0 and be the constant exp(-1)). The explicit `if ξ = 0` branch prevents this. Compiled: `generalizedExtremeValueMap 0 1 0 (exp 2) = -2`, whereas the unbranched formula at ξ = 0 is the constant m. Second subtlety: `Real.log` is junk for e ≤ 0 (`Real.log 0 = 0`, `Real.log (-x) = Real.log x`), so T means nothing there. This is harmless because Exp(1) gives (-∞, 0] measure zero (`ae_pos_expMeasure`). The exp∘log form (rather than `e ^ (-ξ)`) keeps T jointly continuous in (m, s, ξ) at every e, which Continuity.lean uses. Source: Coles, An Introduction to Statistical Modeling of Extreme Values (2001), §3.1.3, eq. (3.2) defines GEV by exactly this cdf, with ξ = 0 read as the Gumbel limit. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b (compiled): value tests at ξ = 0, 1 and -1; standard axioms only.

For e > 0 the map is `if ξ = 0 then m - s log e else m + s * (e ^ (-ξ) - 1) / ξ`, with `e ^ (-ξ)` the real power `Real.rpow`. For a positive base, `Real.rpow e y = exp (log e * y)` (`Real.rpow_def_of_pos`), so exp(-ξ log e) = e^(-ξ). Lean subtlety: `he : 0 < e` is genuinely needed, because `Real.rpow` of a non-positive base is not exp(y log e). Compiled counterexample at e = 0, ξ = 1: the map is 0 (exp(-log 0) = exp 0 = 1), but the rpow form gives 0^(-1) - 1 = -1, since Lean's 0^(-1) is 0. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b (compiled).
For `hξ : ξ ≠ 0`, the map is m + s(exp(-ξ log e) - 1)/ξ, the definition's else-branch. Lean subtlety: `hξ` is exactly what excludes the `x / 0 = 0` junk division.

`generalizedExtremeValueMap m s 0 e = m - s * Real.log e`: at shape zero the map is the Gumbel transformation (the definition's `if ξ = 0` branch). Lean subtlety: no division by ξ happens on this branch, so `x / 0` never enters. `Real.log e` is junk for e ≤ 0, but this identity of the definition holds for every e, and only e > 0 matters for the law.

Correctly stated: this is the generalized extreme-value law GEV(m, s, ξ) in the maximum convention (location m, scale s, shape ξ). Lean ↔ maths: the body is `if 0 < s then (expMeasure 1).map (generalizedExtremeValueMap m s ξ) else 0`. Here `expMeasure 1` is Mathlib's rate-one exponential law (`gammaMeasure 1 1`, Lebesgue measure with density e^(-x) on [0, ∞)), and `Measure.map` is the pushforward along the measurable map T, so for s > 0 the measure is the law of T(E) with E ~ Exp(1). Why that is GEV: Cdf.lean's `cdf_generalizedExtremeValueMeasure_eq` computes, for s > 0 and ξ ≠ 0, cdf(x) = exp(-(1 + ξ(x - m)/s)^(-1/ξ)) when 1 + ξ(x - m)/s > 0. Otherwise the cdf is 0 for ξ > 0 (below the lower endpoint m - s/ξ) and 1 for ξ < 0 (above the upper endpoint). That is Coles' (3.2) on its support, with the standard extension. At ξ = 0, `generalizedExtremeValueMeasure_zero` gives `gumbelMeasure m s`, whose cdf is exp(-exp(-(x - m)/s)), Coles' ξ → 0 member. The signs match Coles: ξ > 0 is Fréchet type (type II) and ξ < 0 is Weibull type (type III). Lean subtlety: (a) s ≤ 0 lies outside the parameter space (Coles requires σ > 0), and there the definition returns the zero measure, which is not a probability law. Every probabilistic statement about it carries `0 < s`. (b) ξ = 0 is a separate branch inside T, so neither -1/ξ = -1/0 = 0 (which would make the naive formula the constant exp(-1)) nor (n^ξ - 1)/ξ = 0/0 = 0 can enter. Max.lean's max-stability and Quantile.lean's quantile also branch explicitly on ξ = 0. (c) The junk values of `Real.log` on e ≤ 0 are invisible because Exp(1) is almost surely positive. (d) `Measure.map` is the genuine pushforward because T is measurable (`measurable_generalizedExtremeValueMap_right`). (e) The cdf formula uses `Real.rpow` only under the guard 0 < 1 + ξ(x - m)/s, so the junk value of rpow on a negative base never appears. Source: Coles (2001) §3.1.3, eq. (3.2), pp. 47–48: σ > 0, ξ ∈ ℝ, and ξ = 0 is the Gumbel limit. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b (compiled): Fréchet witness cdf GEV(0,1,1)(1) = exp(-1/2); Weibull-type witness cdf GEV(0,1,-1)(1) = 1 at the upper endpoint m - s/ξ = 1; Gumbel witness cdf GEV(0,1,0)(0) = exp(-1). Max-stability at ξ = 0, n = 2 gives location m + s log 2 and scale s. The ξ = 0 quantile is m - s log(-log u). Standard axioms only; no GEV law in pinned Mathlib (leansearch, leanfinder, grep).

For s ≤ 0 the measure is 0. Lean subtlety: this is the totalisation outside the parameter space σ > 0. It returns the zero measure, not a probability law, and the lemma states that explicitly so that no consumer mistakes it.

For `hs : 0 < s`, GEV(m, s, ξ) is the pushforward `(expMeasure 1).map (generalizedExtremeValueMap m s ξ)`, the law of T(E) with E ~ Exp(1). It unfolds the definition's `if 0 < s`. Lean subtlety: `hs` selects the non-junk branch; without it the measure is 0.

For s > 0 and ξ ≠ 0, GEV(m, s, ξ) is the law of m + s(E^(-ξ) - 1)/ξ with E ~ Exp(1) and `E ^ (-ξ)` the real power. Lean subtlety: `Real.rpow` is junk on a non-positive base (0^(-ξ) = 0 for ξ ≠ 0; a negative base gives exp(y log|e|)cos(πy)). The proof uses `Measure.map_congr` with `ae_pos_expMeasure` to show those inputs are Exp(1)-null. Both hypotheses are needed: s ≤ 0 makes the left side 0, and ξ = 0 would make the right side the Dirac mass at m, because (e^0 - 1)/0 = 0 in Lean.

GEV(m, s, 0) equals `gumbelMeasure m s` for every s. Coles §3.1.3 makes the ξ = 0 member the Gumbel law exp(-exp(-(x - m)/s)). Lean ↔ maths: for s > 0, `gumbelMeasure m s` is the Exp(1) pushforward by e ↦ m - s log e, which is T's ξ = 0 branch (its cdf is `cdf_gumbelMeasure_eq`); for s ≤ 0 it is 0. Lean subtlety: for s ≤ 0 both sides are the zero measure, so that case holds by the shared totalisation, not by any fact about probability. For s > 0 it is the genuine identity, and no division by ξ occurs. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b (compiled): Gumbel cdf witness exp(-1) at x = m.

Random-variable form: for b > 0, if X ~ GEV(m, s, ξ) under P, then a + bX ~ GEV(a + bm, bs, ξ). Lean subtlety: when s ≤ 0 the hypothesis says that X has the zero law, which forces P = 0; the conclusion is then degenerate but true. For s > 0 the statement is genuine.

If E has law Exp(1) under P, then T(E) has law GEV(m, s, ξ) for s > 0. `HasLaw E (expMeasure 1) P` means that E is P-a.e. measurable and `P.map E = expMeasure 1`. Lean subtlety: T(E) is also evaluated where E ≤ 0 (junk `Real.log`), but that set is P-null. `hs` is needed because the law is the zero measure for s ≤ 0.

If E ~ Exp(1) under P, s > 0 and ξ ≠ 0, then m + s(E^(-ξ) - 1)/ξ has law GEV(m, s, ξ) (the `HasLaw` form of `generalizedExtremeValueMeasure_of_shape_ne_zero`). Lean subtlety: `E ω ^ (-ξ)` is `Real.rpow`, junk where E ≤ 0, which is a P-null set. `hξ` excludes the `x / 0` junk.

For s > 0, GEV(m, s, ξ) has total mass 1 (`IsProbabilityMeasure`): it is the pushforward of the probability measure Exp(1) along a measurable map. Lean subtlety: `hs` is needed, since s ≤ 0 gives the zero measure.

For b > 0, if X ~ GEV(m, s, ξ) then a + bX ~ GEV(a + bm, bs, ξ). `(μ).map (fun x => a + b * x)` is the law of a + bX. The proof is the pointwise identity a + b(m + s(e^(-ξ) - 1)/ξ) = (a + bm) + (bs)(e^(-ξ) - 1)/ξ, together with its ξ = 0 analogue. This is the location-scale closure Coles uses in §3.1.3 (p. 48: G{(z - b_n)/a_n} is another GEV member). Lean subtlety: for s ≤ 0 both sides are the zero measure (b·s ≤ 0), true by the totalisation. `hb` is necessary: compiled, b = 0 gives a Dirac mass at a on the left and the zero measure on the right. Specialised at ξ = 0, it is the Gumbel statement `map_affine_gumbelMeasure` (compiled). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b (compiled).

The map (m, s, ξ, e) ↦ T is Borel measurable jointly in all four reals. `((ℝ × ℝ) × ℝ) × ℝ` carries the product σ-algebra, which is the Borel σ-algebra of ℝ⁴, and the `if ξ = 0` is a case split on the measurable set {ξ = 0}. Lean subtlety: the junk values of `Real.log` on e ≤ 0 are still measurable, so they do not affect the claim.

For fixed (m, s, ξ), e ↦ T(e) is measurable. Lean subtlety: in pinned Mathlib, `Measure.map` along a map that is not a.e.-measurable gives a junk value, not the pushforward. This lemma is what makes `generalizedExtremeValueMeasure` the genuine law of T(E).

(m, s, ξ) ↦ GEV(m, s, ξ) is measurable into `Measure ℝ` with Mathlib's Giry σ-algebra (generated by μ ↦ μ(A) for measurable A), so the family is a measurable kernel in its parameters. The proof branches on the measurable set {0 < s} and uses joint measurability of T. Lean subtlety: the s ≤ 0 branch is the zero measure, so this is a measurable family of finite measures, and probability measures only for s > 0.

Correctly stated: `IsAdmissibleModulus K L 𝔪` says the modulus 𝔪 is admissible for L/K, i.e. the ray subgroup C_K^𝔪 lies in the norm group N_{L/K}(C_L). Lean ↔ mathematics: the body is `raySubgroup 𝔪 ≤ (ideleClassNormMap K L).range`. `raySubgroup 𝔪` is the image in C_K = `IdeleClassGroup (𝓞 K) K` of `ideleCongruenceSubgroup 𝔪` (unit at finite 𝔭 ∤ 𝔪, in 1 + 𝔭^{n_𝔭} at 𝔭 | 𝔪, positive at the real places of 𝔪, free elsewhere), which is Milne's W_𝔪K^×/K^× (CFT v4.03, V §4); `(ideleClassNormMap K L).range` is the image of the idele norm with coordinates ∏_{w|v} N_{L_w/K_v}, i.e. N_{L/K}(C_L); `≤` is subgroup inclusion. For abelian L/K the Artin map C_K → Gal(L/K) has kernel N_{L/K}(C_L) (Milne Thm V.5.3(b)), so the condition says the Artin map factors through the ray class group mod 𝔪, the condition in Milne's Remark V.3.8. Lean subtlety: no abelian hypothesis, so for general L/K this is the norm-group condition, as the docstring says; `Modulus` carries only real places, so complex places impose nothing, as in Milne V §1. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: for ℚ(i)/ℚ compiled that (8)·∞ is admissible while (2)·∞, (4) and (1) are not, matching 𝔣 = (4)·∞.

Correctly stated: if 𝔪 is admissible for L/K and `𝔪 ∣ 𝔫` (finite part of 𝔪 divides that of 𝔫 and its real places are among those of 𝔫, `Modulus.dvd_iff`), then 𝔫 is admissible: 𝔫 imposes stronger congruence and sign conditions, so its ray subgroup is smaller (`raySubgroup_antitone`) and still lies in N_{L/K}(C_L).

Correctly stated: `[Algebra L M] [Algebra K M] [IsScalarTower K L M]` encode a tower K ⊆ L ⊆ M; if C_K^𝔪 ⊆ N_{M/K}(C_M) then C_K^𝔪 ⊆ N_{L/K}(C_L), because N_{M/K}(C_M) = N_{L/K}(N_{M/L}(C_M)) ⊆ N_{L/K}(C_L) (`range_ideleClassNormMap_le_of_algHom` applied to the inclusion `IsScalarTower.toAlgHom K L M`).

Correctly stated: `abelianConductor K L` is the conductor 𝔣(L/K), the least modulus of K (for divisibility) whose ray subgroup of the idele class group lies in the norm group N_{L/K}(C_L). Lean ↔ mathematics: `Modulus K` is a pair (`finitePart`, a nonzero ideal of `𝓞 K`; `infinitePart`, a `Finset` of the subtype `{w : InfinitePlace K // w.IsReal}`), which is Milne's 𝔪 = 𝔪_∞𝔪_0 with 𝔪_0 identified with an ideal and complex places excluded (Milne, CFT v4.03, V §1); `𝔪 ∣ 𝔫` is by `Modulus.dvd_iff` 'finite parts divide and infinite parts are contained', Milne's 𝔪(𝔭) ≤ 𝔫(𝔭) for all 𝔭. `IdeleClassGroup (𝓞 K) K` is Mathlib's `(AdeleRing)ˣ ⧸ unitEmbedding(Kˣ)`, i.e. C_K = 𝕀_K/K^×. `raySubgroup 𝔪` is the image in C_K of `ideleCongruenceSubgroup 𝔪`, whose membership (`mem_ideleCongruenceSubgroup_iff`) is: valuation 1 at finite 𝔭 ∤ 𝔪_0; `Valued.v (x_𝔭 - 1) ≤ exp (-n_𝔭)` at 𝔭 | 𝔪_0, i.e. x_𝔭 ∈ 1 + 𝔭^{n_𝔭} since Mathlib's adic valuation is exp(-ord_𝔭); positive under `extensionEmbeddingOfIsReal` (K_w → ℝ) at the real w in 𝔪_∞; no condition elsewhere. That is exactly Milne's W_𝔪 (V §4), so `raySubgroup 𝔪` = W_𝔪K^×/K^×. `ideleClassNormMap K L` is induced by `ideleNormMap`, whose coordinate at v is ∏_{w|v} N_{L_w/K_v}(x_w) (`ideleFiniteCoord_ideleNormMap`, `ideleInfiniteCoord_ideleNormMap`), Milne's idele norm (V §4); its `.range` is N_{L/K}(C_L), made an `OpenSubgroup` by `isOpen_range_ideleClassNormMap` (cf. Milne Cor. V.4.13: Nm 𝕀_L ⊇ W_𝔪 for some 𝔪). The body `OpenSubgroup.ideleClassConductor U` is `WellFounded.min` (for strict divisibility, well founded by `Modulus.wellFounded_dvd_and_ne`) of {𝔪 | raySubgroup 𝔪 ≤ U}, and `ideleClassConductor_dvd_iff` (via `raySubgroup_gcd`: the admissible moduli are closed under gcd) shows the minimal element is the least: 𝔣 ∣ 𝔪 ↔ raySubgroup 𝔪 ≤ U. For abelian L/K this is Milne's 𝔣(L/K) (Remark V.3.8: the smallest modulus through whose ray class group the Artin map factors), because the Artin map on C_K has kernel exactly N_{L/K}(C_L) (Milne Thm V.5.3(b)). Lean subtlety: the minimum is `WellFounded.min` (a `Classical.choice`) of a set whose nonemptiness is the PROVED theorem `exists_raySubgroup_le_of_isOpen`, not an `sInf`, so there is no `sInf ∅` junk value; and since `∣` is antisymmetric (`Modulus.dvd_antisymm`) the least element is unique, so the choice is irrelevant (compiled: any 𝔣 with ∀ 𝔪, `IsAdmissibleModulus K L 𝔪 ↔ 𝔣 ∣ 𝔪` equals `abelianConductor K L`). There is no abelian or Galois hypothesis: for non-abelian L/K the definition returns the conductor of the norm group, as the docstring says. `K L : Type` (universe 0), the convention of the class-field-theory area; every number field is isomorphic to one in `Type`, so nothing is lost. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: compiled `abelianConductor ℚ ℚ = Modulus.one ℚ`; for every E with `IsCyclotomicExtension {4} ℚ E` (inhabited by `CyclotomicField 4 ℚ`) `finitePart = Ideal.span {4}` and `infinitePart = {∞}`, i.e. 𝔣(ℚ(i)/ℚ) = (4)·∞ (via the downstream `abelianConductor_cyclotomic_eq_ratModulus`); (2)·∞ and (4) are not admissible and (8)·∞ is; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.

Correctly stated: for a tower K ⊆ L ⊆ M (`[IsScalarTower K L M]`), 𝔣(L/K) ∣ 𝔣(M/K) in the sense of `Modulus.dvd_iff`: 𝔣(M/K) is admissible for M/K, hence for L/K (`IsAdmissibleModulus.tower_bot`), hence divisible by 𝔣(L/K). Classically: a subextension has the larger norm group, hence the smaller conductor.

Correctly stated: `abelianConductor K K = Modulus.one K`, the trivial extension has the unit modulus (1) as conductor; `Modulus.one K` has finite part ⊤ = 𝓞_K and empty infinite part. Correctly stated: a modulus 𝔪 is admissible for L/K exactly when the conductor 𝔣(L/K) divides it. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: `lean_minimal_hypotheses` finds `p`, `hw`, `hζ`, `hpn` all load-bearing; the hypotheses are satisfiable (K = ℚ, L = ℚ(i), p = 2, n = 2, as `not_isAdmissibleModulus_one_Qi` instantiates them); standard axioms only.

Correctly defined: `BrauerAlgebra R δ k` is Brauer's algebra B_k(δ) on k strands with loop value δ, over a commutative semiring R. Lean ↔ mathematics: an element is its coefficient function `coeff : BrauerDiagram k →₀ R` (finitely supported functions on diagrams, i.e. the free R-module on the diagrams); `BrauerDiagram k` is `PerfectMatching (Fin k ⊕ Fin k)`, the fixed-point-free involutions of the 2k boundary points (`Sum.inl i` = i-th bottom point, `Sum.inr j` = j-th top point), which are exactly the Brauer diagrams (perfect matchings of k bottom and k top points); the product (`coeff_mul`) is the bilinear map `mulCoeff δ`, which on basis elements gives `of D₁ * of D₂ = δ ^ middleLoopCount D₁ D₂ • of (composeDiagram D₁ D₂)` (`of_mul_of`), where `composeDiagram D₁ D₂` places D₁ above D₂, identifies D₁'s bottom row with D₂'s top row and joins the outer points connected by a strand, and `middleLoopCount D₁ D₂` is the number of connected components of the middle graph (caps of D₁, cups of D₂) all of whose points carry both a cap and a cup, i.e. the closed loops; the unit is the identity diagram `permToBrauer 1` (`one_def`). The algebra laws are proved (associativity from `composeDiagram_assoc` and the loop-count identity `middleLoopCount_add_middleLoopCount_composeDiagram`), the diagrams form a basis (`basis`), the rank is (2k−1)‼ (`finrank_eq_doubleFactorial`) and R[S_k] embeds (`ofPerm_injective`). Lean subtlety: `δ ^ 0 = 1` even when δ = 0, so at δ = 0 a loop-free product keeps coefficient 1 while any product closing a loop vanishes, which is the intended convention; the structure wrapper (as for Mathlib's `MonoidAlgebra`) keeps this product apart from `Finsupp`'s pointwise one; the rank formula uses truncated ℕ subtraction `2 * k - 1`, harmless (see `finrank_eq_doubleFactorial`). Source: The Wikipedia article 'Brauer algebra' (read for this audit) defines B_n(δ) over ℤ[δ] the same way (basis = pairings of 2n points, product = concatenation times δ^r, r = number of closed middle loops removed, dimension (2n−1)‼); the Lean version over any commutative semiring with δ ∈ R is its specialisation. Checks at 5f78b5307b: ranks 1, 1, 3, 15, 105 for k = 0..4 compiled; `Fintype.card (BrauerDiagram 2) = 3` and 'every diagram on 1 strand is the identity' by `decide`; e² = δe at k = 2; in B_4(δ) the relations give (e₀₁e₂₃)² = δ²·e₀₁e₂₃, and over ℤ[X] with δ = X this forces the middle-loop count of that stack to be 2 (loops counted with multiplicity); no instance diamond (Ring/Semiring, AddCommGroup/AddCommMonoid, Algebra.toModule, ℤ-module all agree by `with_reducible_and_instances rfl`); axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Two R-algebra maps f, g from B_k(δ) to an R-algebra A that agree on every diagram basis element `of D` are equal: the `of D` are the basis `basis R δ k`, so the underlying linear maps agree (`Module.Basis.ext`); registered `@[ext]`.

`basis R δ k : Module.Basis (BrauerDiagram k) R (BrauerAlgebra R δ k)` is the diagram basis: a basis indexed by the Brauer diagrams whose coordinate map is `coeffLinearEquiv` (the coefficients), so B_k(δ) is free on the diagrams with `basis R δ k D = of D` (`basis_apply`).
`basis R δ k D = of D`: the D-th basis vector is the basis element of the diagram D (`rfl`).
`(basis R δ k).repr x = x.coeff`: the coordinates of x in the diagram basis are its coefficients (`rfl`).

`coeffAddEquiv R δ k : BrauerAlgebra R δ k ≃+ (BrauerDiagram k →₀ R)` is `coeffEquiv` as an additive isomorphism (Mathlib's `Equiv.addEquiv` for the transported addition): reading off coefficients is additive and bijective.

`coeffEquiv R δ k : BrauerAlgebra R δ k ≃ (BrauerDiagram k →₀ R)` is the bijection between elements and coefficient functions, `toFun := coeff`, `invFun := ofCoeff`, with both inverse laws by `rfl`; the additive and module structures are transported along it, so the algebra's underlying module is the free module on the diagrams.

`coeffLinearEquiv R δ k : BrauerAlgebra R δ k ≃ₗ[R] (BrauerDiagram k →₀ R)` is the R-linear isomorphism with the free module on the Brauer diagrams given by the coefficients; it is the coordinate map (`repr`) of `basis R δ k`.
`coeffLinearEquiv R δ k x = x.coeff`: the linear equivalence reads off the coefficients (`rfl`).
`(coeffLinearEquiv R δ k).symm f = ofCoeff f`: its inverse builds the element with coefficients f (`rfl`).
`(x + y).coeff = x.coeff + y.coeff`: addition is coefficientwise, as in the free module on the diagrams (`rfl`).
`(x * y).coeff = mulCoeff δ x.coeff y.coeff`: the algebra's product is the loop-weighted stacking of the coefficient vectors (by definition, `rfl`).
`(-x).coeff = -x.coeff` over a commutative ring: negation is coefficientwise (transported additive group, `rfl`).
`(of D).coeff = Finsupp.single D 1`: the basis element of D has coefficient 1 at D and 0 at every other diagram (`rfl`).
`(ofCoeff f).coeff = f`: building the element with coefficient function f and reading its coefficients back returns f (structure projection, `rfl`).
The coefficients of `ofPerm R δ k x` are those of x transported along σ ↦ permToBrauer σ (`Finsupp.mapDomain permToBrauer x.coeff`): Σ r_σ σ goes to Σ r_σ [permToBrauer σ].
`(1 : BrauerAlgebra R δ k).coeff = Finsupp.single (permToBrauer 1) 1`: the unit is the identity diagram `permToBrauer 1` with coefficient 1, as in the standard definition.
`(r • x).coeff = r • x.coeff` for r ∈ R: scalar multiplication is coefficientwise, so the R-module is the free module on the diagrams (`rfl`).
`(x - y).coeff = x.coeff - y.coeff` over a commutative ring: subtraction is coefficientwise (`rfl`).
`(0 : BrauerAlgebra R δ k).coeff = 0`: the zero element has all coefficients 0 (additive structure transported from `BrauerDiagram k →₀ R` along `coeffEquiv`, `rfl`).
Uniqueness in the universal property: an algebra map f with f (of D) = F D for every diagram D equals `lift F h_one h_mul` (via `algHom_ext`).
