Two elements of the Brauer algebra with the same coefficient function `coeff` are equal: `BrauerAlgebra` is a one-field structure around `coeff : BrauerDiagram k →₀ R`, so this is its extensionality (proof by `cases`), registered `@[ext]`.

The Brauer algebra B_k(δ) has rank (2k−1)‼ = (2k−1)(2k−3)⋯3·1 over R. Lean ↔ mathematics: `Module.finrank R (BrauerAlgebra R δ k)` is the rank of the free R-module; it equals the size of the basis `basis R δ k` (`Module.finrank_eq_card_basis`), i.e. `Fintype.card (BrauerDiagram k)`, the number of perfect matchings of the 2k boundary points, which `card_brauerDiagram` computes as `(2 * k - 1)‼` (`Nat.doubleFactorial`). `[StrongRankCondition R]` is the hypothesis under which the rank of a free module is the size of any basis; it holds for every nontrivial commutative ring (Mathlib's `commRing_strongRankCondition`, which lives in `Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.FreeModule.StrongRankCondition`, not imported by this file), and some such hypothesis is necessary since over the zero ring `Module.finrank` is 0. Lean subtlety: `2 * k - 1` is truncated ℕ subtraction, so at k = 0 it is 0, not −1, and `0‼ = 1`: coincidentally the correct value, since B_0(δ) = R (one empty diagram) has rank 1, matching the convention (−1)‼ = 1; and `Module.finrank` would be a junk 0 for a module without finite rank, but here a finite basis exists, so the value is genuine. Source: The Wikipedia article 'Brauer algebra' (read for this audit) gives dim B_n(δ) = (2n)!/(2ⁿ n!) = (2n−1)‼. Checks at 5f78b5307b: compiled over a nontrivial commutative ring at k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 giving 1, 1, 3, 15, 105 (the numbers of perfect matchings of 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 points), and `Fintype.card (BrauerDiagram 2) = 3` independently by `decide`; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Over a commutative ring R the Brauer algebra is a ring: `instSemiring` together with the additive group transported from `BrauerDiagram k →₀ R`; `Ring.toSemiring = instSemiring` and the two additive monoid structures agree by `with_reducible_and_instances rfl`, and the ℤ-module from the group agrees with the R-module one at R = ℤ (`with_reducible_and_instances rfl`).

The Brauer algebra is a unital associative semiring: distributivity and the zero laws come from the bilinearity of `mulCoeff`, `mul_assoc` is `mulCoeff_assoc` (the loop-count identity), and `one_mul`/`mul_one` are `mulCoeff_one_left`/`mulCoeff_one_right` for the identity diagram; addition is the free-module addition. Checks: `Ring.toSemiring` of `instRing` is `instSemiring` and the additive monoids agree, both by `with_reducible_and_instances rfl` (no diamond); axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

Universal property of the diagram basis: a function F from Brauer diagrams to an R-algebra A with F(identity diagram) = 1 (`h_one`) and F(D₁)F(D₂) = δ^(middleLoopCount D₁ D₂) • F(composeDiagram D₁ D₂) (`h_mul`, the loop rule) extends to an R-algebra map `BrauerAlgebra R δ k →ₐ[R] A`, namely the linear extension `(basis R δ k).constr R F`, multiplicative because it is so on pairs of basis vectors. The hypotheses are exactly what every algebra map satisfies on the basis, so nothing extra is assumed, and they are satisfiable: lifting `of` itself gives `AlgHom.id` (compiled).
`lift F h_one h_mul (of D) = F D`: the extended algebra map sends each diagram's basis element to its prescribed value.

`mulCoeff δ` is the R-bilinear map on coefficient vectors `BrauerDiagram k →₀ R` extending (D₁, D₂) ↦ δ^c·[D₁∘D₂] with c = `middleLoopCount D₁ D₂` and D₁∘D₂ = `composeDiagram D₁ D₂`: it is `Finsupp.lsum` (linear extension from basis vectors) in each variable with inner value `δ ^ middleLoopCount D₁ D₂ • Finsupp.lsingle (composeDiagram D₁ D₂)`, evaluated by `mulCoeff_single_single`; this is the Brauer product in coordinates. Lean subtlety: `δ ^ 0 = 1` also for δ = 0, so loop-free stacks keep coefficient 1 at δ = 0, the intended convention.

`mulCoeff δ (mulCoeff δ f g) h = mulCoeff δ f (mulCoeff δ g h)` for all coefficient vectors: the Brauer product is associative. By trilinearity (`Finsupp.induction_linear` in each argument) it reduces to basis vectors, where it is (D₁∘D₂)∘D₃ = D₁∘(D₂∘D₃) (`composeDiagram_assoc`) together with c(D₁,D₂) + c(D₁∘D₂,D₃) = c(D₂,D₃) + c(D₁,D₂∘D₃) for the middle-loop counts (`middleLoopCount_add_middleLoopCount_composeDiagram`), so both bracketings carry the same power of δ. This is the substantive associativity theorem, proved rather than assumed; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

`mulCoeff δ (single (permToBrauer 1) 1) f = f`: the identity diagram (bottom i joined to top i), stacked on top with coefficient 1, is a left unit, since it closes no loop and is a unit for `composeDiagram`.
`mulCoeff δ f (single (permToBrauer 1) 1) = f`: the identity diagram stacked below with coefficient 1 is a right unit (no loop, unit for `composeDiagram`).

On basis vectors, `mulCoeff δ (single D₁ a) (single D₂ b) = single (composeDiagram D₁ D₂) (δ ^ middleLoopCount D₁ D₂ * (a * b))`: (a[D₁])·(b[D₂]) = δ^c ab [D₁∘D₂], where `Finsupp.single D r` is r times the basis vector of D; the multiplication table of B_k(δ).
`of D` is the basis element of the diagram D: the element with coefficient function `Finsupp.single D 1` (1 at D, 0 elsewhere); `basis_apply` identifies it with the D-th vector of the diagram basis.
`ofCoeff x.coeff = x`: every element is rebuilt from its coefficients (structure eta, `rfl`).
`ofCoeff (Finsupp.single D r) = r • of D`: the element whose only nonzero coefficient is r at D is r times the basis element of D.

`ofPerm R δ k : MonoidAlgebra R (Equiv.Perm (Fin k)) →ₐ[R] BrauerAlgebra R δ k` is the R-algebra map from the group algebra R[S_k] sending each permutation σ to its diagram `of (permToBrauer σ)` (bottom i joined to top σ(i)); it is `MonoidAlgebra.lift` of the monoid hom σ ↦ of (permToBrauer σ), whose multiplicativity is `of_permToBrauer_mul_of_permToBrauer` and unit law `one_def`. This is the standard copy of the group algebra of S_k inside B_k(δ) (The Wikipedia article 'Brauer algebra' (read for this audit): the subalgebra generated by the s_i is the group algebra of S_n).

The group algebra of S_k embeds in the Brauer algebra: `Function.Injective (ofPerm R δ k)` for every commutative semiring R and every δ. Lean ↔ mathematics: `MonoidAlgebra R (Equiv.Perm (Fin k))` is R[S_k]; `ofPerm` sends σ to the diagram `permToBrauer σ`; by `coeff_ofPerm` the coefficient vector of the image of x is `Finsupp.mapDomain permToBrauer x.coeff`, and since `permToBrauer` is injective (distinct permutations give distinct matchings, `permToBrauer_injective`), `Finsupp.mapDomain` along it is injective (`Finsupp.mapDomain_injective`). Lean subtlety: none beyond generality: no nontriviality or invertibility hypothesis is needed (over the zero ring both sides are 0 and injectivity holds trivially, as it should), and the statement is injectivity only, not surjectivity (for k = 2 the cap-cup diagram is not in the image; compiled). Source: The Wikipedia article 'Brauer algebra' (read for this audit) (the s_i generate the group algebra of S_n inside B_n(δ)). Checks at 5f78b5307b: instantiated over the semiring ℕ; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.
`ofPerm R δ k (MonoidAlgebra.single σ r) = r • of (permToBrauer σ)`: r·σ ∈ R[S_k] goes to r times the diagram of σ.

For a ≠ b, `of (capCup a b) * of (capCup a b) = δ • of (capCup a b)`, Brauer's relation e² = δe: `capCup a b` is the diagram with a cap joining the bottom points a, b, a cup joining the top points a, b and vertical strands elsewhere (the generator e_{a,b}); stacking it on itself returns it and closes exactly one loop. The hypothesis a ≠ b is necessary: `capCup a a` is the identity diagram, and 1·1 = 1 ≠ 2·1 over ℚ with δ = 2 (compiled counterexample). Checked at k = 2.
`of (capCup a b) * of (permToBrauer (swap a b)) = of (capCup a b)`, the relation e·s = e: the transposition diagram of {a, b} stacked below e_{a,b} closes no loop and is absorbed (a = b allowed).

**The loop rule**: `of D₁ * of D₂ = δ ^ middleLoopCount D₁ D₂ • of (composeDiagram D₁ D₂)`, i.e. D₁·D₂ = δ^c (D₁∘D₂) on the diagram basis. Lean ↔ mathematics: `composeDiagram D₁ D₂` places D₁ above D₂, identifies D₁'s bottom row with D₂'s top row, and joins two outer points when a strand connects them; `middleLoopCount D₁ D₂` counts the components of the middle graph (caps of D₁, cups of D₂) made only of points carrying both, i.e. the closed loops that are removed; `•` is the R-action. Lean subtlety: at δ = 0 a loop-free product keeps coefficient `0 ^ 0 = 1`, the intended value; the left factor is the upper diagram, which is the convention that makes `permToBrauer` multiplicative (`of_permToBrauer_mul_of_permToBrauer`). Source: The Wikipedia article 'Brauer algebra' (read for this audit) states the product as concatenation (bottom row of the left factor glued to the top row of the right) times δ^r, r = number of closed middle loops. Checks: compiled e·e = δe at k = 2, and in B_4(δ) (e₀₁e₂₃)² = δ²·e₀₁e₂₃, which over ℤ[X] forces a middle-loop count of 2.

If stacking D₁ above D₂ closes no loop (`middleLoopCount D₁ D₂ = 0`), then `of D₁ * of D₂ = of (composeDiagram D₁ D₂)`: the loop rule with δ^0 = 1; the hypothesis is load-bearing (without it the factor δ^c remains, e.g. e·e = δe).

`of (permToBrauer σ) * of (capCup a b) * of (permToBrauer σ⁻¹) = of (capCup (σ a) (σ b))`, i.e. σ e_{a,b} σ⁻¹ = e_{σ(a),σ(b)}: with `permToBrauer σ` joining bottom i to top σ(i) and the left factor on top, the bottom points capped in the product are the i with σ⁻¹(i) ∈ {a, b}, namely {σ a, σ b}, as stated; no loop closes since permutation diagrams have no caps or cups.

`of (permToBrauer σ) * of (permToBrauer τ) = of (permToBrauer (σ * τ))`: `permToBrauer σ` is the diagram joining bottom i to top σ(i); stacking σ above τ closes no loop and composes to the diagram of σ ∘ τ = σ * τ, so permutation diagrams multiply as in S_k.

`of (permToBrauer (swap a b)) * of (capCup a b) = of (capCup a b)`, the relation s·e = e: the transposition diagram of {a, b} stacked above e_{a,b} closes no loop and is absorbed; also true for a = b, where both diagrams are the identity.
`1 = of (permToBrauer 1)`: the unit of the Brauer algebra is the basis element of the identity diagram (bottom i joined to top i), as in the standard definition.

A smooth proper geometrically integral curve X over k with H¹(X,𝒪_X) = 0 becomes isomorphic to ℙ¹ over some separable extension K/k of degree at most 2. The section variables `[IsProper (X ↘ Spec k)]`, `[SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 (X ↘ Spec k)]` and `[GeometricallyIntegral (X ↘ Spec k)]` are Mathlib's proper, smooth of relative dimension one and geometrically integral, i.e. a smooth proper geometrically integral curve. `hg` is dim_k H¹(X,𝒪_X) = 0. The conclusion `∃ (K : Type u) (_ : Field K) (_ : Algebra k K), FiniteDimensional k K ∧ finrank k K ≤ 2 ∧ Algebra.IsSeparable k K ∧ ∃ e : pullback (X ↘ Spec k) (Spec.map (algebraMap k K)) ≅ projectiveLine K, e.hom ≫ (projectiveLine K ↘ Spec K) = pullback.snd _ _` gives a finite separable extension K/k of degree ≤ 2. It also gives an isomorphism of the fibre product X ×_k K with ℙ¹_K whose composite with ℙ¹_K → Spec K is the second projection, i.e. an isomorphism over K. Lean subtlety: `FiniteDimensional k K` is stated, so `finrank k K ≤ 2` cannot hold through finrank's junk 0. K is quantified in k's universe, which costs nothing since the witness is a residue field κ(x). Red-team checks: proved with K = κ(x) from `exists_finrank_residueField_le_two_and_isSeparable_of_genus_eq_zero` and `exists_iso_projectiveLine_of_isPullback_of_genus_eq_zero` with the identity embedding. Axioms standard.

A smooth proper geometrically integral curve X over k with H¹(X,𝒪_X) = 0 has a point whose residue field is a separable extension of k of degree at most 2. The section variables `[IsProper (X ↘ Spec k)]`, `[SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 (X ↘ Spec k)]` and `[GeometricallyIntegral (X ↘ Spec k)]` are Mathlib's proper, smooth of relative dimension one and geometrically integral, i.e. a smooth proper geometrically integral curve. `hg` is dim_k H¹(X,𝒪_X) = 0. The conclusion `∃ x : X, FiniteDimensional k (X.residueField x) ∧ finrank k (X.residueField x) ≤ 2 ∧ Algebra.IsSeparable k (X.residueField x)` says κ(x) is finite over k, of degree ≤ 2, and separable. κ(x)'s k-algebra structure comes from the structure morphism (`Scheme.residueFieldBaseAlgebra`). Lean subtlety: `finrank k κ(x) ≤ 2` alone would hold at the generic point, where κ = k(X) is infinite-dimensional and finrank is the junk 0. The conjunct `FiniteDimensional k κ(x)` excludes this, so the bound is genuine. Red-team checks: the point is the closed point of a place of degree ≤ 2 with separable residue field (`CodimensionOnePoint.toPlace_surjective`, residue fields identified by `toPlaceResidueFieldAlgEquiv`). Axioms standard. Stacks Tag 0C6N (read in the Stacks source: a Gorenstein proper genus-zero curve with H⁰ = k is a plane conic) is the related classical fact.

A regular proper curve over k with exact constants k, H¹(X,𝒪_X) = 0 and a divisor of degree one is isomorphic to ℙ¹_k over k. The curve, regularity, `hk` and `hg` hypotheses are those of `exists_iso_projectiveLine_of_genus_eq_zero_of_section`: IsCurveOver = integral, proper, dimension one; DVR local rings at codimension-one points; k integrally closed in k(X); dim_k H¹(X,𝒪_X) = 0 for derived-functor sheaf cohomology of 𝒪_X. `hD : SchemeWeilDivisor.relativeDegree (X ↘ Spec k) D = 1`: `relativeDegree f` is by definition `WeilDivisor.weightedDegree` with weight `residueDegree f x` = [κ(x):k] at each codimension-one point x, so hD is deg D = Σ n_x [κ(x):k] = 1. The conclusion `∃ e : X ≅ projectiveLine k, e.hom.IsOver (Spec k)` is a k-isomorphism with Proj k[X₀,X₁] with its canonical structure map (checked by `rfl`). Lean subtlety: finrank's junk 0 on infinite-dimensional spaces is excluded because the proof first proves H¹ finite-dimensional. `residueDegree` would be 0 at a point with infinite residue field, but codimension-one points of a curve are closed with residue field finite over k, so deg D is the true degree. Stacks Tag 0C6U (7), read in the Stacks source: H¹(X,𝒪_X) = 0 and an invertible module of degree 1 give X ≅ ℙ¹_k; on a regular curve Weil divisors are Cartier, so this is the same statement under extra hypotheses (hk is mathematically redundant, see RT-20261105-a5d217). Red-team checks: ℙ¹_k with D the point at infinity satisfies every hypothesis (compiled), so they are not vacuous; axioms standard.

A regular proper curve X over a field k with H¹(X,𝒪_X) = 0, with k integrally closed in k(X), and with a k-rational point is isomorphic to ℙ¹_k over k. `[X.IsCurveOver k]` unfolds (`isCurveOver_iff`) to `IsIntegral X`, `IsProper (X ↘ Spec k)` (separated, finite type, universally closed) and `topologicalKrullDim X = 1`: an integral proper scheme of dimension one over k. `[∀ y : CodimensionOnePoint X, IsDiscreteValuationRing (X.presheaf.stalk y)]` asks for a DVR local ring at every point of coheight one (`CodimensionOnePoint X` is `{x // Order.coheight x = 1}`). On an integral 1-dimensional scheme these are all points except the generic one, whose local ring is the field k(X), so this is regularity. `hk : IsIntegrallyClosedIn k X.functionField` is `IsIntegralClosure k k k(X)`: every element of k(X) integral over k lies in k, so k is the exact constant field. Its k-algebra structure on k(X) is `Scheme.functionFieldBaseAlgebra`, from the structure morphism. `hg : finrank k (Scheme.Modules.Cohomology (InvertibleSheaf.trivial X).obj 1) = 0` is dim_k H¹(X,𝒪_X) = 0. `InvertibleSheaf.trivial X` is the free rank-one 𝒪_X-module. `Scheme.Modules.Cohomology M 1` is Mathlib's `Sheaf.H` (Ext¹ from the constant sheaf ℤ) of the underlying abelian sheaf on the Zariski site: derived-functor sheaf cohomology, not Čech. Its k-structure `cohomologyBaseModule` lets c ∈ k act by the cohomology map of multiplication by c on 𝒪_X. So `hg` is the genus-zero condition, genus = dim_k H¹(X,𝒪_X) as in Stacks Tag 0BY7. `hs : s ≫ (X ↘ Spec k) = 𝟙 _` says `s : Spec k ⟶ X` is a section of the structure map, i.e. a k-rational point. The conclusion `∃ e : X ≅ projectiveLine k, e.hom.IsOver (Spec k)` is a k-isomorphism with the projective line: `projectiveLine k` is `Proj` of the symmetric algebra of k², i.e. Proj k[X₀,X₁], with structure map `Proj.toSpecZero ≫ Spec.map (algebraMap k _)` (checked by `rfl`). `e.hom.IsOver (Spec k)` means e.hom ≫ (ℙ¹_k → Spec k) = (X → Spec k), an isomorphism of k-schemes. Lean subtlety: `Module.finrank` is 0 on an infinite-dimensional space, so `hg` alone would not force H¹ = 0. The proof first proves `FiniteDimensional k H¹` for every regular proper curve (`finiteDimensional_cohomology_one_trivial_of_isProper`), so `hg` really is H¹ = 0. Regularity is imposed only at coheight-one points, which on a curve is all of regularity. `hk` is in fact implied by the rational point (red-team finding RT-20261105-a5d217 compiles the theorem without it), so it narrows nothing. Stacks Tag 0C6U (Characterization of the projective line), read in the Stacks source, states the general form: a proper curve with H¹(X,𝒪_X) = 0 and closed points x_i with normal local rings and gcd[κ(x_i):k] = 1 is ≅ ℙ¹_k. The Lean statement is the case of one rational point on a regular curve. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: ℙ¹_k satisfies every hypothesis (compiled: DVR stalks from smoothness; `hk` via `functionFieldEquiv` and `isIntegrallyClosedIn_ratFunc`; `hg` from `subsingleton_cohomology_one_trivial`; the rational point `infinitySection`), so the hypotheses are consistent and not vacuous. No Riemann–Roch-type input is a hypothesis. Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

If X is a smooth proper geometrically integral curve over k with H¹(X,𝒪_X) = 0 and X has a K-valued point for a field extension K/k, then X ×_k K ≅ ℙ¹_K over K. The section variables `[IsProper (X ↘ Spec k)]`, `[SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 (X ↘ Spec k)]` and `[GeometricallyIntegral (X ↘ Spec k)]` are Mathlib's proper, smooth of relative dimension one and geometrically integral, i.e. a smooth proper geometrically integral curve. `H : IsPullback g (Y ↘ Spec K) (X ↘ Spec k) (Spec.map (algebraMap k K))` says Y with its K-structure map is the fibre product X ×_{Spec k} Spec K. `hg` is dim_k H¹(X,𝒪_X) = 0 for derived-functor sheaf cohomology of 𝒪_X. `x : X` with `φ : X.residueField x →ₐ[k] K` is a k-embedding κ(x) → K, i.e. a K-valued point Spec K → Spec κ(x) → X over k. The conclusion `∃ e : Y ≅ projectiveLine K, e.hom.IsOver (Spec K)` is an isomorphism of K-schemes with Proj K[X₀,X₁]. Lean subtlety: `x` may be any point, even the generic one if k(X) embeds in K. That still is a K-point, so the statement is right as stated. finrank's junk 0 is excluded because H¹ of Y has the same finrank as H¹ of X (`finrank_cohomology_one_trivial_eq_of_isPullback_of_smooth`) and the section theorem proves it finite-dimensional. Red-team checks: the K-point lifts through `H.lift_snd` to a section of Y, reducing to `exists_iso_projectiveLine_of_genus_eq_zero_of_section`. `hg` is satisfied by ℙ¹_k (compiled). Tau Ceti has no compiled `GeometricallyIntegral` instance for ℙ¹_k, so the full hypothesis set is satisfiable by standard mathematics but not by a compiled example. Axioms standard.

Pulling back rational functions along `X.isoProjectiveLine e` sends z ∈ k(t), viewed on ℙ¹_k as `(projectiveLine.functionFieldEquiv k).symm z`, to `e z`: the isomorphism induces e on function fields. Its `@[simp]` LHS is in normal form: `simp?` closes the goal with this lemma alone, and `simp? [-this]` makes no progress.

For a regular proper curve X over k and a k-isomorphism e : k(t) ≃ k(X), this is the isomorphism X ≅ ℙ¹_k whose pullback of rational functions is e. `e : RatFunc k ≃ₐ[k] X.functionField` is a k-algebra isomorphism k(t) ≅ k(X), and the value has type `X ≅ projectiveLine k`, an isomorphism with Proj k[X₀,X₁]. The body composes X ≅ twoChartModel(k(X), e t), the two-chart models' isomorphism induced by e, and twoChartModel(k(t), t) ≅ ℙ¹_k. `functionFieldMap_isoProjectiveLine_hom` shows the induced map on function fields is e, and the in-file instance shows it lies over k. Red-team probe: it equals the general `Scheme.isoOfFunctionFieldAlgEquiv` (Birational/AlgHom) at Y = ℙ¹_k applied to `functionFieldEquiv.trans e`, so it is the canonical isomorphism (finding RT-20261105-4ab565 concerns only the reuse).

The function field of a regular proper curve over k with exact constants k, H¹(X,𝒪_X) = 0 and a divisor of degree one is k-isomorphic to the rational function field k(t). The hypotheses are those of `exists_iso_projectiveLine_of_genus_eq_zero_of_divisor_degree_eq_one`: IsCurveOver plus DVR stalks at codimension-one points = regular proper curve; `hk` = k integrally closed in k(X); `hg` = dim_k H¹(X,𝒪_X) = 0 (sheaf cohomology of 𝒪_X as a k-space); `hD` = Σ n_x [κ(x):k] = 1, since `relativeDegree` weights each point by `residueDegree` = [κ(x):k]. The conclusion `Nonempty (X.functionField ≃ₐ[k] RatFunc k)` is a k-algebra isomorphism k(X) ≅ k(t), with k(X)'s k-algebra structure from the structure morphism. Lean subtlety: `finrank` is 0 on infinite-dimensional spaces, but the proof proves `FiniteDimensional k H¹` before using `hg`, so `hg` means H¹ = 0. Point degrees are finite at the closed points of a curve, so `residueDegree` takes no junk value there. This is the rationality half of Stacks Tag 0C6U (7)/(8), read in the Stacks source. Red-team checks: ℙ¹_k with its point at infinity satisfies all hypotheses (compiled); axioms standard.

For all s and ξ, almost every x under GPD(s, ξ) satisfies x > 0 and 1 + ξx/s > 0, so the law lives on its open support (Coles (4.2)); for ξ < 0 this puts no mass at or beyond the endpoint −s/ξ (compiled for GPD(1, −1/2)). Lean subtlety: at s ≤ 0 it holds because the measure is zero, as the docstring says, so the junk division by s = 0 does not matter.
For fixed s and ξ, e ↦ T_{s,ξ}(e) is continuous on ℝ, since each branch (s·e, or s(e^(ξe) − 1)/ξ with ξ ≠ 0 fixed) is continuous in e.

Defines the transformation T(e) = s(e^(ξe) − 1)/ξ for ξ ≠ 0, and T(e) = s·e for ξ = 0, which sends a rate-one exponential variable to a GPD(s, ξ) variable. The Lean body is literally `if ξ = 0 then s * e else s * (Real.exp (ξ * e) - 1) / ξ`. The zero branch is the pointwise limit of the nonzero formula as ξ → 0, which matches Coles's reading of ξ = 0 as that limit (§4.2.1, (4.4)). It gives the GPD because for E ~ Exp(1), P(T(E) > x) = P(E > log(1 + ξx/s)/ξ) = (1 + ξx/s)^(−1/ξ), which is Coles (4.2). Lean subtlety: division by zero (`x / 0 = 0`). Without the `if ξ = 0` branch the formula at ξ = 0 would be s·0/0 = 0, a constant map with a Dirac law. The separate branch avoids this (compiled: `fun e => 1 * (Real.exp (0 * e) - 1) / 0` is identically 0). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: compiled values T_{2,1}(log 2) = 2 and T_{1,−1}(log 2) = 1/2; the map is exposed downstream only through `generalizedParetoMap_zero` and `generalizedParetoMap_of_shape_ne_zero` (module-checked).
T_{s,ξ}(0) = 0 for every s and ξ, because both branches vanish at e = 0 (s·0, and s(e^0 − 1)/ξ = 0). So the lower support endpoint 0 is the image of the exponential law's endpoint 0.

For s ≠ 0, ξ ≠ 0 and 1 + ξx/s > 0, T_{s,ξ}(log(1 + ξx/s)/ξ) = x. So the logarithm formula is a right inverse of the transformation on {1 + ξx/s > 0}: it is the map E = log(1 + ξX/s)/ξ that sends a GPD variable back to an Exp(1) variable. Lean subtlety: off the positive half-line `Real.log` takes junk values (log 0 = 0, log(−y) = log y), and the divisions by s and by ξ would be junk at 0. The hypotheses hw, hs and hξ exclude exactly these cases, and s ≠ 0 is genuinely needed (compiled counterexample: s = 0, ξ = x = 1).
For s > 0, T_{s,ξ}(e) ≥ 0 if and only if e ≥ 0; this follows from strict monotonicity and T(0) = 0. The hypothesis s > 0 is needed: at s = 0 the left side always holds.

For ξ ≠ 0, `generalizedParetoMap s ξ e = s * (exp (ξ e) − 1) / ξ`, the else-branch of the definition. The hypothesis ξ ≠ 0 is exactly what selects that branch; at ξ = 0 the right side would be the junk value 0 coming from x/0 = 0.
For s > 0 and e > 0, T_{s,ξ}(e) > 0: positive exponential inputs land in the positive part of the open support. This follows from strict monotonicity and T(0) = 0.

At shape ξ = 0 the transformation is e ↦ s·e (the `if` branch of the definition). Lean subtlety: this is a separate branch, not the nonzero formula evaluated at ξ = 0, which would be the junk value s·0/0 = 0.

Claim: `generalizedParetoMeasure s ξ` is the generalized Pareto distribution GPD(s, ξ) with scale s > 0 and any real shape ξ, i.e. the law with survival function (1 + ξx/s)^(−1/ξ) on {x > 0, 1 + ξx/s > 0}, and exp(−x/s) at ξ = 0 (Coles §4.2.1, (4.2)–(4.4)). Lean ↔ maths: the body is `if 0 < s then (expMeasure 1).map (generalizedParetoMap s ξ) else 0`. Here `expMeasure 1` is Mathlib's rate-one exponential law (`gammaMeasure 1 1`, density e^(−x) on x ≥ 0); `generalizedParetoMap s ξ e` is s(e^(ξe) − 1)/ξ for ξ ≠ 0 and s·e for ξ = 0; and `Measure.map` is the pushforward. So for s > 0 this is the law of s(e^(ξE) − 1)/ξ with E ~ Exp(1). Since P(s(e^(ξE) − 1)/ξ > x) = P(E > log(1 + ξx/s)/ξ) = (1 + ξx/s)^(−1/ξ) for either sign of ξ, this is Coles's (4.2). `cdf_generalizedParetoMeasure_eq` (Cdf.lean) proves exactly the cdf `if x ≤ 0 then 0 else if ξ = 0 then 1 − exp(−x/s) else if 0 < 1 + ξx/s then 1 − (1 + ξx/s)^(−1/ξ) else 1`. Every clause of the Voyager bullet is proved, under the stated range. It is a probability measure for s > 0 and every real ξ (`isProbabilityMeasure_generalizedParetoMeasure`). Its density is (1 + ξx/s)^(−ξ⁻¹−1)/s on the open support, exp(−x/s)/s at ξ = 0, and 0 elsewhere (`generalizedParetoPDFReal`, `generalizedParetoMeasure_eq_withDensity`). Its quantile at u ∈ (0, 1) is s((1 − u)^(−ξ) − 1)/ξ, and −s·log(1 − u) at ξ = 0 (`quantile_generalizedParetoMeasure`). Its n-th moment is sⁿ n!/∏_{j<n}(1 − (j + 1)ξ), and the moment exists exactly when nξ < 1 (`integral_pow_generalizedParetoMeasure` with `integrable_pow_generalizedParetoMeasure_iff`; Coles (4.8) is the case n = 1). Threshold stability: for v ≥ 0 with s + ξv > 0, the excess X − v given X > v is GPD(s + ξv, ξ) (`map_sub_cond_generalizedParetoMeasure`; Coles (4.9), σ_u = σ_u0 + ξ(u − u0)). Special cases: GPD(s, 0) = `expMeasure s⁻¹` (rate 1/s); GPD(s, −1) = `uniformMeasure 0 s` (Coles Example 4.3); and for ξ > 0, s/ξ + GPD(s, ξ) = Mathlib's `paretoMeasure (s/ξ) (1/ξ)` (survival (t/y)^r with t = s/ξ, r = 1/ξ). Lean subtlety: (i) Division by zero. ξ = 0 has its own branch, so the nonzero formula's value s·0/0 = 0 (a constant map, i.e. a Dirac law) is never used. Compiled: the nonzero formula at ξ = 0 is identically 0. Every power formula (cdf, density, quantile) carries ξ ≠ 0 or has a separate ξ = 0 branch; otherwise (1 + 0)^(−1/0) = 1^0 = 1 would make the cdf 0. (ii) `Real.rpow` of a negative base is never evaluated. The definition uses only exp, and the cdf and density formulas are guarded by `0 < 1 + ξx/s`. Compiled at s = 1, ξ = −1/2, x = 3 (beyond the endpoint 2): the cdf is 1 and the density 0, whereas the unguarded formula would give the junk value 1 − (−1/2)^2 = 3/4. (iii) A nonpositive scale gives the zero measure, which is not a probability measure (compiled at s = 0), and every probabilistic statement carries 0 < s. (iv) In pinned Mathlib, `Measure.map` along a non-measurable map is a Dirac mass. That is harmless here, since the map is measurable (`measurable_generalizedParetoMap_right`). (v) The Bochner integral is 0 for a non-integrable function, but the moment formula is asserted only where `integrable_pow_generalizedParetoMeasure_iff` proves integrability. At the boundary nξ ≥ 1 the moment is genuinely non-integrable (compiled: n = 1, ξ = 1 and n = 3, ξ = 1/3). The product uses the real `(j + 1 : ℝ)`, so no truncated subtraction occurs, and at n = 0 the empty product and 0! give 1 (compiled). (vi) `cond` of a null set is 0. For admissible v, however, the conditioning set {X > v} has positive mass: compiled, `generalizedParetoMeasure s ξ (Ioi v) ≠ 0` follows from the threshold theorem, because its right side is a probability measure. At the ξ < 0 endpoint v = −s/ξ the set is null (compiled for s = 1, ξ = −1/2), and s + ξv > 0 excludes that v. Sources and checks: Coles, An Introduction to Statistical Modeling of Extreme Values (2001), Thm 4.1 and (4.2)–(4.4) on pp. 75–76, Example 4.3 on p. 77, and (4.8)–(4.9) on pp. 78–79 (read); the n = 2 moment 2s²/((1 − ξ)(1 − 2ξ)) was checked by hand. Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: compiled value tests give cdf of GPD(1, 1) at 1 = 1/2, cdf of GPD(1, −1/2) at 1 = 3/4, and moments 6s³ (n = 3, ξ = 0) and 16s²/3 (n = 2, ξ = 1/4). There is no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate (Mathlib has only `paretoMeasure`). Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

For s ≤ 0, the definition returns the zero measure. Lean subtlety: this totalises the definition outside the parameter range and is not a GPD. It is not a probability measure (compiled), and every probabilistic statement in the family carries 0 < s.

For s > 0, the GPD law is `(expMeasure 1).map (generalizedParetoMap s ξ)`, the pushforward of Mathlib's rate-one exponential law (density e^(−x) on x ≥ 0) by the transformation; this is the `if 0 < s` branch of the definition. Lean subtlety: `Measure.map` is the honest pushforward here because the map is measurable (`measurable_generalizedParetoMap_right`).

For s > 0 and ξ ≠ 0, GPD(s, ξ) is the law of s(e^(ξE) − 1)/ξ with E ~ Exp(1), stated as `(expMeasure 1).map fun e => …`; this is the explicit nonzero-shape form. Both hypotheses are needed: at ξ = 0 the map would be the constant 0 because x/0 = 0 (compiled), and s ≤ 0 gives the zero measure.

For s > 0, GPD(s, 0) = `expMeasure s⁻¹`, Mathlib's exponential law with rate 1/s (density s⁻¹e^(−x/s) on x ≥ 0, mean s). This is Coles (4.4): H(y) = 1 − exp(−y/σ̃), 'an exponential distribution with parameter 1/σ̃'. Lean subtlety: ξ = 0 is a separate branch of the transformation (e ↦ s·e), so no `1/0 = 0` junk enters. Also, `expMeasure` is parametrised by rate (`gammaMeasure 1 r`), so s⁻¹ is the right argument; s would be wrong. The hypothesis 0 < s can in fact be dropped, because Mathlib's `expMeasure` is the zero measure at nonpositive rate (NIT RT-20261105-570d3e). Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: compiled that the ξ = 0 cdf is 1 − exp(−x/s) for x > 0, and that an Exp(1) variable E gives `HasLaw (s * E) (expMeasure s⁻¹)`.

For all s, ξ and e, T_{s,ξ} has derivative s·e^(ξe) at e. This is `HasDerivAt`, a genuine derivative, not the junk-prone `deriv`. At ξ = 0 it reads s, the derivative of s·e (compiled), so the formula is uniform in ξ; it is the Jacobian behind the density in PDF.lean.

If E has law Exp(1) under P, then T_{s,ξ}(E) has law GPD(s, ξ), for s > 0 and every ξ; this is the random-variable form of the construction. `HasLaw E (expMeasure 1) P` means E is a.e.-measurable and P∘E⁻¹ = expMeasure 1. The hypothesis s > 0 is needed: at s ≤ 0 the target law is the zero measure, which no variable on a nonzero P can have.

If E ~ Exp(1) under P, s > 0 and ξ ≠ 0, then s(e^(ξE) − 1)/ξ ~ GPD(s, ξ); this is the explicit-formula form. The hypothesis ξ ≠ 0 is needed because at ξ = 0 the formula is 0 (x/0 = 0). Correct, but it has no consumer and follows in one line from the general HasLaw lemma (MINOR RT-20261105-dacbd6).
If X ~ GPD(s, ξ) under P and c > 0, then cX ~ GPD(cs, ξ); this is the random-variable form of scaling. It holds for every s, because `map_mul_generalizedParetoMeasure` covers the zero branch.

For s > 0 and every ξ, T_{s,ξ}((0, ∞)) = {x : x > 0 and 1 + ξx/s > 0}. That set is (0, ∞) for ξ ≥ 0 and (0, −s/ξ) for ξ < 0, which is exactly the open support of GPD(s, ξ) in Coles (4.2) ('defined on {y : y > 0 and (1 + ξy/σ̃) > 0}'). The hypothesis s > 0 is needed: s = −1, ξ = 0 gives the negative half-line (compiled).

For s ≠ 0 and ξ ≠ 0, the image of ℝ under T_{s,ξ} is {x : 1 + ξx/s > 0}, the domain of the logarithmic inverse. Correct as stated, though the hypothesis ξ ≠ 0 is unnecessary: at ξ = 0 both sides are ℝ (MINOR RT-20261105-17e626). s ≠ 0 is needed: at s = 0 the image is {0} (compiled).

For s > 0 and every real ξ, GPD(s, ξ) has total mass 1 (`IsProbabilityMeasure`), being the pushforward of the probability measure `expMeasure 1` by a measurable map; this covers the bullet's 'for every real shape'. Lean subtlety: s > 0 is required, because s ≤ 0 gives the zero measure, which is not a probability measure (compiled at s = 0).

For c > 0 and all s and ξ, the pushforward of GPD(s, ξ) by x ↦ cx is GPD(cs, ξ): s is a scale parameter and the shape is unchanged, because c·T_{s,ξ} = T_{cs,ξ} in both branches. At s ≤ 0 both sides are the zero measure (cs ≤ 0). The hypothesis c > 0 is needed: c = 0 sends a probability law to a Dirac mass, while GPD(0, ξ) = 0 (compiled). Compiled check: 2·GPD(1, ξ) = GPD(2, ξ).

The map (s, ξ, e) ↦ T_{s,ξ}(e) is jointly Borel measurable on (ℝ × ℝ) × ℝ: it is a piecewise function over the measurable set {ξ = 0} with continuous pieces. This is what makes the family measurable in its parameters (`measurable_generalizedParetoMeasure`).

For fixed s and ξ, e ↦ T_{s,ξ}(e) is measurable (a section of the joint statement). Lean subtlety: this is why `Measure.map (generalizedParetoMap s ξ)` is the honest pushforward, not Mathlib's Dirac-mass junk value for a non-a.e.-measurable map.

The family (s, ξ) ↦ GPD(s, ξ) is measurable from ℝ × ℝ into `Measure ℝ` with Mathlib's Giry σ-algebra (generated by μ ↦ μ(A)), including the s ≤ 0 zero branch. It is a measurable if-then-else over the set {s > 0}, and the pushforward family is measurable because (s, ξ, e) ↦ T_{s,ξ}(e) is jointly measurable. This is what lets the GPD be used as a kernel in its parameters.

For s > 0, every singleton is GPD(s, ξ)-null, i.e. the law has no atoms: it is the pushforward of an atomless law by an injective (strictly increasing) measurable map. Correct, though the hypothesis s > 0 is unnecessary, since at s ≤ 0 the measure is zero (MINOR RT-20261105-d31fff).

For s ≠ 0 and all ξ and e, 1 + ξ·T_{s,ξ}(e)/s = e^(ξe), so the GPD support factor 1 + ξx/s is positive at every transformed point (at ξ = 0 both sides are 1). Lean subtlety: at s = 0 the left side would be 1 because x/0 = 0, which is why s ≠ 0 is assumed (compiled counterexample).

For s > 0 and every real ξ, T_{s,ξ} is strictly increasing on ℝ (`StrictMono`: a < b → T(a) < T(b)). For ξ < 0, both the map e ↦ e^(ξe) − 1 and division by ξ reverse the order, so the composite increases. The hypothesis 0 < s is needed: s = 0 gives the constant 0 (compiled counterexample). This monotonicity is what carries the cdf and the quantile over from the exponential law.

Defines the Verma module M(μ) = U_q(sl₂)/(U·E + U·(K − μ)) of highest weight μ. Lean ↔ maths: `UqSl2 q ⧸ vermaIdeal q μ` is the quotient of `UqSl2 q` is the `RingQuot` of the free ℂ-algebra on E, F, K, K⁻¹ by `UqSl2.Rel q`: K K⁻¹ = K⁻¹ K = 1, K E = q² E K, K F = q⁻² F K, E F − F E = (q − q⁻¹)⁻¹ • (K − K⁻¹), which is the presentation of U_q(sl₂) in Virelizier, Quantum groups §2.3 by the left ideal generated by E and K − μ (`vermaIdeal`); the four instances in the file are the quotient's own additive group, left U-module, ℂ-module and scalar-tower structures (transported by `inferInstanceAs`, no new data), so M(μ) is a left U-module, not an algebra. This is the standard Verma module: it is the induced module U_q(sl₂) ⊗_{U_q(b)} C_μ (Solovyev §2.3), the class v₀ of 1 is killed by E and has weight μ (`e_smul_vec_zero`, `k_smul_vec_zero`), it is universal for such vectors (`lift`, `hom_ext`), and for q, μ ≠ 0 it has basis v, Fv, F²v, … (`basis`), as in Etingof–Semenyakin ex. (11). Lean subtlety: defined for all q, μ ∈ ℂ. At μ = 0, K − 0 is a unit so M(0) = 0 (compiled `Subsingleton (VermaModule q 0)`), matching Virelizier Lemma 3.6 (a highest weight is nonzero because K is invertible); at q = 0, q⁻¹ = 0 and the relations force E = F = 0, so v_j = 0 for j ≥ 1 (compiled); at q = ±1, (q − q⁻¹)⁻¹ = 0⁻¹ = 0 turns the last relation into EF = FE, so M(μ) is then the Verma module of that degenerate algebra rather than of a quantum group. Each theorem with quantum-group content carries q ≠ 0 or genericity explicitly (no `Fact` instance in this file). Sources read: Virelizier, Quantum groups §2.3 and §3.3 (Lemma 3.6, proof of Prop. 3.7); Etingof–Semenyakin, A brief introduction to quantum groups (arXiv:2106.05252) §2 exercises (7), (11), (12); Solovyev (arXiv:2410.18463) §2.3. Red-team checks: E·F ∉ ideal (left, not two-sided), basis F^j v₀ for q, μ ≠ 0, singular vectors exactly at μ = ±q^j for generic q (q = 2: μ = 4, −4 yes, μ = 2 no), all compiled; axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.

For q ≠ 0 and μ ≠ 0, a ℂ-basis of M(μ) indexed by ℕ whose j-th vector is v_j = F^j v₀ (`coe_basis`). Lean ↔ maths: `Module.Basis ℕ ℂ (VermaModule q μ)` is a genuine basis (a linear isomorphism of M(μ) with finitely supported sequences ℕ →₀ ℂ); it is built by `Module.Basis.mk` from `linearIndependent_vec` (independence) and `span_vec_eq_top` (spanning), so both halves are proved. The hypotheses `hq : q ≠ 0` and `hμ : μ ≠ 0` are explicit (no `Fact` instance) and both necessary (compiled: v₁ = 0 at q = 0; M(0) = 0); no genericity is assumed, so the basis exists at roots of unity too, which is correct. Lean subtlety: at q = ±1 the basis also exists (compiled `basis (q := 1)`), but there `UqSl2 q` is the commuting algebra produced by (q − q⁻¹)⁻¹ = 0, so for q = ±1 it is a statement about that algebra; for q ∉ {0, ±1} it is the quantum-group statement. This is Etingof–Semenyakin ex. (11) (the Verma module has basis v, fv, f²v, …). Red-team checks: `(basis hq hμ).repr (vec q μ j) = Finsupp.single j 1` compiled; axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.
The vectors of `basis hq hμ` are exactly the v_j = F^j v₀ (`⇑(basis hq hμ) = vec q μ`), so the basis is (F^j v₀)_{j ∈ ℕ} and not some other basis.

Says E·v_{j+1} = [j+1]_q (q^{−j}μ − q^{j}μ⁻¹)/(q − q⁻¹) · v_j in M(μ), for all q, μ ∈ ℂ. Lean ↔ maths: `quantumInteger q (j + 1)` is by definition (q^{j+1} − q^{−(j+1)})/(q − q⁻¹) (`quantumInteger_def`), the symmetric quantum integer [j+1]_q; `q⁻¹ ^ j * μ - q ^ j * μ⁻¹` is q^{−j}μ − q^{j}μ⁻¹; the scalar acts through the ℂ-structure of M(μ); `vec q μ j` is F^j v₀. Compiled check: at μ = q^k the coefficient equals Virelizier's (q^{k−2n} − q^{−k})(q^{2n+2} − 1)/((q − q⁻¹)(q² − 1)) in the proof of Prop. 3.7 (n = j). Lean subtlety: division by q − q⁻¹ and the inverse μ⁻¹ are Lean's total operations (x/0 = 0, 0⁻¹ = 0). At q = ±1 the right side is 0 by x/0 = 0, and this is true there because the Lean relation EF − FE = (q − q⁻¹)⁻¹(K − K⁻¹) reads EF = FE, so E F^{j+1} v₀ = F^{j+1} E v₀ = 0 (compiled at q = 1); at q = 0 both sides are 0 (E = 0); at μ = 0, M(0) = 0. So no case holds for a wrong reason, but at q = ±1 it describes the degenerate commuting algebra, not a quantum group. Red-team checks: specialisations at q = 2 through `e_smul_vec_succ_eq_zero_iff`; axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.

The singular-vector criterion: for generic q and μ ≠ 0, E·v_{j+1} = 0 in M(μ) iff μ² = q^{2j}, i.e. iff μ = ±q^j. Lean ↔ maths: `IsGenericQuantumParameter q` unfolds to `q ≠ 0 ∧ ∀ n > 0, q ^ n ≠ 1` (q not a root of unity; algebraic values such as q = 2 qualify, transcendence is not required); `hμ : μ ≠ 0` is a nonzero highest weight; `e q • vec q μ (j + 1) = 0` says F^{j+1}v₀ is killed by E, i.e. is a singular vector (of weight q^{−2(j+1)}μ by `vec_mem_weightSpace`); `μ ^ 2 = q ^ (2 * j)` has natural-number exponent 2j. Why: by `e_smul_vec_succ`, E v_{j+1} = c·v_j with c = [j+1]_q (q^{−j}μ − q^{j}μ⁻¹)/(q − q⁻¹); v_j ≠ 0 (`vec_ne_zero`); genericity gives q − q⁻¹ ≠ 0 and [j+1]_q ≠ 0; and q^{−j}μ = q^{j}μ⁻¹ ⟺ μ² = q^{2j}. Exponent check: for μ = q^m the singular vector is F^{m+1}v₀ (j = m), of weight q^{−m−2}, matching Etingof–Semenyakin ex. (12) (M_m contains M_{−m−2} for m ≥ 0 when q is not a root of 1) and the proof of Virelizier Prop. 3.7 (E w_{n+1} = 0 forces n = k). Lean subtlety: the coefficient divides by q − q⁻¹, harmless here because genericity makes it nonzero (`sub_inv_ne_zero`), and [j+1]_q is nonzero by `quantumInteger_ne_zero`. Both hypotheses are needed (compiled counterexamples: at q = 1, E kills every v_j; at q = i, [2]_i = 0 so E v₂ = 0 for μ = 1 although 1 ≠ i² = −1; at μ = 0, M(0) = 0 so the left side holds but 0 ≠ q^{2j}); for a fixed j only q ≠ 0 and q^{2(j+1)} ≠ 1 are needed (compiled, recorded as a NIT). Red-team checks: at q = 2, E v₃ = 0 for μ = 4 and μ = −4 and E v₃ ≠ 0 for μ = 2 (compiled); lean_minimal_hypotheses: both load-bearing; axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.
E·v₀ = 0 in M(μ): the highest vector is killed by E, because E lies in the Verma ideal.
F^n·v_j = v_{n+j} in M(μ), i.e. F^n F^j v₀ = F^{n+j} v₀.
F·v_j = v_{j+1} in M(μ): F moves one step down the string v₀, Fv₀, F²v₀, …
Two U_q(sl₂)-linear maps M(μ) → V that agree at v₀ are equal (uniqueness in the universal property), because M(μ) is generated by v₀; with `lift_vec_zero` it gives ∃! φ, φ v₀ = v (compiled).
K⁻¹·v_j = q^{2j} μ⁻¹ v_j in M(μ), the inverse eigenvalue of `k_smul_vec`. Lean subtlety: μ⁻¹ uses 0⁻¹ = 0, harmless since M(0) = 0.
K⁻¹·v₀ = μ⁻¹ v₀ in M(μ). Lean subtlety: μ⁻¹ is Lean's inverse with 0⁻¹ = 0; at μ = 0 both sides vanish because M(0) = 0 (the proof shows v₀ = K⁻¹K v₀ = 0), so the junk value is harmless.

K·v_j = q^{−2j} μ v_j in M(μ), with q^{−2j} written `(q⁻¹ ^ 2) ^ j`, the standard weight of F^j v₀ (Virelizier Lemma 3.6: F^m v has eigenvalue λq^{−2m}). Lean subtlety: at q = 0, q⁻¹ = 0 so the scalar is 0 for j ≥ 1, but then v_j = 0 (F = 0 in `UqSl2 0`), so the statement stays true.
K·v₀ = μ v₀ in M(μ): v₀ has weight μ, because K − μ·1 lies in the Verma ideal.

For a U_q(sl₂)-module V and v ∈ V with K v = μ v (`v ∈ weightSpace q V μ`, the μ-eigenspace of K) and E v = 0, defines the U-linear map M(μ) → V, class of a ↦ a·v (`Submodule.liftQ` of `LinearMap.toSpanSingleton`, well defined because E and K − μ kill v): the universal property of the Verma module (Frobenius reciprocity for the induced module). Lean subtlety: K⁻¹ v = μ⁻¹ v is not assumed since it follows (and μ = 0 forces v = 0 as K is invertible); `[IsScalarTower ℂ (UqSl2 q) V]` only says V's ℂ-structure is the restriction of its U-structure.
The map M(μ) → V induced by a highest-weight vector v sends the class of a to a·v.
The map M(μ) → V induced by a highest-weight vector v sends v_j = F^j v₀ to F^j·v.
The map M(μ) → V induced by a highest-weight vector v sends v₀ to v (existence in the universal property).

For q ≠ 0 and μ ≠ 0, the vectors v_j = F^j v₀ of M(μ) are linearly independent over ℂ (`LinearIndependent ℂ (vec q μ)`: no nontrivial finite ℂ-linear relation). The proof builds an explicit U_q(sl₂)-action on finitely supported sequences ℕ →₀ ℂ by the action formulas, checks the defining relations (`GeneratorTuple`), and maps M(μ) to it sending v_j to the j-th unit vector. Both hypotheses are needed (compiled: at q = 0, v₁ = 0; at μ = 0, M(0) = 0; lean_minimal_hypotheses: both load-bearing); no genericity is needed. Lean subtlety: the model's E-coefficient has (q − q⁻¹)⁻¹, which is 0 at q = ±1 by 0⁻¹ = 0; this is consistent because `UqSl2 (±1)` has EF = FE, so the statement at q = ±1 is true but concerns that degenerate algebra.
The quotient map U_q(sl₂) → M(μ), a ↦ class of a, as a U-linear map (`Submodule.mkQ` of the Verma ideal), i.e. a ↦ a·v₀ (`mk_eq_smul_vec_zero`).
The class of a ∈ U_q(sl₂) in M(μ) is a·v₀: the quotient map is a ↦ a v₀, because it is U-linear and v₀ is the class of 1.
The class of a in M(μ) is 0 exactly when a lies in the Verma ideal U·E + U·(K − μ) — the defining property of a quotient (`Submodule.Quotient.mk_eq_zero`).
Every element of M(μ) is the class of some a ∈ U_q(sl₂) (`Submodule.mkQ_surjective`).
M(μ) is cyclic, generated as a U_q(sl₂)-module by v₀: `Submodule.span (UqSl2 q) {vec q μ 0} = ⊤` says the U-submodule generated by v₀ is everything, since every class is a·v₀.

The vectors v_j = F^j v₀ span M(μ) over ℂ, for every q and μ: `Submodule.span ℂ (Set.range (vec q μ)) = ⊤` is exactly ℂ-spanning. The proof shows the span is stable under E, F, K, K⁻¹ by the action formulas, hence under all of U_q(sl₂) (`Submodule.smul_mem_of_uqSl2_generators`), and contains v₀, which generates M(μ). Lean subtlety: holds even in the degenerate cases (μ = 0, q = 0), where it is trivially true because the module or the v_j collapse; it is the spanning half of `basis`.

Defines v_j ∈ M(μ) as the class of F^j, which is F^j·v₀ with v₀ the class of 1 (`vec_eq_f_pow_smul`): the lowering vectors v, Fv, F²v, … of Etingof–Semenyakin ex. (11). Lean subtlety: unnormalised (no division by [j]_q!, unlike Virelizier's F^(r)w₀ in L(n)), and v_j = 0 when μ = 0 or (q = 0, j ≥ 1), which is why `basis` assumes q, μ ≠ 0.
v_j = F^j·v₀ in M(μ): the class of F^j is F^j applied to the class of 1.
v_j lies in the weight space of weight q^{−2j}μ: `weightSpace q V λ` is by definition the λ-eigenspace of K acting on V (`mem_weightSpace_iff`: K v = λ v), and K v_j = q^{−2j} μ v_j by `k_smul_vec`.
For q ≠ 0 and μ ≠ 0, every v_j = F^j v₀ is nonzero, since members of a linearly independent family are nonzero; both hypotheses are needed (v₁ = 0 at q = 0, M(0) = 0).
E lies in the Verma ideal U·E + U·(K − μ): it is one of the two generators (`Submodule.subset_span`).
K − μ·1 lies in the Verma ideal (`algebraMap ℂ (UqSl2 q) μ` is the scalar μ·1 of U_q(sl₂)): it is the other generator.

Defines the left ideal U·E + U·(K − μ) of U = U_q(sl₂). Lean ↔ maths: `UqSl2 q` is the `RingQuot` of the free ℂ-algebra on E, F, K, K⁻¹ by `UqSl2.Rel q`: K K⁻¹ = K⁻¹ K = 1, K E = q² E K, K F = q⁻² F K, E F − F E = (q − q⁻¹)⁻¹ • (K − K⁻¹), which is the presentation of U_q(sl₂) in Virelizier, Quantum groups §2.3; a `Submodule (UqSl2 q) (UqSl2 q)` is a subspace of U stable under left multiplication (U acts on itself by a • x = a * x), i.e. a left ideal, and `Submodule.span (UqSl2 q) {e q, k q - algebraMap ℂ (UqSl2 q) μ}` is the smallest one containing E and K − μ·1 (`algebraMap ℂ _ μ` is μ·1), i.e. {aE + b(K − μ) : a, b ∈ U}. It is genuinely one-sided: compiled that E·F ∉ `vermaIdeal 2 2` although E is in it (E·F acts on v₀ by the scalar 1 at q = μ = 2), and that 1 ∉ `vermaIdeal q μ` for q, μ ≠ 0. Lean subtlety: defined for every q, μ; at μ = 0 the generator K − 0 = K is a unit, so the ideal is all of U and the Verma module is 0 (compiled) — this is the honest quotient, not a junk value, and the theorems needing a nonzero module assume μ ≠ 0. This is the annihilator left ideal of the induced module Ind_{U_q(b)}^{U_q(sl₂)} C_μ (E ↦ 0, K ↦ μ) used to define Verma modules in Solovyev §2.3. Red-team checks: membership of both generators (`e_mem_vermaIdeal`, `k_sub_algebraMap_mem_vermaIdeal`); not two-sided; proper for q, μ ≠ 0.

Correctly stated: for Haar μ, μ({f* > s} ∩ {g* > t}) = min(μ{f > s}, μ{g > t}): the rearranged level sets are concentric, so their intersection is the smaller one (Burchard, proof of Lemma 1.6: Vol(A*∩B*) = min{Vol A, Vol B}); valid also when a measure is infinite.

Correctly stated: μ({f* > s} \ {g* > t}) = μ{f > s} − μ{g > t} (truncated subtraction in [0,∞]) for Haar μ, since the rearranged sets are concentric. Lean subtlety: when both measures are ∞ the right side is ∞ − ∞ = 0 in [0,∞], which is correct here because both rearranged sets are the whole space.

Correctly stated: equimeasurability, μ{f* > t} = μ{f > t} for every level t, for an additive Haar measure on a finite-dimensional real normed space. Lean ↔ maths: `schwarzRearrangement μ f` is f* (its value at x is sup{t : μ(ball 0 ‖x‖) < μ{f>t}}, Burchard's A* = {x | ω_n|x|ⁿ < Vol A} applied to the level sets); `μ {x | t < f x}` is the distribution function of f at t; the statement is Burchard (1.2) and Frank's |{f*>τ}| = |{|f|>τ}|. Lean subtlety: no measurability or finiteness hypothesis -- for non-measurable f, μ is the outer measure on both sides, and for an infinite-measure level set both sides are ∞ (compiled at f ≡ 1 on ℝ², level 1/2); dimension zero (μ a positive multiple of the Dirac mass) is handled separately in the proof; it holds for every t ∈ [0,∞], including t = 0 and t = ∞ (both sides 0). Sources: Burchard, A Short Course on Rearrangement Inequalities (2009), (1.2); Frank, Rearrangement methods in the work of Elliott Lieb (arXiv:2207.05153), after (4). Checks (Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): f ≡ 1 instance compiled; no duplicate in Mathlib or Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated: ‖f* − g*‖_p ≤ ‖f − g‖_p for a.e.-measurable f, g, Haar μ and every 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞, the distance measured by `edist` on [0,∞] (= max(a − b, b − a)); this is the nonexpansivity of Burchard's Exercise 1.7 and Frank's Corollary 2, with p = ∞ through the essential supremum.

Correctly stated: for a.e.-measurable f : E → [0,∞] and every exponent p ∈ [0,∞], ‖f*‖_p = ‖f‖_p for an additive Haar measure on a finite-dimensional real normed space. Lean ↔ maths: `schwarzRearrangement μ f` is f* (its value at x is sup{t : μ(ball 0 ‖x‖) < μ{f>t}}, Burchard's A* = {x | ω_n|x|ⁿ < Vol A} applied to the level sets); `eLpNorm g p μ` is the Lᵖ seminorm (∫ gᵖ)^{1/p} for 0 < p < ∞ and the essential supremum for p = ∞; `AEMeasurable f μ` is the source's measurability. Lean subtlety: `eLpNorm g 0 μ = 0` by convention, so p = 0 is a trivial case, not an L⁰ statement; p = ∞ uses `essSup`, which needs no measurability; for 0 < p < ∞ the hypothesis is needed, since for non-measurable f the lower integral of fᵖ can be smaller than ∫ (f*)ᵖ (e.g. the indicator of a set of inner measure 0 and positive outer measure, since f* uses outer measures); no vanishing at infinity is assumed -- f ≡ 1 gives ∞ = ∞ for finite p and 1 = 1 for p = ∞ (the p = ∞ case compiled). Sources: Burchard, A Short Course on Rearrangement Inequalities (2009), Lemma 1.4 (stated there for 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞); Frank, Rearrangement methods in the work of Elliott Lieb (arXiv:2207.05153), eq. (5) for p > 0. Checks (Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): p = ∞ at f ≡ 1 compiled; the measurability hypothesis is load-bearing.
Correctly stated: |f*(x) − g*(x)| ≤ ess sup |f − g| at every x, for Haar μ and arbitrary f, g (the L^∞ contraction, pointwise); `edist` on [0,∞] is max(a − b, b − a).
Correctly stated: essSup f* = essSup f for Haar μ (the L^∞ case of norm preservation), with no measurability hypothesis since `essSup` is defined from the measures of the level sets.

Correctly stated: right continuity of the distribution function -- if c < μ{f > t} then c < μ{f > s} for some s > t, for any measure and any f : α → [0,∞] (no measurability needed: μ{f>t} is the increasing union of μ{f > s_n} for s_n ↓ t). Checks: compiled verbatim with Mathlib-only imports; no Mathlib duplicate found.

Correctly stated: for a.e.-measurable f, g and real p ≥ 1, ∫ |f* − g*|ᵖ ≤ ∫ |f − g|ᵖ for Haar μ (Burchard, Exercise 1.7; Frank, Corollary 2 with j(t) = tᵖ). Lean subtlety: `edist` on [0,∞] is max(a − b, b − a) (Mathlib's `ENNReal.edist_eq_max`), so edist ∞ ∞ = 0 and edist ∞ a = ∞ for finite a, which agrees with |a − b| on finite values.

Correctly stated: the Hardy–Littlewood rearrangement inequality ∫ f g dμ ≤ ∫ f* g* dμ for a.e.-measurable f, g : E → [0,∞] on a finite-dimensional real normed space with an additive Haar measure μ. Lean ↔ maths: `∫⁻` is the Lebesgue integral of [0,∞]-valued functions, so both sides are genuine extended integrals, which is Burchard's reading 'the left side is finite whenever the right side is'; `schwarzRearrangement μ f` is f* (its value at x is sup{t : μ(ball 0 ‖x‖) < μ{f>t}}, Burchard's A* = {x | ω_n|x|ⁿ < Vol A} applied to the level sets); `AEMeasurable f μ`, `AEMeasurable g μ` are the source's measurability (in the weaker a.e. form); `[μ.IsAddHaarMeasure]`, `[FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`, `[BorelSpace E]` contain Lebesgue measure on ℝⁿ (up to a scale, which does not change f*). Lean subtlety: there is no vanishing-at-infinity hypothesis, so the statement is stronger than the textbook one; infinite-measure level sets go to the whole space and the key step μ(A∩B) ≤ min(μA, μB) = μ(A*∩B*) (`addHaar_inter_setOf_lt_schwarzRearrangement`) still holds when a measure is infinite, so nothing holds by a junk value; products use [0,∞] arithmetic with 0·∞ = 0 on both sides, consistent with fg = ∫∫ 1{s<f}1{t<g} ds dt; f*, g* are always measurable and f, g are a.e.-measurable, so neither side is a lower integral of a non-measurable function; the norm may be non-Euclidean (only nested centred balls are used) and dimension zero is included (f* = f). Sources: Burchard, A Short Course on Rearrangement Inequalities (2009), Lemma 1.6; Frank, Rearrangement methods in the work of Elliott Lieb (arXiv:2207.05153), eq. (6). Checks (Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): specialised to indicators it gives Vol(A∩B) ≤ Vol(A*∩B*) (compiled on ℝ²); hypotheses satisfiable (constants); both measurability hypotheses load-bearing in the proof; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.

Correctly stated: ∫ (f*)ᵖ dμ = ∫ fᵖ dμ for a.e.-measurable f and real p > 0, Haar μ (Frank eq. (5); Burchard's proof of Lemma 1.4 via the layer-cake formula); both sides are [0,∞]-valued Lebesgue integrals, so no integrability assumption is needed.
Correctly stated: ∫ f* dμ = ∫ f dμ for a.e.-measurable f, Haar μ (the case p = 1 of `lintegral_rpow_schwarzRearrangement`).

Correctly stated: for a.e.-measurable f, g and real p ≥ 1, ∫ ((f* − g*)⁺)ᵖ ≤ ∫ ((f − g)⁺)ᵖ, Haar μ, where `-` on [0,∞] is truncated subtraction, i.e. the positive part; the one-sided half of the Lᵖ contraction (Frank, Corollary 2 with j convex). p ≥ 1 is needed for convexity.

Correctly stated: t < f*(x) iff μ(ball 0 ‖x‖) < μ{f > t}, i.e. {f* > t} = {f > t}* with A* = {x | μ(ball 0 ‖x‖) < μ A}; this is Frank's eq. (4) and Burchard's Exercise 1.1, and it uses the right continuity of t ↦ μ{f>t} so the strict inequality is exact.

Correctly stated: f* is measurable for every f and every measure (Borel open sets assumed via `OpensMeasurableSpace E`), because {f* > t} is the preimage under the norm of a sublevel set of the monotone function r ↦ μ(ball 0 r); Frank notes this measurability.

Correctly stated: for a.e.-measurable f, f* ∈ Lᵖ iff f ∈ Lᵖ, every p ∈ [0,∞]; `MemLp` is a.e.-strong measurability plus finite `eLpNorm`, and f* is always measurable, so this follows from `eLpNorm_schwarzRearrangement`.

Correctly stated: `schwarzRearrangement μ f` is the Schwarz (symmetric decreasing) rearrangement f* of f : E → [0,∞] with respect to the norm balls of E and the measure μ. Lean ↔ maths: the body is `⨆ t, ⨆ (_ : μ (ball 0 ‖x‖) < μ {y | t < f y}), t`, i.e. f*(x) = sup{t ≥ 0 : x ∈ {f>t}*} with {f>t}* := {x | μ(ball 0 ‖x‖) < μ{f>t}}; Burchard §1.1 defines A* = {x ∈ ℝⁿ | ω_n|x|ⁿ < Vol(A)} -- the same formula, as ω_n|x|ⁿ = Vol(ball 0 |x|) -- and f*(x) = ∫₀^∞ 1_{{f>t}*}(x) dt; I compiled `∫⁻ τ in Ioi 0, 1_{{y | μ(ball 0 ‖y‖) < μ{f > ofReal τ}}}(x) = schwarzRearrangement μ f x` for every measure μ, so the supremum is exactly that layer-cake integral, and, for an additive Haar measure on a nontrivial finite-dimensional space, that when μ{f>t} is finite the set {x | t < f* x} is `ball 0 r` with μ(ball 0 r) = μ{f>t}, the open centred ball of Burchard and Frank. Lean subtlety: the definition is total -- f is [0,∞]-valued (nonnegativity is built in and the value ∞ is allowed) and there is no measurability or vanishing-at-infinity hypothesis, which the textbook requires; a level set of infinite measure is rearranged to the whole space (every Haar ball has finite measure), not to a junk ∅: I compiled f ≡ 1 on ℝ² ↦ f* ≡ 1 and the indicator of any infinite-measure set (e.g. a half-space) ↦ f* ≡ 1, so equimeasurability and the L^∞ identity hold there for the right reason; on functions vanishing at infinity it is the textbook object, elsewhere a natural extension; a level set of measure 0 goes to ∅; `⨆` of the empty family is 0, matching the empty layer-cake integral; for a non-Euclidean norm the balls are norm balls, so it is the rotation-symmetric rearrangement only for the Euclidean norm (the module docstring says this); in dimension zero f* = f (compiled); the value does not depend on the Haar normalisation (`schwarzRearrangement_smul_measure`). Sources: Burchard, A Short Course on Rearrangement Inequalities (2009), §1.1; Frank, Rearrangement methods in the work of Elliott Lieb (arXiv:2207.05153), eqs. (2) and (4). Checks (Red-team audit at 5f78b5307b): witnesses compiled (f ≡ 1, infinite-measure indicator, 1_[0,2] ↦ 1_(-1,1) on ℝ, dimension 0), layer-cake identity and ball identification compiled; Mathlib has no symmetric decreasing rearrangement and the Tau Ceti Steiner symmetrisation is a different object.

Correctly stated: (f + c)* = f* + c for every constant c ∈ [0,∞], Haar μ; for t < c the level set {f + c > t} is the whole space, rearranged to the whole space -- a property of the total definition (f + c does not vanish at infinity), true also in dimension zero.
Correctly stated: f*(0) = essSup f μ, for every measure (ball 0 0 = ∅, so the condition is μ{f > t} > 0); for Haar measure this is the supremum of f*, the textbook ‖f‖_∞.
Correctly stated: f = g μ-a.e. implies f* = g* everywhere, so f* is a well-defined function of the a.e. class and a canonical everywhere-defined representative.
Correctly stated: the defining formula f*(x) = sup{t : μ(ball 0 ‖x‖) < μ{f > t}}, proved by `rfl`; it is the only way an importing module can unfold the unexposed definition.
Correctly stated: ‖x‖ = ‖y‖ implies f*(x) = f*(y), i.e. f* depends only on the norm (radial symmetry; for the Euclidean norm, rotation invariance).

Correctly stated: (c·1_s)* = c·1_{s*} with s* = {x | μ(ball 0 ‖x‖) < μ s}, Burchard's Exercise 1.1 (X_{A*} = (X_A)*); for Haar measure s* is the open centred ball of measure μ s, or the whole space when μ s = ∞ (compiled: 1_[0,2] ↦ 1_(-1,1) on ℝ, and an infinite-measure set ↦ 1).
Correctly stated: f*(x) ≤ essSup f μ for every x, from radial monotonicity and the value at 0.
Correctly stated: ‖x‖ ≤ ‖y‖ implies f*(y) ≤ f*(x), i.e. f* is radially nonincreasing (Frank: 'radially symmetric and nonincreasing'); holds for every measure since balls grow with the radius.
Correctly stated: f ≤ g pointwise implies f* ≤ g* pointwise (Burchard (1.5)).
Correctly stated: f ≤ g μ-a.e. implies f* ≤ g* everywhere (order preservation, Burchard (1.5), here in the stronger a.e. form, since f* depends only on the distribution function).
Correctly stated: (f*)* = f* for Haar μ (idempotence), immediate from equimeasurability and the fact that f* depends only on the distribution function.

Correctly stated: replacing μ by c·μ with 0 < c < ∞ does not change f*, so f* is independent of the normalisation of Haar measure. Both hypotheses are needed: c = 0 gives f* = 0 and c = ∞ changes the strict comparisons (∞·a < ∞·b only if a = 0).
Correctly stated: the set form of `lt_schwarzRearrangement_iff`, {x | t < f* x} = {x | μ(ball 0 ‖x‖) < μ{f > t}} = {f>t}* (Frank eq. (4)).
Correctly stated: if μ{f > s} ≤ μ{g > t} then {f* > s} ⊆ {g* > t}; rearranged level sets are concentric, nested by measure (the step Burchard uses in Lemma 1.6). Holds for every measure.

Correctly stated: if C is a nonempty, bounded, complete convex subset of a nonzero normed space E over ℝ or ℂ, the support functionals of C (the nonzero g ∈ E* whose real part attains its supremum on C) are norm-dense in E*. Lean ↔ maths: `hconv : Convex ℝ C` is ordinary (real) convexity, the right notion over ℂ as well; `hC : IsComplete C` is completeness of C, which holds for every closed C in a Banach space, so this covers the textbook 'closed bounded convex subset of a Banach space'; `hb : Bornology.IsBounded C` is norm-boundedness, `hne : C.Nonempty` is nonemptiness and `[Nontrivial E]` is E ≠ 0; `[NormedSpace ℝ E] [IsScalarTower ℝ 𝕜 E]` only say that the real structure is the restriction of the 𝕜-structure. In the set, `g ≠ 0 ∧ ∃ x ∈ C, IsMaxOn (fun y ↦ re (g y)) C x` says g is nonzero and Re g(y) ≤ Re g(x) for all y ∈ C at some x ∈ C (`IsMaxOn f C x` unfolds to ∀ y ∈ C, f y ≤ f x), i.e. Re g attains sup_C Re g; `Dense` is in the operator-norm topology of `StrongDual 𝕜 E` = `E →L[𝕜] 𝕜`. Lean subtlety: over ℂ the support condition is on Re g, since ℂ is not ordered; this is the standard complex convention, and differs from requiring that |g| attain its supremum on C, which Wikipedia's Bishop–Phelps page records (citing Lomonosov 2000) as false for general complex C. `[Nontrivial E]` is necessary: for E = 0 the set is empty while the dual {0} is not (compiled). Mathematically the other hypotheses are needed too: with C empty there are no support functionals, and for an unbounded C such as a half-plane in ℝ² the support functionals are only the positive multiples of one functional. Source: Phelps' Encyclopedia of Mathematics entry 'Bishop–Phelps theorem' (real Banach spaces) gives 'the same norm density conclusion for the set of functionals in E* which attain their supremum on an arbitrary non-empty closed convex bounded subset C of E (the support functionals of C)'. Checks at 5f78b5307b: specialised to C = [−1, 1] ⊆ ℝ (compiled); axioms standard; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate. The stronger unbounded form, which the proof already contains, is recorded as a MINOR generality finding, not a correctness problem.

Correctly stated: for a complete convex C, a functional f ≠ 0 with Re f bounded above on C, 0 < k < 1 and z ∈ C, there are x ∈ C with k‖f‖‖x − z‖ ≤ Re f(x − z) and a nonzero h ∈ E* with Re h maximal over C at x and Re h > 0 on the open cone {w | k‖f‖‖w‖ < Re f(w)}. This is the Ekeland-plus-separation step of Phelps' proof. In the Lean statement, `BddAbove ((fun y ↦ re (f y)) '' C)` is sup_C Re f < ∞, and `IsMaxOn (fun y ↦ re (h y)) C x` means Re h(y) ≤ Re h(x) for y ∈ C, so h is a support functional at x. The hypotheses are needed: with k = 2, f = id on ℝ, the condition 2|x − z| ≤ x − z forces x = z, and the interior point z = 0 of [−1, 1] has no support functional; k > 0 is Ekeland's ε > 0; f ≠ 0 makes the cone nonempty. Checks: hypotheses satisfiable (C = [−1, 1], f = id, k = 1/2, z = 0, compiled); axioms standard.

Correctly stated: the support points of a complete convex subset C of a normed space over ℝ or ℂ are dense in the boundary of C (Bishop–Phelps for support points). Lean ↔ maths: `frontier C` is the topological boundary, closure C minus interior C; `{x ∈ C | ∃ g : StrongDual 𝕜 E, g ≠ 0 ∧ IsMaxOn (fun y ↦ re (g y)) C x}` is the set of support points, the points of C at which the real part of some nonzero continuous functional attains its supremum over C; `frontier C ⊆ closure S` says every boundary point is a limit of support points. Since every support point is a boundary point (`StrongDual.mem_frontier_of_isMaxOn_re`, in this file), this is exactly 'the support points are dense in ∂C'. `hconv : Convex ℝ C` is convexity and `hC : IsComplete C` completeness, which every closed subset of a Banach space has. Lean subtlety: over ℂ support is measured by Re g, the standard convention; for C = ∅ or C = E the frontier is empty and the statement is rightly trivial; `IsComplete C` makes C closed, which is how the proof puts boundary points in C. Source: Phelps' Encyclopedia of Mathematics entry 'Bishop–Phelps theorem': 'if C is any non-empty closed convex subset of E, … the points of C at which support functionals attain their supremum on C (the support points) are dense in the boundary of C'. Checks at 5f78b5307b: applied at the boundary point 1 of [−1, 1] ⊆ ℝ (compiled); axioms standard; no Mathlib or Tau Ceti duplicate.

Correctly stated: for r ≥ 0 the open cone {y | r‖y − x‖ < Re f(y − x)} with vertex x is (real) convex. It is the strict sublevel set {y | r‖y − x‖ − Re f(y − x) < 0} of a convex function. `hr` is needed: for r = −1 and f = 0 the set is E minus {x}, which is not convex. It is stated for a seminormed E carrying only a 𝕜-module structure compatible with the real one, as the module docstring says.

Correctly stated: if 0 ≤ k < 1, f ≠ 0 and Re h > 0 on the open cone {x | k‖f‖‖x‖ < Re f(x)}, then ‖f − c·h‖ ≤ k‖f‖ for some real c > 0. This is a form of the Bishop–Phelps lemma: a functional positive on a Bishop–Phelps cone of f is, after positive scaling, within k‖f‖ of f. In the Lean statement, `(c : 𝕜) • h` is h scaled by the real number c viewed in 𝕜, and the norms are operator norms. Each hypothesis is needed: f = 0 empties the cone and the conclusion would force h = 0; k = 1 also empties the cone; k = −1 on E = ℝ with f = h = id satisfies the cone hypothesis but makes the bound negative. Checks: hypotheses satisfiable (E = ℝ, f = h = id, k = 1/2, compiled); all explicit hypotheses load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses); the argument was checked step by step (on ker Re h the cone condition gives |Re f| ≤ k‖f‖‖·‖, Hahn–Banach extends this without increasing the norm, Re f minus the extension is a real multiple of Re h, which is positive by testing at a point of the cone, and the real part determines the norm through `extendRCLikeₗᵢ`); axioms standard.

Correctly stated: if g ≠ 0 and Re g attains its maximum over C at a point x ∈ C (`IsMaxOn (fun y ↦ re (g y)) C x`, i.e. Re g(y) ≤ Re g(x) for y ∈ C), then x lies in `frontier C` = closure C minus interior C. So support points are boundary points, with no convexity or completeness needed. Both hypotheses are needed: for g = 0 every point, including interior ones, is a maximiser, and `IsMaxOn` alone does not put x in C (C = [0, 1], g = id, x = 5) (lean_minimal_hypotheses: all load-bearing).

Correctly stated: in every real or complex Banach space E, the continuous linear functionals that attain their norm on the closed unit ball are norm-dense in the dual E* (the Bishop–Phelps theorem). Lean ↔ maths: `RCLike 𝕜` is 𝕜 = ℝ or ℂ, and `[NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] [CompleteSpace E]` make E a Banach space over 𝕜, with no further hypothesis (no `Nontrivial`, separability or reflexivity); `StrongDual 𝕜 E` is by definition (an abbrev) `E →L[𝕜] 𝕜`, the continuous linear functionals, and `‖g‖` is the operator norm `sInf {c | 0 ≤ c ∧ ∀ x, ‖g x‖ ≤ c * ‖x‖}`; the set `{g | ∃ x, ‖x‖ ≤ 1 ∧ ‖g x‖ = ‖g‖}` is literally 'g attains its norm at a point x of the closed unit ball', |g(x)| = ‖g‖ with ‖x‖ ≤ 1; `Dense` refers to the topology of `StrongDual 𝕜 E`, which is the operator-norm topology (checked by `rfl` against the metric topology of `ContinuousLinearMap.toNormedAddCommGroup`), so through `Metric.dense_iff` the conclusion unfolds to: for every f ∈ E* and ε > 0 there is a norm-attaining g with ‖f − g‖ < ε (compiled). Lean subtlety: (i) the closed ball instead of the unit sphere: for g ≠ 0 any witness has ‖x‖ = 1 (‖g‖ = |g x| ≤ ‖g‖‖x‖), and in the real case can be taken with g x = ‖g‖ (compiled), so this is the usual S_E definition; x = 0 is a witness only when ‖g‖ = 0, i.e. g = 0 (compiled), so nothing slips in that way; for E = 0 the sphere is empty and an S_E version would be false (E* = {0} but no functional attains on ∅), while the ball version makes the set all of E*, which the proof handles in its subsingleton branch; (ii) over ℂ, `‖g x‖` is the modulus |g(x)|, equivalent to Re g(x) = ‖g‖ after rotating x by a unimodular scalar (compiled); (iii) `‖g‖` is an `sInf`, but of a nonempty set bounded below for continuous g, so it is the true operator norm, not a junk value. Non-vacuity: the set is not all of E*: on ℓ¹(ℕ, ℝ) (`lp (fun _ => ℝ) 1`, complete) the functional x ↦ Σ (1 − 1/(n+1)) x_n has norm ≥ 1 while |g(x)| < 1 whenever ‖x‖ ≤ 1, and Lean proves it is not in the set, while the theorem still applies to that space. Sources: Aron, Choi, Kim, Lee and Martín, 'The Bishop–Phelps–Bollobás version of Lindenstrauss properties A and B' (arXiv:1305.6420, §1), working over K = ℝ or ℂ, define 'T attains its norm if ‖T‖ = ‖Tx‖ for some x ∈ S_X' and say the Bishop–Phelps theorem 'simply states that NA(X, K) is dense in X* for every Banach space X'; Phelps' Encyclopedia of Mathematics entry 'Bishop–Phelps theorem' states the real case. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only; specialised to 𝕜 = ℝ and 𝕜 = ℂ; no copy in pinned Mathlib 1b1ccf4b08 (grep for Bishop/Phelps/norm-attaining, leanfinder, loogle) or elsewhere in Tau Ceti.

Correctly stated: for a complex algebraic number α of degree d ≥ 2 and a real κ > d/2 + 1, only finitely many rationals ξ satisfy |ξ − α| ≤ H(ξ)^(−κ). `(minpoly ℚ α).natDegree` is the degree [ℚ(α):ℚ] of α ∈ ℂ, and `hd : 2 ≤ (minpoly ℚ α).natDegree` also encodes algebraicity, since `minpoly ℚ α = 0` for transcendental α (compiled: hd implies `IsAlgebraic ℚ α`). `hκ` is `↑d / (2 : ℝ) + 1 < κ` (real division, strict). `mulHeight₁ ξ` is the naive height max(|p|, q) of ξ = p/q in lowest terms (`Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max`), and `‖(ξ : ℂ) − α‖` is the complex modulus |ξ − α|, so `{ξ : ℚ | ‖(ξ : ℂ) − α‖ ≤ mulHeight₁ ξ ^ (−κ)}.Finite` says the inequality has finitely many rational solutions. Lean subtlety: the minimal polynomial of a transcendental number is 0, so the degree bound is the algebraicity hypothesis; `^ (−κ)` is `Real.rpow` with base H(ξ) ≥ 1 > 0; ξ enters ℂ through the cast ℚ → ℂ. For non-real α the statement is elementary (|ξ − α| ≥ |Im α| bounds H(ξ)); the content is the real case, which `thue_approximation_real` restates. Source: Evertse, Diophantine Approximation lecture notes, ch. 6, Theorem 6.9 (p. 115, read) for real α of degree ≥ 3; the docstring says this is a variant allowing complex α and d ≥ 2. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: instantiated at α = √2 ∈ ℂ with κ = 3 (compiled); both hypotheses load-bearing; standard axioms only.

Correctly stated: for a real algebraic number α of degree d ≥ 2 and a real κ > d/2 + 1, only finitely many rationals ξ satisfy |ξ − α| ≤ H(ξ)^(−κ). `(minpoly ℚ α).natDegree` is the degree d = [ℚ(α):ℚ]; there is no separate algebraicity hypothesis because `minpoly ℚ α` is 0 (natDegree 0) when α is transcendental, so `hd : 2 ≤ (minpoly ℚ α).natDegree` says exactly 'α is algebraic of degree at least 2' (compiled: hd implies `IsAlgebraic ℚ α`; a rational α has degree 1 and is excluded). `hκ` elaborates as `↑d / (2 : ℝ) + 1 < κ`, so the division is real division and the hypothesis is κ > d/2 + 1, strict. `mulHeight₁ ξ` is Mathlib's multiplicative height, which `Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max` identifies with max(|p|, q) for ξ = p/q in lowest terms, i.e. Evertse's H(ξ) (compiled values: H(0) = H(1) = 1, H(3/2) = 3, H(−2/4) = 2). The conclusion `{ξ : ℚ | |(ξ : ℝ) − α| ≤ mulHeight₁ ξ ^ (−κ)}.Finite` is 'the inequality |ξ − α| ≤ H(ξ)^(−κ) has finitely many solutions ξ ∈ ℚ', with the non-strict ≤ of Evertse's (6.10). Lean subtlety: the minimal polynomial of a transcendental number is 0, so the degree bound doubles as the algebraicity hypothesis; `^ (−κ)` is `Real.rpow`, harmless because H(ξ) ≥ 1 > 0 (`one_le_mulHeight₁`); `(ξ : ℝ)` is the ordinary cast ℚ → ℝ. Source: Evertse, Diophantine Approximation lecture notes, ch. 6, Theorem 6.9 (p. 115, read), which assumes d ≥ 3; the Lean statement also covers d = 2, as its docstring says (there κ > 2, Roth's range: Tau Ceti's `IsAlgebraic.finite_setOfPred_abs_sub_le_mulHeight₁_rpow_neg` also implies it). Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: instantiated at α = √2 (degree 2 compiled) with κ = 3; κ = d/2 + 1 = 2 is excluded by the strict hypothesis; both hypotheses are load-bearing; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.

Correctly stated in existential form: for a complex algebraic α of degree d ≥ 2 and κ > d/2 + 1 there are C ≥ 1 and λ ≥ 1 such that, whenever ξ₁ ∈ ℚ satisfies |ξ₁ − α| ≤ H(ξ₁)^(−κ) and H(ξ₁) ≥ C, every ξ ∈ ℚ with |ξ − α| ≤ H(ξ)^(−κ) has H(ξ) ≤ H(ξ₁)^λ. `hd : 2 ≤ (minpoly ℚ α).natDegree` and `hκ` encode 'α algebraic of degree d ≥ 2' and κ > d/2 + 1 (minpoly of a transcendental is 0; `/ 2` is real division); `mulHeight₁` is Evertse's H, max(|p|, q) in lowest terms (`Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max`); `‖(ξ : ℂ) − α‖` is |ξ − α|. The quantifier order `∃ C lam, 1 ≤ C ∧ 1 ≤ lam ∧ ∀ ξ₁ ξ, …` makes C and λ depend only on α and κ, as in Evertse; the first hypothesis on ξ₁ is the good-approximation inequality (6.10), the second is H(ξ₁) ≥ C, and ξ ranges over all solutions (ξ = ξ₁ included, harmless because λ ≥ 1 and H ≥ 1). Lean subtlety: Evertse's C and λ are effectively computable, but the Lean statement only asserts that they exist, and in that form it is equivalent to the finiteness theorem (C above the heights of the finitely many solutions makes the hypothesis on ξ₁ unsatisfiable); the module docstring says only existence is stated, and the red team has recorded this as a finding. Also `^ (−κ)` and `^ lam` are `Real.rpow` with base H ≥ 1 > 0. Source: Evertse, Diophantine Approximation lecture notes, ch. 6, Theorem 6.14 (p. 124, read): same threshold κ > d/2 + 1 and same conclusion; Evertse allows any degree, and d ≥ 2 only drops the trivial rational case. Red-team checks at 5f78b5307b: instantiated at α = √2, κ = 3 (compiled); both hypotheses load-bearing; standard axioms only.

Correctly stated: a weak homotopy equivalence f : X → Y between arbitrary topological spaces (no CW hypothesis) induces, for every ring k and every n ≥ 0, an isomorphism f_* : H_n(X; k) → H_n(Y; k) — the homology half of Hatcher's Prop. 4.21 for the coefficient group G = k. Lean ↔ maths: `f.IsWeakHomotopyEquivalence` (TauCeti/Topology/Homotopy/HomotopyGroup/WeakHomotopyEquivalence.lean:78) is a structure with two fields: `exists_joined` (every y : Y is joined by a path to some f x, i.e. surjectivity on path components) and `bijective n x` (for every n : ℕ and every basepoint x : X, `HomotopyGroup.map f rfl : π_n(X, x) → π_n(Y, f x)` is bijective); `HomotopyGroup (Fin n) X x` is Mathlib's set of maps (Iⁿ, ∂Iⁿ) → (X, x) modulo homotopy rel ∂Iⁿ, which is exactly Hatcher's definition of π_n (AT.pdf p. 340), with π_0(X, x) the set of path components, and `HomotopyGroup.map` is post-composition with f; so the predicate is Hatcher's 'isomorphisms π_n(X, x0) → π_n(Y, f(x0)) for all n ≥ 0 and all choices of basepoint x0' (p. 352), the n = 0 case giving injectivity on path components. `singularHomologyFunctor (ModuleCat.{u} k) n` is Mathlib's singular homology: `SSet.chainComplexFunctor` builds, from a coefficient object M, the alternating-face-map complex of n ↦ ∐ over singular n-simplices Δⁿ → X of M, and then takes the n-th homology; at M = `ModuleCat.of k k` this is the free k-module on singular n-simplices with the usual boundary, i.e. C_n(X; k). `.map (TopCat.ofHom f)` is the map induced by pushing simplices forward along f, so `IsIso (…)` says that f_* itself is a k-linear isomorphism, not merely that H_n(X; k) and H_n(Y; k) are abstractly isomorphic. n : ℕ has no lower bound, so H_0 is included. Lean subtlety: (1) universes — X and Y must lie in one universe u (Mathlib's singular homology is a functor on `TopCat.{u}`), and the coefficient ring must also lie in `Type u`, because `ModuleCat.of k k` is an object of `ModuleCat.{u} k`; the spaces are arbitrary, but integer coefficients ℤ : Type apply verbatim only to X : Type, and for X : Type 1 one takes `ULift ℤ` (compiled); (2) the empty space — Hatcher's wording quantifies over basepoints and is vacuous for X = ∅, which would make ∅ → pt a weak equivalence although H_0 differs; the `exists_joined` field excludes this (compiled: ∅ → Unit is not a weak homotopy equivalence, ∅ → ∅ is); (3) basepoints — `bijective` is demanded at every x, and with `exists_joined` this rules out the one-basepoint trap (compiled: the inclusion of a point into the two-point discrete space `Bool`, bijective on every π_n at its only basepoint, is not a weak homotopy equivalence; nor is the constant map Circle → Unit, bijective on path components but not on π_1 ≅ ℤ); (4) `[Ring k]` allows non-commutative k, with `ModuleCat.of k k` the left regular module (compiled at n = 0 for 2×2 rational matrices). No junk values are involved. Sources and checks: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology (AT.pdf from his website), the definition of π_n (p. 340), of weak homotopy equivalence (p. 352) and Prop. 4.21 with its proof (pp. 356-357), read; red-team audit at 5f78b5307b: the identity and every homotopy equivalence satisfy the hypothesis and the theorem instantiates (compiled), the non-witnesses above compiled, `hf` is load-bearing (lean_minimal_hypotheses), axioms propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound only, no Mathlib counterpart (leansearch, leanfinder, loogle, grep of the pinned Mathlib). The coefficients are the ring itself: the form for an arbitrary coefficient module over any ring (hence Hatcher's arbitrary group G, with R = ℤ) follows from this file's local-coefficient theorem at a constant system and is recorded as a generality finding (RT-20261105-04eaf3), not a correctness defect.

Correctly stated: for a weak homotopy equivalence f : X → Y, every local coefficient system L on Y and every n : ℕ, the induced map H_n(X; f*L) → H_n(Y; L) is an isomorphism. `twistedHomologyMap (TopCat.ofHom f) L n` is by definition `homologyMap (twistedChainComplexMap (TopCat.ofHom f) L) n`, the map on n-th homology of the chain map that pushes simplices forward (σ-summand of f*L onto the (f∘σ)-summand of L), and `IsIso` in R-modules is a linear isomorphism; it is the degreewise form of `quasiIso_twistedChainComplexMap`, and for L constant with fibre M it is f_* : H_n(X; M) ≅ H_n(Y; M) (compiled via `twistedHomologyConstantIso_hom_space_naturality`). Lean subtlety: the fibres of L lie in the universe of the spaces (`LocalCoefficientSystem.{u, v, v}`). Hatcher defines H_n(X; E) in §3.H (AT.pdf p. 331).

Correctly stated: for a weak homotopy equivalence f : X → Y and a ring k, the chain map that f induces on normalized cubical singular chains with coefficients in k is a quasi-isomorphism. `normalizedCubicalChainComplex k` is the functor sending a space to its normalized cubical chains (the k-span of singular cubes Iⁿ → X modulo the degenerate ones, with the cubical boundary; Massey's cubical singular chains), `.map (TopCat.ofHom f)` is push-forward of cubes along f, and `QuasiIso` means the induced map on homology is an isomorphism in every degree n ≥ 0; the hypothesis is the predicate `f.IsWeakHomotopyEquivalence` (TauCeti/Topology/Homotopy/HomotopyGroup/WeakHomotopyEquivalence.lean:78) is a structure with two fields: `exists_joined` (every y : Y is joined by a path to some f x, i.e. surjectivity on path components) and `bijective n x` (for every n : ℕ and every basepoint x : X, `HomotopyGroup.map f rfl : π_n(X, x) → π_n(Y, f x)` is bijective), which is Hatcher's definition of weak homotopy equivalence (AT.pdf p. 352) with the empty-source case handled. This is the cubical form of Hatcher's Prop. 4.21 (p. 356), and the named result `isIso_singularHomologyMap` is read off from it through the natural cubical–simplicial comparison. Lean subtlety: the coefficient ring lives in the universe of the spaces (k, X, Y : Type u). Checks: the proof follows Hatcher's mapping-cylinder route (homeomorphism onto the bottom face, deformation of singular cubes into it from the vanishing relative homotopy sets, projection a homotopy equivalence); axioms standard; the file elaborates in under a second.

Correctly stated: for a weak homotopy equivalence f : X → Y and every local coefficient system L on Y, the chain map of normalized cubical chains with local coefficients, from X with coefficients f*L to Y with coefficients L (`normalizedTwistedCubicalChainComplexMap f L`, whose domain and codomain are `((pullback f).obj L).normalizedTwistedCubicalChainComplex` and `L.normalizedTwistedCubicalChainComplex`), is a quasi-isomorphism, i.e. an isomorphism on homology in every degree.
