## What it says
The carrier of a translated polygon is the translated carrier.

- `{n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (P : ConvexPolygon n)`: a convex hyperbolic polygon $P$ with $n$ vertices $v_0, \dots, v_{n-1}$ in $\mathbb{H} \cup \partial\mathbb{H}$, listed counterclockwise (`TauCeti.UpperHalfPlane.ConvexPolygon`); `[NeZero n]` records that $n \neq 0$, which Lean needs to read indices modulo $n$.
- `(h : PSL(2, ℝ))`: an orientation-preserving isometry of $\mathbb{H}$, the Möbius map $z \mapsto (az + b)/(cz + d)$; it acts on $\mathbb{H} \cup \partial\mathbb{H}$ by the same formula, on $\mathbb{H}$ and on $\mathbb{R} \cup \{\infty\}$, and on convex polygons by moving their vertices (the `MulAction` instance of the file).
- The conclusion: `(h • P).carrier = h • P.carrier`, the image of the carrier under $h$.

Isometries carry closed half-planes to closed half-planes and commute with intersections. It is a `@[simp]` lemma.

## What it says
A convex polygon without ideal vertices is a compact convex polygon.

- `{n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (P : ConvexPolygon n)`: a convex hyperbolic polygon $P$ with $n$ vertices $v_0, \dots, v_{n-1}$ in $\mathbb{H} \cup \partial\mathbb{H}$, listed counterclockwise (`TauCeti.UpperHalfPlane.ConvexPolygon`); `[NeZero n]` records that $n \neq 0$, which Lean needs to read indices modulo $n$.

- The conclusion: `∃ Q : CompactConvexPolygon n, Q.toConvexPolygon = P`: some compact convex polygon $Q$ becomes $P$ under the embedding `CompactConvexPolygon.toConvexPolygon`.

With that embedding, it identifies the compact convex polygons with the convex polygons all of whose vertices lie in $\mathbb{H}$.

## What it says
The carrier is geodesically convex: it contains the geodesic segment between any two of its points.

- `{n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (P : ConvexPolygon n)`: a convex hyperbolic polygon $P$ with $n$ vertices $v_0, \dots, v_{n-1}$ in $\mathbb{H} \cup \partial\mathbb{H}$, listed counterclockwise (`TauCeti.UpperHalfPlane.ConvexPolygon`); `[NeZero n]` records that $n \neq 0$, which Lean needs to read indices modulo $n$.

- The conclusion: `geodesicSegment z w ⊆ P.carrier`, where `geodesicSegment z w` is the closed hyperbolic segment from $z$ to $w$ (the point $\{z\}$ if $z = w$).

Each closed half-plane is convex, and so is an intersection of them.

## What it says
The interior angle of a convex polygon at its vertex $v_i$.

- `{n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (P : ConvexPolygon n)`: a convex hyperbolic polygon $P$ with $n$ vertices $v_0, \dots, v_{n-1}$ in $\mathbb{H} \cup \partial\mathbb{H}$, listed counterclockwise (`TauCeti.UpperHalfPlane.ConvexPolygon`); `[NeZero n]` records that $n \neq 0$, which Lean needs to read indices modulo $n$.
- `(i : Fin n)`: the index of the vertex.
- The value: `vertexAngle (P.vertex i) (P.vertex (i - 1)) (P.vertex (i + 1))`: if $v_i$ is a point $A$ of $\mathbb{H}$, the angle in $[0, \pi]$ at $A$ between the geodesic rays from $A$ towards $v_{i-1}$ and towards $v_{i+1}$ (a ray towards an ideal neighbour ends at that ideal point); if $v_i$ is ideal, $0$.

At a finite vertex this is the angle between the two sides meeting there; the polygon being convex, it is the angle inside the polygon, and it lies in $(0, \pi)$. At an ideal vertex the two sides are asymptotic and the interior angle is $0$, the usual convention.

## What it says
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $L$ a Lie algebra over $R$ and $M$ an $R$-module. $\mathfrak a = R(\!(X)\!)\otimes_R L$ (`currentAlgebra R L`), the formal currents, carries the $X$-adic topology: the submodules $\mathfrak a_N$ (`orderSubmodule R L N`), spanned by the $f\otimes x$ with $\operatorname{ord} f\ge N$, form a basis of neighbourhoods of $0$.

- `f : oneCochain R (currentAlgebra R L) M`: an $R$-linear map $f:\mathfrak a\to M$.
- The conclusion: $f$ lies in `continuousOneCochain`, the linear maps vanishing on some neighbourhood of $0$, exactly when there is an integer $N$ with $f(\mathfrak a_N)=0$.

This is the definition of a continuous one-cochain with discrete coefficients made concrete for the order topology: since the $\mathfrak a_N$ form a basis of neighbourhoods of $0$, vanishing near $0$ means vanishing on one $\mathfrak a_N$, which is how continuous cochains on $\mathfrak g(\!(t)\!)$ are described in the literature.

## Lean subtleties
- The coefficients carry no topology. A cochain is called continuous when it vanishes near $0$ (for two-cochains: each partial map vanishes near $0$ and the cochain vanishes near $(0,0)$), which is continuity for the discrete topology on the coefficients (`TauCeti.LieModule.Cohomology.mem_continuousTwoCochain_iff_continuous`).
- $N$ ranges over all integers, negative ones included; the $\mathfrak a_N$ decrease as $N$ grows, so the condition only gets weaker as $N$ decreases.
- `R⸨X⸩` is the ring of Laurent series over $R$ (finitely many negative powers). For a finite free $L$, such as a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field, $\mathfrak a$ is the Lie algebra $L(\!(X)\!)$ of $L$-valued Laurent series; for an infinite-rank $L$ the tensor product is smaller than that.
- The Lie structure of $L$ plays no role in the statement beyond making $\mathfrak a$ a Lie algebra, as cochains require.

## What it says
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $L$ a Lie algebra over $R$ and $M$ an $R$-module. $\mathfrak a = R(\!(X)\!)\otimes_R L$ (`currentAlgebra R L`), the formal currents, carries the $X$-adic topology: the submodules $\mathfrak a_N$ (`orderSubmodule R L N`), spanned by the $f\otimes x$ with $\operatorname{ord} f\ge N$, form a basis of neighbourhoods of $0$.

- `c : twoCochain R (currentAlgebra R L) M`: an alternating $R$-bilinear map $c:\mathfrak a\times\mathfrak a\to M$ ($c(u,u)=0$).
- The conclusion: $c$ lies in `continuousTwoCochain` exactly when (i) for every $u$ there is an $N$ with $c(u,v)=0$ for all $v\in\mathfrak a_N$, and (ii) there is a single $N$ with $c(u,v)=0$ for all $u, v\in\mathfrak a_N$.

This is the joint-continuity criterion for bilinear cochains with discrete coefficients: separate continuity together with vanishing on one $\mathfrak a_N\times\mathfrak a_N$. The roadmap states the criterion in exactly this form.

## What it says
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $L$ a Lie algebra over $R$, with formal currents $\mathfrak a = R(\!(X)\!)\otimes_R L$ in the $X$-adic topology.

- `Φ : LinearMap.BilinForm R L`, `hΦ : Φ.lieInvariant L`, `hΦs : Φ.IsSymm`: an invariant symmetric bilinear form $\Phi$ on $L$.
- The value: the class $[c_\Phi]$ in `continuousSecondCohomology R (currentAlgebra R L) (TrivialLieModule R (currentAlgebra R L) R)`, the continuous second cohomology of $\mathfrak a$ with coefficients in $R$ and trivial action, that is, continuous two-cocycles modulo coboundaries of continuous one-cochains. Here $c_\Phi$ (`twoCochainOfBilinear R L Φ hΦs`) is the residue cocycle $(f\otimes x, g\otimes y)\mapsto \operatorname{Res}(f\,dg)\,\Phi(x,y)$; on modes it sends $(X^m\otimes x, X^n\otimes y)$ to $n\,\delta_{m+n,0}\,\Phi(x,y)$.

This is the residue class of the literature: the class of the cocycle defining the central extension of the formal loop algebra attached to an invariant form.

## What it says
Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero, $L$ a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over $K$ with nondegenerate Killing form, and $Z$ any $K$-vector space, of any dimension, with trivial action of the formal loop algebra $\mathfrak a = L(\!(X)\!)$ (the $X$-adic topology on $\mathfrak a$, $Z$ discrete).

- `Ψ` with `hΨ : Ψ.lieInvariant L`, `hΨs : Ψ.IsSymm`: an invariant symmetric bilinear form on $L$.
- `hspan`: every invariant bilinear form on $L$ is a scalar multiple of $\Psi$.
- `hΨ0 : Ψ ≠ 0`.
- The value: the $K$-linear isomorphism $Z\cong H^2_{\mathrm{cont}}(\mathfrak a; Z)$ sending $z$ to the class of $c_\Psi\otimes z$, the cocycle $(f\otimes x, g\otimes y)\mapsto\operatorname{Res}(f\,dg)\,\Psi(x,y)\,z$.

This is the classification with discrete coefficients the roadmap asks for: for a simple Lie algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, with $\Psi$ the Killing form, $H^2_{\mathrm{cont}}(\mathfrak g(\!(t)\!); Z)\cong Z$, with no finiteness condition on $Z$.

## What it says
`B.IsJordanSplitting π N` is the proposition that the family $(N_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ of submodules of $M$ is a Jordan splitting of the bilinear form $B$ with respect to $\pi$.

- `{R : Type u_1} {M : Type u_2}`, `[CommSemiring R] [AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is a module over a commutative semiring $R$; rings are the case of interest, but no subtraction is needed here.
- `(B : LinearMap.BilinForm R M)`: an $R$-bilinear form $B : M \times M \to R$; Lean writes $B(x, y)$ as `B x y`.
- `(π : R)`: any element of $R$; in the applications a uniformiser of a discrete valuation ring, such as $p$ in $\mathbb{Z}_p$.
- `(N : ℕ → Submodule R M)`: submodules $N_0, N_1, N_2, \dots$ of $M$.

It has three fields:
- `isInternal`: $M$ is the internal direct sum of the $N_i$: the map $\bigoplus_i N_i \to M$ adding up the components is bijective.
- `apply_eq_zero`: for $i \ne k$, $x \in N_i$ and $y \in N_k$, $B(x, y) = 0$. As $i$ and $k$ run over all pairs, this is orthogonality on both sides.
- `isModular`: for each $i$ the restriction of $B$ to $N_i$ is $\pi^i$-modular (`IsModular`): it equals $\pi^i C_i$ for a form $C_i$ on $N_i$ that is a perfect pairing, meaning that $x \mapsto C_i(x, \cdot)$ and $y \mapsto C_i(\cdot, y)$ are both isomorphisms $N_i \to \operatorname{Hom}_R(N_i, R)$.

This is O'Meara's Jordan splitting $L = L_1 \perp \dots \perp L_t$ into modular components of strictly decreasing scales, with each component placed at the exponent of its scale: the component of scale $\pi^i R$ sits at index $i$, and an index with no component carries $N_i = 0$. Since $B$ takes values in $R$, only exponents $i \ge 0$ occur. The definition does not assume that $B$ is symmetric or nondegenerate, and assumes nothing of $\pi$.

A reduction step: to show that the $j$-th constituents of Jordan splittings of two isometric forms are isometric, it suffices to classify their unimodular rescalings from data the splittings provide.

- `{B : LinearMap.BilinForm R M}`: an $R$-bilinear form $B : M \times M \to R$, written `B x y`.
- `{π : R} {N : ℕ → Submodule R M}`, `{M' : Type u_5} [AddCommGroup M'] [Module R M']`, `{B' : LinearMap.BilinForm R M'}`, `{N' : ℕ → Submodule R M'}`: an element $\pi$, a second module $M'$ with a form $B'$, and submodules $N_i$ of $M$ and $N'_i$ of $M'$.

- `(h : B.IsJordanSplitting π N) (h' : B'.IsJordanSplitting π N')`: Jordan splittings of $B$ and $B'$ with respect to $\pi$.
- `(hB : B.IsSymm)`: $B(x, y) = B(y, x)$; `(hBB' : B.Equivalent B')`: $B$ and $B'$ are isometric.
- `(hπ : π ≠ 0) (hπ' : ¬IsUnit π)`: $\pi$ is nonzero and not a unit; `(j : ℕ)`: an index.
- `H`: for all forms $C$ on $N_j$ and $C'$ on $N'_j$ such that both are symmetric, $\pi^j C(x, y) = B(x, y)$ on $N_j$, and in some bases $b$ of $N_j$ and $b'$ of $N'_j$ with the same number $n$ of elements both Gram matrices have unit determinant, and for every linear map $\varphi : N'_j \to N_j$ with $\pi \mid C'(x, y) - C(\varphi x, \varphi y)$ for all $x, y$, and with $\pi^2 \mid C'(x, x) - C(\varphi x, \varphi x)$ for all $x$ whenever $\pi^j \mid B(w, w)$ on $N_{j-1}$ and $\pi^{j+2} \mid B(w, w)$ on $N_{j+1}$: $C$ and $C'$ are isometric.

The proof takes for $C$ and $C'$ the unimodular rescalings of the two constituents and for $\varphi$ the projection to $N_j$ along the other constituents, pulled back through the isometry. So $H$ is the classification of unimodular forms by their reductions, which the theorem leaves to its user.

- `{B : LinearMap.BilinForm R M}`: an $R$-bilinear form $B : M \times M \to R$, written `B x y`.
- `{π : R} {N : ℕ → Submodule R M}`: an element $\pi$ and submodules $N_i$.

- `(h : B.IsJordanSplitting π N)`: the $N_i$ form a Jordan splitting of $B$ with respect to $\pi$.
- `(hB : B.IsSymm)`: $B$ is symmetric; `(hπ : π ≠ 0)`: $\pi$ is nonzero; `(j : ℕ)`: an index.

- O. T. O'Meara, *Introduction to Quadratic Forms*, §91C, for Jordan splittings (as the module docstring records).

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `Module.Free` says that a basis exists; it does not choose one.
- Only the direct-sum condition of the splitting is used; the form and $\pi$ play no part.
- Flatness is the weakest of the usual hypotheses: it holds for free and for projective $M$.

## What it says
A Jordan splitting of a finitely generated module has only finitely many nonzero constituents.

- `{R : Type u_1} {M : Type u_2}`, `[CommSemiring R] [AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is a module over a commutative semiring $R$; rings are the case of interest, but no subtraction is needed here.
- `{B : LinearMap.BilinForm R M}`: an $R$-bilinear form $B : M \times M \to R$; Lean writes $B(x, y)$ as `B x y`.
- `[Module.Finite R M]`: $M$ is finitely generated over $R$.
- `{π : R} {N : ℕ → Submodule R M}` and `(h : B.IsJordanSplitting π N)`: the submodules $N_0, N_1, \dots$ form a Jordan splitting of $B$ with respect to $\pi$: $M = \bigoplus_i N_i$ internally, $B(N_i, N_k) = 0$ for $i \ne k$, and $B$ restricted to $N_i$ is $\pi^i$ times a perfect pairing.
- The conclusion: the set of indices $i$ with $N_i \ne 0$ is finite (`{i : ℕ | N i ≠ ⊥}.Finite`, where `⊥` is the zero submodule).

This is what makes the $\mathbb{N}$-indexed family agree with O'Meara's finite splitting $L_1 \perp \dots \perp L_t$: only finitely many indices carry a constituent.

## References and tests
- O. T. O'Meara, *Introduction to Quadratic Forms*, §91C, for Jordan splittings (as the module docstring records).

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- The proof uses only that $M$ is the internal direct sum of the $N_i$ and is finitely generated; neither the form nor $\pi$ plays a part.
- Under Mathlib's convention that the zero of the submodule lattice is `⊥`, this set is the support of $i \mapsto N_i$, which is where the name comes from.
- It holds over commutative semirings.

## What it says
In a Jordan splitting, the constituents of index at most $j$ and those of index above $j$ span complementary submodules: $M = \bigl(\sum_{i \le j} N_i\bigr) \oplus \bigl(\sum_{i \ge j+1} N_i\bigr)$.

- `{R : Type u_3} {M : Type u_4}`, `[CommRing R] [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is a module over a commutative ring $R$.
- `{B : LinearMap.BilinForm R M}`: an $R$-bilinear form $B : M \times M \to R$, written `B x y`.
- `{π : R} {N : ℕ → Submodule R M}` and `(h : B.IsJordanSplitting π N)`: the submodules $N_0, N_1, \dots$ form a Jordan splitting of $B$ with respect to $\pi$: $M = \bigoplus_i N_i$ internally, $B(N_i, N_k) = 0$ for $i \ne k$, and $B$ restricted to $N_i$ is $\pi^i$ times a perfect pairing.
- `(j : ℕ)`: an index.
- The conclusion: `IsCompl A A'` for $A = \sum_{i \le j} N_i$ (`⨆ i ∈ Set.Iic j, N i`) and $A' = \sum_{i \ge j+1} N_i$ (`⨆ i ∈ Set.Ici (j + 1), N i`): $A \cap A' = 0$ and $A + A' = M$.

It is the coarsening of the direct sum $M = \bigoplus_i N_i$ along the partition of $\mathbb{N}$ into $\{i \le j\}$ and $\{i > j\}$, and it supplies the projection to $A$ along $A'$ used by `IsJordanSplitting.pow_succ_dvd_sub_apply_projectionOnto` and its relatives.

## References and tests
- O. T. O'Meara, *Introduction to Quadratic Forms*, §91C, for Jordan splittings (as the module docstring records).

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `IsCompl` is complementarity in the lattice of submodules, `⊓` and `⊔` being intersection and sum; it is the internal direct-sum decomposition $M = A \oplus A'$.
- Only the direct-sum condition of the splitting is used; the form and $\pi$ play no part.

## What it says
A Jordan splitting moves along an isometry: if $(N_i)$ is a Jordan splitting of $B$ and $e$ is an isometry from $(M, B)$ onto $(M', B')$, then the images $e(N_i)$ are a Jordan splitting of $B'$ with respect to the same $\pi$.

- `{R : Type u_1} {M : Type u_2}`, `[CommSemiring R] [AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is a module over a commutative semiring $R$; rings are the case of interest, but no subtraction is needed here.
- `{B : LinearMap.BilinForm R M}`: an $R$-bilinear form $B : M \times M \to R$; Lean writes $B(x, y)$ as `B x y`.
- `{M' : Type u_3} [AddCommMonoid M'] [Module R M']` and `{B' : LinearMap.BilinForm R M'}`: a second module with a bilinear form $B'$.
- `{π : R} {N : ℕ → Submodule R M}` and `(h : B.IsJordanSplitting π N)`: the submodules $N_0, N_1, \dots$ form a Jordan splitting of $B$ with respect to $\pi$: $M = \bigoplus_i N_i$ internally, $B(N_i, N_k) = 0$ for $i \ne k$, and $B$ restricted to $N_i$ is $\pi^i$ times a perfect pairing.
- `(e : B.IsometryEquiv B')`: an isometry, a linear isomorphism $e : M \to M'$ with $B'(e x, e y) = B(x, y)$ for all $x, y$.
- The conclusion: $i \mapsto e(N_i)$ is a Jordan splitting of $B'$ with respect to $\pi$.

So the existence of a Jordan splitting, and its constituents up to the isometry, depend only on the isometry class of the form, as in O'Meara.

## References and tests
- O. T. O'Meara, *Introduction to Quadratic Forms*, §91C, for Jordan splittings (as the module docstring records).

No test is recorded for it. It is what lets `LinearMap.BilinForm.IsJordanSplitting.finrank_eq_of_equivalent` compare splittings of two isometric forms.

## Lean subtleties
- `e.toLinearEquiv` is the underlying linear isomorphism of the isometry and `↑` views it as a linear map; `Submodule.map` takes the image.
- It holds over commutative semirings.

## What it says
A vector that pairs into $\pi^j R$ with everything lies, modulo $\pi M$, in the sum of the constituents of index at least $j$.

- `{R : Type u_3} {M : Type u_4}`, `[CommRing R] [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is a module over a commutative ring $R$.
- `{B : LinearMap.BilinForm R M}`: an $R$-bilinear form $B : M \times M \to R$, written `B x y`.
- `{π : R} {N : ℕ → Submodule R M}` and `(h : B.IsJordanSplitting π N)`: the submodules $N_0, N_1, \dots$ form a Jordan splitting of $B$ with respect to $\pi$: $M = \bigoplus_i N_i$ internally, $B(N_i, N_k) = 0$ for $i \ne k$, and $B$ restricted to $N_i$ is $\pi^i$ times a perfect pairing.
- `(hπ : π ∈ nonZeroDivisors R)`: $\pi$ is not a zero divisor: $\pi r = 0$ implies $r = 0$.
- `{j : ℕ} {x : M} (hx : ∀ (y : M), π ^ j ∣ (B x) y)`: $x$ is a vector with $\pi^j \mid B(x, y)$ for every $y \in M$.
- The conclusion: $x \in \bigl(\sum_{i \ge j} N_i\bigr) + \pi M$. Here `⨆ i ∈ Set.Ici j, N i` is the sum of the submodules $N_i$ for $i \ge j$, `Ideal.span {π} • ⊤` is $\pi M$, and `⊔` is the sum of submodules.

The components of $x$ in the constituents $N_i$ with $i < j$ pair into $\pi^{i+1} R$ with $N_i$, and $\pi^i$-modularity of $N_i$ then makes them multiples of $\pi$. Together with `IsJordanSplitting.pow_dvd_apply_of_mem_biSup` (the other inclusion), it says that modulo $\pi M$ these vectors are exactly the sums of vectors of the constituents of index at least $j$. This is the step that, with Nakayama's lemma, gives the invariance of the ranks (`IsJordanSplitting.finrank_eq`).

## References and tests
- O. T. O'Meara, *Introduction to Quadratic Forms*, §91C and 91:9, for Jordan splittings and the invariance of the ranks of their constituents (as the module docstring records).

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `nonZeroDivisors R` is the set of non-zero-divisors; in a domain it is the nonzero elements.
- `Set.Ici j` is the set $\{i : i \ge j\}$ of natural numbers. For $j = 0$ the statement is empty, since the sum is all of $M$.

## What it says
In a Jordan splitting, a vector of the $i$-th constituent pairs into $\pi^i R$ with every vector: $\pi^i \mid B(x, y)$ for $x \in N_i$ and all $y \in M$.

- `{R : Type u_1} {M : Type u_2}`, `[CommSemiring R] [AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is a module over a commutative semiring $R$; rings are the case of interest, but no subtraction is needed here.
- `{B : LinearMap.BilinForm R M}`: an $R$-bilinear form $B : M \times M \to R$; Lean writes $B(x, y)$ as `B x y`.
- `{π : R} {N : ℕ → Submodule R M}` and `(h : B.IsJordanSplitting π N)`: the submodules $N_0, N_1, \dots$ form a Jordan splitting of $B$ with respect to $\pi$: $M = \bigoplus_i N_i$ internally, $B(N_i, N_k) = 0$ for $i \ne k$, and $B$ restricted to $N_i$ is $\pi^i$ times a perfect pairing.
- `{i : ℕ} {x : M} (hx : x ∈ N i)`: a vector $x$ of the constituent $N_i$.
- `(y : M)`: any vector of $M$.
- The conclusion: $\pi^i$ divides $B(x, y)$ in $R$.

Writing $y = \sum_k y_k$ with $y_k \in N_k$, only $B(x, y_i)$ survives, and it lies in $\pi^i R$ because $B$ is $\pi^i$ times a form on $N_i$. In O'Meara's language: the scale of the constituent $N_i$, computed against the whole module, is still contained in $\pi^i R$.

## References and tests
- O. T. O'Meara, *Introduction to Quadratic Forms*, §91C, for Jordan splittings (as the module docstring records).

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- Only the first argument is restricted: the statement is about $B(x, y)$ with $x \in N_i$. For a symmetric form the other side follows; symmetry is not assumed.
- `∣` is divisibility in $R$: $B(x, y) = \pi^i c$ for some $c \in R$. For $i = 0$ the statement is empty, since $\pi^0 = 1$.
- It holds over commutative semirings.

## What it says
Projecting to the constituents of index at most $j$ preserves the form modulo $\pi^{j+1}$: $\pi^{j+1} \mid B(x, y) - B(p x, p y)$ for all $x, y$.

- `{R : Type u_3} {M : Type u_4}`, `[CommRing R] [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is a module over a commutative ring $R$.
- `{B : LinearMap.BilinForm R M}`: an $R$-bilinear form $B : M \times M \to R$, written `B x y`.
- `{π : R} {N : ℕ → Submodule R M}` and `(h : B.IsJordanSplitting π N)`: the submodules $N_0, N_1, \dots$ form a Jordan splitting of $B$ with respect to $\pi$: $M = \bigoplus_i N_i$ internally, $B(N_i, N_k) = 0$ for $i \ne k$, and $B$ restricted to $N_i$ is $\pi^i$ times a perfect pairing.
- `(j : ℕ) (x y : M)`: an index and two vectors.

Write $A = \sum_{i \le j} N_i$ and $A' = \sum_{i \ge j+1} N_i$, complementary by `IsJordanSplitting.isCompl_biSup_Iic_biSup_Ici`, and $p : M \to A$ for the projection to $A$ along $A'$ (`(⨆ i ∈ Set.Iic j, N i).projectionOnto (⨆ i ∈ Set.Ici (j + 1), N i) ⋯`, where `⋯` is that complementarity).
- The conclusion: $\pi^{j+1}$ divides $B(x, y) - B(p x, p y)$.

Since $x - p x$ and $y - p y$ lie in $A'$, which is orthogonal to $A$, the difference is $B(x - p x, y - p y)$, a value of $B$ on the constituents of index at least $j + 1$, hence divisible by $\pi^{j+1}$. So $B$ modulo $\pi^{j+1}$ is pulled back from its restriction to $A$.

## References and tests
- O. T. O'Meara, *Introduction to Quadratic Forms*, §91C, for Jordan splittings (as the module docstring records).

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `projectionOnto` takes values in the submodule $A$, and `↑` maps them back into $M$.
- Nothing is assumed of $\pi$ or of $B$ beyond the splitting.

## What it says
When $2 \mid \pi$ and the constituent of index $j + 1$ is even at its own scale, projecting to the constituents of index at most $j$ preserves the self-pairings modulo $2\pi^{j+1}$.

- `{R : Type u_3} {M : Type u_4}`, `[CommRing R] [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is a module over a commutative ring $R$.
- `{B : LinearMap.BilinForm R M}`: an $R$-bilinear form $B : M \times M \to R$, written `B x y`.
- `{π : R} {N : ℕ → Submodule R M}` and `(h : B.IsJordanSplitting π N)`: the submodules $N_0, N_1, \dots$ form a Jordan splitting of $B$ with respect to $\pi$: $M = \bigoplus_i N_i$ internally, $B(N_i, N_k) = 0$ for $i \ne k$, and $B$ restricted to $N_i$ is $\pi^i$ times a perfect pairing.
- `(h2 : 2 ∣ π)`: $2$ divides $\pi$ in $R$, as for $\pi = 2$ in $\mathbb{Z}_2$.
- `{j : ℕ} (hnext : ∀ w ∈ N (j + 1), 2 * π ^ (j + 1) ∣ (B w) w)`: every $w \in N_{j+1}$ has $B(w, w) \in 2\pi^{j+1} R$: the constituent $N_{j+1}$, of scale $\pi^{j+1}$, is even at that scale.
- `(x : M)`: a vector.

Write $A = \sum_{i \le j} N_i$ and $A' = \sum_{i \ge j+1} N_i$, complementary by `IsJordanSplitting.isCompl_biSup_Iic_biSup_Ici`, and $p : M \to A$ for the projection to $A$ along $A'$ (`(⨆ i ∈ Set.Iic j, N i).projectionOnto (⨆ i ∈ Set.Ici (j + 1), N i) ⋯`, where `⋯` is that complementarity).
- The conclusion: $2\pi^{j+1}$ divides $B(x, x) - B(p x, p x)$.

The difference is $B(q, q)$ with $q = x - p x \in A'$; writing $q = a + d$ with $a \in N_{j+1}$ and $d$ in the constituents of index at least $j + 2$, it is $B(a, a) + B(d, d)$. The first term is in $2\pi^{j+1} R$ by `hnext`, the second in $\pi^{j+2} R \subseteq 2\pi^{j+1} R$ by `h2`. It is the quadratic refinement of `IsJordanSplitting.pow_succ_dvd_sub_apply_projectionOnto`, the precision dyadic forms need.

## References and tests
- O. T. O'Meara, *Introduction to Quadratic Forms*, §91C, for Jordan splittings (as the module docstring records).

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `2` is $1 + 1$ in $R$. If $2$ is a unit the statement is the case $x = y$ of `IsJordanSplitting.pow_succ_dvd_sub_apply_projectionOnto`; it is meant for $2 \mid \pi$, the dyadic case.
- `hnext` measures parity against the scale $\pi^{j+1}$ of the constituent, not against $R$.
- `projectionOnto` takes values in $A$, and `↑` maps them back into $M$.

## What it says
A modular form is its own Jordan splitting: if $B$ is $\pi^i$-modular on $M$, then putting all of $M$ at index $i$ and $0$ at every other index gives a Jordan splitting of $B$ with respect to $\pi$.

- `{R : Type u_1} {M : Type u_2}`, `[CommRing R] [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is a module over a commutative ring $R$.
- `{B : LinearMap.BilinForm R M}`: an $R$-bilinear form $B : M \times M \to R$, written `B x y`.
- `{π : R} {i : ℕ}`: an element $\pi$ of $R$ and an index $i$.
- `(h : B.IsModular (π ^ i))`: $B = \pi^i C$ for a perfect pairing $C$ on $M$, one for which $x \mapsto C(x, \cdot)$ and $y \mapsto C(\cdot, y)$ are isomorphisms $M \to \operatorname{Hom}_R(M, R)$.
- The conclusion: the family $N_j = M$ for $j = i$ and $N_j = 0$ otherwise (`if j = i then ⊤ else ⊥`) is a Jordan splitting of $B$ with respect to $\pi$.

This is the one-constituent case of O'Meara's Jordan splitting, a modular lattice. For instance a unimodular form ($i = 0$) is a splitting concentrated at index $0$, and over $\mathbb{Z}_2$ the form $\langle 2 \rangle$ with $\pi = 2$ is one concentrated at index $1$.

## References and tests
- O. T. O'Meara, *Introduction to Quadratic Forms*, §91C, for Jordan splittings (as the module docstring records).

No test is recorded for it. Tau Ceti uses it to compute the dyadic Jordan profile of a modular form (`LinearMap.BilinForm.IsModular.dyadicJordanProfile_ranks`).

## Lean subtleties
- `⊤` is the whole module and `⊥` the zero submodule; the zero submodule is $a$-modular for every $a$, which handles the indices $j \ne i$.
- The statement is over a commutative ring and an additive group, although the definition of a Jordan splitting allows semirings: the proof of the direct-sum condition uses Mathlib's characterisation of internal direct sums by independence, stated for rings.
- Nothing is assumed of $\pi$: for $\pi = 0$ and $i \ge 1$, for instance, $h$ forces $B = 0$, and the conclusion still holds.

text:
## What it says
Jordan splittings exist: over a discrete valuation ring $R$ with uniformiser $\pi$, a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $B$ on a finitely generated $R$-module $M$ makes $M$ an orthogonal direct sum of submodules $N_0, N_1, N_2, \dots$, the form being $\pi^i$-modular on $N_i$.

- `[CommRing R] [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is a module over the commutative ring $R$. The implicit $B$ is a bilinear form $M \times M \to R$.
- `[IsDomain R] [IsDiscreteValuationRing R]`: $R$ is a discrete valuation ring, a local principal ideal domain that is not a field.
- `[Module.Finite R M]`: $M$ is finitely generated over $R$.
- `(hB : B.IsSymm)`: $B$ is symmetric, $B(x, y) = B(y, x)$.
- `(hnd : B.Nondegenerate)`: if $B(x, y) = 0$ for all $y$ then $x = 0$, and likewise on the other side.
- `(hπ : Irreducible π)`: $\pi$ is irreducible in $R$, which in a discrete valuation ring means a uniformiser, a generator of the maximal ideal.
- The conclusion: some family $N$ of submodules of $M$ indexed by $\mathbb{N}$ is a Jordan splitting of $B$ for $\pi$ (`IsJordanSplitting`): $M$ is the internal direct sum of the $N_i$, these are orthogonal to one another for $B$, and on $N_i$ the form is $\pi^i$-modular, $\pi^i$ times a unimodular form.

This is the existence of Jordan splittings in O'Meara's sense, for an integral form: since $B$ takes values in $R$, only exponents $i \ge 0$ occur. O'Meara works over the integers of a local field; here $R$ is any discrete valuation ring, complete or not, of any residue characteristic, $2$ included. Nondegeneracy plays the part of O'Meara's lattice on a regular space.

## References and tests
- O'Meara, *Introduction to Quadratic Forms*, 91:9 — Jordan splittings of a lattice on a regular quadratic space over a local field, which this statement extends to any discrete valuation ring.
- Roadmap IntegralLattices, target 3B, "Jordan splittings exist", for nondegenerate $\mathbb{Z}_p$-lattices ([README line 858 at dd4b28f1](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/IntegralLattices/README.md#L858)); the roadmap's sources give O'Meara section 91C with 91:9 for it.

No test is recorded for it. The roadmap's case, $R = \mathbb{Z}_p$ and $\pi = p$ for the localization of a nondegenerate integral lattice at a prime $p$, is `TauCeti.IntegralLattice.exists_isJordanSplitting_localIntegralForm`, which applies this theorem.

## Lean subtleties
- The family is indexed by all of $\mathbb{N}$: all but finitely many $N_i$ are $0$, as $M$ is finitely generated, and a constituent $0$ is allowed.
- The theorem asserts that a splitting exists, not that it is unique.
- Nondegeneracy forces $M$ to be torsion-free, hence free of finite rank, so no freeness hypothesis is needed. For free $M$ it says that the Gram matrix has nonzero determinant, which is weaker than unimodularity.
- Residue characteristic $2$ is allowed, as for $R = \mathbb{Z}_2$, where a unimodular constituent such as the hyperbolic plane need not be diagonalisable.
- The square-bracket hypotheses are typeclasses, which Lean finds by itself; `[IsDomain R]` is part of what Mathlib asks of a discrete valuation ring.

## What it says
Transporting a form and a family of submodules along a linear isomorphism neither creates nor destroys Jordan splittings: for an isomorphism $e : M \to M'$, the images $e(N_i)$ form a Jordan splitting of the transported form exactly when the $N_i$ form one of $B$.

- `{R : Type u_1} {M : Type u_2}`, `[CommSemiring R] [AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M]`: $M$ is a module over a commutative semiring $R$; rings are the case of interest, but no subtraction is needed here.
- `{B : LinearMap.BilinForm R M}`: an $R$-bilinear form $B : M \times M \to R$; Lean writes $B(x, y)$ as `B x y`.
- `{M' : Type u_3} [AddCommMonoid M'] [Module R M']`: a second $R$-module $M'$.
- `{π : R} {N : ℕ → Submodule R M}`: an element $\pi$ of $R$ and submodules $N_0, N_1, \dots$ of $M$.
- `(e : M ≃ₗ[R] M')`: an $R$-linear isomorphism.
- The conclusion: `(congr e) B`, the form $(x', y') \mapsto B(e^{-1}x', e^{-1}y')$ on $M'$, has $i \mapsto e(N_i)$ as a Jordan splitting with respect to $\pi$ if and only if $B$ has $(N_i)$ as one.

The forward direction applies `IsJordanSplitting.congr` to $e^{-1}$, the backward one is `IsJordanSplitting.congr`.

## References and tests
- O. T. O'Meara, *Introduction to Quadratic Forms*, §91C, for Jordan splittings (as the module docstring records).

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- It is a `@[simp]` lemma: Lean's simplifier rewrites the left side to the right side when it meets a transported splitting.
- `congr e` is `LinearMap.BilinForm.congr e`, transport of forms along $e$, not a congruence of any other kind; `Submodule.map (↑e) (N i)` is the image $e(N_i)$.
- It holds over commutative semirings.

## What it says
If the leading coefficient of $f$ is not positive, its orientation correction is $\sqrt D$.

- `(f : BinaryQuadraticForm ℤ)`: a form $ax^2 + bxy + cy^2$ with integer coefficients.
- `(D : ℤ)` and `[Fact ¬IsSquare D]`: an integer $D$ that is not a square, so that $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt D)$ is a field.
- `(ha : ¬0 < f.a)`: $a \le 0$.
- The conclusion: the element of $K$ underlying `f.idealSignFactor D` is `ω`, the square root of $D$ in
  $K = \mathbb{Q} \oplus \mathbb{Q}\omega$, $\omega^2 = D$.

This is the second branch of the sign clause: a form with $a < 0$ has its ideal multiplied by
$\sqrt D$. The hypothesis also allows $a = 0$, which does not occur when $D$ is the discriminant of $f$.

## References and tests
- TauCetiRoadmap, IntegralLattices, target B2 (Forms and ideal classes): for $\Delta > 0$ a primitive form $f = (a, b, c)$ goes to $\mathfrak a_f$ if $a > 0$ and to $\sqrt\Delta\cdot\mathfrak a_f$ if $a < 0$, in the narrow Picard group of $\mathcal O_\Delta$ ([README, line 1032](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/c9a16a043c3bf2321c63dff75e3f709466373528/TauCetiRoadmap/IntegralLattices/README.md#L1032)).
- `TauCeti.BinaryQuadraticForm.narrowPicClass_discrimTwelveNegativeLeading_ne_one` — the oriented class of $-x^2 + 3y^2$ at $D = 12$ is nontrivial: its correction $\sqrt{12}$ has norm $-12$, while every unit of $\mathcal O_{12} = \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt 3]$ has norm $1$. The value $\sqrt{12}$ comes from this branch, through `norm_idealSignFactor`.

## Lean subtleties
- The statement is about `↑(f.idealSignFactor D)`, the coercion from the unit group of $K$ to $K$,
  since `ω` is an element of $K$.
- `[Fact ¬IsSquare D]` is a hypothesis carried as a typeclass. Since $D$ need not be the discriminant
  of $f$, $a = 0$ is allowed, and gives $\sqrt D$ too.

## What it says
For a form with negative leading coefficient, the oriented ideal is $\sqrt D\cdot\mathfrak a_f$.

- `(f : BinaryQuadraticForm ℤ)`: a form $ax^2 + bxy + cy^2$ with integer coefficients.
- `(D : ℤ)` and `[Fact ¬IsSquare D]`: an integer $D$ that is not a square, so that $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt D)$ is a field.
- `(hf : f.discrim = D)`: the discriminant $b^2 - 4ac$ of $f$ is $D$.

$$\mathrm{Hom}_U(\mathrm{Res}^G_U M, A) \cong \mathrm{Hom}_G(M, \mathrm{Coind}_U^G A).$$

- `(M : SmoothDiscreteTopRep R G)`: a discrete $G$-module over $R$: an $R$-module with the discrete topology on which $G$ acts $R$-linearly with open point stabilisers, that is, continuously.
- `(A : SmoothDiscreteTopRep R ↥U)`: a discrete $U$-module over $R$ in the same sense.

The type `(smoothDiscreteResTopRep U M ⟶ A) ≃+ (M ⟶ coindTopRep R G U A)` is an additive equivalence, a bijection that respects addition of morphisms, from the $U$-equivariant $R$-linear maps $\mathrm{Res}^G_U M \to A$ to the $G$-equivariant $R$-linear maps $M \to \mathrm{Coind}_U^G A$, where `smoothDiscreteResTopRep U M` is $\mathrm{Res}^G_U M$, the module $M$ with its action restricted to $U$, and `coindTopRep R G U A` is $\mathrm{Coind}_U^G A$: the locally constant functions $\phi : G \to A$ with $\phi(ug) = u\,\phi(g)$ for $u \in U$, with $G$ acting by right translation, $(g\phi)(x) = \phi(xg)$, and the discrete topology. This is Ribes–Zalesskii's Lemma 6.10.2 with the same two maps, in greater generality: there $G$ is profinite, the subgroup closed and the modules abelian groups ($R = \mathbb{Z}$). The two sides are written in the order of Mathlib's algebraic `Rep.resCoindHomEquiv`, the reverse of the book's display.

- TauCetiRoadmap, MorseTheory, target M1 ([README, lines 103–108](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/c9a16a043c3bf2321c63dff75e3f709466373528/TauCetiRoadmap/MorseTheory/README.md#L103-L108)), with the normalisation of [lines 83–85](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/c9a16a043c3bf2321c63dff75e3f709466373528/TauCetiRoadmap/MorseTheory/README.md#L83-L85).

## Lean subtleties
- It holds by unfolding the definition (`rfl`): it is a rewriting rule recording how the normalized chart is built, tagged `@[simp]` so that the simplifier uses it.
- `g ⁻¹' S` is the preimage of $S$ under $g$; written with $N^{-1}$ it describes the image under $N$.

## What it says
The normalized linear coordinates of a Morse chart: the linear isomorphism $E \to \mathbb R^n$ sending $v$ to the vector $u$ with
$$u_i = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\,(L v)_{\sigma(i)}, \qquad i = 0, \dots, n-1,$$
where $L$ is the chart's linear change of coordinates and $\sigma$ sorts the weights increasingly, read in Euclidean space.

- `E`, a real normed space (the model); `M`, a space with charts into $E$; `f : M → ℝ`; `x : M`.
- `(φ : MorseChart E f x)`: a Morse chart for $f$ at $x$: a chart $c$ of the maximal smooth atlas with $c(x) = 0$, a linear isomorphism $L : E \to \mathbb R^n$ ($n = \dim E$) and weights $w_j = \pm 1$, exactly $\lambda$ of them negative, with $f(y) = f(x) + \tfrac12 \sum_j w_j (L c(y))_j^2$ on the source of $c$; $\lambda$ = `manifoldMorseIndex 𝓘(ℝ, E) f x` is the Morse index (the number of negative squares of the Hessian).
- `[FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`: $E$ is finite-dimensional.
- The value: a continuous linear isomorphism `E ≃L[ℝ] EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (Module.finrank ℝ E))`, built as $L$, then the reindexing by $\sigma$ = `Tuple.sort φ.weight`, then scaling by $(\sqrt 2)^{-1}$, then the identification of $\mathbb R^n$ with Euclidean space.

These are the coordinates in which $\tfrac12 \sum_j w_j (Lv)_j^2 = -\sum_{i<\lambda} u_i^2 + \sum_{i \ge \lambda} u_i^2$ (`TauCeti.MorseChart.sum_ite_mul_normalizedCoord_sq`): the final linear change of variables of Milnor's normal form.

## References and tests
- J. Milnor, *Morse Theory*, Annals of Mathematics Studies 51, Princeton University Press, 1963, Lemma 2.2 (the lemma of Morse).
- TauCetiRoadmap, MorseTheory, target M1 ([README, lines 103–108](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/c9a16a043c3bf2321c63dff75e3f709466373528/TauCetiRoadmap/MorseTheory/README.md#L103-L108)), with the normalisation of [lines 83–85](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/c9a16a043c3bf2321c63dff75e3f709466373528/TauCetiRoadmap/MorseTheory/README.md#L83-L85).

No declaration of the library tests it; `TauCeti.MorseChart.normalizedCoord_apply` records its value coordinate by coordinate.

## Lean subtleties
- `E ≃L[ℝ] F` is a linear isomorphism that is continuous in both directions; on a finite-dimensional space every linear map is continuous, which is why `[FiniteDimensional ℝ E]` is asked for.
- `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)` is $\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean norm; the chart's own coordinates live in `Fin n → ℝ`, $\mathbb R^n$ with the sup norm. The numbers are the same, only the norm differs.
- The map depends on the data of `φ` ($L$ and the weights), which are not unique; it is the normalisation of this chart, not a canonical object. `Tuple.sort` is one specific sorting permutation.
- `Fin n` is $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and `i.val` its value in ℕ: the coordinates are numbered from $0$, so $i < \lambda$ picks out the first $\lambda$ of them.
- `Module.finrank ℝ E` is the dimension $n$ of $E$; it would be $0$ for an infinite-dimensional $E$, but a Morse chart forces $E \cong \mathbb R^n$, so that case does not arise.

## What it says
The $i$-th normalized coordinate of a vector $v$ is $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}$ times its $\sigma(i)$-th chart coordinate, where $\sigma$ sorts the weights increasingly.

- `E`, a real normed space (the model); `M`, a space with charts into $E$; `f : M → ℝ`; `x : M`.
- `(φ : MorseChart E f x)`: a Morse chart for $f$ at $x$: a chart $c$ of the maximal smooth atlas with $c(x) = 0$, a linear isomorphism $L : E \to \mathbb R^n$ ($n = \dim E$) and weights $w_j = \pm 1$, exactly $\lambda$ of them negative, with $f(y) = f(x) + \tfrac12 \sum_j w_j (L c(y))_j^2$ on the source of $c$; $\lambda$ = `manifoldMorseIndex 𝓘(ℝ, E) f x` is the Morse index (the number of negative squares of the Hessian).
- `[FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`: $E$ is finite-dimensional.
- `(v : E)`, `(i : Fin (Module.finrank ℝ E))`: a vector of the model and a coordinate index.
- The conclusion: `φ.normalizedCoord v i`, the $i$-th coordinate of the normalized coordinates of $v$, equals $(\sqrt 2)^{-1} \cdot (L v)_{\sigma(i)}$ with $\sigma$ = `Tuple.sort φ.weight`.

It is the defining formula of `TauCeti.MorseChart.normalizedCoord`, stated as a rewriting rule.

## References and tests

## Lean subtleties
- `√2` is the real square root of $2$ and `(√2)⁻¹` its reciprocal; $\sqrt 2 \neq 0$, so no junk value of division enters.
- `φ.normalizedCoord v i` reads the $i$-th entry of a vector of `EuclideanSpace`, through Lean's coercion of such a vector to a function on `Fin n`.
- `Fin n` is $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and `i.val` its value in ℕ: the coordinates are numbered from $0$, so $i < \lambda$ picks out the first $\lambda$ of them.
- `Module.finrank ℝ E` is the dimension $n$ of $E$; it would be $0$ for an infinite-dimensional $E$, but a Morse chart forces $E \cong \mathbb R^n$, so that case does not arise.

## What it says
In normalized coordinates the quadratic form of a Morse chart is the standard signed sum of squares of its index:
$$\sum_{i} \varepsilon_i\, u_i^2 = \tfrac12 \sum_j w_j (L v)_j^2, \qquad \varepsilon_i = \begin{cases} -1 & i < \lambda \\ 1 & i \ge \lambda \end{cases}, \quad u = \text{`φ.normalizedCoord v`}.$$

- `E`, a real normed space (the model); `M`, a space with charts into $E$; `f : M → ℝ`; `x : M`.
- `(φ : MorseChart E f x)`: a Morse chart for $f$ at $x$: a chart $c$ of the maximal smooth atlas with $c(x) = 0$, a linear isomorphism $L : E \to \mathbb R^n$ ($n = \dim E$) and weights $w_j = \pm 1$, exactly $\lambda$ of them negative, with $f(y) = f(x) + \tfrac12 \sum_j w_j (L c(y))_j^2$ on the source of $c$; $\lambda$ = `manifoldMorseIndex 𝓘(ℝ, E) f x` is the Morse index (the number of negative squares of the Hessian).
- `[FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`: $E$ is finite-dimensional.
- `(v : E)`: a vector of the model.
- The conclusion: the sum over $i$ of `(if i.val < λ then -1 else 1) * (φ.normalizedCoord v i) ^ 2` equals `2⁻¹ * ∑ j, φ.weight j * (φ.coord v j) ^ 2`.

This is the algebra behind Milnor's normal form: reindex by the sorting permutation (`TauCeti.MorseChart.weight_sort_apply` gives the signs) and absorb the factor $\tfrac12$ into the squares by the division by $\sqrt 2$.

## References and tests
- J. Milnor, *Morse Theory*, Annals of Mathematics Studies 51, Princeton University Press, 1963, Lemma 2.2 (the lemma of Morse).
- TauCetiRoadmap, MorseTheory, target M1 ([README, lines 103–108](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/c9a16a043c3bf2321c63dff75e3f709466373528/TauCetiRoadmap/MorseTheory/README.md#L103-L108)), with the normalisation of [lines 83–85](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/c9a16a043c3bf2321c63dff75e3f709466373528/TauCetiRoadmap/MorseTheory/README.md#L83-L85).

No declaration of the library tests it; it is the step from `TauCeti.MorseChart.eq_quadratic` to `TauCeti.MorseChart.eq_quadratic_normalizedChart`.

## Lean subtleties
- `Fin n` is $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and `i.val` its value in ℕ: the coordinates are numbered from $0$, so $i < \lambda$ picks out the first $\lambda$ of them.
- `Module.finrank ℝ E` is the dimension $n$ of $E$; it would be $0$ for an infinite-dimensional $E$, but a Morse chart forces $E \cong \mathbb R^n$, so that case does not arise.
- `2⁻¹` is the real number $\tfrac12$.
- When $\lambda = 0$ the left side is $\lVert u\rVert^2$, and when $\lambda = n$ it is $-\lVert u\rVert^2$.

## What it says
Sorting the weights of a Morse chart in increasing order puts the $\lambda$ weights $-1$ first, where $\lambda$ is the Morse index.

- `E`, a real normed space (the model); `M`, a space with charts into $E$; `f : M → ℝ`; `x : M`.
- `(φ : MorseChart E f x)`: a Morse chart for $f$ at $x$: a chart $c$ of the maximal smooth atlas with $c(x) = 0$, a linear isomorphism $L : E \to \mathbb R^n$ ($n = \dim E$) and weights $w_j = \pm 1$, exactly $\lambda$ of them negative, with $f(y) = f(x) + \tfrac12 \sum_j w_j (L c(y))_j^2$ on the source of $c$; $\lambda$ = `manifoldMorseIndex 𝓘(ℝ, E) f x` is the Morse index (the number of negative squares of the Hessian).
- `(i : Fin (Module.finrank ℝ E))`: a coordinate index $i \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$.
- The conclusion: with $\sigma$ = `Tuple.sort φ.weight`, a permutation of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ for which $j \mapsto w_{\sigma(j)}$ is increasing, $w_{\sigma(i)} = -1$ when $i < \lambda$ and $w_{\sigma(i)} = 1$ otherwise.

This is the reordering step that turns the diagonal form $\tfrac12 \sum_j w_j z_j^2$ into the normal form with the negative squares first, as in Milnor's statement of the Morse lemma.

## References and tests
- J. Milnor, *Morse Theory*, Annals of Mathematics Studies 51, Princeton University Press, 1963, Lemma 2.2 (the lemma of Morse). The normal form there lists the $\lambda$ negative squares first.
- TauCetiRoadmap, MorseTheory, target M1 ([README, lines 103–108](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/c9a16a043c3bf2321c63dff75e3f709466373528/TauCetiRoadmap/MorseTheory/README.md#L103-L108)), with the normalisation of [lines 83–85](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/c9a16a043c3bf2321c63dff75e3f709466373528/TauCetiRoadmap/MorseTheory/README.md#L83-L85).

No declaration of the library tests it; it is used in the proof of `TauCeti.MorseChart.sum_ite_mul_normalizedCoord_sq`.

## Lean subtleties
- `Fin n` is $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and `i.val` its value in ℕ: the coordinates are numbered from $0$, so $i < \lambda$ picks out the first $\lambda$ of them.
- `Module.finrank ℝ E` is the dimension $n$ of $E$; it would be $0$ for an infinite-dimensional $E$, but a Morse chart forces $E \cong \mathbb R^n$, so that case does not arise.
- `Tuple.sort` is one specific sorting permutation; since the weights are only $\pm 1$, which sorting permutation is used does not affect the conclusion.
- No finite-dimensionality typeclass is assumed here, and none is needed.
- When $\lambda = 0$ every sorted weight is $1$, when $\lambda = n$ every one is $-1$, and for $n = 0$ there is nothing to say.

## What it says
At finitely many nondegenerate critical points of a function on a Hausdorff manifold there are normalized Morse charts with pairwise disjoint sources, each inside a prescribed neighbourhood of its centre.

- `E`, `[FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`: a finite-dimensional real normed space, $n = \dim E$; `H`, `(I : ModelWithCorners ℝ E H)` with `[I.Boundaryless]`: a model space $H$ for $M$, identified with an open subset of $E$ through $I$, with no boundary or corners.
- `M`, `[ChartedSpace H M] [IsManifold I ∞ M]`: a smooth ($C^\infty$) manifold modelled on $I$, of dimension $n$; `f : M → ℝ`; `x : M`.
- `[T2Space M]`: $M$ is Hausdorff.
- `{S : Set M}`, `(hS : S.Finite)`: a finite set $S$ of points of $M$.
- `(hf : ∀ x ∈ S, ∀ᶠ y in 𝓝 x, ContMDiffAt I 𝓘(ℝ) ∞ f y)`: $f$ is $C^\infty$ near each point of $S$.
- `(h : ∀ x ∈ S, IsManifoldNondegenerateCriticalPoint I f x)`: each point of $S$ is a nondegenerate critical point of $f$.
- `{U : M → Set M}`, `(hU : ∀ x ∈ S, U x ∈ 𝓝 x)`: for each $p \in S$ a neighbourhood $U(p)$ of $p$.
- The conclusion: there are partial diffeomorphisms $\psi_p$, one for each $p \in S$, from $M$ onto open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$, such that the sources of $\psi_p$ and $\psi_q$ are disjoint for $p \neq q$, and for each $p$: $p$ lies in the source of $\psi_p$, the source lies in $U(p)$, $\psi_p(p) = 0$, and $f(y) = f(p) - \sum_{i<\lambda_p} \psi_p(y)_i^2 + \sum_{i\ge\lambda_p} \psi_p(y)_i^2$ on the source, with $\lambda_p$ = `manifoldMorseIndex I f p`.

It combines Milnor's Lemma 2.2 at each point with the separation of finitely many points of a Hausdorff space by disjoint open sets.

## References and tests
- J. Milnor, *Morse Theory*, Annals of Mathematics Studies 51, Princeton University Press, 1963, Lemma 2.2 (the lemma of Morse).
- TauCetiRoadmap, MorseTheory, target M1 ([README, lines 103–108](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/c9a16a043c3bf2321c63dff75e3f709466373528/TauCetiRoadmap/MorseTheory/README.md#L103-L108)), with the normalisation of [lines 83–85](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/c9a16a043c3bf2321c63dff75e3f709466373528/TauCetiRoadmap/MorseTheory/README.md#L83-L85).

No declaration of the library tests it; `TauCeti.IsMorse.exists_admissible_morseCharts` uses it for the critical points of a critical level.

## Lean subtleties
- `∀ᶠ y in 𝓝 x, P y` means $P$ holds on some neighbourhood of $x$.
- `Fin n` is $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$: coordinates are numbered from $0$, so `i.val < λ` picks the first $\lambda$ of them.
- `manifoldMorseIndex I f x` is the number of negative squares of the Hessian in the preferred chart at $x$, which is Milnor's index.
- `PartialDiffeomorph I 𝓘(ℝ, ℝⁿ) M ℝⁿ ∞`: a bijection between open subsets of $M$ (the source) and of $\mathbb R^n$ (the target), $C^\infty$ both ways (`∞` is $C^\infty$, not analytic). As a Lean function it is defined on all of $M$; only its values on the source mean anything, and the statements restrict to the source.
- `[I.Boundaryless]`, `[IsManifold I ∞ M]` are hypotheses carried as typeclasses; `𝓘(ℝ)` is ℝ with its usual smooth structure.
- `ψ : S → …` is a family indexed by the points of $S$, viewed as a type; `ψ p p` is $\psi_p$ applied to the point $p$.
- `Pairwise (Disjoint on fun p ↦ (ψ p).source)` says that distinct points of $S$ have disjoint sources.
- `U` is a function on all of $M$, but only its values at points of $S$ matter. The Hausdorff hypothesis is needed: manifolds in Lean need not be Hausdorff.

## What it says
Existence of the trace: on a bounded Lipschitz domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R} \times E$ and for $1 \le p < \infty$, there is a bounded linear operator $T : W^{1,p}(\Omega) \to L^p(\partial\Omega)$ that sends every Sobolev function continuous up to the boundary to its restriction to the frontier.

- `[NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`: $E$ is a finite-dimensional real inner product space. The domain lives in `WithLp 2 (ℝ × E)`, the product $\mathbb{R} \times E$ with the Euclidean norm, a Euclidean space of dimension $n = 1 + \dim E$.
- `[MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E]`: $E$ carries its Borel σ-algebra.
- `[Fact (1 ≤ p)]`: the exponent $p \in [0, \infty]$ is at least $1$.
- `(hp : p ≠ ⊤)`: $p$ is finite.
- `(hΩ : (↑Ω).IsLipschitzDomainWith L)`: the open set $\Omega$ is a Lipschitz domain with constant $L$: it has a Lipschitz graph chart with bound $L$ at every point of its frontier.
- `(hb : Bornology.IsBounded ↑Ω)`: $\Omega$ is bounded.
- The conclusion: there is a continuous real-linear map $T$ from $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$, for Lebesgue measure `volume`, to $L^p$ of the $(\dim E)$-dimensional Euclidean Hausdorff measure restricted to the frontier $\partial\Omega$, such that for every $u$ in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ and every $f : \mathbb{R} \times E \to \mathbb{R}$ that is continuous on the closure $\overline{\Omega}$ and equal to `value u` almost everywhere on $\Omega$, $Tu = f$ almost everywhere on $\partial\Omega$ for that surface measure.

This is the existence half of the trace theorem for bounded Lipschitz domains and $1 \le p < \infty$: $Tu = u|_{\partial\Omega}$ whenever $u$ has a representative continuous on $\overline{\Omega}$. The surface measure is the $(n-1)$-dimensional Hausdorff measure, normalized as Lebesgue measure is, as in the classical statement, and the trace inequality $\|Tu\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)} \le C\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$ is the continuity of $T$, with $C$ its operator norm.

## References and tests
- L. C. Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*, 2nd ed., §5.5, Theorem 1 (the trace theorem): for a bounded $U$ with $C^1$ boundary and $1 \le p < \infty$, a bounded linear $T : W^{1,p}(U) \to L^p(\partial U)$ with $Tu = u|_{\partial U}$ for $u \in W^{1,p}(U) \cap C(\overline{U})$. Here the boundary is only asked to be Lipschitz.
- TauCetiRoadmap, PDE, Lane A, item 6: [the trace operator $W^{1,p}(\Omega) \to L^p(\partial\Omega)$ with kernel $W^{1,p}_0$, for Lipschitz $\partial\Omega$](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/PDE/README.md#L243), with [normalized Euclidean Hausdorff measure $\mu_{HE}[n-1]$ on the frontier](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/PDE/README.md#L252).

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `p` is an `ENNReal`, an element of $[0, \infty]$, and `⊤` is $\infty$. `[Fact (1 ≤ p)]` is the hypothesis $1 \le p$ carried as a typeclass, which Lean finds by itself.
- `WithLp 2 (ℝ × E)` gives the product the Euclidean norm instead of Lean's default maximum norm, so Lipschitz charts and Hausdorff measure are the Euclidean ones; `volume` is its Lebesgue measure.
- An element of `W1p` stores a value and a weak gradient, each a class of functions up to equality almost everywhere, and `value u` is the value, in $L^p(\Omega)$. So "continuous up to the boundary" is said through a representative: some $f$, continuous on the closure, equal to `value u` almost everywhere on $\Omega$. Two such $f$ agree on $\Omega$, as Lebesgue measure charges every nonempty open set, and so on $\overline{\Omega}$ by continuity; the conclusion does not depend on the choice.
- `↑↑` turns an element of `Lp` into a function, and `=ᵐ[…]` is equality almost everywhere for the measure in brackets.
- `euclideanHausdorffMeasure` of dimension $d$ is the $d$-dimensional Hausdorff measure scaled to agree with Lebesgue measure on $d$-dimensional Euclidean spaces; here $d = \dim E = n - 1$. When $E = 0$, $\Omega$ is a bounded open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ such as $(-1, 1)$, and this measure counts the boundary points, so $Tu$ gives the values of $u$ at the endpoints.
- `→L[ℝ]` is a continuous linear map; for linear maps of normed spaces, continuous means bounded.

## What it says
The trace operator of a bounded Lipschitz domain: for a bounded Lipschitz domain $\Omega$ in a Euclidean space and $1 \le p < \infty$, the bounded linear map $W^{1,p}(\Omega) \to L^p(\partial\Omega)$, with surface measure on $\partial\Omega$, that restricts to the boundary every function continuous up to it.

- `[NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`: $E$ is a finite-dimensional real inner product space. The domain lives in $\mathbb{R} \times E$ with the Euclidean norm, a Euclidean space of dimension $n = 1 + \dim E$.
- `[MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E]`: $E$ carries its Borel sets.
- `[Fact (1 ≤ p)]`: the exponent $p \in [0, \infty]$ is at least $1$.
- `(hp : p ≠ ⊤)`: $p$ is finite.
- `(hΩ : (↑Ω).IsLipschitzDomainWith L)`: the open set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R} \times E$ is a Lipschitz domain with constant $L$: it has a Lipschitz graph chart with that bound at every point of its frontier, so near each boundary point it lies on one side of the graph of an $L$-Lipschitz function.
- `(hb : Bornology.IsBounded ↑Ω)`: $\Omega$ is bounded.
- The result: a bounded linear map `→L[ℝ]` from `W1p volume Ω p`, the Sobolev space $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ of $L^p$ functions with weak gradient in $L^p$, to $L^p$ of the frontier $\partial\Omega$ with the measure `euclideanHausdorffMeasure (Module.finrank ℝ E)`, the $(n-1)$-dimensional surface measure.

Its value is an operator chosen among those that the existence theorem `W1p.exists_frontierTrace` provides. By the two theorems its docstring names, it sends every Sobolev function continuous up to the boundary to its restriction to the frontier, and it is the only bounded linear operator doing so.

This is the classical trace theorem. It is usually stated for $C^1$ boundaries; Lipschitz boundaries include them. As there, $p = \infty$ is excluded.

## References and tests
- Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*, §5.5 Thm 1: the bounded linear trace $W^{1,p}(\Omega) \to L^p(\partial\Omega)$ for $1 \le p < \infty$, which restricts functions continuous up to the boundary.
- TauCetiRoadmap, PDE, Lane A, item 6: [the trace operator $W^{1,p}(\Omega) \to L^p(\partial\Omega)$ with kernel $W^{1,p}_0$, for Lipschitz $\partial\Omega$](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/PDE/README.md#L243), with [normalized Euclidean Hausdorff measure $\mu_{HE}[n-1]$ on the frontier](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/PDE/README.md#L252).

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- The ambient space is `WithLp 2 (ℝ × E)`, $\mathbb{R} \times E$ with the norm $\sqrt{t^2 + \|x\|^2}$, so balls, Lipschitz graphs and Hausdorff measure are the Euclidean ones; its dimension is at least $1$.
- `euclideanHausdorffMeasure d` is the $d$-dimensional Hausdorff measure, scaled to agree with Lebesgue measure on $d$-dimensional Euclidean spaces; on the line ($E = 0$) it is counting measure on the endpoints.
- `frontier` is closure minus interior, the topological boundary $\partial\Omega$.
- The value uses classical choice (`Exists.choose`); since only one bounded linear operator has the boundary-value property, the choice is of a unique object.
- Elements of $W^{1,p}$ and of $L^p$ are classes of functions equal almost everywhere, and the trace acts on classes.
- `[Fact (1 ≤ p)]` is a hypothesis carried as a typeclass, and `⊤` is $\infty$ in `ENNReal`, $[0, \infty]$.

## What it says
The trace of a Sobolev function continuous up to the boundary is its restriction to the boundary: on a bounded Lipschitz domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R} \times E$ and for $1 \le p < \infty$, if $u \in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ agrees almost everywhere on $\Omega$ with a function $f$ continuous on $\overline{\Omega}$, then the trace of $u$ is $f$ almost everywhere on $\partial\Omega$ for surface measure.

- `[NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`: $E$ is a finite-dimensional real inner product space. The domain lives in `WithLp 2 (ℝ × E)`, the product $\mathbb{R} \times E$ with the Euclidean norm, a Euclidean space of dimension $n = 1 + \dim E$.
- `[MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E]`: $E$ carries its Borel σ-algebra.
- `[Fact (1 ≤ p)]`: the exponent $p \in [0, \infty]$ is at least $1$.
- `(hp : p ≠ ⊤)`: $p$ is finite.
- `(hΩ : (↑Ω).IsLipschitzDomainWith L)`: the open set $\Omega$ is a Lipschitz domain with constant $L$: it has a Lipschitz graph chart with bound $L$ at every point of its frontier.
- `(hb : Bornology.IsBounded ↑Ω)`: $\Omega$ is bounded.
- `(hf : ContinuousOn f (closure ↑Ω))`: the function $f : \mathbb{R} \times E \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous on the closure $\overline{\Omega}$.
- `(hu : ↑↑(value u) =ᵐ[MeasureTheory.volume.restrict ↑Ω] f)`: the value of the Sobolev function $u \in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$, for Lebesgue measure `volume`, equals $f$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$.
- The conclusion: `frontierTrace hp hΩ hb u`, the trace of $u$, an element of $L^p$ of the $(\dim E)$-dimensional Euclidean Hausdorff measure on the frontier $\partial\Omega$, equals $f$ almost everywhere on $\partial\Omega$ for that measure.

This is the boundary-value property of the trace in its classical form, $Tu = u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for $u \in W^{1,p}(\Omega) \cap C(\overline{\Omega})$: continuity is asked on the closure, not only in $\Omega$, and the surface measure is the $(n-1)$-dimensional Hausdorff measure.

## References and tests
- L. C. Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*, 2nd ed., §5.5, Theorem 1, part (i): for a bounded $U$ with $C^1$ boundary and $1 \le p < \infty$, $Tu = u|_{\partial U}$ for $u \in W^{1,p}(U) \cap C(\overline{U})$. Here the boundary is only asked to be Lipschitz.
- TauCetiRoadmap, PDE, Lane A, item 6: [the trace operator $W^{1,p}(\Omega) \to L^p(\partial\Omega)$ with kernel $W^{1,p}_0$, for Lipschitz $\partial\Omega$](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/PDE/README.md#L243), with [normalized Euclidean Hausdorff measure $\mu_{HE}[n-1]$ on the frontier](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/PDE/README.md#L252).

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `p` is an `ENNReal`, an element of $[0, \infty]$, and `⊤` is $\infty$. `[Fact (1 ≤ p)]` is the hypothesis $1 \le p$ carried as a typeclass, which Lean finds by itself.
- `WithLp 2 (ℝ × E)` gives the product the Euclidean norm instead of Lean's default maximum norm, so Lipschitz charts and Hausdorff measure are the Euclidean ones; `volume` is its Lebesgue measure.
- An element of `W1p` stores a value and a weak gradient, each a class of functions up to equality almost everywhere, and `value u` is the value, in $L^p(\Omega)$. So "continuous up to the boundary" is said through a representative $f$. Two such $f$ agree on $\Omega$, as Lebesgue measure charges every nonempty open set, and so on $\overline{\Omega}$ by continuity: the conclusion does not depend on the choice.
- `↑↑` turns an element of `Lp` into a function, and `=ᵐ[…]` is equality almost everywhere for the measure in brackets.
- `euclideanHausdorffMeasure` of dimension $d$ is the $d$-dimensional Hausdorff measure scaled to agree with Lebesgue measure on $d$-dimensional Euclidean spaces; here $d = \dim E = n - 1$. When $E = 0$, $\Omega$ is a bounded open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ such as $(-1, 1)$; this measure counts the boundary points, and the trace of $u$ at the endpoint $1$ is $f(1)$.
Approves the standard review `31ee1f649aa0ed38`.

## What it says

## What it says
Functions in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ have zero trace: on a bounded Lipschitz domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R} \times E$ and for $1 \le p < \infty$, the subspace $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ of $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ lies in the kernel of the trace operator.

- `[NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]`: $E$ is a finite-dimensional real inner product space. The domain lives in `WithLp 2 (ℝ × E)`, the product $\mathbb{R} \times E$ with the Euclidean norm, a Euclidean space of dimension $1 + \dim E$.
- `[MeasurableSpace E] [BorelSpace E]`: $E$ carries its Borel σ-algebra.
- `[Fact (1 ≤ p)]`: the exponent $p \in [0, \infty]$ is at least $1$.
- `(hp : p ≠ ⊤)`: $p$ is finite.
- `(hΩ : (↑Ω).IsLipschitzDomainWith L)`: the open set $\Omega$ is a Lipschitz domain with constant $L$: it has a Lipschitz graph chart with bound $L$ at every point of its frontier.
- `(hb : Bornology.IsBounded ↑Ω)`: $\Omega$ is bounded.
- The conclusion: `w1p0Submodule MeasureTheory.volume Ω p`, that is $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ for Lebesgue measure, the closure in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ of the test functions $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, is contained in the kernel of `frontierTrace hp hΩ hb`, the trace $W^{1,p}(\Omega) \to L^p(\partial\Omega)$ for the $(\dim E)$-dimensional Euclidean Hausdorff measure on $\partial\Omega$.

This is the easy half of the classical characterization of $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ as the functions of trace zero: a test function supported in the open set $\Omega$ vanishes on $\partial\Omega$, and the kernel of a bounded operator is closed.

## References and tests
- L. C. Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*, 2nd ed., §5.5, Theorem 2 (trace-zero functions in $W^{1,p}$), for a bounded $U$ with $C^1$ boundary; this is its easy direction, $u \in W^{1,p}_0(U) \Rightarrow Tu = 0$. Here the boundary is only asked to be Lipschitz.
- TauCetiRoadmap, PDE, Lane A, item 6: [the trace operator $W^{1,p}(\Omega) \to L^p(\partial\Omega)$ with kernel $W^{1,p}_0$, for Lipschitz $\partial\Omega$](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/PDE/README.md#L243), with [normalized Euclidean Hausdorff measure $\mu_{HE}[n-1]$ on the frontier](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/dd4b28f17c8acb73a121acd119cffe80fe1b232c/TauCetiRoadmap/PDE/README.md#L252).

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `≤` between subspaces is inclusion. `↑` on the left forgets that `w1p0Submodule` is closed; `↑(frontierTrace hp hΩ hb)` forgets that the trace is continuous, keeping the linear map, and `.ker` is its kernel.
- A trace of zero is zero in $L^p(\partial\Omega)$: zero almost everywhere on $\partial\Omega$ for the surface measure.
- `p` is an `ENNReal`, an element of $[0, \infty]$, and `⊤` is $\infty$. `[Fact (1 ≤ p)]` is the hypothesis $1 \le p$ carried as a typeclass, which Lean finds by itself.
- `WithLp 2 (ℝ × E)` gives the product the Euclidean norm instead of Lean's default maximum norm, so Lipschitz charts and Hausdorff measure are the Euclidean ones.

## What it says
The first integral homology of the complement of a knot in a space with $H_1 = H_2 = 0$ is infinite cyclic,
freely generated by the meridian: $k \mapsto k\,\iota(\mu)$ is a bijection
$\mathbb{Z} \to H_1(X \setminus K;\mathbb{Z})$.

- `{X : Type} [TopologicalSpace X] [T2Space X]`: a Hausdorff topological space $X$.
- `{f : Circle → X}` and `{Φ : SolidTorus → X}`: the knot, a loop on the unit circle $S^1 \subset \mathbb{C}$ with image $K$, and a map from the solid torus $D^2 \times S^1$, $D^2$ the closed unit disc of $\mathbb{C}$.
- `h₁`, `h₂`: the reduced singular homology of $X$ with integer coefficients vanishes in degrees $1$ and $2$, that is, $H_1(X;\mathbb{Z}) = H_2(X;\mathbb{Z}) = 0$, as for $S^3$ or an integral homology sphere. They are unnamed in the printed signature.
- `h : IsSolidTorusNeighborhood f Φ`: $\Phi$ is a topological embedding with $\Phi(0, z) = f(z)$ that maps the open solid torus $\{|w| < 1\}$ onto an open set $U \subseteq X$.
- Conclusion: `LinearMap.toSpanSingleton ℤ _ v`, the linear map $\mathbb{Z} \to H_1(X \setminus K)$,
  $k \mapsto k v$, is bijective, where $v = \iota(\mu)$ is the image of the meridian
  `h.framedBoundaryTorus.basis 0`, the class of $t \mapsto \Phi(e^{2\pi i t}, 1)$.

For a knot in $S^3$ this is the classical computation of $H_1$ of a knot complement. Here $S^3$ is replaced by
any Hausdorff space with $H_1 = H_2 = 0$, which is what the Mayer–Vietoris sequence for the cover of $X$ by
$U$ and $X \setminus K$ needs: $H_1(X) = 0$ gives surjectivity and $H_2(X) = 0$ injectivity.

## References and tests
- A. Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, Section 2.2: the Mayer–Vietoris sequence, by which it is proved.
- `TauCeti.framingNumber_unknotSolidTorus` — for the standard solid torus neighbourhood of the unknot in $S^3$, the unit sphere of $\mathbb{R}^4$, the framing number is $0$: its longitude bounds a meridian disc of the complementary solid torus. The framing number is read through the inverse of this bijection; in $S^3$ the
  hypotheses `h₁`, `h₂` hold by `TauCeti.isZero_reducedSingularHomologyFunctor_sphere_of_ne`.

## Lean subtleties
- `IsZero ((reducedSingularHomologyFunctor (↧ℤ) n).obj ↧X)` says that group is zero; reduced homology is ordinary singular homology in positive degrees, so `h₁`, `h₂` say $H_1(X) = H_2(X) = 0$. They are proofs of propositions: nothing depends on which proofs are given.
- `↑(HomologicalComplex.homology ((singularChains ℤ).obj ↧↑(Set.range f)ᶜ) 1)` is $H_1(X \setminus K;\mathbb{Z})$, the degree-$1$ homology of Mathlib's singular chain complex of the complement with the subspace topology.
- `LinearMap.toSpanSingleton` uses the $\mathbb{Z}$-module structure of the homology group, which agrees
  with integer multiples.
- `X : Type` lies in the lowest universe, which the framed boundary torus needs.

## What it says
For a knot with a solid torus neighbourhood in a Hausdorff space, the homomorphism
$H_1(T;\mathbb{Z}) \to H_1(X \setminus K;\mathbb{Z})$ induced by the inclusion of the boundary torus $T$
of the knot exterior into the knot complement.

- `{X : Type} [TopologicalSpace X] [T2Space X]`: a Hausdorff topological space $X$.
- `{f : Circle → X}` and `{Φ : SolidTorus → X}`: the knot, a loop on the unit circle $S^1 \subset \mathbb{C}$ with image $K$, and a map from the solid torus $D^2 \times S^1$, $D^2$ the closed unit disc of $\mathbb{C}$.
- `h : IsSolidTorusNeighborhood f Φ`: $\Phi$ is a topological embedding with $\Phi(0, z) = f(z)$ that maps the open solid torus $\{|w| < 1\}$ onto an open set $U \subseteq X$.
- Value: a $\mathbb{Z}$-linear map from `h.framedBoundaryTorus.H`, the first integral singular homology
  of the frontier of the exterior $X \setminus U$, which is the torus $T = \Phi(S^1 \times S^1)$, to
  $H_1(X \setminus K;\mathbb{Z})$; it is the map induced by the inclusion $T \subseteq X \setminus K$
  (`TauCeti.IsSolidTorusNeighborhood.boundaryHomologyMap_def`).

This is the map whose kernel singles out the preferred longitude (Rolfsen §2E7), with the kernel read in
the complement of the knot rather than in the exterior.

## References and tests
- D. Rolfsen, *Knots and Links*, Publish or Perish (1976), §2E7–2E8 (printed p. 31): up to isotopy a solid torus $V \subset S^3$ has a unique longitude homologically trivial in the exterior $\overline{S^3 \setminus V}$, and the framing with that longitude is the preferred framing.
- `TauCeti.framingNumber_unknotSolidTorus` — for the standard solid torus neighbourhood of the unknot in $S^3$, the unit sphere of $\mathbb{R}^4$, the framing number is $0$: its longitude bounds a meridian disc of the complementary solid torus. Its proof evaluates this map on the longitude through
  `boundaryHomologyMap_def`.

## Lean subtleties
- `X : Type` lies in the lowest universe, which the framed boundary torus needs.
- `[T2Space X]` makes the frontier of the exterior equal to $\Phi(S^1 \times S^1)$ and disjoint from the
  knot, so that the inclusion exists.
- `↑(HomologicalComplex.homology ((singularChains ℤ).obj ↧↑(Set.range f)ᶜ) 1)` is $H_1(X \setminus K;\mathbb{Z})$, the degree-$1$ homology of Mathlib's singular chain complex of the complement with the subspace topology. The domain `h.framedBoundaryTorus.H` is the same construction for $T$.
- Null-homologous here means in the complement $X \setminus K$, while Rolfsen uses the exterior $X \setminus U$. The exterior is a deformation retract of the complement (radially in each disc fibre), a standard fact not formalized here, so the two readings agree.
- The body is not exposed to other modules; `boundaryHomologyMap_def` unfolds it.

## What it says
A map of knot complements that matches the boundary tori, up to a reparametrization of the core circle,
carries a null-homologous longitude to a null-homologous longitude.

- `{X} [TopologicalSpace X] [T2Space X]`, `{f}`, `{Φ}`, and likewise `{Y : Type} [TopologicalSpace Y]
  [T2Space Y]`, `{f' : Circle → Y}`, `{Φ' : SolidTorus → Y}`: two Hausdorff spaces, each with a loop and a
  map from the solid torus $D^2 \times S^1$.
- `h`, `h'`: $\Phi$ and $\Phi'$ are solid torus neighbourhoods of $f$ and $f'$ (embeddings tracing the
  loops on their cores, with open images of the open solid torus).
- `g : C(Circle, Circle)`: a continuous self-map of the circle.
- `m : C(↑(Set.range f)ᶜ, ↑(Set.range f')ᶜ)`: a continuous map from the complement of $f(S^1)$ to that of
  $f'(S^1)$.
- First hypothesis: whenever a point $x$ of the first complement equals $\Phi(w, g(z))$ with $|w| = 1$,
  $m(x) = \Phi'(w, z)$; on the boundary tori, $m \circ \Phi \circ (\mathrm{id} \times g) = \Phi'$.
- Second hypothesis: the longitude of $\Phi$, the class of $t \mapsto \Phi(1, e^{2\pi i t})$, is $0$ in
  $H_1(X \setminus f(S^1);\mathbb{Z})$.
- Conclusion: the longitude of $\Phi'$ is $0$ in $H_1(Y \setminus f'(S^1);\mathbb{Z})$.

The longitude of $\Phi'$ is the image under $m$ of the image under $\Phi \circ (\mathrm{id} \times g)$ of
the class of the curve $(1, e^{2\pi i t})$, which is $\deg g$ times the longitude of $\Phi$. This is a
transport lemma for null-homologous longitudes, not a textbook theorem.

## References and tests
- `TauCeti.ZeroShakeSurface.mapLinearIsometryEquiv` — uses it with $g$ the identity and $m$ a linear
  isometry between the ambient spheres, so the hypotheses are met in practice.

With $g$ and $m$ identities the first hypothesis holds and the lemma returns its second hypothesis.

## Lean subtleties
- The first hypothesis forces $g$ to be injective: if $g(z) = g(z')$, the point $\Phi(1, g(z))$ would map to
  both $\Phi'(1, z)$ and $\Phi'(1, z')$, and $\Phi'$ is injective. So although `g` ranges over all
  continuous self-maps, only homeomorphisms of the circle satisfy it: the lemma is about reparametrizations,
  as its docstring says. The degree of $g$, $\pm 1$, plays no role.
- `SolidTorus.boundaryInclusion` writes the point $(w, z)$ of $S^1 \times S^1$ as the point $(w, z)$ of
  $D^2 \times S^1$ with $|w| = 1$; `↑x` is a point of the complement read in $X$.
- Both spaces are Hausdorff and in the lowest universe `Type`, which the framed boundary tori need.
- Null-homologous is meant in the knot complements, not the exteriors.

## What it says
The map `h.boundaryHomologyMap` is the map on degree-$1$ singular homology induced by the inclusion of the
boundary torus of the knot exterior into the knot complement.

- `{X : Type} [TopologicalSpace X] [T2Space X]`: a Hausdorff topological space $X$.
- `{f : Circle → X}` and `{Φ : SolidTorus → X}`: the knot, a loop on the unit circle $S^1 \subset \mathbb{C}$ with image $K$, and a map from the solid torus $D^2 \times S^1$, $D^2$ the closed unit disc of $\mathbb{C}$.
- `h : IsSolidTorusNeighborhood f Φ`: $\Phi$ is a topological embedding with $\Phi(0, z) = f(z)$ that maps the open solid torus $\{|w| < 1\}$ onto an open set $U \subseteq X$.
- Conclusion: `h.boundaryHomologyMap` equals
  `(HomologicalComplex.homologyMap ((singularChains ℤ).map (TopCat.ofHom (ContinuousMap.inclusion …))) 1).hom`,
  the map on $H_1$ of singular chains with integer coefficients induced by the inclusion
  $T \hookrightarrow X \setminus K$; the elided argument is the proof that the frontier of the exterior
  misses the knot.

It is the defining equation of `boundaryHomologyMap`, true by definition.

## References and tests

## What it says
For a knot $K$ with a solid torus neighbourhood in a Hausdorff space $X$ whose first and second integral homology vanish, an isomorphism $H_1(X \setminus K; \mathbb{Z}) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ that sends the meridian of the neighbourhood to $1$. The knot is a loop `f` from the circle into $X$, with image $K$, and `Φ` maps the solid torus $D^2 \times S^1$ into $X$; both are implicit.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on $X$, a type in the lowest universe.
- `[T2Space X]`: $X$ is Hausdorff.
- `(h₁ : CategoryTheory.Limits.IsZero ((reducedSingularHomologyFunctor (↧ℤ) 1).obj ↧X))`: the reduced singular homology of $X$ with integer coefficients vanishes in degree $1$: $H_1(X; \mathbb{Z}) = 0$.
- `(h₂ : CategoryTheory.Limits.IsZero ((reducedSingularHomologyFunctor (↧ℤ) 2).obj ↧X))`: likewise $H_2(X; \mathbb{Z}) = 0$.
- `(h : IsSolidTorusNeighborhood f Φ)`: `Φ` is a solid torus neighbourhood of the knot: an embedding of $D^2 \times S^1$ whose core $\{0\} \times S^1$ traces `f`, and which maps the open solid torus $\{|w| < 1\} \times S^1$ onto an open subset $U$ of $X$. That openness makes $U$ and $X \setminus K$ an open cover of $X$, to which Mayer–Vietoris applies.
- The result: a $\mathbb{Z}$-linear isomorphism from $H_1$ of the complement $X \setminus K$, with integer coefficients, to $\mathbb{Z}$.

Its value: the map $\mathbb{Z} \to H_1(X \setminus K)$, $m \mapsto m\,[\mu]$, where $[\mu]$ is the class of the meridian (the first vector of the meridian-longitude basis of the boundary torus) pushed into the complement, is bijective; the isomorphism is its inverse, so it sends $[\mu]$ to $1$. That it does so is the theorem `TauCeti.IsSolidTorusNeighborhood.complementHomologyEquiv_boundaryHomologyMap_basis_zero`, which the docstring names.

This is the classical computation of the first homology of a knot complement, usually stated in $S^3$; here $S^3$ is replaced by any Hausdorff space with $H_1 = H_2 = 0$, which is what the Mayer–Vietoris argument uses. In $S^3$ it is the linking number with the knot, as the docstring says.

## References and tests
- Rolfsen §2E — the first homology of a knot complement is $\mathbb{Z}$, generated by the meridian.
- A. Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, Section 2.2 — the Mayer–Vietoris sequence, by which the bijectivity is proved.
- `TauCeti.framingNumber_unknotSolidTorus` — for the standard solid torus neighbourhood of the unknot in $S^3$, the unit sphere of $\mathbb{R}^4$, this isomorphism sends the longitude to $0$ (the framing number is by definition its value on the longitude). The hypotheses `h₁`, `h₂` are met there, by `TauCeti.isZero_reducedSingularHomologyFunctor_sphere_of_ne`, so the isomorphism is not vacuous.
- `TauCeti.ZeroShakeSurface.framingNumber_eq_zero` — for the neighbourhood carried by a $0$-shake surface, whose longitude is null-homologous, it also sends the longitude to $0$.

## Lean subtleties
- `CategoryTheory.Limits.IsZero` says that an object is a zero object: here, that the homology group is trivial.
- `reducedSingularHomologyFunctor` is reduced singular homology, which in positive degrees is ordinary singular homology, so `h₁` and `h₂` are just $H_1(X) = H_2(X) = 0$. `↧X` is $X$ as an object of the category of topological spaces, and `↧ℤ` is $\mathbb{Z}$ as the object of coefficients.
- `↧↑(Set.range f)ᶜ` is the complement of the knot's image with the subspace topology. `HomologicalComplex.homology … 1` is the degree-$1$ homology of its singular chain complex `singularChains ℤ`, and `↑` turns that module into a type.
- `≃ₗ[ℤ]` is an isomorphism of $\mathbb{Z}$-modules, that is, of abelian groups.
- `LinearEquiv.ofBijective` inverts a bijective linear map; it uses choice, but a bijection has only one inverse, so nothing arbitrary enters.
- The sign is fixed by the orientation of the meridian in the framing of the boundary torus.

## What it says
Let $F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on a topological space $X$ and let $Z \subseteq S$ be closed subsets. If all local cohomology sheaves $\mathcal{H}^q_S(F)$ in positive degrees vanish, then for every open $W$ and every degree $j$ the inclusion $\iota : \Gamma_S(F) \to F$ induces a bijection $H^j_Z(W, \Gamma_S(F)) \to H^j_Z(W, F)$.

- `(F : Sheaf (Opens.grothendieckTopology ↑X) AddCommGrpCat)`: a sheaf $F$ of abelian groups on $X$ (the implicit `{X : TopCat}`), an ordinary sheaf on the open sets of $X$.
- `{S Z : TopologicalSpace.Closeds ↑X}`: closed subsets $S$ and $Z$ of $X$.
- `(h : ∀ (q : ℕ), Limits.IsZero (F.supportedHSheaf S (q + 1)))`: for every $q \ge 0$ the sheaf $\mathcal{H}^{q+1}_S(F)$, the sheafification of $W \mapsto H^{q+1}_S(W, F)$, is zero. Only $\mathcal{H}^0_S(F) = \Gamma_S(F)$ may be nonzero.
- `(hZS : Z ≤ S)`: $Z \subseteq S$.
- `(W : TopologicalSpace.Opens ↑X)` and `(j : ℕ)`: an open set $W$ and a degree $j$.
- The conclusion: the homomorphism `(Abelian.Ext.mk₀ (F.supportedSectionsι S)).postcomp _ ⋯` from `(F.supportedSectionsSheaf S).supportedH Z W j`, which is $H^j_Z(W, \Gamma_S(F))$, to `F.supportedH Z W j`, which is $H^j_Z(W, F)$, is bijective. It is the map that $\iota$ induces on cohomology with supports in $Z$.

Since $Z \subseteq S$, a section supported in $Z$ is supported in $S$, so $\Gamma_Z$ factors through $\Gamma_S$. When $\Gamma_S$ has no higher local cohomology on $F$, $F$ and $\Gamma_S(F)$ have the same cohomology with supports in $Z$. This is the case $n = 0$ of the degenerate edge comparison $H^{n+j}_Z(W, F) \cong H^j_Z(W, \mathcal{H}^n_S(F))$, through $\mathcal{H}^0_S(F) \cong \Gamma_S(F)$.
